docs.title: XTM One Documentation Space
docs.text:
Welcome to the XTM One Documentation space. Here you will be able to find all documents and resources about the platform.

Release notes

Please, be sure to also take a look at the XTM One release notes, they may contain important information about releases and deployments.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
XTM One is the core platform of the XTM Platform. OpenCTI (threat intelligence), OpenAEV (adversarial exposure validation) and OpenCRQ (governance, risk and compliance) are its modules: they connect to XTM One, which brings them a shared view of your exposure, common sign-in and integrations, and AI agents that work across all of them. XTM One is open source and AI-native: it lets organizations deploy autonomous agents for threat exposure management, email triage, messaging support, knowledge management and operational automation.

Docker deployment of the full XTM suite (OpenCTI – OpenAEV – XTM One)

If you're looking for information about the deployment of the full eXtended Threat Management (XTM) suite using Docker, please refer to this repository and documentation.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This page covers how to set up a local development environment and contribute to XTM One.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker with Docker Compose 2.24 or later, or Podman (see Podman)
  • Git
  • To run the checks and tests on the host: uv, which also provides Python 3.14, and Node.js 24 (22.18 at minimum) with Yarn

docs.title: Local setup
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one.git && cd xtm-one

# Copy environment file
cp .env.sample .env

# Run the full stack: PostgreSQL + pgvector, Redis, Silo, platform, worker, frontend
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build

docker-compose.dev.yml is an override of the production docker-compose.yml: the same stack, with the platform and the worker running your checkout's backend sources and a Vite dev server in place of the built frontend. To drop the -f flags, set COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.dev.yml in .env (; as the separator on Windows); the commands below then read docker compose ....

The root Makefile wraps these commands: make up, make start, make logs s=platform, make psql, make down (make lists them all). It runs docker compose, or podman compose when docker is not installed; force one with ENGINE=podman (or ENGINE=docker), add profiles with PROFILES="tools ha". make up and make start first check that the stack's host ports are free: when another checkout or process holds one, they stop, name it, and print a free set of host ports for .env.

The frontend is at http://localhost:3100 and the platform API at http://localhost:8100. Both run with hot reload: the platform restarts on a change under backend/app or backend/alembic, the worker on a change under backend/app, and Vite updates the page in place. The platform migrates the database on startup.

  • Run up --build again after a change to backend/pyproject.toml or backend/uv.lock. Frontend dependencies install on every start of the frontend service.
  • Start it in the background with up -d --build, follow it with logs -f platform worker frontend, stop it with stop.
  • Every .env setting reaches the platform and the worker. REDIS_URL and S3_ENDPOINT are the stack's own services and override .env (a Redis password set there is not used); OPENSANDBOX_DOMAIN, BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL default to the stack's own addresses.
  • Every checkout, git worktrees included, is a compose project of its own, with its own database, Redis and bucket. To run two checkouts at once, give the second one free host ports in its .env (see Host ports).
  • Where bind mounts deliver no file change events (podman machine, or a Windows checkout under Docker Desktop), set WATCHFILES_FORCE_POLLING=true and CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=true in .env.
  • Open a database shell with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml exec postgres psql -U copilot. PostgreSQL, Redis and Silo also listen on the host for the tests.
  • Every port is published on 127.0.0.1 only. To reach the stack from another device (a phone, a second laptop), set DEV_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 in .env: PostgreSQL, Redis, Silo and the admin account then answer the network with their dev credentials.

docs.title: Host ports
docs.text:
Each host port the stack publishes is set by a .env variable:

Variable Default Service DEV_FRONTEND_PORT 3100 Vite dev server (FRONTEND_URL follows it) DEV_PLATFORM_PORT 8100 Platform API (BASE_URL follows it) DEV_POSTGRES_PORT 5432 PostgreSQL DEV_REDIS_PORT 6380 Redis DEV_SILO_PORT 9002 Silo S3 API DEV_SILO_CONSOLE_PORT 9003 Silo console DEV_REDISINSIGHT_PORT 5540 RedisInsight (tools profile)

A second checkout running beside the first, for example a git worktree, takes another set in its own .env:

DEV_FRONTEND_PORT=3110
DEV_PLATFORM_PORT=8110
DEV_POSTGRES_PORT=5442
DEV_REDIS_PORT=6390
DEV_SILO_PORT=9012
DEV_SILO_CONSOLE_PORT=9013
DEV_REDISINSIGHT_PORT=5550

Its frontend is then at http://localhost:3110. Tests run from the host against that stack take the matching DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL and S3_ENDPOINT; scripts/ci-local.sh reads them from the running stack.

docs.title: Optional profiles
docs.text:
Profile What it adds tools RedisInsight on http://localhost:5540. ha A Redis Sentinel topology for failover testing; the header of docker-compose.dev.yml lists the .env settings that switch the backend to it.

Enable one with --profile <name>, or with COMPOSE_PROFILES=<name> in .env.

docs.title: OpenSandbox
docs.text: The dev stack always runs the OpenSandbox server of docker-compose.yml (the opensandbox service, which docker-compose.yml alone starts only with the opensandbox profile), which starts the sandboxes as containers through the container engine's socket. In the dev stack it sits on a network that only the platform and the worker join, so no other container reaches it, and it requires a key: OPENSANDBOX_API_KEY from .env, else copilot-dev-opensandbox, which the platform and the worker then send too. The platform uses it with CUSTOM_TOOL_SANDBOX=opensandbox and OPENSANDBOX_API_KEY set in .env. Build the sandbox images it runs once, backend/sandbox/build-image.sh sandbox-python:0.4 and backend/sandbox/build-image.sh sandbox-nodejs:0.4 (the script needs jq and the docker command: with Podman, install podman-docker). The default OPENSANDBOX_IMAGES names those tags, so there is nothing to set in .env.

docs.title: Podman
docs.text:
The compose files run unchanged with podman compose, whichever provider it uses (docker-compose, or podman-compose 1.6 or later):

podman compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build
  • Under podman machine (macOS, Windows) the VM's file share delivers no change events: set WATCHFILES_FORCE_POLLING=true and CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=true in .env, or nothing reloads.
  • On macOS the VM cannot read a checkout under ~/Documents, ~/Desktop or ~/Downloads (bind mounts fail with operation not permitted) unless you grant it access in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders. Keeping the checkout elsewhere also works.
  • Rootless Podman on Linux serves no /var/run/docker.sock, which the opensandbox service mounts, so the stack does not start without it: enable the user socket (systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket) and set CONTAINER_ENGINE_SOCKET=$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock in .env.
  • Bind mounts carry the z option, so they work on SELinux hosts (Fedora, RHEL), and image names are fully qualified (docker.io/...), so Podman's short-name policy never prompts.

docs.title: Python dependencies
docs.text:
The backend (backend/) and the documentation site (docs/) are uv projects: pyproject.toml declares the dependencies and uv.lock pins every one of them, transitive ones included. In either directory:

uv sync                         # install the locked set into .venv
uv add <package>==<version>     # add a dependency and relock; commit pyproject.toml and uv.lock
uv run <command>                # run a command in that environment

CI and the Docker images install with --locked, which fails when pyproject.toml was changed without relocking.

uv run syncs .venv to the checkout's lock before it runs the command. In a worktree whose backend/.venv is a link to another checkout's venv, that rewrites the shared environment: run uv run --no-sync, or set UV_NO_SYNC=1 in that shell.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
xtm-one/
├── backend/           → Python / FastAPI (see backend/AGENTS.md)
├── frontend/          → React 19 / TypeScript (see frontend/AGENTS.md)
├── docs/              → Product documentation (MkDocs)
├── apps/              → Platform app packages
└── docker-compose.yml → Production stack

docs.title: Running checks
docs.text:
# Backend lint and type check
cd backend && uv run ruff check . && uv run mypy

# Frontend lint, type check, dead code (knip) and unit tests
cd frontend && yarn check

# Office add-in type check (an npm package of its own; its unit tests run in `yarn check` above)
cd apps/microsoft-office && npm ci && npm run check

# Backend tests
cd backend && SECRET_KEY=test uv run python -m pytest -m "not integration" -q -n auto

main takes pull requests through a merge queue. On a pull request, the CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs these lint, type and dead-code checks, the migration history check, the secret scan, the ROI ledger's invariants, the frontend ratchet gates and catalog tests, and the frontend build; its tests and database checks skip, as do the jobs of E2E Tests, whose check passes. Once the pull request enters the queue (Merge when ready), the queue runs the suites of both workflows on the commit main would move to: the pull request merged on top of main and of the pull requests ahead of it, since two pull requests each green on their own can break it together. It runs only what the merge group's change reaches - the test files whose imports lead to a changed module, the E2E projects whose code or specs changed, Migrations when the chain's inputs did - and the Test selection job's summary says what ran and why (dev-docs/ci-test-selection.md). A change to what every test runs under (a conftest.py, the dependencies, the workflow) runs everything. A failure takes the pull request out of the queue. main runs both whole nightly, the full pass that catches what the selection missed (a red nightly run opens an issue), and when a file their caches follow changes (the lockfiles, the Dockerfiles, the workflow itself), since only main can save the caches the queue restores. To run them by hand on a branch, open Actions, pick CI (or E2E Tests), click Run workflow and choose the branch, or run gh workflow run ci.yml --ref <branch> and gh workflow run e2e.yml --ref <branch>. Their checks show on the pull request, and a new run on the same branch cancels the previous one. ./scripts/ci-local.sh runs the same suites on your machine (CONTRIBUTING.md).

Since the queue, not a person, pushes to main, the GitHub app's commits feed names github-merge-queue[bot]. On every push to main, the Merge notice workflow (.github/workflows/merge-notice.yml) hands the push to XTM-One-Platform/release, which posts each merged pull request to the team's Teams channel with its author and who merged it (who added it to the queue); the Teams webhook is a secret of that repository (its README, Merge notice).

The Makefile runs both test suites from the host:

  • make test runs the backend unit tests as CI does, from backend/.venv, which it syncs with uv sync --locked whenever pyproject.toml or uv.lock changes (uv provides the Python of backend/.python-version). Narrow the run with ARGS, e.g. make test ARGS="tests/test_x.py -k name".
  • make e2e runs the Playwright core suite against the running dev stack (make start first), at E2E_BASE_URL from frontend/.env.e2e or http://localhost:3100. It logs in with E2E_USER_EMAIL and E2E_USER_PASSWORD from frontend/.env.e2e (copy frontend/.env.e2e.example). One spec: make e2e ARGS="tests_e2e/x.spec.ts". scripts/ci-local.sh --only e2e runs the suite as CI does, on a production build of its own.

docs.title: Running tests in parallel
docs.text:
CI runs every backend suite under pytest-xdist (-n auto locally, -n logical in CI), and so can you. CI also splits each suite between several jobs: with PYTEST_SHARD=<index>/<total> a run keeps every <total>-th test of the sorted test ids (tests/sharding.py), so a test runs in exactly one job. The jobs that run one marker's tests (-m integration, -m chromium) also set PYTEST_MARKED_FILES=<marker>: they collect only the test files whose source spells mark.<marker> (tests/marked_files.py), so such a test applies its marker in its own file. The real-browser tests (-m chromium) are the exception to xdist: they time renders and sign-in redirects, so each of their jobs runs them one at a time. What that asks of a test:

  • No test depends on another one. The suite already runs in random order (pytest-randomly); xdist spreads it over processes too.
  • Every process collects the same test ids. A parametrize value built from uuid.uuid4(), time.time() or a freshly generated key turns into a different id in each worker, and the run stops with Different tests were collected between gw0 and gw1. Give such a parametrization ids= (or pytest.param(..., id=...)): the value can stay random, its name cannot.
  • A PostgreSQL test works in a database of its own, through tests/scratch_database.py. The schema is built once per process into a template database and every scratch database is a copy of it, so a new suite should use scratch_database(...) rather than a CREATE DATABASE + create_all of its own.
  • A test reading the backend's own source (a tripwire over every module under app/) reads it through tests/app_sources.py, which parses the tree once per process instead of once per suite.
  • A module that owns a fixed resource stays on one process. tests/test_bootstrap.py starts one backend on port 8099; it is marked pytest.mark.xdist_group(...) so that all its tests run in the same worker. The group only applies under --dist loadgroup, which CI and scripts/ci-local.sh pass: add it to a local -n run (uv run python -m pytest -m integration -n auto --dist loadgroup).

The integration suite needs PostgreSQL, Redis and Silo, and a database role allowed to create databases: ./scripts/ci-local.sh --only integration starts them and runs it the way CI does.

scripts/ci-local.sh runs one at a time per clone: a run started while another is in progress, from any checkout or worktree, prints Another local CI run is in progress and waits for it to finish, since runs share the machine and the database on port 5432. CI_LOCAL_NO_LOCK=1 skips the wait; CONTRIBUTING.md describes the queue.

The Playwright suite runs in CI as several jobs, each with a stack of its own: E2E_SHARD=<index>/<total> deals the spec files of a project to the jobs by the seconds each took on CI (frontend/tests_e2e/shard-timings.json). The nightly runs measure these seconds and publish the median of their last five measures, which every later run deals by; the committed file is only the fallback, refreshed by hand with backend/scripts/shard_weights.py refresh --kind e2e (dev-docs/ci-test-selection.md).

The suite runs in the merge queue, not on a pull request, whose E2E (Playwright / Chromium) check passes with its shards skipped. In the queue it runs the projects the change reaches: none for docs or unit tests alone, core for any other change, a2a and evaluation for their own code, specs and UI or for what every project runs on (the images, the dependencies, the database). To run it on a branch before, start it by hand: gh workflow run e2e.yml --ref <branch>.

docs.title: Live LLM smoke suite (opt-in)
docs.text:
The provider unit tests run against mocked SDK clients, so they cannot tell whether a real API accepts the requests the platform builds. backend/tests/live/ sends those requests to the real Anthropic, Gemini and OpenRouter APIs with tiny prompts. It spends real money (cents per run), never runs in CI, and is skipped unless LIVE_LLM_SMOKE=1 is set and the provider's key is exported as LLM_PROVIDER_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, LLM_PROVIDER_GEMINI_API_KEY or LLM_PROVIDER_OPENROUTER_API_KEY:

cd backend && LIVE_LLM_SMOKE=1 SECRET_KEY=test uv run python -m pytest tests/live -v -rfEs

A provider whose key is not set is skipped. backend/tests/live/README.md lists the cases, the model overrides and how the keys are kept out of the test output.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Schema changes must use Alembic migrations. Never use inline SQL.

cd backend
uv run python -m alembic -c alembic/alembic.ini revision --autogenerate -m "description of change"

The platform auto-migrates on startup — no manual alembic upgrade needed in production.

docs.title: One head, always
docs.text:
The migration history must have exactly one head. Two pull requests that each add a migration chained off the same parent fork the history the moment both land — and each one is green on its own, because pull request CI validates the branch against main as it was when that run started. This has happened twice on main, and both times it surfaced days later as an unrelated pull request going red.

Three guards catch it:

Guard Where Catches tests/test_migration_integrity.py Backend lint CI job, every pull request, on GitHub's merge of the pull request into its base A fork you created, and one created by another migration that landed on main after your branch was cut The single-head check Migrations (Alembic) CI job, in the merge queue on a change to a migration, a model, a module the chain loads (the migration helpers, the database setup) or the backend's dependencies Two pull requests merged seconds apart: each is tested on top of the ones ahead of it in the queue The nightly run on main Migrations (Alembic) CI job A fork that reached main anyway

If the migration history check fails on your pull request while it passes on your machine, main has moved under you (./scripts/ci-local.sh runs it against the live tip of main too):

git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main
# re-point your earliest migration's down_revision to main's new head
cd backend && uv run python -m pytest tests/test_migration_integrity.py

When a migration lands on main, every open pull request that touches backend/alembic/versions/ also gets an automatic comment asking for that rebase.

Pull requests stacked on an integration branch

CI runs whatever branch you target, merged into that branch, not into main. A fork you introduced is still caught by the first guard above; one created by a migration that landed on main shows once the integration branch itself goes to main. Rebase the integration branch onto main to see it earlier.

Repository settings

The guards above detect a fork; they cannot prevent two green pull requests from being merged seconds apart. The merge queue on main does: the "Merge queue" ruleset of the repository requires it (squash, entries tested on top of the ones ahead of them). Every required check must run on merge_group events or the queue never drains, and must report on the pull request too, or it never enters the queue: on a pull request E2E Tests skips its shards and its check passes, and CI runs its lint jobs. The checks to require are CI verdict (it fails when any job of CI fails, the lint jobs included, reads a skipped one as passed, and runs even when the run is cancelled) and E2E (Playwright / Chromium) - the aggregators, never a shard, and no workflow with a paths filter on pull_request or merge_group.

docs.title: Commit conventions
docs.text:
All commits follow Conventional Commits:

type(scope?): description (#issue)

Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, revert.

docs.title: AI governance
docs.text: This page describes what XTM One shares with AI providers, where that data is processed, and how to control it. Read it alongside Data flow, which covers the request lifecycle and where data is stored.

docs.title: What is shared with an AI provider
docs.text:
When the platform calls an AI provider, the request contains only what the model needs to answer:

  • the agent's persona and system instructions
  • the current conversation or assignment prompt, including recent message history
  • context the agent pulls in to answer — for example, snippets retrieved from a knowledge base, tool results, or an incoming trigger payload
  • the definitions of the tools the agent may call (names and parameters, not their results until a tool runs)

What stays private and is never included in the request to the model:

  • stored integration and channel credentials (encrypted at rest — see Configuration)
  • user passwords and session tokens
  • knowledge bases in full — when an agent answers, only the snippets it retrieves are sent (the full text is sent once to the embedding model when you first add the content, as described below)

XTM One does not train on your data

XTM One never uses your prompts, documents, conversations, memories, or any other data to train, fine-tune, or improve an AI model. Your data is sent to the AI provider you configure only to answer your own requests, in real time. The platform itself trains nothing.

Your AI provider sees your prompts

Whatever an agent puts into a prompt — including retrieved documents and tool results — is sent to the AI provider you configured. The platform does not anonymize, tokenize, or redact prompt content before sending it, and prompts are stored unredacted in your own deployment (see Data flow). Whether the provider retains or trains on the prompts it receives is governed by its terms, not by XTM One — review them, and scope agents' knowledge and tools accordingly. For maximum control, run a local model so no prompt data leaves your network.

docs.title: Adding documents to a knowledge base
docs.text:
To make a knowledge base searchable, XTM One first has to turn its documents into numbers a computer can compare — these numbers are called embeddings. Creating them means sending the document text to an embedding model, which is an AI provider just like the one that answers questions.

Two things are worth knowing:

  • This happens when you add the content, not on every question. The same applies to an agent's saved memories.
  • The embedding model can be a separate provider from the one that answers chats — and it can be a local one (for example Ollama), so the document text never leaves your network. You set it under Settings → AI Models.

docs.title: Where the AI provider runs
docs.text:
You choose the AI provider under Settings → AI Models, or pre-provision it (see the supported providers in Configuration). The provider determines where prompt data is processed:

  • Hosted providers (such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Mistral) process prompts on their own infrastructure, subject to their terms.
  • Self-hosted or local providers (Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on your network) keep prompt data inside your perimeter. This is the recommended option for air-gapped deployments.

docs.title: Scope what agents can access
docs.text:
Because an agent only shares what it is configured to use, you control exposure by scoping the agent:

  • limit which knowledge bases an agent can read
  • limit which integrations and tools an agent can call
  • use assignment-level scoping to further narrow tools and knowledge bases per automation

See the User Guide for how agents, knowledge bases, and tools are configured.

docs.title: Guardrails and safety
docs.text:
XTM One adds several safety layers around every agent run. They lower the risk of misuse, but they are not a substitute for limiting what each agent can access and choosing your AI provider carefully.

  • Per-agent rules — every agent has a separate "guardrails" box where you write hard rules it must always follow (for example, "never send external email" or "only answer questions about our products"). These rules are kept apart from the agent's persona, so an edit to its personality can't accidentally erase them.
  • Injection detection (alert only) — messages coming into an agent are checked for known tricks that try to make the AI ignore its rules ("prompt injection" and "jailbreak" attempts). When one is spotted, XTM One records it as a security event for administrators to review — but it does not block the message. Treat this as an alert to check, not a wall that stops every attack.
  • Treating outside content as data, not orders — anything an agent pulls in from the outside world (web pages it fetches, incoming webhook or integration messages) is wrapped so the AI treats it as information to read, never as instructions to obey. This helps stop a malicious web page or email from hijacking the agent.
  • Built-in security rules — a fixed set of security instructions is added to every agent so it resists attempts to reveal its hidden instructions, override its rules, or pretend to be someone else.
  • Link checking — when an agent's answer includes links to other XTM Suite products, XTM One checks and corrects them automatically, so the agent never hands out made-up links.

docs.title: Human approval of tool calls
docs.text:
When an agent is set to ask before running tools, it stops and asks a person before any tool call that is not known to be read-only: anything that could change something or reach outside the platform. The run stops, the reviewer sees exactly what the agent proposes, and nothing happens until they decide.

Tool approvals are opt-in. No agent asks until an administrator turns it on, for one agent or for every agent; until then every tool call runs as it always has, and no screen shows an approval state. See Turning it on or off. That includes the short list of tools that always ask: they ask only on an agent that asks, so an agent nobody set to ask never stops for a person, whatever tool it calls.

This is not a suggestion the AI can talk itself out of. The platform checks every tool call before it runs, so the pause happens regardless of what the model decides to do.

Where everything lives:

What Where Who Whether approvals are in use, which agents ask, the default every agent follows, the per-tool rules, the connected platforms' policies, the emergency suspend switch Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals Administrators Whether one agent asks The agent → Configuration → Tooling → Ask before running tools Whoever manages the agent The tools you always allow, and Allow every tool for me Profile → Tool approvals (shown once an agent asks, or while you hold a choice) Each person, for themselves only

docs.title: What asks first, and what doesn't
docs.text:
On an agent that asks, every tool asks first unless a rule lets it run without asking. That default matters: a tool nobody has considered yet — a newly connected integration, a custom tool somebody just wrote — asks first rather than acting first.

XTM One ships rules that let tools that only read data (searching, listing, fetching, looking up) run without asking. Threat-intelligence lookups such as lookup_greynoise_ip or lookup_rf_domain are reads; a tool named with a verb that reads for one service and changes data for another (enrich, triage, assess, identify, reverse, resolve, analyze) still asks. Ordinary read-heavy work is therefore unaffected. The same rule is applied to what you connect: the read-classified tools of your integrations and of company-managed, enabled MCP servers run without asking as well, scoped to what is actually connected — a provider you have not connected exempts nothing. The read tools of a connected Suite platform run without asking on the same basis — see Tools from a connected platform. All of it is listed under Tool rules in Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals, grouped by where it came from, and any tool can be made to ask first.

An exemption covers the tool it was decided for, not every tool that carries the name. An MCP server or a custom tool that takes the name of a tool on the list still asks, and a company-managed MCP server's read covers that server's own tool only: a built-in of the same name, such as web_fetch, keeps asking. An entry an administrator adds covers every tool of that name. Tools that download a file (a Jira attachment, a Slack or Google Drive file, a social media post's image) keep asking even though they only read: they pull a document nobody has looked at into the agent's context.

Chat bots are the exception. A Slack, Teams or Discord bot's tools are never exempted automatically, including the ones that only read. Reading a channel means reading people's conversations rather than platform data, which is a decision for a person to make per tool rather than one to infer from a verb. Each configured bot carries its own switch under Settings → Channels instead. Turning it off means two things, and both are deliberate: conversations through that bot run uninterrupted whatever tools the agent reaches for, the tools that always ask included, and the bot's own send/edit/delete tools stop pausing wherever they are called. Only that bot is affected — two bots of the same provider decide separately.

A bot cannot ask, so a gated tool asked for there stops

A chat conversation with a bot has no way to collect an approval today: the bot replies explaining that it stopped, and the turn ends. That is why the switch exists — without it, a gated tool requested through a bot is not delayed, it is unavailable. (An assignment run's approval can be answered from Teams through its pasted link, see Where you answer.)

A few tools that act on nothing at all are exempt for the same reason: asking a person to approve them would only interrupt. request_human_input is the agent choosing to ask a question — gating it would mean pausing for approval to ask for approval — and wait is the agent's timer, bounded by the wait limits in Settings → Parameters and interruptible at any time, so gating it would replace a bounded pause with an unbounded one. check_task_status is the poll beside it, reading whether work the agent already started has finished, on a short fixed budget the model cannot change.

Administrators manage the rules under Tool rules in Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals. The rules can be prepared before any agent asks; the page says they change nothing until one does. You can:

  • Let it run without asking — a tool you trust stops asking, for everyone. Any tool can be added, including destructive ones — the platform warns you rather than refusing. Add a tool by name does the same for a tool not connected yet.
  • Make it ask first — a read-only tool we ship as running without asking starts asking. That decision survives upgrades: a later release that ships the tool exempt again will not silently undo it. Back to the default undoes it.
  • Make all its reads ask first for a whole platform's read tools in one action, and put them back the same way. Ruling on dozens of entries one at a time is not a real choice, so it is offered as one.

A tool's own page, an integration's tool table and a bot's tool list show whether each tool asks first, only while approvals are in use, and link to the rule (for administrators) or to your own approvals (for everyone else). Your own approvals list the tools that ask first and the ones you always allow, so for anyone but an administrator a tool that runs without asking, and that you do not always allow, is shown without a link.

code_interpreter ships whitelisted

The code interpreter runs code the AI writes, and it is on the default whitelist so that routine calculations don't interrupt every run. It is sandboxed, but if your security posture requires a person to see generated code before it runs, this is the first entry to remove.

docs.title: Tools that always ask
docs.text:
On an agent that asks, a few tool calls wait for a person whatever else would let them run: a tool on the whitelist, "Yes, always" or Allow every tool for me. Only a decision on that very call lets it run. Approval stays opt-in, so these calls ask only on an agent set to ask: on an agent set to Don't ask, or that follows a platform default of not asking, they run like every other call, recorded with the agent's setting as the reason. The switch above everything is the platform's own: while approvals are suspended for the whole platform, they run unattended on every agent, recorded with that as the reason. They are calls whose effect a person should see before it happens:

  • act_on_page with submit: a click that saves, creates, sends or deletes in the page the user is on.
  • The Letsignit user writes, create_letsignit_user, update_letsignit_user_variables and delete_letsignit_user: the Letsignit API key reaches every employee, and what they change appears in every email that person sends afterwards. The Letsignit reads (get_letsignit_signature, get_letsignit_user) are not on this list: like the other directory reads (Microsoft Entra's get_entra_user, for instance), they change nothing, and an administrator who wants them asked makes them ask first under Tool rules.

On an agent that asks, while approvals are available, where nobody can answer (a chat bot, a client that does not support approvals, an action an agent scheduled from a conversation), such a call does not run: the agent replies that it stopped, and an exact scheduled action naming such a tool is refused. An assignment run pauses and waits for a person, like any run with a tool that asks.

docs.title: What a reviewer sees
docs.text:
When a run pauses, the reviewer gets the tool's name, what it does, and every argument with its description — so a value like cascade: true can be judged, not guessed at. They can then:

  • Yes — run it as proposed.
  • No — decline it. The agent is told it was declined and can propose something else.
  • Yes, always — see below.

docs.title: Where you answer
docs.text:
Three places, with the same effect and the same record:

  • The run itself — open it and answer there.
  • Operations → Executions — approvals appear inline in the list, so you can answer without opening each run. Filter to Awaiting Input to see only what is paused.
  • The run's link pasted in Microsoft Teams — the link turns into a card that shows each person what their own access allows: whoever may answer the run gets each tool with its arguments and an Approve / Reject choice, or the question with an answer box. The answer is recorded as given from Teams. See Pasted XTM One links.

Someone who sees the card but cannot answer the run can ask the people who can, with Ask the owner to act (or Ask an admin to act on a company-managed run). Those people get a notification in the bell, and the request is listed on the run page, with Dismiss, until the run is answered. It shares nothing: the person who asked still cannot see the run.

The bell tells you a run is waiting and links to it; the decision is made in one of the two places above, because judging a proposal means seeing every argument in full and that does not fit a notification.

docs.title: Answering several at once
docs.text:
Select several rows in Operations → Executions and answer them together. The selection is per run: a run that paused on more than one tool call is answered as a whole, because a half-answered pause cannot resume.

  • Select the N awaiting approval picks exactly the paused rows, skipping notices you cannot act on.
  • Reject asks for one reason, applied to every run in the selection. Give one — with nothing to go on, each agent can only come back and ask you what to do instead, so a reasonless bulk rejection costs more interruptions than it saves.
  • Approve always over a selection lists every tool it would stop asking about before you confirm. Read that list: it is the same durable preference described below, applied to several tools at once.

Each run is recorded as its own decision. If one can no longer be answered — somebody got there first, or the run ended — the others still go through and you are told which did not.

docs.title: Runs a standing approval already covers
docs.text:
Granting "always" (below) stops a tool asking on future calls, but the gate has already run for anything sitting paused — so those runs keep waiting for the tool you just trusted. Where that happens the executions list says how many, and offers to release them in one action.

It is an offer rather than something that happens on its own: a run restarting with no explicit action is surprising, and you may be part-way through deciding something else.

A run is released only when every one of its pending calls is covered. One covered and one uncovered call means it still needs answering by hand — releasing it would approve a call you never consented to. That rule is enforced where the release happens, not where it is offered, so a run that stops qualifying between the offer and the click is refused and named rather than let through.

Nothing is granted by releasing. The exceptions already exist; this only applies them to what was already waiting.

Turning on Allow every tool for me in your profile makes the same offer, for the same reason.

docs.title: "Yes, always"
docs.text:
This saves a preference for you, not for everyone. That tool then runs without asking you again.

Two things to understand before using it:

  • It applies to your scheduled runs too, not just the one you were watching. The approval prompt says so before you confirm.
  • Another user is still asked. Your preference never lowers the bar for anybody else.
  • It does not cover the tools that always ask: "Yes, always" runs the call in front of you, and the next one asks again.

You can review and take back your saved approvals at any time under Profile → Tool approvals, where Tools that ask first also lets you Always allow for me a tool before it ever asks you. If a tool's parameters change after you approved it, the approval is dropped automatically and the tool asks again — your consent described the older version, so it no longer applies.

An approval belongs to the tool you approved, not to every tool carrying its name. A tool from an MCP server is covered only on the server you approved it on: another server advertising the same tool name still asks, and so does a built-in tool sharing the name of an MCP or custom tool you approved. Approving the name again on another server moves your approval to that server. A tool from an MCP server that you approved before the server was recorded asks you once more; answering Yes, always records its server.

docs.title: "Allow every tool for me"
docs.text:
If approving tools one at a time is not how you want to work, Profile → Tool approvals offers the wholesale form: Allow every tool for me. While it is on, none of your conversations or scheduled runs wait for your approval — including tools that delete data or act outside the platform, which is why turning it on asks you to confirm first.

It does not cover the tools that always ask. Like a per-tool approval, this is a preference for you alone; nobody else's runs are affected. Your saved per-tool approvals are kept rather than deleted, so turning the mode off restores exactly the posture you had before. Switching it either way is written to the audit log, and every call that runs under it is recorded with that as the reason.

docs.title: Scheduled runs
docs.text:
A scheduled run that hits a tool needing approval pauses and waits. It does not time out, and nothing is auto-approved. The assignment's owner is notified, and the notification names the tools waiting.

This is deliberate: unattended automation is where an unreviewed destructive action does the most damage. To let one agent's scheduled work run end to end, let the tools it uses run without asking, or set that agent to Don't ask.

docs.title: Turning it on or off
docs.text:
Each agent has an Ask before running tools setting under Configuration → Tooling: Follow the platform default, Ask or Don't ask. It applies to everything the agent does, runs and chats alike. An agent that follows the default takes the platform-wide Every agent asks by default switch under Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals.

That default is off on a new install, and an upgrade changes neither it nor any agent: an install that turned it on, or that a release before approvals were opt-in created with it on, keeps its setting. Otherwise nothing asks until an administrator turns approval on, for one agent or for every agent, agents created later included.

The top of Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals says whether approvals are In use, Not in use or Suspended, and lists the agents that ask (and the General Assistant when it does), each linking to its setting.

The agent's Human in the loop switch is a different thing: it lets the agent choose to ask a person through the request_human_input tool and adds the review prompt. It does not turn the tool approval gate on.

Every tool call is recorded either way, with why it ran: allowed by a rule, covered by a saved approval, approved by a person, or run because approval was off. Changing either setting is audited with the value set, who set it, and when.

docs.title: Suspending approvals for the whole platform
docs.text:
Suspend all approvals, at the bottom of Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals, is the emergency switch. While it is on, no tool call waits for anyone, the General Assistant included, whatever an agent or the platform default says, the tools that always ask included: tool approval is opt-in at platform level, and no tool-level flag turns it back on. Every call that runs under the switch is recorded with that as the reason. The rules and the per-platform policies stay saved but stop applying; Resume approvals puts everything back as it was.

It asks for confirmation and is audited. An administrator's agent with the Platform insights tools reads both switches with get_platform_ai_settings (under tool_approvals: tool_approvals_enabled, approve_tool_calls_default and env_seed, the TOOL_APPROVALS_ENABLED value as deployed) and changes them with update_platform_ai_settings (tool_approvals_enabled: false suspends, true resumes; approve_tool_calls_default is Every agent asks by default), with the same administrator check, the same validation (true or false only) and the same audit entry as this page, marked as coming from the tool. TOOL_APPROVALS_ENABLED=false seeds it suspended: it is read once, when the settings row is created on a fresh install or during the upgrade that adds the switch, and ignored afterwards. Unset, or anything unrecognised, leaves approvals available (which still asks nothing until an agent is set to ask).

Two things to know:

  • A run that has already paused stays paused. Clear those from Operations → Executions: answer them, answer by tool, or dismiss them.
  • The settings are read fail-closed. If they cannot be read, tools gate rather than run.

docs.title: The General Assistant
docs.text: The General Assistant has no agent behind it, so it follows the platform default wherever chat is available. Where it is not, the default reaches only the agents, and Every agent asks by default and its confirmation do not name the General Assistant. The suspend switch and a user's own Allow every tool for me also reach it; so do the tool rules, which are the narrower lever when it keeps asking about a tool you consider routine.

docs.title: Built-in agents
docs.text:
Agents that ship with XTM One are read-only: their persona, tools and settings are managed by the platform and re-synchronised on every restart. Ask before running tools is the exception: an administrator can set it on a built-in agent from the same screen as any other agent. Built-in agents are what an embedded assistant in OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenGRC drives, so without it the only lever would be the platform-wide default.

  • Administrators only, as for everything on a company-managed agent.
  • Your choice survives restarts: the boot-time re-synchronisation does not touch it.

Nothing else about a built-in agent or its assignments becomes editable.

docs.title: Tools from a connected platform
docs.text:
A Suite platform that registers with XTM One — OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenGRC — contributes its own tools, a few hundred of them across the three.

Its read tools skip approval. Every platform tool is classified as reading or changing data, and the ones that only read — searching, listing, fetching, querying — are exempt on the same footing as XTM One's own read tools. Anything that changes the platform still asks. So "require approval" for a connected platform means ask before anything that changes it, not ask before anything from it: an agent can look up a report unattended, and still stops before editing one.

Two things bound that:

  • The classification errs towards asking. A tool whose purpose cannot be established from its name counts as changing data. In particular the consolidated manage_… tools — which can list or create or delete depending on how they are called — always ask, because no single answer about them would be right.
  • One read still asks anyway, by deliberate choice rather than by classification: reading a file's contents into the AI's context, because that loads a third-party document nobody has looked at. Identity and RBAC reads — who the users are, which roles and groups exist, what a role can do — are not held back: they change nothing, and re-gating them where that matters is a deployment's decision, made on the whitelist screen. Half-holding them back would only have looked like a protection: the summary asked while every part of it stayed readable.

If you would rather no platform read ran unattended, Tool rules in Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals groups them per platform and makes the whole set ask first in one action. That decision survives upgrades and survives the platform reconnecting, and the same control puts them back.

Whether the platform's other tools ask is decided per platform under Settings → Access and security → Tool approvals → Approval for connected platforms, which lists whatever is actually connected. Each row shows two separate things:

  • Whether that platform can display an approval prompt. A fact the platform reports about itself when it registers — only it knows. Most builds today have never said, which is not the same as saying they cannot.
  • What happens to its tools while no prompt can be shown. A policy only you can set: gate them, so its agents explain themselves instead of acting, or let them run.

The row also says where the current setting came from — a default, this deployment's configuration, or an administrator — so you can tell whether it is protecting you or merely inherited from an install nobody remembers.

A platform that later ships approval support and re-registers starts gating again on its own, unless an administrator explicitly chose otherwise. In that one case the setting stands and the page offers to restore the safer posture in a click, rather than changing it silently behind you.

Setting the starting point at deploy time

TOOL_APPROVALS_PLATFORM_DEFAULT decides what a platform gets the first time it registers. Set it to skip when deploying beside a platform release that cannot prompt yet, so its agents keep working without anyone making an API call on first boot.

It seeds a value rather than overriding one: whatever it sets is visible and changeable on the settings page, and it never overwrites a choice an administrator has made or applies to platforms already registered.

If you drive XTM One chat from another application, see Chat approvals in client applications.

docs.title: Data retention
docs.text:
All platform data lives in your own deployment (see Data flow). XTM One applies these defaults:

Data Where it is stored Default retention How to control it Conversations and messages PostgreSQL Kept until deleted Delete the conversation, or the agent it belongs to Assignment runs and results PostgreSQL Kept until deleted Delete the run, or the assignment Agent memory — recent interactions Redis 24 hours (auto-expires) Automatic Agent memory — rolling summary Redis 30 days (auto-expires) Automatic Agent memory — long-term facts PostgreSQL 90 days, max 200 per agent Admins can clear an agent's memory at any time LLM traces PostgreSQL (or ClickHouse) Purged after the retention period — 90 days by default Adjustable from 1 to 365 days under Settings → Observability, where Store full payloads off keeps no prompt, answer or tool content and Enable local trace storage off keeps no trace (see What a trace keeps); individual traces can be deleted Daily observability aggregates PostgreSQL Kept indefinitely — they outlive the trace purge on purpose Not covered by the trace retention setting; see What survives the trace purge Audit logs PostgreSQL Audit log retention (days) in Settings > Observability, 90 days by default (each user's most recent sign-in is kept); the entries of a user's own actions are deleted with that user's account Admin-only visibility; entries cannot be edited from the platform Prompt, persona, agent setting and skill versions PostgreSQL Full history by default PROMPT_VERSION_RETENTION_COUNT keeps only the latest N versions of each series (0 = unlimited); a locked version is never pruned Resolved shared state entries PostgreSQL 30 days after resolution SHARED_STATE_RESOLVED_RETENTION_DAYS (0 keeps them until an agent or admin deletes them); active entries are never purged Work items (tasks agents hand to each other) PostgreSQL Done or cancelled items: 30 days. An open item with no activity for 14 days is cancelled, unless it has a start date or deadline still ahead or is a scheduled work item WORK_ITEM_RESOLVED_RETENTION_DAYS and WORK_ITEM_ABANDONED_AFTER_DAYS (0 disables each) Worksets (an agent's scoped document corpus) PostgreSQL and object storage Resolved worksets: 7 days. A workset with its own expiry goes once past it. The corpus the platform creates by itself for an agent's chat or an assignment expires 30 days after its last use WORKSET_RESOLVED_RETENTION_DAYS (0 disables the purge); WORKSET_IMPLICIT_IDLE_DAYS for the agent and assignment corpora (0 keeps them until resolved); a workset a flow creates without an expiry is never purged Flow events PostgreSQL 30 days FLOW_EVENT_RETENTION_DAYS (0 disables the purge); never shorter than the flow run timeout, so a waiting run keeps hearing its event Relayed request records (host, method, status, size, duration) PostgreSQL 30 days RELAY_REQUEST_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS (0 = forever); see Relays Public chat widget visitor uploads Object storage 7 days after the visitor's last message; a file never sent: 1 day PUBLIC_WIDGET_UPLOAD_RETENTION_DAYS (at least 1, cannot be switched off) Sandbox workspaces (files the code interpreter keeps) Object storage Conversation workspace: 7 days unused, or at once when the conversation is archived or deleted. Assignment run workspace: when the run ends CODE_INTERPRETER_WORKSPACE_IDLE_TTL_HOURS (168) and CODE_INTERPRETER_RUN_WORKSPACE_IDLE_TTL_HOURS (24, for a run that has not ended) WhatsApp messages received by a WhatsApp integration PostgreSQL 30 days The integration's inbound_retention_days field, from 1 to 365 days

docs.title: What survives the trace purge
docs.text:
Deleting an expired trace does not delete the KPI it contributed to. Once a day is complete, XTM One rolls its traces up into a small daily aggregate and keeps that aggregate indefinitely, so the Analytics dashboard can still answer "what did last quarter cost?" long after the individual traces are gone. This is why a 30-day or 90-day chart still has data on a platform with 7-day trace retention.

What you keep, and for how long:

Individual traces Daily aggregates Retained for The retention period (1–365 days, default 90) Indefinitely Granularity Every request, with prompts, tool calls and errors (the prompts and tool content only while Store full payloads is on) One row per day, agent, model, source, user, the person the usage counts for and their department Answers "What exactly happened in this conversation?" "How much did this agent, model or person cost, and how fast was it?" Where in the UI Trace explorer, individual trace detail, top errors Cost, volume and latency charts on Analytics

Consequences worth knowing before you choose a retention period:

  • Prompt and response content is not aggregated. Only counts, token totals, cost, latency distributions and feedback averages survive. Nothing a user typed, and no tool result, outlives the retention period.
  • Aggregates are per user. A day's row is keyed by agent, model, source and the user who made the request - and, for a request with no user of its own (an assignment run, a sub-agent, a webhook), the person it counts for - with their department at the time, so per-person and per-department usage and cost stay answerable after the traces are gone. If your retention policy requires per-user usage records to expire as well, treat these aggregates as in scope — the trace retention setting does not clear them.
  • Error details and per-request diagnostics do not survive. The "Top errors" table and trace detail are served from raw traces only, so they are always limited to the retention window.
  • Latency beyond the window is a distribution, not the raw timings. Each day stores a bucketed histogram of its durations, which is what lets percentiles be merged correctly across a long window. Expect percentile values to be accurate to within a bucket rather than exact.
  • A day is never purged before it is aggregated. The maintenance job aggregates first and refuses to delete a day that has no aggregate yet, so lowering the retention period (or a restart longer than it) cannot silently drop a day's KPIs. If a window you select reaches back further than any surviving data, Analytics says so instead of showing zeroes.
  • ClickHouse follows the same retention period. With tracing_store_provider=clickhouse, the maintenance job deletes the expired ClickHouse traces and spans, with their offloaded payloads, on the same window as PostgreSQL, about once an hour. It also declares a table TTL at the retention period plus 7 days on the trace, span and score tables, as a backstop: if maintenance stops, ClickHouse still expires the rows on its own, but their offloaded payload objects stay in the bucket. Long-window dashboards read the PostgreSQL aggregates either way.

To remove the aggregates as well, delete the llm_daily_stats rows (or the deployment's PostgreSQL volume, as below).

Two categories are not retained by XTM One and are governed entirely by your own infrastructure:

  • Application logs are written to standard output. Your container runtime or log aggregator decides how long they are kept and how they are rotated — see Monitoring.
  • Metrics are exposed on the /metrics endpoint and scraped by your Prometheus. The platform holds only current values; historical retention lives in your monitoring stack.

To remove all data, delete the deployment's PostgreSQL, Redis, and object-storage volumes. For selective deletion, delete the specific agents, conversations, or knowledge bases from the application.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review Monitoring to see how AI requests are traced and observed, and Authentication to control who can send them.

docs.title: Editions and licensing
docs.text: XTM One ships as one platform with two editions. Which one you are on decides a single thing: whether AI is licensed, and therefore available. Whether it actually runs is a separate, administrator-held switch (see Running Enterprise Edition without AI).

docs.title: The two editions
docs.text:
Edition When What you get Community Edition No Filigran license is installed and no connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platform is in Enterprise Edition The platform runs with AI off. Identity, settings, platform connections, integrations and the exposure dashboards keep working. Agents, chat and automations are listed and reachable, marked unavailable. Enterprise Edition A Filigran license is installed, or at least one connected platform is in Enterprise Edition Everything is on as long as AI is switched on: agentic chat across your platforms, autonomous agents and assignments, flows, knowledge bases, skills, prompts, MCP servers, custom tools, integrations, Agent-to-Agent interoperability, the full integration catalog and AI adoption analytics.

There is nothing in between. A connected Enterprise Edition platform activates every capability of XTM One, exactly as a license does.

Nothing to redeploy

Every deployment already contains the whole platform. Moving to Enterprise Edition never means installing something new: it is a license key, or a platform connection, away.

docs.title: What a license decides
docs.text:
A Filigran license carries two things and nothing else:

  • Agentic capacity - the number of agentic executions allowed per day, per month and per year. One agentic execution is one complete request handled by the platform - a chat turn, an assignment run, or a background task - however many agents and tools it involves. Requests with no account behind them count too: anonymous channel users, visitors of a public chat widget and calls made with the platform MCP key (see Requests with no account).
  • Module editions - which connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platforms are in Enterprise Edition.

A license never switches individual features on or off. Every capability of XTM One is available to every Enterprise Edition deployment.

docs.title: The included allowance
docs.text:
When Enterprise Edition comes from a connected platform and no Filigran license is installed, the platform runs under an included agentic allowance: 30 executions per day, 100 per month and 300 per year, shared across the deployment. It is sized to discover, test and demonstrate value.

Installing a Filigran license replaces the allowance with the capacity the license carries. Settings > Quotas shows which ceilings apply and where they come from, and lets you set per-user defaults and group or user overrides within them.

A license period with no quota has no ceiling, whether the certificate carries no quota for it or a quota of 0, and whatever the license's start date. Licenses issued from 27 September 2026 write an unlimited period as no quota.

docs.title: Activating Enterprise Edition
docs.text:
You have two ways to activate it, and both work without a redeploy:

  • Connect an Enterprise Edition platform. Register an OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platform that holds its own Enterprise license. XTM One inherits Enterprise Edition as soon as the registration validates.
  • Install a Filigran license. Paste the license PEM in Settings > Parameters, or set the ENTERPRISE_LICENSE environment variable and restart. The instance ID shown on the same page is required to generate the certificate. Set the variable on the platform and on the worker; a worker without it still runs the background AI of the licensed deployment, and says so once in its log.

If you have neither, Start free trial and Contact sales are offered wherever an AI capability is locked - on the home page, in the navigation, on the creation buttons and in the AI settings.

docs.title: What Community Edition looks like
docs.text:
On Community Edition the platform tells you once, clearly, and stays out of the way:

  • The home page leads with the upgrade path and the platform connection instructions.
  • AI entries in the navigation carry a lock; hovering one explains why.
  • A creation button opens the same explanation with the three ways forward.
  • The AI Models settings say that a provider configured now is used as soon as Enterprise Edition is activated, instead of warning that the platform is blocked until one is configured.

You can prepare LLM providers, users, groups and platform connections ahead of activation. Nothing you configure is lost when the edition changes.

docs.title: When Enterprise Edition ends
docs.text:
A deployment returns to Community Edition when its last source of Enterprise Edition goes: the connected Enterprise Edition platform loses its license or is disconnected, or the Filigran license is removed. Within a few seconds the automations configured while it was Enterprise stop running AI too, exactly like the interactive surfaces:

  • Scheduled assignments, integration events, webhooks and channel bots start no AI work. A person writing to a bot, where the bot would answer (a direct message, a mention, a channel it listens to), is told that Enterprise Edition is required and how to activate it; a webhook sender receives a 403 carrying the same explanation.
  • A flow containing an AI step is held back and recorded as skipped with the reason. Flows without AI steps keep running.
  • Work that was scheduled but had not started does not start: it is held. An assignment run waiting on its configured delay, a run resumed from a human-review pause (the answer is kept), a background task that had not begun and the pending runs of an evaluation are shown as Held and run by themselves within about five minutes of Enterprise Edition becoming active again; a conversation waiting on a held background task hears back when the task finally runs. Work held longer than AI_UNAVAILABLE_HOLD_MAX_SECONDS (one week by default, 0 to fail it at its start instead) is recorded as failed with the cause AI not licensed. Deliveries waiting in an assignment's queue stay queued and documents waiting to be indexed stay pending; both are picked up once Enterprise Edition is active again.
  • Nothing is charged to the agentic quota, and nothing is disabled, paused or deleted. Schedules, integration events, webhooks, channel bots and flows resume on their own once Enterprise Edition is active again; a scheduled assignment or flow catches up with one run, not one per occurrence it missed.

Work already running when the edition changes finishes under its own time limit. If the platform briefly cannot read its license state when scheduled work comes due, for example during a database failover, that work is not failed: it is retried shortly afterwards. A channel bot written to meanwhile answers a direct message that the AI service is temporarily unavailable, and stays silent in a group channel.

docs.title: Running Enterprise Edition without AI
docs.text: Enterprise Edition and the AI switch are independent. An administrator can switch AI off on a fully licensed platform; see Running without AI.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review the Settings page for where the license, the quotas and the AI switch live.

docs.title: Emergency stop API
docs.text:
Everything the emergency stop does in the interface is available over REST, plus one route that needs no session at all — the one a printed runbook or a monitoring hook uses. This page describes each route, its inputs, its responses and its errors.

All routes live under /api/v1/panic. None of them is affected by the AI switch: the stop is what switches AI off, so it must keep answering while AI is off.

In the examples, <your-xtm-one> is the platform's full base address. When a reverse proxy serves XTM One under a path (BASE_PATH, see Serving under a path prefix), that path is part of it, for example https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one/api/v1/panic/emergency. The command shown in Settings → Security → Emergency stop and on the printed procedure already includes it.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Two credentials exist, for two situations:

Credential Header Used by What it may do A session token or a personal API key (fcp-…, created in My profile → API Keys) Authorization: Bearer <token> every route except POST /panic/emergency what the signed-in user may do: their own scope for everyone, the whole platform and the token management for administrators The emergency stop token (xes-…, generated in Settings → Security → Emergency stop) Authorization: Bearer xes-… POST /panic/emergency only press the platform-wide stop — nothing else

docs.title: Routes at a glance
docs.text: Method and path Who Purpose POST /panic/stop any user; platform scope needs an administrator press the stop POST /panic/stop/{audit_id}/reason the user who pressed that stop record why, after the fact POST /panic/resume any user; platform scope needs an administrator lift the stop, with a mandatory reason GET /panic/status any user what is paused, whether a stop is in effect, who pressed the last one GET /panic/token administrator whether an emergency token exists (never the token itself) POST /panic/token administrator generate or rotate the emergency token — returned once DELETE /panic/token administrator revoke the emergency token POST /panic/emergency the emergency token press the platform-wide stop without a session

docs.title: Press the stop
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/stop \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope": "platform"}'
Field Values Meaning scope self (default), platform self stops everything that runs for you; platform stops every user's activity, evaluation and autonomous runs, and switches AI off. platform is refused with 403 for a non-administrator

The stop runs immediately and the response says what it did:

{
  "scope": "platform",
  "runs_cancelled": 3,
  "executions_cancelled": 4,
  "sub_agent_tasks_cancelled": 1,
  "chat_turns_cancelled": 0,
  "flow_runs_cancelled": 0,
  "runner_commands_cancelled": 0,
  "evaluation_runs_cancelled": 0,
  "autonomous_runs_cancelled": 0,
  "assignments_paused": 12,
  "ai_disabled": true,
  "late_admissions_cancelled": 0,
  "completed": true,
  "audit_id": "5f0c6d0a-2c8f-4a4e-9a35-1a6c9d2e7b10",
  "stopped_at": "2026-09-18T16:43:04.628632+00:00"
}
Field Meaning runs_cancelled runs stopped — those in progress, queued or waiting for a human, the runs they delegated to, and any run admitted while the stop was being applied executions_cancelled background executions released so no worker resumes them sub_agent_tasks_cancelled background tasks delegated to other agents chat_turns_cancelled chat answers being generated that were asked to stop flow_runs_cancelled flow runs in progress runner_commands_cancelled runner commands not yet dispatched to a machine. One already dispatched cannot be recalled, but it is never sent again evaluation_runs_cancelled, autonomous_runs_cancelled platform scope only assignments_paused assignments whose schedules and triggers no longer fire ai_disabled true when the platform AI switch was turned off (platform scope) late_admissions_cancelled runs a scheduler on another replica admitted while the stop was being applied, cancelled by the follow-up pass — already counted in runs_cancelled, reported apart so you know a second wave happened completed false when cancelling the running work failed after the assignments were paused (and AI turned off, for the platform): the follow-up passes cancelled what they reach, the counts are what was really halted, and the log entry is marked incomplete. Look at the server log, then press the stop again if work is still running audit_id the log entry of this stop — pass it to record the reason stopped_at when the stop took effect

Pressing the stop twice is safe: the second press finds nothing left to cancel and reports zeros.

docs.title: Record why, after the stop
docs.text:
The stop never waits for a justification. Once it has run, attach the reason to the entry it returned:

curl -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/stop/5f0c6d0a-2c8f-4a4e-9a35-1a6c9d2e7b10/reason \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"reason": "Agent looping on the ticket queue, costs climbing fast."}'

{"audit_id": "5f0c6d0a-2c8f-4a4e-9a35-1a6c9d2e7b10", "assignments_annotated": 12}

The reason is written on the stop's log entry and on every assignment that stop paused, where the assignment page and the banner show it. Only the user who pressed the stop may annotate it (404 otherwise). A blank reason is refused with 422; the maximum length is 2000 characters.

docs.title: Lift the stop
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/resume \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope": "platform", "reason": "Loop fixed and deployed, safe to resume."}'
Field Values Meaning scope self (default), platform same rules as the stop reason text, 1–2000 characters, required recorded on the resume entry and on every assignment re-enabled 
{"scope": "platform", "assignments_resumed": 12, "ai_enabled": true}

Only assignments the emergency stop paused are re-enabled; one paused by hand stays paused. For the platform scope the AI switch goes back to what it was before the stop (on, off, or Deployment default), and only if it still reads as the stop left it — a change made in Settings during the stop is kept. ai_enabled reports the effective state after that: on a platform started without AI, or where AI was off before the stop, it stays false.

docs.title: Check the state
docs.text:
curl https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/status -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..."

{
  "self_paused_assignments": 2,
  "self_stop_active": false,
  "platform_paused_assignments": 12,
  "ai_disabled": true,
  "platform_stop_active": true,
  "active": true,
  "last_stop": {
    "at": "2026-09-18T16:43:04.628632+00:00",
    "by": "Alex Admin",
    "scope": "platform",
    "reason": "Agent looping on the ticket queue, costs climbing fast."
  }
}
Field Meaning self_paused_assignments assignments in your scope a self resume would re-enable. One that another person's stop still covers (an assignment you own that runs as them, or the reverse) is not counted: it comes back once their stop is lifted too self_stop_active your own stop is in effect and still covers a paused assignment, even one another person's stop also covers. Your resume stays available while it is true, even when it would re-enable nothing yet platform_paused_assignments the assignments a platform resume would re-enable: the ones a platform-wide stop paused, not a user's own stop — null for a non-administrator ai_disabled whether the platform AI switch is off because of the stop — null for a non-administrator. AI turned off from Settings by hand is not reported here and is not touched by a resume platform_stop_active a platform-wide stop is in effect (the latest one has not been lifted). Visible to everyone, including a user who owns nothing the stop paused active a stop is in effect for you: the platform one, or your own last_stop the most recent stop that concerns you — your own or a platform-wide one — with who (their display name; the log entry keeps the email), when, scope and reason (null until the reason is recorded)

The interface polls this route every fifteen seconds to show the banner.

docs.title: Manage the emergency token
docs.text:
Administrators only.

# Is a token configured? (never returns the token)
curl https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/token -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..."

{
  "configured": true,
  "prefix": "xes-<first 8 characters>...",
  "created_at": "2026-09-18T15:02:11.410000+00:00",
  "created_by": "admin@example.com",
  "last_used_at": null
}

# Generate — or rotate — the token. The token is returned exactly once.
curl -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/token -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..."

{
  "token": "xes-<48 hexadecimal characters>",
  "prefix": "xes-<first 8 characters>...",
  "created_at": "2026-09-18T15:02:11.410000+00:00",
  "created_by": "admin@example.com"
}

There is one token per platform: generating a new one invalidates the previous one immediately. Only a hash is stored, so a lost token cannot be recovered — rotate it. DELETE /panic/token revokes it (204; 404 when none is configured). Generation, rotation and revocation are all recorded in the logs.

docs.title: Press the stop without a session
docs.text:
This is the command the printed procedure carries:

curl -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/panic/emergency \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer xes-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"reason": "Runbook step 3: agent looping on the ticket queue."}'
Field Meaning reason optional, up to 2000 characters — a runbook usually states the cause, a monitoring hook may not. Recorded on the stop's log entry and on the paused assignments when given

The response is the same as POST /panic/stop. The stop always covers the whole platform and is attributed to the administrator who generated the token. If that account is gone, deactivated or no longer an administrator, the stop is attributed to the oldest active administrator instead. When no administrator is active at all, a valid token still works and the stop is attributed to the administrator who generated it, even if that account is deactivated. The token's last_used_at is updated.

A missing or wrong token is refused with 401, and the attempt is recorded in the logs as a security event under the token owner's name. The token cannot call any other route.

The route is rate-limited per client address — ten attempts per ten minutes by default (PANIC_EMERGENCY_RATE_LIMIT, PANIC_EMERGENCY_RATE_WINDOW_SECONDS), counted before the token is checked, so probing it answers 429 with a Retry-After header. The limit fails closed: if the rate limiter cannot be reached, the route answers 503 rather than becoming unlimited. Neither refusal applies to a request that carries the current token's prefix (the xes- and the eight characters shown in Settings): someone who spent the limit from the same address, or a rate limiter outage, cannot lock the holder of the real token out of the stop.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Code When 401 no or invalid credential; on POST /panic/emergency, a missing or wrong emergency token 403 platform scope, or token management, requested by a non-administrator 404 recording a reason on a stop that is not yours, or revoking a token when none is configured 409 re-enabling an assignment the emergency stop paused through PUT /assignments/{id} — lift the stop instead (code: "emergency_stop"); or a self resume while a platform-wide stop is in effect — only an administrator lifting the platform stop resumes it (code: "platform_stop_active") 422 unknown scope, or a missing or blank reason where one is required 429 too many attempts on POST /panic/emergency from one address — wait for Retry-After

docs.title: What "immediately" means
docs.text:
The stop is two steps, in that order. First the door is closed: every assignment in scope is paused and, for the platform, AI is switched off — and this is committed on its own, so every check made after that commit, on any replica, sees a paused assignment and a refused AI gate and admits nothing. Then everything live is cancelled. A run already inside a model or tool call notices within about two seconds through a fast cancel signal; a chat answer being generated, within one second.

A scheduler that had already read the previous state when the first step committed can still create one last run right after it. A follow-up pass right after the stop catches and cancels those, and reports them in late_admissions_cancelled (also in the log entry); a second pass runs a few seconds later, once no server can still hold a cached "AI is on", and counts into the log entry only. For your own activity (self), that second pass leaves alone what you started after the stop: it only cancels runs that were already there, runs of the assignments the stop paused, and runs started by a run the stop cancelled. For the whole platform, both passes also cancel the background tasks and chat answers still live: with AI off, anything found then was admitted by a server whose cache still said "AI is on". Closing the door first is what makes those passes rare and small; the passes are what make the stop complete.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Read Emergency stop for the interface, the printed procedure and what users see while a stop is in effect.

docs.title: Emergency stop
docs.text:
The emergency stop halts every agentic activity at once. Runs, background tasks, chat turns, flows and pending runner commands are cancelled, assignments are paused, and — for the whole platform — AI is switched off so nothing new starts. It is the button you press when an agent misbehaves, costs run away, or an incident requires that no AI activity continues.

Everything the stop does is recorded, labelled where you look for it, and can be lifted once the situation is under control.

docs.title: Who can press it, and how far it reaches
docs.text:
You are Scope you can choose What it covers Any user My activity only Everything that runs for you: your runs and the work they delegated, your background tasks, your in-flight chats, your flow runs, your pending runner commands, and the assignments you own or that run as you An administrator My activity only or Whole platform The same for every user, plus evaluation runs and autonomous runs, plus the platform AI switch

Work already in progress is stopped and does not resume, with two exceptions: a runner command already executing on a machine cannot be recalled and runs to its end, and an answer an agent is already writing for a channel bot, an MCP client or the browser extension finishes under its own time limit. Cancelled runs stay cancelled: lifting the stop re-arms schedules, it does not replay what was cut.

docs.title: What stops and what keeps working
docs.text:
Stopped:

  • runs in progress, queued or waiting for a human answer, and every run they handed work to
  • background tasks delegated to other agents
  • chat turns being generated in the XTM One chat and the chat widget
  • chat turns waiting in the XTM One chat for the approval of a tool call — the turn ends, the prompt is withdrawn and the call does not run
  • flow runs in progress
  • runner commands not yet dispatched to a machine
  • assignments — paused, so their schedules and triggers no longer fire
  • with Whole platform: evaluation runs, autonomous runs, and AI for everyone

Untouched:

  • everything that is not agentic: document processing, knowledge-base synchronisation, integration imports and exports, and flows with no agent step, whose triggers keep firing
  • the triggers of flows: the runs in progress are cancelled, but a flow is not paused like an assignment. With Whole platform, a flow with an agent step waits for AI to be back; with My activity only, your flows' next trigger starts a new run
  • runner commands already executing on a machine — they cannot be recalled, but none is sent to a machine again
  • an answer already being written for a channel bot, an MCP client, the browser extension or the assistant embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ — it finishes under its own time limit; with Whole platform, no new one starts
  • a tool call waiting for approval in an embedded assistant, or left for approval in a conversation whose turn already ended — it runs only if you approve it; with Whole platform, no decision is accepted until AI is back
  • your data: agents, knowledge bases, flows, runs and traces stay readable

docs.title: Press the emergency stop
docs.text:
1. Open your profile menu (your name, top right) and choose Emergency stop.
  2. As an administrator, choose the scope: My activity only or Whole platform.
