docs.text: A manager follows the AI usage of the group's current members in Model usage (under Administration > Observability), and through an agent with the platform insights tools: the agents they use, the costs and the errors. A manager does not have to be a member of the group, and gets no other right. See Group managers.

docs.title: Switching AI off for a group
docs.text:
The AI access card's AI disabled for this group switch turns AI off for every member of the group, the way Running without AI does for the whole platform. It suits a team that policy keeps off models (a works council, a regulated department) while the others keep using AI.

For a member, as long as the group has it off:

  • chat, agents, assistants and every endpoint that answers with a model refuse them with the platform's own ai_disabled refusal, and the AI areas of the navigation are marked unavailable;
  • the assignments, flows and delegated tasks that run as them (the ones they own) are held, as they are while AI is switched off platform-wide, and run by themselves once AI is back; triggering one by hand is refused;
  • no model, embedding or image provider is used for their content, whichever providers they were granted.

A person in several groups is cut off as soon as one of them has AI off. An administrator is held to it like everyone else: nothing an administrator needs to undo it (the groups page, the settings) uses a model. Everything that does not need a model keeps working, the same list as Running without AI.

Members read the change within seconds; a replica that did not serve it follows within five. Switching it on or off is recorded in the audit log, with the previous value. The platform-wide switch wins: with AI off for the platform, a group's setting changes nothing.

docs.title: Auto join
docs.text:
The Auto join card's Single sign-on users join this group switch (default: off) adds everyone who signs in through single sign-on, OIDC or SAML, to the group at every sign-in: an account created at its first sign-in, an account an administrator created for a single sign-on user, and an existing account alike. The Groups list marks such a group with an Auto join badge. It is the way to give every single sign-on user a group's shares, quotas, AI access or provider reservation without adding each one by hand.

  • Once per person. Someone already in the group, however they joined, is left as is. Each membership it adds is recorded in the audit log, with the sign-in as the actor.
  • Only single sign-on. Local accounts, accounts provisioned through SCIM and accounts created through the API join only when they sign in through single sign-on.
  • With SAML group mapping. The mapping manages only the memberships it created, so it never removes one that auto join added, even when the assertion does not name the group.
  • Removing someone. An administrator can remove a member from the Members tab; while the switch stays on, the next single sign-on adds them again.
  • CTEM Viewers. The group XTM One seeds for CTEM read access has the switch on. Every account, however it is created, joins it once, at its creation; single sign-on does not add anyone to it again, so a person an administrator removes stays removed. Switching it off keeps it off.

Switching it on adds nobody at once: each person joins at their next single sign-on. Switching it off removes nobody. Both are recorded in the audit log with the previous value.

docs.title: Terms of Use
docs.text: The Terms of Use are accepted once for the whole platform, by an administrator, not by each user: there is no per-user acceptance to follow here. See Terms of Use acceptance.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Organization profile describes your organization for every agent.

docs.title: Channels and bots
docs.text:
A channel is a messaging platform your users already work in. When a channel bot is connected, people can talk to an XTM One agent from Slack, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or Google Chat instead of opening the web interface, and agents can post messages back into those conversations.

Everything on this page is configured in Settings > Channels & Bots. The per-platform guides then walk through the external setup, one platform at a time.

docs.title: Supported channels
docs.text:
Channel Direction What you connect Web chat Built in Nothing — always available for every user and agent Slack Receive and publish A Slack app with a bot token and signing secret Microsoft Teams Receive and publish An Entra ID app registration, an Azure Bot resource, and a Teams app package WhatsApp Receive and publish A Meta app using the WhatsApp Business Cloud API Telegram Receive and publish A bot created with @BotFather Discord Receive and publish A Discord application with a bot token Google Chat Receive and publish A Google Chat app and a service account key

Web chat is listed in the same screen as Web Chat, with an Always Active badge. It needs no setup and cannot be disabled.

Bots answer as a bot

A channel bot has its own identity: it hears what is addressed to the bot. To let an agent operate a real user account instead - answering when you are mentioned or messaged, or running a dedicated AI user that follows whole channels - see Agent accounts.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need to be an administrator. Only admins can create, edit, or delete channel bots.
  • The deployment needs an active Agentic AI license. Without it, saving a channel bot is rejected.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS. Every platform except Discord delivers messages to a webhook URL built from BASE_URL — see Configuration. A local or private address works for testing only if the messaging platform can reach it.
  • You need administrator rights on the messaging platform itself, or someone who has them. Most steps happen in the external console, not in XTM One.

docs.title: How a channel goes live
docs.text:
The same four steps apply to every platform.

  1. Create the app on the messaging platform. Each platform has its own console — the Slack app directory, the Azure portal, Meta for Developers, and so on. This is where you obtain the credentials and grant permissions.
  2. Connect the bot in XTM One. In Settings > Channels & Bots, select the platform and click Configure, then paste the credentials. Every value is encrypted before it is stored. The card switches to Connected once credentials are saved.
  3. Point the platform at the webhook URL. The connected card shows a Webhook URL you can copy under Receive. Paste it into the messaging platform's webhook or messaging endpoint setting. Discord is the exception — it opens its own outgoing connection and needs no webhook.
  4. Enable the channel on an agent. A newly connected bot does not answer anything yet. Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, enable the channel, and turn on Receive, Publish, or both.

Use the built-in setup guide

Each card in Settings > Channels & Bots has a Setup Guide button. It shows the same steps as the pages here, with the permission list and your deployment's real webhook URL already filled in — including a copy-ready Teams manifest.

docs.title: Receive and publish
docs.text:
Every connected bot has two independent capabilities, shown side by side on the bot card and again on each agent.

  • Receive covers incoming messages: someone writes in a channel or sends a direct message, and an agent answers.
  • Publish covers outgoing messages: an agent uses the bot's tools to post a message, reply in a thread, add a reaction, or upload a file on its own initiative — for example at the end of an assignment.

The two are separate on purpose. An agent can post daily summaries to a channel without ever listening to it, and it can answer questions in a channel without being allowed to post anywhere else.

The Publish capability comes from the bot tools listed on the card. Click the tool count to browse them and test one against the live connection before an agent uses it.

docs.title: Restricting which channels a bot can use
docs.text:
A bot has ambient authority: on the messaging platform it can reach every channel it has been invited to. Channel whitelists narrow that down inside XTM One.

Both lists are edited on the bot card and apply to every agent using the bot:

  • The Receive whitelist limits which channels the platform accepts incoming messages from. Messages from anywhere else are ignored silently.
  • The Publish whitelist limits which channels agents can send to. A blocked send fails with an explicit access-denied error rather than posting to the wrong place.

When a list is empty, no restriction applies at bot level — but a bot with no whitelist at all is reserved for company-managed agents. Non-admin users only see the bot on their own agents once at least one whitelist entry exists, so they cannot silently give a personal agent workspace-wide reach.

Each agent can then narrow the bot's scope further in its own Channels & Bots section. The effective scope is the overlap between the agent's selection and the bot whitelist, never more than the bot allows. Admins can grant an exception per agent with Bypass whitelist. A message the whitelist would have dropped is then let in for those agents only: another agent, or the General Assistant, does not answer it.

docs.title: Tool approvals through a bot
docs.text:
A conversation on an external channel cannot show an approval prompt. When an agent answering through a bot reaches for a tool that needs approval, the bot replies with a refusal and the turn ends: the tool is not delayed, it is unavailable.

The Ask before running tools switch on each bot card decides this. It is on by default.

  • On: tools that need approval stay unavailable in conversations through this bot, and the bot's own send, edit and delete tools ask for approval wherever an agent calls them, including from an assignment.
  • Off: nothing an agent does in a conversation through this bot waits for approval, including tools that change or delete data outside the chat, and the bot's own message tools run without asking everywhere.

Turning it off asks for confirmation, and the change is recorded in the audit log. The security audit in Settings > Security lists every bot with the switch off. The bot's read tools are never exempted from approval automatically, since reading a channel means reading people's conversations: this switch is the only way to let them run without asking.

docs.title: Direct messages, mentions, and anonymous users
docs.text:
Three toggles decide when a bot answers at all. Each exists on the bot card and again on every agent, and the bot setting always wins.

Toggle What it does Precedence Allow private conversations Direct messages reach the agent even when receive channels are restricted If the bot has it off, no agent can turn it back on Only when mentioned In group channels, the bot answers only when it is explicitly @mentioned (not supported on WhatsApp) If the bot has it on, no agent can turn it off Allow anonymous users People without an XTM One account can talk to the agent If the bot has it off, no agent can turn it back on

A few consequences are worth knowing:

  • Direct messages always bypass Only when mentioned. Someone messaging the bot privately never has to mention it.
  • With Only when mentioned on, once the bot has answered in a thread it keeps following that thread for about 24 hours without needing a new mention. This works where the platform reports both mentions and threads — Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Google Chat. On Telegram and Discord the mention is detected but there is no thread tracking, so each new question needs its own mention.
  • Only when mentioned cannot be used on WhatsApp at all: the Cloud API does not report structured mentions, so the condition is never satisfied and the bot stays silent in groups. Leave it off there and scope the bot with the receive whitelist instead.
  • With Allow anonymous users on, the conversation is not attached to a user account. The agent still receives the sender's display name and platform identity as context. The General Assistant is never available anonymously — anonymous traffic is served by agents only.
  • An anonymous conversation reaches what the agent is configured with: its knowledge bases, integrations, handover targets and work-item peers, whatever their Restrict access setting. What it browses across the platform - the agent builder's read tools, template search - is limited to what every user sees: company-managed resources without Restrict access.
  • Anonymous messages count against the platform-wide agentic limits of your license (no per-user limit applies to them). When the platform is at its limit, the sender is told This service is at capacity right now. Please try again later. wherever the bot would otherwise have answered - where it stays silent, it stays silent. See Requests with no account.

Anonymous access is a public door

Turning on Allow anonymous users lets anyone who can reach the channel use the agent, its tools, and its knowledge bases. Restrict the agent's tools and knowledge accordingly, and prefer a dedicated agent for public channels.

docs.title: Commands inside a conversation
docs.text:
Users have two commands on external channels, and they are worth mentioning when you announce a new bot:

  • /reset or /new archives the current conversation and starts a fresh one, which is the way to clear context that has drifted. In a direct message a web conversation was continued in, it ends the continuation instead: the web conversation is kept, and the next message starts a fresh one.
  • /stop mutes the bot in the current thread for seven days. Mentioning the bot again lifts the mute immediately. It works where threads are tracked — Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Chat, and WhatsApp groups. On WhatsApp the mute cannot be lifted early, since mentions are not detected there, so it lasts the full seven days.

docs.title: One conversation across the web, Slack, and Teams
docs.text:
A user can continue the same conversation in the web app and in a direct message with the Slack or Teams bot, in either direction (see Chat). It stays one record: its history, compaction summary, files, pending approvals, agent and session tools.

  • Only direct messages are shared with the web: a Slack DM thread and the Teams personal chat with the bot. Channel threads and group chats are never listed on the web nor continued from it, because other people read them: the web chat, its file upload and the platform chat API refuse them (409). The platform chat API, which runs its turns without the conversation's turn lock, also refuses a Slack or Teams direct-message conversation and a web conversation continued in one.
  • A direct message continues a conversation only when its sender resolves to the conversation's owner. A sender the bot cannot match to an account, or matches to someone else, never reaches it.
  • The conversation keeps its agent. That agent must have the channel enabled with Receive and Publish for the continuation to be offered and answered; a General Assistant conversation answers in any direct message.
  • The continuation is offered, and accepted by the API, only where the bot would answer the direct message: it is checked with the same gates the bot applies to every message it receives (the receive whitelist and Allow private conversations, an agent's Bypass whitelist, Only when mentioned, then the agent's own channel settings). A Slack bot with a receive whitelist and private conversations off drops direct messages, so the option is not offered. A Teams personal chat is never filtered by the whitelist.
  • One turn runs at a time on a conversation, whatever the channel. A Slack or Teams direct message that arrives while a turn runs is queued, acknowledged at once, and answered as the next turn, in arrival order; consecutive messages of one thread are answered together. Up to five messages wait per conversation, for at most an hour; a redelivered event (a Slack retry, a Teams redelivery) is never queued or answered twice. If the process running a turn stops, the scheduler restarts the queue within a minute of that turn's lock expiring, and a queued message that process was answering is answered again, unless its turn had already stored it - a message is started at most twice and stored once. A queued message the bot drops without an answer (it could not be answered twice, or it waited more than an hour) is told so in its thread, in the sender's language. A queued message waits in Redis, its text and the sender's email included, for at most that hour. The files of a queued message that is never answered are deleted. The web refuses a message while a channel turn runs, and the web Stop also stops a turn started from a channel. Direct messages on WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat are not queued.
  • A tool call waiting for approval is decided in the web app. A channel message sent while the turn that proposed it still waits is queued behind it; one that arrives after that turn ended retires the call, as a new web message does, and the reply says so.
  • Continuing in Slack uses the scopes the bot already needs (users:read.email to find the user, chat:write and im:write to open the direct message). Continuing in Teams needs the user to have written to the bot once in a personal chat: Teams lets a bot write first only where it already has a conversation reference.
  • Each continuation is recorded in the audit log (bind / unbind on the conversation).

docs.title: Files in replies
docs.text:
When an agent's answer on a channel includes a file — a report, an export, a generated image — the message carries a link to it. The link works without an XTM One sign-in for 24 hours, so treat it like the file itself.

  • PDFs, plain-text, Markdown and CSV files, WebVTT subtitles, JSON files (JSON Lines and +json types such as JSON-LD included), audio, video, and images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, BMP, TIFF, ICO, HEIC / HEIF, JPEG XL, JPEG 2000) open in the browser. A browser that cannot display or play a format, such as TIFF or HEIC outside Safari, or CSV and JSON Lines in Chrome, saves it instead.
  • HTML pages, SVG drawings, XML files, and every other type are downloaded, never opened: a file an agent or a user wrote can never run as a page on your platform's address.

An image the answer links from the web, such as a GIF found with the GIPHY integration, is sent as an image only when it comes from the media host of an integration (GIPHY's). An image from any other address stays a link: its address is written by the model, and fetching it could hand data from the conversation to whoever owns that address. A reply sends at most four such images.

docs.title: How the bot knows who is talking
docs.text:
XTM One matches the sender to an account by email address:

  • Slack and Google Chat provide the email directly, so matching is automatic.
  • Microsoft Teams provides the email in most messages, and otherwise the platform resolves it from the sender's Entra ID identity.
  • WhatsApp, Telegram, and Discord do not expose an email. Those senders are either treated as anonymous, when the bot allows it, or asked to register.

Once a sender has been matched by email, XTM One also remembers their identity on that platform, so later messages match even without an email. A WhatsApp, Telegram, or Discord sender who never provides an email can be linked to an account by an administrator, through the API only (/api/v1/users/{user_id}/channel-identities). There is no screen for it.

When the sender matches an account, the conversation inherits that user's permissions, personal preferences, and memory — the same as if they had used web chat. Users can also route their own direct messages to a specific agent in My Profile > Channels & Bots.

docs.title: The language of the bot's own messages
docs.text:
Besides the agents' answers, a bot sends short messages of its own: that a message is queued behind the one being answered, that a quota or the run's budget is reached, that an agent is not available on the channel, that something went wrong, the first message of a conversation continued from the web, and the like. The link it adds for a file, presentation or report an agent produced with no name is labelled the same way. They are written in English, French, Spanish or Japanese:

  • A sender matched to an account gets the language set in their profile.
  • A sender with no language of their own (Auto), a sender the bot does not match to an account, and the few replies sent before the bot looks the sender up (AI switched off, /stop, the platform briefly unable to tell whether AI may run) get the platform's default language from Settings > Parameters.
  • When neither is set, they are in English.

The language is never guessed from what the sender writes. The agents' answers are not affected: an agent answers in the language its persona and the conversation lead it to. In the web app, the conversation keeps the platform's own wording of a refusal or an error; only what the channel shows is translated.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Connect one bot per platform and share it. Several agents can use the same bot with different scopes.
  • Set a receive whitelist before inviting the bot to busy channels, then widen it once the behavior is what you expect.
  • Turn on Only when mentioned for shared team channels, and leave it off for a dedicated support channel where the bot should answer everything.
  • Keep publish scopes tight. An agent that only needs to post a daily report needs one channel, not the whole workspace.
  • Review Routing on the bot card: it lists exactly which agents receive from and publish to that channel.
  • Rotate credentials on the messaging platform side, then paste the new value with Edit credentials. Fields left blank keep their stored value.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The bot never answers. Check in this order: the bot card shows Connected; an agent has the channel enabled with Receive on; the channel is in the receive whitelist (or no whitelist is set); the bot has actually been invited to the channel. On group channels, also check whether Only when mentioned is on.

The bot answers in direct messages but not in channels. Almost always the receive whitelist, a missing invitation, or a missing mention.

The messaging platform rejects the webhook URL. Save the bot credentials in XTM One first. Verification requests are signature-checked, so the platform's URL test only succeeds once the secret is stored. Also confirm BASE_URL matches the public HTTPS address you pasted.

The bot answers twice. On Slack, this is caused by subscribing to both message.channels and app_mention. Keep one of the two.

An agent cannot post to a channel. The publish whitelist on the bot, the agent's own publish selection, or both. The effective scope is the overlap of the two.

Nothing works after changing the platform URL. The webhook URL is derived from BASE_URL. Update the endpoint on every messaging platform after the address changes.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Pick the platform you want to connect: Slack, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or Google Chat.

docs.title: Agent accounts
docs.text:
A channel bot is an application with its own identity: people talk to the bot. An agent account is different: an agent operates a real user account of a messaging platform, or a mailbox, through that account's own sign-in. Two modes share one engine:

Mode The account is Typical use Starts with Delegate (on_behalf) Yours "When someone mentions me or messages me on Teams, let my agent answer for me." "Let my agent answer the emails it can, and flag the ones I must answer myself." Your approval before anything is posted, an AI label, a 2-minute grace period, the agent stepping back when you write AI user (ai_user) A dedicated service account everyone knows is an AI, with its own mailbox and calendar An AI colleague that answers direct messages, follows whole channels and decides when to speak - or runs a shared mailbox (support@, executive-assistant@) Replies posted at once, no label, direct messages and mentions answered

Agent accounts are managed in Profile > Agent Accounts. Every user manages their own; administrators see every account with All accounts.

Two platforms are supported: Microsoft Teams (chats and channels) and Microsoft Outlook (a mailbox, see Mailboxes (Microsoft Outlook)). The engine is platform-agnostic: other platforms plug into the same rules, approvals and settings.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• An integration signed in as the account. Connect a Microsoft integration (Integrations > New integration > Microsoft) and sign it in as the account the agent operates: yourself for a delegate, the service account for an AI user. The integration's token must be one you may use - your own integration, or one shared with you with its owner's consent. The scopes the agent needs (Chat.Read, ChatMessage.Send, ChannelMessage.Read.All, ChannelMessage.Send, User.ReadBasic.All for Teams; Mail.Read, Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send for Outlook) are already part of the Microsoft integration.
  • An agent. Its persona, knowledge bases and tools answer. Messages come from other people, who can write anything: prefer an agent whose tools you are comfortable running for them (read-only integration bindings, no destructive tools), and keep approval on for a delegate until you trust it.
  • A public HTTPS address for real time. Microsoft Graph only notifies an HTTPS address, built from BASE_URL. Without one, direct and group chats - and a mailbox's inbox - are polled every minute, and channels cannot be heard.
  • A work or school account: Microsoft Graph does not offer these APIs for personal Microsoft accounts.
  • Microsoft Graph allows one subscription per Microsoft application and chat or channel. When two agent accounts signed in through one application follow the same channel, only one of them hears it, and the other one's card says which account holds it (see When the account does not hear a conversation).
  • One agent account per platform account. A platform account - and an integration, on each platform - is operated by one enabled agent account at a time. One Microsoft integration can therefore run a Teams account and an Outlook mailbox together, but not two Teams accounts. Saving a second one is refused, naming the first when it is yours (another user's account is never named): put the extra behaviour in rules of the first one, or save the second one switched off. Saving reads who the integration is signed in as; when Microsoft cannot say in time, the account is checked again when it starts listening, and stays in error if the platform account is taken.

docs.title: Operating a service account
docs.text:
You can operate several platform accounts from your own XTM One account: yours, and any service account you hold the credentials of. For example, Samuel signs in to XTM One as himself and runs the executive-assistant@ mailbox:

  1. Connect a second Microsoft integration, signed in as executive-assistant@ (name it, for instance, [Executive Assistant] Microsoft).
  2. Create an AI user account with that integration and the Executive Assistant agent. Under Account (integration) the editor shows who the integration is signed in as - check it reads the service account, not you.
  3. Bind Microsoft on the agent (a per-user binding is enough) to give it the account's mailbox and calendar.

In that account's replies, the agent works as the service account:

  • Its Microsoft tools act as the account. Mail, calendar and Teams tools run with the account's integration, whatever the agent's own Microsoft binding would resolve to for you - never your mailbox. An agent with no Microsoft binding gets no Microsoft tools: the account changes which account a tool acts as, never which tools the agent has.
  • It talks to the person who wrote. The agent is told who wrote as the platform reports it, marked unverified, not that it talks to you. Your personal memory (what the assistant remembers about you) and your default knowledge bases and MCP servers are left out of these replies.
  • Your other agent accounts stay out of it. Two agent accounts never answer each other: a message posted by any agent account is left alone by the others, so your delegate and the Executive Assistant cannot reply to each other in a loop.

Every reply still counts against your agentic quota, and its tools run with your permissions.

docs.title: Create an account
docs.text:
1. Open Profile > Agent Accounts and click New account.
  2. Choose Delegate or AI user. The choice only sets starting values; every setting stays editable.
  3. Under General, pick the platform (Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Outlook or WhatsApp; a new account's rules follow it), name the account, pick the integration signed in as the account and the agent that answers. The editor shows who the integration is signed in as, and warns when another agent account already operates that account.
  4. Review the Rules (below), the Replies settings and, if needed, the Schedule.
  5. Use Test to check what the agent would do with a message, then Create.

Saving answers at once. In the background, the account reads who it is from the integration, subscribes to the conversations its rules reach, and starts listening: its card shows Setting up meanwhile, then its status and how it listens (Real time, Polling every minute). Microsoft confirms each subscription by calling the platform back, which can take a few seconds per conversation. When a conversation cannot be heard, the card says why and what to do (see When the account does not hear a conversation).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rules are read top to bottom; the first rule that matches a message decides. A message no rule matches is left alone. Each rule matches on:

Setting Options Where Direct messages, group chats, channels - any combination Specific conversations Chosen from the account's own chats and channels. Empty: every conversation of the selected kinds Only these people Focus the rule on some people (chosen from the directory, or typed as an email) Members of these groups XTM One groups: the rule also covers a sender one of whose Microsoft addresses (mail address or sign-in name) is the email of an active member. With no people and no group, the rule covers anyone Except these people People this rule never answers Trigger Only when the account is mentioned, or Every message (full monitoring). A direct message always counts as addressed to the account. In channels, a rule waiting for a mention hears the mentions only: the channel's other messages - alerts and bot posts included - never reach the account, unless another rule answers every message there Action Answer, or Ignore (stop here) - an ignore rule placed first is how you exclude a conversation or a person entirely Reply Always reply, or AI decides whether to reply: the agent reads the message and stays silent unless its persona says it should speak Follow the thread Once the agent answered in a thread, later messages there count as addressed, and the agent decides whether to answer them. In a channel heard for mentions only, the platform checks that thread every minute for a day after the agent's last answer there, so a follow-up without a mention can take up to a minute to be seen

A rule can also override the account's defaults for the messages it answers: the response mode, the AI label, the grace period, and extra guardrails and instructions ("for my manager, be formal and never commit to a date"). The sparkle button next to the account's instructions and to each rule's guardrails writes or improves them with AI from a short description.

The editor offers ready-made rules: Monitor a channel (AI decides), Focus on some people, Ignore a conversation, Public channels, non-confidential only and Leadership groups, full access (both described below).

docs.title: Access by audience
docs.text:
An agent with deep reach - board material, every integration, a long memory - should not answer everyone with everything. Besides who it answers, each rule decides what the agent may use for the messages it covers, in its Access section:

  • Integrations, knowledge bases, MCP servers, built-in tools, custom tools and skills. The section lists the agent's own; everything is on by default, and switching one off removes it from those replies. This is enforced by the platform, not asked of the model: a knowledge base switched off is not searched, an integration switched off has no tool. A rule only ever narrows the agent - a capability the agent gains later is on for a rule that left the list untouched, never for one that narrowed it.
  • Memory. Use the agent's memory off: the agent neither reads nor writes its memory for those messages, so what it learned in a board chat cannot surface in a public channel, and nothing said there is remembered.
  • Guardrails. The rule's instructions govern what the agent says to that audience ("only information already public inside the company; decline board, financial and HR questions politely"); generate them with AI from a one-line description.

Because the first matching rule decides, order is the policy: put channel rules first. An executive asking the Executive Assistant a question in #general then gets #general's access, not theirs, because everyone in the channel reads the answer. For example:

  1. Public channels, non-confidential only - channels, when mentioned: no confidential knowledge base or integration, memory off, a guardrail.
  2. Leadership groups, full access - direct and group chats, for the members of the Board and ExCo groups: everything the agent has.
  3. Nothing else: anyone outside those groups messaging the account directly is left alone.

The Test tab shows which rule applies and whether it limits access; type an email as the sender to test with the groups of the XTM One user it belongs to. When a rule names groups, it also says who the sender was found to be: XTM One user ..., member of Board, in none of the groups the rules name (add them to the group), or No active XTM One user has the email ... (their XTM One account uses another email, or is deactivated).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Delegate, mentions and DMs only: the default rules. Add Focus on some people above them with Send automatically for your team, so only their questions skip your approval.
  • AI user following an incident channel: a rule on that channel with Every message and AI decides. The agent reads everything and speaks when it has something useful to add.
  • Never in #general: an Ignore rule on that channel, first in the list.

docs.title: WhatsApp business numbers
docs.text:
A WhatsApp agent account operates the business phone number of a WhatsApp integration (WhatsApp Cloud API): as an AI user, the number is the agent's own (a support or assistant number); on behalf, it is a person's business number and the agent answers as them.

  • What it hears. Every message the number receives, in direct conversations (one per phone number) and in the groups the number created, as soon as Meta delivers it to the integration's webhook. No subscription to set up: connect the integration's webhook once (see the WhatsApp integration page) and the account hears what the integration stores. Reactions are not answered.
  • What it sends. A text reply, shown in WhatsApp as a reply to the message answered. What agents send through the integration's tools (messages, templates, files, buttons) appears in the account's activity log.
  • Context. The agent reads the conversation's previous messages as the integration stored them; WhatsApp does not return what the number itself sent.
  • Linked-device gateway backend. An integration whose backend is linked_device_gateway needs no phone number id: the account reads the paired number from the gateway, replies through it and hears what the gateway webhook stores. Every sync checks the number is still paired; an unpaired number puts the account in error and asks to pair it again. The account shows Real time once its rules answer in conversations, on both backends. A refused check names the backend it checked (Cloud API or linked-device gateway).
  • Limits. WhatsApp allows a free-form reply only within 24 hours of the person's last message; after that, only an approved template can be sent.

docs.title: Mailboxes (Microsoft Outlook)
docs.text:
An Outlook agent account watches the account's inbox and handles each email its rules give the agent - your own mailbox as a delegate, or a service account's (support@, executive-assistant@) as an AI user.

Where. A mailbox has two kinds of conversation instead of chats and channels: Emails to the account alone (the account is the only recipient) and Emails with other recipients. The trigger reads Only when the account is in To or Every email, Cc included: an email to the account alone always counts as addressed to it, an email where it is only in Cc does not. A thread of replies is one conversation, named after its subject.

Starting rules. A new mailbox answers the emails sent to the account alone and those with the account in To, the agent deciding for each; emails where the account is only in Cc are left alone. As a delegate, replies wait for your approval, with the AI label, a 2-minute grace period and up to 10 replies per conversation and hour; as an AI user, replies are sent at once, up to 30. Either way, the agent takes up at most 60 emails an hour across the whole mailbox - each new email starts a conversation of its own - and a reply that would go to more than 10 people besides the sender (a reply-all) is handed to you instead of being sent.

Who. Only these people and Except these people take an address or a whole domain written @example.com (that exact domain, not its subdomains): for instance Ignore emails from @newsletter.example.com, or answer @customer.com only.

Triage. For each email a rule hands it, the agent makes one of three choices, and says why in one line:

The agent What happens Shown in the account's page as Answers The reply goes out as the response mode says (sent, waiting for your approval, or recorded in shadow) Answered Hands it to you - it cannot or should not answer (a decision only you can take, missing information, a sensitive topic) Nothing is sent; by default the email is flagged for follow-up, filed in the category Needs your attention, and the notification bell tells you, with the agent's reason Handed to you Leaves it - it needs no reply (a thank-you, an FYI, a confirmation) Nothing is sent; by default the email is filed in No reply needed The agent stayed silent

The choice is read by the platform from a structured answer, not from the wording of a reply. A rule with Always reply lets the agent answer or hand over, never leave an email unanswered. The agent's reason shows under The agent's reason when you open the email in the Decisions tab.

What the mailbox shows (Replies > Mailbox triage): for each of the three outcomes, whether the email is marked as read, the Outlook category it is filed in (empty for none; the category is added to the email's own), and for an email handed to you whether it is flagged and whether you are notified. By default an answered email is marked as read and filed in Answered by AI. In Shadow mode nobody is notified and the mailbox is left untouched, except that an email handed to you is still flagged for follow-up when flagging is on, so you find it. A flag the mailbox refuses shows the email as Failed in the Decisions tab, with the mailbox's error as the account's last error.

Replies. The agent replies in the email's thread - to the sender, or to everyone when others were on the email - with the signature below under the answer and the original email quoted below it, as Outlook does. The agent reads the thread's earlier emails, and the names of the email's attachments, as context. If you answer the email yourself during the grace period, or write in the thread, the agent steps back as on Teams.

Signature (Replies > Signature). A reply the agent sends never goes through Outlook, so a signature add-in installed in Outlook never signs it. The account chooses what it carries:

Signature What the reply carries When to choose it The account's own (default) The signature of the account's latest sent emails, copied Signatures set in Outlook, or a service account whose sent mail is signed From a signature integration The person's current signature from a Letsignit integration, read when each reply is sent: their signature and banner as Letsignit composes them now, its reply variant first Letsignit signs your mail in Outlook (the add-in): the reply looks like one the person sent, banner of the day included None No signature The mail server signs every outgoing email in transit (Letsignit's server-side signature, an SMTP connector): the reply is signed there, once

The signature is looked up by the account's email address and kept for 10 minutes. When the integration cannot be read, or holds no signature for that address, the reply carries the account's own, and the account's card says why until a reply carries the integration's signature again.

Left alone. The account's own emails, drafts, meeting invitations, meeting responses and cancellations with nothing written in them (a bare accept or decline), emails sent by any agent account (each carries a header saying so, so two agent mailboxes never answer each other in a loop), and automated mail - newsletters, mailing lists, notifications, auto-replies and out-of-office messages, recognised by the headers such mail carries (RFC 3834) - shown as Automated mail (a notification, a newsletter, an auto-reply). A meeting response or cancellation in which the sender wrote something ("Declined: ..." with new times proposed) is heard like any email, from the person who answered: the delegate when it was sent on behalf of someone, the rules matching either.

docs.title: Replies
docs.text:
Setting What it does Response mode Send automatically; Ask me first - replies wait in your approval queue; Shadow (record only) - nothing is posted, so you can see what the agent would have said while you tune the rules AI label A line such as Sent by an AI agent on behalf of Sam added to every reply, before or after it. It is added by the platform, never left to the model. {name} stands for the account's name. A rule can turn it on or off Grace period Wait before answering. If the account's human answers meanwhile, the agent stays silent. A restart during the wait does not lose the message Step back after the owner writes Once the human writes in a conversation, the agent stays out of it for this many minutes Replies per conversation and hour A safety limit, for instance between two AI accounts. 0: no limit Agent turns per hour, whole account Every message the agent takes up costs a turn - and an AI quota - whether it answers, hands the message to you or leaves it. Past the limit, the account leaves the next messages until the hour ends, shown as Hourly limit of the account reached. 60 for a new mailbox, where anyone can write new emails; 0 (no limit) for a new Teams account People a reply may reach Mailboxes. The sender of an email chooses who a reply-all reaches: a reply that would go to more people besides the sender is handed to you - flagged, with the reason - instead of being sent. 10 by default; 0: no limit Context messages How many earlier messages of the thread or chat the agent reads. The conversation is replayed from the platform - messages the human wrote themselves included - so the agent answers in context, as a participant. The agent's own earlier replies are part of it (on WhatsApp, read from the account's record of what it sent), so only the messages that arrived since its last reply are the ones it answers Instructions Added to the agent's persona for every reply of this account; can be generated with AI Reactions as feedback On by default. A reaction someone puts on an answer of the agent rates it: by default a thumbs up is positive and a thumbs down negative; click an emoji to make it positive, negative or ignored. See below Notify me when a reply is sent On by default. Each reply the account posts on its own (Send automatically) reaches you in the notification bell - where it was posted, to whom, and the start of what was said - so you can follow what is said on your behalf without reading every conversation. A reply you approve does not notify you again

Files and images. An image pasted into a Teams message and a file shared in it reach the agent with the message: each is downloaded as the account (the files with Files.Read.All, already part of the Microsoft integration, the pasted images with the chat's own Chat.Read or ChannelMessage.Read.All), kept as a file of the reply's turn under your name, and handed to the agent, which reads it with read_file_content and sees an image when its model takes images. At most 10 per message, each under the upload size limit; one that cannot be downloaded is left out and the agent answers with the rest.

Voice notes. A voice message recorded in a Teams chat, or an audio file sent to the account (m4a, mp3, mp4 audio, ogg, opus, wav, webm), is downloaded as the account and transcribed for you with the platform's speech-to-text (the OpenAI provider you may use, as for dictation in the chat; the language is detected). The agent reads it as the message's text, marked [voice note, 0:42, transcribed] ..., after any text the message also carries; it is queued and merged with your other messages like a text. The audio is not kept as a file. When the audio cannot be downloaded or transcribed (no OpenAI provider, a refused download), the agent reads [voice note: transcription failed: <reason>] and can tell you so.

docs.title: Reactions as feedback
docs.text:
When people react to an answer the agent posted, their reaction becomes a rating of that answer in the agent's Feedback tab (and in what the agent's persona improvement reads), next to the thumbs given in the web chat.

  • Anyone who can react counts, colleagues without an XTM One account and guests included. The platform keeps only a keyed fingerprint of who reacted - enough to count one rating per person and to remove it when the reaction is removed - never their name or id.
  • A skin tone counts as the same emoji. Someone holding a positive and a negative emoji on the same answer does not rate it. Emojis you did not map are ignored.
  • A reaction counts for 14 days after the answer was posted. Switching the setting (or the account) off stops reading reactions and keeps the ratings already given. Switching it back on, or changing which emojis count, reads the reactions of every answer still within its 14 days again, so the ratings follow the setting; older answers keep the ratings they had.
  • In AI user mode, the account's own reactions are not ratings (the account is the agent). In On my behalf mode, your own reaction on your delegate's answer counts.
  • Reactions are read as they happen in chats and in channels the account hears in full. In channels heard for mentions only - Microsoft allows one subscription per channel, and that one only carries mentions - and when the platform has no public HTTPS address, the answers are checked every few minutes, then less often as they age. Answers heard as they happen are also checked every few hours, in case Microsoft stops notifying their changes. If Microsoft refuses to notify the reactions of a chat or channel, the account still hears it, its answers are checked instead, and the account's listening problems say so.
  • The account page shows how many positive and negative ratings each answer received (Messages sent tab), and the totals over the period (Overview tab).

The agent never answers the account's own messages, nor messages from apps, bots, workflows and other agent accounts.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text: With Ask me first, each reply waits in Replies waiting for your approval at the top of Profile > Agent Accounts, and the notification bell tells you. For each one you see the message, the conversation and the rule, and you can send the draft, edit it first, or drop it. The AI label is added when the reply is sent. A reply nobody approves expires after a day. Shadow drafts can also be sent from the Replies tab of the account's page.

docs.title: Active hours
docs.text: A weekly schedule with a timezone. During these hours answers only inside the windows; Outside these hours (when I am away) answers only outside them - for instance evenings and weekends for a delegate. A window that ends before it starts runs past midnight.

docs.title: Understanding what happened
docs.text:
The name of an account, or its Activity button, opens the account's page. It keeps every message the account heard over the last 30 days, in three tabs:

  • Overview - over the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days: how many messages the account heard and how many were for the agent, what it did with them (answered, waiting for your approval, stayed silent, handled elsewhere, left alone, failed) and the share it answered, the median time to answer and to approve, the ratings of its answers. Charts show the activity over time, the kinds of conversation and why messages were left alone; tables show what each rule decided and the conversations and people the account heard the most. A figure, a conversation or a person opens the Decisions tab on it. Hide the messages left alone from the timeline to see only what the agent did.
  • Decisions - every message, newest first, filtered by what the account did, the kind of conversation, a conversation, a person or a search, page by page. Handled elsewhere is an email another pipeline of the same agent took first (an assignment run on the mailbox, or another of its agent accounts): this account sent nothing, and the opened row says who took it (Taken by an assignment run of this agent., or Taken by the agent account <name>. with a link to that account; an account you cannot see reads Taken by another agent account of this agent.). The outcome filter wraps onto a second row when its options do not fit. A row opens on why it happened: the reason (The account is not mentioned, No rule covers it, The account owner took over, Hourly reply limit reached...), the rule, how the message was addressed (a direct message, a mention, a follow-up in a thread), whether a grace period ran, and the reply it produced. When a rule names groups, it also shows who the sender was found to be, as in the Test tab.
  • Messages sent - every message the AI sent in the account's name, filtered (All, Replies to a message, Proactive sends, Failed, Awaiting approval, Shadow) or searched: the replies to a message the account heard, with what was posted and how it was rated, and the messages the agent sent on its own (a follow-up or an opening message from a chat, an assignment or a tool call), shown as Proactive send with their recipients and origin in place of the quoted message; the drafts waiting for you (send, edit or drop them here), shadow drafts, and the sends that failed with why. A proactive send is also a row of Decisions, where it opens on what was sent rather than on why, the rule and how it was addressed. A failed send is logged as Failed; a log that cannot be written never fails the send and leaves a warning in the server logs. Messages sent before this log existed are not backfilled.

Use Test in the editor to try a message against unsaved rules.

A message from a conversation no rule covers reads No rule covers it, whoever wrote it. Seeing some after narrowing the rules (for instance from a channel you no longer follow) means the account was still subscribed to it: the first such message triggers a new synchronization, which drops the subscription within a minute or two.

docs.title: Manage accounts from a chat
docs.text:
Agents can read and change agent accounts for you, so you can ask in a conversation instead of opening the editor: "pause my Teams delegate until Monday", "stop answering in #general", "only answer my team in direct messages", "why didn't you answer Bob yesterday?", "create an Outlook account for the Executive Assistant".

  • The General Assistant, and any agent with the agent builder (Agent builder built-in tool), manage every account of yours: list them, read an account (its settings, its rules in order, whether it hears its conversations), create one, change any setting, enable or disable it, add, change, move or remove one rule, delete it, test a sample message against the saved rules or a proposed change, and read the activity log. The same tools are on the XTM One MCP server; a read-only API key gets the reading half.
  • An agent that operates one of your accounts gets the same tools, except creating an account, for the accounts it operates for you only - with no extra built-in tool to enable. Ask the Executive Assistant, in a chat with it, to "answer emails from @customer.com without waiting for my approval" and it changes its own rule. To keep an agent from changing its accounts, add the tools to its tool deny list (update_agent_account, edit_agent_account_rule, delete_agent_account).
  • Never for the people writing to the account. While the agent answers a message someone sent to the account, none of these tools is offered, not even the reading ones: the person writing could otherwise read your rules or widen them. That reply only knows the rule it answers under, and whether the platform adds the AI label to it.

The agent's changes are the editor's: the same checks (an integration and an agent you can use, one agent account per platform account, valid rules), saved the same way, and recorded in the audit log as made through an agent. The Agent Accounts page shows them as soon as the tool returns. A rule the platform cannot apply changes nothing, and the agent is told why.

docs.title: When the account does not hear a conversation
docs.text:
Each synchronization checks every conversation the rules reach. When some cannot be heard, the account card says how many (Not listening to 12 of 14 conversations), when it last checked, and one entry per cause: what is wrong, the conversations it affects (All chats, or the channel by name), what to do, and the button that does it. Technical details shows what Microsoft answered, word for word, for support. While a new check runs, the card keeps the previous check's findings and says so. Once fixed, use Synchronize now (or wait for the next synchronization, within the hour).

The card says What it means What to do The account's integration cannot be used The integration is gone, disconnected, or its token is not one you may use Open the integration and sign it in as the account, or pick another one in the account's settings Microsoft Teams rejected the integration's sign-in The sign-in expired or was revoked Sign the integration in again as the account Microsoft Teams refused to notify the account Microsoft refused the subscription: the integration lacks the permission the card names (Chat.Read for chats, ChannelMessage.Read.All for channels - often an administrator's consent in Entra ID), or the account is no longer a member of the conversation Get the permission granted, sign the integration in again, then synchronize Your agent account ... already follows it / Another user's agent account already follows it Microsoft allows one subscription per application and conversation, and another agent account of this platform holds it Remove the conversation from one of the two accounts' rules, or connect one of them through another Microsoft application ... already follows it through the same app Another platform signed in as this account through the same Microsoft application (for instance a staging instance) holds the subscription Remove it there, or use another Microsoft application for one of the two Microsoft Teams could not reach the platform to confirm the subscription Microsoft calls the platform back before it creates a subscription, and the call never arrived: BASE_URL/api/v1/agent-accounts/notifications/microsoft_teams is not reachable from the internet over HTTPS (behind a VPN or an access proxy, for instance) An administrator makes BASE_URL publicly reachable over HTTPS Channels cannot be heard without a public HTTPS address BASE_URL is not a public HTTPS address: chats are polled every minute, channels cannot be heard An administrator sets BASE_URL to a public HTTPS address The conversation no longer exists, or the account left it The channel or chat is gone, or the account was removed from it Remove it from the rules, or add the account back The rules cover it, but the account does not listen to it A rule answering in every channel follows the first 50 channels of the account; a channel past them, every channel of a team whose channels Microsoft refuses to list, and a channel a rule names without its team are not subscribed to. Technical details says which Name the channel in a rule, or pick it again in the rule Microsoft Teams asked the platform to slow down / did not answer A temporary condition Nothing: the next synchronization tries again

The account keeps hearing every conversation that is not listed: a card with problems and the Active status still answers there.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• An agent account acts with its owner's integration token and agent. It is never shared; administrators can see and edit every account.
  • Messages from other people are untrusted input to an agent that acts as you. The platform's prompt-injection checks and content quarantine apply as on channels, and a tool that needs approval stops the reply instead of posting an explanation - but the safest setup is a delegate with approval and an agent with read-only tools.
  • An account's configuration is yours: the agent-account tools are never offered while the agent answers someone writing to the account (see Manage accounts from a chat). Other tools of the agent still run with your permissions in those replies: narrow them per rule in Access.
  • Group membership is read on every message: someone removed from a group stops reaching what that group could at their next message. A sender is matched to an XTM One user by the addresses the platform reports from its directory (for Microsoft, the mail address and the sign-in name), which the sender cannot type; a sender with no XTM One account belongs to no group. The decisions show only the groups the rules name, never a sender's other memberships.
  • Access limits are enforced by the platform, guardrails by the model. Put what must not leak behind an access limit (a knowledge base switched off, memory off), and use guardrails for tone and for what the agent should decline to discuss.
  • With AI switched off on the platform, no message is answered (each is recorded as AI unavailable); the accounts stay yours to create, edit, synchronize or delete, and their waiting replies to send or drop. Generating instructions with AI waits for AI to be back.
  • Every created, changed, deleted, approved and rejected account or reply is recorded in the audit log, and every agent turn counts against the owner's agentic quota.

docs.title: Discord
docs.text:
Connecting Discord lets people talk to an agent in a server channel or a direct message, and lets agents post messages, reactions, and threads back.

Discord is the one channel that does not use a webhook: the platform opens a persistent connection to Discord itself. That changes one thing in the setup — the connection starts when the platform starts.

Read Channels and bots first for the concepts shared with the other platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need permission to create an application in the Discord developer portal, and to invite a bot to the target server.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • You need to be able to restart the platform after saving the credentials.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Discord application
docs.text:
1. Go to discord.com/developers/applications and create a new application.
  2. Open Bot, click Reset Token, and copy the token.
  3. Under Privileged Gateway Intents, enable Message Content Intent. Without it, Discord delivers empty message content and the agent has nothing to answer.
  4. Optionally copy the application public key from General Information if you plan to use slash commands.

docs.title: Step 2: Invite the bot to your server
docs.text:
1. Open OAuth2 > URL Generator.
  2. Select the bot scope.
  3. Select the permissions Send Messages, Read Message History, and Add Reactions.
  4. Open the generated URL and invite the bot to the server.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the Discord card.
  2. Paste the bot token into Bot Token / Access Token.
  3. Optionally paste the application public key into Application public key. It is only needed for the interactions endpoint used by slash commands, and it enables signature verification on that endpoint.
  4. Click Save Channel.

Restart the platform after saving

The Discord connection is opened at platform startup. A bot saved on a running platform stays offline until the next restart.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable Discord on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable Discord:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers incoming messages.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should post on its own.
  • Decide whether direct messages are allowed with Allow private, and whether people without an account may use the agent with Allow anonymous.

Whitelist entries are Discord channel IDs. To copy one, enable developer mode in Discord, then right-click a channel and choose Copy Channel ID.

docs.title: What to expect on Discord
docs.text:
• Discord does not expose an email address, so senders cannot be matched to an XTM One account automatically. Turn on Allow anonymous users if unknown senders should be served — the agent still receives the username as context.
  • Mentions are detected, so Only when mentioned works in server channels. Thread continuation does not: Discord has no thread identifier narrow enough to track, so a mention is needed for each new question when mention-only is on. /stop is unavailable for the same reason, while /reset works.
  • Answers longer than the Discord limit are split into several messages automatically.

docs.title: What the agent can do in Discord
docs.text: When Publish is on, the agent can send a message, read recent messages in a channel, list the channels it can see, create a thread, add a reaction, pin or unpin a message, and delete one of its own messages.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Restrict the receive whitelist to the channels where the bot is genuinely expected, since a server invitation exposes many channels at once.
  • Use Only when mentioned in community servers so the bot does not answer general chatter.
  • Use a dedicated agent with a narrow tool set when the server is public.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The bot appears offline. The platform has not been restarted since the credentials were saved, or the token is wrong. Restart and check the platform logs for the Discord connection.

Messages arrive empty or are ignored. Message Content Intent is not enabled in the developer portal.

The bot answers in direct messages but not in channels. Check the channel permissions on the Discord side, the receive whitelist, and whether a mention is required.

Slash commands do nothing. The interactions endpoint URL must be configured in the developer portal, and the application public key must be stored in XTM One — Discord probes the endpoint with an invalid signature and expects it to be refused.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Google Chat, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: Google Chat
docs.text:
Connecting Google Chat lets people talk to an agent in a space or a direct message from Google Workspace, and lets agents post messages back into spaces.

Read Channels and bots first for the concepts shared with the other platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need a Google Cloud project and the rights to enable APIs and create service accounts in it.
  • You need a Google Workspace domain where the Chat app can be published to your users.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, because Google Chat posts messages to it.

docs.title: Step 1: Configure the Chat app in Google Cloud
docs.text:
1. In the Google Cloud Console, enable the Google Chat API for your project.
  2. Open the Chat API configuration page and set the app name, description, and avatar. This is what your users see in Google Chat.
  3. Enable the interactive features so the app can receive messages, and choose to receive them in spaces and direct messages.
  4. Under the connection settings, select HTTP endpoint URL and paste the webhook URL shown on the Google Chat card in XTM One — it ends with /api/channels/googlechat/webhook.
  5. Set the visibility so the people who should use the app can install it.

docs.title: Step 2: Create a service account
docs.text:
1. Go to IAM & Admin > Service Accounts and create a service account for the Chat app.
  2. Create a JSON key for it and download the file. This is how the platform sends messages back to Google Chat.
  3. Note the project number from the project overview page — it is the numeric identifier, not the project ID.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the Google Chat card.
  2. Paste the entire contents of the service account JSON key file into Bot Token / Access Token.
  3. Paste the project number into Google Cloud project number. This lets the platform verify that incoming requests really come from Google Chat.
  4. Click Save Channel.

Set the project number

Without it, the webhook accepts any request that reaches the URL. With it, every request must carry a valid Google-signed token issued for your project.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable Google Chat on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable Google Chat:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers incoming messages.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should post on its own.
  • Adjust Allow anonymous, Allow private, and Only mention within what the bot allows.

Whitelist entries are space names, in the spaces/AAAAAAA form used by Google Chat.

docs.title: Step 5: Add the app to spaces
docs.text: In Google Chat, open the space and add the app from the space menu, or start a direct message with it. Like every other channel, the bot only sees the spaces it belongs to.

docs.title: What to expect on Google Chat
docs.text:
• Google Chat provides the sender's email address, so users are matched to their XTM One account automatically and get their own permissions, preferences, and memory.
  • Mentions are detected, so Only when mentioned works in spaces. Google Chat has real threads, so once the bot has answered in a thread it keeps following that thread without a new mention, and /stop mutes a specific thread.
  • There is no typing indicator in the Google Chat API, so a long answer arrives with no visible activity beforehand.
  • Files uploaded with a message reach the agent as files of the conversation, and a file sent without text is still answered. A file larger than the platform's 40 MB upload limit is not passed on, but the message is. A Google Drive file shared in a message is named to the agent with its link, but the Chat app cannot download it: Google Chat only serves uploaded content to an app, and Drive needs the user's own authorization, so an agent reads it through a Google integration.

docs.title: What the agent can do in Google Chat
docs.text: When Publish is on, the agent can send a message to a space, list the spaces it belongs to, read basic information about a space, and delete one of its own messages. It sends text only: Google Chat lets an app upload a file only on behalf of a signed-in user (media.upload requires user authentication), which the Chat app's service account is not.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Restrict app visibility in Google Workspace to the groups that should use it, then use the receive whitelist for finer control per space.
  • Use Only when mentioned in general-purpose spaces and leave it off in a space dedicated to the agent.
  • Keep the service account key in a secrets manager. Rotating it is a matter of creating a new key and pasting it with Edit credentials.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Google rejects the endpoint or the app never delivers messages. Confirm the Chat API is enabled, the app is configured for an HTTP endpoint, and the URL matches the one shown on the card.

Every request is rejected. The project number is wrong. It must be the numeric project number, not the project ID.

The app answers in direct messages but not in a space. It has not been added to that space, the space is not in the receive whitelist, or a mention is required.

The agent cannot post. The service account key is missing or invalid — the key is what authenticates outgoing messages, separately from the incoming webhook.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Slack, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: Microsoft Teams
docs.text:
Connecting Microsoft Teams lets your users chat with an agent from a team channel, a group chat, or a personal chat, and lets agents post messages, cards, and files back into Teams.

Teams has the longest setup of all channels because it involves three Microsoft surfaces: an Entra ID app registration for the identity and permissions, an Azure Bot resource for message delivery, and a Teams app package for installation in the tenant. Read Channels and bots first for the concepts shared with the other platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need an Entra ID (Azure AD) administrator, or someone who can grant admin consent for application permissions.
  • You need permission to upload a custom app to your Teams tenant, or a Teams administrator to do it for you.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, because Teams posts messages to it.

docs.title: Step 1: Register the application in Entra ID
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Entra ID > App registrations > New registration.
  2. Note the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID from the overview page.
  3. Under Certificates & secrets, create a client secret and copy its value immediately — it is shown only once.
  4. Under API permissions, add the Microsoft Graph application permissions listed below, then click Grant admin consent. They must be application permissions, not delegated ones.

docs.title: Application permissions
docs.text: Permission Why it is needed Channel.ReadBasic.All List the channels the bot can work with Chat.Create Start a chat with a user Chat.Read.WhereInstalled Read messages in chats where the app is installed Chat.ReadWrite.WhereInstalled Read and write messages in those chats ChatMember.Read.WhereInstalled Read the members of those chats Team.ReadBasic.All List the teams the bot can work with

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Azure Bot resource
docs.text:
1. Create an Azure Bot resource in the Azure portal.
  2. Choose Single Tenant and Use existing app registration, using the application ID from step 1.
  3. In Settings > Configuration, set the messaging endpoint to the webhook URL shown on the Teams card in XTM One — it ends with /api/channels/teams/messages.
  4. In Channels, add the Microsoft Teams channel.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the Microsoft Teams card.
  2. Paste the application ID into App ID / Client ID.
  3. Paste the client secret into App Password / Client Secret.
  4. Paste the directory ID into Entra ID (Azure AD) Tenant ID.
  5. Click Save Channel. The card shows Connected and displays the webhook URL used in step 2.

The application ID is also what authenticates incoming traffic: XTM One validates the signed token on every Teams request against it, so requests that do not come from the Bot Framework are rejected.

docs.title: Step 4: Build and install the Teams app package
docs.text:
Teams needs an app package to install the bot in your tenant.

  1. Open the Teams Developer Portal and create the app.
  2. Use the manifest template offered by the Setup Guide button on the Teams card — it already carries your deployment name — and replace the placeholders: <YOUR_APP_ID> with the application ID from step 1 (in id, bots[0].botId and webApplicationInfo), your-domain.com with your platform's domain, and the developer block with your organization.
  3. Keep the resource-specific consent permissions listed below under authorization.permissions.resourceSpecific.
  4. Add two icons: color.png, 192×192 in full color, and outline.png, 32×32, a white outline on a transparent background.
  5. Zip manifest.json, color.png, and outline.png together, at the root of the archive: no folder inside the .zip.
  6. Install it through the Teams admin center, or sideload it if your tenant allows custom apps. When you change the manifest later, raise its version so Teams clients pick up the new package.

The template targets manifest schema 1.29 and sets two properties that matter:

  • supportsChannelFeatures: "tier1" lets members add the app to shared and private channels. It is mandatory for an app with the team scope on schema 1.25 and later. Do not also declare supportedChannelTypes: the two are mutually exclusive, and Teams rejects a package that declares both with "We can't read the manifest file".
  • supportsFiles: true lets the bot receive files sent in personal chats. Files shared in group chats and channels are retrieved through Graph and work regardless of this setting.

docs.title: Resource-specific permissions
docs.text: Permission Why it is needed ChannelMessage.Read.Group Read channel messages in teams where the app is installed ChatMessage.Read.Chat Read messages in chats where the app is installed ChannelMember.Read.Group Receive membership events of the shared and private channels the app is added to

docs.title: Step 5: Enable Teams on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable Microsoft Teams:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers Teams messages, and optionally restrict it to specific channels.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should post to Teams on its own, and pick the channels it may post to.
  • Adjust Allow anonymous, Allow private, and Only mention within what the bot allows.

The channel picker resolves team and channel identifiers for you. Group chats are never listed — their identifiers cannot be enumerated — so they are governed by Allow private, Only mention, and agent routing instead of by whitelists.

docs.title: Standard, private, and shared channels
docs.text:
Teams delivers messages differently depending on the channel type, and XTM One compensates for it.

  • In standard channels, every message is delivered to the bot, so mention behavior is entirely up to your settings.
  • In private and shared channels, Microsoft only delivers messages that @mention the bot. After the bot has answered a mention there, XTM One subscribes to that thread through Graph so follow-up messages keep reaching the agent without a new mention. Monitoring stops after seven days of inactivity, and the bot posts a short notice when it does.

docs.title: Graph notifications for private channels
docs.text:
Follow-ups in private and shared channels reach XTM One as Microsoft Graph notifications on <BASE_URL>/api/channels/teams/graph-notifications, a public endpoint Microsoft must be able to reach. Every subscription XTM One creates carries a random secret that Microsoft sends back with each notification; XTM One stores it encrypted and checks it, together with the subscription id, against what it recorded for the channel. Every notification of a delivery is checked before any work is queued for it, so one the verification policy below refuses costs nothing beyond that check. In the default mode, a forged notification that carries what earlier releases accepted (such as the copilot_ value for a channel with no record) is still acted on: one task per distinct message it names, the same message named twice in one delivery counting once. A delivery larger than 4 MiB, far above what Microsoft sends, is refused with HTTP 413, and one XTM One cannot check or record because its Redis does not answer gets HTTP 503, so Microsoft delivers it again later. A follow-up posted while no subscription could notify it - a subscription Microsoft removed, or one XTM One had to recreate - is read back from Microsoft Graph once the channel has a subscription again, up to four hours back, and answered once.

By default, XTM One also acts on a notification that earlier releases acted on without that proof: one carrying the secret of the subscriptions created before 2026-07-02 (copilot_ followed by the team id, which anyone who knows the team id can compute), or the channel's secret under another subscription id. Each case is logged as a warning, at most once every 15 minutes, and reported by the security audit in Settings > Security. Subscriptions created by an earlier release are kept and renewed as before, so nothing changes for your channels on upgrade.

To refuse every notification that does not prove its subscription, turn on Require verified integration notifications in Settings > Security > Security options, or set INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION=true - the switch that also refuses the unverified Slack, Microsoft Graph and LinkedIn notifications of integrations. The maintenance pass, which runs shortly after XTM One starts and then about once an hour, then replaces the subscriptions whose secret is derivable or can no longer be decrypted. Microsoft allows one subscription per channel, so it deletes the old one before creating the new one; what the old one was still delivering is accepted for four hours, and what was posted in between is read back from Microsoft Graph.

If Microsoft refuses the replacement

With the option on, a replacement deletes the old subscription first. If Microsoft Graph then refuses to create the new one, that channel's follow-ups stop until a later pass creates it, and the log says Graph subscription creation failed. With the option off, no subscription is deleted to be replaced.

docs.title: What the agent can do in Teams
docs.text:
When Publish is on, the agent gets Teams tools: send a message or an adaptive card to a channel, a personal chat, or a group chat, edit a message it already sent, read channel messages, chat messages, or thread replies, list teams and channels, list chats, upload a file to a channel, download a file it received, and delete one of its own channel messages.
