Chat and group chat messaging is not governed by channel whitelists — those cover teams and channels. Long answers are split automatically, and images are delivered as separate cards because Teams rejects an activity carrying both text and attachments.

docs.title: Pasted XTM One links
docs.text:
A link to an assignment run (<your XTM One address>/operations/executions/<id>) pasted in a Teams chat or channel turns into a card. The manifest declares it in composeExtensions with a link message handler whose domains is your XTM One host, the same host as validDomains; the Setup Guide template includes it.

  • The posted card names nothing: no run, agent or status. Each person who views it then gets their own version, rendered with their XTM One access, and Teams shows it to them alone.
  • Someone who cannot see the run reads "This run doesn't exist or you don't have access to it", which is also what a link to a run that does not exist shows. A Teams user whose email matches no active XTM One user is asked to sign in with it.
  • When the run waits for a person, whoever may answer it in XTM One - the run's owner, or an administrator for any run - gets the tools it wants to run, with an Approve / Reject choice per tool and an optional reason, or the agent's question with an answer box. Others see the state without the buttons. The answer goes through the same checks as the run page in XTM One, is recorded with the person who gave it, and the run resumes.
  • Someone who sees the card but cannot answer the run can choose Ask the owner to act (Ask an admin to act on a company-managed run). The people who can answer it get a notification in XTM One, and the request is listed on the run page until the run is answered or they dismiss it. Nothing is shared: the person who asked still cannot see the run, and the card answers the same whether the run exists or not.
  • In a conversation of up to 60 members Teams loads each viewer's card on its own; above that, a viewer chooses Refresh card in the message menu.

The app must be installed for the person who pastes the link (deploy it to your whole organization), and a manifest from before this feature must be updated in the Teams admin center. The Teams bot must have its Tenant ID set in XTM One: a card is only rendered and answered for people of that Entra tenant, so someone from another organization whose email matches an XTM One account is never taken for that account. Without it, links unfurl into the neutral card only.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Grant admin consent once and keep the client secret in a password manager. When it expires, Teams stops delivering messages with no other symptom — use Edit credentials to paste the new value.
  • Note the secret expiry date in your calendar. Entra ID secrets are time-limited and this is the most common cause of a bot going silent months after a working setup.
  • Use Only when mentioned for busy team channels; thread continuation keeps follow-up questions working without a new mention.
  • Keep the publish whitelist to the channels the agent genuinely reports into.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The bot is installed but never answers. Check the messaging endpoint in the Azure Bot resource, confirm the Teams channel is added there, and confirm an agent has Teams Receive enabled.

Teams refuses the package with "We can't read the manifest file". Check the package against Step 4: the files at the root of the .zip, the icon sizes, and supportsChannelFeatures without supportedChannelTypes.

It worked and suddenly stopped. The client secret has almost certainly expired. Create a new one and update it in XTM One.

The bot answers in standard channels but not in a private one. That is expected until the bot has been @mentioned in the thread once. After that first mention, follow-ups are picked up for seven days.

Private-channel follow-ups after an upgrade or a SECRET_KEY change. By default nothing changes: a subscription created by an older release keeps working and is renewed, and after a SECRET_KEY change a notification naming the subscription recorded for its channel is still acted on, with a warning. With Require verified integration notifications on, such subscriptions are replaced by the maintenance pass instead (see Graph notifications for private channels). Nothing needs to change in Teams or Entra ID: the same permissions and the same public endpoint are used. Microsoft must be able to reach <BASE_URL>/api/channels/teams/graph-notifications, which also receives the subscription's lifecycle notifications.

Messages are rejected as unauthorized. The application ID stored in XTM One does not match the app the Azure Bot resource uses. They must be the same registration.

The bot cannot read files sent in a chat. Confirm supportsFiles is set in the manifest for personal chats, and that admin consent was granted for the Graph permissions used to fetch files shared in channels.

A pasted run link stays a plain link. The app is not installed for the person who pasted it, or its manifest has no link message handler for your XTM One host. Update the app package from the Setup Guide template.

A pasted run card shows no details. Check that the Teams bot has its Tenant ID set in XTM One. In a conversation of more than 60 members, choose Refresh card in the message menu. Otherwise, check that the person viewing it has an XTM One account with their Teams email address.

Mentions are not detected in group chats. Teams sometimes strips the mention data from the delivered message. XTM One re-reads the message through Graph to recover it, which requires the resource-specific permissions from step 4 to be declared and consented.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Slack, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: Slack
docs.text:
Connecting Slack lets your teams talk to an agent from a channel or a direct message, and lets agents post into Slack on their own — for example to publish a triage summary or reply in an incident thread.

Read Channels and bots first if you have not already: whitelists, mention behavior, and anonymous access work the same on every platform.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need permission to create and install an app in your Slack workspace. In many workspaces this requires a Slack administrator to approve the installation.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, because Slack posts events to it.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Slack app
docs.text:
1. Go to api.slack.com/apps and select Create New App > From scratch. Give it a name and pick your workspace.
  2. Open OAuth & Permissions and add every scope from the table below under Bot Token Scopes.
  3. Open Agents & Assistants and turn on the App Agent toggle. This is what allows the typing indicator while an agent is thinking.
  4. Install the app to the workspace, then copy the Bot User OAuth Token — it starts with xoxb-.
  5. Open Basic Information and copy the Signing Secret.

docs.title: Required scopes
docs.text:
Scope Why it is needed app_mentions:read Receive messages that @mention the bot assistant:write Show the typing indicator while the agent works channels:history Read messages in public channels the bot has joined channels:join Join public channels channels:read Read basic information about public channels chat:write Send messages as the bot groups:history Read messages in private channels the bot has joined groups:read Read basic information about those private channels im:history Read direct message history im:read Read basic direct message information im:write Start a direct message with someone users:read Read workspace profiles users:read.email Match Slack users to XTM One accounts by email

Adding scopes after installation requires reinstalling the app.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the Slack card.
  2. Paste the bot token into Bot Token / Access Token.
  3. Paste the signing secret into Slack signing secret for request verification.
  4. Click Save Channel. The card now shows Connected and displays the webhook URL to use in the next step.

Save the signing secret before configuring events

Slack signs its verification request, and XTM One refuses unsigned traffic. If the signing secret is not stored yet, Slack's URL check fails with a 401. Always complete this step before step 3.

docs.title: Step 3: Subscribe to events
docs.text:
1. Back in the Slack app, open Event Subscriptions and enable events.
  2. Set the Request URL to the webhook URL shown on the Slack card — it ends with /api/channels/slack/events. Slack verifies it immediately.
  3. Under Subscribe to bot events, add the events you need:
Event What it delivers message.im Direct messages with the bot — always add this one app_mention Messages that @mention the bot in a channel message.channels Every message in the public channels the bot has joined

The usual setup is message.im plus app_mention: the bot answers direct messages and mentions. For a dedicated support channel where the bot should answer everything, use message.im plus message.channels instead.

Never subscribe to both channel events

Subscribing to message.channels and app_mention together makes Slack fire two events for the same mention, and the bot answers twice.

docs.title: Step 4: Invite the bot to channels
docs.text: Type /invite @YourBotName in each channel where the bot should be active. The bot only sees channels it belongs to.

docs.title: Step 5: Enable Slack on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable Slack:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers incoming Slack messages, and optionally restrict it to specific channels.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should post to Slack on its own, and pick the channels it may post to.
  • Adjust Allow anonymous, Allow private, and Only mention for this agent, within what the bot allows.

Channel whitelists on the bot use Slack channel IDs. The picker lists the channels the bot can see, so you rarely need to type an ID by hand.

docs.title: What the agent can do in Slack
docs.text:
When Publish is on, the agent gets Slack tools it can use during a conversation or an assignment: send a message, reply in a thread, read recent messages or a thread, list channels and users, look up a user, add or remove a reaction, pin or unpin a message, set a channel topic, and delete one of its own messages.

Replies are converted to Slack formatting automatically, so bold text and links render natively rather than as raw Markdown. Long answers are split into several messages instead of failing.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use Only when mentioned in busy team channels. The bot still follows a thread it has already joined for about 24 hours, so people do not have to mention it in every reply.
  • Prefer a dedicated agent for public channels, with a narrow set of tools and knowledge bases.
  • Set the receive whitelist before inviting the bot to many channels, so a wide invitation does not become wide exposure.
  • Tell users about /reset to start a clean conversation and /stop to mute the bot in a thread that has moved on.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Slack rejects the request URL. The signing secret is missing or wrong in XTM One. Save it on the Slack card, then retry the URL verification.

The bot ignores channel messages. Check that it was invited to the channel, that the right event is subscribed, that the channel is in the receive whitelist, and that an agent has Slack Receive enabled.

Every mention gets two answers. Both message.channels and app_mention are subscribed. Remove one.

No typing indicator. The App Agent toggle is off or assistant:write is missing. Everything else keeps working.

The bot answers but cannot identify the user. The users:read and users:read.email scopes are required to match a Slack user to an account. Without them, senders are unknown and are only served if anonymous access is allowed.

A reply lands in the channel instead of the thread. Slack refuses thread replies on some message types; the platform falls back to posting in the channel rather than losing the answer.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Microsoft Teams, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: Telegram
docs.text:
Connecting Telegram lets people chat with an agent in a private conversation or a group, and lets agents post messages, photos, and polls back. It is the quickest channel to set up: a Telegram bot is created in a few messages with @BotFather.

Read Channels and bots first for the concepts shared with the other platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need a Telegram account.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, because Telegram posts messages to it.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the bot
docs.text:
1. Open Telegram and start a conversation with @BotFather.
  2. Send /newbot and follow the prompts to choose a name and a username.
  3. Copy the token that @BotFather returns. It looks like 123456:ABC-DEF....

docs.title: Step 2: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the Telegram card.
  2. Paste the token into Bot Token / Access Token.
  3. Choose any string as a webhook secret and paste it into Webhook secret token (you define this; pass the same value as secret_token to setWebhook).
  4. Click Save Channel, and copy the webhook URL shown on the card.

docs.title: Step 3: Register the webhook with Telegram
docs.text:
Telegram has no console for this — you register the webhook with one API call, using the same secret you just saved:

curl -X POST "https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_TOKEN>/setWebhook" -d "url=<YOUR_WEBHOOK_URL>" -d "secret_token=<YOUR_SECRET>"

Replace <YOUR_TOKEN> with the bot token, <YOUR_WEBHOOK_URL> with the URL from the Telegram card — it ends with /api/channels/telegram/webhook — and <YOUR_SECRET> with the webhook secret.

The secret is what authenticates Telegram

Telegram sends the secret back with every update, and XTM One checks it. If you skip it, any request that reaches the webhook URL is accepted. If it does not match what is stored, every update is rejected.

Send a message to the bot to confirm the connection works.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable Telegram on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable Telegram:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers incoming messages.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should send messages on its own.
  • Decide whether private chats are allowed with Allow private, and whether people without an account may use the agent with Allow anonymous.

Whitelist entries are Telegram chat IDs.

docs.title: What to expect on Telegram
docs.text:
• Telegram does not expose an email address, so senders cannot be matched to an XTM One account automatically. Turn on Allow anonymous users if unknown senders should be served — the agent still receives the username and display name as context.
  • Mentions are detected, so Only when mentioned works in groups. Thread continuation does not: Telegram has no thread identifier narrow enough to track, so a mention is needed for each new question in a group where mention-only is on.
  • For the same reason, /stop is not available on Telegram. /reset works everywhere.
  • Photos, documents, audio, video, voice messages, and round video messages sent to the bot reach the agent, with their caption as the message. A file sent without a caption is still answered. Telegram lets a bot download files of up to 20 MB: a larger file is not passed on, but its caption is. Stickers are ignored.
  • By default, @BotFather hides group messages from bots. If the bot should read group conversations, send /setprivacy to @BotFather and disable privacy mode for it.

docs.title: What the agent can do in Telegram
docs.text:
When Publish is on, the agent can send a message, send a photo by URL, edit or delete one of its own messages, forward a message between chats, pin or unpin a message, create a poll, and read basic information about a chat, group, or channel.

Pinning and deleting other people's messages requires the bot to be an administrator in the chat.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep the webhook secret in place — it is the only thing authenticating incoming updates.
  • Use a dedicated agent for Telegram when the audience is external, since senders are usually anonymous.
  • In groups, prefer Only when mentioned so the bot stays quiet during normal conversation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing arrives. Check the webhook is registered by calling getWebhookInfo on the Bot API. It reports the current URL and the last delivery error.

Everything is rejected. The secret_token passed to setWebhook does not match the value stored in XTM One. Re-run setWebhook with the right secret.

The bot only sees messages that mention it. Privacy mode is on in @BotFather, or Only when mentioned is on in XTM One.

The bot cannot pin or delete. It is not an administrator in that chat.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Discord, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: WhatsApp: two backends
docs.text:
This page is about the WhatsApp integration that gives agents' tools a number to work with (see WhatsApp in Integrations), not the WhatsApp channel bot that lets people talk to an agent. Messages received on a number that a connected WhatsApp integration operates are stored for that integration's tools and agent accounts, and the channel bot does not answer them.

The WhatsApp integration (Integrations > WhatsApp) runs on one of two backends, chosen per integration with the backend field. The tools keep the same names on both; each backend adds what only it can do.

Meta Cloud API (meta_cloud_api) Linked-device gateway (linked_device_gateway) What it is The official WhatsApp Business Platform from Meta A WhatsApp number paired as a linked device to a hosted gateway (Whapi.Cloud first) Number A business number registered in WhatsApp Manager Any WhatsApp number, paired by scanning a QR code Credentials API Key = system user access token; phone_number_id (required), waba_id, app_secret, verify_token API Key = the gateway channel token; gateway_vendor (default whapi), base_url (default https://gate.whapi.cloud), webhook_secret (inbound) Inbound webhook /api/channels/whatsapp/webhook, shared, routed by phone_number_id /api/channels/whatsapp/gateway/<integration id>?token=<webhook_secret>, one per integration Send text, media, reactions Yes (free-form text needs the 24-hour window, templates outside it) Yes Templates and interactive buttons Yes No Polls No: the Cloud API cannot create a poll, and a received poll arrives as "unsupported" Yes: send_whatsapp_poll (2 to 12 options, single or multiple choice) and get_whatsapp_poll_results (votes per option and who voted, from the votes the webhook stored) Received messages list_whatsapp_conversations, read_whatsapp_messages The same tools: messages, polls and group events (member added, removed, promoted) Sent messages Not readable: the Cloud API does not list what the number sent read_whatsapp_messages also lists the messages the number sent in the conversation, flagged outgoing, with their message id (read live from the gateway) Edit or delete a sent message No Yes: edit_whatsapp_message replaces the text of a text message the number sent, within WhatsApp's 15-minute edit window (the recipient sees it marked Edited; past the window, on a message the number did not send or on a media message it is refused with the reason, nothing changed); delete_whatsapp_message deletes a message for everyone. send_whatsapp_message and send_whatsapp_media answer the message id to pass Groups Only groups the business creates; members join by invite link Any group the paired number is in, including existing ones (list_whatsapp_groups, get_whatsapp_group, send to ...@g.us) Pairing None get_whatsapp_pairing_status (connected, qr, banned, sync_error, starting) and get_whatsapp_pairing_qr (the QR code as an image)

Sending tools, edit, delete and poll creation are write tools and follow the approval rules of every write; reads (groups, poll results, pairing status) are read-only. Message bodies are never logged above debug level.

docs.title: Terms of service: read this before choosing the gateway
docs.text:
A linked-device gateway is not the official WhatsApp Business Platform. It drives a normal WhatsApp account the way WhatsApp Web does. WhatsApp's terms do not allow automated or bulk use of a consumer account, and WhatsApp can ban the paired number, temporarily or for good, without notice.

  • Use a dedicated number for the gateway, never a person's own number.
  • Keep the volume human: no bulk messages, no messages to people who did not expect them.
  • The platform paces every send on the gateway: at most 20 messages per minute per integration and 6 per minute per chat (texts, media and polls together), a random pause of 0.4 to 1.6 seconds before each send, and the typing indicator before a text for about one second per 12 characters (at most 8 seconds). A send over a limit is refused with the seconds to wait; nothing is sent.
  • If the pairing status turns banned, pair another dedicated number; the ban is WhatsApp's decision and the platform cannot lift it.

Choose the Meta Cloud API when you do not need polls or existing groups.

docs.title: Set up the linked-device gateway (Whapi.Cloud)
docs.text:
1. Create a Whapi.Cloud account and a channel; copy its channel token.
  2. In XTM One, Integrations > WhatsApp, set backend to linked_device_gateway, paste the channel token into API Key, leave base_url empty for https://gate.whapi.cloud.
  3. Test Connection reads the channel's health.
  4. Pair the dedicated number: open the integration, tab Configuration, card WhatsApp pairing. While the number is not paired the card shows the gateway's login QR and follows it as it rotates; on the phone open WhatsApp > Settings > Linked devices > Link a device and scan it. The badge turns Paired once linked. The card reads the same state as the agent tools get_whatsapp_pairing_status and get_whatsapp_pairing_qr (connected, qr, starting, sync_error, banned, unknown), which an agent bound to the integration can still run. The QR is shown only to a user who can manage the integration.
  5. Add the number to the groups it must work in, from the phone.
  6. Inbound: set webhook_secret on the integration to a long random value, then in the Whapi.Cloud channel settings > Webhooks add the URL the WhatsApp pairing card shows under Gateway webhook URL (copy button; visible only to a user who can manage the integration, since it carries the secret), that is https://<your XTM One>/api/channels/whatsapp/gateway/<integration id>?token=<webhook_secret> with the events messages (POST and PATCH) and groups. A delivery without the secret, or with a wrong one, is refused (401); an integration without a secret refuses every delivery. The URL answers 404 only when the integration id is unknown, is not a whatsapp integration or is not on backend = linked_device_gateway; the server log then names which ("WhatsApp gateway webhook: no gateway integration : "). Opening the URL in a browser (GET) answers 405 "POST only": that is expected.

docs.title: What the gateway webhook stores
docs.text:
• Received messages (text, link previews, media captions) in the same store as the Meta backend, kept inbound_retention_days (30 by default). What the number sends to others is not stored; what it writes in its own "message yourself" chat is (the self-chat).
  • The self-chat as an instruction channel (off by default): set the extra field self_chat_agent_id to an agent that has an enabled WhatsApp agent account on this integration. Each message the owner writes in the self-chat then starts one turn of that agent, as the integration's owner (the XTM One user who owns the integration, never read from the message), and the reply is posted in the same self-chat. No other chat ever reaches that route: contacts and groups stay data for list_whatsapp_conversations / read_whatsapp_messages, answered only by the account's own rules. The agent's replies echoed back in the self-chat are recognised by message id and never start a turn. An integration without an active owner does not route its self-chat.
  • Voice notes and audio messages (any chat) are downloaded from the gateway and transcribed with the speech-to-text provider of the integration's owner (language detected), then stored as [voice note, 0:42, transcribed, heard in french] ..., the language the model heard named so a switch is never silent. The transcript is judged before it is trusted (both backends): a note whose audio was cut short, that holds far too few words for its length (under 60 a minute past 30 s), or whose speech was mostly decoded unsure (Whisper's own confidence thresholds per segment) is stored as [voice note, 0:56, heard in french: transcription low confidence: <reason>], never as plausible but doubtful text; segments the model writes over silence are dropped. A failed download or transcription is stored as [voice note, 0:42: transcription failed: <reason>], never as an empty message. The audio is held in memory for the transcription only, never kept by the platform; the stored line is followed by [audio of this voice note: media id <id>, download_whatsapp_media fetches it as a file], so an agent can fetch the raw audio from the gateway (as long as the gateway keeps it) and hear it again, for example after a low-confidence transcript. In the self-chat the transcript is the turn's input; elsewhere it is data read by read_whatsapp_messages.
  • A poll, in words (question and options), and its tally: per option, its id and its voters. A new vote replaces the voter's previous choice; get_whatsapp_poll_results answers from the store and asks the gateway only for a poll the webhook never saw.
  • Group events, in words: members added, removed, joined, left, promoted or demoted.

The WhatsApp agent accounts on the integration hear every newly stored message, on both backends.

docs.title: Voice notes on the Meta Cloud API backend
docs.text: A voice note or audio message received on the Meta Cloud API number is transcribed the same way before it is stored: downloaded with the integration's access token (sent only to a Meta host), transcribed with the speech-to-text provider of the integration's owner (language detected), and stored as [voice note, 0:20, transcribed] ... after its caption, if any. A failed download or transcription, or no speech-to-text provider for the owner, is stored as [voice note: transcription failed: <reason>]. read_whatsapp_messages and the WhatsApp agent accounts read the transcript (as data); the audio is not kept by the platform and the transcript is not logged. The stored line names the note's media id, which download_whatsapp_media fetches from Meta as a file of the conversation (as long as Meta keeps the media) for a re-transcription on demand. Voice notes sent to the whatsapp_bot channel bot (a number no integration owns) follow the channel bot's file handling instead (see the WhatsApp channel page).

docs.title: WhatsApp
docs.text:
Connecting WhatsApp lets people reach an agent from a normal WhatsApp conversation, and lets agents send messages, templates, and reactions back. It runs on the WhatsApp Business Cloud API from Meta.

Read Channels and bots first for the concepts shared with the other platforms.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need a Meta developer account and a WhatsApp Business account with a phone number registered for the Cloud API.
  • You need administrator rights in XTM One.
  • The platform must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, because Meta posts messages to it.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Meta app
docs.text:
1. Go to developers.facebook.com > My Apps > Create App and choose the business type.
  2. Add the WhatsApp product to the app.
  3. Open WhatsApp > API Setup and copy the Phone Number ID.
  4. Generate a permanent access token. The temporary token shown on that page expires after 24 hours and is only useful for a first test.

The app needs the whatsapp_business_messaging permission to send and receive messages, and whatsapp_business_management to manage numbers and templates.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect the bot in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Channels & Bots and click Configure on the WhatsApp card.
  2. Paste the access token into Bot Token / Access Token.
  3. Paste the phone number ID into WhatsApp Business phone number ID.
  4. Choose any string as the verify token and paste it into Webhook verification token (you define this). You will enter the same value in Meta.
  5. Optionally paste your Meta app secret into Meta app secret. It is worth doing: it enables signature verification, so the platform can confirm every incoming request really comes from Meta.
  6. Click Save Channel, and copy the webhook URL shown on the card.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the webhook in Meta
docs.text:
1. In the Meta app, go to WhatsApp > Configuration > Webhook.
  2. Set the callback URL to the webhook URL from the WhatsApp card — it ends with /api/channels/whatsapp/webhook.
  3. Enter exactly the same verify token you saved in XTM One.
  4. Subscribe to the messages webhook field.

Meta verifies the URL immediately, so save the credentials in XTM One before this step.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable WhatsApp on an agent
docs.text:
Open the agent, go to Configuration > Channels & Bots, and enable WhatsApp:

  • Turn on Receive so the agent answers incoming messages.
  • Turn on Publish if the agent should send messages on its own.
  • Decide whether direct conversations are allowed with Allow private, and whether people without an account may use the agent with Allow anonymous.

Whitelist entries are phone numbers for direct conversations and group identifiers for groups.

docs.title: What to expect on WhatsApp
docs.text:
WhatsApp behaves differently from the other channels in three ways.

  • No identity. WhatsApp does not expose an email address, so senders cannot be matched to an account automatically. Either turn on Allow anonymous users, which passes the contact name and number to the agent as context, or expect unknown senders to be asked to register.
  • No mentions. The Cloud API does not report structured @mentions, so Only when mentioned cannot work here. Leave it off for WhatsApp, or the bot stays silent in groups. Direct conversations are unaffected. For the same reason, /stop mutes a group for the full seven days — the mute is normally lifted by mentioning the bot again, which WhatsApp cannot signal.
  • The 24-hour window. Meta only allows free-form messages within 24 hours of the person's last message. Outside that window, the agent must use a pre-approved template, configured in Meta Business Manager.

There is also no typing indicator on WhatsApp, so a long answer arrives with no visible activity beforehand.

Photos, documents, audio, voice notes, and videos sent to the bot reach the agent as files of the conversation, with their caption as the message; a file sent without a caption is still answered. A file larger than the platform's 40 MB upload limit is not passed on, but its caption is. Stickers are ignored.

docs.title: What the agent can do in WhatsApp
docs.text: When Publish is on, the agent can send a text message, send an approved template, mark a message as read, and react to a message with an emoji.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated agent for WhatsApp with a narrow tool set, since senders are usually anonymous.
  • Always set the app secret. Without it, the webhook accepts any request that reaches the URL.
  • Prepare and approve templates in Meta Business Manager before relying on the agent to start conversations.
  • In groups, use the group whitelist rather than mention filtering, which WhatsApp cannot support.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Meta rejects the callback URL. The verify token does not match, or the credentials were not saved in XTM One first. The two values must be identical.

Messages arrive but nothing happens. Check that the messages field is subscribed, that an agent has WhatsApp Receive enabled, and that the group or number is in the receive whitelist if one is set.

The bot ignores group messages. Either Only when mentioned is on somewhere — it can never be satisfied on WhatsApp — or the group is not whitelisted.

Sending fails outside a conversation. The 24-hour window has closed. Use a template message instead.

Users are told to register. Anonymous access is off and WhatsApp cannot identify the sender. Turn on Allow anonymous users on the bot and on the agent if that traffic should be served.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Connect another platform, such as Telegram, or review how agents use channels in Agents.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
XTM One supports local accounts and single sign-on (SSO) via OIDC and SAML 2.0. You configure sign-in methods from Settings → Security → Authentication in the UI (admin-only).

A few environment variables also shape authentication. The session and link lifetimes also have a field in Settings → Security → Security options; when you set the variable, it wins and locks that field.

Variable Default What it sets ADMIN_EMAIL, ADMIN_PASSWORD admin@filigran.io, none The bootstrap administrator (see Local accounts) JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES, SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MINUTES 10080, 0 Session lifetime and idle timeout (see Session lifetime and idle timeout) INVITATION_EXPIRE_HOURS 168 How long an invitation link stays valid (1 to 720 hours) PASSWORD_RESET_EXPIRE_HOURS 24 How long a password reset link stays valid (1 to 720 hours) SMTP_* none The mail server that sends invitations and password reset links (see Password reset and email) TERMS_OF_USE_ENABLED, TERMS_OF_USE_VERSION, TERMS_OF_USE_URL, TERMS_OF_USE_EXEMPT_EMAILS see Terms of Use acceptance The Terms of Use gate XTM_HUB_ADMIN_GROUP, PLATFORM_ID none The XTM Hub entitlement gate PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN none Trust between XTM One and OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ (see XTM Suite integration)

The full list is in Configuration.

The first account is always an admin

Whichever way the very first account is created — local registration, admin bootstrap, or the first SSO login — it is granted the admin role. Every later account defaults to the standard user role unless promoted.

docs.title: Local accounts
docs.text:
By default, users authenticate with email and password.

The bootstrap admin account (ADMIN_EMAIL / ADMIN_PASSWORD) is created or reset from environment variables on every startup. Each startup also makes it an administrator again and re-enables it if it was disabled, so it stays a way back into the platform. If you change that password in the UI, the next restart resets it back to the .env value — keep them in sync.

A startup does not touch the account's two-factor enrollment: an administrator who lost their authenticator app signs in with a recovery code, or another administrator resets it (see If a user loses their device and their codes).

Local authentication is governed by two toggles under Settings → Security → Authentication:

  • Local Authentication (default: enabled) — allows email/password sign-in. When disabled, local login and local registration are blocked and users must sign in through SSO (an "SSO-only" deployment). The very first account can always be created, even while this is off, so you are never locked out.
  • Local Registration (default: disabled) — lets users self-register with email and password. When disabled, only admins can create accounts.

docs.title: Restricting new accounts by email domain
docs.text:
Allowed email domains (comma-separated; empty means all domains are allowed) restricts who gets a new account: local registration refuses an email address outside the list, and so does SSO account creation, OIDC and SAML alike (see On-the-fly user creation). The domain is what follows the last @ of the address, compared case-insensitively and exactly: example.com does not admit eu.example.com. The field has its own New accounts section in the settings form, so it stays editable while local authentication is off.

Only account creation is restricted. An account that already exists keeps signing in whatever its domain, an SSO identity is still linked by email to an existing account, and an invitation still registers its invitee.

Changed behaviour. The list used to restrict local registration only, and SSO created an account for any email address the identity provider asserted. An instance that set allowed domains while SSO created accounts outside them now refuses those new accounts (?sso_error=not_provisioned, below).

The domain comes from the identity provider

For an SSO sign-in, the domain is read from the email address the identity provider asserts, so the restriction is only as reliable as that claim. With a multi-tenant provider, make sure it asserts verified addresses only.

docs.title: Admin-managed accounts
docs.text:
Admins manage accounts from the Users page (admin-only). Two mechanisms are available:

  • Create a user directly — add an account and set its role from Users → New user.
  • Send an invitation link — from Users → Invite user, generate a single-use link bound to a specific email address and role. The invitee sets their own password by opening the link.
  • Let a registered product invite — when an XTM One administrator adds someone with no XTM One account in a registered product (OpenCRQ), XTM One sends that person an invitation to create their account, with the user role. Once registered, they continue to the product, on the page they were added to. A pending invitation for the same email is sent again under a new link rather than doubled: the earlier link stops working. Someone who already has an account gets an email telling them they have access instead, and a deactivated account is never invited.

How invitation links work

Each invitation is bound to one email address, carries the role you choose, and can be used once. The link expires after a configurable window (default 7 days, set with INVITATION_EXPIRE_HOURS, capped at 30 days). Invitations bypass the Local Registration and Allowed-domains settings, so you can onboard a specific person without opening self-registration to everyone. The link is sent by email, so inviting someone from the UI needs SMTP.

The day-to-day tasks (roles, disabling an account, setting a password, impersonation, groups) are described in Users and groups.

docs.title: Password reset and email
docs.text:
A local account can get a single-use link to choose a new password in two ways:

  • Self-service. Forgot password? on the sign-in page asks for an email address. If an active account with a local password exists for it, a reset link is emailed. The page answers the same way whether the account exists or not.
  • From an administrator. An administrator sends a reset link from the user's page, or sets a new password directly (see Users and groups).

The link is valid for PASSWORD_RESET_EXPIRE_HOURS (24 hours by default) and works once. A user who only signs in through SSO has no local password and gets no reset link: their identity provider manages their password.

Both the reset links and the invitation links go out by email, through the mail server set by the SMTP_* variables (see Configuration). Without SMTP_HOSTNAME:

  • a self-service request sends nothing and the platform logs a warning; the person sees the usual confirmation and no email arrives;
  • an administrator who sends a reset link or an invitation from the UI gets an error saying email delivery is not configured. Setting a password directly from the user's page still works.

Set the sender name

SMTP_FROM_NAME is the display name of the emails. Set it to your platform's name (.env.sample uses XTM One).

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
People and automations can also reach the API with a personal API key (fcp-…) instead of a web session. A key acts as the person who created it, within the scopes, expiry and limits set on it. Users create their keys in My profile; administrators review every key and set the maximum lifetime in Settings. ADMIN_TOKEN provisions a key for the bootstrap administrator from the environment (see Configuration).

An API key is a machine credential: it is not a web session, so the two-factor step, the session lifetime, the idle timeout and the Terms of Use gate below do not apply to it.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (TOTP)
docs.text:
Any user can add a second factor: a six-digit code from an authenticator app, entered after the first factor on every sign-in. It is enabled per user from Profile → Two-factor — there is nothing to configure at deployment level and no environment variable to set.

The factor is XTM One's own, and it applies whichever way the user signs in — local password, OIDC, or SAML. It is not delegated to the identity provider. That is deliberate: many deployments federate to a provider whose MFA policy they do not control (a customer tenant, a partner IdP, a legacy directory), and being able to enforce a second factor at the application boundary is the point. Where the IdP already enforces one, the two simply stack, and users are free not to enroll.

Any RFC 6238 authenticator app works, including Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, KeePassXC, 1Password, Bitwarden, Aegis and FreeOTP. XTM One uses the parameters those apps assume by default (SHA-1, 6 digits, 30-second period), so enrollment is a QR scan with no per-app tuning. The QR is rendered by your own server, so enrollment works on air-gapped deployments — no third-party service is contacted.

Enrollment is two-phase on purpose: scanning the QR is not enough, the user must type a code back to prove the app was enrolled correctly. Until they do, nothing changes about how they sign in — closing the tab halfway cannot lock anyone out.

docs.title: Recovery codes
docs.text: Enabling two-factor issues 10 single-use recovery codes, displayed once and never again. Each one signs the user in once, in place of the app, if they lose their device. Users can generate a fresh set (invalidating the old one) from their profile, which requires a current code from the app.

docs.title: If a user loses their device and their codes
docs.text:
An admin can clear the enrollment from the user's detail page (Users → select the user → Two-factor → Reset two-factor). The account then signs in with its password alone until the user enrolls a new device. The action is audited.

Administrators never see the secret

The TOTP secret is encrypted at rest with the platform SECRET_KEY, and recovery codes are stored hashed. Neither can be read back by anyone, including admins — resetting is the only recovery path, and it deliberately forces a fresh enrollment.

Rotating SECRET_KEY invalidates every enrollment

The encryption key for stored secrets is derived from SECRET_KEY. Changing it leaves existing enrollments unreadable: affected users can still sign in with a recovery code, and admins can reset their enrollment, but their authenticator app stops working.

docs.title: How it works with SSO
docs.text:
After a successful OIDC or SAML assertion, an enrolled user is returned to the sign-in page for the code step instead of being signed in. No session token is issued until the code is verified, so the extra factor cannot be skipped by replaying the callback URL.

An SSO-only user disables their factor with a code alone — they have no XTM One password to confirm with. Accounts that do hold a local password are asked for both.

Until the code is accepted, the audit log records the event as "Authenticated via OIDC, awaiting second factor", not as a completed login. The completed login is recorded separately, and names the provider it came through.

Local authentication can stay disabled

Two-factor does not require enabling local passwords. An SSO-only deployment (Local Authentication off) can enroll every user in an authenticator app and keep the IdP as the sole first factor.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Two-factor applies to interactive sign-in — local, OIDC, and SAML alike.

That includes the MCP OAuth consent page an MCP client opens to connect to XTM One: after the email and password, the page asks for the code, and the client receives no token until the code is accepted. A failed code there is recorded like one at sign-in (action login), with mcp-oauth as its context.

API keys (fcp-…), channel bots and cross-platform tokens from OpenCTI/OpenAEV are unaffected: they are machine credentials with nowhere to prompt for a code.

Enabling, disabling, recovery-code use and failed verifications are all recorded in the audit log, under the mfa entity type. Each entry is attributed to the flow it came from via its action — login, enable, disable, or update (regenerating recovery codes) — so the audit filters separate a failed code at sign-in from a mistyped one while turning the factor off.

That separation is what makes the log useful for detection: a run of failed second factors with action login and no matching successful login is the signal that someone holds a password but not the device.

docs.title: OIDC (OpenID Connect)
docs.text: Use OIDC to integrate with identity providers such as Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Okta, Google Workspace, or Keycloak. OIDC uses the Authorization Code flow.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A registered OAuth 2.0 / OIDC application in your IdP
  • A Client ID and Client Secret
  • Either a Discovery URL (the .well-known/openid-configuration endpoint — recommended) or the individual authorization, token, and userinfo endpoint URLs
  • The Redirect URI registered in your IdP: {BASE_URL}/api/auth/oidc/callback

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configure OIDC from Settings → Security → Authentication. The fields are:

Field Notes Display Name Label shown on the sign-in button (e.g. "Microsoft") Discovery URL Recommended — auto-resolves the other endpoints. Use the provider's /.well-known/openid-configuration URL, not the issuer URL on its own (for Keycloak, https://<host>/realms/<realm>/.well-known/openid-configuration). Test Connection fetches it and reports the status or the missing key; saving never depends on the result. The server keeps the fetched document for five minutes and drops it when you save Client ID / Client Secret From your IdP application; stored encrypted Scopes Default openid email profile Manual endpoint URLs Optional — set the authorization, token, and userinfo URLs directly if you are not using discovery

The exact Redirect URI to register in your IdP is displayed in the configuration panel.

docs.title: User provisioning
docs.text:
Users are created automatically on first login. XTM One matches the identity in this order:

  1. By the SSO subject (sub) of a previously linked account.
  2. Otherwise by email — if a local (or other) account with the same email exists, it is linked to the OIDC identity.
  3. Otherwise a new account is created, unless on-the-fly user creation is off or the email's domain is not one of the allowed email domains.

The IdP must return an email claim; a login with no email is rejected. The user's name and job title are updated from the IdP claims on each login.

docs.title: Deactivated accounts
docs.text: If step 1 or 2 resolves the identity to an account an administrator has deactivated (Disable on the user's page), the sign-in is refused before anything on the account changes: no profile update, no SSO link, no role change, and no new account is created alongside it. No session is issued; the person returns to the login page with ?sso_error=account_deactivated, and the refusal is written to the audit log as login_refused. Re-enabling the account is the only way back; the next sign-in then completes as usual.

docs.title: On-the-fly user creation
docs.text:
An On-the-fly user creation toggle (default: on) controls step 3 above. When disabled, only pre-provisioned accounts can sign in via OIDC: an identity that matches no existing account (by SSO subject or email) is refused before any account is created, and the person is sent back to the login page with a readable message (?sso_error=not_provisioned). Steps 1 and 2 are unaffected — existing accounts keep signing in and linking by email as before.

While it is on, the allowed email domains, when set, restrict it: an identity whose email domain is not in the list is refused the same way, with the same ?sso_error=not_provisioned, before any account is created.

Use this when account creation must go through an explicit administrative step (invitations, an IdP-side approval flow, or manual provisioning) rather than being implied by IdP access.

docs.title: Automatically admin users
docs.text: An optional Automatically admin users toggle (default: off) grants the admin role to anyone who signs in via OIDC, at every sign-in, existing accounts included: despite its stored name (oidc_auto_admin_new_users), it is not limited to new accounts, and the allowed email domains do not narrow it. It is promote-only — it never demotes existing admins, and turning it off later does not strip roles already granted. OIDC does not support group mapping; use SAML if you need group-driven roles.

docs.title: When sign-in fails
docs.text:
Changed behaviour. A failed or abandoned OIDC sign-in used to leave the browser on a raw JSON error — an API error body, or a validation error about a missing code parameter. It now returns to the login page with a readable message and a marker in the URL:

?sso_error= When What the person sees cancelled They declined the consent screen at the identity provider Sign-in was cancelled; try again when ready not_authorised The XTM Hub entitlement gate declined them (see below) Their account is not authorised for this instance not_provisioned No account matches their identity and none is created for it: on-the-fly user creation is disabled, or their email domain is not one of the allowed email domains No account exists; ask an administrator to create one first account_deactivated Their identity matches an account an administrator deactivated (see above) The account has been deactivated; contact an administrator misconfigured The Discovery URL (or the manual endpoints) gave no usable endpoint: another error status (not 408, 429 or 5xx), a redirect loop, a body that is not a discovery document, or a missing or blank authorization or token endpoint. The server log names the URL, the status and the keys received Single sign-on is not configured correctly; contact your administrator failed Any other provider error, a malformed callback, or the provider being unreachable, slow or rate-limiting (a connection error, a timeout, 408, 429 or 5xx) while its discovery document is fetched Single sign-on failed; contact your administrator

This applies to every OIDC deployment, whether or not the XTM Hub gate below is configured. Nothing about who can sign in changes — only how a failure is presented.

The message is deliberately vague in every case. The specifics — the provider's error code and description, or the reason an account was not entitled — are written to the server log, because someone who has not signed in should not be able to read your identity provider's configuration back out of an error page. The marker is scrubbed from the URL once shown, so a reload does not re-accuse someone who has since signed in successfully.

docs.title: XTM Hub entitlement gate
docs.text:
If this instance is federated through XTM Hub, the Hub can decide which XTM One instances each person may reach, and whether they are an administrator on each one. Set XTM_HUB_ADMIN_GROUP to switch it on — see Configuration. The gate identifies this instance by its PLATFORM_ID, which must be set too.

It is off unless configured, and when on it takes precedence over Automatically admin users above: that toggle only promotes, while the Hub also demotes.

Two consequences are worth knowing before you enable it:

  • A person the Hub has not entitled here is refused before an account is created, so no dormant accounts accumulate — but an existing user who loses their entitlement is also refused on their next sign-in.
  • Administrator is removed when the Hub stops asserting it. The ADMIN_EMAIL account is never demoted for exactly this reason, and local sign-in remains available as a recovery path if the gate is misconfigured.
  • Every role change the Hub causes is written to the audit log, in the same shape as one made from the admin UI, so "who became an administrator, and when" has one answer regardless of who decided it.

docs.title: SAML 2.0
docs.text: Use SAML for enterprise identity providers that require SAML assertions. XTM One acts as the Service Provider in an SP-initiated flow.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Your IdP metadata URL (or XML)
  • The ACS (Assertion Consumer Service) URL: {BASE_URL}/api/auth/saml/acs
  • The Entity ID / SP metadata URL: {BASE_URL}/api/auth/saml/metadata

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configure SAML from Settings → Security → Authentication. The fields are:

Field Notes Display Name Label shown on the sign-in button (e.g. "Corporate SSO") IdP Metadata URL Your identity provider's federation metadata SP Entity ID Optional — leave empty to use the metadata URL

docs.title: User provisioning
docs.text:
Users are created automatically on first login, matched by email in the same order as OIDC (SSO subject, then email linking, then create).

SAML has the same On-the-fly user creation toggle as OIDC (default: on), restricted the same way by the allowed email domains. When it is disabled, or when the email's domain is not an allowed one, an assertion that matches no existing account is refused before any account is created or any group synced, and the browser returns to the login page with ?sso_error=not_provisioned.

A deactivated account is refused exactly as with OIDC (?sso_error=account_deactivated, audited as login_refused), before its group memberships are synced: they stay as they were until the account is re-enabled and signs in again.

docs.title: Automatically admin users
docs.text: Like OIDC, SAML has an Automatically admin users toggle (default: off) that grants the admin role at every SAML sign-in, existing accounts included (saml_auto_admin_new_users). It is promote-only.

docs.title: Group mapping
docs.text:
SAML supports automatic group mapping from IdP group claims (enabled by default). XTM One reads groups from the common claim URIs used by Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, ADFS, and generic SAML providers.

  • Groups from the assertion are synced on every login: the user is added to matching XTM One groups and removed from groups no longer present in the assertion.
  • With Auto-create groups enabled (default), groups in the assertion that do not yet exist in XTM One are created automatically.

Both settings live under the SAML section of Settings → Security → Authentication. See Groups for how groups control entity sharing.

The mapping manages only the memberships it created: it never removes someone from a group they joined by hand, through SCIM, or through Auto join, which adds every single sign-on user (OIDC or SAML) to the groups that have it on, at every sign-in.

docs.title: Session lifetime and idle timeout
docs.text:
A sign-in - local, OIDC, SAML, or the XTM One Desktop sign-in through the browser - opens a web session. Two settings bound it, in Settings → Security → Security options (section Authentication), or with their environment variable, which then wins and locks the field:

Field Variable Default What it does Absolute session lifetime (minutes) JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES 10080 (7 days) The session ends this long after the sign-in, even while it is in use. Idle session timeout (minutes) SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MINUTES 0 (off) The session ends after this many minutes without activity. Activity extends it, never past the absolute lifetime. 0 turns it off; otherwise 5 minutes at least (a smaller variable value is read as 5).

A change applies without a restart, on every replica within 5 seconds, and is recorded in the audit log:

  • Lowering the lifetime ends the sessions already older than the new value, on their next request. Raising it applies from the next sign-in: a session keeps the expiry it was signed in with, and a token issued for it later (a password change, an impersonation, XTM One Desktop) never outlasts it.
  • Turning the idle timeout on applies to the sessions already open. A session with no recorded activity starts counting from its next request, so nobody is signed out the moment it is turned on.
  • Activity is what the person does: clicking, typing, scrolling with the wheel or touch, or coming back to the tab. What the web app does on its own - refreshing a page, the activity stream, an answer streaming into the chat, keepalives - is not activity, so a tab left open goes idle. A minute before an idle sign-out the web app asks Are you still there?; any input keeps the session.
  • The lifetime counts from the sign-in, not from the last token. Changing a password, impersonating a user (the impersonation ends with the administrator's own session, and they share one idle deadline) or signing in to XTM One Desktop through the browser never extends it.

XTM One Desktop follows the same rules: it keeps the session it was signed in with in the machine's OS keychain, so an update or a restart of the app does not sign the person out, and the session still ends with its lifetime or its idle timeout.

When a session ends, every surface refuses it - the API with a 401 whose detail.code is session_expired, and a stream still open (the chat, the activity stream) with a session_expired event - and the web app signs out and returns to the sign-in page, saying why. SSO users sign in again through their identity provider by choosing it there: the web app never opens the identity provider on its own, so an unattended browser is not signed back in. After signing in, the person lands on the page they were on.

The idle timeout needs Redis

The last activity of each session is kept in Redis. While Redis cannot be reached, sessions are not ended for inactivity (the absolute lifetime, carried by the session token, still ends them): refusing every session instead would sign everyone out, and refuse every sign-in, for as long as Redis is down. After a failed read, each replica leaves Redis aside for 30 seconds before trying again, so requests are not held up while it does not answer. A warning is logged, and the Security Audit reports the idle timeout as not enforced (infrastructure.session_idle_timeout_unenforced).

Neither setting applies to API keys (fcp-…), the platform MCP key, MCP OAuth tokens or the tokens OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ sign users in with: they are not web sessions. The Security Audit reports both settings (controls authentication.session_lifetime, hardened at a day or less, and authentication.session_idle_timeout, hardened at 5 to 30 minutes, within the NIST SP 800-63B AAL2 bound).

docs.title: XTM One Desktop sign-in through the browser
docs.text:
XTM One Desktop shows the web app in its own window. Email and password work there; single sign-on runs in the system browser instead, because identity providers often refuse or limit embedded windows. There is nothing to configure.

  1. In the Desktop app, the person picks a single sign-on provider. The app shows Continue in your browser and opens the system browser on that provider.
  2. The person signs in there, then enters their XTM One two-factor code if they enrolled one.
  3. The browser asks Sign in to XTM One Desktop?, naming the machine that asked and who enrolled it. Yes, sign me in there hands the session to the app; Not my machine refuses the request and records the refusal in the audit log.
  4. The app signs in on its own. The browser tab keeps no session.

A request expires after 5 minutes. Only the person who enrolled the machine can confirm a sign-in on it; a company-managed machine accepts any account. A browser session opened through an impersonation or an API key cannot confirm. The confirmed sign-in is recorded in the audit log. The Desktop session follows the session lifetime and idle timeout below.

This requires the runner subsystem, which is on by default (RUNNERS_ENABLED, see Configuration).

docs.title: Signing in to another product through XTM One (OpenID Connect)
docs.text:
Another product (OpenCRQ first) can sign its users in through XTM One with OpenID Connect, on the platform's OAuth server: the person is sent to the XTM One sign-in page (with whatever method is configured above, two-factor included), or reuses the XTM One session already open in the browser, and comes straight back to it signed in. There is no consent page: the products and XTM One are one platform. Other clients (MCP clients, dynamic registration) keep it. The registration token is what makes a product trusted: whoever holds PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN can register a platform with a sign-in client on an origin of their choice, and receive the ID token (email, name, title, role, whether it is the ADMIN_EMAIL account) of any XTM One user who opens one of their links, without a click. The token already grants more, since a registered platform's URL is trusted to sign users in to XTM One by email, so keep it as secret as an administrator credential and set it only on the products you run. A product registered with a loopback platform_url (a development setup) has loopback callbacks: any local program able to open the browser on the authorization URL then completes a sign-in without a click, so keep loopback product URLs to development machines.

  • Discovery: /.well-known/openid-configuration (under a URL path prefix, also /.well-known/openid-configuration/<prefix> at the host root, as for the OAuth documents).
  • Client: the product gets its sign-in client from platform registration (POST /api/v1/platform/register, authenticated by PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN): it sends its callback URLs in sign_in_redirect_uris (on its own platform_url origin, HTTPS or loopback) and the answer carries its sign_in_client_id (xtm-platform-<identifier>, a public client: PKCE S256, no secret). Each registration keeps the client in step: an empty list removes it, an absent field changes nothing. Unregistering the platform, or an administrator purging its registration, removes it too, and the client signs nobody in while its registration is not active. The published default token, which anyone knows, neither creates nor removes it. Clients made through dynamic registration (/mcp/oauth/register, open to anyone) get no OpenID Connect scope.
  • Scopes and claims: openid (always: iss, sub = the XTM One user id, stable, aud = the client id, iat, exp 10 minutes, nonce), email (email), profile (name, and xtm_title: the person's title, null when they have none), xtm_role (xtm_role: admin or user, and xtm_super_admin: true for the ADMIN_EMAIL account only, false for everyone else). Only the scopes both asked and registered are granted; the token response returns them in scope.
  • ID token: returned by the token endpoint beside the access token, signed EdDSA with the platform key published at /xtm/auth/jwks. A product's sign-in client needs the ID token only: it gets no refresh token, and its access token is bound to the client (aud = the client id), so no MCP endpoint accepts it. Authorizations without consent are audited with "consent": false. An administrator impersonating a user is not signed in to products. A product must check state and nonce, since any page can start a sign-in that completes without a click; prompt and max_age are not supported. If the sign-in fails, the page offers to go back to the product, which then receives error=access_denied, and to try again when that can help (not while impersonating, nor when the product's sign-in is no longer available).
  • Sign-in: without an XTM One session in the browser, the person goes through the XTM One sign-in page (any method above) and comes back; the XTM One session then also serves the next product.
  • A client not registered for openid sees no change.

docs.title: Terms of Use acceptance
docs.text:
The Terms of Use are accepted once for the whole platform, by an administrator on behalf of the organization, not by each user.

Until they are accepted, every person who signs in — with any method above — sees a blocking Terms of Use screen and cannot reach any part of the UI:

  • An administrator reads the document (Read the Terms of Use), turns on I have read and accept the Terms of Use on behalf of my organization. and selects Accept and continue. Decline and sign out leaves the platform unaccepted.
  • Anyone else is told that an administrator must accept the Terms of Use first, and can only sign out.

One acceptance opens the platform for everyone. It is recorded with the version, the date and the accepting administrator, and written to the audit log (action accept, entity type terms_of_use). The gate is enforced on the API too, so it cannot be skipped by calling the backend directly. It applies to web sessions only: API keys, channel bots and the tokens OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ sign users in with are never gated.

The gate only applies where Agentic AI is licensed. Community Edition deployments never see it. Switching AI off does not remove it.

Variable Default Purpose TERMS_OF_USE_ENABLED true Set to false to disable the gate entirely — for deployments that handle Terms of Use acceptance outside the product. TERMS_OF_USE_VERSION 2026-07-14 Identifier of the published document. An empty value disables the gate. TERMS_OF_USE_URL https://filigran.io/ai-terms/ Where the document is published. The screen links to it; it is not embedded. TERMS_OF_USE_EXEMPT_EMAILS none Comma-separated emails the gate never applies to, matched exactly and case-insensitively. For the vendor accounts that operate a SaaS instance: they sign in from the first day of the deployment without accepting the Terms of Use on the customer's behalf. The platform stays unaccepted for everyone else until a customer administrator accepts. An exempt address cannot be taken by self-registration or by a user changing their own email; an administrator, an invitation or SSO creates the account.

Changing the version re-prompts everyone

The platform is gated whenever its recorded acceptance does not match TERMS_OF_USE_VERSION. Bumping it is how you roll out a revised document: the screen comes back for everyone (Updated Terms of Use) until an administrator accepts the new version. There is no admin UI toggle — a revision is a deliberate configuration change.

docs.title: Access provisioning summary
docs.text: Method How users are created Where Admin creates a user Admin adds an account and sets its role Users → New user Admin invitation link Single-use, email-bound link the invitee opens to set a password Users → Invite user Self-registration Users register with email and password (optionally domain-restricted) Sign-in page, when Local Registration is enabled SSO auto-provisioning Users are created on first OIDC or SAML login (optionally domain-restricted), linked by email On first SSO login SCIM provisioning An identity provider (Microsoft Entra) creates, updates and deactivates accounts; see Provisioning with SCIM Settings → Access and security → Provisioning

docs.title: Account hardening summary
docs.text: Hardening What it adds Where Two-factor (TOTP) A six-digit code from an authenticator app, required after the password Profile → Two-factor (per user) Admin reset of two-factor Clears an enrollment for a user who lost their device Users → user detail → Reset two-factor Session lifetime and idle timeout Sessions end a set time after sign-in, and after a set time without activity Settings → Security → Security options

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Once authentication is configured, manage accounts and groups in Users and groups. To let OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ users reach XTM One with their own account, see XTM Suite integration.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
This page covers what to back up on a self-hosted XTM One instance, how to restore it, and how to copy an instance to another host. Filigran SaaS instances are backed up by Filigran.

The commands below use the service names of the Docker Compose stack (postgres, minio, platform, worker, worker-preview) and its default database name and user (copilot). Adapt them to your DATABASE_URL and storage settings, or use your managed services' own backup tools.

docs.title: What to back up
docs.text:
What Why Where it lives The PostgreSQL database Every agent, assignment, run, conversation, user, setting and encrypted credential, and the knowledge-base embeddings (the vector extension, pgvector) The postgres service, pgdata volume The object storage bucket Uploaded files, knowledge-base documents, large trace payloads and their images, sandbox workspace files, brand assets The minio service (Silo), minio-data volume, or your S3 bucket (S3_BUCKET, copilot-files by default) SECRET_KEY and the rest of .env SECRET_KEY encrypts every stored credential and two-factor secret, and signs sessions Your .env, or your secret manager

Keep SECRET_KEY with every backup

A database restored without its original SECRET_KEY starts, but every encrypted value in it is unreadable: integration and LLM provider credentials, channel bot tokens, secret variables, OAuth clients, two-factor enrollments. There is no way to recover them. Store SECRET_KEY apart from the database backup, in a place you can reach when the host is gone.

Redis does not need a backup. Losing it costs only short-lived data:

  • background jobs queued and not yet picked up by a worker. A knowledge-base document left waiting is queued again by the scheduler's recovery sweep;
  • invitation and password reset links not used yet, which must be sent again;
  • XTM One Desktop sign-ins in progress, rate-limit counters, and the last activity of each session (the idle timeout starts counting again).

docs.title: A consistent recovery point
docs.text:
The database and the bucket refer to each other: a row points at a file, a trace at its offloaded payload. Back them up at the same moment, or a restored row can point at a file that is missing.

The simplest way is to stop everything that writes, back up both, then start again:

docker compose stop platform worker worker-preview

On Kubernetes, scale the platform and the worker to zero for the same effect. If you cannot stop the service, back up the database first and copy the bucket right after, to keep the gap between them as short as possible.

docs.title: Back up the database
docs.text:
pg_dump in custom format keeps the schema, the data and the vector extension:

docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U copilot -d copilot -Fc > xtm-one-db.dump

docs.title: Back up the object storage
docs.text:
With an external S3 bucket, use your provider's versioning, replication or snapshot features, or copy the bucket with any S3 client.

With the Silo service of the Compose stack, archive its volume while it is stopped. Compose prefixes volume names with the project name (by default the name of the folder holding docker-compose.yml); docker volume ls shows the exact name.

docker compose stop minio
docker run --rm -v <project>_minio-data:/data:ro -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/xtm-one-objects.tgz -C /data .
docker compose up -d

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
Restore onto the same XTM One version as the backup, or a later one: on startup, a later version migrates the restored database forward. An earlier version cannot read a database a later one has migrated.

  1. Put back the .env of the backed-up instance, with its SECRET_KEY, and set the image tags to the version you restore onto.

  2. Stop the platform and the workers if they run, and start the storage services only:

    docker compose stop platform worker worker-preview
docker compose up -d postgres minio

  3. Replace the database with the backup:

    docker compose exec -T postgres dropdb -U copilot --if-exists copilot
docker compose exec -T postgres createdb -U copilot copilot
docker compose exec -T postgres pg_restore -U copilot -d copilot --no-owner < xtm-one-db.dump

    With your own PostgreSQL server, make sure the pgvector extension is installed on it: the dump re-creates the vector extension and needs it to be available.

  4. Replace the objects with the backup:

    docker compose stop minio
docker run --rm -v <project>_minio-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  sh -c "find /data -mindepth 1 -delete && tar xzf /backup/xtm-one-objects.tgz -C /data"

  5. Start the platform. Migrations run on startup if the version is later than the backup's.

    docker compose up -d

docs.title: Copy an instance to another host
docs.text:
A copy is a restore on another host: the same backup, the same SECRET_KEY, the same procedure. What differs is the instance's identity.

  • The instance ID. It is stored in the database, so a restored copy has the same instance ID as the original. PLATFORM_ID forces it: set it to keep the identity stable across restores and re-installs, or to a new UUID to make a copy a separate instance (see Configuration).
  • The XTM Hub registration. It is bound to the instance ID. A copy that keeps the ID keeps the registration. A copy with a new PLATFORM_ID shows Register again in Settings → Parameters, and sends nothing to the XTM Hub until you register it (see XTM Hub registration).
  • Connected platforms and integrations. A copy holds the original's registered OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ platforms, its integrations and their credentials, and its active assignments and flows. Once started, it runs them against the same systems as the original. For a test copy next to a live instance, start it where it cannot reach those systems, or press the emergency stop with the Whole platform scope as soon as you sign in.
  • Its address. Set BASE_URL (and FRONTEND_URL) to the copy's own address, and update the redirect URIs registered in your identity provider if the copy uses single sign-on (see Authentication).

docs.title: Verify after a restore
docs.text:
• /api/health/ready returns 200 (see Monitoring).
  • You can sign in, and the bootstrap administrator is the one set in .env.
  • An integration or an LLM provider answers its connection test: its credential decrypts, so SECRET_KEY is the right one. The security audit names any configuration it cannot decrypt.
  • A knowledge-base document or an attached file opens: the bucket matches the database.
  • Settings → Parameters shows the XTM Hub registration in the state you expect.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Before your next version change, read Upgrade: its rollback procedure relies on the backup described here.

docs.title: Chat approvals in client applications
docs.text:
XTM One agent chat can stop mid-answer and ask a person to approve a tool call before it runs. This page is for anyone driving that chat from outside XTM One — an embedded assistant, a Suite platform, or your own integration.

For what approvals are and how administrators configure them, see AI governance. For how the Suite products connect, see XTM Suite integration.

docs.title: Existing clients keep working
docs.text:
Upgrading XTM One does not break a client that knows nothing about approvals, and no coordinated release is required.

The interactive prompt is opt-in. A client receives one only if it asks, by sending supports_tool_approval: true with the message. Anything that does not — every build predating this feature — gets a normal assistant message instead:

I need approval before running: delete_entity. This chat can't collect that approval, so I've stopped rather than acting without it. You can allow this tool for yourself from the Tools page, or an administrator can allow it for everyone from the same place — or you can ask me to do something else.

Ordinary text, rendered by whatever the client already does with an answer. Nothing hangs, nothing errors, and the user learns why the agent stopped.

Why opt-in, rather than simply pausing for everyone

A client that ignores an approval prompt never answers it. A server that paused anyway would wait indefinitely — no error, no timeout, just a turn that never finishes and a user watching a spinner. Declaring support is a client promising it will answer.

docs.title: Most clients reach XTM One through a proxy
docs.text:
The embedded assistant widget is rarely pointed straight at XTM One. Each Suite platform — OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenGRC — points it at its own backend, which authenticates the browser session, mints a platform token, and forwards the call to XTM One.

flowchart LR
    browser["Assistant widget<br/>(in the platform UI)"]
    proxy["Platform backend<br/>(authenticates, mints token)"]
    xtmone["XTM One<br/>/api/v1/platform/chat/*"]

    browser -->|"1 · message"| proxy
    proxy -->|"2 · forwards"| xtmone
    xtmone -->|"3 · streams events back"| proxy
    proxy -->|"4 · streams through"| browser

That middle hop is why approval has requirements a direct client would never notice. If you operate one, the section below is the checklist.

docs.title: What a proxy must do
docs.text:
If your application forwards chat to XTM One on a user's behalf, four things decide whether approvals work through it.

Forward the whole request body. A proxy that rebuilds the upstream body from a fixed list of fields silently drops supports_tool_approval. The result is safe — XTM One never pauses, and the client gets the plain message — but it is confusing to debug, because from the browser it looks as though the flag was ignored.

Route the decision back. Approval needs a path from the browser to XTM One during a turn, alongside the streaming response. If you already proxy the mid-run steering endpoint, the approval endpoint is the same shape and belongs next to it.

Never time out a streaming turn. This is the one most likely to bite. A paused turn holds its connection open and silent for as long as the reviewer takes, so any read timeout between the browser and XTM One becomes an approval deadline that nobody chose. Set the streaming call's timeout to infinite, and confirm any ingress in front of it does the same.

Pass keepalives through untouched. XTM One keeps the connection warm during silent windows by emitting SSE comment lines (: keepalive) every 15 seconds. These are what stop idle-timeout logic from reaping a legitimate pause, and they only work if your proxy streams bytes through rather than parsing and re-emitting events it recognises.

Accept approval decisions only from a real user session

A decision is a person's consent. Require the same browser session your chat endpoint requires, and reject agent or service identities on that route — an agent approving its own tool call defeats the entire control.

Then tell the reviewer what a rejected decision means. The common case is not an attack, it is an expired session: a paused turn can sit for a long time, and the decision POST is the first request after it.
