Duplicate deliveries — proxy retries, sender at-least-once redelivery, a double-submitted test POST — are deduplicated so a retry returns the original run_id without re-running the assignment. The key is derived in this order:

  1. An explicit header: Idempotency-Key, X-Idempotency-Key, X-GitHub-Delivery, Webhook-Id / Svix-Id, or X-Hook-Signature-Id.
  2. A provider-specific id in the payload (OpenCTI notification_id, Slack event_id, HubSpot eventId, or a JSON-API type + id pair).
  3. A SHA-256 of the URL scope + raw request body.

Send an Idempotency-Key

Step 3 cannot tell a retry apart from a genuine recurrence. Two distinct events carrying byte-identical bodies inside the window — a repeated detection with no timestamp, a state notification with no counter — collapse into a single run, and the second delivery is answered with deduplicated: true. Sending an Idempotency-Key that is unique per logical event removes the ambiguity entirely. Failing that, shorten WEBHOOK_DEDUP_TTL_SECONDS below the sender's event cadence.

docs.title: Assignment auto-pause
docs.text:
A scheduled assignment whose configuration points at a resource its integration can no longer see - a Notion database that was deleted or is no longer shared with the integration - would otherwise fail on every run, forever. Once the integration has reported the same resource missing in two separate runs, the run that uses it again is recorded as failed with the cause Integration resource missing (its summary is kept), and the assignment owner is notified once. After the number of consecutive scheduled runs below, the assignment is paused; the assignment page says which resource and integration are involved and offers Resume. See Operations.

Variable Required Default Description ASSIGNMENT_STALE_REFERENCE_PAUSE_AFTER No 3 Consecutive scheduled runs failed on a stale integration reference after which the assignment is paused. Re-enabling the assignment starts a fresh count; a scheduled run that succeeds or fails for another reason resets it; manual, webhook and event-triggered runs neither advance nor reset it. Built-in and per-user fan-out assignments are reported, never paused. 0 disables the pause (runs still fail and are still reported).

docs.title: CTEM case owner
docs.text:
A CTEM case opened from a signal starts with an owner: the owner of an affected asset in the inventory, else the owner of an asset group that asset belongs to, else the default below. An owner counts only when it is the email of an active account; any other name is skipped, never guessed. Each assignment is written in the case history with how the owner was found.

Variable Required Default Description CTEM_CASE_DEFAULT_OWNER No (empty) Email of the account a new case is assigned to when no affected asset or asset group names an owner with an account. Empty: the case opens without an owner.

docs.title: Messaging channels
docs.text: Variable Required Default Description CHANNEL_AGENT_MENTIONS_ENABLED No false On Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat, let an identified user's @agent-key (an agent's slug, else its hyphenated name) make that agent answer after the routed one, in the same reply - only an agent whose own channel settings let it answer that message (enabled, set to Receive and Publish on that channel, past the bot's receive whitelist, private-conversation and only-mention rules). Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action. false: a channel message is answered by its routed agent alone, whatever it mentions. The web chat's mentions are not affected by this setting. DECISIONS_READ_ENABLED No false Human gates: let the inbox, the bell and the decision cards read the unified decisions store. It takes effect only once every open question (a paused run, a pending tool approval, a flow waiting on a person, a work item waiting for an answer) has its decision: GET /api/v1/decisions/backfill (administrators) shows the count per source and whether the switch is on. false: they read each engine's own state, which stays current either way.

docs.title: Built-in web search
docs.text:
One web search provider is given to every agent without an integration to add. Brave Search wins when its key is set; Google Search is the fallback; with neither key set, agents have no built-in web search.

Variable Required Default Description BUILTIN_BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY No empty Brave Search API subscription token, created in the Brave Search API dashboard. When set, the built-in Brave Search integration gives every agent web, news, image and video search, and Google Search below is not seeded. Its web and image tools also answer to the Google tool names (search_google_web, search_google_images), so agent instructions that name them keep working. BUILTIN_GOOGLE_SEARCH_API_KEY No empty Google Custom Search, as search_engine_id\|\|api_key. Used only when BUILTIN_BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY is empty. Google's Custom Search JSON API is closed to new customers and stops on 1 January 2027: move to Brave Search before then.

docs.title: Microsoft 365 integration
docs.text: Variable Required Default Description MICROSOFT_TEAMS_MESSAGE_TEXT_LIMIT No 4000 The longest text of one message an agent's Teams channel or chat listing shows. A longer message is cut at a word boundary and ends with a [truncated, ...] note giving how many characters are left and the exact call that reads it in full (get_microsoft_channel_message or get_microsoft_chat_message); a message that fits is shown whole. The messages of one listing also share a text budget of 40,000 characters, so on a busy channel the longest messages are cut shorter while the short ones stay whole. A value below 1 fails startup.

docs.title: Runners and XTM One Desktop
docs.text:
A Runner is the pull-based native daemon behind XTM One Desktop (the native client users install on their own machine - chat window plus local execution) and behind the headless runner installed on servers and fleets. A user enrolls it once from the XTM One Desktop page (bottom of the left navigation) and leaves it running. It makes only outbound connections and pulls commands from the platform (the platform never opens a connection to the machine), giving agents genuine full-desktop screenshots, real-browser control, shell + file operations, and synthetic input through the computer_use built-in tool. Enrollment is a single-use, short-lived token exchanged once for a durable credential stored in the machine's OS keychain. Single sign-on from the Desktop app runs in the system browser and hands the session back through the runner-authenticated /api/v1/desktop-login handoff (short-lived Redis records; no extra configuration).

The installers, bare-binary archives, and self-update artifacts are built by the release pipeline and embedded in the platform image — every instance serves its own version-matched downloads directly from the XTM One Desktop page and answers the runners' self-update checks from the same embedded set. There is no external download URL, CDN, or GitHub Releases dependency to configure, and an air-gapped deployment is fully self-sufficient. A source/dev build (no embedded distribution) simply reports downloads as unavailable while everything else — enrollment, transport, computer_use — keeps working with runners you built yourself (apps/runner/build.ps1 / build.sh).

Variable Required Default Description RUNNERS_ENABLED No true Master switch for the whole Runner subsystem: enrollment, the runner transport (WebSocket + long-poll), and the computer_use agent tools. Set false to remove it entirely (every runner endpoint then returns 404 and the Profile tab is hidden). RUNNER_DIST_DIR No runner_dist Directory of the embedded runner distribution inside the image, populated by CI at image build time. Only needs changing if you repackage the image and relocate the artifacts. Empty/absent (source builds) reports downloads as unavailable. RUNNER_MIN_SUPPORTED_VERSION No — Minimum runner binary version accepted at connect (protocol gate). Empty means no floor; a runner below it is told to self-update. Format MAJOR.YYMMDD.SEQ. RUNNER_MAX_PER_USER No 200 Cap on active runners a single user (or the company-managed fleet) may have enrolled at once, enforced at enrollment so an unattended roll-out cannot create unbounded records. 0 = unlimited. RUNNER_MAX_INFLIGHT_COMMANDS No 10 Cap on concurrent in-flight commands per runner; a burst past this is refused with a transient "busy" so parallel tool calls cannot swamp one machine. 0 = unlimited. RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT No false What a restricted runner does with a file command whose path lies inside its allowed folders but leads outside them through a link (symbolic link, junction, mount point). false: it runs, as it always has, with a warning in the command result and the runner log; the security audit (Settings → Security) reports the default while a restricted runner has allowed folders. true: it is refused. The same switch covers a file that is not a regular file - a device (/dev/urandom, a serial port, NUL on Windows), a named pipe or a socket, as the operating system reports the object the command opened, never guessed from its name - on every runner, full control included: false reads and writes it as before, with a warning in the result and the runner log; true refuses it. Needs a runner from this release or later; an older runner ignores it. Also in Settings > Access and security; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS No — (derived) How long an agent's computer_use call waits for a command's result. Unset: as long as the machine may take to report it, counted from the command's delivery - its execution limit (RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 30 s, the wait for its turn on the machine included), then the 50 s it retries a result upload through a platform restart, plus 5 s. That is 205 s with the default limit, and it ends before the command's lease, so a command the wait gives up on is never sent to the machine again. A number: a fixed wait of that many seconds from dispatch. Either way a call never waits past the time the agent run allows one tool call (300 s at most): when that limit comes first, the tool stops 5 s before it and tells the agent the command may still finish, its output then landing in the machine's command history. Upgrading: the default used to be a fixed 180 s, which could end before a command near its limit whose upload rode out a restart had reported (see UPGRADING.md); set 180 to keep it.

Tuning knobs

The transport cadence and timeouts (RUNNER_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, RUNNER_OFFLINE_AFTER_SECONDS, RUNNER_LONG_POLL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES, RUNNER_ENROLLMENT_TTL_SECONDS) have sensible defaults and rarely need changing; .env.sample lists each with its default. RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (120 s) is the execution budget every command is handed: the machine stops a command at that budget + 30 s, the wait for its turn included (a run_shell timeout argument can only shorten it), and both the time before the platform sends a silent command again and the default RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS follow it.

docs.title: Outbound proxy and certificate authorities
docs.text:
The requests that fetch a web page or document at a URL a user, an agent or a remote page chose - the web_fetch tool (agents and flows), the knowledge base URL crawl, Deep Investigation's web pages and the free HTTP sources of a built investigation pack - are sent to the address the destination policy checked, never to the name again, so a DNS answer that changes in between cannot point them at an internal address. Two consequences for the network around the platform:

  • They never go through an outbound proxy. HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and ALL_PROXY are ignored for them (a proxy would resolve the name itself, after the check), and no relay group carries them. A deployment that reaches the web only through a proxy must give the platform and the worker direct outbound access to ports 80 and 443 for these requests; to keep filtering them, do it on the network path (an egress firewall, or a transparent proxy that applies its own destination policy) rather than through the proxy variables. When one of these variables is set, the platform and the worker each log one warning at startup naming the variable (never its value). How other outbound requests treat the proxy variables is unchanged (for MCP servers, see MCP_SERVER_URL_POLICY above).
  • They verify certificates against SSL_CERT_FILE / SSL_CERT_DIR when set, the certifi bundle of public authorities otherwise. Set one of them for a private CA or a TLS-inspecting egress gateway. The file or directory replaces the default bundle for these requests: a file holding only your private CA makes every public site fail its certificate check, so append your CA to a copy of a public bundle. Set the variable, and mount the file, in both the platform and the worker containers (with Docker Compose, in both services' environment).
  • An administrator can add certificates without replacing the bundle. Settings > Access and security > Security options > Trusted certificates for web fetches (WEB_FETCH_TRUSTED_CA_CERTIFICATES, which wins and locks the field) takes one or more PEM certificates - a private certificate authority, or the self-signed certificate of one host - and adds them to the store above for these requests. Verification stays on: the chain must verify to a listed or system certificate and the host name must match the certificate, so a listed self-signed certificate vouches for the host it names and no other. Nothing ever fetches with verification off. The value is checked when it is saved (certificates only; a private key is refused), applies to the next fetch on every replica within seconds, is audited (the audit log and the Security audit show how many certificates, never their text), and is empty by default. These fetches still refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses: a certificate makes a public-facing host trusted, it does not open the internal network.

docs.title: Relays
docs.text:
A relay is a small, separate program you install inside a network the platform cannot reach - a customer data center, an isolated zone - so the integrations, MCP servers and flow HTTP requests you route through it can call the tools there (Splunk, Tanium, an internal API). It opens an outbound connection to the platform and pulls the requests to carry: no inbound flow is ever opened toward that network. Relays are grouped by zone; every relay of a group carries the same traffic, so adding a second one gives the zone high availability. See Relays for enrollment and routing.

The installers (Linux, macOS, Windows), the archives and the self-update artifacts are built by the release pipeline and embedded in the platform image, exactly like the runner's: every instance serves its own version-matched downloads and answers its relays' update checks, and an air-gapped deployment needs nothing else. A container image (xtmone/relay) and a Kubernetes example are published for container platforms.

Variable Required Default Description RELAYS_ENABLED No true Master switch for relays: relay groups, enrollment, the relay transport (WebSocket + long-poll) and routing an integration, an MCP server or a flow HTTP node through a group. Set false to remove them entirely: every relay endpoint returns 404, the Relays page is hidden and nothing is routed - a resource already routed through a group then fails its requests rather than calling directly. RELAY_MIN_SUPPORTED_VERSION No — Minimum relay version accepted at connect. Empty means no floor; a relay below it is refused and told to update. Format MAJOR.YYMMDD.SEQ. The security audit lists the relays older than the floor. RELAY_MAX_PER_GROUP No 50 Cap on relays enrolled in one group, enforced at enrollment. 0 = unlimited. RELAY_REQUEST_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS No 30 Days the platform keeps the record of each relayed request (destination host, method, status, size, duration - never a body or a header value), shown on a group's Activity tab. 0 = forever. RELAY_DIST_DIR No relay_dist Directory of the embedded relay distribution inside the image, populated by CI at image build time. Empty/absent (source builds) reports downloads as unavailable; relays you built yourself still enroll and carry traffic.

Tuning knobs

The transport cadence, timeouts and size limits (RELAY_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, RELAY_OFFLINE_AFTER_SECONDS, RELAY_LONG_POLL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RELAY_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RELAY_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RELAY_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES, RELAY_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES, RELAY_ENROLLMENT_TTL_SECONDS) have sensible defaults and rarely need changing; .env.sample lists each with its default. A request routed to a group with no relay online fails at once with a clear error - it never falls back to a direct call.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
Variable Required Default Description ENABLED_FEATURES No — (none enabled) Comma-separated list of feature flag ids to turn on experimental/in-development features, e.g. MY_FLAG,OTHER_FLAG. Use * to enable all of them. Leaving this unset enables none of them. Changing it requires a restart — there is no toggle in the Settings UI. An unrecognized flag id (e.g. left over from another branch) is logged as a warning and ignored — it never enables anything and never prevents the platform from starting.

The resolved list of enabled flags is also sent to the frontend (as part of the public, boot-time GET /auth/config response), so a flag can control both backend behavior and whether a UI element is shown — with the backend independently enforcing the same flag on any route it gates.

Evaluation (datasets, evaluations and their runs, and the persona rewrites they measure) is off by default, and never available in XTM One mode. In Copilot or dev mode, turn it on with ENABLED_FEATURES=EVALUATION on the platform and the worker, then restart both; * turns it on too. Off, its pages and API are gone, no run starts (scheduled, on agent change, or from an agent's tools) and nothing it stored is deleted: turning it back on picks everything up again.

Custom dashboards (DASHBOARD_STUDIO) are off by default. Turn them on with ENABLED_FEATURES=DASHBOARD_STUDIO on the platform and the worker, then restart both; * turns them on too. Off, the dashboards pages and API are gone (404), the Custom Dashboards built-in tool is neither offered nor run, published links answer like unknown ones and a home dashboard falls back to the platform's. Nothing is deleted: turning it back on restores everything.

The mobile companion (MOBILE_COMPANION) is off by default. Turn it on with ENABLED_FEATURES=MOBILE_COMPANION on the platform and the worker, then restart both; * turns it on too. Off, a phone gets the web app, linking a phone and its routes (/api/v1/mobile-devices, /api/v1/mobile, /api/v1/app-lock) answer 404, nothing is pushed to a phone, the companion PIN never locks anyone out, and agents are not handed the phone tool. Linked phones and PINs are kept: turning it back on picks them up again. See Mobile companion.

Agentic coding labs (AGENTIC_CODING) are off by default, and never available in XTM One mode: they are Filigran's own development tooling, not a product feature. In Copilot or dev mode, turn them on with ENABLED_FEATURES=AGENTIC_CODING on the platform and the worker and set AGENTIC_LABS_NAMESPACE (see Agentic coding labs below); * turns the flag on too, and the labs stay off while the namespace is empty. Off, the sandbox service tools behave as before.

docs.title: Agentic coding labs
docs.text:
With AGENTIC_CODING on (Copilot or dev mode only), sandbox_start_service starts what a checkout declares as a service in a Kubernetes pod of its own, one pod per lab, in the namespace AGENTIC_LABS_NAMESPACE: a workspace container holding the checkout and one container per service, on the pod's shared localhost. The platform talks to the Kubernetes API server with its service-account token; that account needs create, get, list, patch and delete on pods, get on pods/log and create on pods/exec in that namespace, nothing else. A lab is never refused for a quota, never counted against one and never limited in number: the pod carries resource requests so the scheduler can place it, and no limits. Its preview (http://<pod IP>:<port>/) opens in the browser tool and web_fetch while the lab runs. The idle and deadline settings below are hygiene, not limits: 0 turns either off.

Variable Required Default Description AGENTIC_LABS_NAMESPACE No — (labs off) The Kubernetes namespace lab pods are created in. Empty keeps the labs off whatever ENABLED_FEATURES says. AGENTIC_LABS_API_URL No In-cluster address The Kubernetes API server. Empty uses KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST / KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT. AGENTIC_LABS_TOKEN_PATH No /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token The service-account token, read on every call so a rotated token is used. AGENTIC_LABS_CA_PATH No /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt The CA the API server's certificate is checked against. AGENTIC_LABS_CPU_REQUEST No 250m CPU requested per container of a lab pod (no limit is set). AGENTIC_LABS_MEMORY_REQUEST No 512Mi Memory requested per container of a lab pod (no limit is set). AGENTIC_LABS_START_SECONDS No 600 Seconds a lab pod may take to be scheduled and start its workspace container. AGENTIC_LABS_COPY_SECONDS No 300 Seconds one attempt of the checkout copy into a lab may take, apart from the start budget. A copy that times out or loses its stream is tried once more on the same pod before the start answers an error. AGENTIC_LABS_IDLE_HOURS No 12 A lab unused this long is deleted by the hourly sweep. 0 = never. AGENTIC_LABS_DEADLINE_HOURS No 72 Kubernetes ends a lab pod this old (activeDeadlineSeconds). 0 = never. AGENTIC_LABS_LICENSING_URL No — (no licences) Filigran's licensing server. At every lab start the platform asks its /api/ci route for one short-lived ci Enterprise Edition licence per entry of AGENTIC_LABS_LICENCES. AGENTIC_LABS_LICENSING_TOKEN No — (no licences) The licensing server's API-user token (permission to issue CI licences). Kept on the platform: it never reaches a lab pod, an agent or a log. AGENTIC_LABS_LICENCES No — (no licences) ENV_VAR:product name,...: each lab container gets the licence of that product in that variable. A licence that cannot be issued never stops the lab; the start answer names it. AGENTIC_LABS_LICENCE_HOURS No 24 Hours each lab licence is valid for (at most 168). AGENTIC_LABS_MODEL_KEY_ACCOUNT No — (stub model) Email of the account whose short-lived personal API key, scoped to the LLM proxy only, is minted for every lab that declares LAB_MODEL = "live". The key is handed to the pod as LAB_MODEL_API_KEY and revoked when the lab stops; no provider credential ever reaches a lab. AGENTIC_LABS_MODEL_BASE_URL No — (stub model) The LLM proxy as a lab reaches it (https://<host>/v1), handed as LAB_MODEL_BASE_URL. The host must be in the labs' egress allow-list. AGENTIC_LABS_MODEL_NAMES No — Comma-separated model names a live lab's backend offers, handed as LAB_MODEL_NAMES. AGENTIC_LABS_MODEL_KEY_HOURS No 12 Hours a lab's model key is valid for (at most 72); revoked earlier when the lab stops or is reaped.

docs.title: Presentation export
docs.text:
Exporting a presentation to PDF or PowerPoint is a server-side render: the platform opens the deck in its own headless Chromium — the same browser that already ships in the image for the browser tool and the PDF path of generate_file — at a fixed 1920x1080 slide size, and hands back the file. This is what makes an exported slide pixel-identical to the slide on screen, independently of the user's browser, zoom level or print dialog. Nothing needs to be installed for it; the unified and worker images both carry the browser.

The browser loads the deck's render page from the platform itself, authenticated with a short-lived token bound to that one deck (three minutes, read access to the deck's own images only, refused everywhere else in the API). Every other request the page could make — external fonts, scripts, images — is blocked; the deck is entirely self-contained.

Variable Required Default Description PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL No Automatic Origin the headless browser loads the render page from. Empty means automatic: the unified image uses its own loopback address (http://127.0.0.1:4000), so no request goes through the ingress and the pod does not need to resolve its own public hostname; a split development setup (Vite dev server + API) falls back to FRONTEND_URL. PRESENTATION_LAYOUT_CHECK_ENABLED No true Render a deck in the same headless browser right after an agent saves it and report what the schema cannot see — a slide body shrunk to fit, text cut by its box, text painted past the slide's edge — back to the agent in the tool result, so it fixes the slide before answering. Set to false to skip the check everywhere (tool result, get_presentation, POST .../layout-check; the viewer then offers no Layout check button), for example on a deployment without the headless browser.

When to set it

Set PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL when the platform runs behind an ingress the pod cannot reach from the inside, or behind an authentication proxy that would intercept the render page before it reaches the platform — the render token is that page's only credential, and a proxy login screen in its place shows up as an export that fails with a rendering error. Point it at an address that reaches the platform container directly, for example the Kubernetes service name.

At most two exports render at the same time per process; further requests wait for a slot, and a user may request at most six exports a minute from the export buttons (decks and reports together; past that the request is answered 429 with a Retry-After). A render that has not settled after 60 seconds (fonts, images and diagrams all loaded) fails with an explicit error rather than hanging, and the Print to PDF (browser) action on a deck's chat card remains available as a fallback that needs no server rendering.

An agent-generated report exports to PDF the same way, through the same browser, slots, timeout and PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL: the platform opens the report's render page (with a three-minute token bound to that one report) and prints it on A4, exactly as the report's viewer prints it, every annex open. The Export menu of a report (its chat card and its viewer) offers that PDF and Print to PDF (browser) as the fallback; an agent with the report tool exports it as a file of the conversation when the user asks for one.

docs.title: Layout check
docs.text: A slide is a fixed surface, and a schema cannot tell whether six cards and a callout fit on it. So the same headless browser also serves as the layout check that runs after every save an agent makes: the deck is rendered, each slide is measured, and what the audience would see go wrong is reported to the agent in the tool result — a body that had to be shrunk to fit (with the ratio, so "dense" and "overloaded" are told apart), text cut off by a box or the footer, a badge whose text runs past its pill, anything painted past the slide's edge, a statement quote that runs past four lines, a chart with no room to write the values it was asked for (values hidden on chart 2, with the room it had and what to change), a chart whose values had to be turned on their side (values rotated on chart 2, advisory, with a smaller text size or a wider column as the remedy), a pie or a donut whose values had to be set smaller than its text size or written inside its slices (values shrunk on chart 2, advisory, with the legend under the chart or a wider column as the remedy), a row of key figures that had to shrink below its size and no longer matches the same row on the other slides — and, in the other direction, a content slide whose blocks leave more than half of its body bare and that no footer block closes (reported as advisory, with the remedies that slide actually has: more content, a footer block takeaway, or a merge with the neighbouring slide; blocks are sized to their content, so a card or a grid is never stretched to the floor), a content slide whose columns end more than a fifth of the body apart (uneven, advisory, with a block for the shorter column or shared card heights as the remedy), and a body of one block packed under the title over more than 30% of bare body (floating, advisory, with a centred placement or the content that carries it as the remedy). The agent then trims or fills the slide it is told about and saves again, instead of leaving it for the presenter to discover. On screen, a slide whose content does not fit is scaled down to fit rather than overlapping its footer, and the exported PowerPoint carries the same scaled sizes; a row of key figures keeps its size while the rest of the slide shrinks, so it reads the same on every slide. The check is bounded (45 seconds, then it is skipped with a note) and never fails a save; the same measurement is available on demand at POST /api/v1/presentations/{id}/layout-check to whoever can edit the deck (a read-only reader gets a 403).

docs.title: Browser profiles
docs.text:
Browser profiles sign the platform's headless Chromium (the browser already in the image) in to a web application and keep the session, for the agents that browse with them and for Video Studio recordings. They need no feature flag. A sign-in with an interactive MFA runs where it was asked from and waits for the code through Redis, so any replica can receive it; the worker keeps the saved sessions signed in (each profile's "Keep the session alive").

Variable Required Default Description BROWSER_PRIVATE_TARGETS No false Let a browser profile open an application on a private network, on the hosts it declares (operator-network policy: loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses stay refused): its sign-in, the agents browsing with it and Video Studio recordings. Also in Settings > Access and security, where the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. It replaces VIDEO_STUDIO_PRIVATE_TARGETS, which is no longer read: a value an administrator saved in Settings > Access and security moves over by itself, a variable must be renamed.

docs.title: Video Studio
docs.text:
The Video Studio records demo environments in the platform's own headless Chromium (the browser already in the image), composes the video frame by frame in that same browser and encodes it with ffmpeg, which the unified and worker images ship. A recording that acts on a graph's node reads the label painted on the graph with Tesseract (tesseract-ocr), shipped in the same images; a worker without it finds such nodes only by the highlight the graph gives them. Recordings and renders run in the worker, as durable jobs; a sign-in with an interactive MFA runs where it was asked from and waits for the code through Redis, so any replica can receive it.

The Video Studio is off by default: a render needs a worker sized for Chromium and ffmpeg. Turn it on with ENABLED_FEATURES=VIDEO_STUDIO on the platform and the workers, then restart them. Size the workers first (Sizing the workers below):

  • CPU: a request and a limit of 8, the same value. The render estimates from the CPUs the container's quota grants, so a request lower than the limit gives renders fewer CPUs than they were planned for.
  • Memory: a request of 6 GiB and a limit of 24 GiB for the worker that draws whole renders.
  • Pages: leave VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_PAGES at 0.
  • Three workers: one that draws whole renders and scene previews, and two that draw scene previews only (VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_CONCURRENCY=0). docker-compose.yml runs them as worker and two replicas of worker-preview (docker compose up -d --scale worker-preview=N for another count).
  • Restarts: give the workers the same WORKER_TERMINATION_GRACE_SECONDS and WORKER_STARTUP_SECONDS as their pods' terminationGracePeriodSeconds and startup probe. A render under way when its worker is replaced waits that long for the next worker, then resumes where it stopped; 10 minutes when neither is set. With a terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 1260 (docker-compose.yml sets the same stop_grace_period), a worker asked to stop lets the renders it draws past half their frames finish, for up to 20 minutes (VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_DRAIN_SECONDS), and hands the others to a running worker at once. A render handed over keeps its slot: the worker that takes it back gives it priority over the renders queued after it.

On that worker, the estimate for a 130 s, 30-scene 4K video is about 45 minutes, before any render of the platform has been measured. A render that one worker cannot draw within 4 hours is drawn in scene ranges, each on a worker of its own, so more worker replicas also make long 4K renders faster. While it is off, Work > Videos, the Video Studio tool, the Video Production skill, the built-in video templates and the Video Generation and Music Generation models in Settings → AI Models are not offered, and public video links stop answering. Videos already made are kept and come back when it is turned on again.

docs.title: Sizing the workers
docs.text:
A worker's memory is shared between its whole renders, its scene previews and its own jobs:

  • The preview reserve. A worker that draws scene previews keeps 8 GiB that no render ever takes. This is a hard floor: VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_RESERVE_MB may raise it, never lower it. A worker with VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY=0 draws no preview and keeps no reserve.
  • A render's ceiling. A whole render may use 60% of the container's memory limit (VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_MEMORY_MB when set). A 4K (ultra) render may use VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB (16 GiB). Neither ever goes past the limit less the reserve. A worker no bigger than its reserve draws no render at all, and its renders are refused with the memory to give it.
  • A render's pages. A render draws on one page per CPU but one, as many as its ceiling holds at each page's measured peak plus 20%. At 2160p a page peaks at about 3.7 GiB, and 4.6 GiB while it composes a screen insert. The pages are laid out when the render starts, in what the worker has then. From then on, the render holds the budget of the pages it opened, and the rest of its ceiling is left to the previews.
  • A scene preview. A preview draws on its 2 pages, never on one for want of memory. Its ceiling is twice its estimate, kept within the reserve: about 2.7 GiB for a 720p draft, 4.5 GiB at 1080p, 5.4 GiB at 1080p with a screen insert, and 7.5 GiB with three video inserts and a picture. The reserve therefore always holds one preview beside a 4K render. When the worker that took a preview cannot hold its pages, the preview goes to the worker with the most memory free and a preview slot free. When no worker has room, it waits for its pages where it is. Its answer says which, and what holds the worker's memory: its renders and its previews, each with their memory. A worker with the default reserve and 2 preview slots runs its second preview beside a 4K render only once the first ends. When a preview waited for that, its answer says once, for the administrator, the VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_RESERVE_MB that holds every slot at its worst case (16384 for 2 slots) and the memory to add to the container. A second worker that draws scene previews only does the same.

With 8 CPUs and the video of the measured fixture (screen inserts on screen):

Container memory limit Whole render (high) 4K render (ultra) 4K pages, without / with screen inserts Left to previews during that 4K render 16 GiB 8 GiB 8 GiB 1 / 1 10 GiB 24 GiB (recommended) 14.4 GiB 16 GiB 4 / 3 8.6 GiB 32 GiB, VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB=24576 19.2 GiB 24 GiB 6 / 4 11.6 GiB 48 GiB, VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB=40960 28.8 GiB 40 GiB 7 / 7 13.3 GiB

A 4K render with screen inserts takes about 35 GiB to draw on all 7 pages: give the worker a limit of 48 GiB and raise VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB to match. When a render opens fewer pages than the worker has CPUs, the first pre-flight to see it says so once, with the time on the pages opened against the time on all of them and the memory to give. It is said again only when those numbers change.

Workers. The preview workers draw scene previews only, so a 4K render on the first worker never leaves the previews short of memory. They run every other job of the platform too. The preview queue takes one preview per video in turn, and a sweep of every scene of a video queues a preview per scene: with two preview workers, another video's preview starts when the next preview slot frees, not after the whole sweep. A queued preview's answer names the videos whose previews it waits behind, and how many, and how many workers draw previews ("1 worker draws previews, 2 at a time"), counted from the workers that are running, not from what the deployment declares. A preview that waited behind other videos' previews with a single preview worker says once, under platform sizing, that a second one is missing. On Kubernetes, run the same set: one worker deployment that renders, and one with VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_CONCURRENCY=0 and 2 replicas. A worker that renders only (VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY=0) keeps no reserve. Give each worker a memory limit of its own: a worker without one reads the host's memory, and two workers on one host would each count all of it. A long render is split into scene ranges across the workers that draw renders, never onto a preview-only worker. While several videos have previews in the queue, each holds at most its share of the preview slots (the slots over the videos, rounded up), so one video's sweep never keeps every slot while another video's preview waits for its memory or for another worker. A queued preview's answer also says how long it should wait at the queue's pace: its place, the slots, and the median time of the last 20 previews drawn ("about 20 min before it starts at the lane's pace").

A render's CPUs against the other jobs. A whole render's pages share their worker with whatever else it runs: scene previews and recordings, but also the platform's assignment runs, sub-agent tasks and flows, which run in the worker's own process. Scene previews always draw at background priority. A whole render draws in a render lane of its own where the worker allows it: where the worker's container has its own cgroup v2 writable (/sys/fs/cgroup, a delegated cgroup), the worker moves its processes to a xtm-worker child cgroup and each whole render to a xtm-render one weighted VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_CPU_WEIGHT (1000 against the worker's 100), so that on a busy CPU the render keeps about 90% of it however many jobs run beside it; a process started later in the container (docker exec, kubectl exec) joins the worker's. Where the cgroup is read-only, which is the default for Docker and Kubernetes, a worker granted CAP_SYS_NICE (Compose: cap_add: [SYS_NICE]; Kubernetes: securityContext.capabilities.add: ["SYS_NICE"]) starts its renders at a raised priority with the same ratio instead. Without either, a render draws at the worker's own priority, and its estimate says so with what to grant. Whatever the lane, while a worker draws a whole render, new assignment runs, sub-agent tasks and evaluations go to a running worker that draws none (with the default Compose file, the preview workers) and run beside the render only when no such worker takes them within a few seconds. The render's estimate prices the jobs it shares its worker with at the CPU that worker measured for them over the last minute, and names them.

A GPU for the recordings. A recording draws the graphics a page draws itself, in 2D or with WebGL (a graph laid out again, a 3D view orbiting), on the worker's GPU when its Chromium finds one, and on the CPU (SwiftShader) otherwise. On a worker without a GPU, a graph's layout moves may be captured at 5 to 16 frames a second and play stepped. There, each graph is also captured on its own, at reduced quality, and where the capture of the whole page falls short of a layout move, the move is put together from those captures over the page's last full frame, so it keeps 20 frames a second or more while it moves (sharp again once it stops). A move that still plays mostly held frames is said at its step, naming the graph's element and "software GL", and the check when you save a video showing it says "stepping motion". Which worker shape uses what: a GPU worker draws on its GPU (GPU GL) and captures a graph with its page; a CPU worker draws on SwiftShader (software GL) and captures a graph on its own as above. To record on a GPU, run a worker on a GPU node with the GPU passed through and its graphics driver exposed (NVIDIA: the container toolkit with NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,utility,graphics, so Chromium finds the Vulkan driver), and keep the recordings on it: VIDEO_STUDIO_TAKE_CONCURRENCY=0 on the other workers. Each recording says what it was drawn with (GPU GL, or software GL and why), and the worker logs it once at its first recording.

docs.title: Video Studio settings
docs.text:
Variable Required Default Description VIDEO_STUDIO_FFMPEG_PATH No ffmpeg on PATH The ffmpeg binary that encodes recordings and renders. VIDEO_STUDIO_FFPROBE_PATH No ffprobe on PATH The ffprobe binary that reads media durations and sizes. VIDEO_STUDIO_MAX_TAKE_SECONDS No 300 The longest recording, in seconds. VIDEO_STUDIO_MAX_VIDEO_SECONDS No 1200 The longest video a render produces, in seconds. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_CONCURRENCY No 1 Whole renders one worker runs at the same time (each holds Chromium and ffmpeg). Scene previews have a lane of their own (VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY). While a worker has no whole render to make and its preview slots are all busy, these slots take the next scene previews too; a whole render asked meanwhile waits for that one preview to end. 0 = this worker draws no whole render and no scene range: scene previews only (worker-preview in docker-compose.yml). VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY No 2 Scene previews (one scene, at 720p30 or, for a scene showing a figure, a recording or a screen insert, 1080p30) one worker runs at the same time, beside its whole renders, on slots of their own; the queue takes the videos in turn. A preview starts on its 2 pages only, in what the worker's renders and previews leave of its memory limit, which is never less than the preview reserve: on a 24 GiB worker running a 16 GiB ultra render, a preview of up to 8 GiB starts at once. A preview whose pages the worker does not hold goes to the worker with the most memory free and a free preview slot, or waits for its pages, with no attempt spent. Its answer says which. 0 = this worker draws no preview and keeps no reserve. See Sizing the workers. VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY_MAX No 0 The most scene previews one worker runs at the same time while previews are queued. Above VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY, the worker adds a preview slot for each preview queued beyond what its slots run, as many as the CPUs its whole renders leave hold (2 CPUs a preview, on its 2 pages), and drops them as the queue empties: a preview already running keeps its slot. A queued preview's answer says the slots added (preview_slots_added). Raise it only on a worker with CPUs to spare beyond its own slots: on a worker of 4 CPUs and 2 slots it adds none. 0 = the slots stay VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY. VIDEO_STUDIO_TAKE_CONCURRENCY No 2 Recordings one worker runs at the same time. 0 = this worker records nothing, so the recordings run on the workers that do: keep them on a GPU worker this way (see Sizing the workers). At least one worker must record. VIDEO_STUDIO_RECORDING_GL No auto What a recording's browser draws a page's WebGL and 2D graphics on. auto = the worker's GPU when Chromium finds one to draw WebGL on (asked once, at the worker's first recording), the CPU (SwiftShader) otherwise. software = always the CPU, never looking for a GPU. gpu = the recording lane of a GPU node: the worker probes its GPU at start (ANGLE on Vulkan, then on EGL) and logs the WebGL renderer, and records only once Chromium draws WebGL there; a worker that reads a CPU rasterizer (SwiftShader, or Mesa's llvmpipe, softpipe or lavapipe, which Chromium reports as enabled WebGL) claims no recording at all and names what each launch read and what its container holds of the NVIDIA driver (the /dev/nvidia* nodes, NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES and NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, whether libEGL_nvidia.so.0 and libGLX_nvidia.so.0 load or the loader's error naming the missing file, the EGL vendor and Vulkan ICD files, and what libEGL answers under the lane's own EGL environment: its device enumeration and platform extensions, the EGL devices it lists and eglInitialize on the device, surfaceless and default displays), plus the GPUs Chromium's GPU process saw on each launch. A queued recording shows that reason whole. So give it the NVIDIA runtime with the graphics driver capability and keep VIDEO_STUDIO_TAKE_CONCURRENCY=0 on the other workers. On the CPU, a 60 fps recording of a page drawing graphs steps on their transitions: the recording says so and offers 30 fps, and a video's check says each transition on every scene showing it - a brief one the audience still reads as motion as advice, the others as a finding the render waits for. VIDEO_STUDIO_CLIP_CONCURRENCY No 4 AI clip generations one worker waits on at the same time. VIDEO_STUDIO_MAX_RENDERS_PER_USER No 10 Renders one person may have queued or running at once, across all their videos. Beyond it a render is refused with the ones in flight listed; the others wait in the queue with their position. Scene previews are counted apart, per video: every preview asked is queued, and at most this many previews of one video run at once. VIDEO_STUDIO_CLIP_INLINE_WAIT_SECONDS No 200 How long the assistant's generate_video_clip waits for its shot inside the call, the same for every call of a batch, counted from the call's start and never more than the call's own deadline allows. Past it the shot finishes in the background and the answer says why (waiting for a free generation slot, queued at the provider, rate limited). 0 = always in the background. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_PAGES No 0 Headless pages one render draws its frames with, each encoding its own run of the video. 0, the default, follows the rule: the CPUs of the worker container's quota minus one, the CPU left being the worker's own (8 CPUs draw on 7 pages). A render gets faster with more pages as long as each page has a CPU to use. A render never draws on more pages than the worker has CPUs, nor on more than its memory ceiling holds, each page at its measured peak plus a 20% margin: at 2160p one page peaks at about 3.7 GiB, and 4.6 GiB while it composes screen inserts, so an ultra render draws on 4 pages within its 16 GiB, or 3 for a video with screen inserts; drawing on 7 pages with inserts takes a ceiling of about 35 GiB. The pages are laid out when the render starts, in the memory the worker has then. Each page's encoder runs on its share of the CPUs. A scene preview draws on 2 pages at most. Give the container a CPU request as high as its limit. A number sets the pages instead, never more than the CPUs. Each render records the pages and CPUs it used and its frames per second, and the next renders' estimates start from them. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_CPU_WEIGHT No 1000 The CPU weight a whole render's pages and encoders draw at against the 100 of every other job of the worker (assignment runs, scene previews, recordings): a cgroup v2 cpu.weight where the worker's container cgroup is writable, else a raised priority of the same ratio where the worker holds CAP_SYS_NICE (see Sizing the workers). 1 to 10000. 0 = a render draws at the worker's own priority. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_MAX_RANGES No 8 The most scene ranges a render is split into when one worker cannot draw it within 4 hours. Each range is drawn and encoded on a worker of its own, within 4 hours of its own, and the render joins them and mixes the sound once. A range no other worker takes is drawn by the render's own worker after its range, so a single worker still renders it, one range after another. 1 = a render is never split: an ultra render then runs past 4 hours in segments, up to 8. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_SPLIT_MINUTES No 30 A render that would take longer than this many minutes on the pages its worker's memory opens is split into scene ranges across the workers running, as many ranges as bring each one under it (one a worker at most, VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_MAX_RANGES at most), so a long ultra render finishes sooner on a platform with several workers. With a single worker it is drawn whole. 0 = a render is split only past the 4 hours it may run. VIDEO_STUDIO_FRAME_CAPTURE No screenshot How a render takes each frame from its headless page. screenshot captures what the page's compositor shows, all pages in one browser. begin_frame asks Chromium to produce the frame on demand (HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame), 13-29% faster in the render image depending on the scenes, each page drawing in a browser of its own; it is opt-in. auto is begin_frame on Linux and screenshot elsewhere. A page whose frames cannot be begun takes screenshots by itself. Both draw the same frames. Each worker checks begin_frame once when it starts: its Chromium must produce one frame within 2 seconds, else that worker takes screenshots. A worker whose begun frames fail a render takes screenshots until it restarts. The render estimate says which capture the worker uses and why. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_MEMORY_MB No 0 Each render runs in a process of its own; once that process and everything it started (Chromium, ffmpeg) use more than this many MiB, the render is stopped and failed with its peak memory and the scene it was drawing, and nothing else in the worker is touched. 0 = 60% of the worker container's memory limit (4096 MiB when the container sets none). A render whose pages this does not hold, even one page, is not started. The refusal says the memory to give the worker, then the highest quality that fits the worker now, for the person to choose. An ultra render is held to VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB instead when that is higher. Never more than the container's limit less the preview reserve. VIDEO_STUDIO_ULTRA_RENDER_MEMORY_MB No 16384 The memory ceiling of an ultra (2160p60) render, in MiB, at least. Where the worker container has more memory, it is raised to what the pages its CPUs open need at their measured 2160p peak (about 5.9 GiB a page), so a 4K render draws on more pages instead of 2. It is never more than the worker container's memory limit (the host's memory when the container sets none) less 4 GiB kept for the worker's own jobs or the preview reserve, whichever is larger, and never less than VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_MEMORY_MB's ceiling. Raising it past the limit less the reserve gives nothing: give the container more memory too. See Sizing the workers. 0 = an ultra render is held to the same ceiling as the others. VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_RESERVE_MB No 8192 The memory, in MiB, every worker that draws scene previews keeps out of every render's reach. It is a hard floor of 8192: a lower value keeps 8192, a higher one raises it. A render's ceiling is never more than the container's memory limit (the host's memory when the container sets none) less this, and its pages are laid out in what is left when it starts, so a scene preview always starts beside it on its pages. A worker with VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_CONCURRENCY=0 keeps none. VIDEO_STUDIO_PREVIEW_MEMORY_MB No 0 The memory ceiling of a scene preview's process, in MiB: past it the preview is stopped, and nothing else in the worker is touched; it is drawn again at once on one page, and only failed, with its peak memory, when one page does not fit either. 0 = twice the estimate of the preview at its own size on its 2 pages, the screen inserts the scene shows counted on each page (about 2.7 GiB for a 720p preview without inserts and 4.6 GiB with three video inserts and a picture; about 4.5 GiB and 7.5 GiB at 1080p), kept within the preview reserve and never more than the worker's memory. VIDEO_STUDIO_INSERT_FRAMES_MB No 1024 The screen-insert frames, in MiB, a worker keeps in its temporary directory (/tmp, beside the renders' working directories). A frame of a screen insert costs many times a plain frame to draw; once drawn, every render and scene preview on that worker that shows it again at the same size reads it back instead - the next preview of a scene with an insert takes about the time of a scene without one. A 10 s insert at 1080p keeps about 150 to 300 MiB. Never more than a quarter of what that disk has free; the least recently used go first, and what nothing read for 6 hours. Size the worker's /tmp for it: a Kubernetes emptyDir size limit (the Helm chart's tmpSizeLimit) must hold it with the renders' working directories, or the pod is evicted. 0 = no frame is kept. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_STALL_SECONDS No 120 A render whose progress stands still this many seconds, at any stage, is stopped and resumed in place with the frames it had finished kept; after two resumes it is failed as "stalled at X%". 0 = never. VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_DRAIN_SECONDS No 1200 How long a worker asked to stop (a deployment, a restart) waits for the whole renders it draws past half their frames to finish before it hands them to the next worker, counted from the stop signal. It never waits past WORKER_TERMINATION_GRACE_SECONDS less 30 seconds for the hand-over, so it waits only where the deployment gives its workers a longer termination grace than Kubernetes' default 30 seconds. A render under half its frames goes to a running worker at once, and a scene preview is never waited for. An idle worker stops as before. 0 = never waits. WORKER_TERMINATION_GRACE_SECONDS No 0 The worker pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds (Docker Compose: its stop_grace_period), as its deployment sets it. With WORKER_STARTUP_SECONDS, how long a render the worker hands back when it is stopped waits for the next worker: first in the queue, it is failed only once neither its old worker nor a new one could have taken it. It also bounds how long a stopping worker waits for its renders to finish (VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_DRAIN_SECONDS). 0 = not given: 30 s, the Kubernetes default. Never less than 3 minutes together. docker-compose.yml sets 1260 for its workers. WORKER_STARTUP_SECONDS No 0 How long a new worker pod may take to start: its startup probe's initialDelaySeconds plus failureThreshold x periodSeconds, with the image pull if it is slow. 0 = not given: 570 s, so a deployment that sets neither lets a render wait 10 minutes. A render that waited longer fails naming the workers alive and why none took it; rendering it again at the same quality within a day resumes the same render from the frames it kept. VIDEO_STUDIO_MEDIA_RETENTION_DAYS No 30 Days a recording's or an AI shot's media files are kept once no video uses them any more (removed from the last timeline using them, or that video deleted). The media a video uses are never deleted. A rendered video keeps its own MP4; the recording or shot stays listed, marked expired, to be recorded or generated again. 0 = kept forever. VIDEO_STUDIO_UNUSED_MEDIA_RETENTION_DAYS No 14 Days the media of a recording or an AI shot no video ever used are kept after they were made. 0 = kept forever. "Keep its media" on a recording or a shot exempts it from both. VIDEO_STUDIO_FIGURE_STILL_RETENTION_DAYS No 30 Days the editor's still of a figure scene is kept after it was drawn. A still a video still shows is drawn again by the worker the next time the video is saved or previewed. 0 = kept forever. AGENT_CHECK_FILE_RETENTION_DAYS No 7 Days the pictures an assistant makes to check its own work (frames and region crops of a video, contact sheets, screen-insert sweeps, slide captures, page renders) are kept after they were made. They are working files, collapsed under the reply; a picture a video uses (an image scene, a backdrop) is kept. 0 = kept forever. FILE_RETENTION_AGENT_WORKING_DAYS No 60 Days an assistant's working (scratch) file is kept after its last use (a download, a preview, a read by an assistant, an attach). Editable in Settings > Usage and quotas > Storage & retention; set here, it is locked there (the same for every FILE_RETENTION_* variable and AGENT_CHECK_FILE_RETENTION_DAYS). A file an open work item, a workset, an active shared state, a presentation, a report or a video still uses is kept. The content goes; the file stays in the conversation as a deleted card and its download answers 410 Gone. 0 = kept forever. FILE_RETENTION_AGENT_DOWNLOAD_DAYS No 60 The same, for the files an assistant delivers for download. FILE_RETENTION_AGENT_DAYS No 0 Days the other files assistants, tools and MCP servers return are kept after they were made. 0 = kept forever. FILE_RETENTION_CHAT_DAYS No 0 Days the files people attach in a conversation are kept after they were uploaded. 0 = kept forever. FILE_RETENTION_CHANNEL_DAYS No 0 Days the files received from Teams, Outlook and the other channels are kept. 0 = kept forever. VIDEO_QUALITY_CHECK_ENABLED No true Play every saved video in headless Chromium to check what the audience would see go wrong (text covering text, text past the frame, words on screen too briefly) and report it to the assistant and the editor. false skips the check; the layout that keeps text clear of the subtitles and overlays applies either way.

Voice-over and AI clips use the AI providers (Settings > AI Models) the person may use: OpenAI (speech, Sora) and Google Gemini (speech, Veo). Nothing else is configured for them.

How long renders are kept is not an environment variable: administrators set it in Settings > AI Models > Render retention (see Render retention). VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_KEEP_LAST and VIDEO_STUDIO_RENDER_RETENTION_DAYS are no longer read.

docs.title: Waiting arcade
docs.text:
While an agent works, the chat shows a small self-playing Space Invader. Users can take control of it and play a full-screen game over the interface, with a leaderboard shared by everyone on the platform — see The waiting arcade. Scores are stored in the platform's database; a game that cannot reach the server still plays, it just is not saved.

Variable Required Default Description ARCADE_ENABLED No true Offer the playable arcade and its leaderboard. Set to false to keep only the self-playing waiting animation: every /api/v1/arcade route then answers 404, the chat offers no way to take control, and a ?arcade=play link (the invitation of the chat embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ) just opens the page. This is the only switch: users cannot hide the game themselves, and it is left out only for a user whose system asks for reduced motion.

docs.title: Skill loading
docs.text:
An agent's prompt carries a catalog of its attached skills (name + description) and the agent pulls a skill's full content in on demand with the load_skill tool, so prompt size scales with the number of attached skills rather than with the size of their content. A skill that must stay in the prompt at all times can be pinned per agent on the agent's Configuration tab.

These caps bound the worst case and rarely need changing:

Variable Required Default Description SKILL_LOAD_MAX_CHARS No 60000 Maximum characters returned by one load_skill call. Longer content is truncated with an explicit marker naming how much was cut. SKILL_LOAD_BUDGET No 8 Maximum number of distinct skills one run may load. Re-loading an already-loaded skill never counts again. 0 = unlimited. SKILL_RESOURCE_MAX_BYTES No 40000 Maximum bytes returned by one read_skill_resource call (files bundled with a packaged skill).

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text: This page follows a request through XTM One: which components handle it, where its data is stored, and what leaves your network. It is written for administrators and security reviewers deciding how to deploy the platform. The components themselves are described in the Overview; what an agent shares with an AI model, and how to limit it, is in AI governance.

docs.title: How the pieces connect
docs.text:
Two services do the work: the platform, which answers people and systems, and the workers, which run the work nobody waits for on screen. Both read and write the same stores, and both call the AI providers and the tools agents use.

flowchart LR
    U[People and systems] <--> P[Platform]
    P -- run due --> W[Workers]
    P & W <--> ST[(PostgreSQL, Redis,<br/>object storage)]
    P & W <--> AI[AI providers]
    P & W <--> T[Tools: integrations,<br/>MCP servers, sandbox]
    P & W --> TR[(Traces)]
  • Platform: the API, the web application, the chat, and every entry point other systems use. It authenticates each caller, runs every interactive turn, and schedules background work.
  • Workers: assignment runs, sub-agent tasks, and the processing of knowledge-base documents.
  • AI providers: the services hosting the language, embedding, speech and image models. See Configuration.
  • Tools: integrations, MCP servers, built-in tools, and the sandbox that runs custom tools and the code interpreter.
  • Traces: the record of each AI interaction (prompts, tool calls, tokens, timing, errors). Settings > Observability can keep them without their content, or turn them off. See Monitoring.

docs.title: The agent loop
docs.text:
Every agent answer, whether a chat reply or an assignment run, follows the same loop:

  1. The request reaches the platform, which authenticates the caller and loads the agent's configuration.
  2. The prompt is assembled: the agent's persona and instructions, its skills, relevant memory and knowledge, the conversation so far, and the list of tools the agent may use.
  3. The prompt and the tool list go to the configured AI provider.
  4. The model either answers or asks for a tool. It cannot run anything itself: it sends back the name of a tool and its arguments.
  5. The platform or the worker checks the call (permissions, approval rules, budgets) and runs it: searching a knowledge base, calling an integration, delegating to another agent. The result goes back to the model, which can ask for another tool or write its answer.
  6. The answer is delivered and the exchange is recorded as a trace.

What is a tool?

A tool is a function that runs on the platform, such as "search this knowledge base" or "send a Slack message". The AI provider is given a description of each available tool but never touches your systems: it can only request a tool call, and the platform decides whether and how to run it. Credentials never go to the model. See AI governance.

docs.title: A chat message
docs.text:
A message sent from the web application is answered by the platform, while you watch:

sequenceDiagram
    actor You
    participant Platform
    participant Redis
    participant AI as AI provider
    participant Tools

    You->>Platform: Send a message
    Platform->>Platform: Check access, quota and prompt safety
    Platform->>AI: Prompt and available tools
    loop Until the model has an answer
        AI->>Platform: Ask to run a tool
        opt The tool needs approval
            Platform-->>You: Ask for approval
            You->>Platform: Approve or decline
        end
        Platform->>Tools: Run the tool
        Tools-->>Platform: Result
        Platform->>AI: Tool result
    end
    AI->>Platform: Answer, streamed
    Platform->>Redis: Publish the stream
    Redis-->>You: Live answer, on any open tab or device
    Platform->>Platform: Save the conversation and the trace
  • Safety checks. Before the model sees the message, the platform checks your quota and, when Prompt safety (Nova) is connected, screens the message against its rules; a blocked message never reaches the AI provider.
  • Approvals. A tool that changes something can wait for a person to approve it. See Human approval of tool calls.
  • Streaming. The answer streams through Redis, so it reaches you whichever platform replica your browser is connected to. A message you send while the agent is still working is added to the running turn.
  • Long work. A sub-agent the agent delegates to in the background runs on a worker; when it finishes, the worker writes the follow-up answer in the same conversation.

The same path serves the other interactive entry points: the embedded assistant of OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, the Office add-in and the browser extension, the Chat API, the LLM proxy, MCP clients and partner agents.

docs.title: A background run
docs.text:
An assignment runs without anyone watching. The platform decides that a run is due, and a worker carries it out:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Trigger as Trigger (schedule, webhook, event)
    participant Platform
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    participant Redis
    participant Worker
    participant AI as AI provider

    Trigger->>Platform: Schedule tick, webhook or event
    Platform->>PG: Record the run as due
    Platform->>Redis: Wake the workers
    Worker->>PG: Claim the run
    loop Agent loop
        Worker->>AI: Prompt and tools
        AI-->>Worker: Answer or tool call
    end
    Worker->>PG: Save the result
    Worker-->>Platform: Notifications, next assignment
  1. Triggers. A schedule, an assignment webhook, an event from an integration (polled by the platform, or pushed to it, like the notifications OpenCTI and OpenAEV send), a platform event, a work item, or a person pressing Run. See Assignments and triggers.
  2. Recording. The run is written to PostgreSQL before anything else, so it survives a restart of any component.
  3. Claiming. Workers claim the due runs; two workers never take the same run. The worker renews its claim while the run lasts.
  4. Running. The worker runs the agent loop. A run that needs a human answer or an approval pauses, holds no worker while it waits, and resumes when the answer arrives.
  5. Recovery. If a worker stops, its claims expire and another worker resumes the run. A run nobody works on is failed after STALE_ASSIGNMENT_RUN_SECONDS (see Configuration).
  6. Results. The outcome, the notifications and the next chained assignment are recorded; the run appears in Operations.

docs.title: A message from a messaging app
docs.text:
A message sent to a bot in Slack, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord or Google Chat:

  1. The messaging service calls the platform's channel webhook. Discord is the exception: the platform keeps its own connection to Discord.
  2. The platform acknowledges at once and processes the message in the background.
  3. It identifies the sender (by email or a linked identity), applies the bot's rules, and finds the agent and the conversation.
  4. The agent loop runs as for a web chat, with the output shaped for that app.
  5. The answer is sent back through the messaging service, split to its size limits. Files are shared as signed links.

See Channels and bots.

docs.title: A knowledge base
docs.text:
Adding a document and searching it are two separate paths:

flowchart LR
    D[Upload, sync source,<br/>or chat attachment] --> P[Platform]
    P -- original file --> S3[(Object storage)]
    P -- processing job --> R[(Redis queue)]
    R --> W[Worker]
    W -- extract, split --> W
    W -- text of each chunk --> E[Embedding provider]
    E -- vectors --> W
    W -- chunks and vectors --> PG[(PostgreSQL + pgvector)]
    Q[Agent search] --> PG
  • Ingestion. The platform stores the source and queues a processing job. A worker extracts the text (PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint and text formats), splits it into chunks, sends each chunk to the embedding provider, and stores the chunks and their vectors in PostgreSQL. When a knowledge base describes figures, PDF pages are also sent to the chat model as images. Sources kept in sync (websites, Notion, cloud drives, GitHub and others) are fetched by the platform on their schedule.
  • Search. An agent's search combines vector similarity and full-text search in PostgreSQL, so both meaning and exact terms count. Only the chunks it finds go to the model, not the whole knowledge base.

See Knowledge bases.

docs.title: Other systems calling XTM One
docs.text:
Entry point Who uses it Authentication Embedded assistant and platform registration OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ Registration token, then each user's signed identity LLM proxy (/v1) Any OpenAI-compatible client; an agent: model runs an agent Personal API key MCP endpoints (/mcp/...) MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, ...) Personal API key or OAuth Agent-to-agent (/a2a/...) Partner agents Credentials issued to the partner (an OAuth client, or its Microsoft Entra identity); HTTPS only Chat API Your scripts and client apps A session token Assignment webhooks (/api/hooks/...) Your SIEM, SOAR and other systems The assignment's webhook secret Public chat widget Visitors of a website where an agent is published None: the agent is public

Each request runs as an identity the platform knows (a user, or the owner of the assignment or agent), and it reaches only what that identity may use. See XTM Suite integration and Platform MCP servers.

docs.title: Relays and runners
docs.text:
Relays and runners live in your network and open the connection to the platform themselves:

  • Relay. When an integration or MCP server is bound to a relay group, its calls do not leave from the platform. The platform hands each request, encrypted, to a relay of the group through Redis; the relay makes the call on your network and streams the response back. Only metadata (time, target, status) is logged. See Relays.
  • Runner. When an agent acts on a computer, the platform sends the command to that computer's runner over its connection; a shell command can wait for approval first. The runner executes it and returns the result. See XTM One Desktop and runners.

docs.title: Where data is stored
docs.text:
All data stays in the stores you deploy:

Data Where it lives Users, groups, agents, assignments, configuration PostgreSQL Conversations, runs, work items, audit log PostgreSQL Knowledge-base chunks and vectors, long-term memory PostgreSQL (pgvector) Uploaded and generated files, knowledge-base sources, code-interpreter workspaces Object storage (Silo / S3) Job queue, live streams, short-term memory, single-use links, rate limits Redis LLM traces PostgreSQL, or PostgreSQL and ClickHouse when configured; large payloads in object storage (see Monitoring)

Credentials (AI provider keys, integrations, channel bots, MCP servers, secret variables, two-factor secrets) are encrypted before they are written to the database, with a key derived from SECRET_KEY. With a secret vault, the database holds only a reference and the platform reads the secret from the vault when it is used. See Configuration.

How long each kind of data is kept is described in Data retention.

docs.title: What leaves the platform
docs.text:
Destination What is sent When How to control it AI providers Prompts: instructions, conversation, tool results, the knowledge chunks found Every agent turn Choose the provider and models; use a local model to keep everything inside. See AI governance Embedding provider The text of document chunks, and search queries Ingestion and search Settings > AI Models > Embedding Integrations and MCP servers The arguments of the tool calls agents make Tool calls What each agent is given; approvals; relays Langfuse Traces, with prompts and the user's email When connected Settings > Observability SMTP server Password resets, invitations, announcements When configured SMTP_* Filigran telemetry Anonymous counts, never content Every 6 hours TELEMETRY_ENABLED (see Usage telemetry) XTM Hub Platform registration When you register Settings > Parameters

The Filigran license is verified offline: checking it sends nothing to Filigran.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with AI governance to understand what is shared with AI providers and how to control it.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page covers the step-by-step deployment of a self-hosted XTM One instance using Docker Compose. Before starting, read the Overview to understand the deployment models and the architecture.

docs.title: Infrastructure requirements
docs.text: Every deployment runs the same services: the platform, the workers, PostgreSQL, Redis and object storage, plus the optional components you choose. What changes is how much CPU, RAM, and storage you give them. Start from the baseline below, then adjust with What drives sizing.

docs.title: Resource baseline
docs.text:
The official XTM One Helm chart sets the following per-component resource requests and limits. Use them as a starting point and tune to your observed load:

Component CPU request Memory request CPU limit Memory limit Storage Platform 2 4 Gi 4 8 Gi — Worker 1 2 Gi 2 4 Gi — PostgreSQL (per instance, 2 instances) 1 2 Gi 2 4 Gi 64 Gi Redis 0.5 512 Mi — 2 Gi 2 Gi Silo (S3) 0.5 1 Gi — 2 Gi sized to your object volume

The platform and the worker scale differently. See the Scaling model for how to add worker replicas and keep the database connection budget in range.

OS: Any Linux distribution that supports your chosen container runtime. The Docker images are based on python:3.14-slim (Debian).

Disk: 20 GB minimum for the OS, container images, and initial database. Plan for more based on your knowledge base size and file attachment volume — PostgreSQL data and Silo object storage grow over time.

docs.title: What drives sizing
docs.text:
The baseline above suits a typical deployment. Whether you should size up or down depends on how the customer uses the platform. Each resource is driven by a different part of the workload, so profile the use case against these drivers — you rarely need to grow everything at once.

The two dimensions that matter most:

  • Interactive use — how many people chat with agents at the same time, and how heavy each conversation is (long streams, large tool results). This drives the platform and, indirectly, Redis.
  • Automation and data — how many assignments run, how often, and how much content agents ingest and remember. This drives the worker, PostgreSQL, and Silo.

Platform — CPU / RAM. Driven by concurrent interactive users and live chat streaming (SSE, LLM proxy). Size up when many people use chat at once or you see request latency climb — add CPU/RAM and raise WEB_WORKERS. A mostly-automation deployment with few human chat users can stay at the minimum. Chat is stateless per request, so this scales with concurrency, not total user count.

In numbers

WEB_WORKERS is the number of concurrent HTTP/chat processes. The default is 2; the production rule of thumb is 2 × CPU cores + 1, so a 4-core platform runs 9 — roughly ×4 the default's request capacity.

Worker — replicas / CPU. Driven by background-job volume and concurrency — the number of active assignments, how frequently their triggers fire, and how bursty they are (many schedules landing together), plus sub-agent fan-out and knowledge-base ingestion. Size up when runs start queuing or embedding lags. A deployment with a few daily assignments needs one worker; hundreds of assignments, tight schedules, or heavy sub-agent use need replicas.

In numbers

Each worker runs up to MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS assignment runs (default 10) and MAX_CONCURRENT_SUB_AGENT_TASKS sub-agent tasks (default 5) at once, plus up to WORKER_CONCURRENCY queued jobs such as document processing (default 20). Three workers run up to 30 assignment runs at the same time. Throughput scales linearly with replica count, so match the replica count to your peak number of simultaneous runs, and keep the database connection budget in range.

PostgreSQL — storage / RAM. Driven by total data volume — knowledge-base documents and their vector chunks (RAG), agent memory, and run/audit history retention. Storage grows with knowledge bases and history; RAM helps vector search stay fast as embeddings grow. Size up for large or many knowledge bases, long retention, or slow semantic search.

In numbers

Storage is roughly proportional to content — ×2 the ingested documents and history is about ×2 the disk. Start from the chart's 64 Gi baseline and scale from your own corpus size; add RAM only if semantic search slows as embeddings grow.

Redis — RAM. Driven by peak job-queue depth and active-session count — pub/sub for the live activity feed and notifications, plus transient agent state (short/medium-term memory, in-flight chat markers, quota and rate-limit counters). It holds working state, not your data, so it stays small; size up only if you run very high job throughput or many simultaneous active agents. Storage never needs to grow with your knowledge bases.

In numbers

The chart baseline is a 512 Mi request with a 2 Gi limit — roughly ×4 headroom for bursts. Most deployments never approach the limit because working state is transient; treat a rising limit as a signal of extreme queue depth or session concurrency, not routine growth.

Silo / S3 — storage. Driven purely by stored bytes — uploaded knowledge-base documents, chat attachments, and agent-generated files (images, code-interpreter charts). CPU/RAM stay negligible; only disk grows. Size the volume to the customer's expected document and attachment footprint, and prefer a managed S3 (via S3_*) when that footprint is large or must be highly available.

In numbers

Storage equals the sum of stored file sizes — ×2 the uploaded documents and attachments is ×2 the volume. There is no compute multiplier to plan for; provision disk to the customer's raw file footprint plus headroom.

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
You need Docker Engine 24+ with Docker Compose v2.

The repository includes a ready-to-use docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: Get the deployment files
docs.text:
Check Releases for the latest version tag.

Option A — clone a release (builds images from source):

git clone --branch <version-tag> --depth 1 https://github.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one.git && cd xtm-one

Option B — use pre-built images (no build required):

VERSION="<version-tag>"

mkdir xtm-one && cd xtm-one
curl -fSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one/${VERSION}/docker-compose.yml"
curl -fSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one/${VERSION}/.env.sample"

Then create an override to pull images instead of building:

# docker-compose.override.yml
services:
  platform:
    image: xtmone/platform:<version-tag>
    build: !reset null
  worker:
    image: xtmone/worker:<version-tag>
    build: !reset null
  worker-preview:
    image: xtmone/worker:<version-tag>
    build: !reset null

worker-preview is a second worker service of the shipped docker-compose.yml (two containers). It uses the worker image and runs the same jobs, so it needs the same override.

docs.title: Configure environment
docs.text:
cp .env.sample .env
chmod 600 .env
touch .gitignore
grep -qxF ".env" .gitignore || echo ".env" >> .gitignore

Edit .env and fill in the required values. At minimum you must set:

  • SECRET_KEY — generate with python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))"
  • ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD
  • BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL — the public URL of your instance
  • DB_PASSWORD — password for the bundled PostgreSQL
  • S3_ACCESS_KEY and S3_SECRET_KEY — credentials for the bundled Silo object storage

If you connect OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platforms, also set:
