  • PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN — the secret those platforms register with (use the same value on each); generate with python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))". A standalone deployment that connects none can leave it empty. Left empty, Docker Compose falls back to a published placeholder, which only keeps platforms that are already registered connected - it cannot register a new one - and is reported at startup and in the security audit (Settings → Security) until you replace it. While it is in use, the Filigran license certificate is withheld from registration answers, so platforms sub-licensed by your Filigran license cannot prove their Enterprise Edition.

The complete list of available parameters is documented in the Configuration section.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
docker compose up -d

The platform waits for PostgreSQL, Redis, and Silo health checks to pass, then automatically runs migrations, creates the admin user, and seeds default templates.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
docker compose ps          # all services should show "healthy"
curl localhost:4000/api/health/ready   # 200 = fully ready

docs.title: Configure the platform
docs.text:
1. Open your BASE_URL in a browser.
  2. Sign in with ADMIN_EMAIL / ADMIN_PASSWORD.
  3. Go to Settings → AI Models — add at least one LLM provider.
  4. Configure authentication if needed — see Authentication.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text: Port Purpose 4000/tcp Platform HTTP (chat streams over SSE; XTM One Desktop, runners and relays also connect over WebSocket)

docs.title: Exposing the platform
docs.text:
The platform serves plain HTTP on port 4000. In production you put something in front of it that terminates TLS (so users get HTTPS) and forwards traffic to port 4000. Whatever you choose, it must satisfy the same requirements:

Requirement Why Nginx example Forward client IP Needed for rate limiting and audit logs, with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS naming the proxy (below) proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; Forward protocol OAuth callbacks need the real scheme proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; Allow large request bodies Dataset and evaluation ZIP imports can reach 500 MB, knowledge base uploads 50 MB client_max_body_size 500m; HTTP/2 between browsers and the proxy A browser opens at most 6 HTTP/1.1 connections per origin. Every tab of the app holds its activity stream, and a chat tab also its conversation's event stream plus, while an answer is written, its message stream: over HTTP/1.1 a few open tabs use them all up and the app stops loading. HTTP/2 carries them on one connection. The proxy may reach the platform over HTTP/1.1 listen 443 ssl; http2 on; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; before, listen 443 ssl http2;) Do not buffer streamed responses Chat answers stream as server-sent events; a proxy that buffers them shows each answer only once it is complete Nginx honours the X-Accel-Buffering: no header the platform sends; on another proxy, turn response buffering off for /api/ WebSocket upgrade XTM One Desktop, runners and relays connect over WebSocket; without the upgrade they fall back to slower HTTP long-polling. Chat does not use it proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; Generous read/idle timeout LLM calls and streams can run 60s–5min. An idle stream writes a keep-alive every 15 s, so a read timeout must stay above 15 s proxy_read_timeout 300s; Trust the proxy The platform honours the forwarded protocol and client IP only from the proxy you name: without it the audit log records the proxy's address for every user, rate limiting sees one client and the A2A endpoints refuse every request (403 https required) On the platform, not the proxy: FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=<proxy address> (Client address and protocol behind the proxy)

Set BASE_URL to the public https:// URL you expose, regardless of which option you pick.

Option A — Reverse proxy (default). Best for a standard host with a public IP or load balancer. Terminate TLS with any reverse proxy — Nginx, Caddy, Traefik, or a cloud load balancer — and forward to port 4000. Caddy and Traefik obtain and renew certificates automatically; with Nginx, pair it with your own certificate or a tool such as Certbot.

Option B — Connection tunnel. Instead of opening an inbound port, you can front the platform with a tunnel. This fits three cases:

  • Evaluation or demo — a tunnel such as Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) or ngrok gives you a public HTTPS URL in seconds, with no proxy or certificate to configure.
  • No public IP — for a host behind CGNAT, a home lab, or an edge site, an outbound-only tunnel exposes the platform without any inbound firewall rule.
  • Private-only access — a mesh VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard reaches the platform over a private overlay with no public exposure at all.

A tunnel must meet the same requirements as a reverse proxy above. Two points need particular attention:

Watch the tunnel timeout

XTM One makes long LLM calls and holds long-lived SSE streams for chat. A tunnel with a short origin/idle timeout will cut these off — for example, Cloudflare's proxy enforces a ~100-second origin timeout (HTTP 524). Use a tunnel that allows long-lived connections, and confirm chat streaming works end to end before relying on it.

Data residency with public tunnels

A public tunnel (Cloudflare, ngrok) terminates TLS on that provider's edge, so your traffic transits a third party. If you self-host XTM One specifically for data-residency or air-gapped requirements, prefer a reverse proxy you control or a private mesh VPN (Tailscale, WireGuard), which keeps traffic on your own network.

docs.title: Client address and protocol behind the proxy
docs.text:
Behind a proxy the platform's peer is the proxy, not the user: the user's address arrives in X-Forwarded-For and the original scheme in X-Forwarded-Proto. Tell the platform which peer may speak for the client with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS. Uvicorn, which serves the platform, then rewrites the client address and the scheme from those headers for requests from the listed addresses only, and reads X-Forwarded-For from its end, so a client cannot choose its own address even behind a proxy that appends to the header. Without it (uvicorn trusts only 127.0.0.1 by default) every request looks like plain HTTP from the proxy: per-IP rate limiting on /auth/login and /auth/forgot-password becomes one bucket shared by everyone, the audit trail records the proxy's address, and the A2A endpoints, /runners/enroll, /mcp/oauth/register and /mcp/oauth/token report an unconfirmed transport.

TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS trusts any peer

TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true reads the headers from any peer and takes the client from the leftmost X-Forwarded-For value, which the client itself writes behind a proxy that appends to the header, so it suits only a proxy that overwrites the header and is the only thing that reaches the platform. It also takes precedence over FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS when both are set. It is also the Trust proxy headers field of Settings > Access and security > Security options (the variable, when set, wins and locks it). While it is on, the platform logs a warning at startup, or when the field is switched on, and the security audit (/api/v1/security-audit) reports it. FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS is the recommended setting: switch to it with the steps below.

  1. Find the proxy's address as the platform sees it. Every request writes an access-log line whose client_ip field is the peer; with the default settings it is the proxy's address. Name that address, or the network it lives in.
  2. Make sure the proxy sends both headers, as in the examples below. X-Forwarded-Proto must be one value (https): uvicorn ignores a comma-separated list there.
  3. Set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS on the platform container and restart: an IP, a CIDR or a comma-separated list. It is read from the container's environment when the platform starts, so it is not a Settings > Access and security field. Hostnames are not resolved and a CIDR needs its host bits at zero (10.42.0.0/16); any other entry trusts nobody, and the platform names it in a startup warning. Behind several proxies (a CDN, then a load balancer, then an ingress), list every hop between the user and the platform, since the client is the rightmost address that is not listed. Avoid * unless the platform is reachable only through the proxy: it trusts every peer and reads the start of the chain again.
  4. Check it before relying on it: browse to the platform and read your request's access-log line. Its client_ip field is the address the platform uses without TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS, and must now show your own address rather than the proxy's (while the flag is on, forwarded_for shows what the flag reads). If it still shows the proxy, the list does not name it: correct it and restart.
  5. Turn TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS off where it is set: remove TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS (or set it to false) and restart the platform, or, when the variable is not set, turn off Trust proxy headers in Settings > Access and security > Security options.
  6. Check the result: the startup log no longer carries the warning about the flag, the security audit no longer reports it, and the access log's forwarded_for field, written only under TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS, disappears.
NginxTraefikKubernetes ingress 
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

Appending with $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for is safe here: the platform reads the chain from its end. For nginx on the Docker host in front of the Compose stack, the platform sees the Docker bridge gateway of the Compose network (for example 172.18.0.1, docker network inspect <project>_default); for nginx in the same Compose network, its container address or the network's subnet:

FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=172.18.0.1

Traefik sends both headers by default and drops the X-Forwarded-* values a client sent unless the entry point lists the sender in forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs (list a load balancer or CDN in front of Traefik there, not in the platform). Name Traefik itself, by its address or its Docker network's subnet:

FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=172.20.0.0/16

The peer is the ingress controller's pod, so name the cluster's pod network (for example 10.42.0.0/16 on k3s, 10.244.0.0/16 on a kubeadm cluster with Flannel) on the platform container:

env:
  - name: FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS
    value: "10.42.0.0/16"

Neither Helm chart sets it yet: until they gain a first-class value, set it in the platform's env map, xtmOne.platform.env in helm-xtm-one and xtmone.platform.env in helm-xtm-suite:

xtmOne:
  platform:
    env:
      FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS: "10.42.0.0/16"

For an ingress controller on the host network, name the node addresses instead. ingress-nginx writes into X-Forwarded-For the address it received the connection from; behind a cloud load balancer that is the load balancer's unless the service keeps the client address (externalTrafficPolicy: Local, PROXY protocol) or the controller trusts the load balancer's header (use-forwarded-headers with proxy-real-ip-cidr).

docs.title: When the platform reports an undeclared proxy
docs.text:
The platform reads the client address from X-Forwarded-For only, never from X-Real-IP or Forwarded, and only from a peer FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS names. When an audited request - a sign-in, a change an administrator makes - carries X-Forwarded-For from a peer it does not name, whether no proxy is declared or another one is, or names its client only in Forwarded or X-Real-IP, the platform logs one warning naming that peer and what to do, once a day for all its processes and replicas, and again after a restart with another FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS:

A request carried X-Forwarded-For while no reverse proxy is declared - "Trust proxy headers" (TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS) is off and FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS names none beyond this host - so the audit trail recorded the address of the peer that relayed it, 10.42.0.17, instead of the user's. If that peer is your reverse proxy or ingress, set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to its address or CIDR (behind a Kubernetes ingress, the cluster's pod network) and restart. Said once a day for the whole platform; the security audit (Settings > Access and security) reports it too.

The security audit (Settings → Security) reports it as the warning "The audit trail records a proxy's address, not users'", naming the latest such peer any replica saw in the last day, with the exact remedy. A proxy declared under another address than the one it connects from - the Docker host's LAN address for a proxy on that host, which reaches the container from the Compose network's gateway - is reported the same way: name the address the warning gives. With no reverse proxy in front of the platform, such a request carried headers a client sent itself: nothing needs to change, the platform ignores them.

Once the platform has restarted with the proxy named, sign out and sign in again, then open the Audit Logs page: your login shows your own address, not the proxy's. The warning is no longer logged, and the security audit stops reporting the proxy - a proxy it reported for sending no X-Forwarded-For drops out 24 hours after its last such request.

docs.title: Serving under a path prefix
docs.text:
By default the platform expects to be reached at the root of its host (https://xtm.example.com/). To serve it under a path prefix instead — one host shared by several products, such as https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one/ — set BASE_PATH to the prefix and include it in BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL:

BASE_PATH=/xtm-one
BASE_URL=https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one
FRONTEND_URL=https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one

The platform then serves its interface, API, WebSockets and MCP endpoints under /xtm-one/..., and every absolute link it hands out (OAuth callbacks, webhook URLs, SSO redirects, the embeddable chat widget, e-mails) carries the prefix. Both reverse-proxy styles work — the platform recognises a request whether the proxy forwarded the prefix or stripped it — so use whichever your proxy makes natural:

Nginx (prefix forwarded)Nginx (prefix stripped)Traefik 
location /xtm-one/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000;   # no trailing slash: the prefix is forwarded as is
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    client_max_body_size 500m;
}
location = /xtm-one { return 301 /xtm-one/; }

location /xtm-one/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000/;  # trailing slash: nginx strips /xtm-one before forwarding
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix /xtm-one;  # tells the platform the prefix was stripped
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    client_max_body_size 500m;
}
location = /xtm-one { return 301 /xtm-one/; }

http:
  routers:
    xtm-one:
      rule: "Host(`intranet.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/xtm-one`)"
      service: xtm-one
      # Optional - the platform accepts the prefix either way:
      # middlewares: [xtm-one-strip]
  services:
    xtm-one:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://xtm-one-platform:4000"
  middlewares:
    xtm-one-strip:
      stripPrefix:
        prefixes: ["/xtm-one"]

Three constraints:

  • BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL must carry the prefix. The platform routes requests by BASE_PATH, but it builds outgoing links from BASE_URL (OAuth callbacks, webhooks, the MCP resource identifiers) and sends the browser back to FRONTEND_URL after an SSO or OAuth round-trip; when either disagrees it logs a warning at startup and every such link lands on the proxy's 404.
  • The prefix must not start with a namespace the platform serves itself — /api, /v1, /mcp, /xtm, /a2a, /office, /metrics, /assets, /.well-known — nor with the name of one of its static files (/favicon.ico, /logos, /robots.txt, /site.webmanifest, ...), because a stripped request under such a prefix could not be told apart from a direct request for that resource. Such a value is refused at startup.
  • The prefix is a plain path: ASCII letters, digits and -, _, ., ~ between slashes, no percent-encoding, no query string. /xtm-one and /apps/xtm-one are fine (xtm-one/ and /xtm-one/ are read as /xtm-one); /xtm%20one or a prefix with an accented letter is refused.
  • A prefix that is also the address of a platform page (/tools, /agents, /chat, /settings, /login, ...) is refused until you declare the proxy with BASE_PATH_MODE. The platform tells the two proxy styles apart per request - an X-Forwarded-Prefix header naming the prefix means the proxy stripped it, otherwise a path under the prefix was forwarded - and for such a prefix the second reading is ambiguous: behind a stripping proxy the public /tools/tools/123 arrives as /tools/123, which is also the forwarded form of another page. BASE_PATH_MODE=forwarded declares that the proxy keeps the prefix (nginx proxy_pass without a trailing slash, Traefik without StripPrefix); BASE_PATH_MODE=stripped declares that it removes it and sends X-Forwarded-Prefix - Traefik's StripPrefix does so by itself, nginx needs the proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix line of the example above. Any other prefix needs no declaration.

BASE_PATH is the one source of the prefix: X-Forwarded-Prefix is read only as the per-request signal that the prefix it names was stripped (a header naming anything else is ignored), and uvicorn's --root-path is not needed (a deployment that already sets it to the same value keeps working). A request for the bare prefix (https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one, no trailing slash) is answered with a redirect to /xtm-one/ when the proxy forwards it, and served directly when the proxy strips it; that redirect is built from the scheme the platform sees, so behind a TLS-terminating proxy declare it with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS (as for any HTTPS deployment; an nginx reaching a Docker Compose deployment at 127.0.0.1:4000, as in the examples above, connects from the Compose network's gateway - see Client address and protocol behind the proxy) - or keep the location = /xtm-one rule of the examples, which lets the proxy answer it. With Docker Compose, BASE_PATH, BASE_PATH_MODE, BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL set in .env reach both the platform and the worker containers (the worker builds absolute links too). The same values apply to the Helm chart's environment (BASE_PATH / BASE_PATH_MODE on the platform and worker deployments, through the chart's extra env until it gains a first-class value) and to the ingress path; PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL, when set, is an origin and the platform appends the prefix to it itself (a value that already carries a path is used as is). The container itself still answers /api/health, /api/health/ready and /metrics on its own port without the prefix, so liveness / readiness probes and Prometheus scrapes are unchanged.

docs.title: MCP clients authenticating with OAuth
docs.text:
An MCP client (Claude, Cursor, ...) that signs in to this platform's MCP endpoints with OAuth discovers the authorization server from the issuer https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one. RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 put the well-known segment before the issuer's path, so the client asks the root of the host — https://intranet.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/xtm-one and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/xtm-one/mcp/user — which the /xtm-one/ rule above never sees. The platform serves both forms (the path-inserted one and the /xtm-one/.well-known/... one); forward the well-known paths to it as well, without stripping anything:

NginxTraefik 
location /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000; }
location /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/  { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000; }

http:
  routers:
    xtm-one-oauth-discovery:
      rule: "Host(`intranet.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/.well-known/oauth-`)"
      service: xtm-one   # no StripPrefix on this router

Clients authenticating with an API key (fcp-...) and the platform's own connections to other MCP servers need nothing of this.

Not served under a prefix in this release

The Microsoft Office add-in (/office/) is built for the root of the host: its bundle references /office/assets/... and it recognises the platform by that path. Under BASE_PATH the add-in's page is served at /xtm-one/office/ but the add-in itself does not load there; deploy it from a platform served at the root, or wait for the follow-up.

docs.title: Air-gapped deployments
docs.text:
Air-gapped deployments work if you use a local AI provider (Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on your network) and the built-in Silo for storage. To get Docker images into an air-gapped network:

# On a machine with internet access — export the images (pre-built images setup from Option B):
docker compose pull
docker save xtmone/platform:<version-tag> xtmone/worker:<version-tag> pgvector/pgvector:pg17 redis:8-alpine pgsty/silo:latest > xtm-one-images.tar
# With the optional OpenSandbox profile, add its server and sandbox images (see Configuration > OpenSandbox).

# Transfer xtm-one-images.tar to the air-gapped host, then load:
docker load < xtm-one-images.tar

docs.title: Scaling model
docs.text:
What drives sizing tells you which resource to grow for a given use case. This section covers the mechanics — the structural reason the platform and the worker scale in fundamentally different ways, and the one constraint that couples them.

Two different \"workers\"

The word worker means two separate things here. The worker service (the worker container / Helm worker replicas) is the background-job runner you scale horizontally. WEB_WORKERS is unrelated: it sets the number of uvicorn HTTP worker processes inside the platform container, which serve the API and chat. Adding worker replicas does not change WEB_WORKERS, and vice versa.

  • The platform scales vertically first, and can run more than one replica. Give it more CPU/RAM and raise WEB_WORKERS for more throughput. Extra platform replicas are supported for availability (a rollout or a node drain never leaves zero pods serving) and for load: every background service it runs is coordinated across processes, because a single pod already runs WEB_WORKERS processes (2 by default) that each run all of them. See Running more than one platform replica for what is shared, and the few things that stay per process.
  • The worker service scales horizontally — it holds no singleton state, so you add replicas for more background-job throughput. Scaling is manual (there is no autoscaler). The shipped docker-compose.yml starts three worker containers: worker and the two worker-preview containers. See What drives sizing for when to add more.
  • The connection budget couples the two — every platform HTTP worker process and every worker replica opens its own PostgreSQL pool, so max_connections must accommodate (DB_POOL_SIZE + DB_MAX_OVERFLOW) × (WEB_WORKERS × platform replicas + worker replicas) + overhead. Count the rollout too: with a surge rollout (maxSurge: 1) one extra platform pod runs next to the others until the old one is gone. Recalculate it whenever you change a count or the pool sizes (see Configuration).

docs.title: Running more than one platform replica
docs.text:
Each platform process (every uvicorn worker of every replica) runs the same startup and background work. What makes that safe:

What How it is coordinated Database migrations and built-in data seeding PostgreSQL advisory locks: one process migrates / seeds at a time, the others wait and re-run the idempotent steps Vector index builds PostgreSQL advisory lock Assignment scheduler (cron triggers, integration event polling, sweeps, maintenance) Redis window lock: one tick per minute across all processes and replicas Anonymous usage telemetry Redis window lease: one process exports per interval for the whole install, with values read from the database; a process that dies hands over when the lease expires, and a Redis outage skips the export rather than sending one per process A2A stale-task reaper, A2A partner card sweep Rows claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: concurrent sweeps take disjoint work Chat streams Turn state and frames through Redis: a stream on any replica follows a turn running on another, and Stop, steering and approvals reach the turn wherever it runs Runner connections (XTM One Desktop / headless runners) Redis pub/sub wakes the replica holding a runner's socket; results are awaited through Redis on any replica Activity stream (SSE), presence, rate limits, OAuth / MCP OAuth state, desktop sign-in Redis Discord bot Each process opens its own gateway session; the first to claim a message (Redis) answers it Platform branding (name, logo) Each process, the worker service included, re-reads it every minute: an admin change reaches every process within a minute Channel webhooks (Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp, Google Chat), REST and MCP endpoints Stateless per request; Slack events are also de-duplicated in Redis

What stays per process, and what it means:

  • Browser tool sessions. The headless browser an agent drives lives in the process that ran the turn. A later turn served by another process opens a fresh browser (the page and its cookies are gone). Each chat message is its own request, so two turns of a conversation can run in different processes; enable session affinity on the ingress if agents rely on a browser session across turns.
  • Outbound rate limiters for integrations (for example the HubSpot search pacer) are per process: with more processes the combined request rate against a provider can exceed what one process allows itself. Integrations retry on 429, so the effect is extra retries, not failures.
  • Prometheus metrics (/metrics) are per process: a scrape is answered by whichever WEB_WORKERS process takes it, so apart from the gauges recomputed on every scrape (quota, assignment queue, relays, sandbox; see Monitoring) a series is a sample of one process, not a counter to read with rate() or increase(). The logs are the exact record.
  • Caches of licence state, AI settings and LLM provider clients are per process with short expiries (seconds to a few minutes): after a change, other processes follow within that time.

Migrations run on the first new pod to start, while the previous version still serves: a rolling update (with any replica count) relies on every migration staying compatible with the version before it, which the project's migration rules require.

Running more workers (Docker Compose). The worker service has no fixed container name, so you can scale it directly:

docker compose up -d --scale worker=3

Each worker creates its own connection pools, so recalculate the PostgreSQL connection budget accordingly. On Kubernetes, add replicas through the Helm chart instead.

docs.title: Kubernetes and Helm
docs.text:
XTM One can be deployed two ways: the Docker Compose stack described above, which runs the full stack on a single host, or the official Helm chart, which runs the same container images on Kubernetes. Choose the one that fits your infrastructure.

The chart deploys the platform and worker images and can optionally provision the backing services. Its prerequisites are:

  • Kubernetes 1.28+ and Helm 3.12+
  • the CloudNativePG operator for managed PostgreSQL with pgvector
  • an S3-compatible object store: the chart ships Silo, the community-maintained fork of MinIO (or point the platform at an external S3)
  • Redis (deployed separately, or an external Redis)

Wire the health probes as livenessProbe (/api/health) and readinessProbe (/api/health/ready). The worker scales horizontally by adding replicas; the platform scales vertically first and can run more than one replica (see the Scaling model above).

Give the platform pod a terminationGracePeriodSeconds above GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT plus 15 seconds (180 with the default GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT of 120): a stopping platform pod (a rolling update, a scale-in, a node drain) lets its running chat turns finish for GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT, then the ones still running store a reply saying they were interrupted and what they had done. Kubernetes' own default of 30 seconds kills the pod before either happens, and those turns end with no reply. A rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 keeps the old pod serving until the new one is ready.

Under construction

The Helm chart deployment guide is under construction. The chart location, its release status, the full values.yaml reference, and a validated production topology will be documented here soon.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
This page covers how to monitor a self-hosted XTM One instance in production: health probes, metrics, request tracing, and logs. Filigran SaaS instances are monitored by Filigran.

The environment variables referenced here are documented in full in the Configuration section — this page explains what each signal tells you and how to act on it.

docs.title: Health probes
docs.text:
The platform exposes two unauthenticated endpoints for orchestrators and uptime checks:

Endpoint Use for Returns 200 when GET /api/health Liveness probe The HTTP server is running GET /api/health/ready Readiness probe Database, Redis, and object storage are reachable and migrations are complete

Use /api/health as a liveness probe (restart the container if it fails) and /api/health/ready as a readiness probe (stop routing traffic until it passes). The Docker Compose stack already wires /api/health/ready into its health checks so dependent services wait for full startup.

Kubernetes probes

Point livenessProbe at /api/health and readinessProbe at /api/health/ready. Readiness returns non-200 until the database, Redis, and object storage are reachable and migrations have completed, so traffic is held back until the platform is fully started.

Each web worker process (WEB_WORKERS) runs its own startup, and a probe is answered by whichever worker takes it. A worker can therefore be starting while its pod already receives traffic: the replacement uvicorn starts for a worker recycled after MAX_REQUESTS, or a second worker still starting when the first one made the pod ready. Such a worker holds the requests it receives until its startup completes, for up to 8 seconds, and only then answers 503 with Retry-After. It also skips the migrations and the seeding already applied since the container started, so it is serving within about a second. A seeding step the startup logged as retried "on next startup" (the built-in brand assets while the object store was unreachable, for instance) is therefore retried when the container next starts, not by a replacement worker. A worker whose startup failed answers 503 at once, and its /api/health/ready keeps reporting the error. If the database restarts or fails over while a worker starts, the startup waits for it to come back instead of failing: meanwhile /api/health/ready reports startup_retrying with the PostgreSQL error code when there is one (for example database unavailable (25006) for a read-only server, database unavailable (ConnectionRefusedError) otherwise), and the logs give the full error.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
XTM One exposes Prometheus metrics on a token-protected /metrics endpoint.

  1. Set PROMETHEUS_ENABLED=true.
  2. Set PROMETHEUS_BEARER_TOKEN to a secret of at least 16 characters.
  3. Scrape /metrics with an Authorization: Bearer <token> header.

The token is mandatory

When PROMETHEUS_ENABLED=true, the platform refuses to expose /metrics unless a valid PROMETHEUS_BEARER_TOKEN is set. This prevents an unauthenticated metrics endpoint from leaking operational data.

The endpoint serves the platform's own series, all prefixed xtmone_, in the Prometheus text format, together with the standard per-process metrics of the Prometheus client library (Python runtime and garbage collection).

Read from the database, or counted per process

Some gauges are computed from the database at scrape time: the quota, assignment queue, relay and sandbox workspace gauges below. Every process answers the same values for them. The counters and histograms are counted in the process that did the work, and a scrape reads only the process that answers it, so read them as trends, not exact totals (see Running more than one platform replica). The logs and the audit log are the exact record.

docs.title: Quota
docs.text: Metric Type Labels What it reports xtmone_quota_usage gauge user_id, usage_type (agentic, sandbox), model, period (daily, monthly, yearly), platform_id Quota consumed in the current day, month and year, per user, plus a user_id="_global" total

docs.title: Assignments and dispatch
docs.text:
The queue gauges list only the assignments with something queued, running or recently started; an assignment that goes quiet drops out. They carry the assignment's id, never its name. The queue and the variables that size it are described in Configuration.

Metric Type Labels What it reports xtmone_assignment_queue_depth gauge assignment_id, platform_id Deliveries queued for the assignment, waiting for a free slot xtmone_assignment_queue_oldest_age_seconds gauge assignment_id, platform_id Age of the assignment's oldest queued delivery xtmone_assignment_queue_oldest_age_max_seconds gauge platform_id Age of the oldest queued delivery across every assignment not waiting for a human xtmone_assignment_queue_held gauge assignment_id, platform_id 1 while the assignment's queue waits for a human's answer to one of its runs xtmone_assignment_runs_active gauge assignment_id, platform_id Runs of the assignment holding a concurrency slot xtmone_assignment_concurrency_cap gauge assignment_id, platform_id How many runs of the assignment may hold a slot at once xtmone_assignment_dispatch_lag_p95_seconds gauge assignment_id, platform_id 95th percentile of the time from a run's creation to its start, over the last 15 minutes xtmone_event_to_run_seconds histogram kind Seconds from an event (raised by the platform, or handed over by an integration's receiver or poller) to the start of the run it triggered. kind is platform_event, integration_event, the assignment's trigger type for a provider webhook, or platform_event_watch for a one-off watch xtmone_work_item_dispatch_lag_seconds histogram path (tick, wake) Seconds from a work item's last activity (creation, release) to its dispatch to an inbox assignment. wake is the immediate path; a growing tick share means the Redis wake channel is not reaching the processes

docs.title: Runs and resumes
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels What it counts xtmone_run_resumes_total counter entry, cause, graceful, version Assignment runs and background tasks resumed after an interruption (a deployment, a crash), by cause class, whether the stop was graceful, and build xtmone_tasks_orphaned_total counter version Running tasks whose execution lost its lease, by build xtmone_stale_run_warnings_total counter orphan_class Orphaned assignment runs approaching the deadline after which they are failed xtmone_stale_runs_finalized_total counter outcome (failed, completed), orphan_class Orphaned or stale assignment runs the stale-run sweep closed xtmone_turn_resume_results_total counter kind (replayed, truncated) Tool results an interrupted chat turn handed to the turn that resumed it

The version label is the build (the short git commit, else the application version), so you can compare what a rollout cost from one release to the next.

docs.title: Sandbox workspace metrics
docs.text:
The code interpreter's sandbox workspace and the sandboxes behind it report:

Metric Type Labels What it counts xtmone_sandbox_workspaces gauge measure (count, bytes, files, kernel_restarts), platform_id Every workspace of the platform, read from the database at scrape time. xtmone_sandbox_workspace_calls_total counter mode (stateless, session), workspace (mounted, unmounted, unavailable) code_interpreter calls. xtmone_sandbox_workspace_bytes_total counter direction (read, written) Bytes moved into the sandbox and saved from it. xtmone_sandbox_workspace_operations_total counter operation (put, get, list, remove, ingest, materialize_repository, install, gc_delete), outcome Workspace operations; gc_delete carries the sweep's reason (idle, conversation_archived, conversation_deleted, run_deleted, orphan_objects). xtmone_sandbox_workspace_quota_refusals_total counter operation Change sets refused for the quota or the file limit. xtmone_sandbox_kernel_starts_total counter reason (new, restarted, reset) session=true kernels started; a rising restarted means kernels are lost between calls (idle timeout, timeouts, calls reaching another replica). xtmone_sandbox_workspace_sync_seconds histogram phase (materialize, scan, upload, commit) Time moving a workspace in and out of the sandbox. xtmone_sandbox_command_stage_seconds histogram stage (start, command, teardown), outcome Seconds each stage of a sandbox command took. xtmone_sandbox_create_seconds histogram image_key, outcome (ok, timeout, sidecar, error), pooled (true, false) Seconds each OpenSandbox container create attempt took. A timeout series on one image key means its Pool had no warm pod (buffer taken, poolMax reached) or a cold node pulled the image: raise that Pool's bufferMin/bufferMax and poolMax. xtmone_custom_tool_sandbox gauge sandbox (docker, subprocess, opensandbox, docker_unavailable, opensandbox_unavailable, disabled) The sandbox custom tools actually run in: 1 for the active one, 0 for the others.

The audit log records each file put into a workspace (workspace_put), each repository checkout (materialize_repository) and each workspace the sweep deletes, under the entity type sandbox_workspace. Reads change nothing and are not audited: a workspace file handed to a tool (workspace_path) is counted by the metrics only. The workspace of one conversation (size, last clean-up, kernel restarts, bytes moved, files) is served to its owner by GET /api/v1/chat/conversations/{id}/sandbox-workspace.

docs.title: Relays
docs.text:
Reported only while relays are enabled, labelled by the relay group's id, never its name. See Relays.

Metric Type Labels What it reports xtmone_relay_group_relays gauge group_id, state (enrolled, online), platform_id Relays of the group: enrolled, and online now xtmone_relay_group_routed_resources gauge group_id, platform_id Integrations and MCP servers routed through the group

docs.title: Skills and chat
docs.text: Metric Type Labels What it counts xtmone_skill_loads_total counter outcome (loaded, already_loaded, not_found, budget_exceeded) Skills agents loaded during their runs. Never labelled by skill name xtmone_skill_refresh_total counter outcome (success, auth, not_found, client, rate_limit, transient), auth (authenticated, anonymous) Automatic refreshes of skills imported from a URL: tells an expired credential apart from a broken URL or a provider outage xtmone_chat_duplicate_replies_refused_total counter channel Chat replies refused at sending because another run had already answered every message they answer

docs.title: Request tracing
docs.text:
XTM One records a trace for every LLM interaction so you can inspect what an agent did, which tools it called, how many tokens it used, and where time was spent.

A run's trace counts every token of every model call it made, including a run whose calls different providers answered (a provider failover, or a budget downgrade to another provider's model). When different models answered its calls, or their providers report usage in different formats, the run's cost is the sum of its calls' costs, as each call's own trace entry shows them; a run one model answered is priced at that model's rates.

docs.title: Native trace store
docs.text:
By default, traces are stored inside the platform's own database and are browsable from the application under Traces. The store backend is selected with TRACING_STORE_PROVIDER:

  • postgres (default) — traces live in the bundled PostgreSQL. No extra service required.
  • clickhouse — traces are read from a dedicated ClickHouse instance for higher-volume analytics. Provide the CLICKHOUSE_* connection settings.

To investigate an assignment, open it and select View Traces: the Traces page opens scoped to the traces of every run of that assignment, and the other filters (status, failure cause, dates, models) narrow it further. View Traces on a run's page scopes the list to that run alone. The scope shows as a chip above the filters; remove it, or select Clear filters, to see every trace again. Both shortcuts are shown to administrators, who are the ones with access to the Traces page.

docs.title: What a trace keeps
docs.text:
Two switches under Settings → Observability decide what the native trace store keeps, under both store backends:

Enable local trace storage Store full payloads What is stored On (default) On (default) Every trace with its payloads, as described below On Off Every trace without what was said: the prompts, the conversation, the answers, the model's reasoning, tool arguments and tool results are dropped, and an error message keeps its first 200 characters (a provider error can quote the request it refused). Timings, token counts, cost, model, trace and tool names, status, failure cause and metadata are kept, so the Traces list, the analytics and the cost reports keep working Off On or off Nothing: no trace, no span and no user feedback score is written. An administrator's own score on a trace already stored (POST /api/v1/traces/{id}/scores) is still recorded

A change applies within a few seconds on every server and worker, to the traces written from then on — including a trace that was still queued when the switch changed. Traces already stored keep what they hold until the retention period deletes them; delete individual traces from the Traces page to remove them sooner. Deleting an agent deletes none of its traces: they stay until the retention period, listed under the agent's last name, for the people who chatted with it and for its owner (and for administrators). The switches govern the native trace store only: the Langfuse export, while it is enabled, still receives each call's payloads (bounded per field). Turn it off as well to keep payloads inside the platform.

While a switch is off, an agent reading traces (inspect_my_traces, inspect_agent_traces, get_trace_payload, and the same tools on the XTM One MCP server) is told so in the result, so it does not read a run missing from the list, or an empty input or output, as something the run did.

docs.title: Trace payload storage
docs.text:
While Store full payloads is on, trace payloads — the prompt, the conversation, the model's reasoning, tool arguments and results — are stored whole. They are audit material, and the trace store holds the only copy, so nothing is clipped on the way in.

Large payloads are moved out of the database rather than truncated. Above TRACE_PAYLOAD_OFFLOAD_THRESHOLD_BYTES (default 1 MiB), the payload is written to object storage and the trace row keeps a pointer with the exact size, a SHA-256 digest and a short excerpt. In the Traces UI those payloads show a Load full payload action that fetches the complete value on demand; the panes show a bounded preview until you ask for it, so opening a trace with megabyte-sized payloads stays fast.

Images and PDFs inside a payload are stored the same way, one object each: the payload keeps a reference with the blob's content type, byte size and SHA-256, and the span inspector lists them as attachments that render the actual image on demand. This is what makes the screenshot an agent received — or the chart it produced — recoverable from its trace; previously media was replaced by an [image] placeholder, and since the trace store holds the only copy, the picture was gone for good.

Variable What it controls TRACE_PAYLOAD_OFFLOAD_THRESHOLD_BYTES Size above which a payload goes to object storage (default 1 MiB). 0 disables offloading and always stores inline. TRACE_PAYLOAD_HARD_MAX_BYTES Inline fallback ceiling used only when object storage is unreachable (default 32 MiB). Below it the payload is stored inline anyway; above it the trace records that the payload could not be stored, so the gap is visible instead of silent. TRACE_MEDIA_OFFLOAD_ENABLED Whether media blobs are stored (default true). Set to false to replace them with an [image] placeholder instead, as earlier versions did.

Offloading requires the same object storage as file attachments (the S3_* settings). Everything one trace owns — offloaded payloads and media alike — lives under a traces/<trace_id>/ prefix. Plan disk for both volumes accordingly. Trace retention bounds how long payloads and their objects are kept — the retention purge deletes the objects along with the rows, under both store backends.

Langfuse export

When Langfuse is configured, the payloads exported to it still have media replaced by placeholders and long strings truncated, regardless of TRACE_MEDIA_OFFLOAD_ENABLED. Langfuse ingestion has its own size limits, and its SDK would otherwise upload every blob to its own separate media storage. Only the export is reduced; the durable trace keeps everything.

docs.title: Trace retention
docs.text:
How long traces are kept is a platform setting, not an environment variable: set it under Settings → Observability → Trace retention (days) (1–365, 90 by default). It applies to both store backends, in the same maintenance cycle, and each cycle deletes the offloaded payload objects belonging to the traces it expires.

  • PostgreSQL — expired traces are deleted in batches roughly hourly. A day's aggregated statistics (llm_daily_stats) are built before its raw traces are deleted and outlive them, so dashboards keep reporting on days whose traces are gone. A day whose statistics are due to be rebuilt (a repricing filled in costs they were built without) keeps its traces until that rebuild has run.
  • ClickHouse — the same cycle sweeps the expired window: it reads the payload pointers off the expiring rows, deletes the rows, then deletes the objects they pointed at. The tables also carry a TTL as a backstop, re-declared whenever the retention setting changes and re-checked on each cycle, so retention still applies to tables that already exist and to a platform whose maintenance loop is not running.

Why ClickHouse keeps a few extra days

The ClickHouse TTL is deliberately set a week beyond the retention window rather than exactly on it. Offloaded payload objects can only be found through the rows that point at them, so the rows have to outlive the object purge — a TTL on the exact boundary would let ClickHouse drop rows before the sweep had read their pointers, orphaning objects in the bucket. In normal operation the sweep enforces the exact window and the TTL never fires. If the maintenance loop stays down for longer than that margin, the TTL still expires the rows (retention is never silently extended) but their objects are left behind; that is a storage cost, and the sweep logs when it cannot reach object storage.

docs.title: Model usage
docs.text:
Administration > Observability > Model usage (the page was named LLM Analytics) charts what the AI costs and how it behaves over a window. Administrators read the whole platform; a group manager reads the members of the groups they manage, administrators excepted.

  • Window and filters. The window is 24H, 7D, 30D (default), 90D, 6M, 1Y or Custom dates. Below it, the groups, agents, models and sources pickers narrow every card at once; Clear filters resets them. The window and the filters are kept in the URL, so a view can be shared.
  • Key figures. Total cost (with the cost per trace), traces, tokens, average latency, error rate and average feedback, each with its change against the previous window of the same length and, for cost and traces, a daily sparkline.
  • Usage over time. Cost or traces per day, week or month, stacked by model or as one total, with each bar's total written on it (up to 31 bars). The six largest models are drawn and the rest are grouped as Other; select a model in the legend to hide or show it.
  • Rankings. Top agents (by cost, traces, cost per trace or average latency), Top models and Top users (by cost, traces or tokens) and Traces by source, each showing the top 5, 10 or 25 with their share of the total. Select an agent or a source to filter the page on it.
  • Latency. The percentiles (P50 to P99) over the window, the median of each day, or the median and P95 of the ten busiest models.

The Cost breakdown and Top errors cards are tables: every column sorts, a search box narrows the rows, 10, 25, 50 or 100 rows show per page with the page controls above and below, and Export CSV downloads every row that matches the search, in the order shown. Top errors lists up to 500 groups of identical errors over the window, with the agent, the model, the count and when each was last seen.

The same figures are available from the /api/v1/traces/analytics/* endpoints: period takes 24h, 7d, 30d, 90d, 180d, 1y or custom (with date_from and date_to), group_ids narrows them to the current members of the named groups, and GET /api/v1/traces/analytics/errors takes a limit from 1 to 500 (default 20).

docs.title: Cost by agent, user, group and model
docs.text:
The Cost breakdown card splits the window's cost four ways, chosen with its By agent / By user / By group / By model switch (kept in the URL as ?breakdown=users, ?breakdown=groups or ?breakdown=models, so a view can be shared):

  • By agent — every agent that ran in the window, with its owner (the person it belongs to, or Company-managed), traces, cost, share of the total, average cost per trace, average latency and average feedback. The search box matches the owner's name and email too, and the CSV carries the owner's name and email.
  • By user — the users who cost the most over the window, with their email, groups, how many agents they used, traces, tokens, average cost per trace and share of the total. The table holds up to the 500 costliest users; when more users ran traces, it says how many there were in all and counts the rest together as one N other users row on its last page. A deactivated account is marked Inactive, a deleted one Deleted user.
  • By group — every group whose members ran traces, with its active users (members who ran at least one trace) out of its current members, the average cost per active user and its share of the total. Users in no group are shown apart as Users in no group.
  • By model — every model that answered in the window, with its traces, input and output tokens, input and output cost, total cost, share of the total, and P50 and P95 latency.

Both views show the runs no account is behind (anonymous channel senders, public widget visitors, the /mcp/global key, assignment runs without a user) apart, as No user account on their last page, so the user view adds up to the dashboard total.

Groups are read as they are today: traces do not record a group, so a trace counts for the groups its user belongs to now, and moving a user to another group moves their past cost with them. A user in several groups counts in each, so the group rows can add up to more than the total; the card says so when it happens. Both views read the same per-user daily aggregates as the rest of the dashboard on long windows, so they still answer after the traces are purged. The same data is available from GET /api/v1/traces/analytics/cost-by-user (limit, 1-1000, default 100; the users past it are returned together as other_users) and GET /api/v1/traces/analytics/cost-by-group, with the dashboard's filters. For a partition by org unit that never overlaps and never follows a move, use departments.

docs.title: Departments
docs.text:
A group is a membership set - an access list, a distribution list, a SAML claim - and a person belongs to many. A department is an org unit: a person belongs to one, so department figures add up to the platform total. Departments are what the Platform insights analytics tool reads per department; administrators set them in Settings → Observability → Departments:

  • Departments. A name, and optionally its directory values: the other spellings the identity provider or an HR export writes for it (R&D and Research for Engineering). Leave them empty when the directory writes the same name, or when the group rules alone decide. When one group per team already exists, Create from the org-unit groups adds one department and one group rule per group tagged Org unit (the group counts for the department of its name); a group rule can only be added once a department exists for it to point at.
  • Resolution order. A person's department is resolved from the sources in the order chosen: the directory department - the attribute their identity provider sends at sign-in (department by default; the SAML attribute or OIDC claim is named in the same card), matched to a department's name or values in any case - and the group rules: an ordered list of groups, each counting for a department, the first one the person is a member of deciding. A person no source resolves is Unassigned. Usage nobody is behind (the platform's own calls) is Unattributed.
  • HR data. The usual path for an HRIS field (department, team or division) is the identity provider: the HRIS provisions it into the directory, which sends it at sign-in. Import directory departments takes the same data as email,department lines from an HR export; the next sign-in that carries the attribute replaces the imported value.
  • Preview. How many active people the saved mapping resolves, how many it leaves unassigned, and who is in each department.

The simplest setup, three steps: create the departments (or create them from the org-unit groups), add one group rule per team group with the most specific group first (Product Management above Engineering), save and Apply the mapping to history. The page's How does it work? panel and the ? next to each field say the same in place.

The department is recorded with each trace and each daily aggregate when the usage happens, so a person who changes team never moves their past usage, and the figures survive the trace purge. When the first department is created, the usage stored until then is resolved from that mapping once, in the background (the card says how far it got). A later change of the mapping applies to new usage only; Apply the mapping to history resolves every stored usage again from the current mapping, and is recorded in the audit log.

The usage of a trace with no user of its own counts for the person behind it: the identity an assignment run acts as, the person a sub-agent's parent trace counts for, the conversation's owner, or the agent's owner for a webhook or a channel bot. The group's kind (Org unit, Access list, Distribution list, or Not classified, set on the group's page) lets the analytics list org units apart from access and distribution lists.

The mapping is also available from the API (administrators): GET and PUT /api/v1/insights/departments, GET /api/v1/insights/departments/preview, POST /api/v1/insights/departments/directory ({"entries": [{"email", "department"}]}) and POST /api/v1/insights/departments/history. GET /api/v1/insights/analytics/export returns the CSV of an analytics read - the analytics tool's arguments as query parameters - for a spreadsheet or a warehouse load.

docs.title: Models without a price
docs.text: A trace of a model with no price is stored without a cost, and every cost total leaves it out. Once a day, the administrators are told in the notification bell of the models the last 7 days of traces ran on without a price, once per model. Add the price in Settings → Observability → Model pricing with the date it applies from, then reprice with Only from the price's effective date to fill the cost of the traces since that date.

docs.title: Group managers
docs.text:
An administrator can make a user the manager of a group, so they follow how the group's members use AI without becoming an administrator. Open Administration > Users and groups > Groups, the group, then its Managers tab, and pick the people in Add a manager. A manager does not have to be a member of the group, and a group can have several managers. Adding and removing a manager is recorded in the audit log (bind and unbind on the group, with the role manager).

A manager gets Model usage under Administration in the navigation, scoped to their team - the current members of the groups they manage, administrators excepted:

  • Model usage shows the team's usage, with the managed groups named under the title. The groups picker lists only those groups, the By user and By group breakdowns hold only the team and those groups (a group's member count is its team's), and the CSV exports carry the same rows. The figures follow today's membership, like the group breakdown: a person who joins a managed group brings their past usage with them, and one who leaves takes it away. The manager's own usage counts only when they are a member of a group they manage.
  • Administrators are not part of a team. An administrator who is a member of a managed group never shows in the manager's figures, breakdowns or errors; an administrator's own group filter still counts every member.
  • Traces and Sessions stay administrators' pages. A manager does not see them in the navigation, cannot open them, and cannot open a team member's trace or session.

A manager reads the team's analytics; they do not act on it. They cannot edit the group, its members or their agents, and the Refresh Analytics button stays an administrator's. A user who manages no group, and is not an administrator, does not see Model usage.

Through an agent, the Platform insights analytics tool serves a manager the same team: analytics for any team member or managed group. The trace and session listing tools serve a manager their own traces and sessions only, like any user who is not an administrator.

The managers are also available from the API: GET /api/v1/groups/managed (the groups the caller manages, with the number of members their team counts), GET and POST /api/v1/groups/{group_id}/managers and DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group_id}/managers/{user_id} (administrators). The analytics endpoints take group_ids to read one or more of the caller's managed groups. GET /api/v1/traces and GET /api/v1/traces/sessions take group_id for administrators only.

docs.title: Langfuse (optional)
docs.text:
You can additionally forward traces to Langfuse for external observability. Set LANGFUSE_HOST, LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, and LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY. LANGFUSE_HOST defaults to Langfuse Cloud; point it at your self-hosted Langfuse to keep trace data on your own infrastructure.

Langfuse is complementary to the native store — enabling it does not disable native traces. Payloads sent to Langfuse are bounded per field, because its ingestion rejects oversized events; the native store keeps the unabridged copy. The Enable local trace storage and Store full payloads switches do not apply to the export: Langfuse receives each call's payloads for as long as it is enabled.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The platform emits structured logs to stdout, which your container runtime or log aggregator collects.

Variable What it controls LOG_LEVEL Verbosity (debug, info, warning, error, critical) LOG_FORMAT json (structured, for aggregators) or console (human-readable)

One structured http_request line is emitted per HTTP request on the app.access logger. Successful requests to /api/health and /metrics are logged at debug so routine probes and scrapes do not flood your logs; client errors are logged at warning and server errors at error.

In production, keep LOG_FORMAT=json and ship logs to a central aggregator (Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, etc.) so you can search and alert across replicas.

docs.title: Sandbox call logs
docs.text:
Every OpenSandbox-routed call (code interpreter, custom JS tool, custom Python tool) emits one additional structured line, sandbox_call, carrying CPU/RAM usage, execution time, egress policy, and outcome. It ships through the same stdout path as everything else above — no extra infrastructure required. The full field reference (names, types, units, when each is present) lives in Configuration § Sandbox call log fields; this section covers how to query it once it's in Grafana.

Example line (LOG_FORMAT=json):

{"event": "sandbox_call", "usage_type": "code_interpreter", "outcome": "success", "user_id": "3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6", "cpu_used_percentage": 12.5, "cpu_count": 1.0, "memory_used_in_mib": 64.2, "memory_total_in_mib": 128.0, "tte_ms": 842, "egress_default_action": "deny", "egress_allow_list": [], "level": "info", "logger": "app.services.sandbox_call_logging", "timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:00:00.000000Z"}

With logs shipped into Loki, these LogQL queries build directly on the fields above — swap {container="platform"} for whatever stream label your Promtail/Grafana Agent config actually attaches (container name, job, Kubernetes pod label, etc.):

  • All sandbox calls (base query for a Logs panel):
{container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call"
  • Failure rate by usage_type (stat/alert panel — ratio of failing to total calls per interval):
sum by (usage_type) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="failure" [$__interval]))
/
sum by (usage_type) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" [$__interval]))
  • Failure breakdown by reason (table/pie panel — sandbox_ready_timeout, sandbox_create_failed, sandbox_create_error, nonzero_exit, execution_error):
sum by (failure_reason) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="failure" [$__interval]))
  • Average execution time (TTE) per usage_type (time series panel):
avg_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="success" | unwrap tte_ms [5m]) by (usage_type)
  • CPU / memory usage trend (swap cpu_used_percentage for memory_used_in_mib or memory_total_in_mib):
avg_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | unwrap cpu_used_percentage [5m]) by (usage_type)
  • Egress policy audit (confirm what's actually live, per call):
{container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | line_format "{{.usage_type}}: {{.egress_default_action}} allow={{.egress_allow_list}}"

CPU/RAM/TTE fields are simply absent (not null) on records where the sandbox never reached completion — sandbox_ready_timeout, sandbox_create_failed, and sandbox_create_error records have none of them. unwrap queries skip lines missing the unwrapped field rather than erroring, so a TTE/CPU/RAM panel naturally reflects only the calls that actually ran, without extra filtering.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
At a minimum, alert on:

  • /api/health/ready failing for more than a few minutes (platform not serving)
  • A rising rate of 5xx responses in the access logs
  • Worker containers repeatedly restarting (background jobs and assignment runs stall)
  • PostgreSQL connection saturation — see the connection-budget formula in Configuration
  • Disk usage on the PostgreSQL and object-storage volumes, which grow with knowledge bases and file attachments
  • A rising sandbox_call failure rate or an unfamiliar failure_reason for OpenSandbox-routed code interpreter/custom tool calls — see Sandbox call logs above
  • Custom tools running outside the hardened sandbox: xtmone_custom_tool_sandbox{sandbox=~"subprocess|docker_unavailable|opensandbox_unavailable"} == 1. Do not alert on sandbox!="docker": that also fires when custom tools are deliberately turned off (disabled)
  • Queued assignment deliveries waiting too long — see Alert rules below

docs.title: Alert rules
docs.text:
The repository ships a reference set of Prometheus alert rules for assignment dispatch: k8s/prometheus-rules/assignment-dispatch-alerts.yaml. It is a PrometheusRule for the Prometheus operator; apply it with kubectl apply -f k8s/prometheus-rules/assignment-dispatch-alerts.yaml. Its release: kube-prometheus-stack label matches the default rule selector of a kube-prometheus-stack install: adjust it to your Prometheus's selector, or load the group into your own ruler (Mimir, Thanos).

The rules need metrics enabled. They evaluate every minute and take the maximum across replicas.

Alert Fires when For Severity XtmOneAssignmentDispatchLag The oldest queued assignment delivery has waited more than 5 minutes (xtmone_assignment_queue_oldest_age_max_seconds > 300) 2 minutes warning XtmOneAssignmentRunStartLag 95% of an assignment's runs over the last 15 minutes started more than 5 minutes after their trigger (xtmone_assignment_dispatch_lag_p95_seconds > 300) 10 minutes warning

Nothing is lost when they fire: a queued delivery is kept in the database, but automations answer late. To find the cause, compare xtmone_assignment_runs_active with xtmone_assignment_concurrency_cap for the assignment concerned:

  • At its cap: the assignment receives events faster than its runs finish. Raise its max_concurrent_runs trigger setting, or ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS for every assignment.
  • Below its cap: the workers are short. Look at MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS, ASSIGNMENT_DISPATCH_MAX_PENDING_RUNS, the number of worker replicas, or a model provider answering 429.

The worker also logs Assignment dispatch lag with the three oldest queues, at most once a minute while the oldest delivery is older than ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_BACKLOG_SECONDS.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: If a signal points to a problem, continue with Troubleshooting for common issues and how to diagnose them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Before you install, discover how XTM One is built, which services it relies on, and how it can be hosted.

Docker deployment of the full XTM suite (OpenCTI - OpenAEV - XTM One)

If you're looking for information about the deployment of the full eXtended Threat Management (XTM) suite using Docker, please refer to this repository and documentation.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: XTM One is the core platform of the XTM Platform. OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ are its modules: they register with it, sign their users in through it, and reach its agents from their own screens. What you deploy is a small set of services: the platform, one or more workers, and three stores. Everything else is either an external service the platform calls, or an optional component you add when you need it.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph IN[Inbound]
        U[People: web app, Office add-in,<br/>browser extension, messaging apps]
        E[Webhooks, integration<br/>events, schedules]
        X[AI clients: OpenAI-compatible, MCP, A2A<br/>XTM modules: OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ]
    end
    subgraph NET[Your network, optional]
        RL[Relays]
        RN[Runners and<br/>XTM One Desktop]
    end
    subgraph CORE[XTM One]
        P[Platform]
        W[Workers]
        SB[Sandbox, optional]
        P -- "run due, wake-up" --> W
    end
    subgraph ST[Stores]
        PG[(PostgreSQL + pgvector)]
        R[(Redis)]
        S3[(Silo / S3)]
        CH[(ClickHouse, optional)]
    end
    subgraph OUT[Outbound]
        AI[AI providers]
        I[Integrations and<br/>MCP servers]
    end
    IN --> CORE
    NET -- "outbound connection" --> CORE
    CORE <--> ST
    CORE --> OUT

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
The platform image is the service people and systems talk to. It listens on port 4000 and serves:

  • the web application, the REST API, and the live chat (server-sent events);
  • the incoming channel webhooks (/api/channels/...) and assignment webhooks (/api/hooks/...);
  • the OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy (/v1), the MCP endpoints (/mcp/...) and the agent-to-agent endpoints (/a2a/...);
  • the sign-in service the XTM modules use (/xtm/auth/...), their registration, and their embedded assistant;
  • the Office add-in (/office/) and, when enabled, the Prometheus metrics (/metrics).

The platform runs every interactive turn itself: a chat message on the web, in a channel, in a module's embedded assistant, through the LLM proxy, MCP or A2A. It also runs the scheduler (cron triggers, integration polling, knowledge-base syncs, maintenance sweeps) and applies the database migrations when it starts.

It scales vertically first: give it more CPU and memory and raise WEB_WORKERS. More replicas are supported, for availability or for load (see Running more than one platform replica).

docs.title: Workers
docs.text:
The worker image runs the work nobody is waiting for on screen:

  • Agent runs. Assignment runs, sub-agent tasks and scheduled work items are recorded in PostgreSQL as executions. Each worker claims the ones that are due, runs the agent loop under a renewed lease, and hands a run back if it stops: another worker resumes it. Each worker runs up to MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS assignment runs and MAX_CONCURRENT_SUB_AGENT_TASKS sub-agent tasks at once.
  • Queued jobs. Knowledge-base document processing (extraction, chunking and embedding) and workspace indexing go through a Redis queue, up to WORKER_CONCURRENCY jobs per worker.

When a background task started from a chat finishes, the worker also writes the follow-up answer in that conversation. Workers hold no state of their own: add replicas when runs or documents queue up (see Scaling model).

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
Store Role What happens if it is lost PostgreSQL + pgvector System of record: users, agents, conversations, run state, knowledge-base vectors, long-term memory, audit log, and the LLM traces unless ClickHouse holds them. Everything. Back it up (see Backup and restore). Redis Coordination: the job queue, wake-ups between platform and workers, live chat streams, rate limits, short-term memory, single-use links, usage counters not yet written to the database. Work in flight and recent working state. Durable records are not affected. Object storage (Silo / S3) Files: uploads, knowledge-base sources, generated files, code-interpreter workspaces, large trace payloads. Every stored file. Back it up with the database. ClickHouse (optional) A second trace store for high trace volumes: traces are written to PostgreSQL and ClickHouse, and read from ClickHouse. Trace history only.

Each store is set with DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, the S3_* variables and the CLICKHOUSE_* variables: the bundled container or a managed equivalent (RDS or Aurora, managed Redis, S3). See Configuration.

docs.title: AI providers
docs.text: The platform and the workers call AI providers for chat, embeddings, speech and images. Eleven chat providers are supported (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Mistral AI, SpaceXAI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, OpenRouter, Ollama, LiteLLM, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), plus an embedding-only server and ElevenLabs for speech. You configure them in Settings > AI Models or with LLM_PROVIDER_* variables. A local model (Ollama, or an OpenAI-compatible server in your network) keeps every prompt inside your infrastructure.

docs.title: Tools and integrations
docs.text:
Agents act on other systems through tools. The platform or the worker runs every tool call; the AI provider only asks for it.

  • Integrations connect to the XTM modules (OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ) and to more than 100 other services (messaging, email, ticketing, cloud documents, security products). The modules call back in too, through their embedded assistant and the platform MCP servers.
  • MCP servers are reached over HTTP, or started as local processes inside the platform and worker containers.
  • Built-in tools include web search and fetch, a headless browser, and document rendering.
  • Custom tools and the code interpreter run in a sandbox: a local process, a Docker container, or a separate OpenSandbox server. Both are off by default on an XTM One platform.

docs.title: Components in your network
docs.text:
Two optional components run outside the platform and connect to it, never the other way round, so you open no inbound port for them:

  • Relays carry integration and MCP server calls to systems on a private network the platform cannot reach. See Relays.
  • Runners (XTM One Desktop on a workstation, or a headless runner on a server) let an agent act on that computer: commands, files, applications. See XTM One Desktop and runners.

docs.title: Optional services
docs.text:
Service What it adds How to enable it ClickHouse Trace storage at high volume TRACING_STORE_PROVIDER=clickhouse and CLICKHOUSE_* (Configuration) OpenSandbox Isolated containers for custom tools and the code interpreter The opensandbox Docker Compose profile (Configuration) Secret vaults Credentials kept in HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure or 1Password Settings > Security or SECRET_VAULT_* (Secret vaults) Langfuse LLM traces in your Langfuse Settings > Observability or LANGFUSE_* (Monitoring) SMTP server Password resets, invitations, announcements SMTP_* (Configuration) Prometheus Platform metrics and alert rules PROMETHEUS_ENABLED (Monitoring)

How a request travels through these components, and what leaves your network, is described in Data flow. The Installation page turns this into a deployment: Infrastructure requirements gives the CPU and memory figures and the database connection budget.

docs.title: Deployment models
docs.text:
XTM One can be deployed in two ways: Filigran SaaS (Filigran-hosted) and Self-Hosted (you run it).

Filigran SaaS Self-Hosted Hosting Filigran-hosted cloud instance Your infrastructure — on-premises or your own cloud Maintenance Filigran Your team Upgrades Handled by Filigran Manual Network Outbound HTTPS only Your choice — on-premises, private cloud,internet-facing, or fully air-gapped Best for Fastest start, no infrastructure to run Full control, on-premises or data-residencyrequirements, air-gapped environments

docs.title: Filigran SaaS
docs.text:
Filigran hosts and operates XTM One for you as a fully managed cloud private instance. You access the platform through a Filigran-provided URL.

What you need

  • A Filigran subscription
  • A supported web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge)
  • Outbound HTTPS access (port 443) to the platform URL provided during onboarding
  • Outbound HTTPS to your identity provider (if SSO is configured)
  • Outbound HTTPS to any external service your agents connect to (AI providers, messaging platforms, etc.)

Onboarding

  1. Filigran provisions your tenant and sends you a URL and initial admin credentials.
  2. Sign in, then go to Settings to configure AI providers, SSO, and integrations.

Access provisioning

Users can access the platform through:

  • Admin invitation — admins create user accounts from Settings → Users.
  • SSO auto-provisioning — when OIDC or SAML is configured, users are created automatically on first login. SAML supports automatic group mapping from IdP group claims.
  • Self-registration — if enabled by the admin, users can register with a valid email domain.

Your responsibilities

  • User accounts, SSO, and access control
  • AI provider configuration (API keys configured from the Settings UI)
  • Agent, integration, and knowledge base setup

What Filigran manages

  • Infrastructure provisioning and monitoring
  • Platform upgrades and patches
  • Database backups and disaster recovery
  • Availability, performance, and scaling

Infrastructure-level requests — custom domains, network peering or VPN access instead of the public internet, and sizing or capacity changes — go through Filigran. Share your sizing and capacity needs with Filigran so the instance is provisioned accordingly.

Limitations

  • No access to the underlying infrastructure, database, or containers
  • No control over environment variables or performance tuning (worker count, pool sizes)
  • Upgrade timing is controlled by Filigran
  • Custom tool sandbox mode is not configurable

docs.title: Self-Hosted
docs.text:
You deploy and operate XTM One on your own infrastructure. The Architecture above describes the services you run; the Installation page covers the infrastructure requirements and the step-by-step procedure.

What self-hosting means

When you self-host, you take on responsibilities that Filigran handles in the SaaS model:

Area Managed (SaaS) Self-Hosted Upgrades Automatic or coordinated You pull images and restart manually Database backups Managed by Filigran Your responsibility TLS certificates Included You provide certificates and a reverse proxy Monitoring and alerting Included You set up your own (Langfuse, Prometheus, log aggregation) Scaling Managed by Filigran You scale workers and tune connection pools Infrastructure security Managed by Filigran You harden the host, network, and containers

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with the Installation procedure to deploy the platform.

docs.title: Provisioning with SCIM (Microsoft Entra)
docs.text: XTM One serves a SCIM 2.0 endpoint (RFC 7643 and RFC 7644). An identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID uses it to create accounts, keep their name, title and department current, manage group membership, and deactivate accounts when people leave. Deactivating an account through SCIM runs the same cascade as the Disable button on a user's page (see Deactivation).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An XTM One administrator account.
  • In Microsoft Entra: the right to create an enterprise application and configure its provisioning (Application Administrator or Cloud Application Administrator).
  • The XTM One URL reachable from Microsoft Entra (the provisioning service calls it from the internet).

docs.title: 1. Generate a token in XTM One
docs.text:
1. Open Settings > Access and security > Provisioning.
  2. Copy the Endpoint URL. It ends with /api/v1/scim/v2.
  3. Give the token a name (for example Microsoft Entra) and select Generate token.
  4. Copy the token at once. It is shown only this time; XTM One stores only a hash of it.

The token opens the SCIM endpoint and nothing else. Revoke it from the same screen: the identity provider's next call is refused. Each token is limited to SCIM_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE calls per minute (an answer 429 with Retry-After beyond it).

docs.title: 2. Create the enterprise application in Microsoft Entra
docs.text:
1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open Enterprise applications > New application > Create your own application.
  2. Name it (for example XTM One) and choose Integrate any other application you don't find in the gallery (Non-gallery).
  3. Open the application, then Provisioning > Get started, and set Provisioning Mode to Automatic.
  4. Under Admin Credentials:
    • Tenant URL: the Endpoint URL copied in step 1.
    • Secret Token: the token generated in step 1.
  5. Select Test Connection, then Save.

docs.title: 3. Map the attributes
docs.text:
Under Mappings > Provision Microsoft Entra ID Users, keep these mappings and remove the ones XTM One ignores if you want shorter provisioning logs:

Microsoft Entra attribute SCIM attribute XTM One field userPrincipalName (or mail) userName Email, the sign-in identity objectId externalId Link to the Entra user Switch([IsSoftDeleted], ...)
