    xtmone -->|"3 · Reads & updates data"| suite
    client -->|"4 · Uses tools via MCP"| xtmone

The diagram shows four ways XTM One and the Suite products work together:

  1. Registration — each platform registers with XTM One at POST /api/v1/platform/register, authorized by the shared PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN (see below). This one-time handshake enables everything else.
  2. Embedded AI assistant — once registered, OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ surface an in-product AI assistant. The platform streams each request to XTM One over HTTP with Server-Sent Events (/api/v1/platform/chat). The assistant panel also reads the signed-in user's usage quota (GET /api/v1/platform/chat/quota, null on Community Edition), lists their chat prompts (GET /api/v1/platform/chat/prompts) and the conversations they can reference with @ (GET /api/v1/platform/chat/conversation-references) and records their rating of an answer (POST / DELETE /api/v1/platform/chat/conversations/{conversation_id}/messages/{message_id}/feedback), all as that user, like the chat itself.
  3. Reads & updates platform data — to answer, XTM One calls the platform's own GraphQL / REST API. Every call runs as the signed-in user: XTM One signs a short-lived per-user token that the platform verifies against XTM One's public keys at GET /xtm/auth/jwks, so each user's permissions and audit trail apply exactly as if they acted directly (see Acting as the user).
  4. Platform tools over MCP — connecting a platform also exposes its native tools to external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude, custom agents) through XTM One at /mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, and /mcp/opencrq. This is a separate capability from the in-product assistant — see Platform MCP servers.

Registration is authorized by a shared token:

Variable Where it is set Purpose PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN XTM One and each Suite platform Shared secret authorizing a platform to register. Must be identical across all services.

Use the same token everywhere

Every product that registers with XTM One must use the exact same PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN. Set a strong shared secret before connecting production instances, for example the output of python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))".

  • Unset: registration is disabled. Every registration request is refused with a message naming the variable to set.
  • The published default xtm-default-registration-token (the docker-compose.yml fallback): accepted only so the platforms already registered with it stay connected. It cannot register a new platform, change a registered platform's URL, rename one or unregister one: a registered platform's URL is trusted to sign XTM One users in, and its name is what the agents bound to it read, so a token everyone knows must never choose either. Nor can it change the intents and business vertical a platform declares, or clear, downgrade or swap a connected platform's license: only a renewal that XTM One validates - a newer license issued to the same customer and instance - replaces the one registered. XTM One logs a warning at startup and the security audit (Settings → Security) reports a critical finding until you replace it on XTM One and on every platform. Meanwhile the license certificate described below is withheld, so a platform sub-licensed by your Filigran license cannot prove its Enterprise Edition; the registration answer says why (xtm_license_withheld_reason: registration_token_published_default), so the platform can point you to this setting.
  • Failed attempts: after 10 failed attempts in a minute, a client is refused with HTTP 429 until the minute ends, whatever token it presents. A call the published default may not make counts as a failed attempt.

The registration answer can carry your Filigran license

When your Filigran license is what puts a platform in Enterprise Edition (it sub-licenses that platform, or every platform of its type), the registration answer carries the license certificate itself, so the platform can verify its entitlement against Filigran's certificate authority instead of taking XTM One's word for it. That certificate is a license: whoever obtains it can use it until it expires. XTM One sends it only to a caller that presents the registration token, and only in that case, and it refuses every registration while PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN is unset - so treat the token like the license itself: a strong secret, shared only with the platforms you connect, never the placeholder.

Once a platform is registered, its native capabilities become available automatically — including the platform MCP servers (/mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq), which activate as soon as the corresponding platform is connected.

Under construction

The exact registration procedure on the OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ side (which settings to fill, in which UI or configuration file, and how to verify a successful registration from XTM One) is being documented and will be added here.

docs.title: Network reachability
docs.text:
XTM One calls the registered platform's API when an agent works with its data. By default it uses the public platform_url supplied during registration.

The platform_url must be an http:// or https:// address with a host, without credentials, query string, fragment, spaces, control characters or backslashes, and at most 2048 characters long: XTM One refuses any other registration with a 422 response.

For deployments where XTM One and the platforms share an internal network, you can override the API URL XTM One calls:

Variable Effect OPENCTI_API_URL Call the OpenCTI API, fetch its signing keys and send its callbacks on this internal URL instead of the registered public URL OPENAEV_API_URL Same, for OpenAEV OPENCRQ_API_URL Same, for OpenCRQ. The pre-rename name OPENGRC_API_URL is still read, with a deprecation warning in the logs, until 2026-12-31 - see Upgrade

Links stay on the public URL

The override is only where XTM One calls the platform. Every link a person is given - the "Open in ..." links of the platform tools, the platform URL the agents build their links from, the links in their answers, trigger.platform_url in an assignment prompt - is on the registered public URL, the one a browser reaches. A link the agent writes on the internal URL (from a conversation older than the upgrade, for example) is shown on the public URL too, except inside code blocks, which are left as written. With URL_GUARD_ENABLED=false the answers are left as written.

docs.title: Public and internal URLs
docs.text:
In Docker Compose or Kubernetes, each product usually has two URLs: the public one your users open in their browser (http://localhost:8080), and the internal one the other containers reach it on (http://opencti:8080). The signed calls between the products use them for different things:

  • The public URL is the product's identity. It is BASE_URL for XTM One and the base URL a platform registers with (for OpenCTI, APP__BASE_URL). Every token a product signs names it as the issuer, and every token sent to a product must be addressed to it.
  • The internal URL is only where the other side connects: the platform's API, its signing keys and, for OpenAEV, the autonomous run callbacks. No link a person is given is ever on it.

On the XTM One side, the internal URL of a platform is the *_API_URL override above, recorded at the platform's next registration (its heartbeat, every few minutes). On the platform side, it is the XTM One URL the platform is configured with (XTM__XTM_ONE_URL for OpenCTI, OPENAEV_XTM_ONE_URL for OpenAEV): the platform reads XTM One's public identity from GET /xtm/auth/metadata on that URL.

Two settings keep the signed calls working when the URLs differ:

Variable Where Purpose BASE_URL XTM One and its worker The worker signs the tokens of background work (assignments, delegated tasks, autonomous runs). Without it, those tokens carry a default issuer the platforms refuse. Set it to the same value on both containers. XTM_AUTH_ACCEPTED_AUDIENCES XTM One Comma-separated URLs the platforms reach XTM One on when they differ from BASE_URL, for example http://xtm-one:4000. Platform versions that do not read /xtm/auth/metadata address their tokens to that URL, and XTM One refuses them unless it is listed here.

If the embedded assistant answers but every action on the platform's data fails with 401, check the XTM One logs for XTM JWT rejected: the message names the issuer, the audience or the key URL that did not match.

docs.title: Acting as the user
docs.text:
When a Suite platform calls XTM One (or when a request from XTM One calls back into a platform), the action runs as the requesting user, not as a shared service account.

XTM One signs a short-lived, per-user token that the platform verifies, and verifies the platform's tokens the same way. Each product signs its tokens for 10 minutes; XTM One refuses a platform token that carries no expiry or is signed to live longer than 15 minutes, and tolerates up to 60 seconds of clock difference between the products. Keep their clocks synchronised (NTP): a token from a clock more than 60 seconds ahead is refused. Users are matched by email between the two products, so each user's platform permissions, data markings, and audit trail apply exactly as if they acted directly. Platform API tokens are never stored in or proxied through XTM One.

The public keys used to verify these tokens are served from XTM One:

Endpoint Purpose GET /xtm/auth/jwks Public JWKS keys for verifying XTM One's cross-platform tokens (unauthenticated, public) GET /xtm/auth/metadata The issuer XTM One's tokens carry, the audience it expects (both its public BASE_URL, whichever URL you reach it on), its jwks_uri and signing algorithm (unauthenticated, public)

Under construction

The cross-platform token verification setup on the platform side — including how each platform is configured to trust XTM One's JWKS endpoint and how key rotation is handled — is being documented and will be added here.

docs.title: Acting on the platform's page
docs.text: With a decision model set, the embedded "Ask AI" assistant can also act on the page the user is looking at: open a section, switch a tab, type a search term. The assistant in the product performs each click itself, in the user's own session, so it can do nothing the user could not do by hand, and it stops before a button that saves, creates, sends or deletes unless you asked it to. Nothing has to be configured in the product beyond a widget version that supports it; the client protocol uses the approval route the product already forwards.

docs.title: OpenCRQ tools follow each instance
docs.text:
The OpenCRQ tools your agents use follow the OpenCRQ instance you connect. XTM One keeps no list of OpenCRQ versions: each instance describes the operations it serves, and the fields each one accepts, itself.

  • How XTM One learns it. OpenCRQ sends a fingerprint of that description with every registration (its heartbeat, every few minutes). When XTM One does not hold the description for that fingerprint, it asks, and OpenCRQ registers again at once with the description. An OpenCRQ that is not registered with XTM One is not asked ahead of time: its description is read from the instance at the first OpenCRQ call of each conversation or run.
  • A tool the instance cannot serve is hidden from your agents, and refused if something calls it by name. The refusal names what is missing.
  • A field the instance would drop is refused before anything is sent. OpenCRQ drops a field it does not know without saying so, so without this check the tool would look as if it had worked. A field left empty, or one the instance accepts, goes through as usual.
  • The default registration token stores nothing. An OpenCRQ registered with the published default PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN (see above) is accepted without a description being kept: nothing is hidden and no field is checked. Set a registration token of your own.
  • Between two versions, nothing is hidden. While OpenCRQ reports a fingerprint XTM One has no description for, for example just after an upgrade, no tool is hidden and no field is checked. The new description arrives with the next heartbeat, within 5 minutes. A description that is out of date never decides.
  • Several replicas behind one URL. During a rolling deploy the replicas can describe themselves differently, so what is hidden can change from one heartbeat to the next until the rollout ends.

Open the integration and read the OpenCRQ version card of its Overview tab: it shows the connected version, whether XTM One holds the description (up to date, pending, unavailable, or not accepted under the default token), its short fingerprint and when it was received, the tools that are hidden and the operations they miss, and the fields a tool sends that the instance does not accept. Everyone who can open the integration sees it.

Limits

XTM One checks which fields an instance accepts, not their values: OpenCRQ itself refuses a wrong value with an error. An OpenCRQ that does not answer the description is treated as one that hides nothing.

docs.title: Verifying the integration
docs.text:
After registering a platform, confirm the connection from XTM One:

  • The platform MCP server for that product reports Connected in My Profile → MCP Endpoint (and in Settings → MCP Endpoint for admins).
  • The embedded "Ask AI" experience appears inside the registered product.

If a platform shows as not connected, see the platform MCP troubleshooting table and the general Troubleshooting page.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review Data flow to understand how cross-product requests are processed, and AI governance for what is shared with AI providers.

docs.title: Run budgets
docs.text:
A run budget caps what one run costs. A run is a single piece of agent work: one chat turn, or one assignment execution. The budget bounds it along four dimensions at once — money, tokens, tool calls and wall-clock time — and stops the run when any of them is reached.

Budgets exist because the natural limits are the wrong shape. Max iterations counts tool-calling rounds, and a single round can fan out into a dozen parallel tool calls. A run still making progress also goes past it, up to 1000 rounds (see Long runs). A model change can multiply the cost of the same work without changing anything you configured. A budget measures what you actually care about instead: it is what bounds a long run.

docs.title: Where a budget is configured
docs.text:
There are two places, from broadest to narrowest.

The platform, set by an administrator in the deployment's environment. This is the default every run inherits and, just as importantly, the ceiling nobody else can raise. See Agent run budget for the settings themselves.

One agent, on its Value tab, below the agent's ROI. This is where you say "this research agent may spend more than the platform default" or "this triage bot must never spend more than a few cents". It applies wherever that agent runs.

docs.title: The agent's run budget
docs.text:
Open an agent and choose Value (called Budget before; old links still open it): the run budget sits under the agent's ROI. Each of the four limits is a single field, and an empty field means "inherit", not "zero". The placeholder tells you what it would inherit, so you can see the effective budget without saving anything.

That distinction is the whole point of leaving fields empty. A budget that only pins the cost keeps tracking the platform's token, tool-call and time limits — including any later change an administrator makes to them. Typing the inherited numbers in to "be explicit" freezes a copy that silently stops following the platform.

Use the Inherit link next to a field to hand a dimension back.

docs.title: Who may raise a limit
docs.text:
Anyone who can edit an agent may lower any limit. Spending less is never a privilege.

Raising a limit above the platform budget requires an administrator. That is what the platform setting is for: it is the budget a user cannot exceed on their own. If you are not an admin, the tab says so up front, and a field you push above the ceiling is flagged with the platform's value before you attempt to save — you will not discover it as a rejected save.

If your agent genuinely needs a larger budget than the platform allows, ask an administrator to set it. Once they have, the value stays: you can keep editing everything else about the agent without the budget being questioned again, and without being able to raise it further yourself.

Three settings that need no admin

The final-answer reserve, the cheaper-model failsafe and the choice of fallback model are not gated, because none of them can increase what a run spends. The reserve only moves the in-run limit down, and the failsafe keeps the same cost ceiling — it just buys more work under it.

docs.title: The final-answer reserve
docs.text:
A run that spends its entire budget on work has nothing left to pay for the call that turns that work into an answer, so it would return a raw digest of tool output instead of a written result.

The reserve prevents that: a slice of the cost and token ceilings is held back for the closing answer. Work is gated at the remainder; the final answer may spend the full budget. The platform default is 10%, which comfortably covers one closing call.

docs.title: Finishing on a cheaper model instead of stopping
docs.text:
A cost ceiling of, say, $0.50 on an expensive model usually means "don't spend more than $0.50 at this quality" — not "abandon the task". The same $0.50 buys several times more work on a cheaper model.

Turn on Finish on a cheaper model and a run that reaches its cost ceiling switches to a cheaper model and carries on instead of stopping. The rest of the run, including its closing answer, is charged at that model's rates, so the ceiling still holds. The agent is told the switch happened, and the run's trace records it, so cost attribution stays readable per call.

Deliberately bounded:

  • Once per run. Never a ladder that limps along on progressively worse models.
  • Cost only. Tokens, tool calls and time are model-independent — a cheaper model buys no extra wall clock.

Fallback model chooses which model that is. Left on Platform fallback model, it uses the one configured in Settings > AI Models > Fallback Model — the same model the platform already falls back to when a provider fails, so there is one cheaper model to reason about rather than two.

The switch is refused — and the run stops at its ceiling instead — when it could not be made safely: when no pricing is known for the fallback (with no price there is no way to know the next call is actually cheaper), when the fallback's context window cannot hold the agent's system prompt, or when switching would silently drop a structured-output guarantee the run depends on. In each case stopping is the honest outcome; failing mid-run is not.

docs.title: How the layers resolve
docs.text:
Nearest wins, dimension by dimension. For any agent step, each limit is taken from the first layer that pins it:

  1. the agent's own run budget, on its Value tab,
  2. the platform.

Per-dimension is what makes partial budgets safe. An agent budget that pins only the cost does not unbound the token limit — the platform's still applies. Worked through:

Cost Tokens Agent's run budget $2.00 (not set) Platform $5.00 1,000,000 Effective $2.00 1,000,000

docs.title: A budget you did not type yourself
docs.text:
Who may raise a limit governs every way a budget can reach your account, not just a value you type into the tab. Which of two things happens depends on whether you chose the number:

  • you typed it — editing an agent: the save is refused, naming the dimension and the platform's value, so you know exactly what to change;
  • you copied it — duplicating an agent, importing one, restoring an older version: the action goes through and any limit above the platform ceiling arrives lowered to that ceiling. Blocking a duplicate over a number somebody else typed would get in the way of the ordinary "copy the company agent and adapt it" workflow, and lowering it prevents the same escalation.

Either way you cannot end up holding a budget an administrator did not grant. An admin's copy keeps its values, since they could have typed them.

docs.title: What happens when a budget runs out
docs.text:
The run stops making model calls and writes its final answer from the work it completed, using the reserve. The answer says which limit was reached, so the outcome is a shorter result rather than a failure with nothing to show.

Time is the exception in one respect: the duration limit is folded into the run's existing deadline, and whichever bound is tighter applies.

docs.title: When a budget does not apply
docs.text:
Cost needs pricing. The cost ceiling is enforced from the platform's model price table, which is seeded for known models. If no price is known for the model a run uses, cost is not enforced for that run — a warning is logged and the token, tool-call and time limits still apply. Missing pricing data must never be able to stop every run on the platform.

Platform limits bound autonomous work. The platform's own settings apply to assignment runs. A budget you configure on an agent applies wherever that agent runs, chat included — configuring a budget is an explicit act, so it takes effect everywhere.

A budget smaller than one call

A model call the remaining budget cannot cover at the model's full maximum output is made with a lower maximum output, sized to what is left. A limit below the cost or tokens of a single call even with its maximum output lowered to 1,024 tokens makes every run stop immediately and return a summary of tool output. The platform logs an explicit warning at the start of such a run. Raise the budget.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Read Agentic flow for how agents hand work to each other, or Agents for the other tabs on an agent's detail page.

docs.title: Agentic flow
docs.text: Agentic Flow, opened from the main sidebar, shows how your agents cooperate: who hands work to whom, which agents work together as a fleet, and what is scheduled to run.

docs.title: What Agentic Flow is for
docs.text:
Use this view when you want to:

  • understand how one agent hands work to another
  • see the structure behind a shared workflow
  • inspect the path a task can follow
  • review or adjust that structure, if you are allowed to edit it

docs.title: Understand the handover types
docs.text:
The graph uses named connection types between agents.

  • Delegate sends work to another agent in the background.
  • Consult asks another agent for help and returns to the original agent.
  • Transfer moves the conversation to another agent.
  • Mandatory transfer forces the conversation to continue with another agent.

These labels matter because they change how the user experience behaves in chat and in automation.

A consulted agent can consult in turn. When the agent asked needs another agent's answer and has that agent as a Consult handover, it asks it before answering, so its answer carries what the other agent found: an orchestrator consulting a clerk that needs a figure from an analyst gets the clerk's answer with the analyst's figure. While it is being consulted, an agent only consults: it never transfers the conversation and never starts background work. A chain of consults stops at the platform's delegation depth (five levels), and an agent already in the chain is never asked again - a consult that would loop back to it is refused as a circular handover. Each nested consult shows in the Activity tab under the run of the agent that made it.

An agent running a background task can ask the agent that gave it the task a question. Handovers back to an agent already in the chain are refused, so that a task never loops back to its orchestrator; one exception: when the agent that spawned the task is also one of its Consult handovers, the task can consult it, up to three times per run by default (DELEGATED_PARENT_CONSULT_LIMIT, 0 turns it off). The orchestrator answers from what it knows and its own tools, without consulting or delegating to anyone in that answer. A background task back to the orchestrator stays refused.

An agent whose handover agents have no type yet (configured before handover types existed, or through the API without types) shows each of them as All types: it can delegate to, consult or transfer to each one. Types are set per agent, so giving one of them a type, on the agent's configuration page or on this graph, gives every one of them a type: the others become Delegate, and you are shown which ones and asked to confirm first. Saving the agent's handovers without picking a type keeps them All types, and so does adding a handover agent next to them. Once the handover agents have types, removing the only typed one, or deleting that agent, leaves the others Delegate: they never switch back to All types on their own.

An agent can also delegate to itself: faced with a large workload, it can split the work across background copies of itself that run in parallel, even with no handover agent configured. This is on by default. To keep an agent from spawning copies of itself, turn off Parallel copies of itself in the Agent Handover card of its configuration; it can still delegate to its handover agents, and copies already running finish their work. When an administrator has switched the capability off for the whole platform (AGENT_SELF_FANOUT_ENABLED), no agent spawns copies of itself, whatever this option says.

docs.title: The global Agentic Flow page
docs.text:
Choose Agentic Flow from the left sidebar. The page has up to three tabs:

  • Agent-to-agent map, the tab it opens on: the agents in scope and the handovers between them
  • Fleets: the fleets you can see, each with its own page (see Fleets)
  • Flows: the flow library, when your platform has flows turned on

The map has two views, chosen with the switch above it:

  • Graph (the default): your agents in one graph (Mine), or the agents of another segment, the handover links between them, a focus field to isolate one or more agents, on a graph you can pan and zoom
  • Schedule: the assignment triggers and one-off scheduled items of the same agents, on a timeline of the next hour, the next 24 hours or the next 7 days. An agent's Coming up card opens this view narrowed to that agent, and Show every agent widens it back. An old link to /flows/schedule opens this view.

The tab and the view are kept in the address (/flows/map, /flows/map/schedule, /fleets), so a link reopens the same screen and the browser's back and forward move between them.

Scroll the mouse wheel or pinch on a trackpad to zoom in or out where the pointer is. Drag an empty area of the map to move it. Double-click an empty area to fit the whole map back in view. While the pointer is over the map, the page does not scroll.

docs.title: Choose whose agents the map draws
docs.text:
The toolbar above the graph starts with the same visibility filter as every list page: Mine | Company | Shared | All, each with the number of agents it holds. When neither the address (?vis=) nor your last pick names a segment, the map opens on the first one that holds an agent: Mine, else Company, else Shared, else All.

  • Mine draws the agents you own and the handovers between them.
  • Company draws the agents published to the whole company.
  • Shared draws the agents shared with you directly or through a group.
  • All draws every agent you can see.

A handover to an agent outside the segment is not drawn. The counts under the graph (agents, fleets, handovers, runs in flight, open work items) are those of the segment shown. When you own no agent but others are visible, one line under the toolbar says so, with a link to All.

The segment is kept in the address (?vis=mine, ?vis=all...), so a link reopens the same map. A link that focuses an agent (?focus=) and names no segment opens on All. The Filters menu keeps the other filters (agent type, enabled, activity); they apply inside the segment.

docs.title: See fleets as one node
docs.text:
When some of the agents you can see belong to a fleet, the map draws each fleet as a single node by default: the fleet's name and icon in place of its members. A handover from an agent to a member is drawn to the fleet node, a handover from one fleet to another is drawn once between the two fleet nodes, and the handovers inside a fleet are left to the fleet page. The counts under the graph are those of what is drawn, fleets counted apart.

Click a fleet node to open its fleet page. A fleet node is never the start or the end of a new handover: handovers stay between agents, so turn off the Fleets switch in the toolbar to draw every agent and edit their handovers.

docs.title: Follow the map as it changes
docs.text:
When the map changes (another layout, other force settings, the Fleets switch, a focus, a filter, an agent added or moved), the agents slide from where they are to their new place in under a second. New agents fade in where they land and removed ones fade out, so you can follow each agent across the change. If your system asks for reduced motion, the map draws the change at once.

Hover an agent to dim every agent and handover that is not one handover away from it. Click Fit to view in the zoom controls to frame every agent.

Drag an agent to move it: it stays where you drop it, with its handovers, until you change the layout or the agents shown. From the keyboard, focus an agent with Tab and move it with the arrow keys (hold Shift for larger steps). Hold Alt with an arrow key to move the focus to the nearest agent in that direction instead. Dropped or moved onto another agent, it goes to the nearest free spot. A moved agent carries a small dot on its ring. Click Unpin agents in the zoom controls to put every moved agent back in its place. Agents with no handover sit with the other agents of their fleet (under the fleet's name when the map shows several fleets), apart from the other fleets and the agents of the playground. When the map is too dense to draw any name, a hint at the bottom left says to zoom in or hover an agent to read its name.

docs.title: Use the focus field
docs.text:
Large graphs are easier to read when you focus on a few agents.

Use the focus field to:

  • highlight one agent
  • compare a few related agents
  • reduce visual noise in a large environment

You can add and remove focused agents directly from the filter area, or double-click an agent on the graph. A focused agent that is no longer on the graph (a deleted agent, an old link) is ignored: when none of the focused agents is on it, the whole graph is shown.

Once an agent is focused, choose how the graph shows it:

  • Show only (the default) lays out the focused agents alone: each one, every agent it hands work to or receives work from, and the handovers between them. Double-click one of those agents to add it to the focus and bring its own handover agents in, one step at a time. The counts under the graph are those of what is shown. A handover is created between two agents on the graph: to connect an agent that is not shown, add it to the focus or switch to Highlight.
  • Highlight keeps the whole graph and dims every agent outside the focus.

docs.title: Open an agent from the graph
docs.text:
You can open an agent directly from the global graph.

This is useful when you want to move from a visual connection view to the full agent detail page.

docs.title: Editing the global graph
docs.text:
If your role allows it, the global graph is not only a viewer. It can also be an editing surface.

Authorized users may be able to:

  • create a new handover between two agents
  • change the type of an existing handover
  • remove a handover

Click an agent to select it and open its details panel. To create a handover, press the connection icon at the bottom right of an agent you can manage and drag it onto the target agent, then pick the handover type. Releasing the icon without moving starts the handover too: click the target agent to end it, or press Esc to cancel. From the keyboard, press Space on the focused agent to start a handover and Space or Enter on the target to end it; Enter at rest opens the details panel.

Because these are global relationships, a change here affects all users who rely on that agent behavior. When the platform refuses a handover, the message says why: a handover to a member of a fleet that does not expose it to other fleets, for example, names the fleet and points to its orchestrator.

docs.title: Fleets
docs.text: The Fleets tab lists the fleets you can see: groups of agents that work together around an orchestrator and one workspace. Each card shows the fleet's orchestrator, how many home members and connected agents it has, and its workspace. A building icon marks a company-managed fleet, a shared icon a fleet another user shared with you.

docs.title: Create a fleet
docs.text:
The tab offers two ways, on the empty state and above the cards:

  • New fleet opens a form: a name and a description, the workspace the fleet coordinates in (one you manage, or a new one named after the fleet), the orchestrator and the home members, the connected agents with their collaboration instruction and the context they receive, and which home members other fleets may reach (the orchestrator always can). Only agents you manage that have no home fleet yet can be home members, since an agent has one home fleet. Create fleet opens the new fleet's page.
  • Create with a prompt opens the chat with a sentence to finish ("Create a fleet named ... in the workspace ... with ... as orchestrator and ... as members"), on an assistant that carries the Fleets built-in tool. The assistant creates the fleet and answers its link. The button is disabled when no assistant carries the tool: turn on Fleets in an agent's Built-in Tools, or in the General Assistant's.

The Fleets built-in tool lets an agent list, read, create, update and delete fleets, set their members and their exposure. It acts as you: it sees and changes only the fleets and agents you could from the tab, and company-managed fleets stay for administrators.

Click a card to open the fleet page:

  • the header names the fleet, its workspace and its orchestrator, and its Settings button opens the fleet settings
  • Graph draws the handovers between the fleet's agents (its home members and the agents it connects) with the same layouts and toolbar as the agent-to-agent map. An agent that is not a home member is drawn as a ghost node: a dashed outline, less emphasis and the name of its home fleet under its own (nothing for an agent in no fleet). That covers the agents the fleet connects and the agents at the far end of a handover that crosses the fleet's boundary. A ghost node only opens the agent when you click it. Only the handovers the fleet graph returns are drawn: a handover between two agents that are both outside the fleet is left out. A cross-fleet handover that no connected agent governs, or that reaches an agent its own fleet does not expose, is drawn with a dotted line, and its tooltip says which. An agent you cannot read is not drawn.
  • Data flow shows where the fleet's work starts and where it goes, in three lanes: the sources that start its members (integration events, schedules, platform events), the members, and the integrations they write to. Hover a member to light its own sources and outputs; click a source to read its assignments and filters. Opening it reads the configuration only: it starts no run and uses no quota. The address ?view=flow opens it, and so does an older link to the graph's former Data flow switch.
  • Schedule shows the assignment triggers and one-off items of the fleet's home members (the agents it connects keep them in their own fleet)
  • Members lists the home members you can see as the fleet's hierarchy (the orchestrator first, each member under the one it reports to) with their role and their health, what needs a look first: Failing (a run failed in the last 24 hours), Stale (open work items left waiting), Disabled, Idle (no run yet) and OK, with the last run and the runs and work items in flight. Click a member to open the agent. When the fleet has members but none is shared with you, the panel says so. Below them, Connected agents and fleets lists what the fleet calls without owning it.

A fleet lives in one workspace, where its agents coordinate: work items, shared state and knowledge. The workspace survives the fleet, not the reverse: deleting a fleet keeps its workspace with its work items and shared state, a workspace that hosts a fleet cannot be deleted, and one that hosts a live fleet cannot be archived. The workspace's card in Work > Operations > Workspaces names the fleets it hosts (see Fleets and workspaces).

docs.title: Edit a fleet
docs.text:
The owner of a fleet, the people granted configuration on it and administrators edit it from its page. Anyone else sees the same panels with every control disabled and the reason.

Settings opens a side panel: name, description, icon and colour; the workspace the fleet's agents coordinate in (one per fleet); the orchestrator, chosen among the home members; the members other fleets may reach besides the orchestrator; visibility and sharing, as for workspaces; archive or restore; delete. Deleting a fleet never deletes an agent: its members go back to the playground with their handovers and assignments, and the workspace is kept.

The panel's Run defaults section sets what one run of a home member may use when the agent sets nothing of its own: the four budget limits of the agent Budget tab (cost, tokens, tool calls, duration) and Max iterations. An agent's own value always wins, a connected agent keeps its own home fleet's defaults, and an empty field inherits the platform budget; clearing every field removes the fleet's defaults. You can lower a limit below the platform budget; a value above it is outlined with the reason and only an administrator can save it, as on the agent Budget tab.

Under the members panel, the people who manage the fleet see Fleet cost: the priced spend of the runs of its home members over the last 7, 30 or 90 days, in total and by agent. A connected agent's runs count for its own home fleet.

A run's units start unreviewed. Whoever may act on the run (an administrator for a shared run) marks its outcome with PUT /api/v1/roi/records/{record_id}/outcome and {"outcome": "accepted" | "modified" | "rejected", "review_min": 5, "note": "..."}, or {"outcome": null} to clear it. A rejected run counts no value, a modified one counts its value less the review minutes, an unreviewed one counts like an accepted one and is shown apart: each group of the report carries reviewed, unreviewed, rejected and review_rate. Administrators list the records to review with GET /api/v1/roi/records?outcome=unreviewed, and the runs list takes review=unreviewed.

In Members:

  • Add a member offers the agents you manage that have no home fleet: an agent has one home fleet or none.
  • Drag a member onto another to make it report to that one, or onto Top level; from the keyboard, the member's menu has Change parent.... A member never reports to itself or to one of its own reports.
  • The member's menu also sets its role (a label shown beside its name, the agent does not change), exposes it to other fleets, moves it to another fleet you manage, or removes it from the fleet. A move happens in one step: the member leaves this fleet and joins the other at top level, not exposed and without a role. When the other fleet refuses it (archived, company-managed for a personal agent, already connected to that agent), nothing changes and the member stays where it was, role, parent, exposure and orchestrator included. Moving the orchestrator leaves this fleet without one until you choose another. The agent keeps its handovers and assignments. An agent with the fleets tools does the same with move_fleet_member.
  • Connect an agent and Connect a fleet add a connected row; each says when the fleet calls it (the collaboration instruction) and what context it receives (none, a summary or the full conversation).

On the Graph view, the handovers of the home members are edited as on the agent-to-agent map: draw a handover from a member you can manage to another agent of the graph, or click a handover to change its type or remove it. Ghost nodes are never the start of a new handover here; edit them from their own fleet. A handover to a member of another fleet that its fleet does not expose is refused, and the message names the agent and its fleet. Nothing is editable on the graph of an archived fleet. Unlike membership, a handover is part of the source agent's configuration: changing it is an agent update.

Right-click a node of the fleet graph to open its menu:

  • Open the agent opens its page.
  • Focus on its handovers dims every agent except this one and the agents it hands over to or receives a handover from; Clear the focus (or a double click on the node) shows them all again.
  • On a home member of a fleet you can manage, and only while the fleet is not archived: Add a handover from it... picks a target among the home members and a handover type (it needs the right to edit the agent, as drawing the edge does), Change parent... picks who it reports to in the fleet, and Remove from the fleet takes it out after a confirmation; the agent goes back to the playground, unchanged.

A ghost node's menu only opens the agent or focuses on it.

On the graph of a fleet you can manage, and only while it is not archived, drag a home member's node onto another home member to make it report to that member. While you drag, a line follows the pointer: solid over the member it would report to, which is ringed, and dashed grey over a node it cannot report to (itself, one of its own reports, its current parent, a ghost), where the pointer shows it is not allowed and dropping changes nothing. After a drop, the new parent stays ringed for a moment. The drag needs a mouse; from the keyboard, use Change parent... in the member's menu. Press Escape or release outside a member to cancel. A short click still starts a handover. To move a member back to the top level, use Change parent... or the members panel.

None of the membership changes edits an agent: membership never creates a configuration version or triggers an evaluation. An archived fleet keeps its settings editable, to restore it, and its members frozen: adding, changing, removing or exposing a member is refused until it is restored, in the panel, through the API and through the fleets tools alike. Changing the orchestrator never leaves the previous one exposed unless it was exposed on its own.

docs.title: Set a fleet's run defaults and read its cost
docs.text: Run defaults and the fleet's cost are on the fleet page: Run defaults in the Settings panel, and the Fleet cost card under the members panel (see Edit a fleet). A member that sets its own value keeps it; a limit it leaves empty takes the fleet's; what neither sets is the platform's. A connected agent runs on the defaults of its own home fleet, never on those of the fleet that calls it, and its runs count in its own home fleet's cost.

docs.title: Export and apply a fleet spec
docs.text:
A fleet can be kept as code: its spec (apiVersion: xtm-one/fleet/v1, kind: Fleet) carries the fleet's name, description, icon, colour and workspace name, the card's skills and accepted handover types, the fleet's autonomy level (autonomy_level), the orchestrator, and each home member with its role label, whom it reports to, whether it is exposed, its handovers to other members and its agent in the agent export format. Secret values never travel, and an agent you can see but not manage travels by reference only. Connected agents and fleets travel by reference with their collaboration instruction and context inclusion.

  • Export: ask an assistant that carries the Fleets built-in tool to export the fleet (export_fleet_spec).
  • To export the structure only, ask for the spec without the agent bundles (export_fleet_spec with bundles=false). Every member is a reference to its agent (its slug) with its role label, parent, exposure and handovers, a few kilobytes where the agent bundles of a large fleet weigh megabytes. The tool writes the full spec, bundles included, to a file of the conversation and names it; it does the same on its own when the full spec is too long to answer inline. A structure-only spec is a valid spec: applied, each member is adopted by its slug.
  • Apply with the apply_fleet_spec tool (the spec inline, or a file of the conversation holding it, such as the one export_fleet_spec wrote). It runs as a dry run by default: the answer is the plan (each object created, updated, added, removed or unchanged), and nothing is written until you ask the assistant to apply it for real.

Applying is idempotent. The fleet is found by its slug among your own fleets, and each member by its key, the agent's slug: an agent you manage under that slug joins the fleet as it is and is never edited (a difference with the spec is reported as a warning); otherwise the agent is created from its bundle, with its handovers to the other members. Home members the spec does not name leave the fleet, and their agents are kept. A new fleet is created at the spec's autonomy level, so it never runs a moment more autonomous than the spec says; on an existing fleet the spec can lower the level, and a raise is reported as a warning and left to an administrator on the fleet page. The create_fleet tool takes the same autonomy_level. A reference that cannot be resolved for you (an agent you cannot manage, one already home in another fleet, a connected agent you cannot see) is listed and blocks the apply, unless you ask for a partial apply. A spec applies to a personal fleet only: the export of a company-managed fleet applied under its slug is refused whole, dry run included, with the reason, rather than planned as a personal fleet without its company-managed members. Change a company-managed fleet on its fleet page or with the fleet tools, or apply its spec under another slug. A fleet exported, deleted with its agents, and applied again exports the same spec.

docs.title: Fork a fleet
docs.text:
Any fleet you can see can be forked into a personal copy that you can fully edit, a built-in fleet included. Built-in fleets are read-only and rewritten by the platform at every start; a fork is how you adapt one to your own needs. Fork through POST /api/v1/fleets/{id}/fork with an optional name (default Copy of the source's name), an optional workspace_id (default: a new personal workspace) and members:

  • copy (the default): every member agent becomes an editable personal copy, as Duplicate does on an agent page. The hierarchy, exposure, role labels and orchestrator follow, and the handovers between members point at the copies.
  • keep: the orchestrator is copied, and the other members are linked to the fork as connected agents (an agent has one home fleet), with their role label as the collaboration instruction.

The fork also carries the card's skills, the accepted handover types, the run defaults (lowered to your ceiling) and the connected agents and fleets you can see. Every copied automation is created switched off, whatever its state on the source, so a fork starts no run and uses no quota until you enable an automation yourself. The fork records where it came from (forked_from: the source fleet, whether it was built-in, and a fingerprint of its structure at fork time), so a later change to the source can be detected. GET /api/v1/fleets/{id}/source-changes answers whether the source changed since the fork and lists what moved: the fleet card fields, the members added, removed or changed (role, parent, exposure, persona, skills, handovers) and the connected agents and fleets. The platform never touches the fork again.

docs.title: Generate a fleet spec from a prompt
docs.text:
Describe the fleet you want ("an orchestrator that triages incoming alerts, with an analyst, a hunter and a reporter") and let the model write its spec:

  • Ask an assistant that carries the Fleets built-in tool: it calls generate_fleet_spec, shows you the spec and its plan, and applies it with apply_fleet_spec once you agree. Ask it to change the spec before applying; it refines the same spec rather than starting over.

Generating never writes anything: the answer is the spec and the exact dry-run plan of applying it. The model sees the agents, fleets and workspaces you can see. An agent you manage that has no home fleet may be reused as a member; any other existing agent can only be connected. A new member is created with a name, a description and a persona, and nothing else: add its tools, model and integrations on its agent page after the apply. Generating needs AI enabled and the agentic AI licence, like applying.

docs.title: Keep a fleet's documentation current from an assistant
docs.text:
A fleet's About documentation is always generated by AI. An assistant that carries the Fleets built-in tool regenerates it with regenerate_fleet_documentation (the whole documentation, or one section), with the same permission as editing the fleet's configuration. After a change to a fleet's configuration (update_fleet, its members, their hierarchy, a move, an applied spec), the answer says documentation_out_of_date: true when the documentation no longer matches, so the orchestrator knows to regenerate it once. On a built-in fleet the result is a local version; the shipped one can be restored from the About page. Each regeneration is one model call counted on the run or conversation that makes it; nothing regenerates on its own.

A suggestion of the documentation dismissed from the About page or with list_fleet_doc_findings(action="dismiss") stays dismissed however a later regeneration words it: the same kind of point on the same member, about the same subject, keeps its id and stays hidden. A dismissal lapses only when the member it names is reconfigured or after 90 days, and list_fleet_doc_findings then says why next to the suggestion that is back. A change of the fleet's approval gates never lapses a dismissal: a gate that fixes the point removes the suggestion itself.

A home member with no role label is raised as a suggestion at every whole regeneration, one per member, whatever the size of the fleet; it goes as soon as the label is set. An assistant sets or clears a member's role label with set_fleet_member_parent and its role_label argument (an empty label clears it; passed alone, the member keeps its parent), on any fleet it may manage, company-managed included; the answer names the old and the new label, and the change is audited like a change from the member menu.

docs.title: Share a fleet as a one-page datasheet
docs.text: Once a fleet has documentation, Export PDF at the top right of its About page downloads a one-page A4 datasheet: the fleet's purpose and outcome, its status, a small graph of its members, what starts it, its steps and approval gates, the integrations and tools each member uses, the objects it creates, the prerequisites as they stand for you, the automations on, the estimated monthly runs and the unit of work, with the date and version of the documentation. It is built from the stored documentation, so it calls no model, uses no quota and works with AI switched off. A part the documentation does not cover is printed as "Not stated in the documentation"; a long list ends with "+N more" so the sheet always fits on one page.

docs.title: Follow a fleet's operations
docs.text: The fleet page has seven views: Graph, Data flow, About, Members, Schedule, Operations and, for the fleet's managers, ROI. Operations shows what the fleet's home members run, delegate and produce, its orchestrator included and its connected agents left out: Runs (the default), Background Tasks, Work Items, Shared State and Worksets. Each list is the Operations page's own, with its filters, pagination and details, locked on the fleet, so it has no Fleet filter; the same holds for the Operations tab of a workspace, locked on the workspace. The list is kept in the address (?ops=work-items), so a link reopens it. To compare fleets or look across several, use the Fleet filter of the Operations page (see Work history).

docs.title: See an agent's fleet from its page
docs.text:
The Overview of an agent carries a Fleet card:

  • its home fleet, as a link to the fleet page, with who it reports to (Leads the fleet for the orchestrator, Reports to the orchestrator at the top level, At the top level: the fleet has no orchestrator when none is set, or the name of its parent) and its role label;
  • the chips Orchestrator, Reachable from other fleets and Archived when they apply;
  • Connected to: the other fleets that connect this agent, with the context each one receives (No context, A summary, The full conversation, the words of the members panel) and its collaboration instruction;
  • an agent in no fleet says so, with a link to the Fleets tab; an agent whose home fleet you cannot see says In a fleet you cannot see. without naming it.

Without the licence the card is not drawn; any other failed read says The fleet could not be loaded. on the card. The card is read only: Edit in the fleet (or Open the fleet when you cannot manage it) opens the fleet page, where membership is edited. Only the fleets you can see are named.

Fleets are part of the agentic AI features of the Enterprise Edition: without that licence the tab says so instead of listing fleets, and the agent page shows no Fleet card.

docs.title: Good practices for a fleet
docs.text:
These are suggestions drawn from fleets that run in production. The platform refuses nothing that departs from them; adapt them to the fleet's purpose. Every fleet orchestrator carries them as the built-in skill Fleet design and operations, and the setup assistant proposes the first one when you build a fleet. The built-in fleets ship with it: each of their members holds a Consult handover to the fleet's orchestrator.

  1. Two-way coordination. Give each home member a Consult handover to the orchestrator, so it can ask a route, scope or context question; the orchestrator holds the handover types it needs to its members; members report to the orchestrator in the layout. A delegated task may consult the agent that spawned it when that agent is one of its Consult handovers.
  2. One entry point. People talk to the orchestrator; members run from their automations, chat off, unless a person needs one directly.
  3. Reactive first. Wake a member on an event (its work item inbox, a platform event, an integration event); keep a schedule for a permanent cycle someone reads at a fixed time, plus at most one safety net with its exit criterion; temporary work is a timer or a one-off scheduled item.
  4. Work through work items. One key prefix per member, the owner set, a precise ask and deliverable, dedupe by key, not_before to defer and due_at for a real deadline, files attached; something wakes every item; the orchestrator reads results back before using them.
  5. Closed loop. An item whose completion changes what the fleet runs on carries a fleet impact to the orchestrator, which listens on work_item.completed.
  6. Self-healing. Listeners on the orchestrator for run.orphaned, run.failed and frictions; get_fleet_health weekly with the Fleet health advisory skill.
  7. Decisions to people. Park an item for a person with a structured ask (options and a recommendation); read who is waiting live from the items; the run that closes a loop also resolves its shared state and memory.
  8. Shared state hygiene. One stable key per thing, its terminal condition named at creation, resolved when done, lists bounded.
  9. Knowledge and records. Generic, stable personas; procedures in skills, each rule written once and dated; durable facts in a knowledge base; short-lived state in memory or shared state. A fact in the knowledge base is a lead: the system of record wins. In more detail:
    • One shared working knowledge base per fleet, named <Fleet> - Working knowledge: the orchestrator holds the write grant, every member is bound to it read-only, so there is one writer and every member reads the same facts.
    • Members search it at the start of every task and propose updates in their run result (a KNOWLEDGE: line); the orchestrator applies them.
    • Numbered documents, one per subject, rewritten whole in place with a "Last rewritten" date. A good default set: 00 How this knowledge base works, 10 Fleet runbook, 15 Integration routing, 20 Counterparts directory, 30 Members' working notes, 40 Owner's standing preferences, 50 Programs context, 60 to 89 domain documents, 90 Lessons log.
    • The runbook mirrors the live fleet (members, accounts, assignments and their triggers, skills, shared state and memory keys, temporary assignments with their exit criterion, a rules registry, known gaps, a 14-day change log), under a size bound.
    • Credentials, secrets, identity numbers, personal data, message content and confidential figures stay out.
    • A weekly inventory read corrects the runbook against the live fleet; a change of the fleet's shape goes into the change log the same day.
    • Long documents are written in one write from a draft, never assembled across several writes.
    • Consistent names ([<Fleet>] <Member>, skills prefixed by their member, one work item key prefix per member, shared state keys <fleet>:<thing>); a retired member, assignment or skill is deleted once its replacement is verified; members share one settings baseline unless a reason is recorded.
    • Every member ends its internal run summary with what it used and its frictions; these lines stay out of what a person reads.
  10. Smart notifications. Act by default on safe work, ask only for a real decision with a recommendation, tell the affected person once, nothing for a non-event.
  11. Verify. Read back every write, do not assume ids, names or statuses, remove a run's test artefacts in that run.
  12. Least tools. Scope each member's built-in tool groups to what it does.

The fleet's About page reads several of these practices off the configuration and lists what departs from them under Suggestions, with the findings of its documentation. The page computes them each time it opens, with no model call, for the people who manage the fleet:

Suggestion When it shows What you can do Member cannot consult the orchestrator A home member holds no handover to the orchestrator that runs as Consult. Apply adds that Consult handover after one confirmation; the member's other handovers keep their type and the change is versioned on the agent. Member open to chat A home member other than the orchestrator takes chats. Open the agent and turn chat off, or dismiss it when people talk to that member directly. Work items without an inbox A home member owns open work items and has no enabled automation triggered by its work items. Open the agent and add that automation. Orchestrator without listeners The orchestrator has no enabled platform event automation on work_item.completed, run.orphaned or run.failed. Open the orchestrator and add the listeners. No working knowledge base No knowledge base is bound to the orchestrator and every home member, and none the orchestrator writes is read by a member. Create <Fleet> - Working knowledge; the setup assistant (get_fleet_setup) proposes it with five skeleton documents and creates it on your yes. Orchestrator cannot write the knowledge base A knowledge base bound to the orchestrator and every home member has no write grant for the orchestrator. Apply grants the orchestrator write on it after one confirmation, versioned on the agent. Member without the working knowledge base A home member is not bound to the knowledge base the orchestrator writes for the fleet. Apply binds it to the member, read-only, after one confirmation and the same binding checks as an agent edit; dismiss it with a reason when the member is kept isolated on purpose. Knowledge base with several writers A home member other than the orchestrator also writes the working knowledge base. Open the member and keep it read-only, or dismiss it with a reason.

Dismiss and Restore work as for the other suggestions: a dismissal, with its optional reason, holds while the member it names is unchanged. A suggestion goes by itself once the configuration follows the practice. Nothing is refused because of a suggestion.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Work History, where you review runs, waiting items, notifications, and execution details.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: Agents are the main assistants in XTM One. Each one is configured for a particular role, team, or workflow.

docs.title: What an agent is for
docs.text:
Use an agent when you want a more focused assistant than the General Assistant. An agent can answer questions in a specific domain, use selected tools and integrations, search one or more knowledge bases, hand work to other agents, and run background tasks automatically.

An agent works on its own through assignments: a trigger (a schedule, an event, a webhook) and a prompt. See Assignments and triggers.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
Choose Agents from the left sidebar to open the list. You can browse all visible agents, search, filter by visibility or tag, import an agent from a file, and — if your role allows it — create a new one (see Create an agent). Each card is a quick summary: the agent's status, what is attached to it, and whether it is company-managed or shared. Some cards also offer quick actions such as opening a chat or enabling and disabling the agent.

Click the star on an agent's card or row to make it a favorite. Favorites are pinned to the top of the list in both views, above everything else and whichever column you sort by, so the two or three agents you actually work with stay one glance away in a long fleet. The choice is yours alone — it is stored on your account, follows you to any browser, and changes nothing for anyone else. Click the star again to remove it. Filters still come first: a favorite that does not match your search or tag filter is not shown.

The toggle at the right of the filter row switches between the card grid and a sortable list. The list view is the better choice once you manage more than a handful of agents: it puts status, model, assignment count, and attached resources in sortable columns so you can answer questions like "which agents run which model?" by scanning one column. See grid and list views for how sorting and persistence work.

Not every visible agent is editable. Company-managed agents are shared broadly and often read-only for standard users, shared agents come from a group or another owner, and built-in agents are typically read-only. If you open an agent and cannot change it, the page is behaving as designed for your access level.

Connecting a resource to an agent or to one of its assignments (an MCP server, an integration or a channel bot) is limited to the ones you can see yourself, and a save that adds another one is refused; what the agent or the assignment already names stays in place when you save, whoever connected it. An agent shared with you runs with what its owner connected to it - their MCP servers, custom tools, knowledge bases, channel bots and integrations - in its assignment runs, and in your chats too with one exception, integrations: in a chat, an integration you cannot see, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with you, is not used for you (see Sharing an OAuth integration). Your own or a company-wide integration of the same service takes its place when the agent resolves one for you; otherwise a note under the answer names the integration (by its service only when it is not shared with you) and says why, and the agent is told too, so it can say what it cannot do.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Click an agent card to open its detail page. The header gives you direct actions — Chat with Agent, Duplicate, Export, enable or disable, and delete when you can manage the agent. If the agent is designed mainly for assignments, the chat button still works but XTM One warns that it is not optimized for conversation.

The page is organized into tabs (some appear only when your role can see them):

  • Overview is the best first stop: a quick understanding of what the agent does and what is attached to it, without reading the full configuration. Its Coming up card lists what the agent will do next and when: your scheduled work items on it and the next runs of its scheduled assignments, with actions to cancel or reschedule a scheduled item, and Open in Schedule to see them in the fleet's schedule.
  • Configuration is how the agent is set up — persona and instructions, tools and integrations, knowledge and memory, handovers, channels, and intent bindings. For most users this is a reading page; editing is usually reserved for admins. The Intent Bindings card is what makes the agent available inside OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ; see Intents. A built-in tool the agent carries but this deployment has switched off (the code interpreter, Runners, a feature not enabled here) is shown greyed as Unavailable: it does nothing until an administrator enables it, and while editing you can remove it from the agent, not add it. On a company-managed agent that carries Work Items or Shared State, the same card holds its Coordination access: which agents can read and change the company-managed work items it creates and the shared state it owns (see Work history).
  • The Model picker in Configuration chooses what the agent runs on: Platform default, one model, or Platform routing model. The routing model is the lightweight model an administrator sets in Settings > AI Models (the one that already evaluates routing conditions); pick it for an agent that takes a narrow, repeated decision - classify, judge, route - that a small model handles well and for less. The agent then follows whatever routing model the administrator configures. When none is configured, the agent runs on the platform default model, and the Configuration and Overview tabs say so. Choosing a model of its own takes the agent off the routing model.
  • Value shows what the agent returns, then what it may spend. Its ROI section comes first: hours saved, net value and review rate over the last 7, 30 or 90 days, how they are computed, and what the agent delivered from chat. Below it, the run budget caps what one run of the agent may spend — money, tokens, tool calls or time — and can let a run that reaches its cost ceiling finish on a cheaper model instead of stopping. Lowering a limit is open to anyone who can edit the agent; raising one above the platform's own budget is an administrator's decision. See Run budgets. The tab was called Budget and the ROI sat on Overview before; links to either open Value.
  • Versioning lists every version of the persona and of the tracked settings, to compare them and roll back.
  • Memory shows the agent's longer-term memory, where authorized users can search it, review its health, and run maintenance. An entry that no longer holds is marked Superseded (see What the agent remembers).
  • Observability shows how the agent performs over the recent period: traces over 7 days, average cost and latency, error rate, average feedback and quota consumed, then its cost over 30 days, its recent traces, its models, and the feedback it received. It is shown to the people who can see the agent's chats.
  • Chats shows conversations associated with the agent, to review or reopen context.
  • Delegations shows work the agent sent to or received from other agents, useful for understanding how handovers behaved.
  • Feedback gathers every thumbs up and thumbs down given to the agent's work — its chat answers, its assignment runs, its background tasks and the answers it gave when another agent consulted it — with the comments people left, filterable by kind of work and by rating. When feedback criteria are defined (Settings > Quality), it also shows the agent's weighted score and, per criterion, the average, the distribution and the last 30 days. It is shown to the people who can manage the agent.
  • Activity is the agent's run history — review recent executions and spot failures.

docs.title: What the agent remembers
docs.text:
An agent with persistent memory stores what it learns (store_memory), searches it (search_memory), and is given the most relevant entries at the start of each conversation and assignment run.

Some entries describe something that changes: what a document's footer says, how many slides a deck has, the status of a ticket. The agent stores those as state entries, named by the object they describe (a subject such as doc:<id> or presentation:<id>). When it records a newer observation of the same subject, that one replaces the older:

  • The older entry is kept and still found by a search, listed after the current ones and marked Superseded. It is never given to the agent as context again.
  • A state entry reaches the agent dated (as of <date>, verify live), with a reminder that it is a past observation and that the live document, deck or ticket is the one to check before acting on it.
  • The agent can also retire an entry that no longer holds (invalidate_memory), by its id or by its subject. A retired entry is kept and marked Superseded too. The agent's shared entries are retired this way only in a session of the agent's owner or of an administrator.

Entries that name no subject behave as they always did. In a conversation, the agent replaces only the memory it keeps for you, and retires the memory it shares with every user of the agent only for its owner or an administrator: otherwise that shared memory stays as it is for the others, and the newer entry is the one you are shown.

What an assignment run remembers is kept for the user the run acts as, with the memory of that user's conversations with the agent: the next runs as that user, and that user's conversations, read it; nobody else's do.

On the Memory tab, clearing the memory, Optimize, and editing or deleting an entry are for the people who can manage the agent: its owner, an administrator, or a user it is shared with to configure. A user it is shared with read-only sees the memory and changes none of it.

docs.title: What an assignment or a roster may name
docs.text:
An assignment whose trigger listens to an integration reads that integration's events with its credentials, so when you save it, the integration it names must be one you can see: yours, one shared with you or one of your groups, or a company-wide one. Admins may name any. Otherwise the save is refused with the same answer whether the integration exists or not. Editing anything else, or saving the trigger again with the integration it already names, is never refused, even if that integration is no longer visible to you. The agent builder tools apply the same rule; when strict admin access for agent tools is on, an administrator's agent may name only the integrations the administrator sees as their own, shared with them or company-wide.

An agent you create from a template gets the template's assignments and default skills (see Create an agent). A template trigger that names an integration you cannot see is created without it, and then listens to the new agent's own integration of that provider.

The agents you let an agent hand work items to (the Work Items tool's roster) follow the same rule: you can add only agents you can see (admins may add any), and the ones already in the roster stay when you save.

docs.title: Duplicate and export
docs.text:
Two header actions are easy to overlook. Duplicate creates a private copy you can adapt without changing the original, and Export downloads the agent so it can be stored, shared, or imported elsewhere. This is especially helpful when your organization uses standard company-managed agents but you need a private variation.

The copy is yours, so it keeps only what you could connect to an agent of your own. When you copy an agent someone else owns, the integrations, MCP servers, knowledge bases, custom tools, skills, prompts, handover agents, work-item owner agents and channel bots you cannot use are left out, in the copied assignments too, and the confirmation says how many of each kind were left out and why (the warnings of the duplicate response). Everything you can use is copied as it is, a personal OAuth integration shared with you included. Whoever copies, an assignment trigger that listens to an integration you cannot see loses it: the copied trigger then listens to the copy's own integration of that provider. The original agent is not changed: it keeps running with everything its owner connected. Copied assignments start disabled.

Export asks which format you want. The XTM One native bundle (default, JSON) carries everything — assignments, handover routing, memory settings, prompts, skills and variables — so use it for backups and for moving an agent between XTM One instances. Microsoft AgentSchema (YAML) is an open, cross-vendor agent definition that other agent platforms can read, and only what that specification can express goes into its standard fields.

Choosing AgentSchema shows you exactly which of your agent's settings will not be included as standard fields — handover, memory tiers, assignments, integration bindings, prompts and skills among them — before the file is created. Nothing on that list is thrown away: it is preserved in an XTM One section of the document's metadata, so re-importing the same file into XTM One restores everything, while other platforms ignore that section.

Exporting everything is for the people who can manage the agent: its owner, someone it is shared with for configuration, and administrators. If you can see an agent but not manage it, such as a company-managed agent or one shared with you as read-only, Export gives you what its AI Catalog download carries instead, in either format. A credential passed to an MCP server as an argument or in its URL is masked. Custom tools that are not company-managed are left out, unless the agent is published with its personal tools included. A company-managed tool, MCP server, skill or prompt restricted to a group you are not in is left out too, and variables come without their values. The file still imports: re-enter the masked values and fill in the variables afterwards.

docs.title: Read-only integrations
docs.text:
An integration bound to an agent can be made read-only for that agent: the agent keeps the tools that read from it (list, get, search, download) and loses the ones that change it (create, update, delete, send, post, transition, upload and any tool whose action is not clearly a read). The setting is enforced when the agent runs, not by an instruction in its prompt: a write tool of a read-only integration is not offered to the agent, and a call that names it anyway is refused. Removing the integration from the agent removes its read-only mark. The same integration can stay writable on another agent.

A per-user integration (bound under Advanced: Dynamic integrations (per-user) on the agent's Tooling tab, resolved to each user's own connection at run time) has the same switch: turn on Read-only on its card and the agent keeps only that provider's read tools, whichever user's connection it resolves to. The card then shows a Read-only badge outside edit mode. Turning the per-user binding off clears the switch. The API and the create_agent / update_agent tools set it as integration_template_read_only, a list of provider keys that must also be in integration_template_bindings.

docs.title: Building agents from a conversation
docs.text:
An agent with the agent builder tools (the General Assistant, or an agent given the agent_builder built-in tool) can build agents for you in chat:

  • update_agent, create_agent and duplicate_agent accept every built-in group the agent settings offer (files, web, cti, design, coordination, observability and the others), plus the former ids they replaced. builtin_tool_ids follows binding_mode: replace (the default) makes the list the agent's set, add adds groups and keeps the others, remove takes groups out. The answer names the groups added and removed.
  • create_agent sets up a complete agent in one call, with everything update_agent can change: model and temperature, built-in tools, memory, tool scoping and deny list, read-only integrations, handover and channels. If one setting is refused, no agent is created. The answer lists every integration bound to the new agent with its name, so you can check none is missing.
  • clone_agent copies an agent you can see, with integrations, knowledge bases and built-in tools added or removed and the persona replaced or extended. It never copies assignments, sharing, intent bindings or the builtin tag (a copy is not a built-in agent), and it shows what differs from the original, naming each intent binding of the original the copy does not have. With copy_memory it also copies the original's persistent memory you may read, with its dates, types and subjects, and says how many entries it copied; the memory of a company-managed agent is copied by an administrator only. Duplicate takes the same option as copy_memory=true on POST /api/v1/agents/{id}/duplicate.
  • list_agent_intent_bindings, bind_agent_to_intent and unbind_agent_from_intent read and change the intents an agent answers, which decide where a connected platform (OpenCTI, OpenAEV) offers it, for example in a playbook's AI agent step. See Intents.
  • edit_opencti_playbook_graph refuses a node whose configuration names a value outside the choices the component offers, such as an AI agent the playbook step does not list, and says which values are allowed: nothing is saved.
  • list_integration_tools shows which tools of an integration read and which write. For OpenAPI integrations (provider: "openapi") it lists the operations imported from each integration's spec, grouped by integration, with each tool's HTTP method and path; integration_id lists one integration.
  • update_integration shares an integration with groups: members can use it (bind it to their agents and run it) or also manage it. An agent shared with a group only uses, for each member, the integrations that member may use.
  • update_integration with is_company_managed makes an integration company-managed (true, visible platform-wide) or private again (false), as the integration's edit page does. Only an admin can change it. A field the tool does not take is refused by name, so nothing is ignored without a word.
  • update_agent also shares an agent, with groups or with named people outside any group: "share this agent with alice@example.com and marie@example.com, read-only" gives them the agent in their agent list and lets them chat with it; config lets them edit it too. Only people who already have an account here can be named - an address no account matches is refused, and nobody is invited. Removing someone takes their access away at once. The answer, and get_agent, say who the agent is shared with: each group by name with its number of members, each person by name and email, with their level of access. A company-managed agent is already open to everyone and is not shared this way.
