An events stream opened while a request is running first receives a thinking frame flagged "resumed": true, then the steps, the reasoning and the answer written so far, then the rest as it happens; a request your client sent itself is not sent again when it reopens its events stream under the same client_id. A user_message frame (message) is a user message stored from another place.

If your script only cares about its own messages, ignore every frame flagged relayed, except for the request your message was folded into (below).

docs.title: Messages folded into a running request
docs.text:
A conversation runs one request at a time. A message you send while another request is running is folded into it: that request takes your message into account, and you receive:

{"type": "folded_into_active_turn", "conversation_id": "<id>", "folded": true, "turn_id": "<turn id>"}

turn_id names the request that answers your message: its frames follow on the same response, flagged relayed, with that turn_id, up to its end. The agents your message mentions answer it in that request, after the agents of that request, or in the next request when it ends before it can ask them. The REST route that sends a message answers 202 with "status": "folded_into_active_turn" and the same turn_id in that case. Rarely, the message is kept for the next request instead ("folded": false on the stream, "status": "queued_for_next_turn" over REST). turn_id is then present only when a request is running, and that request picks the message up.

docs.title: How a request ends
docs.text:
Every request you are shown ends with a done, cancelled or error frame, including one sent somewhere else, even when the connection to the platform's message broker was briefly lost or the process running the request stopped. When the platform itself had to end it, the error frame carries a reason:

reason Meaning interrupted The request was stopped before it produced its answer (a server restart, for instance). lost The request is over, but how it ended could not be delivered. Read the conversation to see what it stored.

A request still running when a normal server restart stops waiting for it stores an assistant message before that error goes out: it says the request was interrupted and names the tool calls that completed, the ones still running and the last completed action. Read back, the message carries "interrupted": true and the completed calls in tool_call_trace. The REST request that started it gets a 503 with Retry-After; read the conversation before sending the message again.

A request that ended before storing its answer, or whose agent failed, leaves its tool work to the next message of the conversation, streamed or over REST: the tool calls it made and their results reach the agent before that message, so it continues instead of calling the same tools again. This holds for 24 hours.

After a done, the stream that ran the request may send one reply_suggestion frame before it closes: {"type": "reply_suggestion", "conversation_id": ..., "message_id": ..., "text": ...}, the message the user would likely send next, for the answer message_id names. It comes only when the message you sent set "supports_reply_suggestions": true, your administrator enabled reply suggestions and set a routing model, and not for every answer: without the field, the stream closes at the end of the request, with no suggestion to wait for. It is a suggestion to show, never something the platform sends on its own; ignore it if your client has no use for it.

A stopped request can end with two cancelled frames on the stream that runs it: the acknowledgement of the stop, then, once the stop is stored, a second one carrying message_id. In the same way, a request whose agent failed can end with an error (without reason), then, once that reply is stored, a done carrying message_id. Both frames mean the request is over; the second one says what to read back.

Keep a safety check

If your script waits for an answer, also read GET /api/v1/chat/conversations/<conversation_id> when the request stays silent for a long time: is_processing is false once no request is running, and the stored messages show the answer. The platform guarantees the end frame; the check covers a network that drops frames on your side.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Go back to Chat to see how the web app shows the same conversation.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: Chat is where you work directly with XTM One in natural language. It supports both the platform-wide General Assistant and individual agents.

docs.title: What Chat is for
docs.text:
Use Chat when you want to:

  • ask a question in plain language
  • work with a specific assistant
  • upload supporting files
  • reuse a saved prompt
  • continue an earlier conversation
  • speak instead of typing, if your browser supports it

docs.title: The chat layout
docs.text:
Chat has two main areas:

  • the left sidebar for assistant selection and conversation history
  • the main panel for the active conversation

If you are on a smaller screen, the sidebar can collapse so the conversation has more space.

While an agent works, the conversation keeps its end in view: each new command card, output line, status change or wait notice scrolls in as it appears, in the browser and in the desktop app. Scroll up to read and the view stays where you put it, with a Scroll to bottom button; scroll back to the end or press the button and it follows again.

Each command or tool card an agent runs on a machine shows on one line: what it did (Ran a command, Read a file), the first line of the command or the path, the machine, the result (a spinner while it runs, then the exit code or the error) and how long it took. Click the line to see the whole command, its output and the copy and larger-view buttons; a card you open stays open while you are on the page.

docs.title: Choose who you want to talk to
docs.text:
At the top of the sidebar, you choose the assistant for the conversation.

You may see:

  • General Assistant
  • chat-enabled agents
  • assignment-oriented agents shown in a Not recommended for chat section

An agent your company manages carries a Company badge. When an administrator links an agent to the General Assistant, that agent takes the General Assistant's place in the list and carries an Assistant badge.

Choose the General Assistant when you want a broad helper. Choose a specific agent when you want an assistant with a focused role or built-in context.

Picking another assistant in the sidebar while a conversation is open starts a new conversation with it. To keep working in the same conversation with another assistant instead, see Continue a conversation with another agent.

docs.title: Continue a conversation with another agent
docs.text:
A conversation keeps its whole history whatever agent answers in it. To hand the conversation you are in to another agent - because its agent was deleted or disabled, or because another agent should apply what you asked earlier - open Conversation options at the top of the conversation, choose Continue with another agent, pick the agent and click Continue.

  • The agent you pick answers from your next message. It receives the earlier messages of the conversation, and reads the earlier answers labelled with the agent that wrote them, so it does not take them for its own.
  • A note Continued by <agent> on <date> marks the change in the conversation.
  • Only your own conversations in the web chat can be continued this way, between two answers. A Slack or Teams conversation is answered by the agent its channel routes to.
  • The agents offered are the ones you can start a conversation with: enabled and open to chat.

When an agent is deleted, its conversations are kept. Its owner can name another agent to continue them (see Agents); otherwise the conversation shows that its agent was deleted, and you continue it with an agent of yours the same way. The Studios offer the same action next to the conversation's agent (the arrows button).

docs.title: Ask an assistant about your earlier conversations
docs.text:
Every assistant you chat with can read your own conversations back, whichever agent you had them with, a deleted one included. Ask it, for example, "apply what I asked about the launch video in my conversation with Video Bot":

  • list_conversations finds the conversation: by a word of its title, by the agent it was held with (agent, an id or a part of its name, a deleted agent by its last name) or by the video, presentation, report or file it is about (object_id, object_type). Each conversation is listed with its agent.
  • read_conversation_history reads its messages, oldest first and a window at a time, the conversation you are in when no conversation is named. Each message comes with who wrote it (you, or the agent by name), its date, the tools an answer used and the tool results in one line each, and the files, videos, decks and reports it carried, so the assistant can open them with its other tools. search keeps only the messages containing a text. The full content of a tool result is never returned.

Only your own conversations can be read, never another person's, even one shared with you; apart from the conversation you are in, a Slack or Teams channel thread other people read is not read either. Reading a conversation other than the one you are in is recorded in the audit log (read_conversation), once per 15 minutes for the same conversation.

docs.title: Start a new conversation
docs.text:
To start a new conversation:

  1. Open Chat from the sidebar.
  2. Choose the assistant you want.
  3. Click the New conversation button.
  4. Type your message and send it.

If you open Chat from an agent card or an agent detail page, XTM One can preselect that agent for you.

docs.title: Manage conversations from the sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar is not only a list of past chats. It is also your main control area.

From here you can:

  • search conversations by title, preview text, or agent name
  • open an earlier conversation
  • organize conversations in workspaces (see below)
  • archive a single conversation
  • archive all conversations from the Archive all conversations action
  • switch assistants without leaving the page

Archiving removes a conversation from the active list. It is not the same as simply closing the page.

The conversations other people shared with you are listed under Shared with me, below your own; the search narrows them by title, owner and last message too.

docs.title: Organize conversations in workspaces
docs.text:
To keep the conversations of one topic together, and let their agents share work items and shared state, file them in a workspace. The sidebar lists your conversations by workspace, a little like folders:

  • Workspaces lists each workspace you can file into, your default first, with the conversations filed in it. Click a workspace's name to fold or unfold it; the sidebar remembers what you folded.
  • Not in a workspace lists the conversations filed nowhere. That is a normal place for a conversation to be: a new conversation starts there, and it stays there until you file it.

From the sidebar you can:

  • create a workspace with the New workspace button next to Workspaces: type its name and press Enter
  • file a conversation by dragging it onto a workspace, or with the Move to workspace menu of its row, which also offers Remove from workspace; dropping a conversation on Not in a workspace takes it out of its workspace too
  • start a conversation directly in a workspace with the + button of that workspace (New conversation in this workspace)
  • manage a workspace from its Workspace actions menu: Rename, and the same actions as on the Workspaces page — Make default, Knowledge bases, Share, Archive and Delete — plus Open in Workspaces. Archiving asks for a confirmation, then takes the workspace out of the sidebar; its conversations are then listed under Other workspaces. To restore it, open Work > Operations > Workspaces, click Show archived, then choose Restore in its actions menu. Deleting asks for a confirmation and keeps its conversations, which then appear under Not in a workspace; a workspace that still holds work items cannot be deleted

Filing a conversation into a workspace other people can see asks first: its members can then search what was written in it.

Only your own conversations can be filed, into workspaces you can change. A workspace shared with you in read-only shows only while it holds one of your conversations, and a conversation filed in a workspace you can no longer see is listed under Other workspaces. While you search, only the workspaces holding a matching conversation are shown.

You can also file the conversation you are in from the Conversation options menu at the top of the conversation (File in a workspace). An assistant with the XTM One built-in tool can do it for you — switch the tool on in the session tools menu, then ask for example "create a workspace called Acme audit and move this conversation into it".

docs.title: Write your message
docs.text:
The composer at the bottom of the screen supports several input methods.

You can:

  • type a normal message
  • attach files with the paperclip button
  • paste files into the composer
  • drag and drop files onto the page
  • insert a saved prompt template
  • use voice dictation
  • start a full voice conversation

A message holds up to 30 files, each up to 40 MB: a batch of screenshots goes in one message. Past 30, the composer names each file it did not attach and says why ("a message holds at most 30 files"); send them in the next message. While Deep Investigation is on, the composer takes a subject, not files: remove the attachments, or turn it off to send them.

While a response is being generated, Stop generating (or Esc) interrupts it, and you can keep writing: see Add to a reply that is still running.

If a response ends before its answer because XTM One restarted or the reply failed, the work the agent already did is kept: the next message you send in the conversation (Go on, for instance) gets the tools it called and what they returned, so the agent continues from there instead of starting over. A response you stop yourself, and one that ended more than 24 hours ago, start from scratch. A long piece of reasoning with no tool call cannot be kept.

A line under the composer reminds you that AI can make mistakes and that important information should be checked. The same notice appears at the bottom of the embeddable chat widget, between the input box and the "Powered by" line. It is shown in your interface language in the app and in English in the widget.

The lightning icon among the composer buttons counts the agentic actions consumed in the current quota period (the day, month or year your administrator configured), out of your limit when there is one. Hover it for the details. While an assistant works on your message, the action this reply consumes is shown in brackets: 4(+1)/10 means 4 actions before this reply, 1 for it, out of 10. It joins the total when the reply ends, along with any sandbox code runs counted toward the same limit; a reply that fails may have its action credited back instead (see Configuration). The counter is refreshed as well when a reply is stopped or fails, and when a reply you left running by opening another conversation ends.

docs.title: Use a suggested reply
docs.text:
Once an agent has answered, the message box may propose what you would likely ask next, greyed out, with a Tab key beside it. Press Tab (or the right arrow, or click the Tab key) to put it in the box, edit it if you want, then press Enter to send it: a suggestion is never sent by itself. Start typing or press Esc to dismiss it.

There is not always one: the platform proposes nothing when the next step is not obvious, after a reply that failed or that you stopped, or when you already sent another message. The suggestion is made by the routing model your administrator sets in Settings > AI Models, from your message, the agent's answer and the tools it used. Turn suggestions off in your profile.

docs.title: Add to a reply that is still running
docs.text:
You do not have to wait for an answer to correct or complete your request. The composer stays open while the agent works:

  1. Type your message, and attach files if you need to.
  2. Press Enter, or the send button (Send now: the agent folds it in at its next step). The line under the composer reads Enter to send now · Esc to stop generating.

Your message appears in the conversation at once, and the agent takes it into account at its next step, between two tool calls, in the same answer: you get one answer that covers both messages, not two. If the agent was waiting (for a delegated task, for example), your message ends the wait. A message that arrives while the agent is already writing its final answer is answered right after it.

  • A message refused before it reaches the agent (you sent too many messages in a minute, or it could not be saved) is put back in the composer, so you can send it again.
  • A message that mentions another agent, or references another conversation, is held and sent as its own message when the answer ends (see Ask several agents at once with @mentions).
  • A message you send while a reply is running can count as one more agentic action.
  • To abandon the answer instead, use Stop generating (or Esc).

docs.title: See how full the conversation's context is
docs.text:
Once the assistant has answered in a conversation, a small ring and a percentage on the right of the composer show how much of the model's context window the latest answer used. Hover it for the summary (Context used, with the number of tokens); click it to see where the context went: System prompt, Tool definitions, MCP & dynamic tools, Summarized conversation, Tool results and Conversation. The counts are estimates.

The colour follows what happens to the conversation:

  • amber, Context nearly full: older turns will soon be summarized: the oldest messages are about to be replaced by a summary;
  • red, Context overflowed: older content was cut to fit: older content was cut so the answer could run.

When the gauge turns amber or red on a long conversation, starting a new conversation gives the assistant its full context back.

docs.title: Ask several agents at once with @mentions
docs.text:
Type @ in the composer and pick an agent from the list to mention it. You can mention several agents in the same message.

  • In a new conversation, the first agent you mention becomes the conversation's agent.
  • The conversation's agent answers first. Then every other agent you mentioned answers in turn, in the order you mentioned them. Each reply is its own message, labelled with the agent's name.
  • Every mentioned agent receives your full message, including attachments, and can read the replies given before its own in the same turn.
  • Each agent is told which agents answer after it in the turn, so it answers its own part and does not ask you to pass your message on to them.
  • An agent you mention twice answers once.
  • Only agents you can chat with answer: a mention of an agent that is not available to you (not shared with you, disabled, or not open to chat) is ignored, and the others still answer. If an agent fails while answering, a short note replaces its reply and the agents after it still answer.
  • Clicking stop ends the turn: the agents that have not answered yet are not asked.
  • The mentioned agents of one message share a time limit. An agent still answering when it runs out is stopped, and a note names the agents that were not asked.
  • Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action, charged before it starts, exactly as if you had asked it alone; an agent it consults while answering adds nothing. If your agentic quota runs out, the agent that could not be charged says so and the agents after it are not asked. An agent that fails is credited back like any failed answer.
  • Each reply keeps what its own agent produced: its trace (for feedback) and the files it generated.
  • A message you send while an answer is still being written is held and sent as its own message when the answer ends if it mentions another agent, or while several mentioned agents are answering. A message that reaches a running answer anyway (from another device, or through the API) goes to the agent already answering, and the other agents it mentions then answer it, after the agents of the running turn and under the same rules. One that arrives as the answer is ending is answered by them after the next answer in the conversation.

Once an administrator turns them on (CHANNEL_AGENT_MENTIONS_ENABLED=true, see Configuration), mentions also work in messaging channels (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat), for people with an XTM One account. Until then, a channel message is answered by its routed agent alone, whatever it mentions. There is no picker there: type the agent's key after @, the same key the web composer inserts, such as @mail-desk. A mentioned agent answers only when its own channel settings let it answer that message: it is enabled, open to chat, set to Receive on that channel (and on that channel conversation, if it is restricted to some), past the bot's receive whitelist, the private-conversation and only-mention rules, and set to Publish there. With mentions turned on, an administrator decides which agents can answer on a channel in each agent's Channels settings. Any other @ word - a person, a handle, an agent not set up on that channel - is plain text: the routed agent answers alone, as it would without the mention, and no note is added. Anonymous senders cannot mention agents. Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action, as in the web chat, and is told which agents answer after it. When the routed agent has nothing to add, the agents you named still answer. The replies arrive together in one bot message, one section per agent, with a link to every file an agent produced, and are stored as separate messages in the conversation, each with its own agent's files.

docs.title: Point the agent at another conversation with @
docs.text:
To have the agent read another conversation - "@q3-threat-report, what did we decide there?" - type @ in the composer: below the agents, Reference a conversation lists the conversations you can open, the most recent first. Type words of a title to narrow the list, joined with hyphens (@q3-threat finds "Q3 threat report"), then pick one: the composer inserts its key, the title in lowercase with hyphens, such as @q3-threat-report.

  • The list holds your own conversations, from the web chat and from the assistant embedded in OpenCTI or OpenAEV, and those shared with you by name. It leaves out archived and empty conversations, the conversation you are writing in, and conversations only reachable through an organisation link.
  • Only a conversation you picked from the list counts: an @ word you type by hand stays plain text. Deleting the key from your message removes the reference.
  • With your message the agent receives a short brief of each conversation you referenced: its title, the summary and the instructions kept from its earlier messages, and its last few messages. Every agent that answers the message reads it, the mentioned ones included.
  • For the rest of the conversation, the agent can read the referenced conversations in full, page by page. It can read only the conversations referenced in the conversation it answers, and only while you can still open them: one deleted or no longer shared with you is no longer readable.
  • Your message shows a chip for each conversation it referenced. Clicking it opens that conversation. Someone you share your conversation with sees the chips, which name the referenced conversations, but can open only the ones they have access to.
  • A message references at most 5 conversations.
  • A message that references a conversation while an answer is still being written is held and sent when the answer ends: a correction sent to a running answer cannot carry a reference.

The Presentation Studio's composer offers the same list, with conversations only. In the assistant embedded in OpenCTI or OpenAEV, the list appears once the platform enables it.

docs.title: Ask for changes to a file the agent produced
docs.text:
When an agent hands you a file — an HTML briefing, a CSV export, a Markdown report, a JSON bundle — you can ask for a change in plain words: "remove the paragraph about X", "rename the column to Y", "fix the date in the footer". The agent reads the file it produced, applies exactly the change you asked for and returns a new revision of the file. The version you already downloaded is never altered under you.

  • Text-based files (HTML, Markdown, CSV, JSON, YAML, source code, ...) are edited in place, so a one-line change stays a one-line change — the rest of the document is untouched.
  • Rendered documents (PDF, Word) have no editable source: the agent regenerates them from the corrected content.
  • Files you uploaded yourself can be corrected the same way; the result is a new file next to your original.

Tip

Name what you want changed as it appears in the document. The agent matches your words against the file's exact text, so "remove the sentence about JP" works when the document says "JP"; a paraphrase may need one round of clarification.

docs.title: How a reply shows its files
docs.text:
• The files an answer names are shown as cards in the answer. The other files the agent wrote while working on it (a first draft, a scratch file) are shown as compact chips, still downloadable.
  • An answer that names none of its files shows them all as cards.
  • Files that share a name and type in a conversation are numbered v1, v2, ... in the order they were written, and their cards show the exact size in bytes. Every card shows the time its file was written; hover a card to see its file id and the start of its SHA-256 digest.

docs.title: Use prompt templates
docs.text:
If prompts are available in your environment, the prompt button opens a list of reusable prompt templates.

Use this when you want to:

  • start from a standard request
  • keep your wording consistent
  • save time on recurring questions

Selecting a prompt inserts its content into your message box.

docs.title: Use session tools
docs.text:
The wrench button opens the session tools menu. It has one sub-menu per kind of tool, and each sub-menu lists its tools with a switch. Depending on the conversation, you may be able to switch on or off:

  • built-in tools
  • custom tools
  • integrations
  • MCP servers
  • knowledge bases

Each kind shows how many of its tools are on. Switching a tool keeps the menu open, so you can change several in a row. The built-in tools of the Platform Health specialists (Memory Steward, Health Diagnosis, Health Experiments, Health Flow Lab) are Platform Health's own: the menu never lists them, and Disable all leaves them as the agent carries them.

When you use the General Assistant, this menu lets you build a temporary toolset for the conversation. When you use a specific agent, the panel starts from that agent's own toolset and lets you switch built-in tools on or off for the conversation. Work items, shared state and trace inspection act as the agent itself, so they are only offered when the agent already has them or when you can configure the agent. Trace inspection reads the agent's traces, which hold every user's conversations with it, so the one you add, and the one the platform builder (the suite named after the platform) brings along, only work for someone who can read the agent's chats: an admin, its owner, or someone it is shared with as Full access (incl. chats).

A message can only add to the conversation what you could connect to an agent of your own: one that adds a custom tool, MCP server, knowledge base or integration you cannot see is refused with an error that says which kind it is, and nothing is sent. Saving your profile's default tools follows the same rule. What the conversation already has - the tools you selected earlier, your profile defaults, the agent's own toolset and the General Assistant's configuration - is used as it was set up, including what the owner of an agent shared with you connected to it.

Integrations are the one exception, as they always were: an integration you cannot see, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with you, is never used for you in a chat (see Sharing an OAuth integration). Nothing is hidden: when an answer could not use one, a note under it names the integration - by its service only when it is not shared with you - and says why, and the agent is told as well, so it can say what it cannot do. Connect your own integration of that service, or ask the owner to share theirs.

The menu also lets you:

  • reset back to the default configuration
  • enable all visible tools (the ones already on stay on)
  • disable all visible tools
  • hide integrations from the menu and show them again (Show or hide integrations, at the bottom of the Integrations sub-menu)
  • pick the platform an integration scoped to several registered platforms works on (its own sub-menu)

docs.title: Voice options
docs.text:
If your browser supports speech features, Chat can offer two voice modes.

  • Dictate a message, the microphone in the message box, converts your speech into text.
  • Voice call opens a spoken conversation: you speak, the agent answers aloud, and you can interrupt it.

If these controls do not appear, your browser or device does not currently support them.

docs.title: What you may see above the messages
docs.text:
The conversation header can show extra context.

You may see:

  • the active agent name
  • the current channel, such as web chat
  • a transfer banner if another agent handed the conversation over
  • a Return action if you want to go back to the source agent

This is especially useful when the conversation moved from one agent to another.

docs.title: A conversation open in several places
docs.text:
When the same conversation is open in several tabs, on another device, or in voice mode, each one shows the answer as it is written, wherever the message was sent from. Voice mode reads out only the answer to what you said.

When XTM One is updated while a tab stays open, that tab shows A new version is available: select Reload to use the new version. Until you do, the tab keeps working, but it may show an answer started elsewhere as if you had asked it.

To connect your own scripts to a conversation, see the Chat API.

docs.title: Continue a conversation in Slack or Teams, or back on the web
docs.text:
A conversation is not tied to the place it started. The same conversation - its history, files, session tools and agent - can go on in the web app, in a direct message with the Slack bot, or in your personal chat with the Microsoft Teams bot.

  • From Slack or Teams to the web. A direct-message conversation you had with the bot appears in your conversation list, marked with the Slack or Teams icon. Open it and write: the agent answers here, with everything said in Slack or Teams. Each message in the transcript shows where it was written.
  • From the web to Slack or Teams. Open the conversation, then Conversation options > Continue in Slack or Teams, and pick the app. The bot sends you a direct message: in Slack, reply in its thread; in Teams, reply in your chat with the bot. The conversation goes on there, and stays in your list here.
  • Each reply is written where you send your message, with that app's formatting. A message you send in Slack is answered in Slack; one you send here is answered here.
  • The same agent answers everywhere. When your administrator linked the General Assistant to an agent (Settings > General Assistant > Link to Agent), a Slack or Teams conversation with the General Assistant is answered by that agent there and here alike: the chat shows its name, and its tools in the composer. A conversation you started here with the General Assistant before the link keeps the General Assistant in Slack or Teams too.
  • One answer at a time. A message you send in Slack or Teams while another reply in the conversation is being written (here or there) is queued: the bot tells you so right away, and answers it as soon as that reply is done. Several messages you send meanwhile in the same thread or chat are answered together, in one reply, as the web does with a message sent while the agent is still working. Up to five messages can wait; past that the bot asks you to send yours again later. A queued message the bot could not answer - within an hour, or because something failed twice - is dropped, and the bot tells you so in the thread so you can send it again. A queued message keeps the files you sent with it. If the thread stops continuing the conversation before a queued message runs (you send /new or stop the continuation), that message is not answered, and the bot says so. While a reply to a message sent from Slack or Teams is being written, the web refuses a new message and asks you to send it again once the reply arrives.
  • Tool calls waiting for your approval are answered in the web app. Slack and Teams cannot show the proposal. While the turn that proposed the call still waits for your decision, a message you send in Slack or Teams is queued behind it. If that turn ended with the call still waiting, a new message moves the conversation on, as it does on the web: the call is dropped, and the reply starts by saying so.

A few limits:

  • Only the person who owns the conversation can continue it. A conversation shared with you stays read-only, and a conversation from someone who wrote to the bot without an XTM One account is never listed.
  • Group threads stay where they are. A Slack channel thread or a Teams group chat or channel holds other people's messages, and everyone in it reads the agent's answers, so it is not listed here and is continued in Slack or Teams only: you cannot send a message or upload a file into one from here.
  • In Teams, your personal chat with the bot has no threads: once you continue a conversation there, every message you send in that chat continues it, until you send /new or continue another conversation there. Teams also needs you to have written to the bot once, so the bot can write back to you.
  • The option is offered only where the bot would answer you: the conversation's agent must answer on Slack or Teams (a conversation with the General Assistant always can), and the bot must take direct messages. A Slack bot an administrator restricted to some channels with direct messages turned off does not, and the dialog says so.
  • Stop in the same dialog ends the continuation: the next message you send in that Slack thread or Teams chat starts a new conversation.

docs.title: Export a conversation
docs.text: Conversation options > Export as Markdown or Export as PDF downloads the conversation as a document: every message in order, under who wrote it and when. A chart an answer shows (see Platform insights) is written as a table of its values. Anyone who can read the conversation can export it, a shared one included; the 2,000 most recent messages are exported.

docs.title: Share a conversation
docs.text:
To let colleagues read one of your conversations, open Conversation options > Share. The Share conversation dialog gives read access in two ways:

  • People and groups. Type at least two characters of a name in Search people and groups… and pick a person or a group. Each one you add is listed as Can view; the bin icon removes their access at once. The conversation then appears in their sidebar, under Shared with me.
  • Anyone with the link. Turn on Anyone on the platform with the link can view to paste the link in a channel or a ticket without listing recipients first. Readers still have to sign in to XTM One, and the conversation does not appear in anyone's sidebar: it is reached through the link only.

Copy link copies the conversation's address. It is always available: someone who has no access yet simply cannot open it until you add them.

A shared conversation is read-only for the people you share it with: they can read it and download its files, but cannot reply in it, rename it or delete it. Only the owner can share a conversation.

Warning

A conversation can hold results the agent retrieved from integrations or knowledge bases. Sharing it shares those results too, whether or not the people you share it with have access to the source.

docs.title: Rate an answer
docs.text:
Point at an answer to show the thumbs under it: Helpful response or Not helpful. A thumbs down opens a dialog where you can say what went wrong; when your administrators defined feedback criteria (Settings > Quality), the dialog also asks you to score them, for a thumbs up too. Click the thumb you chose again to remove your rating.

Your ratings reach the people who manage the agent, in the agent's Feedback tab. After a reload, an answer you already rated shows its thumbs greyed out (Feedback already submitted), without saying which one you chose.

docs.title: Find the files of a conversation
docs.text:
Conversation options > Conversation files opens a panel listing every file of the conversation: the files you attached (Uploaded) and the files the agent produced (Generated by agent), the most recent first. Filter them with All, Uploaded or Generated. For each file you can:

  • Download it;
  • Show in conversation, which scrolls to the message that carries it;
  • Add to the workspace's sources, when the conversation is filed in a workspace you manage (see Workspaces).

Open in Files opens the Files page on this conversation's files. People you shared the conversation with see the same panel.

docs.title: When an administrator opens someone else's files
docs.text: An administrator who opens the files of a conversation that belongs to another user first sees a confidentiality notice, You are about to open someone else's files, before any file name is shown. To continue, they confirm I have a legitimate need to view these files and I understand this access is logged. and select View files. The access is recorded in the audit log, with the conversation and its owner, and lasts 15 minutes; while the panel is open, a reminder says the files belong to another user. Cancel closes the notice without showing anything; Review notice brings it back.

docs.title: Background task banners
docs.text:
Some requests continue in the background.

When that happens, Chat can show:

  • a banner while background tasks are still running
  • a completion banner when those background tasks finish
  • a failed count if some delegated tasks did not complete successfully

This means the request involved delegation or longer-running work. It is normal behavior, not an error by itself.

Files a delegated task produces (a CSV export, a spreadsheet, a report) belong to the conversation: they appear as download chips on the message the agent posts once the task finishes, and the agent itself can open, check and merge them with its own file tools when it summarizes the result.

Work the agent hands to the background in the Video Studio (a render, an AI shot, a recording, AI music) is shown the same way once the reply ends: a banner says The assistant resumes this conversation when this work finishes and lists each job with how far along it is. When the work ends, the agent comes back on its own and tells you how it went.

docs.title: When a reply stops before it finishes
docs.text: A reply can stop before its end: XTM One was restarted or updated while the agent was working, or the process running it stopped. The conversation never just goes quiet when that happens.

docs.title: The agent resumes by itself
docs.text:
When the platform itself stopped the reply (a deployment, a scale-in or a restart of the platform, or the recycling of a web worker that served its quota of requests), you have nothing to do: once XTM One is back, the agent resumes the same message by itself, from the tool calls it had already completed, and the conversation shows it working again.

It keeps resuming as long as the message makes progress between two stops, for up to 12 hours after the first stop. After three stops in a row that completed no new tool call, it stops resuming and waits for you.

docs.title: The status card
docs.text:
In place of the interrupted reply, the conversation shows one status card for the whole episode: every stop of the same message folds into it, and the card follows what happens live, in every tab and on every device. It reads, for example:

  • Interrupted by a platform restart, resuming by itself, then Interrupted by a platform restart, resumed by itself once the agent answers. A message you send while it resumes goes to the running answer as a correction and does not change the card. The Presentation Studio side chat shows the same card;
  • Interrupted by a worker recycle, resumed by you, when your own message picked the work up and no automatic resume was running;
  • Interrupted by a server shutdown, could not resume by itself, when the agent did not resume (see below).

The chip on the card counts the tool calls the agent had completed (3 tool calls). Click it to see them grouped by tool: the last one completed is highlighted (Last completed), a failed call is counted as failed, and the calls still running when the reply stopped are counted too.

The agent's memory, when it has memory switched on, records the interrupted request and its last completed action.

docs.title: When the agent could not resume
docs.text:
A reply stopped for another reason (the process ran out of memory, for example), or past the limits above, waits for you. The card turns into a warning and offers two buttons to the conversation's owner:

  • Resume sends Continue where you left off. for you. The tool calls the agent had already completed are kept: the agent continues from their results instead of running them again. Sending any other message continues the same way.
  • Dismiss stops offering the resume. The card stays, as not resumed.

A process that crashes or is killed leaves no interrupted reply to draw a card for. The end of the conversation then shows a notice, This response stopped before it finished, with when it stopped and how many completed tool calls are kept, and the same Resume and Dismiss buttons. It stays there after a reload and on your other devices, until a new reply starts. When the reply is already queued to resume by itself, the notice says It is resuming by itself: no need to click anything. and offers no Resume.

If XTM One cannot be reached while you are on the page, the chat keeps trying to reconnect for as long as the page is open, and follows the agent again as soon as it is back. A message XTM One refuses before any reply starts (you sent too many messages in a minute, for example) is never dropped silently: the reason shows in place of the reply.

docs.title: The waiting arcade
docs.text:
While an agent works through a longer request, a small Space Invader appears under the conversation and shoots the waiting message away, letter by letter. It is more than an animation: click it, or its Take control button, and a full Space Invaders game opens over the whole interface. You can also start a game at any time, no wait needed: Play Space Invaders in your user menu (top right), or the command of the same name in the command palette.

The chat embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ invites you here too: while its agent works, its Play Space Invaders in XTM One link opens <your XTM One address>/chat?arcade=play in a new tab, and the game starts as soon as you are signed in - even if you have to sign in first, or wait for an administrator to accept the platform's Terms of Use, as long as that happens within ten minutes of the click.

  • Controls: arrow keys or A/D (Q/D on an AZERTY keyboard) to move, Space to fire (hold it for autofire), right-click or X to send a missile where you aim, P to pause, M to mute, Esc to leave (the first press pauses, the second ends the game and saves it). On a touch screen, drag to move and fire, and tap the rocket for a missile.
  • Waves and bosses: every wave marches faster than the last, and every fifth wave brings a boss. Falling capsules hold power-ups: rapid fire, spread shot, laser, shield, extra missiles, and a few rarer ones.
  • The interface is fair game: your shots and the invaders' leave holes in whatever they hit - buttons, messages, the sidebar. Nothing is really broken: the damage is cosmetic, and everything is rebuilt the moment you leave. Your conversation keeps running underneath.
  • Your answer comes first: when the agent has finished answering, a banner says so - a message it posts along the way before carrying on with its work does not count. Esc (or Read it) takes you straight back to it, and if you had stopped playing, the arcade takes you back by itself after a few seconds. Keep playing lets you finish your game. The game waits for the conversation you started it from: if you switch to another conversation or leave the chat while you play, the game goes on but no longer announces that answer.

docs.title: Leaderboard
docs.text:
Every game you play is scored and saved. The leaderboard - Arcade leaderboard in your user menu, the trophy button next to the waiting game, the Open the leaderboard command, or the pause menu - ranks the best game of each player over the last 24 hours, the last 7 days and all time, shows who is playing right now, and names the holders of three titles: top vandal, sharpshooter and marathon. During a game, the score bar shows whose score you are about to beat.

  • Your callsign is three letters or digits, like on a real arcade cabinet. It defaults to your initials; change it in the leaderboard's My arcade tab. Other players only ever see your callsign - never your name or your email.
  • Turn off Show me on the public leaderboard to keep your scores, titles and live games to yourself, from that moment on - even in a game already running. You still see your own rank.
  • Scores are checked by the server: a score, a number of shots or a count of destroyed interface elements that is not plausible for the time played is refused, and so is a score higher than the waves you reached can yield. The arcade tells you why a score was not recorded. A game in which a cheat code was used is saved but not ranked.

docs.title: Achievements and secrets
docs.text: The leaderboard's Achievements tab lists what you have unlocked. Many achievements are secret until you find them: old cheat codes, a very rare saucer, certain dates on the calendar, and a few things you probably should not shoot. Explore.

docs.title: When the game is not offered
docs.text:
The gamepad always means play: on the waiting panel it opens the game, and nothing in the chat hides it. When your system asks for reduced motion, the waiting panel shows a plain rotating message instead of the invader and the chat offers no game; Play Space Invaders (in your user menu or the command palette) and a ?arcade=play link still start one, since you asked for it. The arcade is not offered while an administrator impersonates a user: nothing is ever recorded under someone else's name. Nor is it offered while the platform's Terms of Use are waiting to be accepted. Administrators can turn the arcade off for the whole platform with ARCADE_ENABLED (see Configuration).

The game and the leaderboard load in the background shortly after you sign in, so a page left open while XTM One is updated can still play. If they could not load before the update (on a Data Saver or 2G connection, for instance), opening them shows Reload to play or Reload to open the leaderboard: Reload reloads the page and opens the game or the leaderboard right away.

docs.title: When an agent is shown as not recommended for chat
docs.text:
Some agents are built mainly for background execution rather than direct conversation.

These agents still appear in the picker, but XTM One marks them so you know they are not optimized for normal chat use.

You can still try them, but the best experience usually comes from:

  • the General Assistant
  • a chat-enabled agent

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
• Start with the General Assistant if you are unsure which agent to use.
  • Use a dedicated agent when the topic belongs to a specific workflow.
  • Attach documents when the answer depends on exact wording or evidence.
  • Open the same conversation again if you want XTM One to keep the discussion context.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Agents, including what the list page shows and how to read an agent detail page.

docs.title: Create an agent
docs.text: You create an agent in three ways: with a guided wizard, with a single form, or by importing a file. All three start from the same page, and all three give you an agent you can keep changing afterwards on its detail page (see Agents).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Creating agents needs Enterprise Edition and AI switched on for the platform (see Editions and licensing). When either is missing, the creation buttons say so instead of opening the page.

An agent you create is yours: it is private until you share it (see Sharing and access). Any integration, knowledge base, tool or skill you attach must be one you can already see. To use a service that is not connected yet, connect it first under Integrations (see Integrations).

docs.title: Open the creation page
docs.text:
Two entry points lead to the same Create New Agent page:

  • New Agent at the top of the Agents list.
  • Create an agent, the featured card of the Agent Studio hub, also listed first under Agent Studio in the sidebar. The hub gathers what agents are made of: Knowledge, Prompts, Templates and Skills.

The page offers three cards:

Card What it does Wizard Builds the agent step by step, with instructions and a tutorial at every step. The easiest way to start. Advanced Picks a template or starts from scratch, then shows one form for the name, persona and required integrations. You set up the rest on the agent's page. Import Creates the agent from an XTM One native bundle or a Microsoft AgentSchema document, in JSON or YAML.

docs.title: Pick a starting point
docs.text:
Wizard and Advanced both open on the template gallery. The first card, From Scratch, gives you an empty agent. Every other card is an agent template: a ready-made role with its persona and, often, pre-configured assignments; the card shows how many. Search the gallery with Search templates... or narrow it with the category pills (All shows everything).

What each template category holds, and what a template brings with it, is described in What an assignment or a roster may name.

docs.title: Build it with the wizard
docs.text:
The wizard shows a live preview of the agent on one side and the current step on the other. The preview follows what you fill in and highlights the part the step is about. Tutorial opens a short explanation of the step, and a step counter tells you where you are.

The wizard walks you through these steps in order:

  1. Identity: the Agent Name (required), an icon and an optional one-line description. The name and icon are how the agent appears everywhere: the agents list, the chat picker, run traces and audit entries.
  2. Persona: the agent's standing instructions (required), written as "You are...". Generate with AI drafts one from a short description, Improve with AI refines what you wrote, and Prompt library lets you start from one of your prompts.
  3. Tools: the built-in and custom tools the agent can call. If you pick nothing, the agent starts with the platform's default tool set.
  4. Integrations: the connected services the agent acts through. A template can require one service type, marked required: you bind a matching connection before you can go on. Connect one takes you to the integration form, and your draft waits for you (see Your draft is kept).
  5. Knowledge bases: the collections the agent searches when it answers. Skip this step if the agent does not need them, unless the template requires one.
  6. Review & create: Create the agent creates it. If a required step is incomplete, the page lists it and the button stays off. With a template, the page says how many pre-configured assignments come with it.

Once you reach the review, the wizard becomes a hub: you can open any step again, and six Advanced options appear below the create button. Each is optional and returns to the hub when you are done:

  • Model: pin the model the agent runs on, or keep Platform default, which follows your administrator's choice.
  • Memory: the four memory tiers (Short-term Memory, Medium-term Memory, Persistent Memory, User Memory), all on by default. Turn them off for an agent that must not keep anything between runs.
  • Guardrails: hard rules the agent must never break, on top of the persona.
  • Skills: packaged instructions the agent loads when a task calls for them (see Skills). A template's default skills that you can use are already selected; remove the ones you do not want.
  • Handovers: the agents this one may hand a conversation over to (see Agentic flow).
  • Budget: caps on what one run may spend. Empty fields inherit the platform limits (see Run budgets).

docs.title: Your draft is kept
docs.text:
Nothing is saved on the platform until you create the agent, but the wizard keeps your draft in the browser tab while you work. If you leave the wizard, for example through Connect one or the sidebar, and come back in the same tab, the draft is restored and a message says Your unsaved draft was restored. Discard draft starts over.

The draft belongs to your account and to that tab only: closing the tab or signing out forgets it, and nobody else signing in on the same browser sees it. A tool, knowledge base, skill, agent or model that is no longer available to you when the draft comes back is marked Unavailable, so you can remove it before you create the agent.

docs.title: Use the Advanced form
docs.text:
Advanced opens the same template gallery, then one form:

  • Agent Name, Description (optional) and Tags.
  • Persona / System Prompt, prefilled from the template when you picked one.
  • Required Integrations, when the template asks for some: pick the connected integration to use for each one, or skip and set it up later.
  • Company-managed agent, for administrators only: the agent is shared with all users, and only administrators can edit it. Before creating it, the platform shows what the agent lends to every user and asks you to confirm.

Create Agent creates it. Everything else (tools, knowledge bases, model, memory, assignments) is set up afterwards on the agent's Configuration tab.

docs.title: Import an agent from a file
docs.text:
Import, on the creation page or at the top of the Agents list, opens Import an agent. Drop a .json, .yaml or .yml file, or click to browse. The platform checks the file before anything is created and shows each check: Reading the file, Detecting the format, Validating against the schema, Resolving references.

  • This file is ready to import. means you can confirm with Import agent.
  • This platform cannot satisfy everything the file references: lists what will be left out, such as an integration or a knowledge base this platform does not have. Suggest fixes with AI explains how to finish the setup.
  • Corrections you can apply before importing: offers to remove a tool that arrives without its code or an MCP server that arrives as an empty placeholder.
  • This file cannot be imported. names what failed. Nothing is created.

What each format carries, and what an import never brings across, is described in Importing an agent.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
After Create the agent, Create Agent or Import agent, the agent's detail page opens. The new agent is enabled.

  • From a template, its pre-configured assignments are created with the agent and switched on. Review them in the agent's Assignments card before you rely on them (see Assignments and triggers).
  • From an imported file, the assignments start switched off, so nothing runs before you have reviewed it.

You can also have an assistant build an agent for you in a conversation (see Building agents from a conversation).

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Give your agent work to do on its own with Assignments and triggers.

docs.title: CTEM signals
docs.text:
A CTEM signal is a change in your exposure: a new vulnerability on something you run, a host that answers on the internet when it should not, a leaked secret, a supplier named in an incident. Signals are where the exposure management loop starts: XTM One checks each signal against your scope and, when it matters, opens a case.

CTEM signals are part of XTM One with an Enterprise Edition license. They are a different feature from the signals of Platform Health.

docs.title: Where to find signals
docs.text:
Open CTEM > Signals in the left navigation (the page address is /ctem/signals). You also reach it from the Home dashboard: the signal counters of the exposure loop, the signal sources button and the activity feed each open the page, filtered where it makes sense. A case shows the signal that opened it under Opened by.

The top of the page shows a summary strip: the signals of the last 30 days, the unmatched signals, the signals that opened a case, and the trigger paths that are connected, with the logos of their sources.

docs.title: Filter the list
docs.text:
• State: the buttons above the table filter on the signal's place in the loop, each with its count: All, New, Confirmed, Unmatched (the signal does not match an asset in your scope yet), Discarded, Watchlist and Case opened.
  • Trigger path and Source: the filters of the table keep one or more trigger paths (see below) or one or more sources, for example Shodan.
  • Search: the search box looks in the subject of the signal, its trigger path and its source.

Each row shows the subject, the trigger path, the source, and when the signal was first and last seen. Sort on any column; the list opens newest first. Click a row to open the signal's loop trace on the side: what the scope check decided, and the case it opened, if any. The filters and the open signal are kept in the page address, so you can share the link.

Select rows to triage them in bulk (for example move them to the watchlist or discard them) or add their assets to the inventory. A signal that opened a case cannot be selected: the case owns it.

docs.title: Lenses
docs.text:
Every signal is seen through one of three lenses:

  • Inside: what runs in your environment, where, which version and configuration.
  • Outside: what the internet can reach.
  • World: advisories, threat intelligence, leaks and suppliers.

Each trigger path has a usual lens; a source may record a signal of a path through another lens.

docs.title: Trigger paths
docs.text:
The trigger path says what kind of change the signal is. There are twelve:

# Trigger path Lens What fires it 1 New vulnerability on a running version World A new or updated vulnerability that may affect what you run 2 Relevant new threat or actor World A threat actor, campaign or malware relevant to your sector or stack 3 Code or dependency flaw before production Inside A flaw in your code or dependencies, before it reaches production 4 Proven exploitable to a primary asset Inside A simulation proved an attack path to a critical asset 5 New exposure Outside Something you own answers on the internet when it should not 6 Stale or orphaned asset Outside An asset that no longer resolves or has not been seen for days 7 Attack-surface drift Outside A host or port on your attack surface that nobody declared 8 Mitigation regression Inside A security control that used to block an attack no longer does 9 Control or evidence decay Inside Evidence that a control works is older than its re-test delay 10 Credential or secret leak World A secret or an account of yours found in a leak 11 Third-party or sub-processor event World A report or incident naming a supplier or sub-processor you track 12 Blind spot or coverage gap Inside An asset that supports a risk scenario with no evidence at all

The trigger path is shown on every row of the list and in the loop trace. Paths 5, 6 and 7 come from the attack surface pass (for example Shodan); paths 1 and 2 mostly from OpenCTI; paths 4 and 8 from OpenAEV; paths 9 and 12 from OpenCRQ.

docs.title: Signal sources
docs.text: The Sources button at the top right of the page opens the signal sources: for each trigger path, what feeds it and whether that source is connected. A path shows Not connected when no integration feeds it, and Off when the integration is connected but its scheduled pass does not run; Turn on takes you to the setting in Settings > Organization. Back to Signals returns to the list.

docs.title: Who sees which signals
docs.text:
• An administrator sees every signal of the organization.
  • A member of a group with a CTEM right sees every signal too: the view right reads them, the decide right also triages them and changes the cases. Your administrator sets these rights on the group.
  • Anyone else sees only the signals they recorded themselves, through their own calls or their agents.

Signals recorded by the platform's own listeners and passes are visible only with one of the first two.

docs.title: Ask an agent about signals
docs.text:
The built-in CTEM agents (the CTEM Assistant and the discovery, prioritization, triage and threat agents) can list signals with the same filters: state, trigger path, lens, source. Any agent you give the CTEM read tools can do the same. For example, ask the CTEM Assistant:

List the CTEM signals with lens outside and trigger path new exposure, stale asset or attack-surface drift, newest first, with their source and last seen date.

The agent sees what the person it acts for sees: when it answers with fewer signals than you expect, it says that the rest is outside that person's reach.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Follow what a signal became in its case: open CTEM > Cases, or the case named in the signal's loop trace.

docs.title: Custom dashboards
docs.text:
A custom dashboard is a page of widgets an agent builds for you: your exposure score and its trend, the stages of your CTEM cycle, a decision waiting for you, what your agents did overnight, the questions worth asking next. You ask for it in the chat; it appears in the conversation, and it keeps its own page you can open on the web, on a computer or a phone.

Custom dashboards are off by default. An administrator turns them on with ENABLED_FEATURES=DASHBOARD_STUDIO (see Configuration). While they are off, the Dashboards pages, the Custom Dashboards tool and the published links are not offered, and nothing stored is deleted.

docs.title: Ask for a dashboard
docs.text:
Ask any agent that has the Custom Dashboards built-in tool, for example:

Build me a dashboard of what I should look at first this morning.

The agent gathers the figures with its other tools (OpenCTI, OpenAEV, your integrations), then composes the dashboard. It appears in the conversation, and under Work > Dashboards.

The General Assistant carries the tool out of the box, as it does the presentation and video tools; an administrator can remove it in Settings > General Assistant. Turn it on for another agent in its configuration (Built-in tools > Custom Dashboards).

docs.title: What a dashboard can show
docs.text:
The agent picks each widget from a fixed catalog and fills its values; XTM One draws it in the platform's look, in dark and light mode, one widget per row on a phone and side by side on a wide screen.

Widget Shows Score A headline figure with its trend line and a few sub-figures Stats A row of figures Stages A cycle or a pipeline, with the progress of each stage Decision Something waiting for you, with its evidence and buttons Feed Recent events, such as what each agent did Callout A highlighted statement Ranked list What to fix first, with severity badges Steps A sequence with its outcomes, such as an attack path Checklist A plan, with what is done Progress Work under way: its status, a bar and its latest lines Prompts Questions you can ask the assistant next Text Paragraphs of prose

An agent cannot write HTML, colours or links to other sites into a dashboard. Its links open pages of XTM One only. A button that asks something never sends it on its own: it opens a new chat with the question in the composer, for you to read, change and send.

docs.title: Make it your dashboard
docs.text:
On a dashboard's page, Use as my dashboard shows it on your Dashboard (/dashboard), and on your home page when your home page is the dashboard, instead of the platform's dashboard. The dashboard list marks it Your dashboard. Use the standard dashboard, on your dashboard or on the dashboard's page, brings back the platform's dashboard. So does deleting the dashboard.

Any dashboard you can open as yourself - yours, one shared with you, a company dashboard - can be your dashboard, one at a time. If it is deleted or no longer shared with you, the platform's dashboard comes back.

docs.title: Keep it up to date
docs.text:
• Refine it in the chat. On the dashboard's page, Refine with the assistant opens a chat that names the dashboard. Ask for a change ("add the open tickets", "drop the feed"); the agent changes the widgets concerned and leaves the others as they are.
  • Refresh it on a schedule. Create an assignment whose prompt asks the agent to update the dashboard (for example every weekday at 7:00). It refreshes the same dashboard, and the page says it was refreshed by a scheduled run, with a link to that run.

The page reads the latest version each time you come back to it.

docs.title: Rearrange or delete it
docs.text:
A dashboard is a grid of 12 columns, with OpenCTI's rows (62 pixels high, 20 apart), so a widget from OpenCTI sits where it sat there. Dashboards made before keep their look: their places are read in these rows. On the dashboard's page, Rearrange lets you drag a widget to move it, drag its corner to resize it, and remove it; with the keyboard, focus a widget, then the arrow keys move it and Shift with the arrow keys resizes it. Each change is saved as you go, and a series of moves made within a minute is kept as one version. A dashboard keeps at least one widget. On a phone or in a narrow chat bubble the widgets are stacked, top to bottom and left to right. If an agent refreshed the dashboard while you were rearranging it, XTM One shows you its latest version and asks you to make your change again.

The trash button deletes the dashboard (its owner only). In a conversation, it then shows as no longer available.

docs.title: See it larger
docs.text: On a dashboard's page, the full-screen button shows the dashboard alone on the screen, and the button that appears over a widget when you point at it shows that widget alone, filling the screen (Escape closes it).

docs.title: History
docs.text: Every change is kept - by an agent, by hand, by a colleague - with who made it and what it changed (the 30 latest). The history button on the dashboard's page lists them and previews one; Restore this version saves it again as the newest version, so a restore can itself be undone. Compare sets the version picked against another (the current one by default): the two definitions side by side or unified, and which widgets were added, changed or removed.

docs.title: Who can see it
docs.text:
A dashboard is private to its owner until they share it. Share on the dashboard's page grants people or groups one of three levels: Can view opens it, Can edit also rearranges, refines and shares it (here or through their own assistant), Can manage also deletes it. An administrator can make it a company dashboard, which everyone opens and only administrators change. Administrators can open any dashboard, and change none they were not given. Only the owner and those who manage it delete a dashboard. The dashboard list marks the ones shared with you.

In Slack, Teams and the chat panels of OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, the agent's answer carries a link to the dashboard's page instead of the dashboard itself.

docs.title: The dashboards list
docs.text:
Work > Dashboards shows your dashboards, those shared with you and the company ones, as cards or as a table (the toggle beside the search). The table sorts by any column - name, tags, access, number of widgets, last update. Search by title or tag, narrow the list to yours, those shared with you or the company ones, and to one or more tags.

The menu of a dashboard (...) offers:

  • Duplicate: a private copy for you, named "(copy)", with its tags and copies of the images it draws. A copy reads its platform widgets through your own integrations: when you cannot use the integration a widget reads, the copy is refused and says why.
  • Edit tags (those who may edit it): the words it is filed under, lower-cased.
  • Delete (its owner). In the table, select several of your dashboards to delete them together; you are asked first.

Administrators also see Public links: every dashboard published as a link, who published it and how fresh its data is, and Turn off for any of them.

docs.title: Dashboard Studio
docs.text:
The Dashboard Studio, part of the same switch, adds:

  • Create and import from the list. New dashboard on the dashboards list asks for a name, a description (Markdown) and what the dashboard should show, and who builds it (Made by: the General Assistant or an agent with the dashboard tools). Create with the assistant makes the dashboard, opens it in the studio and sends your brief as the first message of the studio's chat, so you watch the widgets land and the studio selects each one the assistant adds or changes. Start from an empty dashboard opens it empty, to fill by hand. Import makes one from a file - an OpenCTI dashboard, custom view or widget export, an OpenAEV dashboard export (ZIP) or an XTM One pack - each platform widget reading through your integration of its platform, and opens it in the studio; what the conversion changed is said once it is done. When you have several integrations of one platform, the dialog lets you choose the one its widgets read through; if the file reads that platform and you did not choose, the import says so and names them.
  • Refresh. The refresh button on the dashboard's page and in the studio reads every widget again from its platform at once (a platform answer is otherwise kept a minute), and Auto-refresh does it every minute, 5, 15 or 30 minutes or every hour while the page is open. The interval is yours, kept in this browser for this dashboard.
  • The studio bar. As in the Presentation and Video Studios: the title (renamed in place while editing) and whether everything is saved; Present, the dashboard as its viewers see it, full screen (Esc or Leave fullscreen gives the editor back); the pencil switches between editing and the viewers' view; undo and redo; Refresh (its arrow picks the auto-refresh); the studio; sharing; downloads; and More actions: publish or export, the dashboard source, its history, the settings panel, duplicate and delete.

  • The settings panel folds away. More actions > Hide the settings panel gives the dashboard the whole width; adding an element, a chart or an input brings it back. Its edge is dragged to widen or narrow it (a double-click resets it).

  • The studio. Open in the studio on the dashboard's page opens it beside the assistant, like the Presentation and Video Studios. Drag widgets on the page to place and size them. Click a widget to select it: the assistant is told which one "this widget" is, and the panel on the right shows its configuration (below). A change the assistant saves shows at once, and what you change in the panel is what the assistant then reads: you both work on the same definition.

  • What the assistant does in the studio. It plans the dashboard (each widget, where its data comes from and how fresh it is, and the choices you left open with what it takes by default), then builds it widget by widget: it reads what a widget of OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ can be and looks up the types, filter keys and values in the platform with your access instead of guessing them, reads each data source before saving it, adds each widget with its data source and its place in one step, and checks every widget's data before telling you it is done - looking at a picture of the tab as you see it. The General Assistant carries this method (the Dashboard Design skill) and the tools out of the box.
  • The source editor. Dashboard source (the braces in the studio's bar) shows the dashboard as it is stored: an OpenCTI dashboard manifest. Its widgets are OpenCTI's own widgets and OpenAEV's own widgets (widget_type, widget_config), exactly as those platforms store them, placed on OpenCTI's grid; a text widget is OpenCTI's text widget; its variables are the dashboard inputs, as OpenCTI's dashboard variables (a filter names one as $var:<id>, an OpenAEV filter by its id); and x_xtm_one holds what XTM One adds: its own widgets (x_xtm_one.<type>), the data sources that are not a platform widget, the inputs, the tabs and their layouts (a 12-column grid, or an absolute layout in pixels), interactions, visibility, defaults and applicationProperties. Edit the whole of it, or only the selected widget's visualization or data source, or the defaults (these three as the working definition: dataSources, visualizations, inputs, layout). It is checked when you save: a mistake is shown with the field it is about (for example visualizations.kev.dataSources.primary names no data source 'x') and your text stays in the editor. Those who may not edit see it read-only.

  • Configuration panel. While editing, the panel on the right configures the selected visualization, in these sections:

    • General: its heading and description, its type - any type drawing the same data (a single value becomes a gauge or a ring, a line chart an area or column chart; the options the new type does not have are dropped) - and whether it shows a progress bar while its data is read again and when it was read;
    • Data source: the source it draws (and, for an area, line, column or bar chart, the source of its annotations), Edit the data source in the source editor, or All data sources;
    • Data display: the options of its type, such as the stack mode, the legend, data values, missing values, markers and axes of a chart, the donut hole and labels of a pie, the unit, decimal places, abbreviation, trend and sparkline of a single value, the ends and orientation of a gauge, the rows per page, row numbers and totals of a table, and - for a column, bar, line, area or pie chart - the field that splits it into panels (trellis);
    • Coloring: the series' colours, or a value's colour - the theme's, one colour, or by ranges of the value (below 50 green, from 50 to 80 orange, from 80 red, which you change, add to or remove), written as the dynamic option "> majorValue | rangeValue(majorColorEditorConfig)" with the ranges in the visualization's context; a gauge's own ranges; a colour written as another expression in the source editor is shown as written;
    • Interactions and Visibility (below);
    • Position: its column, row, width and height on a grid (counted from 1, kept within the 12 columns), or its place and size in pixels on an absolute layout;
    • Source: the visualization as JSON, and Open in the source editor.

    Each change is saved as you make it, and undone and redone with the rest. A shape, a line, an icon, an image or markdown has its own options instead. - Toolbar. While editing, the bar above the dashboard adds a chart - any type, on sample data written in the dashboard until you point it at another source in Data source - or an input (a dropdown, a multiselect, a text, a number, a time range or a button, above the tabs and shown in the Inputs panel), adds shapes, icons, images and markdown on an absolute layout (they are greyed on a grid), opens the data sources and the source editor, and switches the dashboard between a light and a dark theme. - Editing and the viewers' view. The studio opens in editing for those who may change the dashboard; the pencil shows it as its viewers see it, and Present shows it so, alone on the screen. - Data sources. The Data panel of the studio lists the dashboard's data sources - where its visualizations' data comes from - with what uses each one (an unused one is greyed). New creates one: data written in the dashboard; the answer of an assignment's last completed run (its text, or a number, a series, a breakdown or rows read from the JSON it answered, at a path such as response.open); a question to an agent, asked only when a viewer presses Ask the agent; a variable (never a secret one, and none while custom variables are turned off); another source passed through steps (where, sort, head, tail, fields, rename, eval with arithmetic only, top, stats, flow), chained one after another; or an OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ widget, built with the same choices as in the product, with a Preview. For OpenCTI: the sixteen widget types of its dashboards; the perspective (entities, knowledge graph, activity & history); up to five data selections (each with its label, the types it counts, its filters - with nested groups, and for relationships the filters of their source and of their target - the date, the attribute counted, the source or target side, the number of results, the sort, a list's columns, a map's zoom and centre); the title, interval, stacked, legend and distributed switches. For OpenAEV: the thirteen widget types of its custom dashboards; series (each with its label, entity and filters), a list's rows, or the fixed series of Security Coverage, Attack Paths and Security Domains (detection or prevention, a simulation); the title, time range (a custom one with its start and end), date, breakdown or interval, number of results, stacked and legend switches, a list's columns and sort. Values are searched in the platform with your access. Every widget type is drawn in XTM One, except OpenCTI's activity & history widgets, shown as a link to the platform. From a source's menu: add a visualization drawing it (placed at the bottom of the tab on screen), edit it, duplicate it, or delete it once nothing uses it. Editing a platform widget keeps everything it holds that the editor does not change; a widget of a type the editor does not know opens in the source editor instead, and saving a widget unchanged writes nothing. Two more sources read data from outside the platforms: an integration tool - one tool of any of your integrations that only reads (a tool that could change something is never called), with the arguments you set, its JSON answer read at a path (a tool that answers in words, not JSON, is drawn as text, or kept as a table by a feed, below) - and a knowledge base table - a table written in a knowledge base document (JSON, JSON lines, CSV or a Markdown table), the whole document or one of its sections, which an assignment can keep up to date; drawn as a breakdown, a table reads its first text column as the labels and its first number column as the values (a severity,count table).
