A source can be read again every refresh (5m, 1h; 30 seconds at least). Where it is read (Read, for the platform, integration, knowledge base, variable and derived sources): on the page, with each viewer's own access (the default); on the server every… 5 minutes, 15 minutes, an hour, 6 hours or a day, whoever has the page open; or on the server, when asked. Read on the server, a source is read with the access of the person who set it and shown to everyone who opens the dashboard, even those who could not read it themselves; its widgets - and those of the sources derived from it - say Data read … with <name>'s access. and offer Refresh now (a source is read at most every 30 seconds on request; the sources read on the server that derive from it are read again with it), and an open page shows each new read without being reloaded. Whoever changes what such a source reads becomes the person it is read as. On the server, a source can also be read on a schedule (a cron expression, UTC, at most every 5 minutes) or on an event: an event of the platform (such as run.completed) or an event an integration raises (such as issues.opened), heard when it reaches the platform for an assignment - its poll or its webhook; however many events arrive, it is read at most once a minute.

What changed, and alerts. Each read on the server is compared with the previous one: the widget says what changed since then - the figure before and after (a number's value, a series' last point, a breakdown's total, a table's row count) and, for a breakdown, the items that moved the most - and a single value shows the change as its trend. A source read on the server can also raise an alert when its figure goes above or below a threshold (Alert when the figure is, in the New data source form; up to five per source through the source editor or the assistant, each info, warning or critical): the dashboard's owner and the person the source is read as are told in their notifications when the figure starts to cross it - once, until it goes back - and on their phone when it is linked (Dashboard alerts, which they can mute there). A read that fails changes nothing: a platform that does not answer never raises or clears an alert.

Feeds. When a widget's data has to be gathered from several places and consolidated, ask the assistant for a feed: it creates an assignment on an agent that has the tools the data takes, on a schedule or an event, whose answer is the data the widget draws, runs it once and adds the widget. The page shows each new answer as soon as the run ends. An assignment source can draw the trend of a figure over its last runs (Trend over the last runs, 2 to 60), and a feed can also keep its consolidated table in a knowledge base document, which other agents then search and read. A platform source reads over its range: a period (1d, 7d, 30d, 1m, 90d, 3m, 6m, 1y; 1m, 3m and 6m count calendar months), fixed dates (2026-01-01/2026-03-31, either end left open), or $time$; without one, the page's. An OpenCTI widget reads it as OpenCTI does: from the start of the day so many days or months back, up to now, as filters on the widget's own date - a list included. - Everyone reads with their own access. Each viewer reads every source as themselves: an assignment's run they may see (another person's private run shows "No completed run of this assignment is visible to you yet"), a variable shared with them, an agent they may chat with - with their own quota. A question is theirs: asking it does not answer it for anyone else, and a person may ask a few questions a minute. The person writing a source may only point it at what they reach themselves. - Periods. A time range input offers the last 24 hours, 7, 30 or 90 days, the last month, 3 or 6 months, the last year, all time (every date, each widget's own period set aside) and a custom range (a start date, an end date, or both). Those who may edit the dashboard can keep the period picked as the dashboard's own (Keep as the dashboard's period): it is what everyone sees first. - Inputs and tokens. The Inputs panel of the studio adds inputs above the tabs: a time range, a dropdown or a multiselect (its choices written one per line as label=value, or read from a data source - which may itself use other inputs' tokens, so one input narrows the next), a text, a number, an entity (a country, a sector, an intrusion set... searched in OpenCTI, or a simulation or a scenario searched in OpenAEV, with the viewer's own access, among the types the input names; the token holds its id), or a button that sets a token and can switch tab. Each input sets a token; a data source names it as $name$ in a filter value, a derived step's value or a platform widget's range ($time$ for a time range input), and a title or a text names it the same way. A source that uses a token with no value waits ("Waiting for input."), except for an entity input set to Read every entity while none is picked ("required": false): until one is picked, the filters on its token are left out and the widget reads every entity, as an OpenAEV dashboard reads every simulation while its simulation parameter is empty. A token's value reaches the platform as a filter value, never as query text. Other tokens: the viewer's own ($env:user$, $env:user_name$, $env:timezone$, $env:locale$, $env:platform$), a data source's result ($<source>:result.<field>$, such as $ds_open:result.value$, and $<source>:job.status$), and computed tokens (expressions.tokens: arithmetic, text, comparisons and if, len, lower, upper, round, coalesce, number). In a text, $name|s$ quotes the value, |h escapes it for HTML, |u encodes it for a URL (the default in a link) and |n writes it as is. The Submit button switch makes inputs change their tokens only when Submit is pressed. The token manager lists every token with its value on the stage, its default (editable), what uses it and what sets it. - Interactions. Pick a visualization in the studio: its Interactions say what a click on it does, in order - set a token from what was clicked (the name of a slice, a bar or a column, its value, the x or y of a point, a field of a table row) or to a written value ($click.value$ and the page's tokens fill it), unset a token, open a link (a page of XTM One, or an http(s) address in a new tab), open another dashboard with tokens (it opens with them, as ?form.<token>= in its address), open the item in OpenCTI or OpenAEV, switch tab, or - on a series - set a time range from a brush ($<token>.earliest$, $<token>.latest$). A clickable chart, value or row shows a pointer; a row is also reached with the keyboard. - Visibility. Show only when and Hide when take an expression on the page's tokens (isSet($host$), in($sev$, "High", "Critical"), $mode$ = "quiet"); Hide when there is no data hides a visualization while its source has nothing to show. The others close up around a hidden one. In the studio every visualization stays on the stage. - Inspect and export. The menu of a visualization drawing data shows Inspect (its data source as stored and the result it drew) and Export CSV (that result as a file; a cell a spreadsheet would run as a formula is neutralised). applicationProperties.hideExport removes the export. - Tabs. A dashboard with several tabs shows a tab bar above its widgets, or on their left (layout.tabs.options: showTabBar, barPosition, also in the panel on the right when nothing is selected); a drag or a resize is saved in the tab on screen. In Edit, the + beside the tabs adds a tab with a grid or with an absolute layout, and the tab's menu renames it, moves it left or right, switches it between a grid and an absolute layout (a tab holding shapes, lines, icons, images or markdown stays absolute: only an absolute layout draws them), and deletes it with what only it shows. - Absolute layouts. A tab with an absolute layout places its widgets in pixels. Its size, and how it fits the screen (Scale to the screen: scaled down to fit, never up; Actual size: its pixels, scrolled; Fit to width), are set in the panel on the right when nothing is selected, with its background: a colour, an image (its size: its own, the whole image, or covering the layout; its opacity). Besides widgets it holds: - shapes: rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, and lines with an arrow at either end; a line's end dragged onto the middle of a side of a block holds to it, and follows it when the block moves; - icons: any icon of the Lucide catalog presentations use, or an SVG you upload; - images you upload (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG, 5 MB each), with the text that describes them to those who cannot see them; - markdown, with its colour, background, size, font and alignment.

Uploaded files belong to the dashboard: whoever can open the dashboard sees them, and they are deleted with it. An uploaded SVG is cleaned of scripts, event handlers and links to other sites before it is stored. Colours are what you pick; a colour left empty follows the theme.
  • Editing an absolute layout. The bar above the dashboard adds an element, brings the selection to the front or sends it to the back (one step at a time from Arrange), aligns two or more items and distributes three or more, duplicates them (with the same data source, or each with a copy of its own), copies, cuts and pastes them, deletes them, and zooms. Click an item to select it, Shift-click to add one, or draw a box around several from an empty spot; drag to move, drag a handle to resize. With the dashboard focused: the arrow keys move the selection by 10 pixels (with Shift, by 1), Alt with the arrow keys resizes it, Delete removes it, Escape clears the selection, and Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) with A, C, X, V, D, Z and Shift+Z or Y selects all, copies, cuts, pastes, duplicates, undoes and redoes. The panel on the right sets the selected item's options and its place. Every change is saved as you go; undo and redo save too, and a series of moves made within a minute is kept as one version.
  • Theme. From the toolbar, or in the panel on the right when nothing is selected, a dashboard can keep a light or a dark theme of its own, whatever the theme of the person viewing it.
  • Defaults. defaults.visualizations.global.options, then defaults.visualizations.<type>.options, are applied under each visualization's own options.
  • Visualizations. A data source can be drawn as a single value (xtm.singlevalue), a single value with an icon (xtm.singlevalueicon) or as a ring (xtm.singlevalueradial), a filler or marker gauge (xtm.fillergauge, xtm.markergauge), an area, line, column or bar chart (xtm.area, xtm.line, xtm.column, xtm.bar), a pie or donut (xtm.pie), a scatter, bubble or punchcard chart (xtm.scatter, xtm.bubble, xtm.punchcard), a list or a table; a distribution or a series also as a radar (xtm.radar, one axis per label, one shape per series), a polar area (xtm.polararea, equal slices reaching out as far as their value), a word cloud (xtm.wordcloud, each label as large as its value, on a log scale) or a heatmap (xtm.heatmap, a row per series and a cell per point, coloured from the lowest value to the highest; colorMin / colorMax). Their options are listed below; an option the type does not have, or a value out of its bounds, is refused when the dashboard is saved, with the field it is about.
  • Panel details. A visualization's description shows under its title; showLastUpdated: true shows when its data was read, showProgressBar: true a thin bar while it is read again.

  • Maps, graphs and flows. Besides charts, a visualization can be:

    • xtm.map: the world (or region: europe, americas, apac) with up to three layers - choropleth (regions coloured in five steps of their value, with a legend), bubble (points sized by value) and marker (points as pins) - drawn on the atlas shipped with XTM One: no map tiles are fetched. Regions are ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes (FR); a country too small to see is a dot.
    • xtm.choropleth.svg: the regions coloured on an SVG of your own (a floor plan, a site map), in options.svg (200 KB at most): each element whose id is a region's code takes its colour. The SVG is cleaned when it is saved (no script, link or external resource), and drawn from its shapes only.
    • xtm.linkgraph (left to right, a table's columns as stages) and xtm.networkgraph (laid out by forces, nodes sized by their links, coloured by group): pan, and zoom with Ctrl and the wheel.
    • xtm.sankey (flows as bands as wide as their value; loops and cycles are left out and counted), xtm.parallelcoordinates (one axis per column of a table, options.fields to choose them), xtm.timeline (events in lanes, with or without an end), xtm.treemap (values on up to three levels, or a distribution).
    • xtm.attackflow: a MITRE Attack Flow, from left to right as its builder draws it - an action's card names its tactic and its technique, a condition branches on true or false, an operator joins steps (AND) or offers a choice (OR), an asset is what an action touches, and the flow's card is where it starts. It reads an Attack Flow as its builder exports it (a STIX bundle, in a knowledge base document, the JSON of an assignment or written in the dashboard), or the graph shape with each node's kind (start, action, condition, operator, asset), technique, tactic, description and operator. To lay out the techniques of an entity (an intrusion set, a report) tactic after tactic, read them from an OpenCTI list of attack patterns with the x_mitre_id and killChainPhases columns, and pass it through a flow step (stage: killChainPhases, label: name, technique: x_mitre_id): each technique is an action in each of its tactics, the tactics in their kill chain's order, joined by OR.

    Static data sources take four more shapes for them: geo (points with lat / lon / value / group, regions with code / value), graph (nodes, edges with source / target / value), events (label, start, optional end and lane, ISO dates) and tree (items with a path of up to three names and a value). A graph, a sankey, a timeline or parallel coordinates also draw a table (sourceField / targetField / valueField, startField / endField / laneField / labelField to pick its columns). - Validation outcomes. Data in the outcomes shape - labels (an expectation type, a security domain, a technique) each with its success, failed and pending counts and optional parts - is drawn as the security posture widgets draw it: a technique matrix (xtm.outcomematrix: a column per group, or per group of a chain in chains with every label of its reference), a path graph (xtm.pathgraph: labels by group, an arrow to those they links to when one is hovered, the run's timeline), an exposure console (xtm.exposureconsole: the exposure score - the share of resolved checks that failed - on an orb, a gate per label, the actions beside it), a score gauge (xtm.scoregauge), a ring gauge (xtm.ringgauge: the first label's successes, failures and pending checks) or domain cards (xtm.domaincards: a card per label with its parts). options.sampleDisplay (full, subtle or off) says whether the exposure console and the gauges show a greyed sample while nothing is counted. Dashboards that used the earlier views (validation gates, exposure gauge, resilience rings, outcome cards, outcome grid) open with their replacement. - Trellis. A column, bar, line, area or pie chart with options.trellis (splitBy: series for a series, group for a hierarchy, or a column of a table; columns: 1-6 or auto; sharedScale: true by default; sort: name, -name, total, -total) is drawn as one small chart per value of the field, at most 24. - View switches. In applicationProperties, hideEdit removes Open in the studio and Rearrange from the dashboard's page, hideExport removes Publish or export, hideOpenInPlatform removes the links to OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ on its widgets, and collapseNavigation folds the navigation on the left to its icons while the dashboard is open (your own choice comes back when you leave it). - Live widgets from OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ. A dashboard can hold the platforms' own widgets: an OpenCTI dashboard widget, an OpenAEV custom dashboard widget, or an OpenCRQ figure (findings, annual loss expectancy by scope or over time, tolerance gaps, the most exposed assets). Their figures are read from the platform each time the page opens, with the access of the person viewing it, through an integration that person can use: sharing a dashboard shares its layout, never your data. An OpenCTI map is drawn as a map of the countries and cities it counts, an OpenCTI tree as a treemap, an OpenCTI timeline as a timeline, its radar, polar area, word cloud and heatmap as such, and its bookmarks widget as cards of the bookmarks of the account OpenCTI answers for; a relationships list also gives each relationship's source and target, so it can be drawn as a graph. OpenAEV's security posture widgets are drawn as OpenAEV draws them, from the queries and lists its own widgets read, with your access: the security coverage as a technique matrix (a kill chain at a time, every technique of each phase, a sub-technique counted in its parent, the coverage and All / Covered / Gaps), an attack path as a path graph (its simulation's techniques by phase, the ones each leads to on hover, the simulation's dates; without a simulation it asks for one), the command center as an exposure console (with your OpenAEV security platforms orbiting the score), the exposure score and a resilience gauge as gauges, the security domains as domain cards (every domain OpenAEV knows, in its order) and the posture radar as a radar. An OpenCTI activity and history widget (read by OpenCTI administrators only) shows a link to the platform. Drawn with its own visualization, a platform widget looks as it does in its platform - the same colours (an entity's, a label's, a status'), number and date formats, sizes and layout - from options its platform sets under the visualization's own; drawn as another visualization, it takes that one's look. Any of these options can still be set in the source. A viewer with no access to the integration sees that the data is not available to them. - A platform widget in one step. Data > New opens on Platform widget (the first of the source types, all shown as tiles). Pick the platform, its integration and the widget - its types are tiles, as in OpenCTI's and OpenAEV's own editors - then Create and place: the data source and its visualization are added together, below the others on the tab on screen, drawn as the platform draws it - in its module's colour, the widget's frame keeping XTM One's. Preview draws it the same way before it is saved. An OpenCTI widget's selection can read one of your OpenCTI saved filters (Saved filter) instead of filters of its own: it is read in OpenCTI, with each viewer's access, every time the widget is. - Widget packs. Widget packs on the dashboards list is a library of ready-made widgets: built-in packs for OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, packs you import from a file - an OpenCTI dashboard, custom view or widget export, an OpenAEV dashboard export (ZIP), an XTM One pack - and packs saved from a dashboard. An import says what it changed or left out. An OpenCTI custom view is a dashboard shown on an entity's page: imported, its widgets read the entity an Entity input of the view's type sets (where OpenCTI reads "the current entity"), and inserting the pack adds that input above the tabs, reading through the same integration as the widgets (once: a second view reading the same token uses the input already there). An OpenCTI dashboard's variables are read too: an entity variable becomes an entity input whose value its widgets read; another kind of variable has no input here, so its widgets read its default value, or are left out when it has none (the import says which). An OpenCTI dashboard's or view's period (its last 3 months, or its start and end dates) is kept by each of its widgets, as whoever edits the dashboard set it. An OpenAEV dashboard's simulation and scenario parameters become entity inputs of that type, reading every one while none is picked: its widgets read them where OpenAEV reads the parameter. Saved as a pack, a dashboard keeps the entity inputs its widgets read, and the OpenCTI saved filters its widgets name are written into them (read with your access), since a pack leaves the OpenCTI they were saved in. In the studio, the Packs panel inserts a pack below the selected widget; each live widget reads through your integration of its platform (you choose when you have several). Built-in packs are duplicated to be changed. - Publish or export. Publish or export sends the dashboard to OpenCTI or OpenAEV as one of their own dashboards, with your own account there, and lists the widgets that platform cannot hold (OpenCTI takes its own widgets and text, OpenAEV its own widgets). The period its OpenCTI widgets read becomes the OpenCTI dashboard's. An input its OpenCTI widgets read goes as one of its dashboard variables when OpenCTI has its type (an entity, a text, a number), and a widget reading another input is left out; OpenCTI custom view sends the dashboard as a custom view of the type of its OpenCTI entity input instead (which needs OpenCTI's customization right there): the widgets reading that input read the entity of the page OpenCTI shows them on. To OpenAEV, its simulation and scenario inputs go as the dashboard's parameters. It also downloads the same files, or the dashboard as a widget pack. The OpenCTI saved filters its widgets name are read with your access and written into the file; one you cannot read keeps its reference, which only its own OpenCTI knows, and the list of what changed says so. OpenCRQ has no custom dashboards: its widgets stay in XTM One. - Share on the XTM Hub. In the same dialog, XTM Hub shares the dashboard on the XTM Hub through your XTM Hub integration: its OpenCTI export becomes a new resource of an OpenCTI custom dashboards library your Hub account may publish to (the library's upload right in your organization). It stays hidden until you activate it on the XTM Hub.

docs.title: Download
docs.text: With the Dashboard Studio on, Download on the dashboard's page and in the studio saves the dashboard as a PDF (every tab, or the tab on screen, each tab starting a page; a very tall tab goes on over several pages) or the tab on screen as a PNG. A visualization's menu offers Download PNG of that one visualization. The file is drawn on the server as you see the dashboard, each source read with your own access, its inputs at their default values (an entity input named, as on screen); a PDF holds pictures of the tabs, like the dashboard on screen. applicationProperties.hideExport removes the downloads.

docs.title: Published link
docs.text:
An administrator can let dashboards be published as links anyone opens without an account (Settings > Access and security > Published dashboard links, off by default). In the Share dialog, the people who manage a dashboard turn its published link on, copy it, replace it or turn it off. A visitor sees a snapshot of the dashboard's data, read on the server with the access of the person who published the link - never live, never with anyone else's access - and when it was read. The snapshot is read again on a visit once older than its interval (every 15 minutes, hour, 4 hours or day) or after the dashboard changed; Read again now reads it at once. Whoever changes what the dashboard reads (its data or widgets, not just where they sit) becomes the link's publisher: from then on the snapshot is read with their access, never with the access of someone who did not choose what it shows. A question to an agent is never asked for a snapshot, nor its answer shown. The visitor receives what draws the dashboard and nothing about where its data comes from (no platform query, integration, assignment, agent or variable), no inputs, no click actions and no links into OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ. The link stops answering when it is turned off or replaced, when the person who published it can no longer edit the dashboard, and while the administrator's switch is off.

A published link can have a marking ceiling (Highest markings shown, offered when the dashboard reads OpenCTI): pick the highest marking of each type the link may show, by name (TLP:AMBER, PAP:GREEN), as an OpenCTI public dashboard's maximum markings. OpenCTI data carrying a marking above them, or a marking of a type you did not pick, is left out of the snapshot (what the data shown reaches above them, such as a relationship's source or target, or an entity counted by a distribution, reads Restricted, as OpenCTI shows what its reader cannot see), and a source holding an agent's written answer is not kept at all (an answer can quote anything). Changing the ceiling reads the snapshot again, with the access of the person who changed it, who becomes the link's publisher. OpenAEV and OpenCRQ data have no markings and are shown as they are.

docs.title: Scheduled export
docs.text: Download > Schedule an export... has one of your agents email the dashboard as a PDF or a PNG on a schedule (UTC): every day, on weekdays, on Mondays, on the first day of each month, or a cron expression. The agent needs its Dashboards built-in tools. The schedule is an assignment on that agent, listed in the dialog (pause it, Send now, delete it) and on the agent's page; its run sends the dashboard with the send_dashboard_export tool through the platform's email. Recipients are the email addresses of people with an account who can open the dashboard (10 at most): each receives the file rendered with their own access, with your subject and message and a link to the dashboard. Any other address is not sent to, and the run says so. An agent can also keep the file with export_dashboard and post it to a channel with its own tools.

docs.title: Visualization options
docs.text:
Visualizations Options Area, line, column, bar stackMode (auto, stacked, stacked100), overlayFields (series drawn as lines over the others), y2Fields and showOverlayY2Axis (a second axis, with y2AxisTitleText, y2AxisScale, y2AxisMin, y2AxisMax), dataValuesDisplay (off, all, minmax), legendDisplay (right, left, top, bottom, off) and legendTruncation, xAxisTitleText, yAxisTitleText and their ...Visibility, yAxisScale (linear, log), yAxisMin, yAxisMax, xAxisLabelRotation, nullValueDisplay (gaps, zero, connect), seriesColors, seriesColorsByField, pointColors (one colour per column of a single series), markerDisplay, lineWidth, areaOpacity, annotationColor, showBrush (a range bar to zoom), resultLimit Pie collapseThreshold (slices under this share of the total are gathered into one, 0.01 by default), collapseLabel, showDonutHole, labelDisplay (off, values, valuesAndPercentage), legendDisplay, seriesColors, seriesColorsByField. Slices and the legend follow the data's order. Scatter, bubble, punchcard xField, yField, sizeField, categoryField (by default the first numeric columns, and the first text column as the category), axis titles, scale and bounds, legendDisplay, seriesColors, bubbleSizeMin, bubbleSizeMax. A punchcard places a circle for each pair of its two text columns, sized by a number. Single value, icon, radial majorValue, trendValue, sparklineValues, trendDisplay (absolute, percent, off), sparklineDisplay (below, before, after, off), showSparklineAreaGraph, unit, unitPosition, numberPrecision, shouldUseThousandSeparators, shouldAbbreviateValue (on by default: 1.2M), shouldAbbreviateTrendValue, underLabel, majorColor, trendColor, backgroundColor, sparklineStrokeColor; with an icon icon (a Lucide icon name), iconColor, iconPosition, showValue; as a ring maxValue, radialStrokeColor, radialBackgroundColor. Filler and marker gauges value, minValue, maxValue, gaugeRanges ([{from, to, value: colour}], which also set the scale), orientation, gaugeColor, labelDisplay and valueDisplay (number, percentage, off), unit, numberPrecision, majorTickInterval. A platform's look (area, line, column, bar, pie, polar area, radar, word cloud, heatmap) palette (material, materialMixed, results) and paletteLead (a first colour before it), paletteNoPale, numberFormat (si 1.5K, siSpaced 1.5 K, compact, locale 1,500), dateFormat (date, longDate, monthYear, year), tooltipContent (labelValue, label), separatorWidth, fill (solid, gradient, with fillOpacityFrom and fillOpacityTo), barRadius, barSize, barGap, colorByPoint, stackTotals, xAxisType (category, time), markerSize, labelMaxLength and labelCut (words, chars), gridLines (both, horizontal, vertical, none), gridOpacity, xAxisFontSize, yAxisFontSize, axisLabelColor, hideAxisLines, valueTickCount, dataValuesStrong, radius, donutHoleSize, colorRanges (heat), valueShades, openLinks (a click opens the item in its platform), emptySample (what a widget without data shows greyed). Single value (a platform's look) valueStyle: standard, difference (the figure under its change over 24 hours), tile (an icon tile, a figure that counts up, a trend chip). List, distribution, timeline A list's listStyle (compact, table, rows, cards), rowHeight, cardsPerRow; a distribution's listStyle (bars, rows); a timeline's timelineStyle (lanes, alternate). Map regionColors (classes, or level: a threat level's colour), basemap (surface, contrast), markerColor, markerSize, markerIcon, zoom, centerLat, centerLng, centerOnFirstMarker. Security posture (coverage matrix, path graph, exposure console, score gauge, ring gauge, domain cards) sampleDisplay (full, subtle, off): how the sample drawn without data shows. Table count (rows per page), headerVisibility (inline, fixed, none), showRowNumbers, showTotals (sums of the numeric columns), columnFormat (per column: width, align, textOverflow, cellType - text, array for a list of items, sparkline for a list of numbers -, data, rowColors, rowBackgroundColors), tableFormat (rowColors, rowBackgroundColors for whole rows).

A colour is one of accent, brand (the colour OpenCTI and OpenAEV draw their widgets in), ai, success, warning, alert, danger, info, neutral, text, muted, chart1 to chart10 (the platform's colours, in light and dark), or a #rgb / #rrggbb value.

docs.title: Dynamic options
docs.text:
An option whose value starts with > is computed from the visualization's data: "majorColor": "> majorValue | rangeValue(ranges)". It starts with a source - primary (the data; table is the same), annotation (the data source named dataSources.annotation, whose first column places a marker on the chart's x and second labels it), or another option of the visualization - then steps separated by |:

  • picking: seriesByName('count'), seriesByIndex(1) (a series' x is index 0), firstPoint(), lastPoint(), delta(-2) (the last point minus the one at that index), min(), max(), sum();
  • formatting, a point or every point of a series: rangeValue(name), matchValue(name), gradient(name), formatByType(name), prefix('text').

A formatter's name is an entry of the visualization's context: rangeValue takes [{from, to, value}] (from included, to excluded), matchValue [{match, value}], gradient {stops: [numbers], colors: [colours]}, formatByType {number: {precision, thousandSeparated, unit, unitPosition, abbreviate}}. For example, a single value turning red past 100:

"options": {"majorColor": "> majorValue | rangeValue(levels)"},
"context": {"levels": [{"to": 100, "value": "success"}, {"from": 100, "value": "danger"}]}

Expressions are read in your browser on the data shown, never run as code; one that does not fit this syntax is refused when the dashboard is saved, and one that finds nothing in the data leaves the option at its default.

If a dashboard holds a widget this version of XTM One does not know (one written by a newer version), the widget shows as a placeholder and the rest of the dashboard is drawn as usual.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Files is the one place that lists every file you and your agents exchanged — the documents you uploaded in a conversation and the outputs your agents produced (reports, exports, generated images, spreadsheets), wherever they were made.

Until now each file lived only behind the context that produced it: the files panel of one conversation, the attachments of one run. Files collects them all so you can find a deliverable again without remembering which chat or which assignment produced it.

docs.title: Open Files
docs.text:
Choose Work > Files from the left sidebar. The Work group holds what your agents produce — Operations (their runs), Presentations (their decks) and Files (everything else they output, plus what you gave them).

The Work hub page itself shows the three at a glance, with counts and the most recently changed items of each.

docs.title: What is listed
docs.text:
You see exactly the files you are allowed to download:

  • files you uploaded, and files generated for you, in your own conversations
  • files of conversations that were shared with you
  • outputs of assignment runs you can open — your own agents' runs, and runs of company-managed agents

Nothing is listed that you could not open: a file that appears in the list can always be downloaded.

Generated files include what an agent brought in from the web: every page or document it reads with Web Fetch is kept as a file of the conversation (a PDF, a spreadsheet or a data file as the document itself, a web page as its HTML source), so it can be downloaded, handed to another tool or added to a knowledge base. Reading the same page twice with identical content keeps one file. A report an agent exported to PDF is a file too.

What is not here

The design assets of presentation templates (logos, diagrams, fonts) are managed from their template under Agent Studio > Templates and are not repeated here — a fresh install ships a few hundred of them, and they would bury your real files. Presentations themselves have their own page, Presentations; a deck exported to PDF or PowerPoint does show up in Files, because the export is a file.

Administrators do not get a wider view here. An administrator reaches another user's conversation files only through the audited break-glass access on the conversation itself, never through this list.

docs.title: Find a file
docs.text:
Four filters sit next to the search box. Each is a segmented control; pick one segment of each.

Filter Segments Question it answers Where the file lives Everywhere · Conversations · Runs · Other in a chat, from an assignment run, or unbound (dataset uploads, tool tests, flow uploads) How it got there Any origin · Uploaded · Generated did a person upload it, or did an agent produce it State Any state · Available · Deleted is the file's content still kept, or was it deleted (see Retention) Visibility Mine · Company · Shared · All your own files and contexts; files of company-managed runs; files shared with you; or every file you can read. With no segment in the address, the page opens on the first one holding a file: Mine, else Company, else Shared, else All

Search matches the file name. The counter on the right of the filter row is the total for the current filters, and the list is paginated when it is long. When Mine holds nothing but other segments do, the page says so and offers Show all.

The visibility segment is kept in the address as ?vis=. An older link that carries ?owner= still opens: ?owner=shared ("Shared with me"), which also listed company-run files, opens on All so it hides none of them, and ?owner=mine opens Mine. The address switches to ?vis= on your next change.

Group (on by default) folds the list by conversation or run, so the files of one piece of work sit together under its title and owner. Switch it off for a flat, most-recent-first list where each row also shows its context.

Filters, search, grouping and page are kept in the URL, so a filtered view can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague — they will see the same view, limited to what they may read.

docs.title: Act on a file
docs.text:
Each row shows the file name, type and size, when it was added and by whom, and a badge telling whether it was Uploaded or Generated. From the row's menu:

  • Download fetches the file.
  • Open conversation / Open run takes you to the place the file came from, so you can read it in context or ask the assistant for a new version.
  • Delete removes the file and its storage object. It is available to the file's owner, the owner of the conversation it lives in, or whoever can manage the run that produced it — someone a conversation was merely shared with can read the file but not delete it.

Deleting a file does not break the message or the deck that referenced it: they show the file as no longer available.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
Files are kept for as long as your administrator set in Settings > Usage and quotas > Storage & retention. By default an agent's working files and the files it delivered go 60 days after their last use: each download, preview or read by an assistant starts the 60 days again. Chat uploads, channel files and the other agent files are kept for good unless your administrator sets a limit. A file an open work item, a workset, an active shared state, a presentation, a report or a video still uses is never deleted.

The row of a file that will go shows Expires <date> if unused.

When a file is deleted, only its content goes. It stays where it was shown, as a muted card with its name, size and Deleted on <date> by the retention policy: in the chat message, the conversation's files panel, a run's attachments and this page (the Deleted state lists them). It can no longer be downloaded (the download answers 410 Gone) and an assistant that tries to read it is told the same, so it can make the file again if it is still needed.

docs.title: Jump from a chat or a run
docs.text: Anywhere the platform shows a file — a chat message, a run's attachments — a link to it in Files opens the page already scoped to that conversation or run, with the file highlighted. The Showing files of chip at the top of the list names the scope; close it to return to the full list with the same filters.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Agents also produce slide decks. See Presentations for how decks are created, shared, and exported.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This chapter introduces what XTM One does, who it is for, and how to find your way around.

docs.title: What XTM One is for
docs.text:
XTM One is the core platform of the XTM Platform. OpenCTI (threat intelligence), OpenAEV (adversarial exposure validation) and OpenCRQ (governance, risk and compliance) are its modules: they connect to XTM One, sign their users in through it, and reach its agents from their own screens. XTM One holds what they share: the common context of your organization, your exposure management view, the shared integrations, and the AI agents that work across all of them.

Use XTM One to work with AI assistants built for cyber, intelligence, operations and business workflows. You can ask for summaries, explanations, extractions and recommendations; follow your exposure across the connected modules; launch or monitor automated work handled by agents and assignments; reuse shared resources such as knowledge bases, prompts, skills, tools and integrations; and review what your agents did before acting.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: XTM One is designed for business users, analysts and operators: you do not need to be an AI specialist. It is useful for teams working with OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, threat intelligence, investigations, reporting and summarization, operational triage, security operations, and email or messaging workflows.

docs.title: Key words in this guide
docs.text:
A few recurring terms appear throughout this documentation:

  • Agent: an AI assistant configured for a specific use case, role, or workflow
  • Assignment: an automation rule that tells an agent when to run and what to do
  • Knowledge Base: searchable internal knowledge used to ground answers and actions
  • Prompt and Skill: reusable instructions that shape how agents behave
  • Tool or MCP Server: capabilities that let agents query, fetch, or act outside the chat itself
  • Integration: a connection to another system such as messaging, email, or external platforms

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text: Open the XTM One sign-in page and choose the login method available in your organization: a company account, email and password, or a local account if that is allowed. If your organization uses single sign-on, you are redirected to your identity provider and brought back automatically.

docs.title: Find your way around
docs.text:
After signing in you land on the Dashboard. The left navigation moves you between sections, the top bar holds search, notifications and your user menu, and the center shows the current page.

The left navigation reads from top to bottom:

  • Home and Chat: your overview and your conversations with assistants.
  • Orchestration: your agents and what they form and follow. It holds Agents, Fleets, Agentic Flow (the map of how agents work together) and, for administrators, Intents.
  • Work: what your agents produce. It holds Operations (their runs, background tasks, work items, shared state, worksets and workspaces), Value, Presentations, Videos, Dashboards and Files, the last ones where your deployment offers them.
  • Agent Studio: what your agents are made of. It holds Knowledge, Prompts, Templates, Skills and Investigation packs. Create an agent is a button of the hub and of the Agents page, and a destination of the command palette.
  • Tools & Integrations: what your agents act through. It holds MCP Servers, Tools, Integrations and Connections (Browser profiles, plus Variables and Relays where your deployment offers them).
  • Administration (administrators): Observability (Model usage, Outcomes, Traces and Sessions), AI Adoption, Evaluations, Platform Health, Users and groups, Objects, Audit logs and Settings. A group manager sees Model usage for the members of their groups.

Orchestration, Work, Agent Studio and Tools & Integrations are groups: click a group's name to open its hub page, which presents each of its pages as a card, and the arrow next to it to fold or unfold the group. A row that gathers several pages (Observability, Users and groups, Connections) opens the first of them, with one row of tabs to the others. The navigation can also shrink to a rail of icons, with the toggle at its foot.

The product switcher at the top of the navigation (Switch product) lists the OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ platforms connected to XTM One and the XTM Hub, each with its connection status, and opens the one you pick.

docs.title: What you can access
docs.text:
What you see depends on your role and on your organization's edition. Some users only use the shared platform experience, some use ready-made assistants, and some create and manage their own agents and resources. The Administration section is for administrators.

An area that needs AI stays listed when AI is not available, marked with a lock: on Community Edition (see Editions and licensing), or when an administrator has switched AI off (see Running without AI). Point at it to see why. You can still open it and read what it holds.

If a section is missing altogether, it is not enabled for your deployment or your account. This guide explains those differences only when they matter for a task.

docs.title: Search with the command palette
docs.text:
The search box at the left of the top bar (Search…) opens the command palette. Press ⌘K on a Mac, or Ctrl K elsewhere, to open it from anywhere, even while you type in a field.

  • Type the name of a page to go to it: every page of the navigation is listed.
  • Type > to run a command, such as Play Space Invaders.
  • Type @ to jump to a section of the page you are on.
  • Type ? for help on these modes.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The bell in the top bar shows how many notifications you have not read. It collects what your agents and the platform want you to know:

  • runs, flows and work items waiting for your input or decision, listed first and marked Action needed until you answer them;
  • the results of assignments set to notify you when they complete;
  • flow notifications and questions, reminders and messages from agents;
  • problems that need you: an integration that can no longer sign in, a resource an assignment keeps missing, a chained run that could not start, security and API key notices.

Click a notification to open the page it is about; opening it marks it read. Point at one and use Mark as read to mark it read without opening it, or Mark all read for all of them. A notification waiting for your answer stays unread until you answer it: opening it does not read it, it has no Mark as read, and Mark all read leaves it unread; while one waits, the bell's count turns red. A work item you cannot open is never listed. View all opens Operations > Executions on its Notifications filter. What you mark read is kept on your account, so your other devices agree.

docs.title: The top bar
docs.text:
Besides search and notifications, the top bar holds:

  • Quick triggers, when you have assignments you can start by hand: start one from there with Run now;
  • the AI Catalog button, when your administrator has enabled the catalog: it opens the catalog of published agents and resources in a new tab;
  • your user menu: My Profile, Get XTM One Desktop (or My machines once the desktop app is installed), the arcade, Settings for administrators, the About window, Emergency stop and Sign out.

When your deployment offers it, Get XTM One Desktop opens the page to download XTM One Desktop, the desktop app through which an agent can act on your computer. See XTM One Desktop and runners.

docs.title: XTM One in the other modules
docs.text: Depending on your deployment, you also use XTM One from inside OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ. There it appears as an assistant panel or an AI action inside the product where you already work, while the agents, resources and automations are still managed in XTM One. See XTM One in the XTM Suite.

docs.title: Start with the dashboard
docs.text: If you are not sure where to begin, open the Dashboard first. It is the best place to see what waits for you, check your exposure and recent activity, and find the next action to take.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Once you are signed in and comfortable with the layout, move to the Foundations section. Start with Foundations Overview, then continue to Data model before moving into the Dashboard and the rest of the UI chapters.

docs.title: Platform Health
docs.text: When Platform Health is on, it looks for ways to improve the agents and flows of the platform, tries them on sandbox copies, and files improvement proposals. A proposal changes nothing until someone who manages the target approves it.

docs.title: Where to find them
docs.text:
• Agent page > Overview > Improvements: the proposals on the agent, its skills and its assignments, and the Platform Health cycles on the agent.
  • A flow's page > Improvements (the compass in its toolbar): the proposals and cycles of the flow.
  • Administrators: the Platform Health page (/health) lists every proposal.

These appear only to the people who may manage the agent or flow: its owner, a person or group it is shared with at the config level, and administrators for a company-managed one. Read-only sharing does not show them.

docs.title: The Overview tab
docs.text:
The Overview tab of the Platform Health page opens first. Every figure on it comes from checks that run on a schedule without any model call, so reading it consumes no agentic quota.

  • Module cards: one card per module, with its score out of 100, its open findings by severity and the change over the last 7 days. Agents and fleets appear in every deployment; XTM One, OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ appear in XTM One deployments.
  • Score history: each module's daily score over 7, 30 or 90 days (administrators).
  • Findings: what the checks found, most severe first, with search and filters by severity, module and category. The switch above the list shows the open, dismissed or resolved findings with their counts. Open a row to read its evidence, its recommendation and a link to the documentation.
  • Dismiss finding: sets an open finding aside for 7, 30 or 90 days or until it resolves, with a reason. A dismissed finding leaves the score; the reason is recorded in the audit trail. It comes back if it is still failing when the dismissal lapses.
  • Dismiss all and Restore all: act on the selected rows, or on every finding of the list when none is selected, with one reason for a dismissal. Restore on a dismissed finding brings it back to the open list at once. Every change is recorded in the audit trail.

Administrators see every module. Anyone else sees the findings of the agents they manage (owner, or shared at the config level), without the module cards of the platforms.

docs.title: On the home dashboard
docs.text:
The home dashboard reads the same findings, for administrators:

  • Product pills: the dot of the OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ pill turns red when the platform is unreachable or its module holds an open critical finding, and amber on an open warning. Point at the pill to read the count.
  • Critical findings notice: when critical findings are open, a notice at the top of the dashboard gives their count and the most recent one; Review opens this tab. Model configuration and knowledge base findings keep their own notices, which every user sees.

docs.title: Reading a proposal
docs.text:
Each proposal shows:

  • its type (persona, skill, assignment prompt, flow repair, flow optimization, new flow, agent to flow) and its status;
  • the measured result of its experiment: a measured gain, no measured change, or Unmeasured when it could not be measured, with the reason;
  • how many of the experiment's writes were simulated rather than replayed from recorded calls;
  • its evidence: links to the traces, ratings and runs you may open. Evidence you may not open is counted, not linked.

Approve or reject it from the target's page. An approved change is applied as a new version of the target and watched: if it regresses within the watch window it is rolled back, unless someone edited the target meanwhile, in which case that edit is kept.

docs.title: Improve with Platform Health
docs.text:
The Improve with … button (it carries the orchestrator's name), on the agent page and on a flow's page, asks Platform Health to investigate that agent or flow now. It is offered to the people who may manage it. Platform Health says so when it cannot start:

  • it is already working on this target;
  • the target is outside its supervision scope;
  • its budget per cycle or per month is reached;
  • agentic AI is off on the platform.

What it finds appears under Improvements once its cycle ends.

docs.title: The companion
docs.text:
The companion is a small animated pet in the bottom-right corner of the screen that shows what Platform Health found, and what your own work is doing. It is offered to administrators, who are the people who can open the Platform Health page; other users see neither the pet nor its profile card. It is off until you turn it on in Profile > Profile > Companion, where you also pick the pet. The Butler, with a silver tray, is the built-in pet and the default one.

The pet When Waves It appears Looks worried A Platform Health cycle, or one of your runs, failed in the last 30 minutes Checks its watch One of your runs is waiting for your approval Presents a letter A proposal waits for a decision you may take Is at work A Platform Health cycle is running, one of your runs is running, or the chat on screen is answering Stands by Nothing of the above

Click the pet to read what it shows: first the open findings, the most severe kind with its count (for example "2 critical findings are open.", or "No open finding."), then what is happening now. From there you open the Platform Health page or hide the pet; you can show it again from your profile. When your system asks for reduced motion, the pet holds still. It reads only what you may already see, without calling any model.

docs.title: Home dashboard
docs.text: The Dashboard is the landing page of XTM One, and Dashboard at the top of the left navigation brings you back to it. In XTM One it is the CTEM command center: one view of your exposure across the modules connected to XTM One (OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ) and of the agents that work on it.

docs.title: What the Dashboard is for
docs.text:
Use the Dashboard to:

  • see your exposure posture and each stage of your exposure management loop
  • read your AI exposure briefing and its recommended actions
  • check which modules are connected and healthy
  • see what waits for you: notices, work items, setup steps
  • follow recent agent activity and open the main work areas

docs.title: What you see first
docs.text:
What the Dashboard shows depends on whether a module is connected yet and on your edition:

  • No module connected yet: the welcome page. It introduces XTM One and shows a Connect OpenCTI card and a Connect OpenAEV card, each with the steps to connect that platform. Administrators also see the Registration token to give the platforms. This page is mainly for the initial rollout: your administrator usually completes it.
  • Community Edition, the first time: a one-time introduction. Once a module is connected, a Community Edition platform shows a page that presents what Enterprise Edition adds, with the connected modules. Explore the command center takes you to the command center, which you land on directly from then on. Start Free Trial and Contact Sales open Filigran's pages, and administrators can Activate License.
  • Otherwise: the command center, described below.

When an administrator has switched AI off, the home page says so instead (see Running without AI).

docs.title: Dashboard notices
docs.text:
The top of the Dashboard gathers what needs attention, each as a notice you can click:

  • N work items are waiting for you: work items that wait for your decision, or items of yours that no agent owns and that are past their due date. The notice names the item waiting longest. Review opens that item when it is the only one; when several wait, it opens Tasks > Work Items on the Waiting for me view with the All scope, which lists every item the notice counts (your own, company-managed and shared ones), oldest first. Pick Mine there to narrow the list to your own items; the link keeps the scope, so a bookmark reopens the same list.
  • Model configuration: No default model configured or No embedding provider configured, when agents or knowledge bases cannot run yet. Administrators get a Configure button.
  • Knowledge base health: a knowledge base that needs attention, indexing stalled, re-indexing in progress or stale embeddings, with a link to the documentation or the settings.
  • Platform Health (administrators): the critical findings open in Platform Health, their count and the most recent one, with Review.
  • Your own OAuth integrations that share your personal credentials with other people, with Stop sharing and Keep sharing.
  • On Community Edition, the upgrade path to Enterprise Edition.

When nothing needs attention, no notice is shown.

docs.title: The command center
docs.text:
The command center opens with a greeting, a summary of your exposure posture, and the Start chatting button. Next to it you see when the exposure data was last synced; the refresh button next to that time fetches your data again, for you only.

The product pills under the greeting show each module: OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, then the XTM Hub. A connected module shows its edition, version and health, and opens the platform when you click it. For an administrator the health dot also reads Platform Health: red on an open critical finding, amber on an open warning, with the count when you point at it. A module that is not connected offers Connect OpenCTI (or Connect OpenAEV), which explains how to connect it; OpenCRQ shows Soon until an OpenCRQ platform connects.

The XTM Hub pill follows the platform's registration with the XTM Hub: a green dot while the XTM Hub confirms it, a red one when it did not at the last hourly check or when the platform must be registered again. A platform that is not registered shows the XTM Hub integrations you can use instead (a green dot while one is connected), and otherwise reads Connect XTM Hub: it opens the registration for an administrator and the integration form for anyone else. The pill opens your XTM Hub. See the XTM Hub integration for what agents can do with it.

docs.title: Exposure posture
docs.text:
The posture score, out of 100, sums up your exposure across the five stages of the exposure lifecycle. Click the posture ring (or the Exposure posture card) to see How the Exposure Posture is computed: a weighted average of the five stage scores, with the weight and score of each stage. A stage with no connected module is left out of the average, so it never drags the score down.

A row of cards follows:

  • Exposure posture, with the number of stages covered;
  • three cards specific to the vertical you chose, for example Known-exploited, Detection coverage and Validation success for Cyber. Each one opens the matching page in the module that provides it;
  • Agents, with the number of active assignments;
  • Agentic executions over the last 30 days, which opens Operations > Executions (see Operations).

A figure that has no data yet is shown greyed as a sample, so you see what the card will hold once the module is connected.

docs.title: Act now
docs.text:
Act now lists what to do first: the work items and tool approvals waiting for you, then the facts read from the connected modules (known-exploited exposures, failed simulation expectations, detection coverage gaps) and the setup steps left. Each row says in one line why it is there; click it to open the stage page that holds the figures behind it. Ask AI opens a new chat with the row's context already written in the message box, asking the assistant to guide you step by step through the fix; review it and send it yourself.

When the rows come from module-wide figures rather than from your organization context, the card says These actions are generic, and administrators get Set up organization context to fill it in.

When the organization context lists a software inventory, the known-exploited row counts only the known-exploited vulnerabilities that OpenCTI relates to the software of that stack (matched by CPE, else by product and vendor), and its line names the products it matched, for example Known-exploited and affects Fortinet FortiOS in your software inventory. This row is then tailored, so the generic notice no longer counts it. Without a software inventory, or when OpenCTI holds no matching software, the row keeps the module-wide count.

The same notice appears on the other widgets whose content does not use your organization context yet:

  • Exposure briefing says This briefing is generic while no organization context was ever saved: the briefing analyst reads the sector, regions, primary assets, software inventory and PIRs of the context to rank its findings. Set it up, then generate the briefing again.
  • Stats and coverage says These figures are module-wide when its known-exploited figure counts every such vulnerability in OpenCTI because the context has no software inventory. Each figure under Findings opens the stage page that holds it.

Administrators get the Set up organization context (or Review organization context) action; other users are told that an administrator can set it up.

docs.title: Choose a vertical
docs.text: The switcher at the top right of the Dashboard chooses the vertical the command center reads your exposure for: Cyber (cyber attack-surface exposure, the default), FIMI (foreign information manipulation and interference) or Fraud (digital fraud, phishing and brand abuse). The posture, the stage cards, their analysts and the briefing all change with it. Your choice is kept on your profile.

docs.title: Exposure lifecycle stages
docs.text:
The Exposure lifecycle row shows one card per stage: Scoping, Discovery, Prioritization, Validation and Remediation. Each card gives the stage score and its main figures, its trend, the agent that analyses it (Owned by its name), and, when a module that feeds it is missing, a button to connect it.

Click a card to open the stage page. It shows the stage score, the AI assessment of the stage (a headline, what it means and a Recommended action), all its metrics, its history and the modules that feed it. Refresh (or Generate, the first time) writes a new assessment for you and your current vertical, using only what you can see in the connected modules. The Company Context card invites you to describe your software inventory, primary-asset assets and risk priorities in the Company Context knowledge base, so the analyst can judge what actually matters to you.

The sixth card, Governance & Risk, is reserved for OpenCRQ: until an OpenCRQ platform joins, it shows greyed sample figures.

Note

AI assessments are an Enterprise Edition capability. On Community Edition, the stage scores and metrics stay available and the assessment is replaced by an explanation.

docs.title: AI exposure briefing
docs.text:
The Latest exposure briefing card is written by the Exposure Briefing Analyst agent: a summary of your exposure, its key findings and the focus for the week. It is generated for each user every month, from what that user can see in the connected modules, and Generate my briefing writes yours now. Until your first briefing exists, the card shows a sample preview.

View full briefing opens the Exposure briefing page: the headline and summary, the posture trend, the cross-product insight, every key finding with its recommended action, the Next steps and the Recommended focus. From there you can follow up on a step in a chat or hand it to an agent. Refresh writes a new briefing for you and your current vertical.

The Recommended actions card lists what to fix first: the steps of your briefing, and actions such as triaging known-exploited exposures, closing validation gaps or connecting a missing module, each with its own button. Open briefing opens the full briefing.

Note

The exposure briefing is an Enterprise Edition capability. On Community Edition, the card and the page explain this and your numeric posture stays available.

docs.title: Value and top value drivers
docs.text:
On a Copilot deployment, the Value card shows the hours saved and the net value of the last 30 days: the whole organization for an administrator, your own agents and fleets otherwise. See the value opens the Value page.

The Top value drivers card beside it ranks the agents of the same report by hours saved: each row shows the agent, its share of the first agent's hours, the hours saved and its runs, and opens the agent. All agents opens the By agent tab of the Value page. A narrow card keeps the name and the hours. An agent that no longer exists is shown as Deleted agent, without a link. Until a unit of work is declared, the card offers Declare a unit of work.

An administrator sets who sees the organization's value in Settings > Organization > Rates by role, card Value visibility and privacy: Organization totals for every user lets every user switch the Value page to the organization's figures; Smallest group shown apart (5 people by default, 2 to 50) folds any fleet, agent, unit of work or week backed by fewer people into Other for users who are not administrators, in exports and agent tools too; By person breakdown for administrators turns on that breakdown, and every read of it is written to the audit log.

docs.title: Live Activity and latest results
docs.text:
Live Activity lists the latest agent runs as they happen. All opens Operations > Executions. Until a first run exists, the panel shows a greyed sample.

Latest Results & Digests shows the most recent digests and reports your agents produced. Click one to open its run, or View all to list them all in Operations > Executions.

docs.title: How to use the Dashboard day to day
docs.text:
1. Read the notices at the top and deal with what waits for you.
  2. Check the posture and the stage that changed the most, and open its page if you need the details.
  3. Read your briefing and pick a recommended action.
  4. Use Start chatting to work on it with an assistant.
  5. Open Work > Operations to see what your agents already did.

docs.title: Customize the dashboard
docs.text:
You can build your own dashboard: it is a grid of widgets you move, resize, remove and add back. The widgets are the posture overview, each KPI card, the AI exposure briefing, the exposure lifecycle title, each stage of the exposure lifecycle (and the Governance & Risk card), the recommended actions, the live activity, and the latest results and digests.

  1. Select Customize, next to the vertical switcher at the top right of the dashboard. The widgets stay on screen, framed, and a bar at the top lists what you can do.
  2. Drag a widget to move it; the others make room. Drag its bottom right corner to resize it.
  3. Select the cross on a widget to remove it. Add a widget lists the widgets you removed; one you add back goes below the others.
  4. Select Done to use the dashboard again: while you customize it, its widgets do not open anything.

Each change is saved to your profile at once, so the dashboard looks the same on your next sign-in and on any device. Each vertical (Cyber, FIMI, Fraud) keeps its own layout.

The dashboard of a Copilot deployment is built the same way, with Customize at its top right. Its widgets are the status header, each KPI card (agents, conversations, agentic executions, integrations, documents), the agent list, the last conversations, the live activity, the latest results and digests, the Value card and the Top value drivers card beside it. It keeps one layout. Reset to default puts it back to the original layout. Your layout is yours only: it does not change anyone else's dashboard.

A widget adapts to the size you give it: the smaller it is, the fewer secondary details it shows, the most important ones staying. For example, a small posture overview shows the posture score next to its title instead of the posture ring, and the connected products as logos (point at one to see its name, version and health); a small stage card keeps its score and its main figures; the recommended actions show as many actions as fit. Make a widget bigger to see everything again.

In a narrow window the widgets are shown one below the other, in the order of your layout, and cannot be rearranged until you widen the window.

docs.title: If the dashboard looks different from another user's
docs.text:
That is usually normal. The dashboard varies based on:

  • which modules are connected, and your edition
  • the vertical each person chose
  • what each person can see in the connected modules: the briefing and the stage assessments are written for you, from your own access
  • whether your account has access to the related areas
  • the layout each person built (see Customize the dashboard)

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Chat, which is the fastest way to start working with XTM One.

docs.title: Mobile companion
docs.text:
Off by default

The mobile companion is turned on by your administrator with the MOBILE_COMPANION feature flag (ENABLED_FEATURES, see Configuration). Until then, a phone opens the web app, and the Phones tab of your profile is not shown.

On a phone, XTM One is a companion to the platform rather than the full platform on a small screen. It shows what you need away from your desk, and the platform reaches you there with notifications.

The device decides, not the size of the screen. A phone gets the companion even held sideways, and a tablet or a computer gets the full platform.

docs.title: The three tabs
docs.text:
• Today: the platform's home dashboard (XTM One's command center, or the Copilot dashboard), the one the web app opens on, under a short greeting.
  • Inbox: your notifications, the same ones as the bell of the web app. What waits on you comes first and is answered right there: approve or reject the tool calls a run proposes, or answer its question.
  • Ask: the assistant.

Any other page of the platform, for example a link to an agent's settings, says it is made for a computer, with a button back to Today.

What you read on the phone is read on the computer too, and the other way around: read state is kept by the platform, not by each browser.

docs.title: Install it as an app
docs.text:
You can install the companion on your home screen. It then opens full screen, like any other app.

  • Android (Chrome, Edge, Samsung Internet): tap Install on the banner at the top of the companion, or Install the app in the menu next to the greeting on Today.
  • iPhone (Safari): the banner reminds you how: tap Share, then Add to Home Screen.

Not now hides the banner on that phone for a month. A long press on the installed app's icon offers its tabs as shortcuts.

The installed app keeps no offline copy of your data or conversations: it needs a connection, and shows a short "You are offline" page when there is none.

docs.title: Notifications on your phone
docs.text:
Tap Turn on notifications on Today or in the Inbox, then allow notifications when your browser asks. That links the phone to your account. On iPhone, install the app first (iOS 16.4 or later): Safari gives notifications only to installed apps.

Your phone then receives what your notification bell shows:

  • runs waiting for your approval or your answer;
  • the results of runs set to notify you;
  • reminders an agent scheduled for you;
  • messages an agent sends you (see below);
  • integration problems, security audit findings, API keys about to expire, and the other notices of the bell.

A tap opens the notification's page in the companion.

docs.title: Approve or reject from the notification
docs.text:
A run waiting on tool approvals arrives with Approve and Reject buttons (on Android; Safari on iPhone shows no buttons, the notification opens the Inbox instead; with a PIN lock on, there are no buttons either). A button decides every tool call the run waits on, exactly as the web app would, and it works:

  • once: the other button, and any copy of the notification, stop working as soon as the run is decided, from anywhere;
  • for 15 minutes;
  • only if the run still waits on the same tool calls;
  • only while the phone it was sent to is still linked to your account.

To look at the details first, tap the notification instead: the Inbox shows each tool call and its arguments.

docs.title: Manage your phones
docs.text:
Profile > Phones on the computer lists your linked phones. For each one you can:

  • send a test notification;
  • turn notifications off or on;
  • choose what it notifies about (runs, reminders, messages from agents, analytics, flows, security audit findings). Approvals and questions waiting on you always notify;
  • set quiet hours (22:00 to 07:00 in your time zone): nothing is pushed in between, and what arrives waits in the Inbox;
  • unlink it: it stops receiving notifications, and the buttons of the notifications already on it stop working.

The QR code on that page opens the platform on your phone. It holds only the address: you sign in on the phone as usual.

An administrator can see and unlink a person's phones (for example when someone leaves), and cannot send them anything. The Phone notification content option (Settings > Access and security, or PHONE_NOTIFICATION_CONTENT) set to minimal makes every phone notification say only "New notification", with no buttons, for deployments that want nothing on a lock screen; so does a PIN lock, for the person who turned it on. The content of a notification is encrypted for the phone: the browser's push service (Google, Apple, Mozilla or Microsoft) carries it without being able to read it.

docs.title: Lock the companion with a PIN
docs.text:
A PIN of your own keeps your data out of reach of anyone who picks up your phone. While the PIN lock is on, the companion shows nothing and approves nothing until the PIN is entered: not your home dashboard, not your name, not a notification's content.

  • Turn it on from the companion (Today > menu > Protect with a PIN) or from Profile > Phones on the computer. A PIN has 6 to 8 digits, and cannot be one digit repeated or a run like 123456.
  • The companion asks for it each time it opens, after half a minute in the background, and after 10 minutes without use. Lock now in the Today menu locks it at once.
  • Five wrong PINs in a row sign the phone out. Sign in again on the phone to continue.
  • While the PIN lock is on, a phone notification says only "New notification", with no Approve or Reject buttons: a lock screen shows nothing either. Tap it, enter the PIN, and the Inbox has the details.
  • To change the PIN or turn the lock off, open Profile > Phones on a computer. Forgot your PIN? Sign out on the phone, choose a new one there (the computer never asks for the current one), then sign in again on the phone.

The PIN applies only to the companion on a phone. On a computer, nothing changes.

An administrator can require a PIN for everyone with the Require a PIN on the mobile companion option (Settings > Access and security, or COMPANION_PIN_REQUIRED). Each person then chooses a PIN the first time the companion opens on their phone, and cannot turn it off.

docs.title: What agents can do with your phone
docs.text:
• Notify you. An agent with the Phone Notifications built-in tool can send a short notification to your linked phones, for something that deserves your attention while you are away: a critical finding, a run that needs you, a result you asked to be told about. It reaches only the person the agent acts for, follows your quiet hours and choices, links only to pages of the platform, and is capped (3 per run, 20 per hour across all agents). It also lands in your bell.
  • Remind you. Ask any agent to remind you of something ("remind me tomorrow at 9 to check the patch window"). The reminder is a scheduled work item, and it reaches your phone when it is due.
  • Ask you. When a run needs your approval or your answer, the notification brings it to your phone, with buttons for approvals.

docs.title: Share to XTM One
docs.text: On Android, once the app is installed, XTM One appears in the share sheet of other apps. Share a link, some text, a screenshot or a document: the companion opens a new conversation with it in the message box and the files attached. Nothing is sent until you add your question and send it.

docs.title: My profile
docs.text: My Profile is where you manage your personal experience in XTM One. Unlike Settings, which is shared platform configuration, this page is about your own account.

docs.title: What you can do here
docs.text:
Use My Profile to:

  • update your account details
  • set your time zone and theme
  • change your password, if you use a local account
  • protect your account with two-factor authentication
  • choose your default chat agent
  • tailor the General Assistant to your needs
  • review the tools you let run without asking you
  • control your private channel routing
  • let an agent operate a messaging account or a mailbox
  • review and clear memory
  • check your quotas
  • create API keys
  • manage your personal MCP exposure
  • press the emergency stop, and lift it

docs.title: The main profile tabs
docs.text:
The current profile page is organized into:

  • Profile
  • Tool approvals, once an agent asks before running tools, or while you hold an approval of your own
  • Channels & Bots
  • Agent Accounts
  • Memory
  • Quotas
  • API Keys
  • MCP Endpoint

Looking for the runners tab?

Downloading the native app and managing your machines moved to the XTM One Desktop page: Get XTM One Desktop in your user menu. The old Profile > Runners address redirects there. See XTM One Desktop and runners.

docs.title: Profile tab
docs.text:
The Profile tab contains your personal account information.

You can usually review or update:

  • full name
  • title
  • time zone
  • theme
  • authentication method

Your email address is shown but not editable: the other Filigran platforms find your account by it, so an administrator changes it for you.

If you use SSO, the page shows that clearly so you know sign-in is handled by your identity provider.

Reply suggestions turns off the next-message suggestion the chat shows once an agent has answered (see Chat). It is on by default, and only works when your administrator has set a routing model.

docs.title: Password changes
docs.text:
If you use a local account, the Profile tab also includes a password change area.

If you sign in with SSO, password changes are usually managed outside XTM One by your identity provider.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text:
Right below the password area, the Profile tab lets you protect your account with a second factor: a six-digit code from an authenticator app, asked for every time you sign in — after your password, or after your identity provider if you use SSO.

To turn it on:

  1. Select Set up. A QR code appears.
  2. Scan it with your authenticator app — Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, KeePassXC, 1Password, Bitwarden, or any other. If you cannot scan (for example KeePassXC on a desktop), choose Enter the key manually and type the key it shows.
  3. Type the six-digit code your app displays and select Enable two-factor.

XTM One then shows 10 recovery codes.

Save your recovery codes now

This is the only time they can be displayed. Each one signs you in once, in place of your app, if you lose your phone. Nobody can retrieve them for you afterwards — not even an administrator.

Once enabled, signing in becomes two steps: your password, then the code. If your phone is not to hand, choose Use a recovery code on the code screen.

From the same area you can:

  • Generate new recovery codes — replaces your current set. Requires a code from your app.
  • Disable two-factor — requires both your password and a current code, so neither an unlocked browser nor your phone alone is enough to remove it.

If you lose both your device and your recovery codes, ask an administrator to reset your two-factor enrollment. Your account then signs in with your password alone until you set it up again on a new device.

Works with SSO too

If you sign in through an identity provider, you can still enable two-factor here. XTM One asks for the code after your provider signs you in, so the extra factor applies even when your organisation's identity provider does not enforce one. If your account has no XTM One password, disabling only asks for a code.

docs.title: General Assistant Tools
docs.text:
The Profile tab also contains your personal General Assistant tool overrides.

This is where you can review or override access to:

  • built-in tools
  • integrations
  • MCP servers
  • custom tools
  • knowledge bases

This matters when you want your own General Assistant experience to differ from the platform default.

You can also reset your personal choices back to the platform default.

docs.title: Tool approvals tab
docs.text: Tool approvals lists the tools you let run without asking you, and lets you take each approval back so the tool asks you again.
