Under Tools that ask first, you can always allow a tool for yourself before it ever asks you, and Allow every tool for me turns approvals off for you alone. Your choices never change what other people are asked. See Human approval of tool calls.

docs.title: Channels & Bots tab
docs.text:
Channels & Bots controls how your own chat routing works.

This tab currently lets you:

  • choose your default web chat agent
  • assign a different agent for your private conversations on supported channels
  • fall back to default routing when you do not want a personal override

If connected channel bots are available, you can set a different direct-message agent for each channel. Group-channel behavior remains governed by the shared admin routing, described in Channels and bots.

docs.title: Agent Accounts tab
docs.text: Agent Accounts is where you let an agent operate a real messaging account or mailbox: your own, as a delegate, or a dedicated service account, as an AI user. Each account names the integration signed in as that account, the agent that answers, and the rules for what it answers. See Agent accounts.

docs.title: Memory tab
docs.text:
Memory shows what XTM One remembers about you.

It is split into two main parts:

  • a Cross-Agent Profile shared across agents
  • per-agent memory for agents you have interacted with

The cross-agent profile holds only facts about you: your name and role, time zone, language, writing and signature preferences, and key contacts with their roles. Notes about an agent's work for you, such as a pull request on hold, a review pending, a mail-triage rule or an incident, belong to the agent whose work produced them. No other agent reads them. A note about something that can change is shown to its agent as unverified with the date it was written, and is dropped after 72 hours.

A profile saved before profiles and agent notes were kept apart is shown as Not reorganized yet. No agent reads it until it is split into your profile and each agent's notes. The split happens on its own in the background, or at your next exchanges with your agents.

From this tab you can:

  • review consolidated memory
  • inspect recent interactions
  • clear the cross-agent profile
  • clear memory for one specific agent, including the notes its work left in your profile
  • purge all your memory if you want a full reset

This is the best place to check when an agent seems to be remembering something you no longer want it to keep.

docs.title: Quotas tab
docs.text:
Quotas shows your personal usage against the limits that apply to your account.

In XTM One, this usually focuses on agentic executions. Some other deployments can also show additional quota types.

When your limit is the platform-wide pool of the license, the gauge shows the whole platform's usage against it, including requests with no account behind them (anonymous channel users, public chat widget visitors, calls made with the platform MCP key).

Use this tab to understand:

  • your current consumption
  • your limit period
  • whether the limit comes from a user rule, group rule, or platform default

docs.title: API Keys tab
docs.text:
API Keys lets you create personal keys for controlled programmatic access.

From this tab you can:

  • create a key: a name, and optionally its scopes, expiry and limits (see below)
  • copy it when it is first shown: it is never shown again
  • review your keys: each one shows its prefix, what it reaches (Full access, or its surfaces, Read-only and its agents), its expiry, its own limits with what it used of its quota this period, its request count and its last use
  • edit a key's name, scopes, expiry and limits with the pencil button
  • delete a key you no longer need: anything using it stops working at once

A key that expired, or that an administrator revoked, stays listed and marked as such until you delete it. A key created before an administrator set a maximum lifetime and outliving it is marked Beyond the maximum lifetime: it keeps working until you give it an expiry within the limit.

The page also shows the Platform API endpoint and basic usage guidance. In some non-XTM deployments, an additional LLM proxy section can appear.

A key acts as you: it can never do more than your account can, and what your account loses (a role, a share, the account itself) the key loses too. You can narrow it further.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
When you create a key, you choose:

  • Where it can be used: the REST API (/api/v1), the LLM proxy (/v1, Copilot deployments only) and the MCP endpoints (/mcp/user, /mcp/xtm, /mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq). A request on any other surface is refused with 403.

  • Read-only or read-write. A read-only key never changes anything:

    Surface A read-only key can It cannot REST API GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests any POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, including a POST that only searches LLM proxy list the models, call a model, count tokens run an agent (agent:<slug>), which acts with the agent's tools MCP endpoints connect, list tools and call the tools that only read call a tool that changes data; on /mcp/user every tool runs an agent, so it gets none

  • Optionally, a set of agents. The key then only reaches those agents: the agent:<slug> models of the LLM proxy, the tools of /mcp/user, and on the REST API the agent's own routes (/api/v1/agents/<id>/...) and the conversations with it. Everything else is refused: raw models, /mcp/xtm, the platform MCP servers and every other REST route.

A key created before scopes existed keeps working as it always did: every surface, read-write, every agent. Narrow it by editing it.

docs.title: Expiry
docs.text: A key can carry an expiry date; from that moment it is refused everywhere (401 API key expired). The dialog offers 7, 30 or 90 days or a year (90 days for a new key), Pick a date, and No expiry while no maximum lifetime is set; editing a key keeps its expiry unless you choose another. Your administrator may set a maximum lifetime: a key you create or re-date must then expire within it, and a key created without a date gets the longest one allowed. You are notified in the notification bell 7 days and 1 day before a key expires, and when an administrator revokes one; the notification opens this tab.

docs.title: Limits of its own
docs.text: A key can carry its own rate limit (requests per minute) and its own quota (requests per day or per month). They count every request the key makes on a surface it may use, on top of your own quotas, which keep applying. A key over its own limit is refused with 429 and a Retry-After header, while your other keys keep working.

docs.title: Keys made by a key
docs.text: A key can create or change keys through the API, but never one that reaches further than itself: more surfaces, read-write when it is read-only, more agents, a later expiry, or looser limits than its own are refused. A key with a rate limit or a quota of its own creates no key at all, since each new key would bring a fresh budget of its own; it can still edit keys within its limits.

docs.title: MCP Endpoint tab
docs.text:
MCP Endpoint is for users who want to connect external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude Desktop, and others) to XTM One.

From this tab you can:

  • copy your personal MCP endpoint URL
  • review the connection snippet
  • choose which agents are exposed
  • remove agents from that exposed list

If you do not choose a restricted list, the endpoint can default to all eligible visible agents.

The same tab also shows the Platform MCP Servers card (unless an administrator has disabled the feature). Each connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ platform gets its own native MCP server (/mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq) exposing its business tools, with the endpoint URL, live connection status, and a ready-to-copy client configuration; platforms that are not yet connected appear dimmed as Not connected until they are registered. See Platform MCP servers for the full guide.

When an administrator has enabled it, a Platform Tools MCP Server card appears too. It exposes XTM One's own tools on /mcp/xtm — agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, and variables — scoped to what you can already see and manage. It is how you read an agent's traces from Claude Desktop or Cursor and fix its configuration there. The card also offers a downloadable installer package for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and any Agent Plugins client — with One-click install on, the package already contains the endpoint URL and a freshly created API key, so there is nothing to configure (and the file is then a secret: delete it once installed). See Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: Emergency stop
docs.text:
Your profile menu — your name, top right — also holds the Emergency stop entry. It cancels every agentic activity that runs for you and pauses your assignments; an administrator can extend it to the whole platform. You confirm by typing a code shown in the dialog, and you are asked why right after.

Once a stop is in effect, the same menu offers Resume my activity (and, for an administrator, Resume the whole platform), and a red banner on every page offers Resume directly. See Emergency stop.

docs.title: What to change first
docs.text:
For most customer users, the most useful first changes are:

  • name and title
  • time zone
  • default chat agent
  • General Assistant tool preferences

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The Settings page explains where administrators manage shared platform behavior.

docs.title: Office add-in
docs.text: The Office add-in brings XTM One chat into Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook. It opens as a side panel next to your document or email: you pick an agent, ask about what you have open, and put the agent's reply into the document with one click.

docs.title: What the add-in does
docs.text:
• Chat with your agents from inside Office, with the same agents and the same conversations as the web app.
  • Send what you have open with each message: your selection and part of the document or email around it, so you do not have to copy and paste.
  • Run quick actions such as Summarize, Translate or Improve without writing a prompt.
  • Put a reply into the document: replace your selection, add the text to the document, or add it as a comment.

The add-in is part of the platform: there is nothing else to deploy. Your platform serves it at its own address followed by /office/.

Platforms served under a path prefix

The add-in only loads from a platform served at the root of its host. On a platform served under a path prefix it does not load. See Serving under a path prefix.

docs.title: Install the add-in
docs.text:
An administrator installs the add-in for the organization, or you install it for yourself to try it. Office installs an add-in from a manifest file, and the add-in has two:

Manifest Adds the button to manifest.prod.xml Word, Excel and PowerPoint manifest.outlook.xml Outlook

Both are in the apps/microsoft-office/manifest folder of the XTM One source code. The platform does not offer them for download.

  1. Open the manifest in a text editor and replace every COPILOT_URL with the address of your platform, for example https://xtm-one.example.com.
  2. Upload it to Office:
    • For the whole organization: in the Microsoft 365 admin center, Settings > Integrated apps, upload the manifest as a custom app. For Outlook, choose Deploy add-in, then Upload custom app with the manifest file, and assign it to the users or groups who need it.
    • For yourself, in Word on the web: Insert > Office Add-ins > Upload My Add-in.
    • For yourself, in Outlook on the web: the settings gear > Add-ins > My add-ins > Custom add-ins > Add a custom add-in > Add from file.

The button carries the name XTM One. To give it your platform's own name, the manifests can be generated again with that name: the README.md of the apps/microsoft-office folder explains how.

What the add-in loads

The add-in's panel loads Microsoft's Office library from Microsoft and its typefaces from Google Fonts. If your network or proxy filters outbound traffic, see Security headers for the sources it uses.

docs.title: Open the add-in
docs.text:
• Word, Excel and PowerPoint: select the XTM One button on the Home tab.
  • Outlook: the button appears in the ribbon when you read an email, when you write or reply to one, and when you organize a meeting.

The button is not in the ribbon

Office collapses add-in buttons when the window is narrow. Look in the overflow menu (...) at the right end of the ribbon. In Outlook, a newly deployed add-in can take a few minutes to appear and may need Outlook to restart.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
The panel shows your platform's name and Office Add-in. If the add-in finds a session of the web app it can reuse, it opens directly on the list of agents. Otherwise it asks you to sign in with your Email and Password, then Sign In.

The form takes an email and a password only. An account that uses two-factor authentication cannot sign in through it: the add-in says so.

To sign out, select the sign-out icon at the top right of the agent list.

docs.title: Choose an agent
docs.text:
After you sign in, the panel lists who you can talk to under Select an Agent:

  • The General Assistant, always first.
  • Recent: the agents you already have a conversation with in the add-in, marked Resume. Select one to pick up where you left off.
  • Every agent you can see: your own, the ones shared with you, and the company-managed ones, marked Shared. An agent that is disabled, or set not to chat, is not listed.

Type in Search agents... to filter the list by name or description. The refresh icon at the top reloads the list, and the sun or moon icon switches between the dark and the light theme.

docs.title: Chat about your document
docs.text:
Once you choose an agent, the panel opens its conversation. Type your question in Ask about your Word document... (the host's name changes with the application), then press Enter or the send button. Shift+Enter starts a new line.

  • When you have something selected, a strip above the messages shows the start of your selection, so you know what goes with your message.
  • + at the top starts a new conversation with the same agent.
  • The back arrow returns to the agent list. The next time you choose that agent, the add-in starts a new conversation.

The add-in's conversations are ordinary XTM One conversations. When the same conversation is open in the web app too, a message sent there shows up in the panel, and on a turn that several agents answer, each reply is labelled with the agent that wrote it, as in the web chat. See A conversation open in several places.

docs.title: What the agent receives
docs.text:
Each message carries what you have open, not the whole document:

Application What goes with your message Word Your selection, the beginning of the document, its headings, and its word and table counts Excel The selected cells, the first rows of the active sheet, and the names of the workbook's sheets PowerPoint Your selection and the number of slides Outlook The email's subject, sender and recipients, and the beginning of its body

In Word, a message that asks for a summary or about the whole document (for example "summarize this" or "review the entire document") sends the full text of the document instead. A long document is cut after its first 12,000 characters.

The context is part of your message

The panel shows only what you typed, but the message stored in the conversation holds this context too. When you open the conversation in the web app, or reopen it in the panel, you see your message with the document content that went with it.

docs.title: Quick actions
docs.text:
Select the sparkle icon at the left of the message box to open the quick actions. The first four also appear as buttons in an empty conversation. Each one sends a ready-made request about your selection or your document:

Application Quick actions Word Interpret, Summarize, Translate, Modify, Improve, Comment, Review Doc, Insert Table, Insert HTML Excel Interpret, Summarize, Translate, Modify, Formula, Comment, Insert Table PowerPoint Interpret, Summarize, Translate, Modify, Improve, Insert HTML Outlook Summarize, Interpret, Draft Reply, Improve, Translate

In Word, Interpret and Summarize work on the whole document when nothing is selected, and Review Doc asks the agent for review comments on the whole document, section by section.

docs.title: Put a reply into your document
docs.text:
Under each reply, buttons put it into what you have open:

Button Word Excel PowerPoint Outlook Replace Replaces your selection Writes into the selected cells, one line per row and tab-separated columns Replaces the selected text Replaces the whole body of the email you are writing Insert below Adds the text at the end of the document Changes nothing Adds a new slide with the text Inserts the text at your cursor in the email you are writing Comment Adds a comment on your selection, or on the first paragraph when nothing is selected Adds a comment on the selected cells Not shown Not shown

The × button dismisses the buttons. Once a reply is applied, it shows Applied to document.

The text goes in as plain text

The buttons insert the reply's text. Formatting in the reply, such as bold or a table, arrives as its raw characters, not as formatted content. In Outlook, the buttons only change an email you are writing, never one you are reading.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text: The add-in cannot show a tool approval. When an agent needs your approval before running a tool, it stops and explains why in its reply instead of acting. To allow the tool, or for how approvals work in clients such as this one, see Chat approvals in client applications.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see What to do Reconnecting... under the messages The add-in lost its connection and tries again on its own, up to three times. Connection lost — please refresh Close the panel and open it again. Not connected — please wait or refresh Wait a moment for the connection, then send your message again. Session expired Close the panel, open it again, and sign in. No agents available No agent you can see is enabled for chat, and the list, General Assistant included, stays empty. Ask an administrator to share an agent with you.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: To learn what you can do in the full chat, including files, workspaces and @mentions, see Chat.

docs.title: Platform insights
docs.text:
Platform insights is a built-in tool suite that lets an agent answer questions about the platform itself: what the AI costs, who uses it, what was created and when, how adoption evolves, who changed what. It reads the same figures as the administration pages - LLM Analytics, AI Adoption, Objects and the audit log - so what an agent tells you matches what those pages show.

Ask, for example:

  • "Graph the cost of AI agents for the group Customer Success over the last 90 days."
  • "What did each department spend on LLMs per month this year, and what should we budget for next year?"
  • "Top five agents of Engineering, and everyone outside our seven named departments."
  • "How many presentations were created each week since each release?"
  • "Which models cost the most this month, and how does it compare with last month?"
  • "Who deleted an agent last week?"
  • "What does this platform hold today?"

The answer comes with a chart drawn in the conversation when it helps, and with the warnings the dashboards show next to the same figures.

docs.title: Who can use it
docs.text:
The suite is one built-in tool, Platform insights, chosen in the Built-in Tools card of an agent's configuration.

  • Administrators read the whole platform: every user, group, agent and object.
  • Group managers read their team's LLM analytics as well: the usage of the current members of the groups they manage, administrators excepted, and those groups. Ask, for example, "List the agents my team used in the last 30 days with their cost". Everything else stays their own slice, traces and sessions included.
  • Anyone else reads their own slice only: the objects they own, the usage they generated, the groups they belong to, the audit entries of their own actions. Naming another person, or a group they are neither a member nor a manager of, is refused.

Every result says which of the three it served. When strict admin access for agent tools (access.agent_tools_strict_admin_access, see Settings) is on, an administrator's agent reads their own slice as well.

The General Assistant carries the suite by default for administrators (Settings > General Assistant lists it, and an administrator can remove it there). It is offered to group managers' General Assistant too, serving them their team's analytics, and not to other users'; an agent that carries it serves them their own slice.

All the tools read only. They never ask for approval, and the audit log tool records each of its own reads in the audit log (once per identical read every 15 minutes), so reading who did what leaves a trace of who looked.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text: Tool What it reads query_platform_analytics LLM usage - cost, tokens (input, output, cached), traces, errors, error rate, active users, duration, latency, feedback and cost per active user, per trace or per 1,000 tokens - as a total or per department, group, user, agent (with each agent's owner and status), model, source, day, week, month or release, split by a second dimension; with a projection, a comparison with the previous period, or as a CSV file query_platform_objects The objects of the platform - agents, assignments, runs, conversations, presentations, videos, reports, files, flows, fleets, workspaces, work items and more - listed, counted per type, or counted per day, week, month or release of their creation get_platform_release_history The builds the platform has run, with when each was first and last seen, and where the rollout of the newest stands. With no argument every recorded build comes back, oldest first; last_n (the newest N) and since (first seen at or after an ISO-8601 instant) answer newest first with a window naming what was served, and running_only answers the running build, its first boot, the previous release and the rollout alone query_ai_adoption The AI Adoption dashboard (agentic AI on this platform): the overview (active users, top users) and the adoption gaps (inactive and low-activity people, monthly adoption rate) list_platform_traces The Traces page as rows: when, which agent, model and user, source, status, failure cause, duration, tokens, cost and the start of the error message, filtered by period, users, groups, agents, models, sources, status and text, sorted like the page and 100 at most per call. A row says what a trace is, never what it holds. A run that stored its rollup when it closed carries it (numbers only: wall, model, tool and wait time in ms, iterations, tool calls and errors, input, output and cache tokens, tool result size), and the page adds rollup_percentiles: the p50 and p90 of each figure over its rows list_platform_sessions The Sessions page as rows: each conversation with its user, first and last activity, traces, errors, agents, models, tokens and cost, with the same filters query_audit_log Audit entries filtered by actor, action, entity, period and text, 200 at most per call get_platform_overview What the platform holds today: its identity (instance: the Instance ID of Settings > Parameters, PLATFORM_ID when forced, the platform name and its URL, answered to every caller), objects per type, agents by state, assignments by trigger, integrations by provider, knowledge base chunks, machines online, the sandbox pods per image key with how many are running, creating or pulling their image (sandbox_pods_by_image_key, administrators only), file storage (in total and per file source in files_by_source: agent_check, video_take, agent_working, chat...), the deployed build, the feature flags on, trace retention and whether the analytics aggregation is fresh query_platform_metrics The backend's own Prometheus series (the xtmone_* families the /metrics endpoint exports): a counter or gauge as one row per label set, a histogram as count, sum, mean and p50 / p95 estimated from its buckets. Administrators only; see Platform metrics query_platform_frictions The friction ledger counted: what agent runs struggled with (tool errors, retries, approval pauses, sandbox and runner failures, resumed turns, frictions an agent recorded itself) and whether each was disposed of. Totals over the window (recorded, occurrences with repeats, undisposed), and the same per agent, kind, class, tool or disposition and / or per day, week or month, as rows render_chart draws render_chart Draws the rows another tool returned as a chart in the answer

docs.title: Platform AI settings
docs.text:
Administrators also get get_platform_ai_settings (a read) and update_platform_ai_settings (a write, gated like any other for an agent that asks before running tools). They cover the settings that bound every agent run: the wait policy, the default reasoning effort, the default chat model and its provider, and the two switches of Settings > Access and security > Tool approvals:

  • tool_approvals_enabled: false suspends every tool approval platform-wide (Suspend all approvals), true resumes;
  • approve_tool_calls_default: whether an agent that follows the platform default asks before running tools (Every agent asks by default).

Both take true or false (null leaves them as they are), are refused with the 403 sentence for anyone who is not an administrator, and are audited exactly as the Settings page does, marked via: update_platform_ai_settings. The read reports them under tool_approvals, with env_seed, the TOOL_APPROVALS_ENABLED value as deployed (read once when the settings row is created). Every switch an administrator changes in the UI there is readable and writable by these tools.

docs.title: The default chat model and provider
docs.text:
The read reports the default under default_model: agent_default_model, agent_default_provider, agent_default_provider_id, env_locked (whether DEFAULT_MODEL pins it) and serving_providers, the configured providers that list the default model, the current one flagged current. An agent watching the providers moves the default with update_platform_ai_settings and agent_default_provider (an id of serving_providers, or a provider key that names one of them), and optionally agent_default_model, in a call of their own. The write goes through the handler of Settings > AI and models > Models: the same validation, the same audit entry (model_defaults_changed, each value before and after) and the same announcement rules. It is refused with its reason, nothing written, for a provider that is not configured, a provider that does not serve the model, a default pinned by DEFAULT_MODEL (the refusal names it) or a person who is not an administrator. The answer is the setting read back after the write, with changed naming each value before and after.

Every default of Settings > AI and models > Models is read under default_routes: agent_default, routing, fallback, decision, image and embedding, each with provider_id, provider, model and env_managed (the embedding route also with dimensions). update_platform_ai_settings with default_routes moves any of them in a call of its own, for example {"routing": {"provider": "bedrock"}}: a provider by id or key, an optional model (the current one by default). The checks are those of the Settings page: the provider must be configured and list the model; the embedding route changes provider only (same model and dimensions, so nothing is re-embedded); a route an environment variable pins is refused with the variable named. One refused route writes none of the others. The write goes through the Settings page handler (its audit entry with the values before and after), plus an entry naming the agent run.

Whenever a default route changes provider or model, the platform raises platform.default_model_route.changed, once per route, whatever made the change: settings_page, agent_tool, provider_deleted, env_provider_prune or system. The payload carries route, before and after (provider_id, provider, model), cause and actor_user_id, and no credential. A save that changes nothing raises nothing. The event is platform-wide, so an assignment with a platform_event trigger on it (filter keys route, cause, after.provider and the others list_platform_events names) runs once per change, with no need to poll get_platform_ai_settings.

docs.title: Purging working storage
docs.text:
Administrators also get purge_platform_storage, a write that asks for approval like any other. It applies the storage retention now instead of waiting for the hourly sweeps, with an age threshold older_than_days (0: everything older than one hour; the last hour is never touched):

  • agent_check: the check files agents made to look at their own work (frames, contact sheets, insert crops, screenshots);
  • unused_recording and unused_shot: the media of ready Video Studio recordings and AI shots no video uses (video, keyframes, poster, contact sheet, frames). The library entry stays, marked expired, as with the regular expiry;
  • figure_stills: the editor's figure stills, drawn again by the next preview that needs one.

It never deletes a file a video needs, a recording or shot a video's timeline names or marked Keep its media, nor a video's renders, posters and captions. dry_run is true by default and only counts the files and bytes per category: run it first, then again with dry_run: false. Each call handles at most limit items per category (5,000 by default); more: true says another call finds the rest. A real purge is written to the audit log.

docs.title: Reading the figures right
docs.text:
The agent repeats the warnings that come with a figure. They are the same ones the dashboards show:

  • Departments never overlap; groups do. A person counts for one department, so department rows add up to the platform total. Groups are current membership: a trace counts for the groups its user belongs to today, and a person in several groups counts in each of them, so group totals can add up to more than the platform total. Ask for org units only to leave access and distribution lists out.
  • Unattributed and ungrouped usage. Usage nobody is behind - the platform's own calls, or a run whose agent was deleted since - and people in no group are reported apart, never dropped.
  • Missing prices. Usage of a model with no price has no cost, and every cost total leaves it out. The result names those models; set their price in Settings > Observability > Model pricing.
  • Stale aggregation. When the daily analytics aggregation has not run for more than 48 hours, older days may still move once it catches up.
  • Coverage start. A window that reaches further back than the oldest data the platform still holds is flagged: the missing days are missing data, not zero activity. The daily aggregates outlive the trace retention, so a monthly series reaches further back than the traces.
  • Hidden costs. When cost data is hidden on the platform, every cost is reported as unavailable, never as zero, and no chart is drawn of it.
  • Partial buckets. The first and last week or month of a window cover only the part of it inside the window, and are flagged.

Every metric has every breakdown and every split, except latency (the median), which is computed as a total, per model and per day; duration, the average, has them all. A request outside that is refused with the nearest one that is computed.

docs.title: Who the usage counts for
docs.text:
Many traces have no user of their own: an assignment run, a sub-agent consulted by another agent, a webhook, a message on a channel. Their usage counts for the person behind them, in this order:

  1. the trace's own user;
  2. for an assignment run, the person who triggered it, else the identity it runs as, else the assignment's owner;
  3. for a sub-agent or a background copy, the person its parent trace counts for;
  4. the owner of its conversation;
  5. the owner of its agent, for a webhook or a channel bot.

What none of them names is reported apart, by reason: the platform's own calls, a conversation with nobody behind it, or an agent or run deleted since. Ask for the traces' own users instead ("raw attribution") to read usage the way the Traces page does.

docs.title: Departments
docs.text:
Departments are the org units an administrator sets in Settings > Observability > Departments (see Monitoring). A person's department is the one their identity provider sends as their directory department, else the first group rule they match, else Unassigned. It is recorded with the usage when it happens: a person who changes team brings no past usage with them.

A read can name departments, groups and people together, leave some out, or ask for everyone outside the ones named - "everyone but the seven named departments" is the Others bucket.

docs.title: Budgeting
docs.text:
• Per head. Active users counts the distinct people with usage in a bucket; cost per active user, per trace and per 1,000 tokens are computed per row.
  • Projection. A monthly series can be projected up to 36 months ahead with a linear trend, a compound monthly growth rate or the average of the last months. The fit uses complete months only - the current month is shown as its run rate so far - and says how well it reads the past (R² and mean percentage error).
  • Comparison. Any breakdown can be compared with the previous period of the same length, row by row.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text: Any read can be exported as a CSV file of every row, every metric as a column, without the bounds of a chart. The agent attaches the file to its answer. Administrators can also download the same CSV from GET /api/v1/insights/analytics/export, with the tool's arguments as query parameters, for a spreadsheet or a data warehouse load.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
The platform records each build it boots with - the version shown in the About dialog and its commit - and when it was first and last seen. A count or a cost can then be cut per release: a release is the deployed one from its first boot until the next build's.

The history starts at the first boot of a release that records it; nothing before it is backfilled. Whatever predates it is counted under before_release_history, and the agent says so. Analytics are kept per day, so a day on which a new build was first seen counts for that build.

The release history and the overview also say where the rollout of the newest build stands, so "is this fix deployed" is answered from the platform rather than from the deploy pipeline: in progress (a newer build booted and recorded itself while the pod answering still runs the previous one: its commit and the time its first pod booted are given), draining (the newest build answers, but the previous one was still seen minutes ago and may still be serving), complete, or rolled back (the newest recorded build has not been seen for a while and an older one answers). A deploy is known from the first boot of one of its pods: before that, nothing is recorded and the previous build is the deployed one.

docs.title: Platform metrics
docs.text:
query_platform_metrics reads the series the backend exports to Prometheus, which the deployment scrapes inside the cluster, so an administrator's agent can check them without access to that scrape: the sandbox container create times (xtmone_sandbox_create_seconds), the tasks a rollout orphaned (xtmone_tasks_orphaned_total, per build) and the resumed runs (xtmone_run_resumes_total, per entry, cause, graceful and build), the assignment queue gauges and every other xtmone_* series.

  • Called without series, it lists the series it serves with their type and how many label sets each has.
  • labels keeps only the rows whose labels equal the values given, for example {"version": "f474aac6"}.
  • Only xtmone_* series are served. Any other name, and any PromQL expression, is refused by name.
  • The view is process-local: the values of the one backend worker that answered, since it started. Other workers and pods keep their own counts and a restart starts them from zero, so the figures are a sample, not the cluster-wide total. The result names the host, process and build that answered (view) and says so in its caveats.
  • Histogram percentiles are estimated from the buckets, the way Prometheus histogram_quantile does.
  • A caller who is not an administrator gets their scope and no series.

docs.title: Charts in the conversation
docs.text:
render_chart turns query rows into a bar, stacked bar, line, area, pie or donut chart drawn in the answer, with its title and a caption. A chart holds at most 16 categories and 6 series - the same bounds as a chart in a presentation - so a 90-day window is charted per week or per month.

A chart never invents a figure: a hidden cost, or a missing value of an average, refuses the chart instead of drawing a zero.

When the conversation is exported (the chat menu's Export as Markdown and Export as PDF), or when the answer is delivered to Slack or Teams, each chart is written as a table of its values.

docs.title: Presentations
docs.text:
For a written document rather than slides, ask for a report.

A presentation is a slide deck your assistant builds for you, in a conversation, from a plain-language request. It renders right inside the chat, plays like a real deck (keyboard, touch, fullscreen, speaker notes), stays editable by asking for changes, and exports to PDF and PowerPoint that look exactly like the slides on screen.

Every deck you can see is listed under Work > Presentations in the sidebar — your own, the ones colleagues shared with you, and the ones published to the whole company. The Work group is where what your agents produce lives: their runs under Operations, their decks here, and every other file they output or you gave them under Files.

docs.title: Create a deck
docs.text:
Ask any assistant that can generate presentations — the General Assistant, or an agent with the presentation tool enabled — for slides, in your own words:

Create a 10-slide all-hands deck for Q3: highlights, the three numbers that matter, the roadmap for Q4, and a closing slide with my contact details.

The assistant composes the slides, and the deck appears in the conversation as an interactive card. When several templates are available to you and your request does not name one, the assistant first asks which template to use (see Template and theme). You can also start from the Presentations page: New presentation lets you pick the template and the theme, then opens the chat with the beginning of a request already typed for you.

Brief it like a designer

A good brief names the audience, the one message to remember, and the numbers you want on screen. The assistant chooses the slide compositions — a two-column comparison, a wall of key figures, a before/after, a diagram with an explanation, a roadmap, a takeaways slide — and keeps each slide readable from the back of the room. Ask for a short outline first when the deck is long, then let it build the whole thing in one pass.

Start from the last edition

For a deck you make again and again — the quarterly update, the monthly report — ask the assistant to copy the last one: "copy Quarterly Review, Q3 2026 as Quarterly Review, Q4 2026, then update the numbers". The copy keeps the template, the theme, the slide size, the header and footer settings and every slide with its speaker notes, so the new edition starts from the approved layout rather than from a fresh draft, and a footer that shows the deck's title shows the new one. The copy is yours: it is shared with nobody, starts with no comments, and the original is not changed. Any deck you can open can be copied this way, one shared with you as Can view or published to the company included. The assistant then changes only what differs, slide by slide (see Change a deck). When you no longer need a copy, ask the assistant to delete it ("delete My draft of the Q4 review"): it deletes a deck only when you ask, and only one you own - a deck shared with you, even as Can edit, stays as it is. Deleting is final: there is no trash to restore from, and the deck's history, comments, sharing and public link go with it, exactly as with Delete on the Presentations page.

Slides can carry text, bullet and check lists, callouts, key figures, tables, feature grids, timelines, process flows, numbered cards, quotes, images (a product screenshot can wear a browser window, a slim browser window with a thinner bar for several screenshots side by side, or a device frame, on a glow in the brand colours), a challenge-and-answer pair (two stacked cards joined by an arrow), logo grids, native charts, org charts, and diagrams drawn from a text description (flowcharts, sequences, mind maps). The assistant can highlight a word or a phrase with bold, emphasis, code style, or a colored tone — for example an accent to point at the one thing that matters, or success / warning / error for a verdict.

Architecture and ecosystem diagrams

Ask for "an architecture diagram of the platform", "how the modules feed each other" or "the ecosystem around the product" and the assistant draws a native diagram in the deck's own palette and fonts: product logos from the template inside the boxes, labeled arrows between them ("Threat data", "Findings"), a highlighted core the rest runs on, a band across the top for a portal or a marketplace, a titled panel around the modules of a platform, and a legend. A box or a panel can also wear a colour of the template's palette — on the brand decks, the product colours: XTM One purple, OpenCTI blue, OpenAEV orange, OpenCRQ blue — as its border, a tint of its body, its icon and the chips inside it (ask for "each product in its own colour"); the colour follows the slide's theme, dark or light, and the PowerPoint exports carry it as shown. The arrows are routed so they never run through a box - when the two plain elbows between two boxes are both blocked, the arrow takes the free lane between the rows or the columns - an exchange in both directions runs as two parallel lines that do not cross, every arrow lands on the middle of a side (the plain ties from a highlighted core fan out onto the middle of each box's top edge), and a label never sits on a box or on another label: it slides along its arrow, or beside it, to a clear spot. The drawing is never blown up to fill the slide - a diagram on three columns keeps the same box and type sizes as one on five - and a diagram a little too tall for its place closes its rows up before anything is made smaller. A box that only gives context (a "ghost") can carry its icon inline before its label (icon_tile: false) so its label stays centred and two such boxes on one row line up. A panel can be headed by the platform's own logo from the template, in its top-left corner, with or without its title after it (ask for "the platform's logo on the panel"), and by a row of up to six small pills on the same line - the platform's capabilities, in its top-right corner by default, or right after the logo and title - which takes no room from the boxes inside the panel (ask for "the platform's capabilities in the panel's corner"). The template's own mark or logo placed in a box, a panel, an image or a row of logos reads exactly as it does in the slide's corner: in the slide's accent on a light slide and its light colour on a dark one, so a white mark is never lost on a pale slide; and the layout check names any logo painted at under 1.5:1 contrast against what is under it; the pills are never wrapped onto a second line, and when a row is too long for its panel the layout check says so and names the panel. A logo or a row of capabilities can also sit bare inside a panel, with no box around it (frame: false); the arrows to it end on the logo or the words themselves. An arrow can be told which side of a box it leaves and enters (source_side / target_side: top, right, bottom or left) - ask for "the request out of the left of the core into the top of the product, and the answer back the same way" and the two are drawn as two squared, parallel paths - and the router keeps that side even when it faces away, bending around the box. Two arrows between the same two boxes, one each way, are drawn as two parallel lines at the same height on both boxes, flat when the boxes sit on one row; lane: 1 and lane: 2 say which one runs on top. An arrow can also end on a panel's border instead of on a box (target: "zone:platform", the panel carrying the id platform) - context feeding the whole platform - with its head on the border and no hidden box taking a row inside the panel. In the live deck the diagram is interactive: hover or focus a box to light up what it connects to, click it to read the detail the assistant wrote for it, Escape to release. Everything is vector — the PDF export stays sharp at any size.

Org charts

Ask for "the leadership team", "the engineering org with its headcount" or "the hiring plan for next year" and the assistant draws a native org chart: every seat says who it reports to, and the deck lays the tree out itself - one line of cards per level, every card of a level as wide and as tall as the others, each manager centred over their reports and joined to them by one line along the gap, and a secondary manager drawn as a dashed line routed around the cards. Each kind of seat looks the same on every slide: a person (their photo from the template's people photos, or their initials, the name on one line and the role under it), an open seat (dashed, in the warning colour, marked Open role, with its target date), a planned hire (in the accent colour, with the period it is planned for - "+3 Platform engineers" for three of them), a team drawn as one card with its headcount, a team drawn as a bubble whose area is its headcount, and an external seat (a contractor, a partner or an agency, muted with a dotted outline). Ask for "the headcount under each manager" and every manager carries the roll-up the chart computes from the tree - people count one, teams their headcount, open and planned seats apart ("14 · +3 open · +4 planned") - or today against the target ("14 → 47"). Other looks: left to right, a leadership wheel around the root, compact cards, everything as bubbles, or cards over bubbles (the people as cards, their teams as bubbles under them), one tinted zone per branch, and a legend of the kinds drawn. A large organisation folds: from a level you choose, a manager's reports become one card with their count, or only the first levels are drawn; when a level is wider than the slide its last level stacks into a column under one line, and a chart that would still need type too small to read is refused with a notice rather than shrunk - the layout check then tells the assistant to fold teams or draw them as bubbles. In the live deck, hover or focus a seat to read its whole team's headcount, its tags, its note and its dotted managers; click a folded team (or press Enter) to open it in place - the deck itself does not change; the arrow keys walk the tree. The PowerPoint export (editable shapes) carries the chart as native shapes - each seat a group of its card or circle, its words as text - and its lines as connectors, so it can be edited in PowerPoint; the PDF stays vector. In a video, an org chart is built level by level (see Video Studio).

Positioning maps

Ask for "a competitive landscape", "where the vendors sit on coverage and openness" or "a 2x2 of the options" and the assistant draws a native positioning map: two real axes with arrowheads, each with its title and the meaning of both ends ("Single stage" to "Whole loop"), crossing at the centre or running along the left and bottom edges, four named quadrants over a faint tint, and every item placed at its own position on both axes (0 to 100), anywhere on the plane rather than snapped to a cell. Every vendor mark is drawn at one size in a small square, its plain name beside it; the item the slide is about is larger, in the template's accent; context items can be dimmed. Names are moved to a free side of their mark so they never cover another name; when no side is free, the layout check names the crowded items. Up to four short callouts under or beside the map say why the highlighted item sits where it does, and each item can carry a one-sentence note shown on hover. Two maps fit side by side on one slide, same top and same height, and the editable PowerPoint export writes the axes, tints, marks and names as shapes.

Charts and dashboard slides

Give the assistant the numbers — "ARR by quarter for the last eight quarters", "the share of Community versus Enterprise", "trials against a target of 150" — and it draws a native chart in the deck's own palette and fonts: bar, stacked bar, line, area, pie, donut, a gauge against a target, a bar and line combined, a waterfall for a bridge, or a butterfly - two groups compared rung by rung, such as individual contributors and managers per seniority level, the first drawn to the left of a central spine and the second to the right, every number written as a plain size with no minus sign, a level one group does not have (a 0) left empty on its side - no bar and no number, the level names on the spine (or on the left axis), and each side's total under the legend if you ask for it; or a world map coloured by country (see "Maps by country" below). Values read the way a board expects (€16.5M, 86%, thousands separators in your language) and are written on the figure: a small upright label just above each bar of a grouped bar chart, as on a dashboard card — set smaller where it would touch its neighbour, and turned on its side only when even the smallest size would — and, on a stacked bar, inside each segment that has room for it, with the stack's total above - or, on a horizontal bar chart, just past the end of each bar, where the chart keeps room for the widest total so a 100% on a chart of shares is never cut by its frame. A segment too thin for its number - a series worth a few percent of each stack - writes it just past the stack instead, after the total: a small figure in the series' colour, tied to its segment by a short line, several of them stacked neatly when one bar has more than one; the PowerPoint export draws them in the same place. Ask for smaller or larger chart text ("label size sm", as on a Metabase card; "lg" for a figure read from the back of the room): the values and the axis text follow, in the viewer and in the exports. To size the numbers apart from the axis text, ask for a value size - one of those text sizes, or a size in pixels from 10 to 32 ("values at 20px", two under the slide's 22) - and only the numbers on the bars, points and stacks change, set smaller from there if they must; the axis text keeps its size, in the PowerPoint export too. In the editor this is Value text size on the chart. When the values of a bar, stacked bar or combined chart are wider than the room between two bars - two series over seven quarters in half a slide - you choose what they do instead of being set smaller or turned: ask for them on two rows ("stagger the values") and every value keeps its size, upright, just above its bar - only a value that would touch the one beside it moves a row higher, and on a chart that combines bars and a line, a value the line would run through moves above the line, so no number is crossed out by it; or ask to keep them upright, and every value keeps its size in its place: a value that would touch its neighbour or the line moves just one row higher when that row is free, without moving any bar, and one that would still touch something there is left out, which the layout check reports. Either way the bars stand a little further apart, or narrow a little, to make room - except the bars of a grouped bar chart, which keep the tight groups they always have, so each period still reads as one group: there a value wider than its bar runs over the gap and the bar beside it, its halo keeping it legible on that bar, and only another value moves it a row higher or leaves it out. The PowerPoint export spaces its bars the same way. A horizontal bar or stacked bar chart takes the same choice: staggered, every value keeps its text size - one that would touch the value in the next row moves along its row just past it, and a segment's number too long for its segment is written past the stack, after the total, at the same size and tied to its segment by a short line - so two share charts on one slide read at one size; kept upright, a value that would touch another, or that its segment cannot hold, is left out, which the layout check reports. In the editor this is Value labels on the chart. On a pie or a donut each value sits just outside its slice, at the end of a short line, and the pie leaves exactly the room its values need, so a value is never cut by the card or written over the legend: in a narrow panel the pie is drawn a little smaller, and the values are set smaller only when the pie would otherwise shrink too far. When even the smallest size leaves no room outside - a pie squeezed beside a long legend - the values are written inside the slices large enough to hold them, in a colour that reads on each slice, and a slice too small keeps its number in the tooltip. The PowerPoint export writes the values at the same size and on the same side of each slice. Values turned on their side are reported by the layout check (values rotated on chart 2) so the assistant can put them on two rows, pick a smaller text size or a wider column; so are a pie's values set smaller than its text size (values shrunk on chart 2), so the assistant can move the legend under the chart or give it a wider column. Should a chart have truly no room for its numbers, the layout check says so (values hidden on chart 2) so the assistant gives it more room or fewer series; values are never dropped without a word. For a stacked chart it only suggests a taller or wider chart when that would actually bring the numbers back; when no size would, it says so and suggests leaving that series' numbers to the tooltip, or leaving the chart as it is - the totals are written either way. Figures are as precise as they need to be: a value under 10 keeps two significant digits (0.96x, 1.4h), and two different values never read the same (1.57x and 1.56x, not 1.5x twice). When a slide states its figures to a given precision, ask for it - "two decimals on the burn multiple" - and every value read against that axis, its ticks and tooltips included, is written with exactly that many decimals (1.27x, €19.14M), in the exports too. By default each amount takes its own unit, so one chart can read €480k next to €1.2M; ask for one unit - "all in millions", or thousands, or billions - and every amount on the chart, its ticks, tooltips and target included, is written in it with the chart's decimals (€0.25M next to €2.50M, an amount too small for the unit reading €0.00M rather than disappearing), in the exports too. Pies, donuts and gauges keep their own amounts. A gauge stands in the middle of its card or dashboard panel, its dial filling the start of its track and rounded at the value; ask for a small, medium or large one ("size sm", md by default, lg: a dial 240, 360 or 480 px across, in a dashboard panel too), or for one that fills its room ("fill"), and the dial grows as far as the room allows without cutting its number or its target label - in the PowerPoint export too, where the gauge is a picture of the figure. A line drawn over bars writes its values as well - each next to its point, over it or under it, on the bar with a white halo where the point falls in one, never on an axis label or one number over another: a value set too close to another moves just clear of it, and a line's first value slides clear of the axis beside it. A line or an area whose values would run into one another in a single row - eight quarters in a one-third dashboard panel - writes them alternately above and below the points, at the largest size that gives each value two points' room, before it sets them smaller or leaves any out; the PowerPoint export places them the same way. A chart where nothing touches is drawn exactly as before. To part a line from the bars on purpose, ask for an axis range - "make the left axis go up to €60M", "start the right axis at -€5M" - or set Axis maximum / Right axis minimum in the editor; the range always keeps zero and every value of its axis. To leave one series' numbers to the tooltip, ask for it ("no values on the burn bars", or on the small series of a stacked chart, whose stack totals still count it). A target shows as a dashed reference line named in the legend, and the chart follows the theme when you switch it between dark and light. The legend sits above the plot - on the panel's title row in a dashboard, beside a chart's own title - unless you say otherwise: ask for "the legend under the chart" (or set Legend position to Bottom in the editor) when a narrow panel's entries would otherwise wrap beside the title, and it moves to one centred line under the axis with the plot taking the room; Right stacks the entries beside the plot, the natural place for a donut's slices. The PowerPoint export puts the legend on the same side. A chart stands on a card — the deck's card surface and a fine border, like the key figures beside it and the panels of a dashboard — with its legend and caption inside; ask for a chart "without its card" (or turn Framed off in the editor) to draw it straight on the slide. Give a chart a title ("title it Monthly signups", or the Title field in the editor) and it is written at the top of the card, as a dashboard panel titles its chart, with the legend on the same row; the caption stays the note under the plot. Two by two charts on a slide, each titled and asked to fill its space, take their cards to the bottom; a chart in a dashboard panel is titled by the panel, which refuses a second title. The card is there from the first frame and stays while the bars grow in, and the editable PowerPoint carries it as a plain shape under the chart. Two units can share one chart — new logos as bars next to the average sales price as a line, or burn in millions next to the burn multiple: the second series reads against an axis on the right, written in its own unit (€300k, 1.5x) and drawn in that series' colour, with a target line of its own if you give one. In the live deck a chart is interactive: hover a bar or a point for its exact value, click a legend entry to hide or show a series. A chart asked to fill its space — on its own, under a heading in one of two columns, or inside a card that fills its column — takes the height left once the blocks around it are placed, and never less than a readable plot: when there is not even that, the layout check reports the chart as too short, so the assistant trims what surrounds it. A waterfall shows a bridge — "the ARR bridge from Q2 to Q3: opening, new logos, expansion, churn, ending": the opening and ending stand on the axis, each change floats from where the previous one left the total — rises in green, falls in red — and dashed lines carry the level from bar to bar. The platform adds the bars up: an ending that does not equal the opening plus the changes (beyond half a percent of what the changes moved, the slack of rounded figures) is refused with the gap named — "ending €19.14M vs running sum €19.2M, gap €0.06M" — so the assistant corrects the figure that is wrong. When the gap is real, ask for it to be shown: it is drawn as its own Unexplained bar before the total instead of being hidden in it. For a slide that reproduces a dashboard, ask for a dashboard slide: a row of key figures across the top — each can carry a small trend line beside its value — and up to six panels of charts, tables or figures on a grid below, sized to fit the slide without shrinking. Two panels can also share the grid half and half - a chart beside a table: ask for "two equal columns" (in the editor, Panel columns set to 2 on the slide) and they sit side by side at the same width, up to four panels on the slide; the PDF and PowerPoint exports draw the same two columns. When five or six key figures each carry a long comparison under them ("Q3 25 EUR 4.5M · Q2 EUR 6.7M"), ask for small tiles (or set Tile size to Small on the slide in the editor): the figures and their notes are set smaller so each note stays on one line, and the panels below get the room back, in the PDF and PowerPoint exports too. A row of key figures on a content slide comes in three sizes — small, medium (the default) and large — and a size reads the same on every slide: when a slide holds more than fits and is shrunk to fit, what surrounds the row shrinks, not the figures, so a KPI row repeated across a deck keeps the same size from one slide to the next, in the PDF and PowerPoint exports too. Only a slide too full to fit even that way shrinks its figures as well, and the layout check says so. A key figure's change is green when it rises and red when it falls, unless you say which way is good news: when lower is better - a loss, a burn, churn, costs - the assistant shows a fall in green with its arrow still pointing down ("-18.4% QoQ"), and a rise in red. In the editor, Delta tone sets that colour on a figure by hand, and the PDF and both PowerPoint exports show the same colours.

Maps by country

Ask for "customers by country" or "headcount per country" and the assistant draws a world map (a choropleth): each country with a figure is coloured on a ramp of the template's chart colour, from a light wash for the lowest figure to the full colour for the highest, and the countries without one stay in the muted surface colour, in the dark and the light theme alike. The countries are named by their two-letter ISO 3166-1 code (FR, US, GB); a code that is not one — UK for the United Kingdom, a country name — is refused with its position named, so the assistant corrects it before the deck is saved. Hover a country to read its name, in your language, and its figure; with values shown, the figure is also written inside every country large enough to hold it, as large as the country allows, and a country too small to see (Singapore, Malta) gets a dot in its colour. The legend is the ramp itself, with the lowest and the highest figure. Ask for a stepped legend instead and the figures are grouped into at most five classes, cut where they naturally part (or into the number of classes you ask for, from two to seven): each class is one flat shade of the same colour, every country takes the shade of its class, and the legend lists the classes beside the map, a dot and a range each — 43 for a class of one figure, 12 - 39 for a range, 120 + for the top class. Ask for no dots and the small countries keep their colour only, however tiny that is at the map's scale; a territory with no shape of its own on the map (Réunion, French Guiana) keeps its dot, so its figure is never lost. In the editor, the Map legend, Map classes and Small-country markers controls set the same. To zoom, ask for the map of Europe, the Americas or Asia-Pacific: the neighbouring countries are still drawn at the edges, and the layout check names a country that falls outside the region. A map takes a title, a caption, a frame, the full height of its slide and the text sizes like any chart, on a content slide or in a dashboard panel. In the PDF it is vector, like every chart; in the editable PowerPoint it is a high-resolution picture of the map, its title, caption and legend written as text beside it — PowerPoint's own map chart only opens in Office with an internet connection, so it is not used.

Agenda slides

A short agenda is a numbered list — one column up to four items, two columns up to six. From seven items the assistant lays it out as a board-deck grid: three columns of N. | TITLE cells, each with a one-line description under the title, so a long agenda still reads from the back of the room. The grid holds six to nine items — two to three full rows — and past nine the agenda returns to a two-column list rather than shrinking. Ask for "the agenda as a grid" or "as a list" to choose the look yourself, or "in three columns" to get the grid from six items; a description on any one item reserves that line on every cell, so the board stays even.

Logo walls

Ask for "our customers by sector" or "a logo wall of our partners" and the assistant groups the logos into equal cards — one per sector or category, its title and icon on one line — that fill the slide, each card's logos spread across its full width. Every logo is sized by its visible mark, not by its file: the transparent margin a logo was exported with is cropped away, so "small", "medium", "large" and "extra large" (28 / 40 / 56 / 72 px on the slide) are the height you actually see, and a round seal is drawn a little taller than a long wordmark so both carry the same weight. A logo row that is too narrow shrinks all its logos together, never one alone. Ask for the logos in one colour (the slide's text colour, or a muted grey) for a quiet "trusted by" band — it is also how white brand logos stay visible on a light slide; hovering a logo in the live deck shows its original colours. Labels under the logos are off unless you ask for them. Boxes of text follow the same idea: ask for "a card" instead of a tinted panel, with the icon on the title line and the content using the full width.

Formulas and configuration cards

Ask for "core + modules + capacity = one license" and the assistant draws a formula: two to five cards joined by +, =, - or x, each with an icon, a logo or a row of logos, a title and a subtitle, and a coloured bar on its top edge; the last card can be the result, drawn in the deck's brand gradient with white text. Under it, configuration cards show two to four example setups side by side: each card stacks up to six rows, a logo or a name on the left and a status chip on the right (for example Included or Enterprise Edition); a row that is available but not used is greyed, its chip dashed. Cards are centred by default and a product wordmark can stand alone as a card's name. Configuration cards can carry a heading with a rule over them ("Example configurations"), frame each row, line their chips up at the right and close each card with a tinted band (for example Agentic capacity on the left, Included allowance on the right). Both follow the theme in light and dark, and both export to PowerPoint as native shapes and text you can edit, the result card keeping its gradient.

Customer quotes

Ask for "a customer quote slide" or "the customer's quote as a statement" and the assistant makes the quote the slide itself: large and bold, centred on the slide, with an oversized quote mark in the deck's accent colour, the speaker's name, role and company underneath and, when you give them, two to four facts about the customer ("Employees 80K", "Revenue $30B") as figures in the accent colour. A quote can also sit beside other content as a pull quote with a large accent rule, or be a testimonial card with the speaker's portrait or the company logo. In the editor, a selected quote offers its four looks as thumbnails, the size (up to the size of a title-slide headline), the alignment, the quote marks, the portrait and the logo picked from the deck's template, and the figures. Key figures anywhere on a slide can drop their card the same way (the plain variant of a metric), so a row of numbers sits under a paragraph without turning into boxes.

Funding rounds and partner logos

Ask for "our funding rounds with the lead investors' logos" and the assistant draws a timeline whose steps each carry their investor's logo, under the step's description and centred on its step, all the logos on one row. In the editor, each step of a timeline has a logo picker over the template's logos. A logo grid with a set number of columns shares its width in equal cells, each logo centred in its own, so a grid placed under a timeline of as many steps lines up with it; Stretch spreads the logos edge to edge instead.

Sales and marketing collateral has its own building blocks: a feature matrix (a comparison table with an accented "us" column and check / cross marks), editions and plans as tier cards with one recommended tier and a call-to-action button each, a fact sheet made of badges (certifications, hosting regions, community numbers) and label / value rows, personas — two to four audience cards naming the role, what hurts today and what changes for them — and a banner for a hero header or a closing call to action with buttons that link to a page or an e-mail address. Ask for "a battlecard against a legacy TIP", "the editions slide", "who it is for" or "a closing slide with a demo button" and the assistant reaches for them.

Pages, not only slides

Not everything is presented from a stage. Ask for a product brief, a one-pager, a datasheet or a case study and the assistant lays it out on a portrait page — A4 or US Letter — instead of a 16:9 slide: a hero banner, a fact sheet, a feature matrix, the editions, and a call to action, denser than a slide because it is read, not projected. A page exports to a PDF on real A4 / Letter paper and to a portrait PowerPoint of the same size. On screen it is not a slide show — see Read a page.

Images come from the predefined assets of the deck's template rather than from the assistant's imagination: add your architecture diagram, product screenshots or partner logos to a template, ask for "the architecture diagram" or "a logo wall of our partners", and the assistant places the actual figure — every one is described so it can be picked by what it shows, and the assistant asks the template for one role or keyword at a time rather than reading the whole inventory. See Templates.

docs.title: Play a deck
docs.text:
The card in the chat is a live deck. Everything you operate it with sits in the toolbar along its top edge — nothing is drawn over the slide itself: no corner arrows, no progress bar, no counter on the slide.

  • The middle of the bar is navigation: previous / next, and the slide counter (3 / 12), which opens a go-to-slide menu listing every slide by title, with a number field for long decks.
  • Present — the one highlighted button on the bar — takes the deck, toolbar included, to the whole screen. The slide fills the screen edge to edge: a 16:9 deck on a 16:9 monitor has no border at all, and on a screen of another shape (a 16:10 laptop, an ultrawide) the bands around it are black, like any player, whatever theme the deck or the app is in. The bar floats over the top edge for a moment, then slides away with the pointer after a moment of stillness and comes back as soon as you move the pointer — never when you press a key, so stepping through the slides with the arrows or a clicker never makes it flash; press Esc (or the bar's exit button) to leave. The keyboard is always active while presenting. Where the browser will not hand over the screen — a locked-down kiosk, an embedded desktop window — the deck fills the application window instead, with the same bar and the same keys; and from a chat embedded in another product, Present opens the standalone viewer, which can go fullscreen.
  • Open in studio, on the card in the chat, lands on the standalone viewer at /presentations/<id> — the same page a deck opens on from the Presentations list, with the editor, the comments, the history and the sharing controls — and opens the studio beside it, carrying this very conversation along so the assistant keeps everything it already knows about the deck. It is also the page you put on a projector or share as a link: no product menus, only the deck's own toolbar. Open in a new tab, in the More menu, opens that page beside the chat.
  • Comments opens the review notes on the deck and History its revisions (see Work on a deck together); the count on Comments is the number of notes still open. The initials beside Present are whoever else has the deck open right now.
  • The More menu holds the rarer presenter actions: the slide overview, the black screen, the speaker view with your notes and the next slide, the printable notes handout, and the list of keyboard shortcuts.

In the chat, the keyboard belongs to the page until you click the deck or its toolbar; from then on the deck has the keys, until you click somewhere else. In the viewer and while presenting the deck always has them.

Keys What they do Right Space N Page Down / Left P Page Up Next / previous slide Home / End First / last slide G Go to a slide O Slide overview F / Esc Present / stop presenting (Esc also closes the overview) B or . Black screen S Speaker view A Present to a meeting (audience window) ? or F1 Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts pause while you type in a field or use a menu, so a key never turns the page by accident.

The deck is authored at a fixed 16:9 slide size (or 4:3 if you asked for it) and scales to whatever space it is given — a chat card, a laptop screen, a projector — so what you rehearse is what the room sees.

docs.title: Present with your notes
docs.text:
Every slide can carry speaker notes — what you say over it, not what the room reads. The assistant writes them with the deck (ask for "speaker notes on every slide, conversational, two or three sentences each" and it does; the note under each slide in the editor panel shows the words and the speaking time it adds up to), and reports back which content slides still have none. They live in the deck, travel with it in the PowerPoint export, and are read from the speaker view.

S, or Speaker view in the More menu, opens the speaker view in a window of its own — from the standalone viewer or from the card in the chat alike. Put the deck on the room's screen and keep this window on your laptop:

  • The current slide on top, so you know what the room sees without turning round — with a "screen is black" notice while the deck is paused.
  • Your notes in large type under it, the reason the window exists: bullets as bullets, emphasis as emphasis. + / - set the type size once and it is remembered.
  • The next slide in the side column, so the transition is spoken before it appears.
  • A stopwatch that starts on your first slide change (pause, resume, reset at will), the wall clock, and your pacing: the notes give every slide an estimated speaking time, so the window knows how far ahead of or behind the plan you are, and how much spoken time is left. Type a target length in minutes and the plan is re-scaled to the slot you actually have.
  • The transport: previous / next, a go-to-slide menu, the black screen — every one with the same key as the deck.

The window follows the deck: whichever screen is playing it — the viewer, a chat card, the fullscreen stage — announces where it is, and the keys pressed in the speaker window move the room's screen. Your clicker moves both. With no deck window open it runs in rehearsal mode, and says so: same notes, same timer, its own position — the way to practise the talk before the room is there. Edits made from the studio while you rehearse land in the notes and the previews without a reload.

Notes handout, in the same menu (and in the speaker window's header), opens every slide with its notes as one printable document at /presentations/<id>/notes — the sheets for the lectern, or for the colleague who presents the deck in your place. Only slides with notes leaves the section dividers out; print it to paper or to PDF from the browser.

If the speaker window does not open

Browsers block windows a page opens without a click behind them. Allow pop-ups for this site and press S again — the speaker view is a new window, never a popup drawn over the deck.

docs.title: Present to a meeting
docs.text:
A, or Present to a meeting in the More menu, opens the audience window: the slides and nothing else, letterboxed in black at any window size, with no toolbar and no pointer. It is a plain browser window, so share it in Teams, Zoom or Google Meet while the speaker view stays on your own screen. It follows the deck and the speaker view, takes the deck keys from the first moment (a clicker works at once), and a click on a slide moves to the next one (Shift + click goes back). Press S in it to bring the speaker view back; close it with its own window button.

The speaker view is the hub of the meeting: its header says whether an audience window is live (Audience window live or No audience window), and Open audience window opens one, or Bring back audience window brings the open one to the front at the current slide without reloading it, so the share the meeting tool holds is kept. With two screens, in a browser that supports window placement (Chrome and Edge), the browser asks once for permission to manage windows; once allowed, the audience window opens over the whole of the screen the speaker view is not on. Refused, or on one screen, it opens as a plain 16:9 window to share.

Hand the clicker. A co-presenter on another computer can move your slides. In the speaker view, Hand the clicker asks for a person; only someone who can already open the deck can receive it (a public-link viewer cannot). They get one in-app notice, open the deck on their own machine and drive it from the bar at the bottom of the viewer: previous, next and the slide you are on. Their moves reach your stage and your audience window through the server, so it works whatever meeting tool you use. One person holds the clicker at a time; your own keys keep working, Take back returns it to you in one click, the holder can Give back too, and a holder whose connection drops loses it after 45 seconds. Every hand-over and take-back is in the audit log.

docs.title: Read a page
docs.text:
A portrait presentation — a brief, a one-pager, a datasheet on A4 or Letter — is a document, and the platform treats it as one. Instead of a stage it opens as a reader: every page stacked on a scrolling surface as a sheet of paper, the same toolbar along the top edge, and nothing that only makes sense for a slide show — no fullscreen, no transitions, no speaker view.

  • The middle of the bar is navigation: previous / next page, and the page counter (1 / 2), which opens a go-to-page menu listing every page by its heading. Scrolling moves the counter too — the current page is the one under the top of the reader.
  • The zoom controls sit beside it: zoom in / out in steps, and Fit width, which sizes each sheet to the reader. Ctrl + mouse wheel zooms as well.
  • Open in studio, on the card in the chat, lands on the standalone reader at /presentations/<id> with the studio open beside it and the document's actions (edit, comments, history, share, export) alongside; Open in a new tab in the More menu opens it beside the chat.
Keys What they do Right N Page Down / Left P Page Up Next / previous page Home / End First / last page G Go to a page + / - / 0 Zoom in / zoom out / fit width ? or F1 Keyboard shortcuts

What you see is what prints: each sheet on screen is the page the PDF export produces, scaled as a whole, so a line that fits on screen fits on paper.
