A keyed screen never blinks: on a still shot (Follow the camera off) the screen is filled once from its first frame rather than keyed again on every frame - what crosses it still stays in front, its edge softened by the key's feather, and the tolerance decides how much of the shot's green around the bezel the key takes -, and on a moving one the key is read over five frames together, so the edge of the insert does not jitter with the footage's compression. The glow is a soft halo in the picture's own colour, kept to the screen's bezel: it never lights the wall around the monitor, and a keyed screen glows only when you ask it to. Room light (15 % by default) is how much of the shot's own light and reflections play over the insert - a window's glare across the monitor, a lamp's falloff - laid on as light, never as a tint of the room's colour or of the green screen: a screen lit evenly adds nothing, and 0 draws the picture exactly as it is. The editor's preview plays the insert as the render draws it - keyed, following the camera, the recording moving - once it has been drawn in the background (the scene says it is being prepared meanwhile, and shows the inserted media mapped onto the surface); the scene's thumbnail in the timeline shows its first frame (never the green screen it covers); the inspector lists the insert with its fit, glow, room light, key and timing. On footage whose camera moves, turn on Follow the camera (or ask the assistant): the screen's corners, read off the frame the insert comes in on, are followed in perspective through the footage - by the surface and the frame around it - so the insert stays on its surface. A frame where that following is unsure (a plain wall, a screen whose own picture moves) keeps the screen's edges as that frame shows them, so a nearly still shot is followed from its first frame; saving the video snaps the corners to the screen's edges on that first frame and says how its frames were placed ("track: 190 frames by the tracker, 2 by the bezel read") or where the surface would be lost. When the surface is lost (the camera cuts away, something covers it), the render and the scene preview fail with surface lost at t=... and the frame where it was lost, rather than draw the insert off its surface. On an AI shot whose camera was locked off after it was made, the insert is followed through the shot as the model made it and placed where the locked-off shot shows the screen, so it does not jitter; when locking the camera cropped into the screen, the render fails as "screen cropped" at that frame instead of drawing half an insert (generate the shot again without stabilisation, and the insert follows its camera). A wall of screens is one insert: ask for several panes on the one surface ("show OpenCTI, OpenAEV and XTM One on the three screens of the wall"), side by side or in rows and columns, each showing its own picture or video with a thin gap between them; the panes follow the wall together, in its perspective, and share its key. The corners you give are a starting point: on every frame the render reads the edge of the screen's bezel around them and snaps the insert to it, so a quad a few pixels off still sits square on the monitor and follows it as the camera moves, and the insert is drawn sharp at the quality you render at (never drawn on the shot and enlarged with it). On a still shot you can leave the corners out altogether: when the video is saved, the screen's bezel is found on the frame the insert comes in on - the flat green, blue or magenta screen the shot shows, in the key's colour when the insert has one - and stored as the insert's corners, so the first preview already draws it on its bezel; the save is refused, that frame attached, only when it shows no such screen. Corners you give within 2 % of the frame's width of the bezel are snapped to it when the video is saved; further off, the save says so and you leave them out to take the bezel. One insert per scene can find its corners so, and an insert that follows the camera takes corners given. A curved screen - one whose edges bow by more than 5 % of their length, the points along the edge confirming it - cannot take a flat insert (each edge is judged only on the part nothing stands in front of: an edge mostly hidden by a person or an object is said as covered and not judged, so a subject standing at the bezel never makes a straight screen look curved): a shot meant to carry an insert that starts from a picture with such a screen is refused before anything is paid, a take that bends its screen fails, and the save says so of an insert on it - generate the shot again with a flat screen. A render that finds a screen curved where the shot's own check passed it on the same take says it disagrees with that check, as a warning that never holds the render. A flat screen seen from the side or from below is fine: the insert is drawn in its perspective exactly, and the assistant only says how far it is turned ("seen at 35 degrees"). Only a shot that carries an insert is checked - a screen replacement, a shot the assistant says will carry one, or a shot a scene already draws an insert on - so a mug or a lamp in an ordinary shot never stops it, and the assistant can say a shot carries no insert at all (then no screen is checked on it, and its stray screens are not cleaned). A rounded or glowing object of a screen's colour is never taken for one: a screen has four straight edges around a flat key colour or a dark fill, and is never the brightest thing in the picture. Under a chroma key the screen is painted flat behind the insert - nothing of the green shows through -, and it stays covered on every frame of its scene, both transitions included: before the insert comes in and after it goes, the screen shows as switched off (the bezel's dark colour, else black, the room's light on it), the insert fades in and out over that, a screen showing two inserts one after the other hands over from one to the next, and a cut or a fade to the next scene blends the two finished pictures - the green never shows, not even for a frame. An insert that lasts as long as its scene or longer never fades out: it stays whole to the scene's very last frame, however much longer the scene plays than planned (a cut moved onto the music's beat, a held last frame), through the fade into the next scene too. Every preview and render reads its own video back, frame by frame: a screen showing one flat colour, or a picture other than the insert's, on a frame where the insert should show fails as insert missing, with that frame. On a transition's frames - a crossfade into the next scene - the insert is blended with the scene coming in, so it is read with that scene taken out of the frame, never against the insert alone: a crossfade never fails an insert that is there, a screen that really went black still does, and the finding says how much of the insert the frame showed there (its alpha). Frames where less than half of it still shows are not judged, and the answer says how many. A transition that blurs or dims the whole picture - a blur, a fade_black, a zoom, a flash - or the video's fade from or to black blurs and dims the insert with it: there the screen is judged against the frame around it, so it fails only when it is flat while the rest of the picture keeps its detail, and the answer says how many of its frames it judged so. The matte is steadied from frame to frame so it never flickers, the key's shade and how unevenly the screen is lit are both read off the shot, and the green fringe on whoever stands in front is taken out without turning it magenta. A screen partly out of frame keeps its true corners outside it and the insert shows through the visible part: never squeeze the quad to the frame's edge, which skews the insert (the save says so as advice). The save also says when an insert's text would be too small to read: a recording, an uploaded screenshot or an uploaded video whose smallest text is drawn under 10 pixels of a 1080p frame is said as advice, under 6 pixels as a finding the render waits for - typically a wall of many panes, each showing a full-size recording. Both offer only what brings its text to 12 pixels and keeps the page's own layout: the share of the frame the insert needs (fewer panes on a wall), or a camera push on the insert - ask the assistant to "push in on the alerts panel": the insert's zoom draws its picture up to 4 times larger within its surface, easing in between two moments and panned to the region you name. A larger surface or a push is offered only at a size the picture stays sharp at in the quality you render the video at (its latest render's, High before the first), so a push the save suggests is never one the render refuses. When the picture cannot be drawn that large, the advice names what can: the pixel ratio to record it at again (the same layout, more pixels), the picture size to use, or, for a recording, the largest push it stays sharp at and the browser zoom to record it at again so its text is larger in the same pixels. A push sharp at 1080p that a 4K render would refuse says so. A picture drawn under 0.3 of its own size shows as a whole page - a dashboard on a wall screen -, which a push would crop: it is offered no push, and the advice says why. Recording it again with its text larger for its width - on a screen under 40 % of the frame's width the browser zoom (the page zoomed in, its window and frame keeping their size), on a wider one a narrower window - is suggested only when the recording's page keeps its layout at the width it would then be laid out at: once a recording is made, its page is narrowed step by step to find where its layout changes (a menu collapses, cards stack, the page scrolls sideways), and the recording says how far down it holds. A dashboard told to record again zoomed in, or in a window, too narrow for its desktop layout would come back as its mobile layout, cropped and over-zoomed on a wall screen. A recording asked at a browser zoom its page does not fit at is refused before anything is recorded: the assistant is told the width the page is laid out at, how far it overflows and the largest zoom that keeps its layout ("at zoom 190 the page lays out at 842 px and overflows by 225 px; the largest zoom that keeps its layout is 150"), and a page that overflows below its minimum width says that width exactly ("its page keeps this layout down to 1067 px"). A larger share of the frame is suggested only when the scene has it: two monitors side by side cannot each take 68 % of the frame, so when the inserts sharing its width would together need more than all of it, the advice says so and suggests what needs no more of the frame - a push, the recording made again at a higher browser zoom up to the largest its page keeps its layout at ("largest safe zoom 150 on this page"), or a tighter page, such as a single dashboard panel recorded on its own. How much the source is scaled down is given with it, but is not the test: a recording at pixel ratio 2 is drawn at under half its size and stays readable when its text is large enough. AI shots and logos are not judged, nor an insert that is scenery: three monitors sharing one frame show their recordings far too small to read by design, so the assistant marks each such insert ambient and the check gives the size its smallest text is drawn at as a fact ("ambient, not judged - its smallest text, about 24 px in the source, reads about 5 px on the 1080p frame"), rather than advise on it. Marking an insert so changes nothing it draws, and keeps the scene's preview. The advice always offers to mark an insert ambient when it is scenery. The assistant is told the advice once per insert - the panes of a wall together -, not on every save; the finding, every time. The render and the scene preview also fail an insert drawn over what stands in front of its surface - on a single frame, on more than half a percent of the screen, even seen through it (insert over foreground, with that frame and the spot cut at 100 %) -, a picture kept whole with Fit inside the frame that has a letterbox baked into it (insert padded: bands on two opposite sides in a colour that is not the picture's own sides - a transparent margin, or a plate the logo sits on, is never one, and Fill the frame is never judged), a logo inserted that stops showing (logo lost), an insert whose colours came out different from the picture itself, keyed or not (insert colour shift: its blacks lifted by more than 5 % of the range, or its colours tinted or turned by more than a few degrees - "tinted blue, with its blacks lifted 18%" - with its luminance, saturation and contrast against the picture, on five frames or more; lower its Room light when the room's light lifts its blacks, otherwise the finding names what shows through it; read away from whoever stands in front and its soft edge, and not read at all on a frame they cover more than 30 % of the screen, the answer saying so), an insert that could not be drawn at all - a logo the template has no file for, an SVG that could not be drawn - which would leave the video model's own drawing on screen (insert missing, with the reason), a Fill the frame fit that cuts the recording's own content - a sidebar, a right column - to fill the screen (insert cropped: use Fit inside the frame, or a screen of the recording's proportions), a quad more than half a percent of the frame's width off the bezel the shot shows - on average or on any one side - on five frames in a row (insert off its bezel, with what fixes it - leave the corners out so the save measures the bezel, follow the camera when the screen moves, or generate the shot again when the screen is curved: on a still shot, a frame or two where the render caught a line drawn on the screen for its bezel keep the bezel of the frames around them, and fail nothing), a quad that jumps on one frame against the frame before it by more than a tenth of a percent of the frame's width, beyond the way the screen moves through the frames around it (insert jitters: 0.4% between 26.000 s and 26.017 s: a blinking screen however close to its bezel it stays on average, the two frames attached side by side, the insert's region at 100 %; a screen that steps with a shot slower than the video, or a pan, never counts), the key's colour left inside or just around the surface (residual key: the quad stops short of the screen, or the key does not take the whole screen - the finding says where it sits, inside the screen, on the screen running past the quad, or past the bezel, and on which side; when the shot's green panel runs past the monitor's bezel, the key takes that green too at its tolerance and paints it in the bezel's colour, so the shot's own green never fails a take; the key's colour is looked for inside the screen and half a percent of the frame's width around it, and fails only past 0.3 % of the screen on five frames or more, or on a single frame of a cut or a transition between two scenes, where nothing hides it - under it, a few pixels nobody sees, the answer says it and nothing fails -, while the shot's own green farther out, its screen's glow on the bezel or a spill on the desk, is taken out of the picture on every frame instead, the answer saying how much; green the inserted picture itself shows - a chart, a ring, a button of the product's own colour - is its own and never counted, the answer saying how much of the screen it covers, and the half percent around the screen shows the bezel's own colour), a matte or a despill that flickers from frame to frame, or an insert missing from one frame of its scene while drawn on the frames around it (insert flickers), the key showing on a screen at a cut or through a transition, read back off the video once it is encoded - each scene's own picture there, so a green in the scene beside it is never taken for the key (insert dropped at t=..., with that frame: nothing in the video causes it, render again) -, an insert drawn soft (insert soft: a source with too few pixels for the screen it is drawn on at the quality you render at - a 1280-pixel recording stretched over an 1800-pixel screen of a 4K frame reads soft; the finding names the recording and the size it needs, for a recording the pixel ratio to record it at again - or an insert region that comes out blurred against its source) and a green or magenta halo along whoever stands in front on five frames or more (insert halo, measured after the edge despill and said as the edge spill it leaves at its width, with that edge cut at 100 % and the advice to widen the despill - or turn it on - before generating the shot again; where that edge crosses green the picture itself shows, it is the picture's; the colours of what stands in front itself are left out and said, and a magenta the compositing itself made on that edge is said apart, so the edge's length, the spill, the subject's own colour and the compositing's share read apart without opening the crop; when two previews at different settings leave the same halo, the finding says it is no setting but the subject's own colour, named, to declare in the insert's despill.own_hues - or to accept), each with its time, its scene, the frame that shows it, its value against its threshold, what was left out of the measure (the picture's own key colour, whoever stands in front, the bands beside a picture kept whole) and one fix - never a key tolerance or feather to try, which does not move these measures. Every check reads only the pixels it owns: whoever stands in front of the screen - from its first frame on a still shot too, where they stay in front of the insert - is left out of the bezel's edges, the colours and the key's colour alike. The save, a scene preview and a render measure an insert the same way, at any resolution: when a render finds what the save or a preview of the same scene, unchanged, passed, its finding says it disagrees with that save or preview and is a warning, never what holds the render. A defect nothing in the video causes on one frame alone - one frame the page drew and the encoder dropped - is the render's own, never your video's: a render draws the same frames every time and no edit of the video changes them, so it is never a finding and never holds a render. It is listed once for the administrator with the frame that shows it, and not again when the same scene, unchanged, is drawn with it on the same frames. An insert missing, dropped or not drawn on more frames than that is a finding that holds the render. So is an insert the render did not measure where it is drawn (insert measurement lost): the screen's edge its save and its scene's preview found and the render's frames did not, or the picture read off the video showing the insert beside the box read rather than under it - its finding names the frame, the box and the size each one read it at, and nothing it read of that insert is said as a fact. A High or Ultra render, drawn with motion blur, measures every screen insert on every frame as its scene's preview does. One whose frames all lie in a transition says what keeps the insert off them instead - making that transition a cut, or ending the insert before it (starting it after it, for a transition in) - and holds the render like any other finding. A frame of a transition that shows under two thirds of the insert, the scene coming in outweighing it, is counted as faint and never judged. What the scene draws over the insert - a statement's lines and chips, an overlay, burned-in subtitles - is left out of that reading: the insert is compared on the part of it they leave uncovered, and a frame where they cover more than 60 % of it is counted as covered and never judged. Two drawings of the same join - the preview of the scene on each side of it, or a render - that read the insert differently there (present in one, missing in the other) say so, and neither warns. A screen insert is judged on the frames its scene owns in the encoded video, to its last one: never on the first frame of the scene after a cut, even with motion blur, whose shutter on that frame still shows a little of the scene before. Whether its layer is drawn on every frame (insert flickers) is judged the same way, on the very frames the check of the encoded video reads and the flicker the answer gives counts: the frames its scene is on screen alone, and the frames of a transition into or out of it that show two thirds of the insert or more - never the first frame of a transition into its scene, which still shows the scene before whole. It is said only where the encoded video itself shows the insert missing, on a frame that shows it whole: a frame the render's own log missed but that shows the insert drawn is no finding, and a transition's frame is never one. A frame the insert is not drawn on counts in that flicker, so the answer never lists such a frame while it says the flicker is 0. The answer gives each join's frames measured and its residual key; whether the insert was seen there is said with the rest of the encoded video's check. The answer to a preview or a render also gives these numbers for every insert - how far the quad was from the bezel, how far it jumped from one frame to the next at most, the residual key, the flicker, the sharpness, the halo, and its colours at its room light (luminance, black level, tint or hue, saturation, contrast), so the light can be tuned - and attaches the insert's region cut at 100 % of the rendered frame at its first, middle and last frame - the first and last frames its scene is on screen alone, after its transition in and before its transition out, never a frame blended with the scene before or after, and the assistant says where they were cut - and, for a residual key, the side of the screen where most of it sits -, so you judge the compositing on the real pixels rather than on a downsized frame; the frame of each insert's worst finding is attached too, a failed render's included - at most twelve pictures an answer, the others named so the assistant opens any of them when it needs it - and the assistant opens all of them again like the scene's own frames, and can cut the same region at any other moment of a render, at 100 %. It says which resolution the numbers and the crops come from: a preview's are its draft's, and a 4K render measures and crops them again on its own 2160p frames. Recordings are made at a pixel ratio of 2 by default, sharp enough for a 4K render on most screens. The check for a soft insert runs when the video is saved and with every scene preview, for each quality you may render at (standard, high and ultra): a recording too small for its screen in a 4K render is said then ("soft at ultra"), with the size it needs, as advice that refuses nothing - a scene preview is drawn at 1080p and would never show it. Ask the assistant to record it again for that screen at that quality: it reads the screen's size from the saved video and picks the window and pixel ratio, widening the window and zooming the page in as much when it must, so the page keeps its layout. A whole render at a quality where an insert would be soft is still refused before it is paid for. A whole render also keeps the first, middle and last frame of every scene with a screen insert or a replaced screen at the render's own size - a 720p preview hides what a 4K frame shows - and the assistant looks at them before calling the screens right.
  • A screen partly hidden behind someone: when a person or an object stands over one side of a keyed screen, so that side's bezel cannot be seen, the save places that side where the screen's key colour ends rather than at the person's edge, and says so ("right side hidden behind the foreground: placed at the key colour's extent, x 0.985"). If a preview still finds the key colour running on from one side of the quad, the finding names the side and the value to widen it to ("widen the quad's right side to x 0.780: the screen continues there"). It never suggests a retake or a despill for that case, because the green there is the screen itself.
  • Many frames at once, to check a render: the assistant can sweep a stretch of a video ("every second of the dashboard insert") in one step: up to 60 frames, or a region of each such as one screen insert at full resolution, laid out as one contact sheet with each frame's moment under it, every frame kept as a picture it can open. An agent running on a schedule (an assignment) can open every picture a render's answer names (its poster, its insert crops, its findings' frames, its captions) as well as a chat can, and reads a long video's scenes a range at a time ("scenes 18 to 24") instead of a cut-off spec.
  • A frame of your footage as a picture: the assistant can keep one frame of a recording (the frame after one of its steps, or at a moment), of an AI shot or of a video file as a picture of its own ("keep the frame of the dashboard step as a picture"), at up to 4K, and use it as an image scene, behind a statement, or as the picture an AI shot starts from. An image scene or a statement's backdrop can also name the recording and its step (or a moment) directly: the frame is kept as a picture when the video is saved, once, and taken again only when the recording or the moment changes. A render of the video is a video file too: the assistant can look at any moment of a finished render before you call it final, whoever rendered it, as long as you can open the video.
  • Slides: a deck slide plays as a picture with a camera motion; chrome: false (ask the assistant) draws it without the deck's footer, logo and slide number, for a slide shown inside the film rather than presented. When subtitles are shown over a slide, it is scaled to stand above them, so they never cover its footer.
  • Animated figures: one diagram of a deck - an architecture, a process flow, a timeline, a roadmap's phases, a chart, a diagram, an org chart - drawn alone in the video's colours and built in step by step: an architecture's zones first, then each node on its own, row by row, each link drawn once both its ends are there; a process flow's steps and a roadmap's phases in order; chart series growing; an org chart level by level - the root, then each level's cards, then its teams' bubbles growing to their size, every headcount counting up, the dotted lines last. Each step fades in as it rises into place, and the camera moves to it before ending on the whole figure for the scene's last two seconds. Built, the figure keeps moving to the end of its scene: it drifts in slowly, a light pulse runs along each link from its source to its target, and the core node's glow breathes. The figure is framed on everything it draws - a label wider than its node included - and its drift is fitted to the frame: drifted and leaned or turned in space as it is drawn, it always keeps 3% of the frame clear on every side; where only a drift too small to see would, it holds still once built instead. When the assistant saves a video, it is told the drift each figure plays and how close to the frame's edge it comes. Ask the assistant for it ("show the architecture of slide 4 building up while I explain it"); it takes the block from a deck, or writes one for the film. A figure taken from a deck follows its slide, and is drawn in the video's theme: a template logo the slide places for the other theme - a light deck's dark-on-light product logos on a dark video - is drawn as the twin its template declares for this one, so pointing a scene at another deck's slide is one edit, never a copy of the block with its logos swapped by hand; the assistant is told which logos it swapped. A template logo kept as a picture for the slides that already place it - soft past 1080p - and replaced by a vector version that its template names is drawn as that vector, in the video's theme: a light deck's opencrq-logo-light.png draws opencrq-logo.svg on a dark video, sharp at 4K. The deck stays as it is, and the assistant is told which picture was drawn as which vector. In the editor, the Animated figure section sets how long it lasts, whether it builds step by step or all at once, whether the steps come in evenly over the scene or as the narration says their names (measured on the spoken voice once it is generated; a name is recognised however the narration writes it - in any case, with or without a hyphen or a possessive, in the plural, in one word or two, or by its product name alone, as "OpenCTI" for "OpenCTI - Threat intelligence"; a subtitle shows its whole line at once, so a step named in it comes in when that line appears, never after it, even when the voice reaches the name later in the sentence; the steps it does not name are spread evenly around those it does, up to the end of the scene), how long each step stays on screen before the next one (Time on each step, 0.8 s by default: steps a short scene has no room for come in a few at a time), whether the camera follows the steps or keeps the whole figure still, and what the figure does once built (Once built: keeps moving, the default, or holds still). A figure built with its narration stays on screen long enough after it for the step named last to come in when it is said. The figure keeps clear of the subtitles: it is centred, at its full width, between the top margin of the frame and the top of the subtitles' pill (between the subtitles and the bottom margin when they are at the top), and when the assistant saves a video it is told where each figure spans ("Its figure spans 14% to 72% of the frame's height"). When the assistant saves a video, it is told when each step of each figure comes in and which words of the narration bring it in. The editor shows the figure built in whole on the scene's thumbnail and when you select the scene; it is drawn in the background once the video is saved - saving never waits for it - and the preview says Figure being drawn until it is; a figure nobody opened for a while is drawn again the next time the video is opened. The figure's build then plays on the stage where the scene plays: move the playhead through the scene, or hover the scene in the timeline to watch it build under the pointer.
  • Pictures brought to life: turn on Animate with the video model on an image scene (a product screenshot, a team photo, a diagram), and describe how it moves if you like ("a slow push in, the charts light up one after the other"). The video model makes a silent shot from that very image when the video is saved; the scene plays the shot once it is made, and the still with its camera motion until then - or for good when no video model is available, which the assistant tells you. A picture no video model can read is refused when the video is saved, never discovered at render. The assistant animates the stills of a film by itself when AI shots are available. A photo with words in it - a team holding a banner, a sign, a caption - keeps them: ask the assistant to keep that region as it is, and the photo's own pixels are drawn back over it in every frame of the shot, following its camera, so the words are never redrawn. A shot whose camera cannot be followed fails as kept region lost and can be generated again with a calmer move; keep a region nothing in the shot moves across.
  • Screenshots in motion, without a model: a video model redraws the words of a product screenshot, so a screenshot is animated with effects drawn on the real picture instead, its text untouched: panels of the interface lifted off it in depth as the camera moves (parallax), a band of light sweeping across it, a glow pulsing on one region - a gauge, a score, an alert. Ask the assistant ("lift the alerts panel and pulse the risk score"); the preview plays the effects exactly as the render does. A picture moves by the video model or by effects, not both.

docs.title: Motion design
docs.text:
Everything a video draws - its cards, statements, overlays and motion graphics - moves the brand's way, set once for the whole video under Video > Motion:

  • Personality: Precise (crisp, measured moves - the platform's own motion), Calm (slow, soft reveals), Energetic (snappy springs, titles letter by letter), Cinematic (long blurred reveals and a light sweeping across the accent words) or Playful (bouncy springs). It sets every timing and easing at once: how a title comes in, how far a line rises, how fast the lines of a statement follow each other, how a card's logo appears. Speed makes the whole video's motion faster or slower, and Titles come in by overrides how titles split (lines, words or letters). A template presets its personality, and a brand template locks it.
  • Motion graphics: a Motion graphics scene (Add scene in the timeline, or Media > Cards) lays out a whole animated scene from a few words - a kinetic title, the brand's logo revealed, a figure counted up ("6,000+"), a list built item by item, a statement split across windows, a quote, a title over a moving constellation - in the video's colours and personality, whatever its format: a 9:16 version of the same scene stays readable. Choose its Composition in the inspector and write its words. The assistant can also draw a motion scene of its own: text set letter by letter, shapes and lines drawn stroke by stroke, one shape turning into another, pictures and logos moving along a path, a 3D camera moving through the elements, particles, and Lottie animations exported from After Effects (Bodymovin JSON with its images embedded and its text as glyphs; a file that loads anything from outside itself is refused when the video is saved, and expressions are not played - the animation plays its keyframes).
  • On the beat: with music, Cuts on the beat makes each scene play a little longer - never shorter, a second at most - so the cut lands on a beat; Cuts and builds on the beat also brings a statement's lines and a motion scene's elements in on the beats. A built-in score's beats are known from its tempo; an AI track or an uploaded sound is listened to once, and a sound with no steady beat is left as it is - a warning of the save, with the two ways out (a track with a steady beat, or beat sync off); so is beat sync on a video with no music.
  • Motion blur: what moves blurs as it would on film. It is drawn at the High and Ultra qualities only, so previews stay fast, and a render with it takes about three times as long.
  • Figures in space: an animated figure can stand in 3D while it builds (In space: leaning back and turning towards the camera, or turning slowly side to side).

Every frame is still drawn from the time alone, never from the frame before it: a scene preview, a render split across workers and a render drawn again show exactly the same motion.

docs.title: Good to watch by construction
docs.text:
Every frame is laid out so that nothing covers anything else, whatever the assistant (or you) wrote:

  • The subtitles keep their band. While someone speaks, the text of a card or a statement, a lower third and a recording's browser window stay above the subtitles (below them when they are at the top) - burned in or not, because a player draws the subtitle track in that same band. A card's whole text, not just its title, is scaled down to fit the room left, and a word too long for the width (a URL) is scaled into it.
  • Overlays find their place. A badge or a callout asked where the scene's text already is takes the first free corner; two callouts on one element stand on either side of it, or one above the other; a lower third stands above the subtitles.
  • Subtitles are readable. A subtitle holds on two lines, set a little smaller when its sentence is long.

  • The watermark leaves the stage to the brand. Title and closing cards already carry the brand: the corner watermark leaves while they play and comes back with the content, a moment after it starts and once the card has left the frame, however long the transition. A statement does not draw its logo while the video has a watermark: the watermark already shows the brand, and the logo shows again once the watermark is off. The brand mark is never drawn twice on one frame. The brand film templates open on a centred title card with the logo.

  • Transitions cut like an editor. Left on Automatic (the default, and what every built-in template but the Filigran Product Video uses: a demo crossfades calmly from scene to scene), each cut is picked from the scenes on either side: the opening card pushes into the video, words dissolve into pictures and pictures into words, a run of AI shots dissolves from one to the next (or, at a Dynamic rhythm, alternates a push through the frame and a whip pan), the closing card comes after a dip to black, and a shot too short to dissolve is cut. Video > Transitions sets the rhythm - Calm, Dynamic, or Classic, which only cuts, crossfades and fades to black, the grammar of a brand film (the brand film templates use it) - or one transition for every cut - cut, crossfade, fade through black, slide, zoom, blur, wipe, whip or flash - and a scene's Transition in overrides it for that scene, which says what it comes in with. The assistant is told the transition planned into every scene each time it saves or reads the video, so it can check the cuts before rendering.

  • Footage keeps moving to the end of its scene. A scene lasts as long as its narration. When the narration is longer than the AI shot, the animated picture or the video behind a statement, the footage plays slower to fill the scene, down to 70% of its speed. A shot whose own sound you keep plays at its speed, because slowing it would slow its sound. A recording first plays the pauses it sped up more slowly, never slower than twice real time, so a page loading still reads sped up; the steps keep their real speed, and pauses set to Cut stay cut. A recording still shorter than its narration is then slowed down by the save itself, to the speed at which it lasts as long, never below half speed: the assistant is told "speed set to 0.69 automatically" and has nothing to type back. Only a recording still too short at half speed is reported, with the seconds still missing (record more of the flow, or shorten the narration). Setting the scene's fit to off keeps the speed you chose. Whatever is still missing holds the last frame, drifting slowly in until the next scene, so the picture never stops dead before a transition. Your own Hold the last frame is kept as you set it: a still moment, which does not drift. The preview and the render play it the same way.
  • A demo is told as a product manager tells it. On the Filigran Product Video template a recording keeps its camera still - a scene asking for a detail moves it calmly, no deeper than 1.3 times, in moves of 2 seconds -, the scenes crossfade calmly, a callout stays 3 seconds and the opening card is centred (left on the card the template adds, under template_scenes, leaves the right of the frame to the backdrop). Every save holds each recording scene to it, as advice that never blocks a render: a narration that reads its screen - an action said as an instruction ("Click the layered button"), a count of what the screen draws ("23 entities"), a name of two words or more its frames show while it is said (each frame read once by your chat model; the brand's names and the video's title are not counted) -, an automatic camera making more than 4 moves a minute of its scene (one is always allowed) or moving in on an element covering over 40% of the page, and a recording slowed under 0.7 times to last as long as its narration, with the narration length that keeps it at 0.8 times.
  • A video can be dynamic by construction. A video's pace set to dynamic (for a short social cut) presets the quick version of everything the video leaves unset: recordings cut their pauses instead of speeding them up, the camera moves quicker with half-second zooms, a recording keeps only 0.3 s after its last step, transitions cut at the dynamic rhythm, statements reveal their words one by one - and a recording longer than its narration is sped up to end with it, up to 1.25 times, the assistant told the speed it set. A scene can say its narration a little faster or slower than the rest (its own narration speed), and the voice-over's style can be the energetic or calm preset. Every save says how the video reads: words a minute of voice-over, the average and the longest scene, and how long each recording's screen stays still - the cursor still, the page unchanged - while the voice speaks; a scene over 20 seconds, or still for more than 3 seconds under its narration, is flagged with what to change.
  • A recording can fill the frame. A recording scene set to fill is drawn edge to edge - no margin, no browser bar, no rounded corner or halo - for a screen whose details must be read; the subtitles still keep their band. A template that locks the browser window leaves it to each scene, unless it locks fill off.

What a layout cannot fix is measured: after each save, the video is played in the render's compositor at the moments that matter and checked for text covering text, text cut by or touching the edge of the frame, text scaled down so far it gets hard to read, text still appearing when its scene ends, words on screen too briefly to be read, subtitles too fast to follow, words over a backdrop not darkened enough, overlays too short to read, and the brand mark drawn twice on one frame (brand mark drawn twice: the watermark, a card's logo or a picture overlay of the brand's mark together, with the time of the frame and what to switch off to keep one). The assistant reads the findings with the result of every save and fixes them before it renders; you see them in the editor under the header.

The pictures and the sound are checked too, scene by scene, each finding saying what to change: an AI shot that failed (the render would refuse it) or is still being made, a ready shot being generated again or whose last regeneration failed (advice only, said once whatever the number of scenes showing it, naming the take that plays: its previous take plays, in a render too), an animated image whose animation failed or is still being made (advice only: the scene plays the still image), a shot asked with a still camera whose camera moved (camera moved on a locked-off shot; a real product screen drawn into a shot follows the camera, so it is not flagged for it; set motion: intended on the clip scene when the move is wanted, and a preview of every scene showing the shot that passes clears it, the check naming that preview and its revision), an image smaller than the frame it is drawn on (it would look soft), a screen insert whose corner leaves the frame (advice: the screen keeps its true corners and the insert shows through the visible part - a quad mostly outside the footage the frame shows is a failure; the render and the scene preview also check every frame an insert draws, above), music that ends before the video with Loop off, music too quiet to be heard (silent, a long quiet passage, or lost under the voice - advice only, see "Music"), a narration no voice will speak (the voice-over off, or no speech model available), a narration spoken by another voice than the video's because the video's voice failed it (see below), a card or a statement that writes the brand name its logo already spells (Filigran in the kicker under the Filigran logo: the audience reads it twice), and an AI shot or a recording still holding its last frame for more than a second and a half under a longer narration (advice: generate a longer shot, continue it with a shot made from its last frame, record more of the flow, or shorten the narration). A shot or a recording shorter than its narration says the speed that makes it last as long, beside Zoom to fill the scene, and a screen insert running past the point where a looping shot starts again says where that seam falls and the length that ends the insert before it. When a recording is made, the assistant is told how long it plays at each speed and how much narration that carries, before it writes one. These are read from what the platform knows of your media, so they are shown even where the layout cannot be measured, and the editor reads them again when a shot is generated again, without waiting for the next save.

Before a scene preview or a render starts, everything it would find without drawing a frame - a screen insert off its bezel or on a screen that is not flat, footage shorter than its narration, a frozen last frame, an insert past a loop's seam, text that does not fit or covers other text, a shot or a recording not ready - is checked at once, and the start is refused with the whole list in one answer, each finding saying first when only a new shot fixes it. Corners a little off the bezel are snapped and saved as a new version of the video before the start, said in the answer. Whether a screen is flat is measured once, on the shot itself when the video is saved, so a scene preview and a 4K render give the same answer; a screen that bows a little is no finding when the insert drawn on it still covers it - on its edges, none of the green showing past them - and the save says so as a fact. On a transition's frames drawn smaller than the shot (a 1080p render of 4K footage), a reading of the screen's bezel that disagrees with the save's is set aside for it and said to the administrator in that render's answer, never as a finding of the video.

A recording scene whose kept seconds play its page still loading is flagged at save and refused before any preview or render (scene_loading_span): from a click that opened a page or a view to the moment the wait after it saw the page settle, and every span the recording logged a progress indicator or a blank drawing area. A click that stays on its page and sets a drawing moving (a graph laid out again, a legend folded, a view kept in the page address) is not a page loading: its motion is what the scene shows, and only a progress indicator or a blank drawing area it shows counts. The finding names the scene, the recording, the seconds it plays and the fix: move the scene's start past the moment the page settled, cut the scene in two around it, or cut its pauses. Under 0.3 s, a click's own response, it is tolerated.

Two faults that only the whole video would show are refused when the video is saved, before any preview: the same sentence in the narrations of two scenes (each preview hears its own narration only, the whole video would say it twice and fail its sound check), naming both scenes; and a recording on a screen insert that the quality the video is made for - the quality of its last render, 4K before its first - would draw soft, with the window size and the pixel ratio to record it again at, so it is recorded once.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A video template keeps every video of a team to the same look. It is a template like the ones that dress presentations - listed under Agent Studio > Templates, shared, duplicated and published the same way - and it carries:

  • what it is made for: product demo, brand film, event, launch, explainer or social - New video suggests a template for each of these kinds of video;
  • the palette, fonts, logos and pictures of the brand (the same colours as the brand's deck);
  • the look it presets: the backdrop, the watermark, how its videos move (see Motion design), the transitions, the captions, the voice-over style, how a statement reads, how a recording sits on screen (the browser window, the cursor, the camera). A preset fills only what the video leaves unset: the editor's Watermark field shows the template's corner until you pick another one or None, and when a video draws no watermark while its template draws one, saving it says so;
  • the art direction of its AI shots: the look every AI shot made for the video takes (the light, the lens, the materials, the palette) and what no shot ever shows - see AI shots wear the template's art direction;
  • the cards it adds: a title card before the first scene and a closing card after the last, when the video has none of its own - a starting point, never locked: a video's own first title card (last closing card), written in the editor or by the assistant, replaces the template's and takes its look;
  • the choices it locks: a locked choice always takes the template's value, whatever the video asks for; the editor shows it locked, and the assistant is told so when the video is saved.

These templates ship with the platform:

Template Where Made for What it does Filigran Product Video Filigran Copilot Product demo The Filigran palette (dark or light) on the aurora backdrop, the Filigran mark as a watermark, every recording in the same browser window with a still camera, calm crossfades, a voice presenting like a product manager, a centred Filigran title card and a "Book a demo" closing card. Locks the colours, the backdrop, the watermark, the captions and the browser window (a scene may still fill the frame). Filigran Brand Film Filigran Copilot Brand film, launch Statements revealed line by line over AI shots and event footage, the brand palette on the aurora backdrop, the Filigran deck's pictures and logos, cuts, crossfades and fades to black only, and the "Uncover threats. Take action." closing card. Filigran Event Loop Filigran Copilot Event A silent loop for a booth or stage screen (16:9 or vertical for a totem): no voice-over, no captions, short statements alternating with AI shots and product screenshots, the tagline at the end. THREAD Conference Video Filigran Copilot Event, launch The THREAD Color Set, dark like the stage, every card and recording drawn over the THREAD pixel mosaic, Elms Sans titles, the mosaic emblem as a watermark, the edition on the title card and a "See you there" closing card under the THREAD logo. Formats 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1. XTM One Product Video Every platform Product demo The XTM One palette on the mesh backdrop, recordings in the same browser window, an XTM One title card. Locks only the colours and the browser window. XTM One Brand Film Every platform Brand film, launch, event Statements over AI shots and real footage, figures counted up, the XTM One palette on the mesh backdrop, cuts, crossfades and fades to black only. Threat Briefing Every platform Explainer One threat, campaign or vulnerability explained from your intelligence: figures and ATT&CK techniques in statements, your intelligence platform's own screens as the evidence, AI shots that set the scene, a calm analyst voice-over with captions, a "Threat briefing" title card. Social Teaser Every platform Social, launch 15-30 s, vertical first: a hook in the first two seconds, words revealed one by one, quick cuts, captions burned in for muted viewing.

Every one of them directs its AI shots: filmed rather than rendered - natural light, real places and materials, the brand's own tones, no lettering, logos or invented screens - and never laser beams, starfields, lens flares, glowing networks, holograms or the other stock images of a generated "cyber" picture. They never limit how many AI shots a video has: a video made of AI shots, product demos and animated pictures alone is a complete video.

Each one also moves its own way (see Motion design): the product videos are Precise, the Filigran one revealing its logo from the left and sweeping a light across its accent words; the brand films are Cinematic, cut on the music's beat, with motion blur; THREAD and the event loop are Energetic, on the beat, with motion blur; the threat briefing is Calm; the social teaser is Energetic and a little faster, its titles word by word. The Filigran templates and THREAD lock their personality; a video still sets its own speed, beat sync and motion blur.

A video an assistant creates in a chat without naming a template wears the platform's default one: the Filigran one in Copilot mode, the XTM One one elsewhere. Free style (the look New video starts in, also under Video > Template in the editor) applies no template at all: no added cards, nothing locked, every choice is the video's. A video keeps its look when the assistant rewrites it: its template, or free style, until a template is chosen.

To make your own, duplicate a template and change it: its palette in the Design editor, its rules under Configuration > Advanced (JSON) in extra_metadata.video (see Templates). A template change restyles the next render of every video wearing it.

docs.title: Recordings and browser profiles
docs.text:
A recording is captured in the platform's own headless browser - nothing to install - at a high resolution (2400x1350 by default), with human pacing: the cursor glides to each element, typing has a natural rhythm, scrolling is smooth and steady (a scroll step can be given how long it takes, else it moves at the recording's pace; a header pinned while the page scrolls under it, and what the page draws over a graph it zooms, stay exactly as painted on every frame): the wheel turns once a frame of the recording, the same distance each time - 1200 px over 2 seconds is 120 turns of 10 px at 60 fps - and a scroll to the top or the bottom of the page moves it the same way, never by the browser's own smooth scroll. A browser paints a page that large only a few times a second, so while a step scrolls, the recording notes where the page stands 60 times a second and draws the scroll again at 30 frames a second (60 for a video rendered at 60 fps) from what the browser painted: a scroll plays smooth on a screen insert, whatever the size it was recorded at - the page's own scroll or a panel of it that scrolls on its own, a page that repaints slowly included, which scrolls at the pace the wheel turned however late it paints, never repeating a frame it painted late. A scroll over a graph the page draws itself, in 2D or with WebGL - a knowledge graph, a report graph - zooms the graph instead: the wheel then turns at the recording's frame rate, each turn painted before the next, and the zoom is drawn again at that rate from what the browser painted, the toolbars over the graph left still. A hover, a click or typing that fades a tooltip in or opens a menu is drawn again the same way, over the time its animation lasts. A scroll the browser painted at the recording's rate but unevenly - a frame repeated, then one twice as far, the move-move-hold cadence that reads as judder - is drawn again at that rate too. Each scroll keeps how evenly it moves from one frame to the next (the rate it was painted at, the largest, mean and spread of its distance a frame), and a step whose spread exceeds half its mean is said as stepping motion in its recording's action log. The assistant is told the frame rate each recording plays at ("scrolls at 30 fps (27 frames a second synthesised between keyframes)"), and each scroll and animation step's own (the rate the browser painted it at, whether it was drawn again, and the panel it scrolled), and a recording whose scrolls or animations play under 24 frames a second is a finding when you save a video that shows it, naming the step ("take 38f88e75 carries 2.1 fps on step 3 (scroll): scrolls will step"): record it again - with the seconds it gives for a scroll faster than the page could paint. A frame the browser hands over at another size or scale than the rest of the recording (painted while a graph of the page was read, not what the page showed) is dropped, the frame before held in its place, and the recording's answer lists each run (step, time, frames). Frames that still draw the page at another scale during a wait, a pause, a highlight or a hover, between two frames that are alike, are a capture fault, not a motion of the page: the recording's answer says "off-scale frames at step 24 (pause, 103.0-103.4 s, 0.4 s, 2 frame(s))", and saving a video that shows them is a finding on each scene playing them, naming the frames: record that take again rather than slow it. When a step does not find what it looks for, the assistant is told the closest names the page offered and what the page was filtered by then (a search term a list page kept, the parameters of its address). Each recording keeps its action log (what was clicked, where, when), which is what the camera, the cursor and the callouts are drawn from. Sensitive parts of a page can be blurred in every frame or hidden (a cookie banner). Recordings are made by the assistant from a step script: Record a new flow with the assistant in the editor's Media tab asks it. A step marked optional (a banner that may not show) gives up after 3 seconds instead of 15, and the time it spent looking is cut from the video, whatever the idle setting. A wait after a click that opens another page or switches a tab holds until the page has loaded - no progress bar or spinner left, the page and its graphs still for half a second - up to 10 seconds past the time it asked for, and the assistant is told when the page settled. A spinner or a placeholder shimmer drawn by an animation that never ends counts as loading too, as long as it moves on screen, even when nothing else on the page changes; an element of the page's own that always animates holds such a wait until its timeout, and the assistant is told so it can turn the wait's settling off. A wait, a pause or a highlight whose frames still show a page loading (a progress bar, a graph not drawn yet) is pointed out to the assistant with the recording ("step 5 holds on a loading page for 2.1 s"), so it records it again before using it, and is noted as advice when you save a video that shows it. When the assistant looks at a page before scripting a recording, it is told how long the page took to settle once it opened, so it gives its waits the time the page needs. A step choosing an option works on any list, not only a classic drop-down: a picker such as a tenant or organisation selector is opened, the option is found by the name it shows (typed first in a picker you search in), and the cursor moves to it and clicks it; the camera frames the picker and its choice. An option the list does not have stops the recording naming the options it offered. A step naming an element by its role and name also finds it under a close role - a menu entry that toggles (menuitemcheckbox) for a menuitem, a switch for a checkbox, a tree entry for an option, and a menu entry for a button when its name is exact and unique - its own role first; the action log says which role it matched. A recording lasts 5 minutes at most (VIDEO_STUDIO_MAX_TAKE_SECONDS): before it starts, its script is timed (its waits, its actions, its typing), and one that would take more than 90% of that is refused, naming the step that crosses the limit and the last marker before it to split the script at. A recording that still reaches the limit - a page slower than expected - is kept up to there, ready (truncated at step N), with its contact sheet. A recording never types a password: a step typing into a password field, or typing one of the profile's stored credentials, is refused (its action log would keep what it typed) - keep the credentials on the browser profile, which signs in by itself. The contact sheet the assistant checks a recording with - and every poster or screen it shows you - is a file of the conversation, so it opens again when you come back to the conversation later.

To record an application you sign in to, use a browser profile (Tools & Integrations > Browser profiles, or Browser profiles at the top of Work > Videos): the start URL, the sign-in URL if it differs, the account to use, and the session its sign-in saved. The same profiles let your agents browse the application signed in; their sign-in, MFA, sessions and timeouts are described on that page.

A recording can act on a graph the page draws itself (a knowledge graph, an attack path), where nodes and links are not elements a step can name. A click, double-click, right-click, hover, drag or wheel step may act on a point of the page - in pixels of the window, or relative to an element such as the graph (0.5, 0.5 is its centre, so the point holds whatever the window's size) - or on a node by its label. Nothing is needed from the application filmed - any release, any instance, a third-party tool: the recorder finds the node's entry in the list a graph keeps for screen readers (one entry per node, invisible on screen), reads the label painted under the node on the graph, and when it cannot read it (labels overlapping, a dense cluster, a graph zoomed out too far to show labels) makes that entry the active one, as a keyboard user does, and takes the node the graph highlights. It does so again before every step, so a node moved by a pan, a zoom or a new layout is followed, and the recording's log says how each node was found and where the cursor acted on it - for a recording that stopped too. A label drawn on a link (along it, turned with it or in italic) and a card that repeats the node's name over the graph are never taken for the node's label. The cursor glides to the node and rests on it a quarter of a second, as a person hovering before a right-click does, then clicks; a right-click notes the menu it opened and checks it is the node's - the graph heads it with the node's name - so a right-click beside the node stops the recording right there, saying what the menu was headed with and where the cursor was, with a picture of the graph marking that point in the contact sheet; a drag moves smoothly to where it releases (a lasso, a node moved, another node), a wheel zooms, and keys can be held meanwhile (Control + click adds to a selection). The camera zooms on a node clicked as it does on a button. A label the graph's list does not hold stops the recording naming its three closest entries; a node neither painted nor highlighted on the graph stops it too, saying which, with a picture of the graph in the contact sheet. A step on an entry of the list a graph keeps for screen readers only stops the recording at that step, naming the node step to use instead: a click there would land beside the graph.

Animations are captured at the recording's frame rate. Before the first step, the recording measures how fast this server can capture frames of its size. When it cannot keep up with the recording's frame rate, the recording is made at pixel ratio 1.5 if that keeps up (the assistant is told). Otherwise it is refused, naming the largest window and pixel ratio this server was measured to keep up at (measured then, or remembered from the recordings made on it in the last 15 minutes) and, for a 60 fps recording, 30 fps at the size asked when that keeps up. The assistant can ask for either fallback in advance, so the recording is made on it instead of being refused, and the recording says which it used. When the server is busy with other work - scene previews, a render or another recording - and that is what keeps it from keeping up, the recording is not refused: it waits in the recording lane of the render queue, and starts by itself once that work has eased enough to keep up. Meanwhile the assistant says its place in the lane, the recordings ahead of it and what it waits for ("busy: 2 scene previews and 1 render on its worker"); once made, the recording says how long it waited. A recording is refused only when the server itself cannot keep up with nothing else running, or after waiting six hours; that refusal names the work that was still running, and asking again queues it once more. A recording whose server was stopped under it (a deploy, a restart) is not charged a retry for it: one whose steps were done is finished from the frames it captured, its steps not played again, and says so; one started again from its script on a server that cannot yet keep up with its frame rate waits up to 30 minutes in the recording lane for one that can, instead of being refused. Scene previews always give way to a recording, never the reverse. A graph the page draws itself, in 2D or with WebGL, is drawn on the server's GPU when it has one, and by the browser's software GPU otherwise, so it animates on a server without one too, more slowly: the recording says which (GPU GL or software GL). The recording keeps how many frames it captured each second and each step's rate, and a stretch where the page animated at under 20 frames a second for more than a second is said when it is made and when you save a video showing it (low capture rate at step 4 (12 fps for 2.3 s)): record it again. Each such graph is also measured on its own: every transition it plays (a graph laid out again) is listed at its step in the recording's action log, naming the graph's element, how long it moved and the rate it was captured at, and one under 20 frames a second is said the same way, however short (low capture rate at step 4, with the graph's element, its rate, how long it moved and software GL). Drawn by the software GPU, it is recorded faster only on a server with a GPU: your administrator can add one (see the deployment's "Sizing the workers"). A recording scene played slowed down (speed under 1) over such a stretch blends the frames on either side instead of holding each one longer. On a server without a GPU, a 60 fps recording of a graph steps on its transitions: the recording says so when it is made and offers 30 fps, which halves the frames each transition has to fill. When you save, each such transition is said on every scene that shows it, in one check: a brief one painted fast enough to still read as motion is advice, a longer one or one that holds a frame on screen for more than a quarter of a second is a finding the render waits for. The finding offers slowing the scene only where the recording kept the frames to blend there.

The assistant looks before it records: it can open a page of the signed-in application in the profile's saved session, without typing anything or running a step, and read its screenshot and the names of what can be clicked or typed in - the names the menu really shows ("Agentic Flow", not "Flows") - so the recording's steps find their elements the first time. It looks at the page in the same clean state a recording starts in (below), so the names it reads are the names the recording finds. A step that still misses its element is reported with the three closest names the page offered at that moment, the page's address and title, and how many elements of that kind it showed; when one of your recent recordings with the same profile found that element, the report says which one and at which address ("the page is in another state"). The contact sheet keeps the frame where the step failed, also for a recording the failure stopped.

Every recording starts from a clean page state. An application often remembers how you left a page: a graph's layout, a list's filters, kept in the browser's storage and sometimes written into the page's address. A browser profile's saved session would carry that from one recording to the next, so a recording that changed a graph's layout would leave the next one on a page its steps were not written for. Once the session is checked, each recording opens its start page exactly as given, after clearing what the application kept in the browser's storage for that site. Cookies are never cleared, and neither are the storage keys the profile lists as part of its sign-in (keep_storage_keys, on the browser profile). The first line of the recording's action log says what was cleared and the address the recording opened on. The assistant can keep the page state as the session carried it, choose what is cleared, or clear it again before a step that opens a page. When clearing the storage signs the application out, the recording stops and says so, naming the keys it cleared: list the sign-in keys on the profile.

Recordings start signed in, or not at all: every recording checks the session before its first step. When it has ended, a profile that can sign in by itself (its password and TOTP secret, or the identity provider's saved session) signs in again first; otherwise the recording stops with profile not authenticated: landed on <page> and makes no video - sign the profile in, then record again. Some applications show their sign-in page for a moment while they read the session, then open: the recording waits for the application to show signed in (the element or the address you set on the profile, else the same check as the session check) and starts only then, so its first frame is the application, never its sign-in page. An application that does not open signed in within the profile's sign-in timeout stops the recording the same way. A recording may use any profile you may use; the profile does not need to be given to the assistant.

Recordings reach public addresses only, unless an administrator allows browser profiles on private networks and the profile declares the hosts.

Screen inserts are checked on every frame: a render reads every frame of each screen insert it draws - a stroke of the inserted page seen through the person in front, a ghost of the mask, a halo, a frame off the bezel - not only its first, middle and last frames, and fails on a defect that lasts a few frames. Its quality report says, per insert, how many of its frames were read (every frame or sampled) and when its worst frame is. To look at an insert whole, ask the assistant for an insert sweep: one picture per scene, the insert's region at 100 % every second (or the step you ask), each moment labelled with its time and the failing ones framed in red.

docs.title: AI shots, voice-over and music
docs.text:
• AI shots are animated footage generated by a video model - an opening shot, b-roll behind a statement, a place or people at work that sets the scene - optionally starting from a picture or from a frame of your own footage, so the shot opens on something real. That frame can be an image, a step of a recording (the frame its contact sheet shows after that step), a moment of an uploaded or rendered video, or the last frame of a recording or of another shot, which the new shot then continues: placed right after that footage, it carries on from where the footage stops. Ask the assistant for it ("start a shot from the dashboard step of my recording"). Before it pays for the shot, the assistant looks at that frame and moves it if it is not the right picture; a page caught still loading (a spinner, a blank page) is noticed, and the shot starts once the page has settled instead. The frame taken from your footage is kept as a file of the conversation: the assistant shows it with the finished shot, the inspector shows it under First frame with where it was taken, and a shot generated again starts from that same picture, even once the recording is gone. A frame of your footage must have the shot's shape: a landscape recording does not start a vertical shot unless the assistant is asked to crop it, which keeps the middle of the frame at the shot's shape (a picture is used as it is). They are scenes of a video like recordings: generate one from the editor's Media tab (or ask the assistant) and it joins the video at once, shown as being generated until it is ready. They use the video model your administrator chose under Settings > AI Models > Video Generation (see Video generation): Veo on Google Gemini, or what an OpenAI-compatible gateway such as LiteLLM serves (Veo on Vertex AI, Runway); the editor lets you pick another listed model for one shot. A model named for a shot, or for a shot generated again, is made by the provider that lists it - never by the one chosen in Settings - and a model two of your providers offer is made by the one your video's shots of that model are made on (a shot generated again: the one it was made on), else by the one chosen in Settings, and the shot says which - you say which only when neither of them offers it. A model its provider has retired is never offered or used - OpenAI retired its Sora video models on 2026-09-24 - and when no video model is available at all, the assistant says why before it plans the video, and nothing is generated to fail. When a model does not make the size, length or resolution asked, the shot is made at one it does and the shot says so; a provider that is busy or briefly unreachable (its load, an outage, no answer) never fails the shot nor hands it to another model: the shot waits in the queue for that very model and is asked again after 30 s, then 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, then every 10 minutes, for up to a day - the assistant and the inspector say provider busy, next try at 17:45, 3 tries. A provider's rate limit or quota never fails a shot on the spot (see below). A shot is never paid for twice: a generation interrupted by a restart of the platform is picked up where the provider is, and a video already made is kept even if what follows it fails. The platform generates a few shots at a time (four by default, VIDEO_STUDIO_CLIP_CONCURRENCY), so when the assistant asks for more at once, the others wait their turn: the assistant waits for each shot for a few minutes at most (VIDEO_STUDIO_CLIP_INLINE_WAIT_SECONDS), and a shot still being made after that goes on in the background. The assistant is told why - waiting for a free slot, queued at the provider, rate limited - and how far the shot is, and checks on it before rendering.
  • The same subject in every shot: a shot can be given one to three reference pictures - a character, an animal, a garment, a product, a logo - that the video model keeps the same, wherever it stands in the frame: give every shot of a film the same references and the subject no longer changes from shot to shot. A start frame is for continuity (the shot carries on from a picture), reference pictures for consistency. Only some video models take them (Veo 3.1 and Veo 3.1 Fast, without a start frame and at 8 seconds; Kling 3.0 Omni, beside a start frame; Seedance 2 on Runway, without a start frame); the assistant is told which, and a shot asked with references on a model that takes none is refused before anything is paid. A shot generated again keeps its references. A shot is asked in one of three modes - a start frame only, reference pictures only, or both on the models that take them together - and the assistant is told which each time. Generating a shot again switches between them: giving it references on a model that takes one or the other drops its start frame by itself (Start frame dropped); the assistant can also drop the start frame on purpose (start_frame: false), go back to a start frame alone, which drops the references (start_frame: true with the picture to start from: Reference images dropped), or start the shot from another picture or another moment of its footage. The picture it started from stays in the conversation. Before generating many shots at once, the assistant can check them all first (validate_only): every check runs - the model, the references, the start frame and its shape - and the answer says the mode and whether the provider cools; nothing is generated or paid; a combination the model cannot take is refused at once, naming the model and the two ways out.
  • Ingredients - your logo, your product, a character: in place of bare reference pictures, a shot can be given one to three ingredients, each with what it is and, if you like, its name ("the Filigran logo"), and it keeps the picture it starts from on any video model. A model that takes reference pictures beside that start receives them; any other model is told to keep each one exactly as in the picture the shot starts from, so that picture must show them - the assistant composes it first when needed. On such a model a logo is also drawn back onto the finished shot with its own pixels: it is found in the picture the shot starts from (or placed where the assistant says), followed through every frame as the camera moves, and drawn over what the model made of it, so it is never misspelt. It is drawn in exactly one place in every frame: on an object that moves past something else (a mug falling over a table), the surface carrying the logo is followed, never what lies behind it. When the object turns its logo away from the camera (a mug that rolls), the logo fades out over three frames instead of being squeezed into a smear, is not drawn while it faces away, and fades back in where it faces the camera again; an object at rest keeps its logo perfectly still. A shot that loses sight of a logo facing the camera (the camera cuts away, a hand covers it) fails as logo lost, its video kept to look at. Every finished shot is checked for its logo showing twice in a frame: such a shot says logo duplicated at t=... with that frame, and a scene preview or a render of a scene playing it fails until the shot is generated again. The shot says which way its ingredients went (sent, named, composited or tracked), and a shot generated again keeps them.
  • A logo on a subject the shot does not open on. An establishing shot of a building or a street, with the branded subject walking in later, has no logo in the picture it starts from. Give the logo its subject instead: a picture of the subject wearing the logo (a conversation file, or a frame saved from another shot) and, if you like, what to call it ("the cow in the navy blanket"). Once the shot is made, the subject is found in its frames, the surface the logo sits on - the blanket, the garment, the panel - is followed through every frame, and the logo is drawn there with its own pixels, in perspective and under the light of the scene, on every instance of the subject (a herd each wearing it gets one logo each), from the frame it enters to the frame it leaves. This works on every video model, with or without a start picture; a model that takes reference pictures is sent the logo first, and the logo is drawn onto the subject only when that take does not show it as given. A shot whose subject never appears fails as ingredient subject not found; one whose surface cannot be followed past a frame (a hand over it, a fast turn) fails as ingredient surface lost at t=..., that frame kept to look at. The shot says the share of its frames the logo was drawn on. Ask the assistant ("the cow wears our logo on its blanket - it walks into the street shot").
  • Every shot's frames are kept and measured: once a shot is made, its first, middle and last frames are kept with it - the assistant sees them with the shot, the inspector shows them under The shot's frames - with how close its first frame stayed to the picture it started from, the share of that picture's words it still reads, and how far its last frame moved from its first. Ask for a minimum likeness ("keep the first frame close to the screenshot") and a take that drifted further from its picture fails as drifted from reference, its video kept for you to see, to be generated again in place.
  • The same prop or character in every scene: a recurring prop - the branded rug the hero wears, a product, a mascot - tends to drift from one AI shot to the next (a collar appears, the piping changes colour) while every shot passes its own checks, because each is read against its own prompt and start picture only. Give the video references: a picture of the prop or character as it should look (a crop saved from the scene that got it right, with save_video_frame, or a portrait), with a name and, if you like, a few words on what must stay the same. Then name the references each shot's scene must match (consistency).
