Administrators can turn public video links off for the whole platform in Settings > Access and security > Security options (Public video links, or VIDEO_PUBLIC_LINKS_ENABLED=false, see Security options): every link then stops working at once and none can be created; turning the option back on restores the links that were not turned off.

docs.title: Render retention
docs.text:
Every render keeps its own MP4, poster, captions and frames, so a video's renders are kept for a while, not forever. Once a night, a render is deleted with its files when nothing keeps it and its days are over:

  • a failed or cancelled render, 1 day after it ended;

A whole render that fails at one of its checks after its frames were drawn (a picture gate, the frozen-picture watch, any quality check on the finished video) also keeps its drawn frames for 24 hours (RENDER_FAILED_KEEP_SECONDS = 86400). While they are kept, the render says frames kept until <UTC time> in Renders and in the assistant's answer. The next render of the same revision at the same quality, drawn from exactly the same inputs, resumes from them: it draws only the segments missing, its frozen-picture watch goes on where the failed one stood, and its notes say Resumed from kept frames of render <id> at <s> s. A revision that changes what is drawn ignores them and they are deleted; past 24 hours the hourly cleanup deletes them. A successful render keeps no frames beyond its end.

  • a scene preview, 7 days after it ended - and as soon as a new preview of the same scene is ready, which replaces it;
  • an older ready render, one a newer ready render of the same quality replaced, 30 days after it ended.

Never deleted: the newest ready render of each quality (your newest 1080p cut and your newest 4K, say), the current render - the one the library card, the chat card and the public link play - a render in progress, and a render you kept with Keep it in its menu. Administrators set the days (see Render retention). Each render in Renders says what keeps it or until when it is kept.

docs.title: Clean up renders
docs.text:
To free the space at once, Clean up renders in Renders deletes many renders together, with their files. Choose what goes:

  • Everything but the newest ready render of each quality (the default), or keep only the newest render of one quality - your 1080p final, say - and let a 4K draft go too;
  • Failed and cancelled renders;
  • Scene previews;
  • Everything, the newest ready renders too, only once you confirm it: the video then has nothing to play until it is rendered again.

Only renders made before limits the cleanup to older renders. The dialog lists every render the cleanup would delete, keep or refuse, and why, with what it frees, before anything is deleted. A render still in progress is refused (cancel it first), and so is the render the public link plays, unless you confirm it: the link then plays the newest ready render left. On a video shared with you to watch only, you can delete only the renders you asked for. Frames you saved in a conversation stay. Delete, in a render's menu, still removes a single render.

Your assistant does the same when you ask ("delete the old renders of this video, keep the 1080p final"): it can list what would go first, and says what it deleted, how much space it freed and which render the video plays now. Every cleanup is in the audit log.

docs.title: Delete a video
docs.text:
Deleting a video in the Video Studio deletes it for good: there is no trash. Its renders and scene previews go with it, with their files; its recordings and AI shots stay in your library, and the ones no other video uses are deleted after their retention days (see Media and their retention).

Your assistant deletes a video only when you ask it to ("delete the video Launch film"), and only a video you own (an administrator for a company-managed one): a video shared with you is refused. When other people open the video (shared with people or groups, or with a public link on), it asks you to confirm first, since deleting it removes it for them too. A card of the video in a conversation then reads that it is no longer available. Every deletion is in the audit log.

Administrators find every video, whoever made it, under Administration > Objects (filter Videos), see Objects. A video posted in a conversation on another channel (Slack, Teams, email) is a link to its page.

docs.title: Limits and settings
docs.text: Administrators set the recording and video length limits, the number of renders that run at once, the media retention and the ffmpeg location in the deployment configuration (see Video Studio settings), and the render retention in Settings (see Render retention).

docs.title: Publish an agent on a website
Publish an agent on a website
docs.text:
You can put an agent on any website as a chat widget: a floating button in the bottom-right corner of the page that opens a chat panel. Your visitors talk to the agent without an XTM One account and without signing in.

This page covers how to turn the widget on, where to get the embed code, what visitors see, what the agent can do for them, and the limits that apply to anonymous visitors.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need to be able to edit the agent: you own it, it is shared with you with configuration access, or you are an administrator. On a company-managed agent, only administrators can change it.
  • The widget answers only where chat is available. On Community Edition, or when an administrator has turned AI off, visitors get an error instead of an answer. See Editions and licensing.

Anyone can reach the agent

Once the widget is on, anyone who has the embed code, or opens a page that carries it, can chat with the agent. The agent's persona and knowledge bases answer people you do not know. Expose only an agent whose knowledge you are willing to make public.

docs.title: Turn on web exposure
docs.text:
1. Open the agent, then Configuration > Channels & Bots.
  2. In the Web Exposure card, marked Danger Zone, turn on Expose on Web.
  3. If XTM One shows what the change lends to new people, read it and select Enable to go on. See Sharing and access.

The card then shows a Live badge, and Get Embed Code appears for the people who can edit the agent: the embed code chats as the agent's owner, so the people it is shared with read-only see the widget is live, not its code. On the Agents list, the agent carries the Web Exposure indicator, and you can filter the list on it.

Turn Expose on Web off to stop the widget on every site that uses it. The embed code does not change: when you turn the switch back on, the pages that still carry the old code work again.

Copies start without the widget

When you duplicate, clone or export an agent, the copy has web exposure and visitor uploads turned off, and gets its own embed code once you turn them on.

docs.title: Get the embed code
docs.text:
1. Select Get Embed Code. The Embed Code dialog opens.
  2. Select Copy to copy the snippet.
  3. Paste it into your website's HTML, just before the closing </body> tag.

The snippet carries two attributes:

  • data-token is required. It identifies the agent, and it is the only key to it: treat it like a password you chose to publish.
  • data-context is optional. It is a JSON object that describes the page the widget is on, such as the page, the product, the section or the role of the user. The widget sends it with every message, so the agent can adapt its answer. Replace the example values with your own, or remove the attribute.

Keep secrets out of the page context

data-context is written in your page, so every visitor can read it and change it. Use it for hints, never for anything private or for a decision the agent must trust.

There is no list of allowed sites: the widget works on any page that carries its embed code.

docs.title: Add suggested prompts
docs.text:
Suggested prompts are the clickable conversation starters the widget shows under its greeting. They appear in the Web Exposure card once the widget is on.

  • Type a prompt in Add a suggested prompt… and press Enter, or select the plus button.
  • Select Generate with AI to have prompts proposed for you.
  • Remove a prompt with the cross on it.
  • Select Save Prompts to publish your changes, or Cancel to drop them.

docs.title: What visitors see
docs.text:
The widget shows a button in the bottom-right corner of the page. Selecting it opens a panel with:

  • the agent's name, and a greeting with its description and your suggested prompts;
  • New conversation, to start over, and Maximize / Restore default size, to change the panel's size;
  • a box that reads Ask a question…;
  • the reminder that AI can make mistakes, and a "Powered by" line with your platform's name.

The widget's own text is in English. Answers stream as the agent writes them.

A visitor who comes back with the same browser finds their last conversation again, and an answer still being written resumes. Clearing the browser's site data, or selecting New conversation, starts a new one.

docs.title: What the agent can do on the widget
docs.text:
Conversations use the agent's persona and its knowledge bases. A widget conversation is more limited than a chat in XTM One:

  • No integrations, MCP servers or custom tools. The agent cannot act with the tools and credentials it uses elsewhere, so a visitor can never drive them.
  • No approvals. A visitor cannot approve a tool call. If the agent requires approval for a tool, the turn stops with an error instead of waiting.
  • No downloadable files. The agent cannot generate files for the visitor; file generation stays available in authenticated chat.
  • No agent memory. What the agent remembers from its other conversations is never used on the widget.

A message that looks like an attempt to take control of the agent is refused with a polite answer. If an administrator has connected a prompt guard, it can also check visitors' messages and the agent's answers. See Configuration.

docs.title: Let visitors attach files
docs.text:
Visitors can only type until you allow uploads. In the Web Exposure card, turn on Allow visitor uploads. The widget then shows an Attach files button, and visitors can also paste a screenshot or drop a file on the panel.

Uploads are open to anyone

Anyone who can open a page with the widget can send files, without an account. Leave uploads off unless your visitors need them. The security audit lists every widget that allows them.

What a visitor can attach:

  • Types: PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, text and data files (such as .txt, .md, .csv, .json, .xml, .yaml, .log, .html) and images (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp). No SVG, archive, audio or video. Each file is checked against its content, not only its name.
  • Size: 40 MB a file, and at most 10 files and 100 MB per conversation.
  • Budgets: uploads are counted per visitor and per widget each hour. The widget as a whole also has a storage limit across all its conversations.

The agent reads a document as its text and sees an image as a picture.

When a file is refused, the widget shows the reason next to its name: its type, its size, a budget, the storage limit, or the content check. A file refused for what it is leaves the tray. A file the platform cannot take right now, because it is busy or a budget is reached, stays in the tray so the visitor can send again later.

Visitor files belong to their conversation. Only the visitor's own browser downloads them, and on the platform only administrators can open them. They are deleted after a period without new messages in the conversation, 7 days by default. A file never sent with a message is deleted after a day. Turning Allow visitor uploads off stops new uploads; files already attached follow the same deletion rules.

The exact rules, and the retention an administrator can change, are in Visitor uploads on the public chat widget.

docs.title: Limits for anonymous visitors
docs.text:
Visitors have no account, so their use is bounded per visitor address and per widget:

  • 10 new conversations an hour from one address;
  • 30 messages a minute from one address, across all widgets;
  • 20 messages a minute from one address to the same widget.

Every widget message counts against the platform-wide agentic limits, like any other request. When those limits are reached, visitors read This service is at capacity right now. Please try again later. Their use is never attributed to you or to any other user. See Requests with no account.

How visitor addresses are grouped, and what happens when the rate-limit store cannot be reached, are set by an administrator. See Configuration.

docs.title: Review widget conversations
docs.text: Widget conversations appear in the agent's Chats tab, under the Embedded Chat channel, with the other conversations of the agent. You can read them if you own the agent, if it is shared with you with access to its chats, or if you are an administrator. See Agents.

docs.title: When the host site has its own security policy
docs.text:
The widget runs inside the page of the site that embeds it. If that site sends a Content-Security-Policy, the policy must allow what the widget loads, or the widget does not appear or renders unstyled. Give your web team The embeddable chat widget.

An administrator can also make the widget render answers more strictly, showing only the images the platform serves. See Configuration.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Sharing and access to see everyone your agent reaches, or with Agents to put the same agent on Slack, Microsoft Teams or another messaging platform.

docs.title: Webhook triggers
docs.text:
A webhook trigger lets another system start an assignment. Your SIEM raises an alert, your SOAR runs a playbook, your ticketing tool opens a case — each of them can post to a URL, and the agent starts working on what it received.

This page covers where to find that URL, how to authenticate a call to it, and how to wire it up from a SOAR playbook.

docs.title: Find the URL and the secret
docs.text:
Open the agent, find the assignment in the Assignments card, and open it. On the Trigger card of an assignment whose Trigger type is Webhook you will see:

  • Webhook URL — the address the sending system posts to. It already contains the assignment identifier, so there is nothing else to configure.
  • Webhook secret — the credential the sending system must present. Every webhook assignment gets one automatically.
  • How to trigger — a ready-to-paste request you can copy, adapt, and test with before you touch the other system.

Who can see the secret

The secret is only shown to people who can manage the assignment. If the Trigger card shows the URL but no secret, ask whoever owns the assignment for it.

docs.title: Authenticate the request
docs.text:
Send the secret in one of these headers — verbatim, except in the Authorization form, which takes the Bearer prefix:

Header Value X-Webhook-Token the secret, verbatim X-Webhook-Secret the same thing, under the name the Webhook secret label suggests Authorization Bearer <secret>, for senders that only offer standard authentication fields X-OpenCTI-Token the original spelling, still accepted so existing senders keep working — use one of the names above for anything new

This is what almost every SIEM and SOAR webhook action can produce, and it is the scheme to reach for first. A secret with non-ASCII characters is matched whether the sender writes the header in UTF-8 or in latin-1.

If your sender can compute an HMAC over the request body, you can sign it instead and keep the secret off the wire: put the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body in X-Signature. Provider-specific signatures — GitHub, Slack — are recognized as well.

A correct URL is not enough

A request that carries none of these headers is refused with 401, even when the URL and the secret are both right. The most common cause is a header sent under a name that is not on the list above. Every webhook assignment is created with a secret, and administrators can additionally require one platform-wide — see Configuration.

docs.title: Trigger from a Google SecOps SOAR playbook
docs.text:
The native webhook action in a SecOps SOAR playbook only offers a URL and a token, with nowhere to put a header. Use the generic Execute HTTP request action instead, configured like this:

Field Value Method POST URL Path the Webhook URL from the Trigger card Headers {"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Webhook-Token": "<the webhook secret>"} Body Payload the JSON you want the agent to receive, for example {"case_id": "[Case.case_id]", "alert_name": "[Alert.alert_name]"} Fail on 4xx/5xx true Request Timeout 120

Do not paste the secret in clear

Store it in the SecOps SOAR credential store (or an environment parameter) and reference it as a placeholder instead of the literal value. Playbooks are exported, cloned between environments and often committed, and this credential is long-lived and travels on the wire with every delivery. Anyone who obtains a copy can authenticate any body against your assignment until someone rotates the secret. An X-Signature HMAC is bound to the exact body it signed and never puts the secret on the wire at all, so senders that can compute one should prefer it.

Three things to get right:

  • Write plain JSON in Headers and Body Payload. The field expects JSON as-is. Escaping the quotes — {\"Content-Type\": \"application/json\"} — makes the playbook reject the value before the request is ever sent, with a message about an invalid JSON structure.
  • Keep the placeholders inside the quotes. "[Alert.alert_name]" is valid JSON; an unbalanced quote around a placeholder is not, and the request fails for a reason that has nothing to do with XTM One.
  • Leave Fail on 4xx/5xx on. It is what makes a refused or throttled delivery visible in the playbook instead of passing for a success.

docs.title: Event matching
docs.text:
A trigger that selects events - an integration event such as GitHub pull_request, or the events list of a webhook trigger - runs on exactly the events it selects:

  • pull_request runs on pull_request and its actions (pull_request.opened, pull_request.closed, ...), never on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, whose names only start with it.
  • An events entry works the same way: issues.opened matches issues.opened, never issues.opened_by_bot.

A trigger saved on a version before exact matching keeps the prefix match it always had, so nothing that ran before stops running: pull_request also runs on pull_request_review, an events entry also matches any event whose name starts with it, and a GitHub trigger on its dedicated URL runs on every delivery it receives, ping included. It keeps that through every edit that leaves its events alone - a new name, prompt, delay, filter or integration - and through every copy: duplicate, import, catalog clone.

The Trigger card says which mode an assignment uses: Exact event matching with what it runs on, or Legacy event matching with the events it also runs on because of the prefix match. A legacy trigger switches to exact matching when you:

  • choose Use exact matching on its Trigger card, or
  • choose its events again in the trigger editor - another event, provider or trigger type. The editor says so before you save.

Administrators can apply exact matching to every trigger at once: Settings > Access and security > Exact event matching for every trigger, or WEBHOOK_EXACT_EVENT_MATCHING=true, which wins. See Configuration.

Triggers the agent builder created before this version

The agent builder used to store an integration event under event_type, a key the platform does not read: such a trigger runs on every event its provider delivers by webhook, and a polled one (a new email, a new message) never runs. It keeps behaving that way until you choose Use exact matching on its Trigger card: it then runs only on the event it names, and a polled one starts with its next new event. The Trigger card and the security audit point these triggers out.

docs.title: When something does not arrive
docs.text:
Read the response the sending system got:

What you see What it means 401 Missing webhook signature… No recognized credential header. Check the header name first — the secret is usually fine. The rest of the message lists the headers you can send. 401 Invalid webhook token A token header is right, its value is not. Copy the secret again from the Trigger card. 401 Invalid webhook bearer token Same, for the Authorization: Bearer form. 401 Invalid webhook signature The body was signed with a different secret, or the signature was computed over a modified body. 429 Too many deliveries, or too many already waiting. Retry after the delay given in the response. "status": "ignored" The delivery was accepted but matched nothing — the assignment is disabled, deleted, or not a webhook assignment. "reason": "event not selected" A GitHub delivery to the dedicated URL of an integration-event assignment that matches exactly, for an event its trigger does not select. Check the event on the Trigger card, or the events the GitHub webhook sends (see Event matching).

Everything that did start is in Operations, including runs still waiting behind an active one. An assignment runs up to ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS deliveries at once (10 by default, or its trigger's max_concurrent_runs), so a delivery arriving while they are all going is queued rather than lost, and starts as soon as one ends. A pushed integration event arriving then - a GitHub delivery to an integration-event assignment, for example - is skipped instead, unless an administrator turned on INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED; a polled one (an email, a Teams or Slack message) always waits in the queue. See Webhook delivery.

Administrators can tune the delivery limits, the queue depth, and the de-duplication window — see Configuration.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Operations to follow what your triggered runs actually did, with Assignments and triggers for the other triggers, or with Agents if you still have to create the agent behind the assignment.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Operations is where you review what agents have already done and what they are working on. It is the operational record for runs, waiting items, notifications, and failures.

docs.title: What Operations is for
docs.text:
Use Operations when you want to:

  • check whether a task is still running
  • review a completed result
  • respond to a request for human input
  • isolate notifications or digests
  • follow work that moved between agents

docs.title: Open Operations
docs.text:
Choose Work > Operations from the left sidebar. The Work group gathers what your agents produce — Operations (their runs), Presentations (their decks) and Files (their outputs and your uploads) — and the Work hub page shows the three at a glance.

Operations opens on its Executions tab, which is the run history described in this chapter. The other tabs — Background Tasks, Work Items, Shared State, Worksets — cover the delegations, durable work items, cross-run state and corpora your agents coordinate through. The last one, Workspaces, lists the environments that group conversations and keep that coordination apart per topic (see Workspaces). An agent builds a workset when it carries the Coordination built-in tools, chosen in the Built-in Tools card of its configuration: on an assignment the corpus belongs to that assignment and the person it runs as, and is kept between its runs; in a chat each agent has its own corpus, one per person and per workspace. A company-managed agent's chat corpus is itself company-managed, so whatever you add through that chat is listed in Worksets for every user, just like the work items and shared state such an agent produces. When an admin makes an agent company-managed, the worksets it has already built (on its assignments and in its chats) become company-managed with it, and they go back to their owners alone when it is made private again. Its automatic summaries stop at a call budget per corpus, after which the agent has to write the missing ones.

Some agents keep one corpus per conversation instead, such as the built-in FIMI Analyst. What such an agent reads in a chat is yours alone, whether or not the agent is company-managed. It is kept apart from your other conversations and deleted 30 days after the agent last used it. An agent with a workset can also send the whole result of a search or a listing into its corpus instead of reading it in the conversation. It then gets back only a receipt: how many items were stored, which were left out and why, and which dates it could not read. It reads the stored items with its workset tools, which keeps long sources cheap to go through.

Note

Agents chatted with before each one got its own corpus wrote into a single shared corpus per person. That older corpus is no longer read by chats; it stays listed under Worksets until you delete it.

Every tab has the same visibility control, after the search box: Mine | Company | Shared | All, the control of every list page of XTM One. With no segment in the address (?vis=), a tab opens on the first segment holding a row: Mine, else Company, else Shared, else All. A segment named in the address always wins, an empty Mine included.

  • Mine is what you are responsible for: what you created, and what the agents you own created or own.
  • Shared is the work of agents shared with you, directly or through a group, that is neither yours nor company-managed.
  • Company is the work of company-managed agents and runs that is not yours.
  • All is everything you can see.

A background task always belongs to the person who started it and is never shared, so Background Tasks offers Mine and All only; All is every user's tasks for an administrator and your own for anyone else. When Mine holds nothing but other segments do, the tab says so and offers Show all. Your choice is kept in the page address as ?vis=, so going back or sharing the link keeps it, and the counts follow it. An older link that carries ?ownership= or ?scope= still opens: ?ownership=shared (or company_managed), which used to list shared and company-managed work together, opens on All so it hides none of it, and the other values open the segment they named. The address switches to ?vis= on your next change.

Work items and shared state written by a company-managed agent are company-managed: everyone who can use that agent sees them, and they are read-only for everyone else. Only company-managed agents (whoever they are working for) and administrators can change them, claim them or delete them; a company-managed flow can also claim and settle the company-managed work items its work-item trigger picks up. Your own agents and flows can read them but not change them, and on these tabs only an administrator can resolve, complete or delete a company-managed entry, including one created while you were chatting with a company-managed agent.

A company-managed agent can narrow this for what it produces: its Coordination access, in the Built-in Tools card of its configuration, says which agents can read and which can change the work items it creates and the shared state it owns - everyone and every company-managed agent (the default), selected company-managed agents, or only itself. An agent that can change them can always read them, and the agent a work item is assigned to, and the agent that claimed it, can always work on it. An agent left out of an entry never sees it, so two groups of agents narrowed to themselves can each use the same key for their own entry. The setting applies at once to what the agent already created. It only concerns agents: these tabs show the same rows as before, and administrators keep full access.

docs.title: Reading a work item
docs.text:
Each row of the Work Items tab names the agent that owns the item (the one expected to act on it), the agent that created it, the chat, assignment run or flow run it came from, and the person it acts for. An agent that is not shared with you is shown as an agent you cannot open, never by name, and so is a run or a chat you cannot open. Filter the list by owner agent with the picker next to the status filters.

The view switch at the end of the toolbar shows the items as a list, as cards or as a Graph of what depends on what, and keeps your choice. The graph draws the items the filters, the scope and the search match: an arrow goes from an item to what it waits for (another item, a pull request, an issue, a deployment, a workflow run, or the person a decision card asks), a dashed line from a program to its items. An item a filtered-out item waits for is drawn with a dashed border so the chain does not stop short. Done and cancelled items are hidden until you show them, and items with no dependency are counted under the toolbar rather than drawn. Select a node to light the chain it waits for and the chain that waits for it; an item only a person can release has a red border. The open button of a node opens the same details as the list.

A badge says what will act on the item:

  • Picked up automatically: an inbox (an assignment or a flow triggered by work items) drains the owner agent's queue and takes the item within about a minute. Picked up once due is the same for an item with a due date still to come.
  • No automatic pickup: no inbox drains the owner agent's queue, so the item waits until someone asks that agent to process its work items, or completes it by hand.
  • Not picked up: filtered out: the owner agent has an inbox, but its minimum priority or correlation key prefix leaves this item out.
  • Unassigned: nothing picks it up: no owner agent is set.
  • Being worked on and Blocked: not picked up: an agent holds the item, or it was blocked, for example after repeated failed dispatches.
  • Waiting for CI on #N: the item names an open pull request whose CI is still running. When the CI completes, the platform hands the item to its owner agent at once, with the conclusion and a link to the run. An item that also waits for other work items keeps showing Blocked on N items: the CI end only adds a note, and the item goes back to the queue when those items are done.

docs.title: Pull requests on a work item
docs.text:
A work item can name the pull requests it waits on, in payload.pull_requests (repo as owner/name and number). An agent fills this in when it opens a pull request for the item: the GitHub create_github_pr tool takes an optional work_item_id. Each row links to its pull requests.

When the GitHub integration's signed webhook receives the CI events of a pull request (workflow_run, check_suite, pull_request), the item reacts:

  • CI completed: once every CI run of the head commit has completed, or one has failed, the item is handed to its owner's work-item inbox at once. The run's trigger context has reason: pr_ci_completed, the conclusion and the run link. If a live run already holds the item, that run gets a dated note instead of a second run being started. The same head commit and conclusion dispatch only once: a repeated delivery, or another workflow failing or cancelled on a head already red, is dropped and counted on the pull request's CI record (dropped); a re-run of a workflow (a new attempt of the same run) that concludes wakes the item once more, red or green, and a late delivery of an older attempt is ignored. A run is counted as concluded only once it reports both completed and a conclusion. A run that does not test the pull request's own CI (on GitHub, a pull_request_target run such as a branch deploy, or a third-party app's check suite, which can finish before the workflows of the head are even requested) or a skipped check can fail a head but never makes it green alone: the head is green once at least one of its own CI runs succeeded and none is left running. When no CI delivery came, the live read also waits for every check the base branch requires to report.
  • New commits: the CI of the previous head no longer counts.
  • Draft or ready: the item records whether each pull request is a draft, when it is opened or pushed to and when it is marked ready or turned back into a draft. If an inbox run ends with the item still open on a pull request, the item waits for that pull request's merge or closing. A draft is the exception, because it is waiting for a review before it is marked ready. If its CI is still running, the item is blocked with a reason that names the CI completion, and that completion hands it back. If its CI has already completed, the item goes back in the queue a little later. The run's end reads each open pull request live first (draft or ready, its head, its CI), so a pull request marked ready during the run is seen. When a UX review round is open on the pull request, draft or ready, the item waits for that round's verdict, not for the CI or the merge. When a ready pull request's CI already finished green and no completion is left to hand the item back, it goes back in the queue at once for its next step. An item the run left blocked stays blocked.
  • CI read when no event came: an item blocked with only a reason (nothing else releases it) on an open pull request is not left waiting for a CI event that never comes, for example when the webhook is unsigned or the head was made by merging the base branch. A few minutes after the item goes quiet, the platform reads the pull request's current head and its checks with the owner's credential. Once every check of that head has completed, or one has failed, the item is handed to its owner's inbox as if the CI event had come, once per head and conclusion, with a note saying it was read.
  • Merged or closed: the item gets a dated note. If its payload sets complete_on_merge: true, it is completed with the merge SHA once every pull request it names is merged. An item blocked on its pull requests alone (a reason only, no blocking item, no open reference, no person to answer) goes back to the queue once none of them is open any more.
  • Items waiting for it: when the pull request is on a repository whose deployments the platform observes (WORK_ITEM_DEPLOYMENT_REPOSITORIES), every item blocked on this one also waits for the pull request's deployment, with a note saying so. It is put back in the queue by the first running build that carries the merge, not by this item's completion at the merge.

This needs the GitHub integration's webhook with a signing secret and the workflow_run, check_suite and pull_request events. An unsigned delivery is ignored.

A note added to an item while an agent run is working on it reaches that run: the run sees it before its next step, marked as a new note on the item it holds, so a "duplicate, stop here" note written by another agent or by you takes effect at once. A note the run writes itself is not sent back to it. When no run is working on the item, the note simply stays on the item for the next run to read.

Open a row for the full picture: why you see the item (yours, company-managed, or filed in a workspace you can see), each inbox with whether it takes the item, the full description, result and payload, its timeline, and when the retention sweep would cancel an item nobody picks up or delete a finished one.

Mark done and Cancel work item ask for confirmation and let you record what was done, or why it is no longer needed. Put back in the queue reopens a claimed, blocked or finished item with its claim and failed dispatch attempts cleared, so an inbox can take it again. An item can wait for other work items (blocked_on, set by the agent that creates or updates it): it shows Blocked on 1 item (or more) with each item it waits for linked by its title, is never flagged stale, and goes back to the queue by itself once every one of them is done, at the very write that finishes the last one (an agent's update that drops one still open while the item stays blocked is refused, the item named, unless it passes drop_open_blockers); if one of them is cancelled, the item goes back to its owner with a surfaced: note naming the cancelled item (references it still waits for keep it blocked). When an item it waits for already names a pull request on a repository whose deployments are observed, it waits for the build that carries that pull request, whichever was written first. An item waiting for a check (a retest) can ask to go back only when it passed: with blocked_on_release_on set to passed, it reopens once every item it waits for is done with the verdict PASS (the optional verdict of complete_work_item: PASS, FAIL or INCONCLUSIVE); one done FAIL, INCONCLUSIVE or without a verdict keeps it blocked, with the claim note still blocked: <id> completed FAIL, and no run starts on it. An item can also wait for pull requests or issues (blocked_on_refs: the repository, the number and whether it waits for the merge, the close or either): it goes back to the queue by itself once every one of them merged or closed as asked, with a dated released: line on top of its description that gives the time the code host states for the merge or the close and, when later, the time of the release (released: owner/name#12 merged at 2026-11-04T00:59:04Z; released at 2026-11-04T01:22:19Z); a pull request closed without a merge that the item wanted merged keeps it blocked, with a claim note. An item can also wait for a change to be live (blocked_on_refs with kind deployment, naming a pull request or a commit): it waits for the merge first, then for the first build of the platform that contains the merged commit, and goes back to the queue within a minute of that build starting; meanwhile its Waits for line reads deployment of owner/name#12 (merged 1a2b3c4, not in build <version>), and its released: line names the build. Nothing polls for it: the check runs when a new build starts and once when the item is blocked. An inbox takes a released item 45 seconds after the release (its not_before, which the released: line names), so the run that merged the pull request completes the item itself instead of a second run being started on it. The release follows the code host's events at once; for a repository that sends none, or a pull request that merged before the item was blocked on it, the platform also reads the state of the references itself every few minutes, with the item owner's own access to the code host, so the item is released within about five minutes. A blocked item is black or white: setting Blocked needs an owner agent and something that releases it, either the items or references it waits for, an open pull request bound to the item (its CI completion hands it back), or a person's decision (needs_human with an ask card: the question, at least two options and a recommendation); it is refused otherwise. A reason in words (blocked_reason) is context, never the blocker; an item deferred to later stays open with a not_before. An item it waits for that is cancelled hands it back to its owner. An item blocked before this rule keeps its state, and the fleet health lists it until it is given a real blocker or reopened. A claim made by an assignment run or a background task is held by that run: when the run ends without finishing the item (it failed, timed out, was cancelled or was stopped by a platform restart), the item goes back to the queue on its own within a minute, with a dated note saying which run released it, and its description and progress are kept; another run that claims it in the meantime takes it over, while an item held by a run still working stays refused to everyone else. Another agent run cannot take such an item either: its update or completion that puts it back to Open, blocks it or finishes it is refused, naming the holding run, unless it passes take_over; then the write lands, the claim goes, a finished_under_holder claim note says who did it, and the holding run is told to stop at its next step: a pause it is in ends at once with the stop, whether it is an assignment run, a background task, or a run that claimed the item mid-run. From then on that run's updates and completions on the item, a note included, are refused with the same stop, naming the item's state and its new holder, unless it passes take_over to take it back. A person's change goes through the same way without the flag. Adding a note or changing the priority never needs it from another run. A claim that names no run (made in a chat, or before runs were recorded) goes back to the queue the same way once the item has been quiet for 10 minutes and its agent has no run still working that started before the claim; an item put back to Open by hand loses its claim at once. An item whose holding run has ended is no longer shown as held or being worked on. Items created before this view existed show no origin: it was not recorded then.

docs.title: What the agent working on an item receives
docs.text:
The agent an item is assigned to reads it in full: its whole description, its payload, its result and the files attached to it. When an inbox picks the item up, the run it starts receives all of it. An agent that creates a work item in a chat or a run can attach up to 10 files of that chat or run (a file you uploaded, a file an agent generated or downloaded) rather than copying their content into the description. The agent working on the item can open them whatever chat or run it works in, and no agent that cannot see the item can. Each file stays in the chat or run it came from.

The Executions tab shows runs across your visible agents. It is designed for filtering first and investigation second.

docs.title: Use the main filter tabs
docs.text:
At the top of the page, XTM One provides quick filter tabs.

You can switch between:

  • All
  • Notifications
  • Digests
  • Running
  • Awaiting input
  • Completed
  • Failed
  • Cancelled

These tabs are the fastest way to narrow the page to the type of work you care about.

docs.title: Use the other filters
docs.text:
In addition to the main tabs, you can refine the list with:

  • search
  • visibility
  • agent selection
  • fleet selection

The Fleet filter (All fleets by default) keeps the runs of the fleet's current home members, its orchestrator included and its connected agents left out. The same filter sits on Background Tasks (tasks whose delegating or delegated agent is a home member), Work Items (owned or created by a home member), Shared State and Worksets (owned by a home member). Membership is read when the list loads, so a member added or removed counts at once. With a fleet chosen, the agent selection offers its home members only, the run type is the members' assignment runs, and Select all matching is not offered for a bulk delete. The fleet is kept in the address (?fleet=), so a link reopens the same filtered list. The Operations view of a fleet page and the Operations tab of a workspace have no Fleet filter: their lists are already locked on the fleet or the workspace.

Visibility has four segments:

  • Mine
  • Shared
  • Company
  • All

This is useful when you work in a shared environment and only want to focus on your own workload, on runs shared with you, or on the company-managed runs.

docs.title: Understand the run cards
docs.text:
Each run card gives you a quick status summary.

You may see:

  • the agent name
  • the assignment or run title
  • a short summary
  • the current state
  • the creation time
  • delegation indicators

Typical states include:

  • running
  • awaiting human input
  • completed
  • failed
  • cancelled — a run cut by the emergency stop carries the cause Stopped by an emergency stop.

docs.title: Notifications and digests
docs.text:
The Notifications and Digests filters are there for communication-oriented runs.

Use them when you want to:

  • review automated updates sent by the platform
  • separate digest-style outputs from normal task runs
  • find communication outputs without scanning every run

docs.title: When a run is waiting for you
docs.text:
Some runs pause and ask for human input.

When that happens:

  • the run appears under Awaiting input
  • the run detail page shows the question or pending action
  • you can respond directly from the run
  • you can dismiss the waiting item if it is no longer needed

This is the main place where human approval or clarification appears in the UI.

docs.title: When an integration resource goes missing
docs.text:
An assignment can keep pointing at something its integration can no longer see - a Notion database that was deleted, moved, or is no longer shared with the integration. A single miss can be a typo in one run, so it changes nothing. When the integration reports the same resource missing in two separate runs, the platform treats it as the assignment's configuration:

  • the run that used it again is marked failed with the cause Integration resource missing, and its error names the resource and the integration; whatever the agent produced stays in the result
  • the assignment owner gets one notification when this starts, not one per run
  • after a few consecutive scheduled runs like this (three by default), the assignment is paused; the assignment page shows why, and Resume switches it back on

To fix it, share the resource with the integration again, or update the assignment so it no longer uses it, then resume the assignment. Resuming starts a fresh count, and a scheduled run that succeeds ends the episode. Only a resource the agent used counts: an id it only read along the way - the target of a relation, a child block, a search result - never fails a run.

docs.title: When an assignment's owner is deactivated
docs.text:
While an administrator has disabled the account that owns an assignment, nothing starts that assignment unless it is company-managed - an assignment whose agent is shared with a group or a person pauses too: not its schedule, webhooks, integration events or work items, not a chained assignment or a retry, not a flow step, and not a manual run, whoever asks - an administrator included. The assignment page and the agent's assignment list show it as paused because its owner's account is deactivated.

  • nothing about the assignment itself changes: its own on / off switch and any pause its owner set are kept, so re-enabling the account resumes it exactly as it was, and a schedule that came due meanwhile runs once, as after a resume
  • a run that was already waiting to start (a delayed run, a queued webhook delivery, a retry) is marked skipped with the reason when it would have started; a run in progress finishes, but one that stopped to wait (for a partner's answer, for example) is marked skipped - stopped before resuming - when it would go on
  • a webhook delivery to it is answered ignored with the reason; a question it asked stays pending until the account is back (dismissing it still works)
  • company-managed assignments are not affected: they keep running even when the administrator who created them is deactivated
  • to keep one running while the account stays disabled - a shared agent other people rely on, for example - an administrator transfers its agent to an active owner or makes the agent company-managed

docs.title: Open a run detail page
docs.text:
Click any run to open the detailed view.

The run detail page usually includes:

  • the run title
  • the status
  • the agent
  • the trigger that started the run
  • timestamps for created, started, and completed states
  • shortcuts to the related agent, assignment, or parent run

docs.title: Review the result
docs.text:
For completed runs, the detail page helps you understand what happened.

Depending on the run, you may see:

  • a final summary
  • tool actions
  • intermediate reasoning or step history
  • output sent to another system
  • child runs created through delegation

This makes the page useful both for everyday checking and for troubleshooting.

docs.title: When a run stopped before it was done
docs.text:
A run can end on one of its limits rather than because the agent finished: it used all its Max iterations, its timeout ran out, the run budget cut its answer short, the model did not answer in time, or delegated tasks were still running when it stopped waiting. The agent still writes up what it has, so the run is completed and keeps that result, but the Result card says it is partial and names the limit, instead of showing it as a finished task.

For a run that used all its iterations, check the assignment's Max iterations first: when the assignment sets its own value, it is the one the run uses, whatever the agent's value is. The assignment page shows the value it uses, marked Inherited when it takes the agent's or the platform's.

docs.title: What the run struggled with
docs.text:
A run that met difficulties shows a Frictions card on its page, with the number of frictions it recorded: what this run struggled with, and what carries each fix. The card is shown only for a run that recorded at least one, and lists up to 50, the oldest first.

Each row names:

  • the kind of friction, as the platform writes it: a tool error (tool_error), a retry, an approval pause, a sandbox or runner failure, a friction the agent recorded itself (manual), and a few others;
  • the tool involved, when there is one, and Met N times when the run met the same friction more than once;
  • its class, once the friction has been classified;
  • what carries its fix: a work item, a shared state entry, a skill or prompt edit, each with its reference, or accepted when the behaviour is fine as it is. A friction nobody has dealt with yet reads Undisposed, and the card's header counts them.

Evidence unfolds the error or the call as it was recorded.

The platform records every tool error a run meets by itself, and the same error met again counts once more on the same row instead of adding one. An agent that carries the Coordination built-in tools can also record a friction, list the frictions of its runs, and classify one and name what carries its fix. Use the card to see why a run took longer than expected, or which fixes are still owed.

docs.title: Rate the result
docs.text:
Once a run has completed or failed, the Result card asks Was this result useful? with a thumbs up and a thumbs down, like the buttons under an answer in the chat. A thumbs down lets you say what went wrong. Your rating is yours: rating again replaces it, and clicking the thumb you chose removes it.

The same rating is offered wherever an agent's work can be read: on a finished background task that was started from a chat (in Operations > Background Tasks; a task started by an assignment is rated on its run page), and on the answer an agent gave when another agent consulted it for you, in the agent's Delegations tab (a background task is rated as the task or its run, and a transferred conversation in the chat, so the same work is never rated twice). The people who manage the agent see every rating in its Feedback tab, with a link to the rated run or conversation when they may open it.

When your administrators have defined feedback criteria (Settings > Quality), the dialog also asks you to score each of them, such as the accuracy of the answer on a scale of 1 to 5 or its tone. Score what matters to you and skip the rest: a thumb alone is still a complete rating.

docs.title: Follow delegated work
docs.text:
One run can create more runs if work is handed to another agent.

Use the Executions list and the detail page together to understand:

  • where the work started
  • whether another agent took over
  • which parts succeeded or failed

This is especially important in environments that use multi-agent flows.

docs.title: Bulk actions
docs.text:
The Executions tab also supports selection and cleanup actions.

Depending on your permissions, you may be able to:

  • select multiple visible runs
  • delete selected runs
  • select all runs matching the current filters

Bulk actions are useful when you need to clean up large sets of test runs or old operational records.

docs.title: Administrator-only cleanup
docs.text:
Administrators can also see Cleanup Stale Runs.

This action is meant for recovery situations, such as:

  • a restart left some runs stuck
  • a run exceeded its timeout
  • the page still shows work as running when it should have failed

The cleanup action marks those stale runs as failed so the list becomes accurate again.

docs.title: Cancelling runs that have not started
docs.text:
When an agent piles up runs it cannot start (its daily quota is exhausted, or a burst of events arrived on a busy assignment), an administrator can cancel every run of an agent or an assignment that is still pending, delayed or queued in one call, optionally only those created before a given time. The runs stay in the history with the status cancelled and the reason Cancelled by <your name>; runs already running are never touched. The same action is available to an administrator's agent as the cancel_runs tool (with dry_run to count first), and through the API as POST /api/v1/assignments/runs/bulk-cancel (dry_run: true answers the count without changing anything).

On Operations > Executions, an administrator filters the list on one agent and clicks Cancel runs not started. The page first counts the agent's runs that are still pending, delayed or queued and asks for confirmation with that count ("Cancel 12 runs that have not started?"); nothing changes until you confirm. Once confirmed, the list switches to the Cancelled status filter and shows the runs that were just cancelled. Without an agent filter the action is disabled: a cancel on status alone would reach every waiting run of the platform, and the API refuses it. The per-run actions are unchanged.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter covers Resources, which includes knowledge bases, prompts, skills, MCP servers, tools, variables, and integrations.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is a named environment for one line of work — an audit, a customer, a research topic. You file conversations into it, and the agents working in those conversations share what they collect there: the work items they create and the shared state they keep. You can also record which knowledge bases the workspace works with.

Workspaces are an Enterprise Edition feature (see Editions and licensing). Managing them calls no model, so they keep working when AI is switched off.

docs.title: What a workspace is for
docs.text:
Use a workspace when you want to:

  • keep the conversations of one topic together
  • let agents in those conversations work from the same work items and shared state, and stay apart from other topics
  • note which knowledge bases belong to that work

A conversation that is filed in no workspace works as it always has: its agents use your own work items and shared state.

docs.title: Open Workspaces
docs.text:
Choose Work > Operations from the left sidebar, then the Workspaces tab. The other tabs of Operations — Work Items, Shared State, Worksets — list what agents build inside and outside workspaces (see Work history).

Each workspace is a card showing:

  • its name, with a default badge on your default workspace and an archived badge on an archived one, and a badge saying when it is company-managed, shared (by you, or by whom when it is someone else's) or read-only for you
  • its description
  • what it holds: conversations, work items (with how many are still open), shared state, worksets and knowledge bases — or Nothing filed here yet. For a workspace that hosts a fleet, the work items, shared state and worksets include what the fleet's agents created that you can see, the same ones its Operations tab lists (see Fleets and workspaces)
  • when it was last updated

Use the search field to find a workspace by name, and Show archived to list archived ones too.

docs.title: Your default workspace
docs.text:
Everyone has exactly one default workspace, named General, created the first time you open the list. It is listed first. Nothing is filed in it on its own: a new conversation is in no workspace until you file it, and a conversation stays in no workspace for as long as you like.

The default workspace cannot be archived, deleted or made company-managed. You can share it. To change it, open another workspace's actions menu and choose Make default. Only a workspace you own, that is not archived and not company-managed, can be your default.

docs.title: Create a workspace
docs.text:
1. Click New workspace.
  2. Enter a name and, if you like, a description of what it is for.
  3. Click Create.

The workspace is yours: nobody else sees it unless it is shared with them.

docs.title: Manage a workspace
docs.text:
Click a workspace's name to rename it or change its description. Open workspace in its actions menu opens the workspace's own page: your conversations filed there on the left, its knowledge on the right, and New conversation to start one already filed in it. Renaming keeps its handle (shown under the name), so existing links keep working.

The actions menu of each card offers the following. The same actions are in the Workspace actions menu of each workspace in the Chat sidebar (see Organize conversations in workspaces).

  • Make default — see Your default workspace.
  • Share — see Share a workspace.
  • Knowledge bases — choose the knowledge bases this workspace works with. Binding moves and copies nothing, and grants nobody access: each knowledge base keeps its own owner and sharing, and you can only bind one you can see. Someone who opens the workspace sees only the bound knowledge bases they can see themselves.
  • Archive / Restore — archiving asks for a confirmation, then hides the workspace from every picker and keeps everything it holds. To restore it, click Show archived, then Restore in its actions menu. Nothing can be filed into an archived workspace until it is restored.
  • Delete — removes the workspace after a confirmation. Its conversations are kept, in no workspace (never moved to a default workspace), its worksets are deleted together with its instructions, its sources and the index of its conversations, and bound knowledge bases and linked skills are left untouched. A workspace that still holds work items cannot be deleted: archive it instead, or clear its work items first.

These actions are greyed out when they do not apply: the default workspace cannot be archived or deleted, and a workspace you may only read cannot be changed. When an action is greyed out because of a fleet, the menu says why under it.

docs.title: Fleets and workspaces
docs.text:
A fleet lives in one workspace: the workspace is where the fleet's agents coordinate (work items, shared state, knowledge). The card and the page of a workspace that hosts a fleet say Hosts fleet followed by the fleet's name; click it to open the fleet. A fleet you cannot see is counted, not named. Three rules follow:

  • a workspace that hosts a fleet cannot be deleted: move the fleet to another workspace or delete the fleet first
  • a workspace that hosts a live fleet cannot be archived: archive the fleet or move it first (a workspace whose fleets are all archived can be archived)
  • deleting a fleet never deletes its workspace: the workspace stays with its work items and shared state

A work item created by an agent of the fleet is filed in the fleet's workspace when the agent names no workspace and you may change that workspace; a workspace the agent names always wins. Moving an agent to another fleet later moves none of its work items. Work items the fleet's agents created before this rule were filed in the fleet's workspace on upgrade when they belong to the workspace's owner; the others stay where they were and still appear in the workspace's Operations tab and counts. Only the work items that are filed in a workspace stop it from being deleted.

docs.title: Give a workspace its knowledge
docs.text:
Open the workspace's page (Open workspace), or, in a conversation filed in it, Workspace knowledge in the Conversation options menu. Every agent working in a conversation of the workspace - any agent, the General Assistant, the agents it consults or delegates to, and a flow's agents wired to a workspace node - receives:

  • Instructions — up to 8,000 characters on how agents should work there.
  • Sources — documents the agents work with. Manage sources adds uploaded files, pasted text, a website and synchronised sources (Notion, Google Drive, OneDrive / SharePoint, GitHub…), with the same formats, limits and synchronisation as a knowledge base. While they fit in a share of the model's context window (see Workspace knowledge), they are given whole; beyond it, they are searched. A file attached in one of the workspace's conversations can be added from the conversation's Conversation files panel (Add to the workspace's sources).
  • Knowledge bases — the ones bound to the workspace (Manage, or Knowledge bases in the actions menu).
  • Skills — library skills linked to the workspace: always in the agent's catalogue, loaded when needed.
  • Conversation search — the agents can search the conversations filed in the workspace, once each has been quiet for a while (30 minutes by default). What people wrote, the agents' answers and the text of attached files are indexed, with a summary; the results of tools never are, nor are group channel threads. A conversation unfiled, moved, archived or deleted leaves the search at once, and so does one whose owner no longer sees the workspace.

Who sees what: anyone who sees the workspace sees its instructions, its sources and the counts of its conversation search, and its agents can search every conversation filed in it. Only people who can change the workspace (Can configure) change its knowledge. The sources live in a knowledge base the workspace owns: it appears in the knowledge bases list with a Workspace badge, read-only there, and is never offered for binding elsewhere. Bound knowledge bases and linked skills each keep their own sharing: someone who cannot see one does not get it, in the panel or in their agents' turns.

docs.title: File a conversation in a workspace
docs.text:
The quickest way is the Chat sidebar, which lists your conversations by workspace: drag a conversation onto a workspace, or use its Move to workspace menu. See Organize conversations in workspaces.

From the conversation itself:

  1. Open the conversation in Chat.
  2. Open the Conversation options menu at the top of the conversation and choose File in a workspace.
  3. Pick a workspace, or No workspace to take the conversation out of the one it is in.

The change applies from the next message: from then on, agents in that conversation create and read work items and shared state in that workspace.

Only the owner of a conversation can file it, and only into a workspace they can change. Archived workspaces, and workspaces you may only read, are not offered.

Filing into a workspace other people can see asks first: its members' agents will be able to search what was written in the conversation.

docs.title: Share a workspace
docs.text:
A workspace follows the same scopes as other resources (see Containers and scopes). To share one, open its actions menu and choose Share:

  1. Switch on Share with people and groups.
  2. Search for a person or a group and add them.
  3. Choose what each one may do:
    • Read only — they see the workspace and what its agents built there, but cannot file conversations into it or change it.
    • Can configure — they can also file their own conversations into it, and change it: rename it, bind knowledge bases, share it with anyone, archive it, or delete it.
  4. Click Save.

Who can see this workspace says, in words, who the settings let in; while you have unsaved changes it adds Applies when you save.

Admins also see Company-managed workspace: switched on, the workspace is visible to everyone and changed only by admins. Restrict access then limits it to the people and groups listed. The default workspace stays personal, so this switch is not available for it.

Only someone who can change a workspace can share it. The owner keeps it whatever a grantee does: a grantee cannot take it over or remove the owner's access, and only an admin can transfer it. Removing a person's access does not unfile their conversations: they stay filed, but their agents no longer read or write that workspace's work items and shared state, and they can move them elsewhere.

docs.title: Workspaces shared with you
docs.text:
A workspace shared with you appears in your list with a Shared by badge naming its owner, and a Read-only badge when you may only read it. With Read only you see it and what its agents built there; with Can configure you can also file your conversations into it, change it, share it and delete it. A company-managed workspace is visible to everyone and changed only by admins. Someone else's default workspace shared with you is not yours: it carries no default badge and cannot be made your default.

The same rule applies to what agents do there: an agent reads the work items and shared state of every workspace its user can see that is not archived, and writes only where that user can change the workspace.

docs.title: Let your assistant manage workspaces
docs.text:
The XTM One built-in tool (the agent builder) can do all of the above from a conversation. It is not on by default: switch it on for the conversation in the session tools menu (the wrench button), or have an admin add it to the General Assistant, or add it to an agent's configuration. Then you can ask, for example:

  • "Create a workspace called Acme audit and move this conversation into it."
  • "Which workspace is this conversation in?"
  • "Move all my conversations about Acme into the Acme audit workspace."
  • "Take this conversation out of its workspace."
  • "Bind the Policies knowledge base to the Acme audit workspace."
  • "Archive the Q2 review workspace."
  • "Make Research my default workspace."

Any agent can also file the conversation you are in, or create a workspace for it, when you ask ("file this conversation in Acme audit") — no tool to switch on. Into a workspace other people can see, the move waits for your approval on the approval card, whatever the agent's approval settings, and "always" is not offered: each such move is approved on its own. Where no approval card can be shown (a Slack or Teams thread, the MCP server, a scheduled run), the assistant cannot file into a shared workspace: move the conversation from its menu in XTM One.

The assistant can list your workspaces with what each holds, find your conversations by title, workspace or unfiled ones, and file several at once — when you mention no conversation, it files the one you are in. You can refer to a workspace by its exact name. It applies exactly the same rules as the pages above: it only moves your own conversations, into workspaces you can change and that are not archived, it never binds a knowledge base you cannot see, and it refuses to archive or delete your default workspace or to delete one that still holds work items. A move of several conversations is all or nothing. Deleting a workspace cannot be undone, so the assistant is instructed to check with you first. Creating, changing and deleting a workspace through the assistant is recorded in the audit log, as it is from the page; filing a conversation is not, from the assistant or from the page. The assistant can also clear a workspace's description or color, and put its default icon back. A workspace you no longer see, by name or by id, matches none of your conversations, even those still filed in it: they are listed as being in a workspace you no longer see.

The same tools are available through the Platform tools MCP server. There is no current conversation there, so conversations are named by their ids.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Operations to follow the runs, work items and shared state your agents produce.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
This section introduces the concepts behind the product before the rest of the guide walks through individual screens. It is most useful when you are new to XTM One, when the object names still feel abstract, or when you are moving between XTM One and other Filigran products.

The pages cover:

  • Data model — the main platform objects.
  • Relationships and nesting — how one object references another.
  • Containers and scopes — how work is grouped and where visibility applies.
  • Reuse and deduplication — when to reuse a shared object and when to create a copy.
  • Trust, review, and confidence — how to judge AI outputs operationally.
  • Meaning of dates and status — the timestamps and status labels you see across the product.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Start with Data model, then continue through the rest of the Foundations pages before the screen-by-screen guides.

docs.title: Containers and scopes
docs.text: Some pages in XTM One are about one specific object. Others are about a container that groups many objects, or a scope that sets a visibility boundary.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A container is any object or view whose main role is to hold and organize related work. It usually shows the items it contains and lets you add or remove them. The main ones:

  • Conversations keep the messages, context, and history of one chat thread together.
  • Workspaces group conversations on one topic, with the work items and shared state their agents build there and the knowledge bases the work relies on (see Workspaces).
  • Knowledge bases group documents and import sources into one searchable corpus.
  • AI Catalog entries group shareable resources into published packages that other users can review and clone.

Being inside a container does not always mean ownership: a prompt attached to an agent is still reusable elsewhere, and a catalog item added to your account usually becomes a new local copy rather than a live link to the source.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A scope is the boundary that decides where an object is visible and who can edit it:

  • Personal — belongs to one user; the safest place to experiment, since edits stay local.
  • Shared — visible to the groups or people it is shared with. Each share has a permission: Can configure lets them edit it too, Full access (incl. chats) (agents only) also lets them read the agent's conversations and its traces (its Observability tab, and trace inspection in a conversation or a run they trigger, even when the agent carries it itself), which hold those conversations, and Read only lets them look but not change it; a read-only share shows a Read-only badge and says so instead of offering an Edit button.
  • Company-managed — visible to everyone but usually edited only by admins; the broadest scope in day-to-day use.

docs.title: Before you change something
docs.text: Ask whether you are editing the container itself or an item inside it, and whether the change affects only you, your group, or the whole company. Those two questions prevent most accidental changes.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Reuse and deduplication, which explains when XTM One keeps a shared object, when it creates a copy, and how to avoid duplicate setup.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
XTM One is easier to understand when you treat it as a set of connected objects rather than a set of disconnected screens. The same object can appear in Chat, the Agentic Flow graph, Operations, and the AI Catalog without becoming four different things.

At a high level there are three kinds of things: assistants that do work, resources those assistants rely on, and records that show what happened.

docs.title: Assistants and records
docs.text:
• Agents are the main assistants. An agent bundles its instructions and persona, tools, knowledge bases, prompts and skills, assignments, handovers, and memory. If you remember one object type, remember this one.
  • Assignments are automation rules inside an agent — they define what triggers the work and what the agent does when it runs. They are not separate assistants.
  • Runs are the execution records created when assignments or other background work happen. They tell you whether the work ran, is still running, failed, is waiting for a person, or what it produced — the operational layer of the product.
  • Conversations are the chat sessions between a user and the General Assistant or a specific agent. The conversation holds the discussion; the agent stays the reusable assistant behind it.
  • Fleets are named groups of agents that work together: an orchestrator and the agents that report to it. An agent belongs to at most one fleet (its home); a fleet can also connect agents or other fleets it calls without owning them. Every fleet coordinates in exactly one workspace (its work items, shared state, worksets and knowledge), and publishes a fleet card: what it does, its entry agent and the agents other fleets may hand over to. A fleet shows its handover graph (including the handovers that cross into or out of it, and whether a connected link governs each one), its declared hierarchy, its schedule, its recent activity and the health of each member; agents in no fleet form the playground. An agent in no fleet works exactly as before. Removing an agent from a fleet, or deleting the fleet, never deletes the agent nor changes its handovers.

docs.title: Reusable resources
docs.text: The Resources area holds the building blocks agents and chats depend on: knowledge bases (searchable documents), prompts (reusable instructions), skills (reusable instruction packages), MCP servers (external tools over the Model Context Protocol), tools (built-in or custom actions), and integrations (connections to outside systems).

docs.title: Access and sharing
docs.text: Users have personal settings and access; groups are used for controlled sharing. Most objects have one visibility state — personal, shared with a group, or company-managed — which decides who can edit them and whether you should reuse an object or copy it.

docs.title: How it appears in the UI
docs.text: Most areas follow the same pattern: a list page, a detail page, and tabs for overview, configuration, activity, and related records. The UI is not inventing a new concept on every screen — it shows different views of the same underlying objects. In practice they chain together: a user opens an agent, the agent contains assignments and references resources, running it creates a run in History, and chatting with it is stored in a conversation.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Relationships and nesting, which explains how these objects point to one another and where configuration actually lives.

docs.title: Meaning of dates and status
docs.text: XTM One shows many timestamps and status labels, and they do not all mean the same thing. The common confusion is between when a record was created or changed in XTM One, when outside data was last refreshed, when a run started or finished, and whether an assistant or connection is healthy right now.

docs.title: Two families of dates
docs.text:
Technical dates describe what happened inside XTM One — created, updated, refreshed, synced, last heartbeat. They tell you about platform freshness and maintenance state.

Operational dates describe the lifecycle of work — scheduled for, started, completed, awaiting input since, last run. They tell you what happened in the workflow.

A few worth pinning down: created/updated are when a record was made or last changed in XTM One; started/completed are when a run began and finished; last heartbeat is when a connected platform last reported health; synced/refreshed is when imported content was last updated from its source.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text: Dates read best alongside status. Enabled/disabled describe whether an object is active for use. Connected, stale, or disconnected describe the health of an external connection. Running, awaiting input, completed, and failed describe the state of a run.

docs.title: How to read a page
docs.text: On configuration pages, dates usually describe the object record. On history pages, they describe execution lifecycle. On connection cards, they describe freshness or health. For example, an agent with a recent updated date changed its configuration recently — it does not mean it ran recently; and a run with an old started time and no completion may be stuck or waiting.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Return to the main guide and continue with the Home Dashboard chapter.

docs.title: Reuse and deduplication
docs.text: XTM One works best when teams reuse shared building blocks instead of recreating the same setup many times. Without a clear reuse model, you quickly end up with duplicate agents, copied prompts that drift apart, repeated tool configuration, and confusion about which version is the real one.

docs.title: Reuse first
docs.text:
Before creating something new, check whether the platform already has a shared agent, a reusable prompt or skill, an existing knowledge base, a configured MCP server or integration, or a catalog item you can add instead of rebuilding. In many environments, reuse is the right default.

The platform keeps one shared object when several agents point to the same prompt, skill, MCP server, or knowledge base, or when a company-managed or group-shared object is intentionally reused. It is not silently duplicated.

docs.title: When to make a copy
docs.text:
XTM One creates or expects a copy when you duplicate an agent, add a catalog item to your account, or export and re-import an object. Do this on purpose when you need different behavior, are testing a private variation, do not have edit rights on the shared original, or want the shared object to stay stable for everyone else.

The practical rule: edit the shared object when the whole team should benefit; duplicate it when only your version should change. This matters most for prompts, skills, and agents. Do not create a copy just because you found the shared version first.

docs.title: Avoiding duplicate setups
docs.text:
• Search before creating.
  • Check whether a company-managed or shared version already exists.
  • Use Duplicate only when behavior must diverge.
  • Reuse prompts, skills, MCP servers, and knowledge bases whenever possible.
  • Use the AI Catalog when you want a structured starting point rather than a manual rebuild.

XTM One also deduplicates operationally — for example, agent memory maintenance avoids storing the same fact repeatedly. From a user perspective the key idea is simple: prefer a stable shared source when one already exists.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Trust, review, and confidence, which explains how to judge AI output and understand operational trust signals in XTM One.

docs.title: Relationships and nesting
docs.text: Objects in XTM One are rarely isolated. Most of the platform works because one object references, includes, or configures another. When you look at a page, it helps to know whether you are editing the object itself, editing a child that belongs to it, or linking a reusable object that lives elsewhere.

docs.title: Linked resources vs. nested configuration
docs.text:
Two patterns cover most of the product:

  • Linked resources are references between standalone objects — an agent references knowledge bases, prompts, skills, integrations, MCP servers, and tools; a group gives users access to shared objects.
