The referenced object keeps its own identity and life elsewhere, so one prompt, skill, MCP server, or knowledge base can serve many agents. Changing a shared resource can therefore affect more than one page.
  • Nested configuration is stored inside a parent object rather than as a separate shared item — an assignment belongs to one agent, a persona belongs to its agent, channel behavior belongs to the agent or the shared bot, personal tool overrides belong to the user profile. Here you are editing the current object, not a library item.

Agents are where most of this comes together — they contain assignments, reference reusable resources, point to handover targets, and expose themselves through chat, channels, or MCP. That is why the agent detail page is often the best place to understand the rest of the model.

docs.title: Overrides and inheritance
docs.text: Some settings inherit rather than link one-to-one: channel behavior can inherit from the channel bot, profile preferences can override platform defaults, and user-level MCP exposure can be narrower than the global setting. When a value is empty, it usually means inherit, not disabled.

docs.title: How to read a page
docs.text: If the page shows a reusable entity card or picker, you are usually linking objects, and a change can affect shared behavior. If it shows inline form fields with no separate entity page, you are usually editing nested configuration that stays local.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Containers and scopes, which explains how work is grouped and where organizational boundaries apply.

docs.title: Trust, review, and confidence
docs.text: XTM One does not reduce trust to a single score. You judge it through ownership, run status, review steps, and source visibility — deciding whether an answer is ready to use, still needs review, where it came from, and who owns the underlying configuration.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Who manages an object is the first trust signal. Personal objects are yours — good for testing, but not a shared standard. Group-shared objects are collaborative team assets that can change as the group edits them. Company-managed objects usually represent the most stable, broadly approved standard, and are often the best starting point.

docs.title: Run status
docs.text:
Execution state is the second signal. Running means work is still in progress. Awaiting input means the system is waiting for a human decision, so the output is not final. Completed means the run finished normally, though you may still want to review the result before acting on it externally. Failed means the work did not complete and should not be treated as final.

Some workflows pause for a person on purpose — a draft to review before sending, a question that needs a human answer, an approval gate mid-workflow. When you see this, the platform is intentionally asking for human judgment.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: To judge an output, look at which agent produced it, which tools or integrations were used, which knowledge base or source material was involved, and whether the configuration was shared or private. The run detail page and the surrounding object pages are the best places to inspect that context.

docs.title: Good working habits
docs.text:
• Treat AI output as proposed work, not automatic truth.
  • Prefer company-managed or well-reviewed shared resources for important tasks.
  • Review Awaiting Input and draft states carefully.
  • Open the related run or object page when you need more context.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Meaning of dates and status, which explains how to interpret timestamps and lifecycle signals across XTM One.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Resources are the reusable building blocks behind agents and conversations. If agents are the assistants, resources are what those assistants know and act through. In the left navigation they sit in two groups:

  • Agent Studio holds what defines your agents: Create an agent, Knowledge, Prompts, Templates, and Skills.
  • Tools & Integrations holds what your agents act through: MCP Servers, Tools, Integrations, Browser profiles, Variables, and Relays.

Click a group's name to open its overview page, with one card per area. You usually come here when you are preparing an agent, improving an existing setup, or checking how a workflow gets its data and actions.

docs.title: Agent Studio
docs.text:
• Knowledge bases store documents and indexed content that agents can search, so answers are grounded in trusted material. Content can be uploaded directly or kept in sync from external sources such as websites, Notion, cloud storage, and GitHub.
  • Prompts are reusable text instructions that keep wording consistent across chat requests, agent behavior, and recurring workflows.
  • Templates hold the brand behind generated presentations, reports and dashboards — palette, typefaces, layouts, logos and composition guidance — so the same request produces on-brand output for everyone. A read-only brand template, the XTM One Brand Deck, ships with every platform.
  • Skills are reusable instruction sets — a packaged behavior or method — that can be attached to agents. A skill can be authored directly or fetched from a source URL.

To build an agent from these pieces, see Create an agent.

docs.title: Tools & Integrations
docs.text:
• MCP servers expose external tools to XTM One in a controlled way. Use them when agents need capabilities such as search, data lookups, or system actions provided through MCP. See also Connect an external MCP server and MCP catalogs.
  • Tools are the actions agents can use directly: the built-in tools (files, web, browser, design, the platform tool and others). Custom tools are off by default in XTM One; an administrator can turn them on.
  • Integrations connect XTM One to external services such as email, ticketing, messaging, and cloud document systems, giving agents live access to those systems.
  • Browser profiles are saved sign-ins to web applications: an agent given one opens the application signed in with its Browser tool, without seeing the credentials.
  • Variables store reusable values that resolve at runtime in prompts, personas, skills, and tools, so key values are not repeated by hand. Values can be marked Secret. Variables are off by default in XTM One; an administrator can turn them on.
  • Relays let XTM One reach services inside a network it cannot reach directly, without opening an inbound flow toward that network.

docs.title: Other related pages
docs.text:
• XTM One Desktop and runners: the native app, and the machines your agents can act on.
  • Agent-to-agent (A2A): how your agents work with agents outside XTM One.
  • Sharing and access: who can use what you lend, and through what.
  • Platform MCP servers and Platform tools MCP server: XTM One as an MCP server for your own clients.

docs.title: Grid and list views
docs.text:
Every resource list page — and the Agents page — can be displayed two ways. The toggle sits at the right of the filter row, next to the item count.

  • Grid is the default: one card per item, optimized for browsing and recognizing things at a glance.
  • List shows the same items as table rows. It fits far more per screen and exposes extra attributes side by side, so you can compare a whole fleet at once — which model each agent runs, which tools are enabled, how many documents each knowledge base holds.

On the Agents page, favorites (the star on a card or row) sit above every other item in both views — sorting a column reorders the favorites among themselves rather than sending them back into the pile.

In list view, click a column header to sort by it; click again to reverse the order. Items with no value for that column (no model pinned, never fetched) always stay at the bottom, in both directions. Every action available on a card — opening the item, enabling or disabling it, starting a chat, copying a variable reference — is available on the matching row.

Your choice is remembered per page and across sessions, so a page you prefer as a table stays a table the next time you sign in.

docs.title: Platform MCP servers
docs.text:
XTM One is not only an MCP client — it is also an MCP server for the connected Filigran platforms. As soon as an OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ instance is registered with XTM One, external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude Desktop, and others) can connect to /mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, and /mcp/opencrq with a personal API key and work with threat intelligence, exposure validation, and governance-risk-compliance content directly.

See Platform MCP servers for endpoints, authentication, the tool surface, and client configuration.

docs.title: Platform tools MCP server
docs.text:
XTM One also exposes itself over MCP, on /mcp/xtm: agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, and variables — scoped to what the calling user can already see and manage. It is how you read an agent's traces from Claude Desktop or Cursor and fix its configuration without leaving the client. Off by default; an administrator enables it in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

See Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: How the resource types work together
docs.text:
In a typical workflow:

  • an integration connects to the outside system
  • a knowledge base provides trusted context
  • a prompt or skill shapes the behavior
  • a tool performs an action
  • a variable avoids repeating key values

This is why resources matter so much: they are where assistants become usable and consistent.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with the detailed guide of the resource type you need, starting with Integrations.

docs.title: Agent-to-agent (A2A)
docs.text:
A2A is an open protocol that lets agents on different platforms give each other work. With it, an agent running on a partner's platform — Azure Foundry, Google Agent Platform, or another XTM One deployment — can send a task to one of your agents, and one of your agents can send a task to a partner's agent.

This page covers both directions: exposing one of your agents to a partner, and calling a partner's agent from XTM One.

Not the same as handovers

Agents on your own platform hand work to each other without A2A. That cooperation is shown in Agentic Flow. A2A is for agents that live on another platform.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
A2A is available while agentic chat is: AI is switched on and the platform runs in Enterprise Edition (see Editions and licensing). There is nothing else to enable. When agentic chat is not available, the A2A cards in the integration catalog explain what is missing, and an agent that already has A2A bindings keeps them: its agent card is not served and no delegation tool is offered until agentic chat is back.

Partners reach your agents over HTTPS only. A request XTM One cannot confirm as encrypted is refused, not redirected. If your platform sits behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, your administrator must name that proxy as trusted, or every partner request is refused: see FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS in Configuration.

docs.title: Choose a mechanism and a direction
docs.text:
Every A2A relationship is an integration. Open Integrations, search the catalog for A2A (the cards carry the Agent to Agent (A2A) tag), and pick the mechanism your partner supports:

Catalog entry Use it when the partner OAuth A2A can exchange a client ID and secret for a token on its own — Google ADK, or another XTM One deployment Foundry A2A runs on Azure Foundry and authenticates with Microsoft Entra Google Agent Platform A2A runs on Google Agent Platform (Vertex AI Agent Runtime)

The creation form then asks for a Direction:

  • Inbound: a partner tasks our agents — binding this integration to an agent exposes that agent to the partner.
  • Outbound: our agents task a partner — binding this integration to an agent gives it a tool to delegate work to the partner.

An integration serves one direction. To change it later, unbind it from every agent first. An agent that builds the integration with the create_integration tool sets the direction with its a2a_direction argument (inbound when omitted), changes it with update_integration, and reads it with get_integration. The agent's Overview tab shows which way each A2A binding points, with an Exposes agent or a Delegates to partner badge.

docs.title: Expose one of your agents
docs.text:
There is no separate switch: an agent is reachable by a partner exactly while it is bound to an inbound A2A integration.

  1. Create the integration with the Inbound: a partner tasks our agents direction.
  2. Give it the partner's credential details:
    • OAuth A2A: save the integration, then on its Configuration tab, in the Partner credential card, choose Generate credential. The client secret is shown once, at that moment — copy it before you leave the page.
    • Foundry A2A: fill in the partner's tenant ID, the audience of a dedicated app registration that represents XTM One, and the one partner identity allowed to call. The setup guide walks through the Azure side.
    • Google Agent Platform A2A: fill in the audience the partner's tokens carry and the one service account allowed to call.
  3. Open the agent, then Configuration > Tooling. In the Integrations card, choose Edit, click the integration to bind it, and Save.

The Partner reachability card on the integration's Configuration tab tells you what is still missing — no credential yet, no pins, or no agent bound — and whether the partner has connected.

Binding is a change to the agent, so it follows the same rule as editing it: the owner, an administrator, or someone the agent is shared with at configuration level. A company-managed agent, built-in agents included, can be exposed only by an administrator. A company-managed agent that is not built in can be bound only to company-managed integrations.

One credential per partner

An OAuth A2A credential works on every agent its integration is bound to. To keep a leak limited to one agent, create one integration per agent.

docs.title: Share the agent card URL
docs.text:
Each exposed agent gets its own agent card URL: the address the partner registers on its side. The card is public and tells the partner what the agent does and how to authenticate.

Find it on the integration's Configuration tab, in the Agent card URLs card: one row per bound agent, with a button to copy it. Send the partner:

  • OAuth A2A: the card URL, the Client ID and the client secret. The partner exchanges them for a short-lived token at the address the card gives.
  • Foundry A2A and Google Agent Platform A2A: the card URL only. No secret is stored on either side; the partner presents a token its own cloud issues, and XTM One checks it against the values you entered.

docs.title: Whose identity the work runs as
docs.text:
A partner's task runs as the agent's owner — never as the person who bound the integration. For a company-managed agent, that is the account that created it, often an administrator. The Integrations card on the agent's Tooling tab names that user in a line that starts with External work runs as.

Read that line before you send the card URL. The partner reaches everything that user can see, their personal and group-shared data included, through the agent's whole tool set and the agents it hands work to. There is no per-partner narrowing of tools. If that is too much, do not expose the agent, or duplicate it under an owner whose reach fits.

The work counts against that user's agentic quota. A partner is still treated as an outside caller: it gets no trace inspection, cannot change platform objects and cannot drive the owner's machines (XTM One Desktop runners), whatever the owner may do. See Sharing and access for how this fits with the agent's other audiences.

docs.title: What a partner can do
docs.text:
Once connected, the partner can:

  • send a task and read its status and answer;
  • cancel a task that is still running, including the work the agent passed on;
  • register a callback address to be told when a task changes, instead of asking repeatedly;
  • send a follow-up in the same conversation.

The agent accepts text and structured data. A message with a file is refused before any work starts. Answers are not streamed, and the partner cannot list its tasks: it keeps the ID of each task it created. Submissions are rate-limited per partner.

When the request is unclear, the agent can ask the calling agent a question. The task waits for the caller's answer, never for a person, and the agent asks at most three times. The run that asked reads Waiting on caller and shows the question; the caller's answer continues the task in a new run, and each of the two runs links to the other.

Work a partner submits shows on the integration's Activity tab — only that partner's own — and in the agent's activity with a badge naming the A2A provider that submitted it.

docs.title: Call a partner agent
docs.text:
1. Ask the partner for the card URL of each agent you may task, and for a credential.
  2. Create the integration with the Outbound: our agents task a partner direction, paste the card URLs (separated by commas or new lines), and enter the credential:
    • OAuth A2A: the partner's token endpoint, the client ID and the client secret it issued you. From another XTM One deployment, these come from its inbound OAuth A2A integration.
    • Foundry A2A: your own Entra tenant ID, application (client) ID and client secret.
    • Google Agent Platform A2A: impersonation of a service account the partner names, or a service account key JSON.
  3. Save. XTM One fetches and checks each card, and the Partner verification card shows what each partner agent declares and whether it is reachable.
  4. Bind the integration to each agent that should delegate: Configuration > Tooling > Integrations.

Each partner agent that passes verification becomes one delegation tool for the bound agents, named after the agent it reaches. The integration also gives them a tool to stop a task still running at the partner, which the agent uses only when you ask. The What this brings your agents card lists these tools.

A delegation sends only the message the agent writes for it — not your conversation, nor any credential of yours. The partner's answer comes back as a quote from an outside party, not as instructions. When the partner runs XTM One, the agents your credential reaches appear on their own, without anyone typing their URLs.

To tell the partner which instance is calling, set Send this instance's identity to On on the outbound integration. Every message it sends then carries, in its metadata under xtmOneInstance, this platform's Instance ID (Settings > Parameters) and its name; nothing else is added. It is Off by default, and each integration is set on its own.

Card URLs must be HTTPS

A card URL that is not HTTPS, or that points at a private or loopback address, is refused.

docs.title: Check a partner's health
docs.text:
The Partner verification card on an outbound integration shows how many partner agents are reachable (2 of 3 reachable, for example), with a panel per partner agent: its verdict, what it Accepts and Produces, whether its card is signed, and when it was Last verified. Use Verify now on one agent or Verify all.

When the partner changes its card in a way that matters, delegation to that agent pauses until you review the change and choose Accept card change. The Work sent to this partner card, shown to the people who can manage the integration, lists each delegation and how it ended.

docs.title: Revoke access
docs.text:
• Stop exposing one agent. Unbind the integration from the agent (Configuration > Tooling > Integrations > Edit). Its card URL stops working at once. Binding it again creates a new card URL, which you must send to the partner.
  • Cut off an OAuth A2A partner. Choose Regenerate secret in the Partner credential card. The old secret stops working at once on every agent the integration is bound to.
  • Change who may call a Foundry A2A or Google Agent Platform A2A integration. Edit its values: the next partner request is checked against them.

XTM One also revokes an exposure on its own when the agent's owner changes, when the agent moves between personal and company-managed, when its sharing changes, or when it is disabled or deleted. When the agent is still enabled and bound, it gets a new card URL to send to the partner. Deactivating the user an exposure runs as pauses it; reactivating the account restores it with the same card URL.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: See Sharing and access for everyone else an agent reaches, and Integrations for the integration screens.

docs.title: Browser profiles
docs.text:
A browser profile is a web application and its sign-in, kept by the platform: the start URL, the sign-in URL if it differs, the account to use and the session that sign-in saved. Give a profile to an agent and its Browser tool opens the application signed in - to answer a question, write a report, build a presentation from a dashboard, or record a demo in the Video Studio - without ever seeing the credentials.

Profiles are listed under Tools & Integrations > Browser profiles. They need no feature flag: they work whether or not the Video Studio is turned on.

docs.title: Create a profile
docs.text:
New browser profile asks for:

  • Name and Start URL: the application's home page, where every session opens and is checked.
  • Sign-in URL (optional): the page that starts the sign-in when it is not the start URL - for single sign-on, the page the application's "Sign in with SSO" button opens.
  • Username, Password and TOTP secret: stored encrypted and never shown again. A blank field keeps what is stored, Clear removes it (Keep undoes it before you save). They are typed here only: the assistant can create a profile and set its addresses and sign-in options, but never takes a credential in the chat - what a tool receives stays in the conversation - so it asks you to add them on this page.
  • From a vault: instead of typing a credential, pick it from a secret vault your administrator granted you - the password and the one-time password of a 1Password item, or a secret in HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Google Cloud or Azure. The profile then stores a reference, and the platform reads the credential from the vault each time its browser signs in: rotate the password in the vault and the profile follows. The field shows the vault, the path and the key; the card shows From a vault.
  • Private-network hosts (optional): see Private networks.
  • Keep the session alive: how often the platform refreshes the saved session so it does not expire between uses. A new profile refreshes it every 4 hours; Never turns it off.

An administrator can publish a profile to the whole company: everyone can then use it, with their agents and their recordings, without ever seeing its credentials.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Sign in runs the sign-in in the platform's own browser, in the profile's own session: signing in to the application in a tab of your own browser does not sign the profile in.

  • Single sign-on: an application that sends you to a hosted identity provider (SAML or OpenID Connect) works like a first-party sign-in form. Set the sign-in URL to the page that starts the single sign-on, or set confirm_selector to the application's single sign-on button. The sign-in follows the whole way back to the application and is done only once the start URL shows the signed-in application.
  • MFA: with the account's TOTP secret (the key an authenticator app is enrolled with, as base32 or as the otpauth:// link of its QR code), the sign-in answers the code prompt by itself. Paste the secret, or pick it From a vault (a 1Password item's one-time password field, or a vault secret holding the key): the platform checks it is a real key - when you save it, or when it reads it from the vault. A password manager's own reference syntax (op://..., a ${...} placeholder) is refused, saying how to pick it from a vault instead. Without a TOTP secret, an MFA prompt pauses the sign-in, with the platform's browser kept open on the prompt for 5 minutes (MFA window): type the code on the profile's card, or give it to the assistant in the chat. A push approval shows the screenshot of the prompt and the number to enter in your authenticator app; the sign-in continues by itself once you approve.
  • Passkeys and security keys: when the account's default MFA method is a passkey, Windows Hello or a FIDO security key, the platform's browser cannot use it (there is no device to tap). The sign-in detects this, backs out to "Sign in another way", and chooses a code method instead - an authenticator code (which it answers from the TOTP secret) or a text message. Give the profile the account's TOTP secret so these accounts sign in unattended; if the account offers only a passkey and a phone-approval push, the sign-in asks you to approve the push.
  • Test a sign-in: Test sign-in on the profile's card runs the whole sign-in once without saving anything, and shows where it got to - the steps it took and the page it ended on. Use it to check a profile signs in cleanly without touching the session a recording relies on.
  • Renews by itself: by default, every profile the platform can sign in without a person carries a Renews by itself badge: one with the account's username and password whose sign-in asks for no code (a local login), one with the password and a valid TOTP secret, or one with a saved single-sign-on session. A sign-in that has to ask someone for a code or an approval removes the badge until a TOTP secret is added or the credentials change. With the badge, the platform signs it in again on its own when the session expires, so recordings and agents keep working without anyone signing in again. Credentials read from a vault count.
  • A vault that does not answer: when a credential read from a vault cannot be read (the vault is down, the secret was moved, the grant of its provider changed), the sign-in stops at once and says which credential and why, the card shows the failure, and an agent is told to have an administrator check the vault rather than to ask you to sign in. A saved session that still works keeps working meanwhile.
  • Sessions: once signed in, the profile keeps the session - the cookies of the identity provider and of the application, and the application's storage. A profile reads Signed in only when the start URL, opened with the saved session, shows the signed-in application; otherwise it reads Session expired (lands on login page) with the page it landed on. Check the session checks it now. When the application cannot answer - it is restarting, overloaded or limits the rate of requests (an HTTP 5xx or 429) - the check opens it again a few times over about half a minute, then says so (start_url answered HTTP 503: the application is unavailable...). The profile then reads Saved, not checked rather than Session expired, it is not signed in again (by the keep-alive, Check the session, a recording or an agent), a recording stops with profile session not checked, and an agent's Browser tool says the application did not answer instead of asking you to sign the profile in; check again once the application is back. A recording whose own page is refused that way reloads it before its first step. When the application answers that way to the last check of a sign-in (or of Test sign-in), it ends Signed in, not checked rather than failed: a sign-in still saves its session, which reads Saved, not checked. Check the session answers within about a minute and a half, the sign-in again of a profile that renews by itself included: a sign-in still running then goes on in the background, and the card shows Signing in... until it ends.
  • Timeouts: under Sign-in selectors and timeouts, the sign-in timeout (120 s by default) counts from the last page change; a sign-in that stops moving fails and names its stage and the last page it was on.
  • Session storage keys: a Video Studio recording clears what the application kept in the browser's storage before it starts, so it never opens on a page a previous recording left changed (a graph's layout, a list's filters). Cookies are never cleared. An application that keeps its sign-in in that storage rather than in a cookie lists those keys in keep_storage_keys, separated by commas: a recording keeps them. A recording whose clearing signs the application out stops and names the keys it cleared.
  • Applications without a session cookie: an application that keeps its sign-in as a token in the browser's local storage (XTM One does) is signed in and saved like any other: the saved session carries that storage, so the session check, snapshots and recordings open it signed in. When a saved session still does not reopen the application, the message says what it kept ("session not persisted (no cookie of ...; localStorage keys: ...)"); a sign-in form that comes back without an error says which field was left empty ("email field left empty"): set username_selector then.
  • A signed-in selector that no longer matches: when the profile's signed-in selector is not on a page that otherwise renders the signed-in application (no sign-in form, the application's own host, not the page it shows without a session), the check passes and says the selector is stale: update it or clear it. When the page is a sign-in page, the failure names the selector it looked for.
  • Sign-in page and application at the same address: when the application shows its sign-in form and its dashboard at the same URL (its sign-in URL is its start URL) and keeps its session in local storage, the check compares the page with what that URL shows without a session instead of failing on the address. A session kept in local storage alone, without any cookie, is a saved session.

docs.title: Give a profile to an agent
docs.text:
On an agent's Configuration > Tooling tab, with the Browser tool on, the Browser profiles card lists the profiles the agent may sign in with. Binding is explicit: an agent never reaches every login its users can see.

  • The agent lists them with the browser's profiles action and opens one with navigate and the profile's name. The session it opens is checked first; when it has expired and the profile can sign in by itself (its password and TOTP secret, or a saved identity provider session), it signs in again. When the sign-in needs a person (an MFA code with no TOTP secret), the agent says so: sign the profile in on its card, then ask again.
  • A run opens a profile only for a person who may use it - its owner, the people and groups it is shared with, or everyone for a company profile. An administrator's role does not widen that: a run never opens someone else's private profile. A run that acts for nobody (an anonymous visitor of a public widget, a company assignment without a run-as user) opens none. A credential read from a vault is read for whoever may use the profile, as with any secret field: sharing the profile lends its sign-in, never the credential. Who may store or move such a reference is the vault's grant: an edit that changes the profile's start URL, sign-in URL or private hosts while it keeps a reference you could not have stored is refused, unless the same edit replaces that credential.
  • Read-only: a binding marked read-only lets the agent navigate to URLs and read the pages (their text, their accessibility tree, screenshots, the console, at the window size it sets), never click, type, press a key, hover or run a script. A page reached by a link can still change something in an application that changes state on a simple visit; give such an application to an agent you trust.
  • When the agent closes the session, or after five idle minutes, the platform saves the refreshed session - only if it still opens the application, and only if nobody saved a newer one meanwhile.
  • Save a session the agent signed in: when you complete a single sign-on with the agent in its browser (you approve the prompt or give it the code it asks for), ask it to save the session into the profile: the browser's save_session action keeps only the cookies and storage of the profile's hosts, nothing of the other sites it browsed, and only once the profile's start URL opens the signed-in application with them; the profile then reads Signed in. It needs a binding that is not read-only and a profile you may edit, and the browser has to be on the application, not signed in with another profile. Each save, kept or refused, is in the audit log (browser_profile, action update).

Every time an agent opens a profile, the audit log records it (browser_profile, action use) with the agent and the person it acted for.

Your own General Assistant uses the profiles you give it under My profile > General Assistant Tools > Browser profiles, shown once its Browser tool is on. There is no platform default: a profile is a login, given by its user.

docs.title: Private networks
docs.text: Browser profiles reach public addresses only, like the agent browser tool. An application on a private network needs two things: an administrator turns on Browser profiles on private networks (Settings > Access and security, or BROWSER_PRIVATE_TARGETS, see Configuration), and the profile names the hosts it may reach (Private-network hosts). Loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses stay refused either way.

docs.title: Connect an external MCP server
docs.text: An external MCP server gives your agents the tools of another system — GitHub, a SIEM, a sandbox, a threat-intelligence feed — through the Model Context Protocol. This page explains how to configure one so XTM One can call it. For a tour of the screens once a server exists, see MCP servers. For the opposite direction — an external MCP client calling XTM One — see Platform MCP servers.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Edition. Adding or importing a server requires AI to be switched on and the platform to be licensed for agentic AI (Enterprise Edition, see Editions and licensing). When AI is switched off, the action shows the AI-disabled notice; when the agentic AI license is missing, it opens the Enterprise Edition dialog.
  • Who. Any user can add a server for themselves. Only an administrator can create a Company-managed server. Every user of the platform can see and use it, unless an administrator turns on Restrict access in its sharing settings to limit it to named people and groups; only administrators can edit it.
  • What you need from the provider. For a remote server, its endpoint URL and either an API key or an OAuth login. For a local (subprocess) server, the package or binary to run and the environment variables it expects.

docs.title: Choose a transport
docs.text: Transport Use it when What XTM One does Streamable HTTP The provider hosts the server and gives you a URL (usually ending in /mcp). The recommended choice for remote servers. Connects to the URL over HTTP, sending your headers or OAuth token. SSE (legacy) The provider only offers the older Server-Sent Events endpoint (usually ending in /sse). Same as above, over the legacy protocol. Subprocess (stdio) The server is distributed as a package or binary you run yourself (npx …, uvx …). Starts the command as a child process of the XTM One backend and worker, and talks to it over its standard input and output.

docs.title: Add a server
docs.text:
1. In the left navigation, open Tools & Integrations > MCP Servers.
  2. Under Connected MCP Servers, click Add Server.
  3. Pick a preset, or Custom Server to configure any server by hand. A preset fills the transport, command or URL and the expected variables, and shows a short note about where to get the credentials it needs (for example, the scopes of a GitHub token).
  4. Fill in the form described below, then click Create Server.
  5. On the server page, click Test connection (see Test the connection).
  6. Attach the server to an agent (see Give an agent access).

Every server needs a Server Name. Names are labels for people; the tools the model sees keep their own names (see Tool names). Tags are free-form labels used to filter the list.

docs.title: Subprocess (stdio) servers
docs.text:
• Command: the executable to run, for example npx or uvx. It must be found on the PATH of the backend and worker containers, or be an absolute path to an executable file.
  • Arguments (space-separated): for example -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github. The field is split on spaces, so a single argument cannot contain a space. A preset placeholder such as /path/to/allowed/dir must be replaced before the server can be created.
  • Environment Variables (secrets): one Variable Name / Value pair per variable the server reads, such as GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN. Values are stored encrypted and are never displayed again. When you edit the server, leave the list empty to keep the stored variables; entering any variable replaces the whole stored set.

Put credentials in environment variables, never in the arguments: arguments are stored in clear and shown to everyone who can configure the server.

What the process can rely on:

  • Runtimes. The official images ship Node.js (for npx) and uv (for uvx; when only uv is present, uvx … runs as uv tool run …). They do not include the Docker CLI, so a server started with docker run … needs an image you build with it, and access to a Docker daemon. The presets started this way (VulnCheck, TheHive, Elastic Security, ReversingLabs) show this warning when you pick them.
  • Environment. The process does not inherit the platform's configuration or secrets. It starts with a minimal environment (PATH, HOME, the locale and temporary-directory variables, PYTHON* variables) plus the variables you configured. A server that needs a proxy or a custom CA must be given the corresponding variables explicitly; NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED in particular is never passed through from the platform.
  • Network. npx and uvx download the package on first start, so the containers need access to the npm or PyPI registry (or your mirror). The first start, download included, must complete within the 60-second connection limit.
  • Isolation. The process runs with the permissions of the backend and worker, without a sandbox. Only run servers you trust, and prefer a remote transport for anything third-party.
  • No relay. A stdio server runs on the platform itself, so it cannot be routed through a relay group.

docs.title: Remote servers (Streamable HTTP or SSE)
docs.text:
• Server URL (or SSE URL): the endpoint given by the provider, for example https://mcp.example.com/mcp. XTM One connects to it from its backend and worker, so it must be reachable from there.
  • Route through: Direct (from the platform) by default. To reach a server inside a network the platform cannot reach, choose a relay group: every request the server makes — its tools, the connection test, OAuth detection, sign-in and token refresh — then leaves from that network through one of its relays, and fails rather than falling back to a direct call when no relay is online. See Relays.
  • Authentication: Secret Headers or OAuth 2.0. Presets for hosted servers default to OAuth 2.0.

docs.title: Secret headers
docs.text: Use this when the provider gives you a static API key. Add one Header Name / Header Value pair per header, typically Authorization with Bearer <your key>, or the provider's own header such as X-API-Key. Headers are stored encrypted and never displayed again. When you edit the server, leave the header list empty to keep the stored headers; entering any header replaces the whole stored set, so re-enter every header the server needs.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Use this when the provider asks you to sign in. In most cases you only need the server URL:

  1. Choose OAuth 2.0 and click Detect settings. XTM One reads the server's published OAuth metadata (RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, then the authorization server's RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect metadata) and fills Authorize URL, Token URL and Registration URL (optional). Every discovered endpoint must use https:// (http:// is accepted only for localhost).
  2. Leave Client ID (optional) and Client Secret (optional) empty unless the provider gave you a client. Without one, XTM One registers itself with the provider automatically (RFC 7591). It first requests a public client and uses PKCE; if the provider rejects that registration mode, it retries without selecting an authentication method and securely stores any client secret the provider returns.
  3. Set Scopes (space-separated) if the provider documents required scopes.
  4. Create the server, then open its Configuration tab and click Authorize in the OAuth Connection card. You are sent to the provider to sign in and consent, then back to the server page, which shows OAuth connected and discovers the tools.

Values you type by hand always take precedence over discovered ones. If nothing can be discovered, enter the Authorize URL and Token URL from the provider's documentation.

If the provider requires a pre-registered client, create an OAuth application on the provider's side and register this redirect URI:

<BASE_URL>/api/oauth/callback

<BASE_URL> is the platform's public URL, including its base path when it is served under one (see Installation). Then enter the Client ID and, for a confidential client, the Client Secret the provider issued.

One connection per server

The token belongs to the server, not to each user: everyone who uses the server calls it with the account that authorized it, just as they would share its API key. On a personal server only its owner can authorize; on a company-managed server only an administrator can, and the configuration screen says so. Choose the account you authorize with accordingly — typically a service account with the least privileges the agents need.

Tokens are refreshed automatically before they expire when the provider issued a refresh token. The OAuth Connection card shows Connected, Error (a refresh failed: click Re-authorize) or Not connected. Switching the server back to Secret Headers discards the stored tokens.

Administrators control two related settings: MCP_OUTBOUND_DCR_ENABLED turns automatic client registration off (every OAuth server then needs a client ID), and OAUTH_TOKEN_URL_STRICT restricts which token URLs are accepted. See MCP OAuth and Security.

docs.title: Import from a client configuration
docs.text:
Import on the list page creates servers from a configuration you already have, either From a file (a .json file) or From a URL (Configuration URL, then Fetch). It accepts:

  • the mcpServers object used by Claude Desktop, Cursor and similar clients;
  • the servers object used by VS Code;
  • an MCP registry server.json, whose packages map to npx (npm), uvx (PyPI) or docker (OCI).

The review step lists every server found; select the ones to create. Placeholder values in environment variables and headers are dropped and reported as Still needs a value for …; placeholders in command arguments are imported as written, so review and replace them before using the server. Open each imported server afterwards and fill in any missing values. Imported servers use header authentication; switch a server to OAuth 2.0 in its configuration if it needs it. A configuration URL must use https:// and point to a public address. A file is limited to 1 MB and 100 servers.

docs.title: Test the connection
docs.text:
On the server page, Test connection connects, lists the server's tools and saves them. It has three outcomes:

  • Connection successful, with the number of tools discovered;
  • Authorization required: the server refused the request or publishes OAuth metadata while no credential is set — authorize it, or switch Authentication to OAuth 2.0 and authorize it;
  • an error message, which usually names the cause (see Troubleshooting).

In the Discovered Tools card of the Configuration tab, Discover Tools or Refresh Tools lists the tools again, and Test on a tool runs it once with arguments you provide. Refresh after any change to the transport, URL or credentials. Testing requires the right to configure the server.

docs.title: Give an agent access
docs.text:
An agent only uses the MCP servers attached to it:

  1. Open the agent, then Configuration > Tooling.
  2. In MCP Tool Servers, click Edit and click a server to attach or detach it.
  3. Optionally use the tool scope button (All tools by default) to keep only the tools the agent needs. Fewer tools means a clearer choice for the model and fewer actions it could take.

Only servers you can see are offered, and only enabled ones. A company-managed agent can only use company-managed servers. Assignment runs use the agent's servers and tool scope.

In chat, the tools panel of a conversation lets you add MCP servers to the General Assistant for that conversation, and your profile holds the servers selected by default. A server whose Hide from chat switch is on (edit view of its Configuration tab) is left out of these chat pickers but can still be attached to agents.

docs.title: Tool names
docs.text: The model sees each tool under the name the server gives it, not prefixed with the server name (characters other than letters, digits, _ and - are replaced with _, and names are cut to 64 characters). If two sources attached to the same agent or conversation expose a tool with the same name, only one of them is offered. Limit the tool scope, or avoid attaching two servers that publish the same tool names.

docs.title: Approvals, limits and files
docs.text:
• Approvals. MCP tools go through the platform's human approval of tool calls: on an agent that asks before running tools, a tool asks for a person's decision first unless a rule lets it run. The read tools of company-managed, enabled servers run without asking automatically; the tools of a personal server ask unless a rule or an approval covers them.
  • Time. Connecting (start, handshake and tool listing) is limited to 60 seconds. A tool call is limited by the run's tool timeout (300 seconds by default). After repeated connection failures the platform stops retrying a server for 5 minutes; Test connection always retries immediately.
  • Size. A tool result is cut to fit the model's context: at most 15% of the model's context window, and never more than 150,000 characters. Files a tool returns are kept as files of the conversation or run. When the agent follows a linked resource with read_mcp_resource, that read stores at most 40 MB in total — see Files an MCP tool returns.

docs.title: Sharing and company-managed servers
docs.text:
A server can be shared with groups or users as Read only (use it, cannot edit) or Can configure (use and edit, test included). Sharing a server lends its credentials: whoever can use it calls the external system with your headers, environment variables or OAuth token. XTM One asks you to confirm before lending them; see Sharing and access.

For a server the whole organisation relies on, prefer a company-managed server created by an administrator, authorized with a dedicated service account. Restrict access limits it to named people and groups when it should not reach everyone. Its read tools are also the only MCP tools that run without asking automatically on an agent that asks before running tools.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix command '…' was not found in PATH The command is not installed in the backend and worker images. Install it in your image, or give an absolute path to an executable. … does not exist or is not executable The absolute path is wrong, or the file lacks the execute permission. The test times out on a stdio server The first npx / uvx download is slow or blocked. Check the containers' access to the package registry, or pre-install the package in your image. Authorization required The server needs credentials: set headers, or switch to OAuth 2.0 and click Authorize. On a server you do not own, its owner (or an administrator, for a company-managed server) has to authorize it. Connection test failed: the server redirects to … The server answered with a redirect the connection does not follow (another host, or one that changes the request). If the address it names is the intended server, save the server with that URL. Automatic OAuth client registration is disabled on this platform… MCP_OUTBOUND_DCR_ENABLED is off. Create a client at the provider (redirect URI <BASE_URL>/api/oauth/callback) and enter its Client ID. …enter the Authorize URL and Token URL in the server configuration. The server publishes no OAuth metadata. Copy both URLs from the provider's documentation. The provider shows an error instead of its sign-in page, or OAuth failed after signing in The provider rejected the client or the redirect URI. Check that the redirect URI registered at the provider is exactly <BASE_URL>/api/oauth/callback, and that the client ID and secret are the ones it issued. OAuth status Error The token could not be refreshed (revoked consent, expired refresh token). Click Re-authorize. The server is not offered when editing an agent It is not visible to you, or the agent is company-managed and the server is not. The agent does not use an expected tool Check the agent's tool scope for that server, Refresh Tools on the server, and whether another attached source exposes a tool with the same name.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Once the server is attached, try it from a chat with the agent, then review its calls in the server's Activity tab (see MCP servers).

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
An integration connects XTM One to an external service, such as email, ticketing, messaging or cloud documents, and gives agents live access to it. This page gives you a quick tour of the integration screens.

Each first-party provider card in the integration catalog carries a diagonal corner ribbon. Certified marks the integrations Filigran qualifies and supports: the Filigran products (OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ and the XTM Hub) and the integrations Filigran runs its own agents on every day: Ashby, Atlassian Jira, Concord, DocuSign, Drata, Figma, GitHub, Google, Google Search, Grafana, HackerOne, HiBob, HubSpot, Letsignit, LinkedIn, Metabase, Microsoft, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview, Notion, OpenAPI / Swagger, Perk, Planhat, Slack and WhatsApp. The catalog serves the qualification as is_certified on each provider. Preview marks every other catalog entry. Custom providers you import yourself carry no ribbon — the qualification is ours to make about our own catalog, not about your bundles — and are identified by their Custom badge instead.

An integration of an imported custom provider calls its API at the base URL set in its configuration. Like an OpenAPI integration, it can reach public hosts and private-network hosts, so an intranet API works, but loopback, link-local, reserved and cloud-metadata addresses are refused. The base URL is checked when the integration is saved (a host name that does not resolve yet is accepted), and again on every tool call and Test connection, where each connection goes to the address that was checked. For an integration routed through a relay group, the relay checks the destination, and saving refuses only a base URL that is a cloud-metadata address.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, open Tools & Integrations > Integrations. The list page answers one practical question fast: which external connections are usable right now.

Each card is status-heavy by design, so the list already works as a health dashboard. The status badge is the signal to read first — it distinguishes a connection that is ready, one that is configured but not yet authorized, and one that needs re-authorization because permissions changed or the provider refused its refresh token or client credentials. You can search by name or provider and filter by visibility, tags, or category to narrow a long list.

If you have permission, New Integration starts a new connection. Credentials are always encrypted in the database.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Opening an integration shows a header with the connection status and the actions that make sense for it — a setup guide for provider prerequisites, Test connection to validate the live connection, Authorize or Re-authorize to resolve OAuth state, and delete. The detail page itself is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

A provider whose authentication modes are set up apart (Planhat: OAuth or an API key) has one setup guide per mode: the creation page shows the guide of the mode you pick, and an integration's page the guide of the mode it uses. The catalog card shows a guide that covers every mode.

When an integration is built on an open-source project, its setup guide credits that project under the title: its name links to the project's repository, followed by its author and its license. The Nova integration, for example, credits NOVA by Thomas Roccia, released under the MIT license; see Prompt safety (Nova).

Some integrations add pages of their own after those three tabs — the API Spec of an integration imported from an OpenAPI or Swagger document, or the rules of the Nova integration, which only administrators see. These pages are tabs of the integration: open the integration from Tools & Integrations > Integrations to reach them. Integrations are never listed one by one in the left navigation. Anyone who opens such a page from a link without being allowed to see it is told it is not available to them, with a way back to the Overview.

When Test connection reports a failure the platform recorded earlier - such as the last rule sync of the Nova integration - the stored error is shown only to the people who can manage the integration (administrators, for a company-managed integration). Everyone else sees that the check failed and a sentence saying who can see the details; the server log always keeps the full error.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview tells you not only whether the integration works, but why it does or does not. It combines usage figures, the connection state (authentication method, credential readiness, authorized and missing scopes), and cards showing which agents — and, for sync sources, which knowledge bases — depend on it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is a richer screen than most other resources because it mixes three concerns: the integration's identity, its authentication and provider setup, and its visibility and reuse in the workspace. The description field matters more than it looks — the UI passes it to agents as tool context.

This tab is also where you see what the integration actually does:

  • The available tools are split into read tools (retrieve or inspect information) and write tools (change something in the connected system). That split helps you judge risk. When the integration is connected, you can test a tool with real credentials before binding it to an agent.
  • If the provider supports events, an event triggers card explains, in business language, which external changes an agent can react to and how they are delivered (webhook, polling, or hybrid).
  • A webhooks card shows how external events enter XTM One. Depending on the provider it can display a URL to copy or, for GitHub, let you create and remove repository webhooks directly from the UI. What it shows follows the provider and the OAuth app the integration uses:
    • Microsoft 365: new emails and Teams messages are picked up by polling every 5 minutes, so there is no webhook to configure.
    • Slack: new messages are picked up by polling every 5 minutes. For real-time events, the card shows the shared Slack notifications endpoint to set as the Request URL in the Event Subscriptions of the Slack app the integration uses; the integration's Signing secret field (or, on your administrator's Slack app, the Slack OAuth default's) is what verifies them. See Slack message events below.
    • Other providers with events: an integration created on your administrator's OAuth app (you left its client ID empty and the administrator configured OAuth defaults for the provider) gets its events through the webhook the administrator set up, so the card says so instead of showing a URL. An integration on your own OAuth app shows its own webhook URL to configure in that app.
    • Replacing the client ID moves an integration to your own OAuth app. The tokens issued to the previous app are removed, so authorize the integration again before it is used.
    • For integrations created before XTM One recorded which OAuth app they use, the card compares the integration's client ID with the administrator's current OAuth default: the same ID means the administrator's app, any other means your own. Only when that comparison cannot be made does the card follow whether the provider has OAuth defaults, as it did before.

docs.title: Slack message events
docs.text:
New Slack message assignments receive messages in two ways. The event poller reads the monitored channels every 5 minutes with the integration's own token. It needs no setup and serves every assignment whose trigger names the integration (the assignment editor always sets one) or whose agent is bound to it. For real-time delivery, the Slack app the integration runs on sends its Events API deliveries to /api/v1/integrations/notifications/slack.

That endpoint checks every delivery against the app's Signing Secret (Slack app > Basic Information). Nothing has to be set up for events to keep arriving: with no Signing Secret stored, a delivery is accepted without a verified signature, exactly as before signatures were checked, and XTM One says so with a warning in the log and a Security Audit finding. Storing the secret turns verification on for the integrations of that app:

  • An integration running on its own Slack app: put the secret in the integration's Signing secret field.
  • An integration created with the Slack app your administrator provides (Settings > OAuth defaults): the administrator stores the secret in the Signing secret field of the Slack OAuth default, once for everyone.

Once a Signing Secret is stored, a delivery it does not prove never reaches the integrations of that app, and a verified event reaches only what it concerns:

  • It reaches only the integrations running on the app that signed it, and only those of the Slack workspace it was sent for.
  • It then reaches the assignments whose agent is connected to one of those integrations, under the rules the poller applies: for an OAuth integration bound to the agent, the token is the agent owner's own, or shared with its owner's explicit acknowledgement. An assignment whose acting user can no longer see the integration still receives the event, as polled events are delivered, and the log says so.
  • A message outside a public channel (private channel, direct or group message) reaches only the integration of its author or of the user Slack authorized the event for. Everyone else still receives it through the poller if their own token can read it.
  • The trigger's channel selection applies, as the poller applies it.
  • An assignment whose agent is connected to no Slack integration at all has no app or workspace to be matched against: it receives the event as before.

An event the platform cannot verify with what it holds (no usable Signing Secret for the app that sent it) is handed out as before signatures were checked: to every New Slack message assignment whose channel selection admits it, except those connected only to integrations whose app Signing Secret is stored.

Each message runs an assignment once. The real-time path and the poller claim it under the same key, and a Slack retry of the same event is skipped. A message an assignment's own run posted does not run that assignment again; any other assignment watching the channel still runs on it.

To refuse every event that cannot be verified, an administrator turns on Require verified integration notifications in Settings > Access and security (or sets INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION=true, which wins and locks the field). The messages of integrations without a stored Signing Secret then arrive through the poller only, and the Security Audit says how many integrations are concerned. If Slack disabled the app's Event Subscriptions after refused deliveries, re-enable them once the secret is stored.

docs.title: OpenRouter
docs.text:
The OpenRouter integration connects an OpenRouter account - one API key for hundreds of models. It takes the account's API key and, optionally, a management key (OpenRouter > Settings > Management keys): the management key cannot run models, but it unlocks the credits, the activity and the API key management below. Test connection checks both keys.

Its three pages, tabs of the integration shown to the people who manage it:

  • Usage - what the key spent today, this week and this month, its spending limit, the credits left on the account, and the spend per day and per model over the last 30 days, with the providers that served each model.
  • Models - the catalog the key may use (text and embedding models): prices per million tokens, context, tool calling, reasoning, image input, and for each model the providers serving it with their price, uptime and latency. An administrator uses it to feed the platform's OpenRouter LLM provider: offer the models you want, mark the default one, and create the provider - or link an OpenRouter provider made in Settings > AI Models. The provider keeps a copy of the integration's API key, replaced whenever the key is replaced in the integration, and the context window of every newly offered model is taken from OpenRouter's catalog. Only a company-managed integration can feed the platform provider: the provider is shared by every user. Making the integration private again, unlinking it or deleting it leaves the provider running on the key it holds. In Settings > AI Models such a provider carries an Integration badge that leads back here.

The integration's Overview says whether the platform runs on it: the provider it feeds and its models, or, for an administrator, what is missing and a link to the Models page that creates it. Adding an OpenRouter provider in Settings > AI Models while a company-managed OpenRouter integration holding its API key feeds none points there too, so the key is not entered a second time.

docs.title: LM Studio
docs.text:
The LM Studio integration connects an LM Studio server (0.4 or later). When the platform can reach the server - an LM Studio on the same machine or the same network - leave Route through relay on Direct: the platform calls the server itself. When it cannot, route the integration through a relay group, and every request leaves from a relay installed next to the server (see Relays). It takes the server URL as the platform, or the relay, reaches it (for example http://gpu-host:1234, or http://host.docker.internal:1234 for an LM Studio running on the machine that hosts the platform's containers; a /v1 suffix is removed) and, only when Require Authentication is on in LM Studio's server settings, an API token (masked, never shown again). The integration is connected as soon as its server URL is set. Test Connection lists the server's models, on the integration's route.

Its Models page is for the people who manage the integration:

  • the models on the server - chat, embedding and decision models, loaded or not - with their size, quantization, maximum context, tool calling, reasoning and image input, and each loaded instance with the context it is served with;
  • Load a model with its options (context length, flash attention, KV cache on the GPU) and unload an instance; Download a model from the LM Studio catalog (openai/gpt-oss-20b) or a Hugging Face link, with a quantization for a Hugging Face link, and follow the download. Loading, unloading and downloading are for the holder of the server: an administrator for a company-managed integration, its owner otherwise;
  • the platform's LM Studio LLM provider: an administrator offers the models they want, marks the default one and creates the provider from a company-managed integration. The provider holds no URL and no token: it reads them, and the relay group, from the integration on every request, so an edit of the integration applies to it at once: its requests go through the relay group when it has one, directly otherwise. A newly offered model gets the context it is loaded with (the smallest of its instances), else its maximum. Unlinking the provider, deleting the integration or making it private stops it: its requests are refused. An LM Studio provider is created only this way, never from Settings > AI Models.
  • API Keys - the keys of the account (management key): their spend, limit and expiry. The holder of the account - an administrator for a company-managed integration, its owner otherwise - can create a key with its own spending limit and reset period, rename it, change its limit, disable it or delete it. A new key is shown once; XTM One does not keep it. The key the integration runs on, and the key of the platform LLM provider, cannot be disabled or deleted from here.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: Teams meeting recording and recurring events
docs.text:
The Microsoft integration's calendar tools act as the account that authorized it, on its default calendar or on any calendar passed as calendar_id (a secondary calendar, or one shared with the account).

  • Recording and transcription. When an agent creates or updates a Teams meeting, it can turn on Record and transcribe automatically, and allow or block transcription and recording. The tool changes the event's Teams meeting, then reads the options back from Microsoft and reports what Teams kept: when Teams does not keep a change (a Teams meeting policy of the organizer can forbid recording or transcription), the agent gets an error, never a success. Reading an event also shows its Teams meeting options: recording, transcription, who can bypass the lobby and who can present.
  • Recurring series. An agent can create a daily, weekly, monthly or yearly series, list its occurrences between two dates (with the ones already cancelled), and move or cancel one occurrence without touching the rest. Cancelling a meeting the account organizes sends its attendees a cancellation notice, with an optional message. A series has one Teams meeting, so its recording options cover every occurrence.

Only the organizer of a meeting can change its options, so connect the integration with the account that organizes the meetings (a dedicated service mailbox, for example). The options use the delegated Microsoft Graph permission OnlineMeetings.ReadWrite, which the integration requests; acting as the signed-in account, it needs no Teams application access policy. If a tool answers that the token lacks OnlineMeetings.ReadWrite (for example in a tenant where users cannot consent to it), an administrator adds it to the delegated permissions of the integration's app registration in Microsoft Entra ID and grants admin consent, then the integration is re-authorized (Re-authorize on its page) so its new token carries the permission.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: answering a meeting invitation
docs.text:
An agent can accept, tentatively accept or decline a meeting invitation the account received, as Outlook's buttons do, with an optional comment to the organizer. It answers the invitation only and never changes the meeting: a meeting the account organizes is refused, and a cancelled one too.

  • One occurrence or the series. An occurrence of a recurring meeting (from the list of its occurrences) answers that occurrence only; the series answers every occurrence.
  • Without notifying the organizer. The response is sent to the organizer by default; the agent can also record it in the calendar only.
  • Proposing another time. With a tentative acceptance or a decline, the agent can propose a new time, sent to the organizer with the response, when the organizer allows new time proposals.
  • What the agent reports. After answering, the tool reads the event back from Microsoft: its subject, start, end, the response Microsoft now shows (accepted, tentatively accepted or declined), whether the organizer was notified, and its link. A response Microsoft does not show is reported as not confirmed, never as done. When Outlook takes a declined meeting off the calendar, the agent says so.
  • It is a write: an agent whose Microsoft binding is read-only does not get it. It uses the delegated permission Calendars.ReadWrite, which the integration already requests.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: telling a meeting message from an email
docs.text:
A meeting invitation reads like any email when its body holds no Teams join link, an in-person meeting above all. The mail tools say which messages are meeting messages, read from the type Microsoft gives the message, with no extra request.

  • Reading one email. Message type: is message for an email, else meetingRequest, meetingCancelled, meetingAccepted, meetingTentativelyAccepted or meetingDeclined.
  • Listings and search. The full listing and the search carry the same line; the one-line listing adds meetingRequest, meetingCancelled or meetingResponse to the message's state.
  • New email triggers. The event carries message_type. The filter exclude_meeting_messages drops meeting requests, cancellations and answers before any run; {"message_type": "meetingRequest"} in an expression keeps only invitations.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: Teams meeting transcripts
docs.text:
An agent reads what was said in a Teams meeting from its transcript, as the account that authorized the integration: in meetings it organized and in meetings it was invited to. Each line names its speaker.

  • Why there is no transcript. When Microsoft lists no transcript for a meeting, the agent gets Microsoft's reason and message: either Microsoft exposes no transcript for the meeting, or Microsoft refused to list it. A refusal is a permission problem, not a missing transcript, and the answer names the permission to grant, OnlineMeetingTranscript.Read.All. Listing recent transcripts counts the refused meetings apart from the meetings without a transcript.
  • From the recording. A transcribed meeting also keeps its transcript inside its recording: it is what the Teams player shows. When Microsoft lists no transcript, the join-URL transcript tool reads the one inside the meeting's recording, in the Recordings folder of your OneDrive (whatever its name in your language), where Teams saves an automatic recording of a meeting you organize. The answer names the recording it read, and the other recordings made at that time if there are any.
  • From a recording link. get_microsoft_recording_transcript reads the transcript of a recording from its OneDrive or SharePoint link (a sharing link or the address of the video), or finds a meeting's recording in your OneDrive from the meeting ID. Use the link for a recording saved in someone else's OneDrive: Teams saves a recording in the OneDrive of the person who started it.
  • Only the transcript is read: the video is never downloaded.
  • Reading the transcript inside a recording goes through SharePoint, so it needs the delegated permission AllSites.Read (Office 365 SharePoint Online) on the integration's app registration, like the transcripts of channel meetings. If the agent answers that it could not obtain a SharePoint access token, an administrator adds that permission in Microsoft Entra ID and grants admin consent, then the integration is re-authorized (Re-authorize on its page).

docs.title: Microsoft 365: reading a Teams message in full
docs.text:
When an agent lists a Teams channel or chat, it sees each message whole, up to 4,000 characters of text (an administrator can change this with MICROSOFT_TEAMS_MESSAGE_TEXT_LIMIT, see Configuration). A longer message, such as a memo with sections and lists, is cut at the end of a word and ends with a note: [truncated, N more characters: read it in full with get_microsoft_channel_message(team_id=..., channel_id=..., message_id=...)]. The note names the exact call, with the message's own IDs, so the agent can read the rest. A message without the note is complete.

  • One message, in full. get_microsoft_channel_message reads one post or thread reply of a channel, and get_microsoft_chat_message one message of a chat. The agent gets the whole text (including cards posted by apps and workflows, and quoted messages), the author, when it was posted, edited or deleted, its reactions, attached files, pasted images, mentions and its Teams link. For a channel post, it also gets the number of replies and the IDs of the newest ones.
  • From a link. Paste a Teams message link (Copy link on a message in Teams) in the conversation: the agent passes it to the tool, which reads the team, channel, message and thread from the link.
  • Busy channels. All the messages of one listing share a text budget, so a channel with many long messages stays readable: the longest ones are cut shorter, the short ones stay whole, and every cut message carries its note.
  • Both tools are reads. A Teams channel Scope(s) limits the channel tool to the selected channels (a link to another channel is refused) and removes the chat tool.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: posting a file in a Teams channel
docs.text:
An agent can post a file of its conversation or run in a Teams channel, as the account that authorized the integration: a deck it exported as a PDF, a report, a file a user attached. The tool is send_microsoft_channel_file, and the file is its file_id, the id the tool that produced or received the file returns (export_presentation for a deck).

  • The file is uploaded unchanged into the channel's Files folder (its SharePoint folder), then the message is posted with the file attached, so it opens from the message like a file a person shared. A file of the same name in that folder is replaced, as a new version of it.
  • The post is a new message with an optional text, or a reply in a thread (reply_to_message_id). One file per message, up to 100 MB.
  • The agent gets back the link to the message and the file's SharePoint links.
  • A file that cannot be uploaded posts nothing, and a channel that does not exist (or that the account cannot reach) is reported with nothing uploaded.
  • It is a write: a read-only binding of the integration does not offer it, and a Teams channel Scope(s) limits it to the selected channels. The account must be a member of the team; the delegated permissions ChannelMessage.Send and Files.ReadWrite.All, which the integration requests, cover the post and the upload.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: sending a file in a Teams chat
docs.text:
An agent can send a file of its conversation or run into a Teams chat, 1:1 or group, as the account that authorized the integration: a report it exported as a PDF, a file a user attached. The tool is send_microsoft_chat_file, and the file is its file_id.

  • The file is uploaded unchanged into the sending account's OneDrive, folder Microsoft Teams Chat Files, where Teams itself keeps chat files.
  • Before the message is posted, every member of the chat except the sender is given read-only access to the file, signed in and without an invitation email. The file's permissions are then read back: each member must be listed with access.
  • A grant that fails, or a member Microsoft does not list with access, returns an error naming the member and posts no message: nobody receives a file card they could not open. The file stays uploaded, and the error carries its link.
  • On success the agent gets back the message id, where the file is stored and the members the read access was granted to.
  • It is a write: a read-only binding of the integration does not offer it. The delegated permissions ChatMember.ReadWrite (to read the chat's members), Chat.ReadWrite and Files.ReadWrite.All, which the integration requests, cover the share and the post.

An agent account bound to Teams sends the files its answer names the same way. A [[FILE:id]] marker in the answer is taken out of the text and the file posted with the reply as a Teams file card:

  • In a chat, the file goes to the account's Microsoft Teams Chat Files folder and is shared read-only with the chat's members, checked as above, before the reply is posted.
  • In a channel thread, the file goes to the channel's Files folder, which the team's members already read.
  • A file that cannot be uploaded, shared or carded, or a file past 100 MB, is not attached: the reply carries one plain line File not attached: <name> instead, never a raw marker. A marker naming a file of another user is dropped.
  • A reply without a marker is posted as before.

The other markers of an answer become links, on Teams as on every account (Outlook, Gmail, WhatsApp): a deck, a report, a video or a dashboard ([[PRESENTATION:id]], [[REPORT:id]], [[VIDEO:id]], [[DASHBOARD:id]]) is posted as a link to its page on XTM One, labelled with its title, and a deck marker that names a slide ([[PRESENTATION:id#/slide]]) opens the deck on that slide. A marker naming an item of another user is dropped, never posted raw; an investigation or a scheduled work item marker is removed.

Editing a message keeps its file. update_microsoft_chat_message and update_microsoft_channel_message send a message whole again, and Teams drops a file card the edit leaves out, so both tools read the message first and send its files back with the new text. The answer names the files kept. A card the message carried is replaced by the edit's own card, as before. A message that cannot be read is still edited, and the answer warns that a file it carried may no longer show. Files in a channel need no new grant: they sit in the channel's Files folder, which the team's members already read.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: people in a Teams group chat
docs.text:
An agent can see who is in a Teams chat and change the members of a group chat, as the account that authorized the integration. The chat keeps its thread: no new chat is created.

  • Who is in the chat. list_microsoft_chat_members lists each member with their name, email, role and membership id.
  • Adding people. add_microsoft_chat_members adds one or more people, by email address or Microsoft Entra user ID. By default they see the whole conversation since the chat was created; with include_history set to false they see only what is posted after they join. Someone already in the chat is left unchanged. The answer is the chat's member list after the change.
  • Removing someone. remove_microsoft_chat_member removes one person, by email address, user ID or the membership id the listing gives. The answer is the member list after the change.
  • A one-on-one chat cannot take new members (Microsoft Teams does not allow it): the agent is told so and nothing changes. Start a group chat with create_microsoft_chat instead.
  • Adding and removing are writes: a read-only binding of the integration offers only the listing. A Teams channel Scope(s) removes all three tools, like the other chat tools.
  • They need the delegated permission ChatMember.ReadWrite, which the integration now requests.
