    • For the authorization code and implicit flows, register <platform URL>/api/oauth/callback as the redirect URI in the API's OAuth app, create the integration, then click Authorize. An implicit token cannot be refreshed: click Authorize again when it expires.
    • With a device code, Authorize shows a code and a link: open the API's sign-in page, enter the code and approve. No redirect URI is needed.
    • Client-credentials and password tokens are requested when tools run and reused until they expire. The password flow takes the username and password of the account the API should act as; its client ID and secret are only needed when the API asks for them.
    • An OpenID Connect scheme is read from its discovery document when the spec loads, and offers the flows its provider supports; its sign-in requests the openid scope, plus offline_access when the provider supports it.
    • A client certificate can be added to any option, under Client certificate: paste or load the PEM certificate, its private key, and the key's passphrase when it is encrypted. It is sent on every call and every token request. An expired certificate is refused, and calls stop with a message saying so; from 30 days before its expiry, the API Spec tab and the integration's overview flag it. To rotate it, have the new certificate issued before the old one expires, then click Replace under Client certificate in the API Spec tab: the next call presents the new one.
  • The operations to expose, grouped by tag. Deprecated operations start switched off, and Read only keeps only the operations that read (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY). The pencil next to an operation renames its tool or rewrites its description; agents choose tools by these, so a clear name and description help.

The name and description of the integration can be set on the same page. The description is filled from the spec, and agents read it as context for every tool of the API.

Operations that upload a file become tools too: a multipart file field, or a request body in a file format such as application/octet-stream, an image, a PDF or XML. The agent passes a file available in the conversation, such as a file the user attached, or text it writes, such as a CSV it builds. These operations carry a File badge in the list.

Every HTTP method becomes a tool, including HEAD and OPTIONS, which answer with the response status and headers, and the OpenAPI 3.2 QUERY method and custom methods. TRACE and CONNECT never do: TRACE echoes the request back, credentials included, and CONNECT opens a tunnel instead of calling the API. OpenAPI 3.2 documents are read with their additions too: a querystring parameter is one argument that holds the whole query string, JSON Lines bodies take a list of items, a $self URL is the base of the document's relative links, and tag summaries name the groups of operations.

Some operations cannot become tools, and the preview says why for each: file content in a query, header or path parameter or in a URL-encoded form, TRACE and CONNECT, and definitions that cannot be resolved (a referenced file that cannot be downloaded, for example). An operation the spec marks as public (security: []) is called without the credential. So is an operation the spec places on another server than the base URL (another host, scheme or port), so that a spec cannot send the credential elsewhere; the preview flags these operations.

Calls can reach public hosts and private-network hosts, so an intranet API works. Loopback, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused, for the spec download, the files it references, and every tool call and token request. Each connection goes to the address that was checked, so a host name that resolves differently a moment later cannot redirect it. Behind an HTTP proxy, which makes the connections itself, each request's URL is checked before it is sent.

An OpenAPI integration adds an API Spec tab to its detail page. It shows where the spec came from, its version and authentication, and lets you change which operations are tools, and their names and descriptions, without importing again. Refresh from URL downloads a URL-sourced spec again: selected operations that disappeared are dropped, new ones stay off until you select them, and the names and descriptions you set are kept. Replace spec loads a different URL, file or archive; the new document must offer an authentication that uses the same kind of credential. An OpenAPI integration that holds no spec yet (one created before spec import existed) gets its first spec the same way, through PUT /api/v1/integrations/{id}/openapi or the agent builder's update_integration with openapi: its stored credential is kept, and the spec's absolute server becomes the base URL when none is set. The OAuth endpoints and scopes follow the chosen option: the ones it changes are updated, the others keep your edits. The tab also shows the OAuth endpoints and scopes, which you can edit, and the client certificate: its subject, issuer and expiry, with Replace and Remove. Test connection calls one enabled GET operation that needs no argument.

Agents bind an OpenAPI integration as that specific integration. There is no per-user binding for it, because each OpenAPI integration is a different API. For the members of a shared agent to use its tools, share the integration with their groups.

Admins can switch the whole provider off from the integration catalog, like any other provider.

docs.title: Several accounts of one provider on an agent
docs.text:
When an agent binds two or more integrations of the same provider (two Microsoft accounts, for example), each account's tools get a suffix so the agent can tell them apart: list_microsoft_calendar_events__corporate and list_microsoft_calendar_events__personal. The suffix is the integration's tool suffix (tool_slug in the API). It is derived once from the integration's name when the integration is created and does not change when the integration is renamed, so the agents, skills, prompts and assignment gates that name a suffixed tool keep working after a rename.

To change it, set tool_slug through the integrations API (PUT /api/v1/integrations/{id}) or the agent builder's update_integration tool (create_integration takes it too): lowercase letters, digits and underscores, at most 21 characters, unique among the owner's integrations of that provider. An invalid value is refused before anything is written, and a suffix another integration of the same provider and owner holds is refused with the reason. The new name is used from the next run; anything that names the old suffixed tool must be updated. The agent builder's list_integrations and get_integration tools show each integration's suffix, and get_agent shows the suffix of each binding.

An assignment's tool gate (activation_check) can name one account's tool without its suffix, by its base name and the integration id: "tool": "list_microsoft_calendar_events@<integration id>", or "tool": "list_microsoft_calendar_events" with an "integration_id" key. The current suffixed name is found when the gate runs, so the gate survives any change of the suffix.

docs.title: Read-only and managed nuances
docs.text: Integrations can have more nuanced edit behavior than other resources. Company-managed integrations are read-only for non-admins, and some suite-level registrations behave like centrally managed records rather than personal connections. Status, tools, and related usage stay visible even when editing is restricted.

docs.title: Sharing an OAuth integration
docs.text:
An OAuth integration is connected with one person's account: whoever authorized it. You can share it like any other integration - with groups, with individual users, or company-wide by making it company-managed - and once it is shared, everyone it is shared with acts using that connected account. Their agents, assignments and flows use the owner's token, so actions in the external service appear as the owner.

That is the default. When sharing is turned on in Configuration, a notice says so, with one switch below it:

  • Don't share my connected account (off by default; an admin editing someone else's integration sees Don't share the owner's connected account) keeps the integration shared without the owner's account: the owner keeps their connection and is the only one who uses it, and everyone else it is shared with authorizes the integration with their own account (see below). The choice is kept: authorizing the integration again never shares the owner's account. Only the owner or an admin can turn it on or off.
  • Reconnecting a shared integration that shares its account shares the account used to reconnect it; the Authorize button says so. A group-shared or user-shared integration is reconnected by its owner. A company-managed integration can be reconnected by any admin, who then becomes its owner. Turning Don't share my connected account off again shares the owner's account and disconnects everyone's own.
  • Saving asks once: a confirmation names whose account it is, who will act with it and how to avoid it. Confirming shares it; cancelling changes nothing.
  • A member who edits a shared integration without being its owner or an admin cannot share the owner's account: if the owner never shared it, saving a new share shares the integration without it, and the confirmation says so before anything is saved.
  • Stopping sharing - removing every group and user and turning company-managed off - makes the integration personal again: only its owner uses the account until it is shared again.

In a chat, people who cannot see the integration, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with them, use their own account of the same provider instead when they have one; when they do not, a note under the answer says the integration was not used for them and why, and the agent is told too. What carries it - an agent's runs, public link and channels, a flow, a knowledge base import source, a skill's source - acts with its account for that thing's audience, as the next section explains.

The dashboard reminds owners which of their integrations share their connected account, with a shortcut to stop sharing.

Through the API, the choice is the keep_oauth_credentials_on_share field of POST /api/v1/integrations and PUT /api/v1/integrations/{id}: true shares the connected account, false shares the integration without it. A request that shares the integration without the field keeps the account private, as it always did: an account whose sharing was never consented to stays its owner's, and everyone else authorizes their own. An edit that does not change sharing and sends no choice changes nothing.

An agent makes the same choice with the share_connected_account argument of the create_integration and update_integration tools (false is Don't share my connected account; credential_mode per_user or shared says the same). It is written exactly as the switch writes it, and true is refused for someone who is not the owner, the account's holder or an admin. get_integration and list_integrations report the mode of an OAuth integration and, when it is per_user, how many people connected their own account. The mode protects the other people's chats: the owner's own agents keep acting with the owner's account in their assignments and flows.

docs.title: Shared without the connected account: each person authorizes their own
docs.text:
On an OAuth integration shared with Don't share my connected account:

  • Everyone it is shared with sees a Your account block on the integration's page: Connect your account opens the provider's sign-in for their own account (the integration's OAuth app, the same one for everyone), with its status and Disconnect my account. The integrations list says whether their account is connected.
  • Every run acts with the account of the person it runs for: a chat, the person chatting; an assignment, the person it runs as (else the agent's owner); a flow, its owner; the public widget, event polling and notifications, the agent's owner. Never with someone else's: someone who has not connected theirs gets no tools from the integration, and a note under the answer links to the page where they connect it.
  • The owner connects first and keeps their own connection; the integration reads as connected when theirs is. The people who manage it see who connected an account (names and status, never the account) and can disconnect anyone.
  • A new OAuth app (client ID) disconnects everyone's own account, and someone who can no longer see the integration loses theirs. A skill's private source cannot use such an integration: a skill is shared and refreshed unattended, with no one person whose account it would act with.

This works for every OAuth integration, OpenAPI ones included. Through the API, the choice stays keep_oauth_credentials_on_share (false shares the integration without the account); the integration reports it as credential_mode (shared or per_user). A person disconnects their own account with DELETE /api/v1/integrations/{id}/my-credential; the managers list the connected people with GET /api/v1/integrations/{id}/credentials and disconnect one with DELETE /api/v1/integrations/{id}/credentials/{user_id}.

docs.title: Lending your integrations through a shared agent
docs.text:
An agent you share with groups or people can be bound to your personal integrations. You choose, per agent, what the people it is shared with get when they chat with it:

  • Use my integrations through this agent. The agent runs with your connected accounts in their chats too, under its persona, guardrails and tool scoping. The integration stays yours: it is not listed on their Integrations page, they cannot bind it to their own agents or use it in their own chats, and they never see the credential. Assignments, flows, the web widget and channels already act with the agent's integrations.
  • Switch to per-user. When they chat, members use their own connected integration of the same provider; your account stays for the agent's assignments and flows. An imported OpenAPI integration cannot switch: each one is its own API.
  • Share the integration itself (from the integration's page, see above) is a different grant: it becomes theirs to use everywhere, not only through this agent.

Through the API, an agent's owner lends with lent_integration_ids on PUT /api/v1/agents/{id}: only the owner, only their own integrations, only ones the agent binds ([] lends nothing). The agent reports it as integration_lending (the ids, who set it and when). Binding a new personal integration does not lend it until the owner chooses again; unbinding one stops lending it.

An agent sets it with the platform tools: update_agent (or create_agent) with integration_lending='true' lends every personal integration of the owner the agent binds (company-managed and per-user integrations are never lent), 'false' stops lending, blank leaves it as it is. The same rule applies: only the agent's owner, never an editor or an administrator on their behalf. get_agent shows the lending (on or off, the integrations lent, who set it and when) and list_agents with detail='full' shows it per agent. A copy of an agent (clone_agent, a fleet export or apply, a catalog install) never carries the lending: it starts off, as in the settings page. A fleet health check (get_fleet_health) reports a shared member bound to its owner's personal integrations it does not lend (shared_agent_without_lending); only the owner fixes it.

An agent another agent consults, delegates to or transfers to uses its own lending for the person in the chat: when both the assistant and the desk it consults lend, the desk runs with its owner's integrations for that person.

docs.title: Sharing a personal credential, everywhere
docs.text:
Any stored credential - an OAuth account, a personal access token, an API key, a bot token, a service-account secret - is used by more than the people an integration is shared with. Everything that carries the integration lends it to its own audience:

  • An agent bound to it: its assignments, its flows, its public web widget, the people who message it on a channel without an account and the platform MCP key all act with the agent's integrations. In a chat, someone the integration is not shared with uses their own account instead, or is told under the answer that it was not used.
  • An assignment that overrides the agent's integrations or listens to an integration's events, for everyone who can use the agent.
  • A flow node, for the flow's audience.
  • A knowledge base import source: its readers see what is synced with it.
  • A skill's private source: it is refreshed with it.
  • The General Assistant's platform bindings, for every user, and a user's own assistant, for that user.

Sharing is never refused. Before a change that lets new people act with someone's credential - sharing an integration, an agent, a knowledge base or a skill, making one company-managed, binding an integration to an agent, an assignment, a flow node, an import source or the General Assistant, enabling an agent's web widget, transferring an owner - one confirmation says whose credential it is ("your GitHub token", "Alice's Jira connected account"), who will be able to use it (with counts, and the public link, anonymous channel users or the MCP key when they apply), through what, what they can do with it (the provider, and the scopes when known) and how to avoid it: Don't share my connected account, switching the agent to per-user integrations, or a company integration. Nothing is asked when nobody new is reached.

The integration's Overview has a Sharing and access section for the people who manage it: every way the credential reaches people, with the reason (shared directly, bound to an agent, an assignment override or trigger, a per-user binding an assignment resolves to the person it runs as, a flow node, an import source, a skill source, the assistants), the audience and a link. An entity you cannot open is named by its owner only. The integration cards show the same thing compactly (Shared - 3 ways), with the breakdown on hover.

The same answers are available to API clients, read-only: GET /api/v1/integrations/{id}/exposure, GET /api/v1/integrations/exposure/summary and POST /api/v1/integrations/exposure/preview (see Sharing and access for every moment you are asked, and the routes every lent resource has).

docs.title: Scope(s): boundary or guidance
docs.text:
An agent, and each of its assignments, can narrow an integration to specific elements in its Scope(s) card (repositories, channels, CRM object types). The card says which kind of selection it is.

By default every selection is Guidance only: it is given to the agent as instructions ("focus your work on these specific resources"), and its tools can still reach other elements. This is also what every selection made before the choice existed stays.

A selection of one of the four element types below can instead be a hard boundary: turn on Enforce as a boundary next to it, in the agent's or the assignment's Scope(s) card, and save. The card then reads Enforced. The choice is made on each selection, so an agent can enforce its repositories while its Slack channels stay guidance. The Security Audit lists, for information, the selections of these types that are kept as guidance; it does not change the audit's score.

  • Enforced - GitHub repositories. The agent's GitHub tools cannot work on any other repository, in assignments and in chat. A request for another repository is refused with the list of allowed ones, whichever way it names that repository. Repository listings and searches, a team's repositories, sub-issues and project boards show only the selected repositories, and a project card of another repository cannot be changed (draft cards belong to no repository and stay available). The tools that reach repositories without naming one - the raw GraphQL query and its query-only sibling, repository search, the notification inbox - are not offered, and creating or transferring a repository, changing a team's members and comparing with a branch of another repository are refused. Organization, team, project and user details stay readable.
  • Enforced - Slack channels. The agent's Slack tools cannot read, post to, react in or manage any other conversation, in assignments and in chat; a channel may be named by its ID or its #name. Channel listings and message and file searches show only the selected channels, listing files needs a selected channel, and a file named by its ID is read or deleted only when it is shared in one of them. Direct messages and creating a channel are not offered. Workspace members stay readable. A Slack channel bot the agent posts through is bound by the bot's own publish channels, not by this selection.
  • Enforced - Microsoft Teams channels. The agent's Teams tools cannot read, post to, reply in or list the members of any other channel, in assignments and in chat; a channel meeting's recordings and transcripts are read only in a selected channel (by name or ID), and so is an image pasted in a channel message. The teams-and-channels listing shows the selected channels. Teams chats (1:1 and group) and creating a channel are not offered. The selection applies to Teams only: Outlook mail, calendar, OneDrive, SharePoint, To Do and your own online meetings keep their tools.
  • Enforced - HubSpot CRM object types. The HubSpot tools of an object type that is not selected (contacts, companies, deals, tickets) are not offered, in assignments and in chat, and associations, record deletion, record attachments and the associations a record read includes are refused for any other object type. Marketing email campaigns and the file manager (file search and upload) are not a CRM object type and are not offered; a file is downloaded through the record of a selected type it is attached to. Emails, notes, calls, meetings and tasks are read through a record of a selected type (its timeline, an engagement search on it, its associations), and one associated with no such record is refused. Forms and their submissions, sequences and the inbound report are offered only when contacts are selected. Owners, teams, pipeline and property definitions stay readable. A custom object is selected and named by its object type ID (2-...).
  • Guidance only - every other element type (GitHub organizations, Jira projects, ...): these have no switch and cannot be enforced. The selection is given to the agent as instructions, but its tools can still reach other elements. Do not rely on it as an access boundary; restrict the integration's own credentials instead.

An assignment refines the agent's selection, and the stricter of the two wins: a type is a boundary for an assignment's runs when the agent or the assignment enforces it. A type the agent enforces is a boundary for every assignment of that agent (the assignment's switch shows it on and locked), and an assignment can enforce a type its agent keeps as guidance. The boundary is then the assignment's refinement of the agent's selection, and one that leaves no valid element (an entry that is not a valid owner/name, or an assignment enforcing repositories its agent does not offer) allows nothing.

The work an agent hands over - to a consulted or transferred agent, or as a background task - stays within the boundaries of the run that handed it over, narrowed further by the other agent's own selection of those types. A selection the delegating run only has as guidance does not follow the work: the other agent keeps working from its own selection, as the prompt it receives says.

What the boundary does not cover

The boundary applies to the GitHub integration's own tools. It does not restrict another route to GitHub the agent may have - an MCP server that exposes GitHub, a custom tool, the code interpreter or the web tools - nor a flow's integration nodes, nor the General Assistant, which has no Scope(s). It does not govern the selected repository's own automation either: a workflow the agent starts runs with that repository's own token and secrets, and GitHub serves the commits of a repository's forks through the repository itself. After a transfer, the conversation continues under the new agent's own selection.

docs.title: Who receives an integration's events
docs.text:
An assignment with an integration-event trigger listens to the integration its trigger names, or, when it names none, to its agent's first integration of that provider. A flow's integration-event trigger names one too. XTM One reads those events with the integration's credentials and hands them to a run, and checks whether the run's user can see the integration:

  • for an assignment, the user its runs act as: its Run as user, else its owner (the agent's owner);
  • for a flow, the flow's owner.

Seeing the integration means the usual rule: it is theirs, it is shared with them or one of their groups, or it is company-managed and not restricted to an audience. Admins see every integration. A company-managed assignment with neither an owner nor a Run as user keeps the connected-account rule above, as before.

When that user cannot see it, the events are still delivered, as they always were, and never silently: the worker log names the assignment (or the flow and its trigger node) once an hour, and the security audit (GET /api/v1/security-audit, Settings > Security) lists it as a warning. Share the integration with that user, or pick one they can see.

docs.title: OpenAEV tenants
docs.text:
On a multi-tenant OpenAEV, every OpenAEV tool request acts on one tenant: the one in the integration's Tenant ID field (the tenant's ID in OpenAEV).

  • Left empty (the default), the tenant is chosen the way OpenAEV does for a request that names none: the account's only tenant, or the default tenant when the account belongs to several, it among them. A single-tenant OpenAEV, and an account in the default tenant, need nothing more.
  • Set, every request goes to that tenant. The account must belong to it: otherwise OpenAEV answers TENANT_ACCESS_DENIED, and the error names the tenant the request went to.
  • An account that belongs to several tenants, none of them the default, needs the field: until then creates fail, with an error that says so.

Where to set it:

  • OpenAEV registered with XTM One (the default xtm_one mode): the integration is created and kept up to date by the registration and its page is read-only, except the Tenant ID field, which an administrator edits there. A new registration keeps it. Its token is each user's own, so with the field set, every user of the integration works in that tenant and must belong to it.
  • API-key integration (copilot and dev modes): the field is on the integration form. To work in several tenants, create one integration per tenant and bind each to the agents that work there.

docs.title: OpenCRQ tools
docs.text: An OpenCRQ integration follows the OpenCRQ instance it is connected to. The OpenCRQ version card of its Overview tab shows the connected version, whether XTM One holds the description of the instance's operations, the tools hidden from your agents because the instance cannot serve them, and the fields a tool sends that the instance does not accept. A tool that sends such a field is refused before anything is sent. The card is shown to everyone who can open the integration, and turns amber when the description is pending, unavailable, or not kept because OpenCRQ registered with the default registration token. For an OpenCRQ that is not registered with XTM One, the description is read from the instance at the first OpenCRQ call of each conversation or run. How each instance describes itself is in OpenCRQ tools follow each instance.

docs.title: XTM Hub
docs.text:
The XTM Hub integration gives agents the catalog of the XTM Hub, the Filigran ecosystem hub: the ready-to-use resources it publishes for the XTM Platform, namely OpenCTI custom dashboards, custom views, playbooks and integrations (connectors, CSV / TAXII / RSS feeds, live streams, third-party integrations), and OpenAEV scenarios. An agent bound to it can:

  • list the catalogs;
  • search one catalog, or all of them, by text, use case and compatible OpenCTI / OpenAEV version, and for OpenCTI integrations by type, verified status, connector-manager deployment and license;
  • read one resource in full, from its slug or its XTM Hub link;
  • list the newest and the most deployed resources, and the use cases resources are tagged with.

These need no account: keep the authentication mode None. Leave the XTM Hub URL empty to use the platform's default XTM Hub (https://hub.filigran.io unless XTM_HUB_DEFAULT_URL names another), or set the address of another XTM Hub.

With an XTM Hub API token, the agent also works as you in one of your XTM Hub organizations. It can:

  • say whom the token acts as, in which organization, and whether it is read only;
  • list the libraries you reach, private organization libraries included, and search their resources;
  • list the platforms registered with the XTM Hub in that organization;
  • download a resource's file as a file of the conversation or run, which other tools can then use. A downloaded OpenCTI dashboard can be imported into OpenCTI by its file: import_opencti_dashboard takes a file of the conversation as well as JSON, and checks it the same way;
  • with a read and write token, publish a file of the conversation (an OpenCTI dashboard, view or playbook export, an OpenAEV scenario) to a library of yours where you may upload. Each publication is made in your name and stays inactive until someone activates it on the XTM Hub: an agent cannot publish a resource visible at once. Updating or deleting a published resource is done on the XTM Hub.

Once an administrator turns on tool approvals, the download and the publication each wait for your approval; the other XTM Hub tools only read and run without asking.

To set it up, open your profile on the XTM Hub, create a token under API tokens for the organization agents should act in, switch the integration's authentication mode to API Key and paste the token (it starts with xhp_ and the XTM Hub shows it once). A read only token is enough for everything but publishing. The token never signs in, manages tokens or changes who can access what. XTM One sends it only over HTTPS, or to an XTM Hub on the same machine, and only once the XTM Hub says it accepts API tokens. A token belongs to the XTM Hub it was made on: changing the integration's XTM Hub URL, or switching back to None, removes it. A token on a shared integration acts as you for everyone it is shared with, so prefer a read only token there.

Test connection checks that the address answers as an XTM Hub and lists its catalogs, and with a token names the user and organization it acts as.

Each public result carries the resource's XTM Hub page. Deploying a resource into OpenCTI or OpenAEV is done from that page, with your own XTM Hub session.

Resources are published by the Filigran community. Their names and descriptions reach the agent as untrusted data, never as instructions.

The integration also appears on the home dashboard, next to OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ.

The integration also exists as an import bundle, to distribute it as a package: build it with python -m scripts.build_xtm_hub_bundle from backend/ (it writes xtm-hub-integration-<version>.zip) and import it as an administrator. The bundle creates the custom:xtm-hub provider and an XTM Hub integration pointing at the public XTM Hub. Its tools send the same catalog queries as the built-in integration, each a fixed query whose variables alone the agent chooses, but each search needs the catalog's id from list_xtm_hub_catalogs first and their answers are the XTM Hub's JSON, read with a size limit and handed to the agent as untrusted data, like the built-in tools' answers. Its tools need bundles that support constant values and untrusted answers, which arrived with this integration: on an earlier XTM One the bundle imports, but its tools fail.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Read the status badge before editing anything.
  • Use Test connection before assuming the agent is broken.
  • Use the available tools card to understand what the integration really provides.
  • Check scopes and re-authorization warnings when OAuth behavior changes. The platform also marks an OAuth integration as needing re-authorization, and stops refreshing its token, when the provider says the refresh token is revoked or invalid, or rejects the integration's client ID / secret (invalid_client). GitHub and Slack report both inside an otherwise successful answer, and the platform reads them there too: bad_refresh_token (GitHub) and invalid_refresh_token (Slack) for the refresh token, incorrect_client_credentials (GitHub), invalid_client_id and bad_client_secret (Slack) for the client ID / secret. In that last case, update the client ID / secret in Configuration first, then re-authorize: a new consent with the rejected credentials fails the same way. The mark stays until a new authorization succeeds: the platform never retries such an integration on its own, and saving a new client secret, token URL or scopes alone neither reconnects it nor retries the refresh. Saving a new client ID removes the tokens issued to the previous app, so the integration then shows as configured but not yet authorized until you authorize it. A temporary provider failure (a network error, an outage, rate limiting, such as Slack's ratelimited or service_unavailable) never produces this mark; the platform just retries later.
  • Look at the Agents count on Overview before editing a shared integration.

docs.title: Knowledge bases
docs.text: A knowledge base stores documents and indexed content that agents search, so their answers are grounded in trusted material. This page gives you a quick tour of the knowledge base screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, open Agent Studio > Knowledge. The list page is where you start: search by name or description, filter by visibility or tags, and compare existing collections before creating a new one so you avoid duplicate silos. Each card shows enough to judge a collection at a glance — what it is about, its visibility, and how much indexed content it holds. If you have permission, New Knowledge Base creates one from files, GitHub, Notion, or cloud storage.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Opening a knowledge base shows a header with the name, its badges (System managed, Company-managed, Shared, Read-only), and a few actions that serve different purposes:

  • Test Search lets you judge answer quality before changing anything. It is disabled until the knowledge base has indexed content.
  • Re-embed is a maintenance action that refreshes the searchable index.
  • delete removes the whole knowledge base, not a single document.

The detail page is organized into tabs. Overview, Configuration, and Activity are always present; Documents and Import Sources appear for knowledge bases you populate yourself (Import Sources is hidden for system-managed ones).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview is the fastest way to understand the current state: how much content is indexed, how often it is queried, the embedding model, and which agents are bound to it.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
Documents is the main content view — upload files, paste text, download, delete, and reprocess documents that are stuck or failed. Open it when your real question is whether the source content is actually present, whether ingestion failed, or whether an old file version is still indexed.

Each document keeps its original source text, not just the searchable chunks it was split into. That is what makes download return the file you put in, and it is also what agents read when they need a whole document rather than the fragments semantic search returns.

docs.title: Import Sources
docs.text:
Import Sources manages automatic sync (website, Notion, OneDrive/SharePoint, Google Drive, GitHub, and more). It shows each source's schedule and last-sync status, so it is useful both for setup and for answering "why isn't the knowledge base up to date?". Some source types require a connected integration first; when that is missing, the option stays visible but disabled and the UI explains what is needed.

A knowledge base can hold several sources of the same type, for example two Notion pages or two repositories. Each sync replaces and removes only the documents its own source imported, so the sources add up rather than replace each other, and Force re-sync purges only that source's documents and the documents of its type that belong to no source. A page or file two sources both reach is stored once. Documents synced before this rule existed belong to no source yet: the next sync of each source takes over the ones it finds, and may still remove the ones another source of the same type has not taken over yet, which that source imports again at its own next sync. After every source has synced once, they no longer touch each other's documents.

A OneDrive / SharePoint source can read several whole folders and leave some out. Its configuration holds folder_paths, the folders it reads (each like Folder path, new files picked up at every sync), and exclude, what it never reads: a folder or file name matched at any depth (XX. Archives leaves out every folder of that name and all it holds), a path from the top of the drive, or a pattern with * and ?, case ignored. An excluded folder is never opened and an excluded file never imported, and a document imported before the exclusion is removed at the next sync.

Agents manage the same settings with three tools of the platform group: get_knowledge_base_sources lists a knowledge base's sources with their scope, schedule and last sync; update_knowledge_base_source sets the folders, exclusions and subfolder setting of a OneDrive / SharePoint source; resync_knowledge_base starts a sync of one source or of every enabled one, and with full purges each source's documents first like Force re-sync. They follow the rules of this tab: anyone who can open the knowledge base reads its sources, and only the people who can manage it (administrators for a company-managed one) change a source or start a sync.

When you choose a specific integration for a source, you can only choose one you can see. The source then syncs with that integration every time, on its schedule or with Sync now, whoever starts it. If the person the source syncs for (whoever set it up, else the knowledge base's owner) later loses access to that integration - it is no longer shared with them, or Restrict access leaves them out - the source keeps syncing with it, and the security audit lists the source so that an administrator can share the integration with them or have the source use another one.

When a sync fails, the full error is shown only to the people who can manage the knowledge base: its owner, the people it is shared with who may configure it, and administrators (only administrators for a company-managed knowledge base). That text is what fixing the source takes, and it can name internal hosts, addresses or paths. Everyone else who can open the knowledge base sees a short, fixed description instead - for example The sync timed out. or The source was disabled after repeated failed syncs. - followed by a note that people who can manage the knowledge base can see the details. The full error is always kept, and the server log records it with the knowledge base and source ids.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration covers the knowledge base's identity (name, description, tags), its visibility and sharing, and the Read-only content, Index HTML as rendered text and Describe PDF figures switches. System-managed knowledge bases stay read-only here.

Turn Read-only content on when a collection is ground truth — the authoritative version of something other work is checked against. A read-only knowledge base stays fully searchable, so agents keep using it for answers; what changes is that nothing can rewrite it. Agents lose write access to it even if an agent's configuration grants writing, its documents cannot be added, edited or deleted, and the knowledge base itself cannot be deleted until you turn the switch back off.

Two things deliberately keep working on a read-only knowledge base: configured Import Sources still refresh it, and Re-embed still works. That is so a collection whose authority lives in another system — a policy wiki, a specification repository — stays both locked against edits and up to date. To freeze such a knowledge base completely, disable its import sources as well.

Index HTML as rendered text (off by default) decides how HTML documents are searched. Off, an HTML document is indexed as its source markup, exactly as before the switch existed. On, it is indexed as the text a reader sees: the page text in reading order, with a summary of the data its scripts embed first, and styles, scripts and SVG drawing instructions left out. Turn it on for exported pages and reports, whose markup often outweighs their text so much that searches match tags instead of sentences. The stored document does not change either way (opening or downloading it still returns the original HTML), and only what is indexed differs. Changing the switch re-indexes nothing by itself: it applies to documents added or changed afterwards (by hand, by an agent or by an import source), and Re-embed applies it to the documents already there. It only affects documents that are HTML; data, text and code files (JSON, CSV, Markdown, plain text, scripts), and text an import source has already converted, such as Markdown from a crawl, are indexed as they are. A page with no visible text or data, a page too large to render whole, or one that cannot be rendered is indexed as its source; with the switch on, the Embedding completed entry Activity shows for an HTML document says which of the two it was indexed as.

Describe PDF figures (off by default) decides whether what a PDF shows as pictures is searchable. Off, a PDF is indexed from its text layer only: a diagram, a graph, a chart, a screenshot, or a page with no text layer at all (a scan, an export whose text was converted to outlines) is not. On, each PDF uploaded to the knowledge base (with the Upload button, through the API, or as a workspace source) is read page by page when it is indexed: the pages that carry an image, vector drawings or almost no text are rendered and described by the chat model the platform uses for the person who added the document, and each description is indexed right after its page's text. A graph is described as its nodes and its oriented relations, a screenshot by the text it shows, a chart by its values, and a page without text layer is transcribed whole. Text read from an image is treated as quoted content, never as instructions. The stored document does not change (opening or downloading it still returns the PDF's text layer).

Each described page costs one model call, and at most 30 pages are described per document (the pages without text layer first). The platform's chat model must accept images. The switch applies to PDFs uploaded while it is on: PDFs uploaded before, documents from an import source and pasted text are indexed as before. When the figures of a document could not all be described (the model is unavailable, cannot read images or timed out, the 30-page cap), the document is still searchable by its text and Documents marks it Figures partly described or Figures not described, with the reason on hover; the Embedding completed entry in Activity says the same. Re-embed retries the pages that failed, for up to 7 days after the upload; pages already described are never paid for again. Turning the switch off indexes the text layer alone from the next re-embed. An exported knowledge base carries the descriptions, so an imported copy indexes the same text.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
Activity is the audit view — when content changed, whether a sync ran recently, and who edited the configuration. Check it when answer quality shifts. Document updated entries also cover agent write-backs: an agent with write access to a knowledge base can revise a stored document, which re-indexes it. The document shows pending until re-indexing finishes, so a document an agent just changed is briefly not searchable — that is expected, not a failure.

Sync entries follow the same rule as Import Sources: a failed sync, a sync alert, a quarantined source and a configuration error show the full error to people who can manage the knowledge base, and a fixed sentence to everyone else. The activity search only looks through what you are shown, so it never finds text you cannot see.

When a sync source is quarantined (disabled after repeated failures, repeated "not found" errors or repeated hangs), the knowledge base owner gets a notification in the platform naming the knowledge base; on a company-managed knowledge base every administrator gets it too, each person once. The source stays disabled until it is re-enabled or force re-synced.

docs.title: Badges that set expectations
docs.text:
• System managed means the platform maintains the content automatically; Documents may be read-only and point you to Import Sources instead.
  • Content locked (Locked on the list page) means the knowledge base is marked read-only: searchable as usual, but nothing writes to it. This is about the content.
  • Company-managed plus Read-only means you can view it but not change it. This one is about permissions — who may administer the knowledge base — which is why a collection can carry both badges for different reasons.
  • Shared means the knowledge base belongs to a shared group rather than to one person.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Start on Overview before editing anything.
  • Use Test Search before deciding a knowledge base is weak.
  • Check Documents when results look incomplete, and Import Sources when freshness is the issue.
  • Read the badges first — they explain why some actions are missing.
  • Mark authoritative collections Read-only rather than relying on each agent's configuration being right — the lock lives on the knowledge base, so it holds no matter what an agent is granted later.
  • Keep very large documents out of knowledge bases you expect agents to read whole. A document above roughly 200 000 characters is not loaded into an agent's context at all: the platform records it as a work item instead, and the agent is steered to search it for the relevant passages. Splitting it into meaningful documents usually works better than leaving one enormous file.

docs.title: MCP catalogs
docs.text:
XTM One publishes its MCP servers in the official MCP Registry, the catalog that VS Code, the GitHub MCP registry and other MCP clients read. You can install a server from your client's catalog instead of copying its address by hand.

Availability

The catalog listing is rolling out with an upcoming release. Until XTM One appears in your client's catalog, add a server by its address as a custom connector (Add XTM One to Claude) or with an API key (Use an API key instead).

docs.title: What is listed
docs.text:
Catalog entry Endpoint What it gives you XTM One platform tools /mcp/xtm XTM One's own tools: agents, assignments, runs, traces, knowledge bases, prompts and skills. See Platform tools MCP server. XTM One agents /mcp/user The agents you selected in My Profile > MCP Endpoint or, if you selected none, every agent you can chat with; each one is a tool that runs the agent on your request. An API key limited to some agents exposes those only. OpenCTI (via XTM One) /mcp/opencti The OpenCTI tools of the platform MCP servers. OpenAEV (via XTM One) /mcp/openaev The OpenAEV tools of the platform MCP servers. OpenCRQ (via XTM One) /mcp/opencrq The OpenCRQ tools of the platform MCP servers.

Every entry works with your own XTM One instance: the catalog does not host anything, it tells your client how to reach your instance.

The global agent endpoint (/mcp/global) is not listed: it signs in with an administrator key for the whole instance rather than with your account.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Check with your administrator that what you want to install is available on your instance:

  • XTM One platform tools: the server is turned on in Settings > MCP Endpoint. It is off by default.
  • OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ: the platform is connected to XTM One, and the platform MCP servers are on in Settings > MCP Endpoint.
  • XTM One agents: the instance runs Enterprise Edition, and the agents you want are enabled and available in chat.
  • All of them: AI is turned on.

docs.title: Install from a catalog
docs.text:
1. Search your client's MCP catalog for XTM One, OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ.
  2. Install the entry. Your client asks for the host of your XTM One instance: enter its host name, for example xtm.example.com. If your instance is served under a path, include it, for example example.com/xtm-one. A client that installs several XTM One entries can reuse the same answer.
  3. Your client opens an XTM One page in your browser. Sign in, check the name of the client, and approve it.

The page names the client and the site it comes from, for example Claude Code (claude.ai). Approve only a client you are installing yourself.

Every tool call then runs as you, with your permissions. The tools carry standard annotations, so your client knows which calls only read and which change or delete something, and most clients ask you before a destructive call.

docs.title: Add XTM One to Claude
docs.text:
Until XTM One is listed in Claude's own connector directory, add a server to Claude as a custom connector: in Claude, open Settings > Connectors, choose Add custom connector, and paste the address of the endpoint, for example https://xtm.example.com/mcp/xtm. Claude opens the same XTM One sign-in page.

Note

claude.ai connects from Anthropic's servers, not from your computer. Your XTM One instance must be reachable from the internet for a custom connector added in claude.ai, Claude Desktop or Claude mobile. Claude Code runs on your computer and only needs to reach your instance from there.

docs.title: Use an API key instead
docs.text: A client that does not support OAuth connects with a personal API key (fcp-...), created in My Profile > API Keys and sent as a bearer token. The configuration snippets in My Profile > MCP Endpoint already carry the right address.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The client says the server does not exist (404): the platform behind it (OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ) is not connected to your instance.
  • The client is refused (403): the server is turned off, AI is off, or, for the agents server, the instance does not run Enterprise Edition. Ask your administrator.
  • No browser page opens: your client does not support OAuth sign-in. Use an API key.
  • The sign-in page refuses the client: an administrator may have turned off client self-registration or client metadata documents in Settings > Security. Use an API key, or ask your administrator.
  • A web-based client is refused (403) before it signs in: XTM One only answers web pages served from its own address or from an address your administrator allows.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Explore what you can do with the platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text: This page gives you a quick tour of the MCP server screens. To configure a new server — transport, credentials, OAuth, testing and attaching it to an agent — see Connect an external MCP server.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, open Tools & Integrations > MCP Servers — the first entry of the group, because an MCP server is the richest capability an agent acts through (a whole tool server rather than one function). The page also carries the MCP endpoints this platform itself exposes; see Platform MCP servers and Platform tools MCP server. The list page is built for quick scanning: search by name, command, or URL, and filter by visibility or tags. Each card answers two questions at a glance — is the server likely usable right now (enabled or disabled, transport type), and what kind of setup sits behind it (subprocess vs. HTTP, whether OAuth or environment variables are involved) if something goes wrong later. If you have permission, Add Server connects a new external toolset, and Import creates servers from a client configuration you already have (see Import from a client configuration).

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a server shows a header with its name, transport, enabled state, and OAuth status when relevant. Test connection is the main action — try it first after any setup or credential change, because it tells you whether the problem is the server connection itself or something later in the agent workflow. The page is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview shows whether the server is meaningfully ready: how many tools it discovered, how often they are called, its connection details, and which agents depend on it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is the most operationally important screen. It covers the server's identity and connection (transport, command or URL, environment variables or headers) and its visibility and sharing. You can switch transport directly here between subprocess (stdio), Streamable HTTP, and SSE.

The URL of a Streamable HTTP or SSE server must be an http or https URL. The platform connects to it from its own network, so it checks the address before every connection - and when you save it - against the MCP server URL policy an administrator sets in Settings > Access and security:

  • By default (Permissive) only cloud metadata addresses (such as 169.254.169.254) are refused; a server on localhost or on a private network works.
  • Private networks also refuses loopback (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1), link-local and other reserved addresses. A server on a private network (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) still works.
  • Public only refuses every internal address. Reach a server inside your network through a relay group (Route through) instead.

A redirect is checked the same way, and so are the OAuth discovery requests the platform makes to connect an OAuth server. The connection follows a redirect only within the server's own origin (a trailing slash, http to https on the same host) and only when it keeps the request: a server that redirects anywhere else (to www., to another host, with a 301 / 302 on a request that posts) fails the test with a message naming the address it points to, without its query. If that is the intended server, save it with that URL. An address the policy refuses gives the message "This MCP server URL is not allowed": when the server is one you trust, ask an administrator to list its origin in Trusted MCP server origins. See MCP_SERVER_URL_POLICY in Configuration for the full rules.

The arguments field reads like a command line: arguments are separated by spaces, and an argument that holds a space is written in double quotes (--header "Authorization: Bearer ..."), where \" and \\ stand for a quote and a backslash. An argument with a space is shown that way too, so it stays one argument when you save.

A credential written into the arguments or a URL is shown masked to everyone who can see the server, its owner included: a token keeps its first characters (ghp_ab***), and the value of a secret-named flag or variable (--token ***, GITHUB_TOKEN=***), a URL's password or secret query value, and a Bearer token become ***. Saving leaves a masked value as stored, wherever it now sits in the arguments, so you can rename, tag, share or add an argument without retyping it. To change a credential, type its full value. A save is refused, with nothing changed, when a masked value no longer matches one stored value: a *** moved after another flag, a URL edited around its masked password, or one of two tokens that look the same once masked removed. Type the full value of each masked argument or URL then. The full values are in the server's export, for the people who can edit it.

The same screen holds the discovered tools card, where you discover or refresh the server's tools, read each tool's description, and test an individual tool. This matters because most MCP questions are not about the server object itself — they are about whether the expected tool is actually visible and callable. When the server uses OAuth, an OAuth connection card shows whether it is configured but not yet authenticated, with an authorize or re-authorize action. On a company-managed server that action is admin-only, because the resulting connection is a single shared one — every user of the platform calls the server through the token the admin authorized, just as they all share its API key when it authenticates with headers.

Once authorized, the connection stays usable without re-authorizing, even when the authorization server issues short-lived access tokens (a few minutes). The platform refreshes the token before it expires, refreshes it again when a connection finds it about to expire, and replaces it once when the server refuses it. For this to work, the authorization server must issue a refresh token. When its metadata lists offline_access (Okta, Entra ID and Auth0 issue refresh tokens only on request), Authorize adds that scope to the server's scopes, before it registers a client for the platform. A server authorized before this change gets it the next time someone clicks Re-authorize, unless the platform registered its client automatically without that scope: clear the client ID in the configuration, then click Re-authorize to register a new client that asks for it. If the server still asks for authorization a few minutes after each connection, its authorization server issues no refresh token: check that the client is allowed the refresh token grant.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity is the traceable history — whether the server changed recently, whether calls were made, and whether an issue started after an edit.

docs.title: Files an MCP tool returns
docs.text: A file an MCP tool sends back (an image, a document, an embedded resource) is kept as a file of the conversation or run: the agent reads it, you get a download card, and the agent can hand it to any other tool that takes a file. A tool may instead return a link to a resource without its content, often because it is large. The agent sees the link, and when it needs the file it asks the same MCP server for it (read_mcp_resource), over the server's own connection: the file is then kept like any other. Only a link the server's own tools returned in the run can be read this way, up to the platform's 40 MB file limit.

docs.title: Shared, company, and read-only states
docs.text: Ownership rules shape these pages: private servers are editable by their owner, shared servers are reused across group members, and company-managed servers are visible more widely but read-only for non-admins. Testing a server (Test connection, Discover Tools, a tool's Test) requires the same right as editing it: a Read only share lets you use the server from your agents, not test it.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use Test connection before troubleshooting the agent itself.
  • Refresh discovered tools after changing transport or credentials.
  • Read the discovered tool list, not just the server name.
  • Notice the difference between a configured server and an OAuth-connected one.

docs.title: Platform MCP servers
docs.text:
XTM One embeds a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for every connected Filigran platform. This means any MCP-compatible client — Cursor, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or your own agents — can connect to OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ through XTM One and work with your threat intelligence, exposure validation, and governance-risk-compliance content directly.

This page explains what the platform MCP servers are, where to find them, and how to connect a client.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
One dedicated MCP endpoint per platform:

Endpoint Platform What it exposes https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti OpenCTI Threat intelligence knowledge: search, entities (SDOs), observables (SCOs), relationships, indicators, containers (reports, cases, groupings), notes, labels, markings, statistics https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev OpenAEV Adversarial exposure validation: scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, atomic tests, expectations, findings, vulnerabilities, assets, media content, lessons learned, reports https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencrq OpenCRQ Governance, risk & compliance: frameworks, requirements, control capabilities, compliance assessments, risk scenarios, attack outcomes, CRQ financial summaries, assets, vulnerability findings and posture, CVE search, threats, treatment plans, budget reviews, risk dashboard

All endpoints use the MCP Streamable HTTP transport, the modern standard supported by all major MCP clients, and speak the protocol revisions 2026-07-28, 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26: your client gets the revision it asks for. A call from a web page is accepted only from the platform's own address or one listed in CORS_ORIGINS; desktop, command-line and hosted clients send no such origin and are not concerned.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
The platform MCP servers are a Community Edition feature. There is nothing to install and nothing extra to license:

  • A server becomes available as soon as the corresponding platform is registered with XTM One — the same registration that powers the embedded "Ask AI" experience in OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ.
  • While no platform of that type is connected, the endpoint simply answers that the platform is not registered.
  • Administrators can turn all platform servers off globally with the Platform MCP Servers toggle in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

docs.title: Where to find your endpoints
docs.text:
Open My Profile > MCP Endpoint.

The Platform MCP Servers card is always visible there (as long as an administrator has not disabled the feature) and lists every platform server with its live status. For each connected platform it shows:

  • the endpoint URL, with a copy button
  • the live connection status (Connected or Registered)
  • a Config button that copies a ready-to-paste MCP client configuration

A platform that is not yet connected appears dimmed as Not connected, with a reminder that its MCP server activates automatically once the platform is registered with XTM One.

Administrators see the same information, along with the global enable/disable toggle, in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The servers accept a standard bearer token:

  • a personal API key (fcp-...), created in My Profile > API Keys, or
  • an OAuth 2.1 access token — MCP clients that support OAuth discover the authorization flow automatically. Clients such as claude.ai, Claude Code and VS Code identify themselves with a client metadata document and need no registration; others register themselves. Either way you sign in and approve the client on an XTM One page that names it.

Every tool call runs as you on the platform. XTM One signs a short-lived token for your user (matched by email on the platform side), so your platform permissions, data markings, and audit trail all apply exactly as if you performed the action yourself. The platform's own API token is never stored in or proxied through XTM One.

docs.title: Connect a client
docs.text:
Copy the configuration from the Config button in your profile, or use this template (keep only the servers you need):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "opencti": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    },
    "openaev": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    },
    "opencrq": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencrq",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Where to paste it:

  • Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json in your project (or the global MCP settings)
  • Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json
  • Other clients: any client supporting MCP Streamable HTTP with custom headers

You can verify the connection from a terminal:

curl -s -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}'

docs.title: What the tools cover
docs.text:
The tools are the same battle-tested tools used by XTM One agents through the native platform integrations.

For OpenCTI, you can:

  • search and read any STIX entity, observable, relationship, or container
  • create and update entities, observables, indicators, relationships, containers, and notes
  • manage labels, markings, and container membership
  • promote observables to indicators
  • retrieve statistics, top related entities, and modification history

For OpenAEV, you can:

  • search and read scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, findings, assets, and ATT&CK content
  • create and manage scenarios, simulations, injects, expectations, and atomic tests
  • create and manage payloads, findings, and vulnerabilities
  • work with documents, media channels, articles, challenges, lessons learned, and reports

For OpenCRQ, you can:

  • browse tenants, organizations, compliance frameworks, and their requirements
  • read control capabilities (strength, coverage) and declare their assessment, declare or clear a capability's posture for one organization's scope, add, remove, restore or reset the ATT&CK techniques it covers, and read and answer compliance assessments
  • create and manage risk scenarios, set a scenario's or an organization's risk tolerance (a scenario's can be cleared), and read attack outcomes and CRQ financial summaries
  • list primary and supporting assets, set every field of a supporting asset (subcategory, URL, linked person, tags, machine, identity or AI target properties) and clear the optional ones with an empty string, change the roles of dependency links, delete a manually added vulnerability evidence, hand an evidence state or a whole asset back to its connectors, and search CVEs
  • read vulnerability findings, the top vulnerabilities, asset posture scores, and what attack simulations prevented and detected
  • browse the threat catalog, the threats relevant to a risk scenario, and the threats exploiting a CVE
  • read risk treatment plans and budget reviews with their simulated loss reduction, the risk dashboard, and the posture attack simulations proved for a control

OpenCRQ is multi-tenant: every tool accepts an optional tenant identifier and resolves your sole tenant automatically when omitted.

The OpenCRQ tools follow the OpenCRQ instance that is connected: an instance that does not serve a tool does not have it offered to your client. The tool count shown for OpenCRQ is the full list. See OpenCRQ tools follow each instance.

Every tool comes with a title and the standard MCP annotations, so your client knows what a call does before making it:

  • reads (search, get, list) are marked read-only;
  • writes that only add something (create, add, run a simulation) are marked not destructive;
  • writes that change or remove what exists (update, delete, remove, manage) are marked destructive, and most clients ask you to confirm them.

The annotations are hints for your client. What a call may actually do is still decided by your permissions on the platform.

docs.title: What the tools deliberately do not cover
docs.text:
The platform MCP servers expose business and knowledge tools only. Platform administration is out of scope by design:

  • no user, group, role, tenant, or organization management
  • no playbooks, dashboards, or workspace administration
  • no notification, customization, ingestion, or data-sharing configuration
  • no connector or platform settings management

This is enforced server-side with a strict allow-list: a tool that is not explicitly allowed can never be listed or executed through these endpoints.

OpenCTI writes are direct

Knowledge changes made through the OpenCTI MCP server are applied directly to the live knowledge graph, with your user's permissions. The draft-review workflow used by XTM One agents does not apply to MCP clients — review changes on the client side before running write tools.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Meaning What to do 401 Unauthorized Missing or invalid token Check the Authorization header and that your API key is active 403 Forbidden Platform MCP servers are disabled Ask an administrator to enable them in Settings > MCP Endpoint 404 Not Found The platform is not registered with XTM One Connect the OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ instance to XTM One first Tool result contains an error message The platform rejected the call (permissions, invalid input, connectivity) Read the message — it reflects your own permissions on the platform

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Create a dedicated API key per MCP client so you can revoke access independently.
  • Remember that every action is performed as you — write tools modify real platform data.
  • If a tool you expect is missing, it is most likely excluded on purpose (platform administration) rather than misconfigured.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
If you also want to expose XTM One agents (not platform tools) to your MCP clients, continue with the MCP Endpoint tab described in My Profile.

To read agent traces and manage XTM One's own objects from an MCP client, see Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: Platform tools MCP server
docs.text:
Alongside the platform MCP servers — which bridge the connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ instances — XTM One exposes itself over MCP.

One endpoint, /mcp/xtm, lets any MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, your own agents) read your agent traces and manage the objects you work with every day: agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, MCP servers, variables, and workspaces (with the conversations you file in them).

The typical use: an agent misbehaved, so you read its traces from your client, spot the step that failed, and fix the agent's configuration — without leaving the client.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Endpoint What it exposes https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm XTM One's own tools: agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases (including semantic search), prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, MCP servers, variables, workspaces

The transport is MCP Streamable HTTP, the same as every other XTM One MCP endpoint, in the protocol revisions 2026-07-28, 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• inspect_agent_traces — recent traces, filterable by period, status, source, and model. Naming a target_agent_id scopes to one agent; omitting it lists traces across agents, which is how you find which agent failed before drilling into it. With include_spans (the default), each trace carries a rollup computed from all its spans: iterations, model calls, tool calls and tool errors, tokens and cost, per-tool calls and result size, and the five largest tool results with their span id, so you can see where a run spent its tokens and read any of those results with get_trace_payload. A run that stored a rollup when it ended also carries it, in every mode (without spans too): wall time, time in model calls, in tools and in wait, cache-read and cache-write tokens, and the rollup's own cost (overhead_ms); the listing then adds rollup_percentiles, the p50 and p90 of each figure over the runs it lists.
  • get_trace_payload — the full stored value of any trace or span field. Listings return bounded previews; this reads the rest, one page at a time. A model's reasoning shows as [reasoning omitted], here and in listings: read back into a prompt, Claude may decline it. Pass include_reasoning: true to read it, paging from offset 0.

Trace access follows the same rule as the Trace Explorer in the UI: the cross-agent listing is an administrator surface, and a non-admin reads the agents they can manage. A deleted agent's traces stay until the retention period removes them: name its id as target_agent_id to read the runs of it you made, or all of them if it was yours; a query matches its last name.

Every inspect_agent_traces listing, and every get_trace_payload read of a trace that is not the calling agent's own, is recorded in the audit log (inspect_traces). The same read by the same person - a listing of the same agents, or the same field of the same trace - is recorded once every 15 minutes: paging through one payload or changing a listing's filters writes one entry, and the entry says so in window_seconds. A listing of other agents, another trace or another field is recorded at once.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Everything the REST API and the UI offer for the objects you own or share:

  • Agents — list, read, create, update, delete, plus templates and the available-resources catalog
  • Assignments and runs — list, read, create, update, trigger, and read execution history
  • Knowledge bases — list, read, create, update, delete, add and read documents, revise a document (with automatic re-embedding), and search_knowledge for semantic search across everything you can read
  • Prompts, skills, variables — full CRUD, plus load_skill / read_skill_resource to open a skill's bundled files
  • Custom tools, integrations, MCP servers — full CRUD

Every tool comes with a title and the standard MCP annotations: reads (list_*, get_*, inspect_agent_traces, search_knowledge) are marked read-only, create_* are marked not destructive, and update_*, delete_* and trigger_assignment (which starts an agent run) are marked destructive, which most clients ask you to confirm. These are hints for your client; your permissions decide what a call may do.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Off by default. Unlike the platform MCP servers, this one exposes this instance's own configuration surface, so an administrator has to enable it explicitly:

Settings > MCP Endpoint > Platform Tools MCP Server

While it is disabled, the endpoint answers 403 with a message saying so.

It also needs agentic AI to be licensed (Enterprise Edition). Its tools create and change agents, assignments, flows and knowledge bases, which the REST API only allows on a licensed deployment, so on Community Edition the endpoint answers 403 with detail.code set to license_required. With AI turned off, it answers 403 with detail.code set to ai_disabled. Unlike this server, the platform MCP servers stay available on Community Edition.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The tool surface is resolved per request, from the calling user. There is no separate permission model to configure: every tool enforces the same three-tier gates as the REST API and the UI.

  • Built-in objects are read-only for everyone.
  • Company-managed objects are read-only for non-administrators.
  • Group-shared objects need a config-tier grant to modify.
  • Knowledge bases you can read are searchable; only the ones you can manage are writable.

A caller sees and changes exactly what they could see and change in the interface — never more.

docs.title: Where to find your endpoint
docs.text: Open My Profile > MCP Endpoint. Once an administrator has enabled the server, a Platform Tools MCP Server card shows the endpoint URL, a copy button, and — under Install in your client — a downloadable package for each supported client.

docs.title: Install with a package
docs.text:
Three formats, all carrying the same skill so the model knows how to use the tools rather than guessing:

Package For How you install it Claude Code plugin (.zip) Claude Code claude --plugin-dir ./xtm-one-platform, or add it as a local marketplace to keep it across sessions Claude Desktop extension (.mcpb) Claude Desktop Double-click the file, or drag it into the Claude Desktop window Agent Plugins package (.zip) Any Agent Plugins v1.0.0 client Unzip it and point your client at the directory

Each package already contains the endpoint URL, and the skill inside carries a tool reference generated from the surface that server offered you — so it lists the tools your permissions actually reach, not a maintained-by-hand list.

docs.title: One package, one server
docs.text:
The same three formats also package the platform MCP servers — OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ — for the platforms actually registered with XTM One. When more than one server is live, clicking a format asks which one you want; with only one there is nothing to ask and the download starts.

There is deliberately no "all of them" package. A client loads every tool definition of every server it connects to, and the four servers together currently come to more than two hundred tools — well past the point where tool selection degrades and every request carries the weight. Installing a second package stays available; it is your explicit choice rather than a default.

A bridge package ships the generated catalogue of that platform's tools and no hand-written guidance: those tools belong to OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, whose own documentation is the authority on what they mean, and invented prose here would rot unnoticed as those products move.

docs.title: Other clients
docs.text:
The Other button covers the clients that install by editing a file rather than by opening a package:

Client File Notes Codex CLI, Codex IDE extension, ChatGPT desktop app ~/.codex/config.toml One file for all three — they share this configuration Cursor ~/.cursor/mcp.json Also accepts .cursor/mcp.json per project VS Code — Needs no snippet: it reads the Agent Plugins package directly, so download that one

Those two files already hold your other MCP servers, so what you get is a fragment to merge, not a file to replace — shown with a copy button and the path to paste it into. The one-click choice applies here too: with a key, it is written into the fragment; without, the fragment points at a XTM_ONE_API_KEY environment variable instead, which is what both clients document for keeping a token out of a file that often ends up in a dotfiles repository.

ChatGPT desktop, outside Codex

ChatGPT's own Developer mode (Settings → Apps) takes a public HTTPS URL and authenticates with OAuth or not at all — it accepts no custom header, so an API key has no place there and http://localhost will not connect. /mcp/xtm publishes OAuth 2.1 Protected Resource Metadata, so that route works on an HTTPS deployment. The ~/.codex/config.toml entry above is what covers the ChatGPT desktop app locally.

docs.title: One-click install
docs.text:
The One-click install switch (on by default) makes the download self-contained: the platform creates a new API key dedicated to that package, names it after the client, and writes it into the configuration files. Install it and you are done — nothing to paste.

The trade-off is stated plainly because it is real: the downloaded file is then a live credential.
