Do not commit or share it, delete it once installed, and revoke the key from My Profile > API Keys if it goes anywhere it should not. It is a key of its own, so revoking it affects nothing else. It is also scoped to the MCP endpoints only - it cannot call the REST API or the LLM proxy - and expires within the maximum lifetime your administrator set, if any (see API Keys tab).

A new key is created rather than reused because there is nothing to reuse: keys are stored as bcrypt hashes and the plaintext exists only at creation, so no existing key can be read back into a package.

Turn the switch off and the packages carry no credential — your client asks for the key at install time and keeps it in its own secure storage. If you have no API key at all, the card says so and points you at the API Keys tab.

docs.title: The Agent Plugins package never carries a key
docs.text: Agent Plugins 1.0.0 states that configured headers are literal, visible package data that must not contain credentials, and defines no portable credential-reference field. Embedding a key would make the package non-conformant — which is the one property that format exists for. It therefore always downloads credential-free, whatever the switch says, and its README explains where to add the bearer token in your own client.

docs.title: Why the Claude Desktop bundle contains a script
docs.text:
The .mcpb format runs a local MCP server over stdio, but this server is remote and speaks Streamable HTTP. The bundle therefore carries a small bridge (server/index.js) that forwards each JSON-RPC message over HTTPS. It has no dependencies, fetches nothing at runtime, and is about a hundred readable lines — check it before installing if you would rather verify than trust.

If you want no local process at all, add the endpoint as a Claude Desktop custom connector instead, using the URL from the same card.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
A standard bearer token:

  • a personal API key (fcp-...), created in My Profile > API Keys, or
  • an OAuth 2.1 access token — clients that support OAuth discover the flow automatically (RFC 9728), and the token is audience-bound to /mcp/xtm, so a token minted for another endpoint is refused here. Clients such as claude.ai, Claude Code and VS Code identify themselves with a client metadata document and need no registration.

docs.title: Configure a client by hand
docs.text:
For a client with no package of its own — Cursor, an internal tool, your own agent — configure it directly:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "xtm-one-platform": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Where to paste it:

  • Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json in your project (or the global MCP settings)
  • Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json
  • Other clients: any client supporting MCP Streamable HTTP with custom headers

Verify from a terminal:

curl -s -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Meaning What to do 401 Unauthorized Missing or invalid token Check the Authorization header and that your API key is active. A one-click package whose key you later revoked will fail this way — download it again 403 Forbidden The server is disabled, AI is turned off on this deployment (ai_disabled), or agentic AI is not licensed (license_required) Ask an administrator to enable it in Settings > MCP Endpoint, turn AI on, or activate Enterprise Edition, as the message says A tool is missing from tools/list You have nothing in scope for it search_knowledge only appears when you can read at least one knowledge base; load_skill only when at least one skill is visible to you A trace listing is refused The cross-agent listing needs administrator rights Name a target_agent_id for an agent you manage

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Create a dedicated API key per MCP client so you can revoke access independently — revoking a user's keys cuts that client off immediately. The one-click packages already do this: each download gets its own key, named after the client.
  • Delete a one-click package file once it is installed. The client has stored what it needs, and the file is a live credential until you do.
  • Remember that write tools change real platform objects. Review what your client proposes before letting it run them.
  • Leave the server disabled on deployments where no one needs it; it is a configuration surface, not a read-only report.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: To expose XTM One agents as tools (rather than platform management), see the MCP Endpoint tab described in My Profile. For the connected OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ platforms, see Platform MCP servers.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text: A prompt is a reusable text instruction: it keeps the same wording across chat requests, agent personas and recurring work. This page gives you a quick tour of the prompt screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, open Agent Studio > Prompts. The list page is a reusable library: search by name or a remembered wording fragment, filter by visibility or tags, and check whether a prompt already exists before creating another version. Each card shows a content preview so you can judge relevance and style before opening it. If you have permission, Add Prompt creates a repeatable instruction others can reuse.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a prompt shows a header with its name, badges (Company-managed, Shared, Read-only), and a delete action when you can manage it. The page is organized into Overview, Configuration, Versioning, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview combines usage metrics with a readable content preview. It helps you tell whether the prompt is a draft or already reused in real workflows, and — through the Agents Using card — how many downstream uses an edit would affect.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is where you read and edit the prompt. The distinctions that matter are durable:

  • editing the content changes what the prompt says
  • Hide from chat changes where it is surfaced (it drops the prompt from the chat picker while keeping it available for agent configuration)
  • sharing settings change who can reuse it

The content editor includes a variable insert control, so you can add platform variables without memorizing the syntax.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Each time you save a change to the prompt's content, a new version is recorded. Versioning lists them, newest first, with the date, the author and the commit message, and marks the Active one.

  • Select two versions, then Compare, to see what changed between them.
  • The rollback button of a version makes its content the current one again. You can add a commit message; the content you replace stays in the list.
  • Administrators can also lock a version so it cannot be deleted, and delete a version that is not active.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity answers who changed the prompt, when, and whether a recent run problem started after an edit — especially useful for shared prompts.

docs.title: Read-only and shared states
docs.text: Private prompts are editable by their owner, shared prompts are visible in a group context, and company-managed prompts are visible to everyone but read-only for non-admins. When a prompt is read-only, you can still inspect its content and usage.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Read the content preview before creating a duplicate prompt.
  • Check Agents Using before editing a shared prompt.
  • Use Hide from chat when the prompt is operational and not meant for casual use.
  • Keep names and descriptions clear enough that other teams can reuse the prompt without guessing.

docs.title: Relays
docs.text:
A relay lets XTM One reach the tools that live inside a network it cannot reach directly - a Splunk in your data center, a Tanium server, an internal API, an on-premises OpenCTI - without opening a single inbound flow toward that network.

You install the relay on a machine or in a container inside the network. It connects out to XTM One over HTTPS and pulls the requests it should carry. When an integration, an MCP server or a flow step is routed through it, its calls leave from that network, through the relay, instead of leaving from the platform. Nothing listens for inbound connections, and there is no VPN to set up.

You find them under Tools & Integrations > Relays. A platform administrator can turn relays off entirely with RELAYS_ENABLED=false (see Configuration).

docs.title: Relay groups
docs.text:
Relays belong to a relay group, and a group stands for one network: a data center, a cloud account, a site, an OT zone. You route a resource through a group, never through one particular relay: every relay of the group can carry its requests, and the platform balances them across the relays that are online. Two or more relays in a group give you redundancy - when one stops, the others keep carrying the traffic.

Only administrators create relay groups. A group is either available to every user (company-managed) or shared with specific groups and people, like any other resource (see Sharing and access). Once a group is shared with you, you can route your own integrations through it.

To create one:

  1. Open Relays and select New relay group.
  2. Give it a name (for example Paris datacenter), an optional zone and a description of what the network holds.
  3. Optionally list the allowed destinations (host:port, *.corp.local:443, 10.20.0.0/16:8089). The platform then refuses any request to anything else before it reaches a relay. Each relay also enforces its own list, which always has the last word.
  4. Select Create and enroll a relay.

docs.title: Enroll a relay
docs.text:
Enroll a relay (on the group's page) walks you through the install:

  1. Choose where the relay runs: Linux, Windows, macOS, Docker or Kubernetes.
  2. Optionally name it (the machine's hostname is used otherwise) and set the destinations it may reach. With an empty list the relay reaches nothing.
  3. Select Generate the install command and run the command it shows inside the network:
    • on Linux and macOS, as root - it downloads the relay from your XTM One instance, checks its signature, installs it as a system service and enrolls it (on Linux it needs glibc 2.35 or newer: Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 or a later distribution);
    • on Windows, in an elevated PowerShell - same steps, as a Windows service;
    • with Docker, on a host inside the network;
    • with Kubernetes, with kubectl against a cluster inside the network - each replica enrolls as its own relay.
  4. The dialog waits until the relay connects, then tells you it is online.

The enrollment key in the command is shown only once. A key for one machine enrolls one relay and expires soon; a key for several replicas (Kubernetes) stays valid for 7 days.

Every instance serves the relay installers and updates itself, matching its own version, so an air-gapped deployment needs nothing else. A relay installed as a service updates itself; a relay in a container is updated by pulling a newer image.

docs.title: Route a resource through a relay group
docs.text:
On the configuration of an integration, a remote MCP server, or a flow HTTP request step, choose the group under Route through. Direct (from the platform) keeps the usual behavior.

Once a resource is routed, every request it makes - its tools, its connectivity test, its OAuth sign-in and token refresh, its event polling - goes through the group. When no relay of the group is online, those requests fail with a clear message: a routed resource never falls back to a direct call.

Local MCP servers

A stdio MCP server runs on the platform itself, so only a remote MCP server can be routed through a relay group.

docs.title: Follow a group
docs.text:
The group's page has six tabs:

  • Overview - relays online, requests and failures over the last 24 hours, average latency, traffic, and the destination policy.
  • Relays - each relay with its status, version, connection type (WebSocket or long-poll), what its own list lets it reach and when it was last seen. From here you revoke or delete a relay, and manage the enrollment keys.
  • Routed resources - the integrations, MCP servers and flows routed through the group.
  • Activity - every request a relay carried: when, which relay, the destination host, the method, the outcome, the size and the duration. Only this metadata is kept - never a header, a body or a credential.
  • Diagnostics - send one test request to a destination from the group's network, and the commands to run on the relay's machine when something does not connect.
  • Settings - the group's name, zone, allowed destinations and sharing, and deleting it. A group that something is still routed through cannot be deleted: route those resources elsewhere first.

docs.title: Configure a relay
docs.text:
A relay reads a few settings from relay.toml:

  • /etc/xtm-one-relay/relay.toml on Linux;
  • /Library/Application Support/XTM One Relay/relay.toml on macOS;
  • %ProgramData%\XTM One Relay\relay.toml on Windows.

It reloads the file when it changes. The settings you are most likely to need:

Setting What it does allowed_destinations The hosts, wildcards and networks the relay may reach, each with its port (splunk.corp.local:8089, 10.20.0.0/16:443). Anything else is refused. * allows every destination - the security audit flags it. ca_bundle A file of internal certificate authorities to trust, for services signed by your own CA. insecure_tls_destinations Hosts whose certificate the relay does not check. Use it only for a lab. upstream_proxy An outbound proxy the relay must use to reach XTM One. transport auto (WebSocket, falling back to long-poll), websocket or long_poll - for proxies that refuse WebSocket upgrades. max_concurrent_requests How many requests the relay carries at once. health_listen An address for a local health endpoint (for example 127.0.0.1:9180): GET /healthz answers 200 while the relay is connected to the platform.

In a container, every setting is an environment variable instead (XTM_RELAY_ALLOWED_DESTINATIONS, XTM_RELAY_CA_BUNDLE, ...).

The relay trusts the Mozilla roots built into it and the operating system's certificate store. Keep the host's CA certificates package up to date: the relay cannot drop a root the host still trusts.

On the relay's machine:

  • xtm-one-relay status says whether it is enrolled and connected (exit code 0 when online);
  • xtm-one-relay check-config shows the configuration it runs with and its effective allow-list;
  • xtm-one-relay test-destination https://splunk.corp.local:8089/ sends the same request from the machine, through the relay's own checks.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The relay only ever connects out. Its credential is stored on the machine, readable by the relay's service account only, and an administrator can revoke it at any time from the Relays tab.
  • Two lists decide what a relay reaches: the group's (checked by the platform) and the relay's own (checked on the machine). A request must pass both.
  • The relay checks the addresses it is about to connect to, after resolving the name, so a name that resolves somewhere unexpected is caught. It never reaches a cloud metadata endpoint, whatever its list says, and * does not cover its own machine or link-local addresses.
  • The security audit reports relays that allow every destination, relays older than the minimum supported version, groups in use with no relay online, and groups with a single relay.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Route one of your integrations or MCP servers through the group you created.

docs.title: XTM One Desktop and runners
docs.text:
XTM One Desktop is the native XTM One app for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It gives you two things in one install:

  • A real window for your agents. Your chat, your conversation history and your agent selection - everything the web app does - in a native window that stays in your system tray and comes back with one shortcut (Ctrl+Alt+Space).
  • An assistant that can act on the machine you are sitting at. From that chat, agents can run commands, read and edit files, capture a genuine full-desktop screenshot, and drive a browser you are already logged into - on this machine, within its permission model, with your approval inline in the chat, and with every command audited.

The second half is a runner: the small pull-based daemon the Desktop app embeds, which connects outbound to XTM One and pulls the work agents send to this machine. A runner also exists on its own, without the window: the headless runner you install on servers, VMs, and MDM-managed fleets where nobody sits at a desktop (see Install headless). Both appear as machines on the XTM One Desktop page, both obey the same permission model, and both are what the computer_use agent tools target.

Runners exist for the cases a headless browser cannot cover. When an auditor wants a screenshot with the real desktop, the OS clock, and the signed-in identity - not an AI-generated or headless render - a runner captures the true screen of a real session. The same channel lets an agent operate an authenticated browser or run a check directly on a workstation or server.

Runners are pull-based: the app connects outbound to XTM One and pulls work. The platform never opens a port on your machine, and there is nothing inbound to firewall.

docs.title: Install XTM One Desktop
docs.text:
Everything starts from the XTM One Desktop page: open your user menu, at the top right, and choose Get XTM One Desktop (My machines inside the Desktop app), or search for Get XTM One Desktop in the command palette. On a personal machine the graphical installer needs no command line; for servers and fleets there is a fully headless command-line path (see the next section).

  1. Open the XTM One Desktop page and download the installer for your operating system - the page detects it and offers it first; the other platforms are listed below. The main button is the x86_64 (Intel/AMD) build; ARM machines take the arm64 link next to it. Macs need no choice at all - one universal bundle covers both Intel and Apple Silicon.
  2. Run the installer (next, next, finish on Windows; drag to Applications on macOS; an AppImage or a .deb / .rpm on Linux). On Linux it needs glibc 2.35 or newer: Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 or a later distribution.
  3. Launch XTM One Desktop. On the Connect this machine screen, paste this instance's URL and an enrollment key, then connect. The chat window opens on your instance: sign in as you would in a browser. (Single sign-on opens your system browser - see Signing in below.)

If the OS blocks the first launch

A build that is not code-signed for your operating system trips the first-open gate: Windows SmartScreen shows "unrecognized app" (click More info > Run anyway), and macOS reports it "could not verify ... is free of malware" - click Done (not Move to Trash), then open System Settings > Privacy & Security, click Open Anyway, and launch again. This only ever concerns the first manual install: self-updates are signature-verified and never re-prompt, and the headless install path is not affected.

Create an enrollment key from the same page, under Connect a machine. The key carries the permissions the enrolled machine starts with, as one of three presets:

  • Desktop (recommended) - every capability enabled. This is the preset for the machine you sit at: usable from the very first message. Shell commands run as the agent sends them; turn on Shell commands need approval on the key if you want each one held for your approval in the chat (off unless you turn it on).
  • Locked down - screenshots and browser control only, no approval gate; enable more later from the machine's card. The historical default.
  • Custom - choose the mode, the capabilities and the approval gate yourself (this is where fleet keys for servers are configured).

A key is single-use for the first machine but can be configured for reuse across a fleet, and it can carry labels so an unattended roll-out lands already configured. After enrollment the app stores a durable credential in the machine's OS keychain and stays connected across reboots - you never paste the key again.

One record per machine

Each enrolled machine is one runner. Installing on ten machines gives you ten runners you can name, label, and target individually - not ten integrations. Re-enrolling a machine that is already in the list (a reinstall, a re-run of the install script) updates its existing record - new credential, refreshed host facts, your name/permissions/labels kept - instead of creating a duplicate. Revoked runners stay revoked: enrolling that machine again deliberately creates a fresh record.

docs.title: Install headless (command line)
docs.text:
Servers, VMs, and MDM-managed fleets rarely have someone sitting at a desktop, and have no use for a chat window. For those machines, the XTM One Desktop page also shows a one-line install command per operating system under Servers and headless machines (command line): copy it, replace the key placeholder with an enrollment key, and run it on the target machine - no graphical session is ever needed. What it installs is the headless runner: the same binary as the Desktop app without the window and the tray, serving shell, file and browser commands to your agents exactly as before.

The command downloads the runner build matched to your instance's version, verifies its integrity, installs the binary, enrolls the machine, and registers it to start automatically (a LaunchAgent on macOS, a systemd user service on Linux, a logon task on Windows). The same binary is also a CLI afterwards: xtm-one-runner status, xtm-one-runner run, and xtm-one-runner reset manage it without any UI.

If the integrity check cannot run - the host has no sha256sum / shasum, or no .sha256 is available next to the archive - the installer still installs but warns INTEGRITY NOT VERIFIED and says why. For fleet and MDM rollouts, add --require-checksum (-RequireChecksum on Windows) or set XTM_RUNNER_REQUIRE_CHECKSUM=1 so an unverified binary is refused instead. A checksum that does not match, or a .sha256 that holds no checksum, always stops the install. The checksum is served by your instance next to the archive, so it proves the download arrived intact rather than who built it: use an https:// address for your instance, since over plain HTTP both could be swapped in transit and the installer warns about it. If the installer cannot get the archive from your instance, it reports the HTTP status it received, so a proxy or firewall problem - or a sign-in page from an authentication proxy answering in its place - is not mistaken for a build without embedded downloads.

The installer also checks the release signature: every release signs its runner archives, and the installer verifies the archive's .minisig against the release public keys it carries (the signature names which key made it, so a new release key can be trusted before releases are signed with it), so when that signature is there to check, a binary that was not built by the release - swapped on a mirror or behind a proxy, together with its checksum - is refused. The signature must also have been made for the archive this machine needs, so a signed build of another platform or flavor served in its place is refused too. Release signatures also name the runner version they were made for: when the archive comes from your instance, a signature for another version - an older signed build served in place of the current one - is refused, and the installer prints the version it verified. Archives signed before versions were signed install as before, and say so. The same checks guard the runner's own self-updates, which never install a build older than the running one. On macOS and Linux it uses minisign when installed, otherwise OpenSSL 3, otherwise (when upgrading) the runner already installed; on Windows it needs nothing extra. A signature that does not verify always stops the install. When the signature cannot be checked - no .minisig next to the archive (a build made without the release signing key), one that is not a signature at all (an error page from a mirror or a proxy, for example), a signature whose trusted comment names no file, or no verifier on the host (for example a first install on a macOS machine with neither minisign nor OpenSSL 3) - the installer warns SIGNATURE NOT VERIFIED; add --require-signature (-RequireSignature on Windows) or set XTM_RUNNER_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1 to refuse instead. Without it, whoever can swap the archive can also withhold its .minisig and leave only that warning, so always add it for a mirror (--download-base) and for MDM or other unattended rollouts, where nobody reads the warning. If you build and sign the runner with your own key, an instance built from your fork serves installers that already trust the key of its tauri.conf.json; an installer taken from anywhere else needs XTM_RUNNER_MINISIGN_PUBKEY set to your public key: the key line of your .pub file, or the base64 value tauri.conf.json carries. The installer then says which key ID it checks against - the ID your .pub file prints - so you can confirm it is yours.

docs.title: The headless build (Linux servers)
docs.text:
On Linux the installer picks between two builds of the same runner:

Build Ships Capabilities Desktop (default) Everywhere else, and any Linux with a graphical session Screenshots, mouse/keyboard, shell, files, browser Headless Linux hosts with no graphical session Shell, files, browser

This is not a matter of taste. The desktop build links the desktop libraries (GTK, X11) at load time, so on a server without them it fails before it runs - no flag or setting can work around that. The headless build links none of them.

The installer decides from the environment: no DISPLAY and no WAYLAND_DISPLAY, and no graphical session on the machine, means headless — so SSH-ing into your own Linux desktop to run the installer still gets you the desktop build. Force either one with --headless or --desktop (or XTM_RUNNER_FLAVOR=headless for cloud-init and MDM). The choice sticks: a headless runner is only ever offered headless updates.

Two things a server does differently:

  • Credential storage. Servers usually run no keyring daemon. When there is no OS keychain, the runner stores its credential in a file readable only by its own user, next to its config, and says so in the log.
  • Staying up after logout. The service runs under your user account, so enable lingering or it stops when your SSH session ends. The installer does it for you when it can: sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>.

Desktop capabilities need a desktop

Screenshots and mouse/keyboard control require a logged-in graphical session. Shell commands, file operations, and browser control work on fully headless servers. A headless runner asked for a screenshot answers with a clear error rather than a black frame - assign that work to a runner on a real desktop.

libxdo.so.3: cannot open shared object file

A runner installed before this error was fixed needs one library that a stock Ubuntu desktop does not ship (it lives in universe). Install it once with sudo apt install libxdo3; the runner then starts and updates itself to a build that no longer needs it. Newer builds synthesize input over the X11 protocol directly and require nothing extra to install. That is a packaging fix, not new Wayland support: synthetic input reaches X11 and XWayland windows, so a Wayland-native application still does not receive computer_action keystrokes or clicks.

docs.title: The XTM One Desktop app
docs.text:
Once enrolled, the app opens your instance in its own window and lives in the system tray (or menu bar) behind the XTM One icon. From there you can:

  • open the chat window - or press Ctrl+Alt+Space from anywhere
  • see live status - Online, Connecting, Reconnecting, or Update required when your instance no longer accepts this version of the app (update it from the connection panel)
  • open the connection panel: the machine's name, the enrolled instance URL, the app version, and the host facts reported to the platform (OS build, available shells, installed browsers, monitors, timezone and locale)
  • change a few settings - automatic updates, launch-at-login, and the browser CDP URL
  • unenroll the machine locally

The same actions are in the app's own menu, so you never have to find the tray icon: the File and Help menus of the chat window on Windows and Linux, the menu bar on macOS (where Cmd+, opens the settings). Check for updates..., in the Help menu (the app menu on macOS), asks your instance for a newer build and, when there is one, installs it and restarts the app.

Closing a window hides the app to the tray; the runner keeps serving. To stop the app, use Quit in the tray or in the app's menu; while an update is being installed, Quit waits up to a minute for you to answer or cancel its password prompt, and the connection panel says so. The window stays on your instance: links that would open a new tab, and any link to another site, open in your default browser, and downloads land in your Downloads folder. The app updates itself from signed bundles matched to your instance, so a fleet stays current without anyone touching each machine. When an update restarts the app, the windows you had open come back, with the chat on the page you were on.

On Linux, only the AppImage updates unattended. A .deb / .rpm install updates through your package manager, which asks for an administrator password, so the app does not install those updates on its own: it opens the connection panel to announce the new version, and Install version ... installs it when you choose to. For a Linux desktop that should stay current with nobody at the keyboard, install the AppImage (or the headless build on a server). A .deb / .rpm install from an earlier version gets this behaviour through one last update applied the old way: until you accept it, that version asks for the password on its own each time it checks for updates.

docs.title: Upgrading from XTM One Runner
docs.text:
An installed runner updates itself into XTM One Desktop; the enrollment, the credential and the launch-at-login choice are kept. A few things change name along the way:

  • Windows: XTM One Desktop installs into a new XTM One Desktop folder and removes the former install. The Start menu and desktop shortcuts and a taskbar pin keep their XTM One Runner name but start XTM One Desktop; XTM One Runner leaves Installed apps. A machine updated before this was fixed may still list XTM One Runner in Installed apps: do not uninstall it, as that removes the machine's enrollment and sign-in. The next update removes it for you.
  • macOS: the app bundle is swapped in place. A Mac upgraded from the runner keeps its old folder name until you reinstall from a fresh download.
  • Linux: the AppImage updates in place. The .deb / .rpm package is now named xtm-one-desktop; it declares that it replaces xtm-one-runner, so a package-manager upgrade removes the old package for you.

Headless runners on servers are not affected: they keep their own update channel and the same command line.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
Email and password work inside the window like anywhere else. Single sign-on runs in your system browser: identity providers refuse or degrade embedded browsers (conditional access, passkeys, Windows Hello, "use the browser you are already signed in to"), and the app's window shares no session with the browser you use all day. So a Continue with ... button in the app opens your browser on your instance's sign-in; you finish there as usual, the browser then shows which machine is asking (the name of your XTM One Desktop machine and who enrolled it) and asks you to confirm, and the app signs itself in a moment later. The browser tab keeps no session - you asked to sign in on the desktop.

The confirmation matters: a sign-in request can only be started by an enrolled XTM One Desktop, and can only land on a machine that is yours (you enrolled it) or company-managed (a shared machine your administrator provisioned). A machine someone else enrolled is refused, even one shared with your group: that share lets the machine run your commands, it does not let whoever holds the machine act as you. If the machine named is not yours, choose Not my machine: the request is dropped so nobody else can complete it, the refusal is recorded in the audit log, and you should tell your administrator.

Once signed in, you stay signed in when the app restarts - after an update, a reboot or a crash - under exactly the rules of the browser: the session ends when its lifetime or its idle timeout set by your administrator ends it (see Session lifetime and idle timeout), or when you sign out. The app keeps your session in the machine's OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Secret Service on Linux) next to its own credential, so it no longer depends on the window's browser storage, which an unclean shutdown can damage.

docs.title: Acting on this machine
docs.text:
Every message you send from the app carries the machine it was typed on, so the agent's computer_use tools default to it: "run the tests", "what is in ~/Downloads", "take a screenshot" act here, without naming a runner. Fleet targeting still works - name another machine and the agent reaches it, within the usual rules. Above the composer, a small bar shows the machine, its connection state and a switch to turn local execution off for a conversation.

When the machine's permission model holds a shell command for approval (the Shell commands need approval switch, on the enrollment key or on the machine's card), the request appears in the chat, above the composer: what the agent wants to run and on which machine, with Approve, Always allow, Reject and Always block. The agent waits for your decision and the command's output lands in the same reply. A decision you do not take in time leaves the command queued on the XTM One Desktop page, where you can still approve it.

docs.title: Seeing what the agent does on a machine
docs.text:
Every command an agent sends to a machine shows up in the conversation as a card, above the reply it leads to - in the Desktop app and in the browser alike:

  • a shell command is a small terminal window: the prompt and the command, a live timer while it runs, then its exit code, how long it took and its output (errors in their own colour), with buttons to copy the command or the output and a larger view;
  • a file read or written shows its path and a preview of the content;
  • a folder listing shows the folder's entries, folders first;
  • a screenshot shows a thumbnail you can enlarge;
  • a mouse, keyboard or browser action says what was done (text typed through the agent is shown as a character count, never as text).

A command held for your approval, blocked by the machine's policy, refused because the machine was busy or offline, or cut short when the reply ended says so on its card. The cards are saved with the conversation, so they are still there after a reload and for the people you share it with; a very long output is shortened on the card, and the reply's reasoning details (the i icon) keep more of it.

While a shell command runs, its card has a Stop button (only the square icon on a narrow card). Stopping ends the command and every process it started; what it printed until then stays on the card, and the agent is told that the command was stopped and when. You can stop a command that runs for you, and so can the people who manage the machine. A stopped card says who stopped it: Stopped by you, or Stopped by followed by the person's name for everyone else who reads the conversation.

Inside XTM One Desktop, the paths on a card whose command ran on this machine get Open (with its default application), Show in folder and Copy path, and so do absolute paths the agent quotes in its reply, such as C:\Users\me\Desktop\disks.txt or a file:/// link: a click opens the item, Alt (Option on macOS) + click shows it in its folder. Only documents, images, media and plain-text files are opened that way - an executable, a script, a shortcut, an installer, a web page or a document able to carry macros is only ever shown in its folder - and a network address (a \\server\share path, a link that leads onto one) is never opened from the chat; a drive letter you mapped to a share yourself works like any other drive.

When a long reply finishes while the app is behind another window, the taskbar entry flashes (the Dock icon bounces on macOS) so you know it is ready.

docs.title: Uninstall and re-enroll
docs.text:
Uninstalling the app removes the local enrollment with it - the stored credential, your sign-in, the configuration, and the launch-at-login entry - so the next install always starts fresh at the Connect form. The runner's record on the platform is deliberately left alone (an uninstall can happen offline): revoke it on the XTM One Desktop page when you retire a machine for good.

If a running runner's record is revoked on the platform, the app shows a fatal error with a Re-enroll this machine button: one click drops the dead local credential and reopens the Connect form, prefilled with your instance URL and ready for a fresh enrollment key.

Revoking takes effect on every server at once: from that moment no new command is queued for the machine or handed to it and nothing more is accepted from it, its queued and running commands end, and its live connection closes right away, or at its next heartbeat (every 30 seconds by default) at the latest. A command handed to it a moment before the revocation may still reach it; it is recorded as cancelled and its result is refused.

docs.title: Permissions the first time
docs.text:
• macOS asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility permission the first time an agent captures the screen or controls input. Grant them in System Settings > Privacy & Security; the app links you straight there and shows whether each one is granted.
  • Linux capture and input need a graphical session. On Wayland, capture goes through the desktop portal; the app warns when the current session cannot be captured.

docs.title: What an agent can do on a runner
docs.text:
When an agent has the computer_use built-in tool and at least one of your runners is online, it can:

  • take a full-desktop screenshot (the audit-evidence case)
  • perform mouse and keyboard actions
  • run a shell command, and keep a long one running in the background (see Long commands in the background)
  • read, write, and list files
  • control a browser you already authenticated

Browser control attaches to a browser you started with remote debugging, at the browser CDP URL of the app's settings (http://127.0.0.1:9222 by default): start Chrome or Edge with --remote-debugging-port=9222 and a profile of its own (--user-data-dir=...; recent versions ignore the port on your everyday profile), and sign in there once. The agent acts on one tab and keeps it from one command to the next: list_tabs shows the open tabs, the one the agent drives and the one you used last, and select_tab switches to another tab (the one you used last when no tab is named), for instance after you signed in in a new tab. Opening tabs or signing in in that browser does not break the connection; if it drops anyway, the next command reconnects to the same tab. When the browser cannot be reached because an administrator policy turns its remote debugging off (RemoteDebuggingAllowed), the error says so.

Typing into a page field brings the driven tab to the front and focuses the field first, then reads it back: when the field still holds nothing (it could not take the focus), the action fails and names the field, never the text.

Typing and scrolling are bounded by the command's time budget, never by a length: text of any size is typed in small chunks, and when the budget runs out the action stops between two chunks and says how far it got, so nothing is typed after the command is reported as timed out. A shell command's output and its errors are each kept up to 1 MiB; past that the output is cut and the result says so. The data a command returns - that output, a folder listing, a page's content - may take up to 16 MiB once written as JSON, where escaping counts (a control character takes six bytes), and a file it returns up to RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES. A larger result is not kept: the command fails at once and its error says why, so the agent can ask for less.

Flows can drive runners too: the Runner command node dispatches the same command kinds through the same transport — the runner's permission mode, allow-lists, and approval gating apply unchanged — and can wait for the result. A flow reads at most 1 MiB of that result, written as JSON: a larger one reaches the node's outputs cut to fit, each cut text ending with a [TRUNCATED ...] marker and flow_truncated giving its full size, while the machine's command history keeps it whole. Flows can also react to runner lifecycle through the built-in Runner online, Runner offline, and Runner command completed event types with the On event and Wait for event nodes. Runner offline fires when a machine is revoked while online, or when it has been silent for RUNNER_OFFLINE_AFTER_SECONDS (75 seconds by default): the scheduler's presence sweep, which runs about once a minute and handles up to 500 machines per pass, then declares it offline. Runner online fires once the machine is heard from again, so the two always alternate. A platform restart or upgrade drops every runner connection for a few seconds; a machine back within that window fires neither. The machine rides the restart out: it retries its polls, heartbeats and result uploads with back-off, so a command that finishes while the platform restarts still reports its result once the platform is back within about 50 seconds.

The agent waits for a command's result as long as the machine may take to report it: from the moment the machine takes the command, its execution limit and then those 50 seconds of upload retries (205 seconds in all by default, RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS sets a fixed wait instead), never longer than the agent run allows one tool call. When that limit ends the wait first, the agent is told the command may still finish.

A command is never sent later to nobody: when the agent stops waiting for it (its wait ran out or you stopped the turn) or the flow run waiting for it ends, a command the machine had not picked up yet is cancelled, including one still waiting for your approval in a flow, and one the machine already took is not sent again. If that one still finishes, its output is in the machine's command history.

Screenshots and file reads come back into the conversation as inline images or downloadable files, exactly like other tool results, so they can flow straight into an evidence workflow. The PNG is also forwarded to the model as a native vision block (high-detail, PNG preserved) so the agent can read the URL bar, labels, errors, and OS clock itself - it should never ask you to describe or verify the capture.

docs.title: Long commands in the background
docs.text:
A command that takes long - a large download, a build, a server that keeps running - can run as a background job. The agent gets an answer at once with the job's id and its first lines of output, and the command keeps running on the machine, its output kept in a log file there. The agent then follows the job with its shell_jobs tool: it lists the machine's jobs, reads a job's output from where it left off, and stops a job with every process it started.

In the conversation, the card of a background job reads Background while the job runs, and keeps its Stop button after the reply ends. Stopping a job asks you to confirm first. Once the job is over, the card shows its exit code (Ended when there is none), or Stopped by you if you stopped it.

On the XTM One Desktop page, the card of a machine you manage lists its Background jobs, running ones first, each with a Stop button. The list is read from the machine when you open its card, after a stop, and when you click Refresh. Every read is a command in the machine's history, so the list is not refreshed on its own. When the machine is offline, busy or does not answer, the list says so.

A machine whose app is too old for background jobs refuses them before anything is sent, and the agent is told which version it needs: update XTM One Desktop or the runner, or run the command without the background option.

docs.title: Control what a runner allows
docs.text:
Each runner carries its own permission model, set on the XTM One Desktop page (the machine's card):

  • Restricted (default) - least privilege. Only the capabilities you enable are allowed (screenshot, mouse/keyboard, shell, file operations, browser control). Enabling a capability is the consent: once it is on, it runs without further prompts. Shell commands are the exception and get finer control:
    • Allow-list (standing approvals) - a matching command runs immediately and never asks for approval. With approval off, only allow-listed commands can run at all.
    • Block-list (standing refusals) - a command containing a blocked word or phrase is always refused. It never runs and never reaches the approval queue, and the block-list wins over the allow-list.
    • Require approval - any shell command not covered by the lists waits for a human decision: inline in the chat when the command was asked for from XTM One Desktop, otherwise on the XTM One Desktop page. When approving or rejecting, Approve & always allow / Reject & always block saves the exact command, whatever its length, into the corresponding list, so the same command never asks again. Approval applies to shell commands only - screenshots, input, file operations and browser control never queue.
    • File operations can additionally be narrowed with a path allow-list. The platform checks the path as written against it, and the runner resolves links to see where the path really leads. A path inside the allowed folders that leads outside them through a link (a symbolic link, a junction, a mount point) still runs by default, as it always has, with a warning in its result and in the runner log; with RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT=true (see Configuration) it is refused (to reach what such a link leads to, add that folder to the allowed paths). A link that stays inside the allowed folders keeps working either way, an allowed folder that does not exist yet can be written into (the runner creates it), and a path written as a network share or automount path (\\server\share, /net/host) is only looked up inside an allowed folder that is itself on it. After opening a file or folder the runner re-checks the handle it actually got: its type in every mode, and in strict mode its real path too, so a link swapped in between the check and the open is caught and nothing is truncated or written until that check passes (only a folder the write has to create is made before it, so a link swapped in at that moment can leave an empty folder where it leads; on a volume the OS cannot resolve paths on, some RAM disks and VirtualBox shared folders, the handle cannot be named and the pre-open check stands). What no mode prevents: a link in an allowed folder that leads onto a share is followed to see where it leads, which can reach that host, and a hard link is the file itself under a second name, so one inside an allowed folder is served like any file there.
  • Full control - a deliberate opt-in that allows every capability and every command with no lists and no approval. It is clearly flagged in the UI, and every command is still audited. An agent listing its runners (list_runners) sees every capability on a full-control runner, whatever capability toggles were saved before the switch.

Whatever the mode, every command is recorded server-side with its result, and revoking a runner invalidates its credential immediately - the next command fails and the app stops. A command still queued when a runner's permissions are tightened is checked again when it is delivered, and cancelled if they no longer allow it.

File operations read and write regular files as they always have. A path goes to the operating system as written and is never judged by its name: what the OS opens for it decides, and when the OS refuses it, its error is the result. A file that is not a regular file - a character or block device (a serial port, /dev/urandom, /dev/zero, NUL on Windows, a volume or disk opened raw such as \\.\C:), a named pipe (FIFO) or a socket, as the OS reports the object opened - is also read and written as before, on every runner, with a warning in the result and in the runner log saying what it is. With RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT=true (see Configuration) it is refused, on every runner, full control included; on Windows a device is refused once it is opened, before anything is read or written, since its handle is what tells. A name Windows opens as a file is a file, whatever it looks like - con.log, aux.c or nul.txt on Windows 11, a folder named aux, a drive, share or volume location behind a \\.\, \??\ or \\?\ prefix, a file in a volume shadow copy (\\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\...) - and is served as one, with no warning, strict or not. Reading a Windows device such as NUL, or a raw volume, fails as it always did: Windows cannot describe it for the size check before the read. Such a file is opened without waiting and then used as a plain open would, so a named pipe with no program at its other end returns at once (empty for a read, an error for a write) instead of holding a runner worker for good; a socket cannot be opened as a file at all. A restricted runner with allowed folders only reaches one inside those folders; a device path never lies under a drive-letter folder.

A read never asks for more than a positive result size limit (RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES, the largest file a runner may upload) or 256 KiB, whichever is larger. What comes back as a file - binary content, or text past 256 KiB - is cut to the limit and flagged as incomplete; the 256 KiB of text that comes back inline has never met that limit, so under a smaller limit a runner from this release still returns such text whole (an older runner cuts it to the limit, as before). A limit of 0 or less keeps its meaning - every non-empty file result is refused at upload and reads are not bounded - and is reported at startup and by the security audit (Settings → Security).

A read that stops at its size before the end of the file says so in its result: how many bytes were read, and how to read the rest - a larger max_bytes, or, at the result size limit, another way such as a shell command that splits or compresses the file. A runner from before this release cannot tell, so a read it returns at exactly the size it was asked for is flagged as possibly incomplete.

docs.title: Choose which machines an agent can reach
docs.text:
Runners are targeted, not global:

  • Give runners labels (for example audit, eu-west, workstation).
  • On an agent, set a runner selector - specific runners or a set of labels - so the agent can only reach the machines you intend.
  • An assignment can refine that selection further, never widen it, so an agent-driven automation can never reach a machine its agent could not. A flow's Runner command node targets one explicit runner instead — gated by the runner's own permission mode, allow-lists, and visibility (a flow can only use runners visible to the person who runs it: their own, group-shared, or company-managed).

When more than one eligible machine is online, mutating actions require the agent to name the target runner explicitly, so a command can never land on the wrong machine by accident. The list_runners tool lets an agent see which machines are online before acting.

docs.title: Availability and limits
docs.text: The whole subsystem is governed by platform configuration: an administrator enables it, sets where installers are downloaded from, and can cap how many runners a user may enroll and how many commands may run on one machine at once. If downloads are not configured on your deployment, the page explains it and you can still enroll a runner you obtained separately. See the runner variables in Configuration for the full list.

docs.title: Fleet oversight for administrators
docs.text: The XTM One Desktop page lists your machines: the ones you enrolled, the ones shared with you, and the company-managed fleet - for administrators too. To see every machine enrolled with the platform, whoever enrolled it, an administrator opens Administration > Objects and filters by Machines: each row shows the machine's owner, operating system, live connection state (Online, Offline with the time it was last seen, or Revoked) and runner version, and opens the machine's own page with the same permission editor and revoke / delete actions as here. Reading the command history of a machine you neither own nor hold a configure-level share on (a company-managed machine is yours to manage and is not counted) is recorded in the audit log. See Objects.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Name each machine so you can tell an agent exactly where to work.
  • Start in Restricted mode and enable only the capabilities you need; reserve Full control for machines you fully trust.
  • Use labels for fleets and set agent selectors so each agent reaches only its own machines.
  • Turn on shell-command approval when a person should stay in the loop, and build up the allow/block lists from real decisions with "Approve & always allow" / "Reject & always block".
  • Revoke a runner as soon as a machine is decommissioned.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The XTM One Desktop page (Get XTM One Desktop, or My machines inside the app, in the profile menu) - where you download the app, create enrollment keys and manage your machines.
  • Agents - bind the computer_use tool and set the runner selector.
  • Configuration - the RUNNERS_ENABLED and RUNNER_* deployment variables.

docs.title: Sharing and access
docs.text: When you share something, you may also be lending what it carries. An agent bound to your GitHub token lets everyone who can start one of its runs act with your token; an MCP server with your API key in its headers answers for everyone whose agent uses it. XTM One always says so, and never blocks you.

docs.title: What can be lent
docs.text:
Resource What the people it reaches act with Integration its stored credential: an OAuth connected account, a personal access token, an API key, a bot token MCP server its headers, its environment variables, or its own OAuth token Custom tool its code, run on their behalf Channel bot its bot token (bots are platform-wide and managed by administrators) Variable its value, secret or not Knowledge base its documents, searched and read in full, and written to where the agent may write Skill its instructions and files Prompt its text

A knowledge base, a skill or a prompt is lent by what attaches it: an agent reads the ones it attaches as their owner may, for everyone it serves, whoever is chatting - and so do a flow's knowledge base and skill nodes and the General Assistant's knowledge bases. The confirmation names each one a change lends to new people. A change to the knowledge base, skill or prompt itself (sharing, unsharing or deleting it) does not list it, only what it carries.

docs.title: Through what
docs.text:
A resource reaches people in two ways:

  • Directly: it is shared with people, with groups, or with everyone (company-managed, optionally restricted to named people and groups).
  • Through something that carries it: an agent bound to it, an assignment override or trigger, a flow node, a knowledge base sync source, a skill's private source, a prompt or custom tool that references a variable, or the General Assistant's platform bindings. What an agent or the General Assistant attaches carries its resources into their runs too: an attached prompt's or skill's variables, a skill's private source, a knowledge base's sync source (attached prompt, attached skill, attached knowledge base on the card).
  • Through a per-user binding: an agent bound "per user" to a provider has each person use their own integration in a chat, but its assignments run as one person - the agent's owner, or the run-as user of a company-managed assignment - and use that person's own integration of the provider for everyone who sees their work, or, while that person has none connected, the company-wide integration of the provider they may use. The integration's card lists those assignments (per-user binding); a per-user fan-out assignment (Run for all users) uses each user's own.

An agent's audience includes more than the people it is shared with: anyone with its public chat link, anyone who messages it on a channel that accepts people without an account, its A2A partners, anyone holding the platform MCP key when the agent is exposed there, and anyone holding the URL of one of its webhook assignments. A flow's audience includes anyone holding the URL of its webhook trigger once it is active. An A2A partner's task runs as the identity its exposure records, but it is an outside caller like a channel sender without an account: it gets no trace inspection, and the platform builder only reads, as a caller without an account (company-managed objects), and never writes, whatever that identity may do. What the people without an account run counts against the platform-wide agentic limits (see Requests with no account).

Two honest caveats:

  • In a chat, people who cannot see an integration bound to an agent, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with them, use their own connected integration of the same provider instead; when they have none, a note under the answer says the integration was not used and why. The agent's runs, public link, channels and A2A partners act with the bound one. So an integration bound to an agent is counted as usable by the agent's owner, its callers without an account, the people who can configure the agent (they can add an assignment), and, when the agent has an enabled assignment that uses the agent's integrations and that they may trigger, everyone who sees the agent - not by the people who only chat with it. Adding someone to a group the agent is shared with announces the integration only on those terms.
  • A variable resolves only for someone who can see it, or in a run acting as someone who can (the agent's owner by default).
  • An agent bound to an integration its owner can no longer see (the share was revoked, or the owner left the group it was shared with) holds an orphaned binding: none of its runs (chats, assignments, public link, channels, A2A, scheduled work items) uses the integration, its tools are refused with the reason owner_lost_access, and the owner is no longer counted among the people who can use the integration. The integration's Who can use it card flags the agent (Owner no longer has access) with an Unbind action for whoever can edit the agent, the agent's settings page names the integrations its owner lost, and get_integration and get_agent report it. Restore the owner's access or remove the binding to clear it.
  • When an agent stops reaching someone (their share or their group's removed, they leave the group or it is deleted, a company-managed agent made private, the agent given to another owner), their agents stop handing over to it and filing work items for it: it is removed from their handover targets and work-item owners. An agent you keep reaching stays where you named it.
  • Before a change that would orphan bindings (unsharing an integration from a group or a person, making it private, removing a member from a group), the confirmation lists the agents that would lose the integration under These agents would lose this integration, with their owner, and Unbind them too (checked by default) removes those bindings in the same step for every agent you can edit. The preview API reports them per item as orphaned_agents.

An OAuth connected account shared without its owner's consent is shared without the account: the owner keeps it, and the people it reaches authorize the integration with their own - on the integration itself, and every run acts with the account of the person it runs for (see Integrations).

docs.title: Where you see it
docs.text:
• On the resource's page: a Sharing and access card lists every path - shared with a group, with people, company-managed, through an agent, an assignment, a flow, a knowledge base, a skill, a prompt, a custom tool or the General Assistant - with who it reaches and a link to each one you can open. Something you cannot open is named by its owner, without its name. Integrations, MCP servers and custom tools show it on their overview, variables in their edit dialog, channel bots in their tools dialog (Settings > Channels & Bots).
  • On an integration's overview: the card is Who can use it, one list grouped by access path with one total at the top: the direct shares (company, groups with their member count, people), then each agent bound to it once (its owner, who it reaches, and what runs with the integration: chats, its assignments, its public link, its channels), then the other entities that carry it. It replaces the former Sharing and access and Agents Using This Integration cards, which listed every bound agent twice.
  • On the resource's card: a Shared - N ways badge, with the breakdown in its tooltip.

Both are shown to the people who can manage the resource, and both follow every change as soon as it is saved.

docs.title: When a person or a group is deleted
docs.text: When an administrator deletes an account or a group, it leaves the sharing of everything it was given, with its access level, and a resource shared with nobody else reads as not shared. A share with that person saved at the same moment either lands first and is removed with the rest, or is refused because the account is gone. Group shares are not checked that way yet: a sharing form opened before a group was deleted can still save that group back onto its resource, where it grants nothing (the group has no members left) and stays listed until someone removes it. A flow run keeps the audience its flow had when it ran.

docs.title: When you are asked
docs.text:
Before a change that lends something to new people, or takes it from people who use it, one dialog lists each resource concerned: whose it is ("your MCP server Tickets and its headers", "Alice's GitHub connected account"), who newly gets it or loses it, through what, what they can do with it and how to avoid it (a company-managed resource instead of a personal one, per-user integrations, Don't share my connected account). One click proceeds; nothing is refused and there is no setting. The dialog only opens when someone other than you and the resource's owner is concerned.

You are asked when you:

  • share a resource or something that carries one: people, groups, company-managed (a flow's too), lifting an access restriction, an owner transfer (an agent, a flow, a skill, a knowledge base, a prompt, an integration, an MCP server, a custom tool), an agent's public web widget, an agent's channels, sharing an agent's personal integrations with its groups from its Sharing card;
  • bind a resource to something shared: an agent's integrations (fixed or per user), pipeline steps, MCP servers, custom tools, channel bots, knowledge bases, skills and prompts, persona, guardrails and human-in-the-loop prompt (variables), an assignment's overrides, trigger, channels, prompt and run-as identity, a flow node, a knowledge base import source, a skill's private source, a prompt's or skill's content, the General Assistant's bindings, knowledge bases and channels;
  • open a public entry point: activating a flow with a webhook trigger, resuming a webhook assignment, letting a channel bot answer people without an account, exposing an agent on the platform MCP endpoint or generating its key;
  • change a group's members: an administrator adding someone to a group (or removing them) is told what its shares lend them, by name;
  • create something already shared: a company-managed integration, agent, prompt, skill, MCP server or custom tool, a channel bot, an assignment on a shared agent;
  • unshare or unbind: the dialog says who stops having access, with Unshare and Keep sharing - switching an agent to per-user integrations, unrouting an agent from a channel bot, removing an agent from the platform MCP endpoint or revoking its key included;
  • delete an agent, an assignment, a flow, an integration, an MCP server, a custom tool, a prompt, a skill, a knowledge base, a channel bot or a variable that others use: the dialog says who loses what, and replaces the usual confirmation.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Every route is read-only and additive:

  • GET /api/v1/exposure/{resources}/{id}: every path of one resource, with its reason, its audience and, for a carrier, who acts with the resource through it (lent). For the people who can manage the resource (an administrator who opens it from a direct link or Administration > Objects included).
  • GET /api/v1/exposure/{resources}/summary: the number of ways each resource you can see and manage is shared, for the list cards.
  • POST /api/v1/exposure/preview: before a change, which resources it lends to new people (gained) and takes from people who could use them (lost). Body: entity_type (a resource type, or agent, assignment, flow, knowledge_base, skill, prompt, general_assistant, and for administrators group and platform_mcp), entity_id (omitted when creating), parent_id (the agent, when creating an assignment) and change (only the fields the change sets, plus new_owner_id for an owner transfer and delete: true for a deletion; remove_channel for an agent unrouted from a channel; add_user_ids / remove_user_ids for a group; mcp_exposed_agent_ids / has_mcp_key for the platform MCP endpoint; status: "active" for a flow's activation).

{resources} is integrations, mcp-servers, custom-tools, channel-bots or variables; a preview item may also be a knowledge_base, a skill or a prompt an agent, a flow or the General Assistant attaches. GET /api/v1/integrations/{id}/exposure, GET /api/v1/integrations/exposure/summary and POST /api/v1/integrations/exposure/preview give the same answer for integrations, computed by the same engine, with integration-specific names (credential, credential_usable, credentials, reached). The routes never return a secret value, and a carrier you cannot open is listed without its name.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: A skill is a reusable instruction set, a packaged method that you attach to agents. This page gives you a quick tour of the skill screens, then explains how agents use skills and how packages are imported.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, open Agent Studio > Skills. The list page is a reusable behavior library: search by name, description, or purpose, and filter by visibility or tags. Each card answers three questions without opening the detail page — is the skill currently active, is it centrally maintained or locally owned, and (for URL-based skills) whether it should be edited here or refreshed from its source. If you have permission, Add Skill creates one by URL, paste, or file upload, and Import Package imports one or more skills from a file (see Importing skills from an archive).

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a skill shows a header with its name, its source type (URL-based Skill or Direct Content Skill), its Enabled or Disabled state, and badges. Export downloads the skill. For URL-based skills the header also has Refresh, which fetches the content again from the source URL — the quickest way to answer "did the source change outside XTM One, and do I need the latest version here?". The page is organized into Catalog, Instructions, Resources, Versioning, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
Catalog holds what describes the skill and who can reach it:

  • Name and Description. The description is what agents read to decide when to load the skill (see How a skill reaches the agent).
  • Compatibility and Tags.
  • URL, and for a skill kept in GitHub, Private repository access and Tracked branch (see Skills from a private GitHub repository).
  • Enabled controls whether the skill is currently available to agents — a skill can stay saved but stop affecting agents immediately, including mid-conversation.
  • Hide from chat controls discoverability in chat, not whether the skill exists.
  • Sharing settings control who can reuse it.
  • License is the skill's licence and copyright notice (the license field of a SKILL.md frontmatter is read into it). The License and attribution section shows it with the full text of the licence the skill bundles as LICENSE.md at its root. It is metadata about the skill: the agent never reads it, and it travels with the skill when it is exported or installed from the AI Catalog.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
Instructions shows the SKILL.md as rendered markdown, with its frontmatter kept as a raw block above it. Images in the text are not loaded: a skill can come from another user or a remote URL, and the page does not fetch what it points to.

Edit opens the markdown content, where the actual operating method lives. The editor includes a variable insert control for reusable values.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Resources lists the custom tools a skill package created, next to the resource path each one came from, with a link to open each tool (see What a package's files become).

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Each content change records a new version. Versioning lists them with their date, author and commit message, and marks the Active one. Select two versions, then Compare, to see what changed; the rollback button of a version makes its content current again, and the content you replace stays in the list. Administrators can also lock a version so it cannot be deleted, and delete a version that is not active.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity is the audit view. During troubleshooting it helps you tell a skill change apart from an agent configuration change or a normal difference in model behavior.

docs.title: How a skill reaches the agent
docs.text:
An agent does not carry the full text of every skill attached to it. Its prompt carries a catalog: one entry per skill with the name, the description, the compatibility note, and the names of any bundled files (except its LICENSE.md). When a task matches an entry, the agent calls load_skill and the full instructions arrive at that point in the conversation. If the skill is a package, the agent can then read individual bundled files with read_skill_resource.

A long skill written with Markdown headings can also be read one section at a time: load_skill with section (the heading text, or its number such as 16) returns only that section and its subsections. A section read does not count as a load, so it also brings a rule back after the conversation pruned the first full load; a title that matches no section, or several, answers the list of the skill's sections. Headings inside code blocks are not sections.

On a long skill the agent can look before it reads: load_skill with outline: true lists every heading with its index and size, and nothing else. section also accepts that index (#12) or a heading path (Rules > Holds), as get_skill does. A section longer than one answer is read by window: max_chars sets the size (at most the per-load cap), and a cut answer names the offset the next call continues from. An outline or a windowed read does not count as a load either.

docs.title: Editing a long skill from a conversation
docs.text:
An agent with the agent builder tools reads and changes a long skill by section, never resending it whole:

  • get_skill with outline lists the headings (index, level, offset, length); with section (a heading text as load_skill accepts it, a heading path such as Rules > Holds, or an index such as #3) it returns that section verbatim.
  • update_skill takes a mode: replace (the whole body, the default), replace_section (one section, its heading line included, every other character kept), insert_after (a new section after the one named), append, or edit (a list of exact find/replace operations; nothing changes unless every one applies, and a text found more than once needs replace_all).
  • A replace that would remove more than half of a skill of 2,000 characters or more is refused unless confirm_shrink is set. A content that is only a placeholder, or shorter than 50 characters, never replaces such a skill: the refusal names the current length and nothing changes.
  • Every content change made this way writes a skill version, so a bad edit is rolled back from the skill's history like an edit made in the page.
  • update_skill and update_prompt also change who owns and who reaches the skill or prompt: owner (an email or user id) transfers it, an administrator's action recorded in the audit log; users with users_permission (use, the default, or manage) shares it with people, and shared_group_ids with shared_group_permissions with groups, each list applied by binding_mode (replace, the default, add or remove; none clears it). The owner named in users is reported, never stored, and a company-managed skill is not shared with individual people. get_skill and get_prompt read back the owner, the groups and the people with their access.

This is why the description matters more than it looks: it is the only thing the agent sees until it decides to load. A description that does not say when to use the skill leaves the agent guessing.

Three consequences worth knowing:

  • attaching ten skills costs about the same prompt space as attaching one — the cost scales with the number of skills, not the size of their content
  • every load shows up in the run trace as a tool call, so a trace finally answers "which skill actually influenced this answer?"
  • a skill that is disabled, unshared, or made private stops being loadable immediately, even in a conversation that is already running (detaching a skill from the agent takes effect on the next message or run, like every other change to an agent's configuration)

docs.title: Keeping one skill always loaded
docs.text:
On an agent's Configuration tab, each attached skill has a pin. Pinning it puts the full instructions in the system prompt on every turn, exactly as before this behaviour existed — the right choice for the one skill that defines how the agent works, rather than one it should reach for occasionally. A pinned skill does not appear in the catalog, because there is nothing left to load.

Pin sparingly. Pinning every skill re-creates the oversized prompt the catalog exists to avoid.

docs.title: Skills from a private GitHub repository
docs.text:
A URL-based skill normally fetches its SKILL.md anonymously, which only works for a public file. When the file lives in a private repository, select a connected GitHub integration under Private repository access, and every fetch is authenticated with that integration's stored credential instead.

Both GitHub integration types work, because both authenticate the same API:

  • a personal access token — a fine-grained token must list the repository and grant Contents: Read
  • an OAuth App or GitHub App connection — the current token is read on every refresh, so a rotated token is picked up with no change to the skill

Nothing is copied onto the skill. It stores only a reference to the integration, so rotating the credential in Integrations is the single place a token is ever managed. You can attach any integration you can already see: your own, one shared with your groups, or a company-managed one.

Tracked branch decides which version is served:

  • leave it empty to follow the repository's default branch, which means each refresh returns the latest commit merged there — the usual choice when skills are reviewed by pull request and merged
  • set a branch name to follow that branch instead
  • set a commit SHA to deliberately pin a fixed version that will not move

The URL you paste may point at the GitHub file page (github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<branch>/…), at raw.githubusercontent.com, or at the contents API. All three are recognised. A branch name containing a / is ambiguous in those URLs, so set Tracked branch explicitly in that case.

The content is validated when you save: XTM One reads the file once with the credential you selected, and refuses to save with a specific message when the token is rejected, when the token cannot see the repository, or when the path does not exist on the tracked branch. You therefore find out immediately rather than discovering a stale skill later.

After that, refresh is on the normal schedule: URL-based skills are re-fetched when their cached content is more than a day old, and the check runs hourly. A newly merged change appears within one refresh cycle rather than instantly — use Refresh in the header when you need it right away.

docs.title: When the credential stops working
docs.text:
If the attached credential expires, is revoked, or loses access to the repository, the skill shows a Credential rejected badge on both the list page and the detail header.

That state is deliberately different from a broken URL:

  • the skill stays enabled and agents keep using the last content that was successfully fetched
  • refresh keeps retrying daily instead of quarantining the skill, because the fix is rotating a token, not repairing a URL
  • as soon as the credential works again, the next refresh clears the badge on its own

To recover, re-authorize the integration in Integrations, or attach a different one to the skill. Operators also get distinct log entries for an authentication failure, a missing path, and a provider outage, so a token problem is never reported as a dead URL.

Setting Private repository access back to Public repository (no credential) detaches the credential. That is a configuration change only: it does not re-read the source, so it works even when the repository is private and unreadable without a token. The content already cached is kept, and the next scheduled refresh then behaves like any other unreachable URL.

docs.title: Importing skills from an archive
docs.text:
Import Package on the list page accepts a single SKILL.md / .txt file, or a .zip archive.

A ZIP may hold several skills at once — a folder exported from a repository, or a collection shared by another team. Nothing is written straight away: XTM One reads the archive first and opens a review screen listing the skills it found (with their description, resource and version counts), the files it ignored grouped by reason (a README with no frontmatter, an image, archive metadata such as __MACOSX), and a checkbox per skill. A single-skill package goes through the same review, showing one row.

docs.title: What counts as a skill in the archive
docs.text:
