A skill is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter declaring name and description, and the directory holding it is that skill's root. Those roots are found wherever they are in the archive, so all of these work — mixed together in the same ZIP if need be:

  • <skill-name>/SKILL.md with its scripts/, references/, assets/, examples/ and versionning/ folders — the Agent Skills layout, repeated as many times as needed
  • <skill-name>/<anything>.md — folders that name the file after the skill rather than using SKILL.md
  • <skill-name>.md at the root of the archive — a flat folder of skill files
  • any of the above under one or more wrapper folders, which is what zipping a skills/ directory produces (skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md), README included

The frontmatter name is always what the skill is called, even when the folder is named differently — a mismatch is a warning on the review screen, not an error. When a folder contains both SKILL.md and other markdown files, SKILL.md is the skill and the rest is ignored.

Files inside a skill's scripts/, references/, assets/, examples/ and versionning/ folders belong to that skill at any depth, and are never mistaken for skills of their own even when they carry frontmatter — a reference document stays a reference document, and a versionning/ snapshot stays a version. Anything else inside a skill folder (an unmapped templates/ directory, for instance) is listed as ignored rather than imported. When a single folder holds several skill files, resources cannot be attributed to one of them: they are listed as ignored and the skills are imported without them.

docs.title: Collisions and partial failures
docs.text:
A skill whose name you already have is flagged on the review screen, with a choice per skill: Skip leaves the existing skill untouched (the default), Replace overwrites it with the archive's version, Import as new creates a copy under a suffixed name.

Each skill is then imported on its own. A skill that fails — malformed frontmatter, a duplicate name inside the archive, a package requiring a tool this platform does not have — never rolls back the skills that already landed. The result screen lists every skill as created, replaced, skipped or failed, with the reason.

docs.title: What a package's files become
docs.text: A skill package is more than its SKILL.md. The mapped folders are turned into real platform objects at import time.

docs.title: scripts/ become Custom Tools
docs.text:
Custom tools are off by default

In XTM One, custom tools are switched off by default. The tools a package creates are still created, but agents cannot run them until an administrator turns custom tools on (see Tools).

Every executable script in scripts/ is imported as an enabled Custom Tool, so the agents using the skill can actually run it. The tool is named <skill-name>-<file-name> (pdf-extract-convert for scripts/convert.py), described as Imported from scripts/convert.py, and tagged skill-import plus the skill name so you can find every tool a skill created. Language comes from the extension: .py is Python, .js / .mjs / .cjs are JavaScript. A file with any other extension is not turned into a tool — it is still stored with the skill and downloadable from it, and the import reports Skipped non-executable script resources so the omission is visible rather than silent.

There are two shapes:

  • One tool per file — the default. Each script stands on its own.
  • One tool for the whole folder — used when scripts/ looks like a Python project, which XTM One detects as an __init__.py alongside more than one .py file. Modules that import each other only work if they are unpacked together, so the entire scripts/ tree is embedded in a single tool: at run time it is extracted into a temporary directory, that directory is put on sys.path and becomes the working directory, and the entrypoint runs as __main__. Anything passed as the tool's argv input becomes sys.argv for the script.

The entrypoint of a Python project is chosen among the top-level scripts that contain __main__, preferring main.py, then run.py, then the first in alphabetical order; when several qualify, the import says which one it picked. The embedded workspace is capped at 10 MB compressed — a larger scripts/ folder is refused with a message asking you to reduce or split the package. Imported tools execute in the same hardened sandbox as any other Custom Tool: importing a package does not create a privileged execution path.

docs.title: Who can run them, and what happens on delete
docs.text:
Materialized tools inherit the skill's visibility — a company-managed or group-shared skill produces company-managed or group-shared tools, because agents belonging to other users must be able to execute them. A private skill produces private tools. A tool name that is already taken is suffixed rather than overwriting anything.

Agents that already reference the skill are wired up automatically: the new tools (and reference knowledge bases) are added to their configuration, so an existing agent does not silently miss the scripts of a skill it already uses. Deleting the skill deletes the tools and knowledge bases its import created and removes them from every agent that had been linked; re-importing with Replace does the same cleanup first, so repeated imports never accumulate orphaned tools. The tools a skill created are listed on its Resources tab, next to the resource path each one came from.

docs.title: references/ become Knowledge Base documents
docs.text:
Text files in references/ (or reference/) are imported as documents in a knowledge base named <skill-name>-references, tagged the same way, and bound to the agents using the skill. Files whose type cannot be read as text are skipped and reported as Skipped non-text reference resources.

The knowledge base and its documents exist as soon as the import returns, but the documents are queued for vectorization like any uploaded document — they stay pending until the platform worker processes them, and only then are they searchable by agents. A knowledge base whose documents are all still pending means the worker has not picked them up yet, not that the import missed them. assets/ and examples/ are stored with the skill as-is, and are never turned into tools or documents.

docs.title: Controlling the mapping: assets/xtm-resource-map.json
docs.text:
Everything above is inference — convenient defaults for a package that ships nothing but files. A package can decide for itself instead by including assets/xtm-resource-map.json:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "builtins": ["web_search"],
  "scripts": [
    {
      "path": "scripts/convert.py",
      "tool": {
        "name": "pdf-to-markdown",
        "description": "Convert a PDF to markdown",
        "language": "python",
        "workspace_mode": "project",
        "input_schema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "argv": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } } }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "references": [{ "path": "references/format.md" }]
}

Points that matter when writing one:

  • listing scripts replaces inference — only the entries you list become tools, which is how a Python project exposes more than one entrypoint
  • workspace_mode is single_file or project, and overrides the detection described above
  • input_schema is the tool's input contract; without it the tool takes no declared input
  • builtins requests platform built-in tools by ID. The platform refuses to import a package asking for a built-in it does not have, and the bulk review screen flags it before you approve rather than at write time
  • a malformed manifest fails the import with the exact field at fault, instead of falling back to inference

Exporting a skill writes this manifest back into the package with the mapping that was actually resolved, so a skill exported from one platform and imported into another creates the same tools.

docs.title: Packaged skills carry their own resources
docs.text:
The skill card and picker show what a skill carries, for example 1 KB · 2 tools. Those resources belong to the skill, not to the agent:

  • attaching such a skill to an agent also attaches the knowledge bases and custom tools it carries, so instructions that say "consult references/playbook.md" actually reach the content
  • detaching the skill removes them again
  • in the agent's Knowledge Bases and Custom Tools sections they are marked Via skill and cannot be detached by hand — detach the skill instead

Two consequences are worth knowing. A company-managed agent only accepts company-managed knowledge bases, so a packaged knowledge base that is not company-managed is skipped rather than attached — publish the skill company-managed if its references must follow it there. And resources you attached yourself are never touched by this: only the ones a package created are added and removed automatically.

Deleting the skill, or re-importing its package with replace, deletes the resources that import created and unbinds them everywhere.

docs.title: Exporting a skill
docs.text:
A skill is exported as a package (a ZIP holding SKILL.md, its resources and its versionning/ history) or as JSON. A package needs a name and a description in the frontmatter of SKILL.md and of every version snapshot, but a skill created by pasting or uploading plain instructions keeps them in its own Name and Description fields. The export writes the missing ones from those fields, so you do not have to repeat them in the content:

  • a value the frontmatter already has is never changed, and the stored content is not modified;
  • the exported name is the skill's name in package format: lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, 64 characters at most (Code Review becomes code-review), and it names the package's root folder;
  • when the skill's name has no usable character (for example only non-Latin letters), the export stays unavailable and the skill page says which field to fix.

docs.title: Read-only states
docs.text: Company-managed skills can be read-only for non-admins, shared skills stay editable in a group context, and some built-in skills are non-editable. When a page is read-only, inspection still works.

docs.title: Empty states on the list page
docs.text:
If no skills exist yet, the page suggests creating the first skill by URL, paste, or file upload.

If filters remove all visible skills, the page shows No skills match your filter.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Check whether a skill is enabled before blaming the agent for missing behavior.
  • When an agent ignored a skill, read the run trace: no load_skill call means the description did not match the task, which is a description problem, not a content problem.
  • Write descriptions that say when to use the skill, not just what it contains.
  • Use Refresh on URL-based skills when the source was updated.
  • Treat a Credential rejected badge as an integration task, not a skill task — fix the token in Integrations.
  • Check which agents use a shared skill before changing it.
  • Keep compatibility and description fields meaningful so reuse stays easy.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template is a design your presentations wear: a palette per theme, the heading and body typefaces, the logos drawn on every slide, the predefined assets a deck may place (figures, screenshots, badges, partner / integration / customer logos), the layouts it may use, and a few sentences of guidance on how to compose in that brand. Agents find templates by name, kind, aspect ratio, tag and by the themes they support, so the same request produces on-brand output for everyone. The page lists, for each template, the themes it supports — Dark, Light or both.

A template has one of three kinds, chosen when it is created: Presentation dresses slide decks and pages, Report dresses executive reports, Video dresses the videos of the Video Studio (see Video templates). Whatever its kind, its assets are readable by any deck — there is no separate "asset pack" kind, the assets belong to the template whose brand they serve.

Templates live under Agent Studio > Templates in the sidebar. The page opens with the three steps of using one; they are spelled out below.

docs.title: Use a template
docs.text:
1. Design it. A template declares the themes it supports — Dark, Light or both — with two switches, when it is created and at any time on the Configuration tab (Themes this template supports); at least one stays on. Each supported theme gets its own palette: the base palette carries the full set of colours and the typefaces and is read as Dark or Light from its background colour, and the other supported theme gets a variant palette in which only the colours you set differ — the accent, fonts and logos carry over. A template that supports a single theme limits every deck wearing it to that theme; switching a theme off removes the choice from those decks (a deck already in that theme is snapped to a supported one at its next save, and the note says so). The template's Preview renders a sample deck in each supported theme so the palettes can be judged before any deck exists.

2. Choose it when you create a presentation. New presentation, on the Presentations page or on a template's own page (New presentation with this template), asks which template the deck starts in and which of its supported themes to use, then opens the chat with the request written for you. In a chat, when you can see several templates, the template is your choice, never the assistant's: an assistant asked for a presentation without a template named lists your templates and asks which one to use before creating anything (it may recommend one, but a new deck is never created in a template you did not pick); name it ("in the Sales template") and it does not ask, ask for "no template" and the deck is drawn in the plain built-in look. Automations, and chats where the assistant cannot ask, use the platform's default presentation template — the built-in brand deck (the XTM One Brand Deck on an XTM One platform, the Filigran Brand Deck on Filigran Copilot) unless an administrator chose another company template in Settings > Parameters.

3. Change it anytime. A deck stays linked to its template rather than copying it: the palette, fonts and logos are read from the template every time the deck is drawn, so editing the template restyles every deck wearing it, at once. The deck's own Design section (Edit slides in the viewer) applies another template, or none, with a live preview, and offers the Dark / Light theme among the ones the chosen template supports. The slides, their words, the images uploaded to the deck and the theme it picked belong to the deck; deleting a template leaves its decks intact, in the plain look.

A template can also fix the deck defaults of new decks made from it, so nobody has to ask for the brand look each time — the theme (a default theme the template does not support is snapped to one it does), the 16:9 or 4:3 aspect ratio, the slide transition, and the covers: the hero backdrop, its colour and the theme of the title and closing slides, so a brand deck opens and closes on a dark gradient cover whatever the body's theme (the Filigran Brand Deck and the XTM One Brand Deck do: their decks open and close on their gradient cover). Every deck offers the Plain, Gradient, Split and Spotlight covers; the tiled ones — Mosaic, Cascade, Horizon and Pillar — are a brand's own artwork, offered only by a template that lists them under heroes in its Extra metadata ("heroes": ["mosaic", "cascade", "horizon", "pillar"], as the THREAD Conference Deck does). A cover default must be one of the covers the template offers. Deck defaults live in the template's Extra metadata and in the Design editor, and they dress new decks only — an existing deck is never restyled by them. A template can define the header and footer every deck wearing it fills once, and it carries the agent guidance every assistant reads before composing a deck in that brand: which slide opens, where the numbers go, how sparingly to use the accent color. The logo_mark asset — the symbol without the wordmark — is what the gradient cover draws as a faint watermark in its corner.

A template also decides how long a deck may run. A deck holds up to 100 slides unless its template says otherwise: max_slides in the template's Extra metadata raises the limit for the kind of deck the template is for — a board pack or a quarterly review that gives every dense dashboard its own slide outgrows a pitch deck's budget — up to 300, the platform's ceiling. The Filigran Brand Deck ships with 150; the XTM One Brand Deck keeps the default. The limit applies when a deck grows: the assistant's insert_slide and the editor's Add slide and Duplicate stop at it and say which limit it is, a deck without a template keeps the default, and a deck that is already longer than its template now allows (the template was changed, or the deck was moved to a shorter one) stays editable as it is — it simply cannot take more slides until it is back under the limit. Exports and the viewer handle a long deck like any other.

Only the template's palette, fonts, logos and footer pattern reach a deck. A template can restyle a presentation, but it can never inject arbitrary styling or scripts into the pages that render it.

docs.title: Header and footer
docs.text:
The line at the bottom of every slide of a deck is not written on the slides — it is drawn from a few deck settings. A template decides what that line says for every deck wearing it, as a pattern with placeholders:

{{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}
  • {{title}}, {{subtitle}} and {{event}} are always available: the deck's title, the subtitle of its opening slide (as plain text — inline emphasis such as [[accent:...]] is not drawn in a footer) and the event the deck names. They need no declaration.
  • Every other placeholder is a variable the template declares — a key (classification), the label the deck's settings show (Classification), an optional hint and an optional default. A deck fills its variables once, in its Header & footer settings; until it does, a variable reads the template's default, or nothing when the template declares none.
  • An empty placeholder disappears with its separator: a deck with no event reads Quarterly review - Confidential, not - Quarterly review - Confidential. Everything that is not a placeholder is drawn as written.
  • A header pattern is optional and follows the same rules; it is drawn along the top of the same slides as the footer, and hides with it.

The XTM One Brand Deck defines {{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}. The event and the classification are both optional and have no default, so a new deck reads its own title on every slide, and "mark it Confidential" is one field, not a slide-by-slide edit.

On the Configuration tab, the Design editor's Header & footer card holds the footer pattern, the optional header pattern and the variables (up to eight), and previews the line with sample values as you type. The declaration is checked before it is saved — a placeholder no variable declares, a variable no pattern uses, a key that is not a lowercase word, a missing label — and a declaration with a problem is refused rather than drawn literally on every slide. Overview shows the pattern and the variables of a template that has them. A template with no pattern leaves the footer to each deck, which writes an event and a free footer text in the same settings. Changing the pattern restyles every deck wearing the template, like the palette; a field a deck set for a former pattern is kept, and the deck's settings say when no footer reads it.

The pattern is part of the design an assistant authoring a template can set (chrome in the template's metadata, with footer, header and variables), and get_template shows it to any assistant composing a deck, which is how "set the event to FIC 2026" reaches the right field.

docs.title: Brand watermark
docs.text: The same card has a Brand watermark switch. On, every content, agenda, roadmap, takeaways and dashboard slide of a deck wearing the template carries the template's mark (its logo_mark asset) faint in the top-right corner, over a soft glow of the brand gradient rising from the bottom corners — the cover's watermark, quietened for slides that have work to show. Title, section and closing slides keep their own backdrops. The mark is inked for the slide's theme, so it reads on a light slide as well as on a dark one. A template with no logo_mark asset draws nothing, and a deck that hides its logo hides the watermark with it. In the PowerPoint export the watermark is one picture under each body slide, behind blocks that all stay editable. An assistant sets it with "watermark": true in the template's chrome. The Filigran Brand Deck has it off: following the Brand team's flat design rules, its body slides carry the corner emblem instead, and its footer reads the deck title, the event and the classification separated by middle dots ({{title}} · {{event}} · {{classification}}), each part optional. Its colours are the exact brand values: a flat #0A0C1C page with a Sky Blue accent in the Dark theme, an ice blue #E6F7FF page with a Royal Blue accent in the Light theme, chart series in brand colours with no grey.

docs.title: Corner emblem
docs.text: The Corner emblem switch, next to it, draws the template's mark small and in full colour in the top-right corner of every slide except the title and closing ones, which keep their cover. Unlike the watermark it also appears on section slides, so the brand sign stays in view through the whole talk. A template with no logo_mark asset draws nothing, and a deck that hides its logo hides the emblem with it. In the PowerPoint export the emblem is a picture of its own, like the logo. An assistant sets it with "emblem": true in the template's chrome. The THREAD Conference Deck has it on.

docs.title: The built-in brand deck
docs.text:
Every platform ships the XTM One Brand Deck, a company-managed template: the product's own purple palette on dark surfaces (it supports the Dark theme only), Geologica and IBM Plex typefaces, six ordered colours for the series of a chart, four brand colours (the XTM One, OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ product colours, which the boxes of an architecture diagram can wear), the XTM One logo and mark, and the product material of the XTM platform as predefined assets: the OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ, XTM Hub, XTM One and XTM Platform logos and marks, the XTM platform architecture and product-flow diagrams, and product screenshots. It is the working example of a template every platform has, and the default presentation template of an XTM One platform; Filigran Copilot, Filigran's internal edition, also ships the Filigran Brand Deck and defaults to it.

Filigran Copilot also ships the THREAD Conference Deck, for the keynotes of THREAD, Filigran's conference: the colours of the THREAD design kit's color set on near-black slides (Cyan for highlights, the Lime-to-Blue gradient), and a Light theme drawn in the same set on Alabaster (the logo in dark ink, Cobalt Blue for highlights and the gradient's start, the mosaic tiles in their own colours); Elms Sans headings; title and closing slides on the Cascade cover of the THREAD marketing kit (the logo large in the top-left corner, tiles stepping down from the top-right one, the headline low over a thin rule and the speakers and date row), with Mosaic, Horizon and Pillar one click away in the slide's Selection tab - these four tiled covers are THREAD's own, offered by no other template; the "thread, powered by Filigran" logo in the corner and the mosaic "t" as the corner emblem. Its footer signs every slide with the edition, the talk's title and its classification (THREAD 2026 - The Road Ahead - Public): the edition reads THREAD 2026 until a deck sets another, and the classification is one field of the deck's Header & footer settings. It carries the same Filigran product, partner, integration and customer logos as the Filigran Brand Deck, plus the THREAD mosaic artworks, and its assistant guidance is written for a keynote: the session type above the title, every speaker and the date and room on the cover, numbered section dividers, few blocks per slide, and a closing slide with the speaker's contacts.

The logo is drawn automatically on every slide of a deck made from it. To give an assistant your own figures to place — your architecture diagram, your screenshots, your partners' logos — duplicate it or create a template of your own and add them on its Assets tab.

docs.title: Predefined assets
docs.text:
The assets of a template are what an assistant places when you ask for a figure, so it uses the actual one instead of drawing an approximation.

Every asset has a description that says what the figure shows and which surface (dark or light) it is drawn for; assistants read these descriptions to pick the right file, and you see them in the Assets tab. A template can hold hundreds of assets, so an assistant never reads the whole list: it asks the template for one role ("the partner logos") or one keyword and gets only what matches — ask for "a logo wall of our partners" and it lays the right logos out in a logo grid.

Upgrading an XTM One platform

Earlier versions also shipped the Filigran Brand Deck, Filigran's own house style, on XTM One platforms. It is reserved to Filigran's internal edition: on the first start after the upgrade — whether AI is switched on or off — it is removed together with every one of its assets and their stored files, and whatever the object store could not delete at that start is deleted within the hour once it answers again. The decks made from it keep their slides and are drawn in the plain look until you choose another template in their Design section, such as the XTM One Brand Deck. A picture a slide had placed from it is removed with it and nothing is drawn in its place; editing that slide, asking an assistant to rewrite the deck or restoring an earlier revision still works — the picture stays gone and the history says how many pictures were left empty — and you can put another picture in its place at any time. If an administrator had chosen it as the Default Presentation Template, the setting returns to the built-in default. A copy you made with Duplicate is your own template and stays: delete it from the Templates page if it should go too.

Upgrading from the asset libraries

Earlier versions shipped the partner, integration and customer logos as three separate asset-library templates next to the brand deck. On an XTM One platform the first start after the upgrade removes them, logos included. On Filigran Copilot, which ships the Filigran Brand Deck, it moves their logos into that deck instead — the same files under the same identifiers, so every slide that already placed one keeps it — and removes the three emptied libraries. A template of that former kind you created yourself keeps working with its assets, but no new one can be created: give the logos to a Presentation template instead. Import refuses a package of that kind and names it, so edit the kind in the export first; Duplicate copies such a template as a Presentation one, keeping the palette keys and layouts a presentation honours; whatever it had to leave out is listed in the audit log entry of the copy.

Built-in templates carry a Built-in badge and are read-only: they are kept in sync with the platform on every startup, so an edit would be undone by the next upgrade. To derive your own palette from one, use Duplicate — the copy is yours to change.

docs.title: Video templates
docs.text:
A Video template keeps every video that wears it to the same look. Its palette (per theme), fonts and logos work as they do for a deck - the logo and logo_light assets are drawn on the title and closing cards, the logo_mark asset is the watermark - and its rules live in extra_metadata.video:

  • aspect_ratios — the formats the brand ships, the first one the default (16:9, 9:16, 1:1, 4:5);
  • purposes — what the template is made for: product_demo, brand_film, event, launch, explainer, social (New video suggests it for those kinds of video);
  • defaults — what a video gets when it leaves it unset: theme (mode, background - aurora, gradient, mesh, grid, mosaic or solid - and watermark, the corner the mark is drawn in: a video writing none keeps none, and saving it says the template draws one), default_transition ({"type": "auto", "pace": "calm"} or "dynamic" to pick each cut from the scenes on either side, or one named type with an optional duration), captions, voiceover (enabled, voice, style, speed, and pronunciations: the brand's product names as the voice must say them), music (the brand's sound: a built-in track - bright-horizon, deep-focus, signal, ascent, late-notes, momentum or quiet-light - with its volume, ducking, duck_db, fade_in and fade_out; a video naming its own music keeps it, and "music": {"enabled": false} plays none);
  • scene_defaults and overlay_defaults — the same per scene type (title, statement, recording, slide, clip, image, outro: the card style, how a statement is revealed and aligned and how dark its backdrop is, the browser window, the cursor, the camera) and per overlay type (style, position, duration, and a picture overlay's width and opacity). What a scene shows - its text, its lines, its recording, its backdrop, its narration - is never a template's to preset, with one exception: a scene type's defaults may add the brand's marks as picture overlays by their role, never a file - "clip": {"overlays": [{"type": "image", "asset": "logo_mark", "position": "top_right", "width": 0.06, "duration": 60}]} puts the template's mark on every AI shot and video clip, before the scene's own overlays, unless the scene draws that mark itself;
  • intro and outro — {"required": true, "scene": {...}}: the title card added before the first scene and the closing card added after the last when the video has none ({title} in a text is the video's title); with required: false the card only lends its look to one the video writes;
  • locked — the paths whose template value always wins, such as theme.background, captions.style or scenes.recording.frame, plus theme.palette, which keeps the template's colours and logo over any the video names;
  • shots — the art direction of every AI shot made for a video wearing the template (see AI shots wear the template's art direction): style, the look added to the prompt of a shot drawn from a description (up to 600 characters: the light, the lens, the materials, the palette in words, the motion); avoid, what no shot shows, one term each (up to 16: added to the negative prompt of a video model that takes one, and read on the finished shot's frames, which says when it shows one - name visual things, never text or a logo, which a shot made from a real screenshot carries). For example "shots": {"style": "Photographic, natural light, deep navy and cyan tones.", "avoid": ["laser beams", "starfields", "holograms"]}. It steers the shots, never limits how many a video has.

Every preset must make a valid video and every lock must name a preset: a rule that does not is refused when the template is saved, with the field named. The Overview tab shows the rules (Video rules), and New video with this template starts a video in it. Video templates ship with the platform for every kind of video: Filigran Product Video, Filigran Brand Film, Filigran Event Loop and THREAD Conference Video on Filigran Copilot, XTM One Product Video, XTM One Brand Film, Threat Briefing and Social Teaser on every platform (see Video Studio templates). Every built-in video template carries the assets of its brand's deck: the four Filigran ones the whole library of the Filigran Brand Deck (product screenshots, diagrams, badges, team and event photos, and the product, partner, integration and customer logos), the THREAD one that of the THREAD Conference Deck, and the XTM One ones the product logos, diagrams and screenshots of the XTM One Brand Deck. The assistant places them as image scenes or statement backdrops, draws a screenshot onto a screen in a picture, or animates them as a figure - a wall of customer logos, an architecture whose boxes wear the product marks. The first product video a platform ships is the default of a video an assistant creates without naming a template, and freestyle: true opts a video out of any template (New video starts in free style unless a template is chosen or suggested for the kind of video).

docs.title: Create a template
docs.text:
From Templates, Add Template opens the creation form: a name, a description, the kind (Presentation for slide decks and pages, Report for executive reports, Video for Video Studio videos), the aspect ratio, tags, and — for administrators — whether the template is company-managed. A Presentation template also declares the themes it supports with two switches, Dark and Light — both on by default, at least one stays on. Generate with AI drafts the palette from a brief (see below) and proposes the themes its palettes read as, which you can still change; Preview renders a sample deck in it before you save.

Once the template exists, its detail page has three tabs:

  • Overview — the description, the Design (the palette per theme, marked Supported or Not supported), the attributes agents search by (kind, aspect ratio, tags), the layout catalog, and how many times agents retrieved the template
  • Configuration — the editable fields, the Design editor (Themes this template supports, one palette per supported theme with its colours — the base palette comes first and also carries the fonts — and the deck defaults), the layouts and the sharing settings; the raw JSON stays available under Advanced (JSON). Every palette shows its chart series (chart_1 to chart_6, drawn as a small bar preview that follows each keystroke; each theme tunes its own, and an empty series keeps the built-in colour, chart_1 the accent) and its optional brand hues (brand_1 to brand_4, the product colours an architecture node or zone can wear; an empty one falls back to the chart series of the same rank, and a variant palette inherits the base palette's). An empty field shows, dashed, the colour a deck draws instead: the colour it falls back to, or what a variant palette inherits from the base palette - its accent, gradient and brand hues, and every colour when the base palette's background is not set. When Advanced (JSON) also holds a variant for the base palette's own theme, which decks in that theme lay over the base, the form names the keys it sets, and editing one of them in the base palette removes it from that variant - except background, which decides the base palette's theme: remove a variant's background in Advanced (JSON). Preview the unsaved design opens the template preview on everything being edited - the name, the aspect ratio, the layouts, the palettes and the deck defaults - so it shows what saving would produce; a name, an aspect ratio or layouts the save would refuse (a blank or over-long name, an over-long aspect ratio, layouts JSON that does not parse) are previewed as saved, and a palette value the save would refuse is left out of the preview.
  • Assets — the files bound to the template

The old theme label

Templates created before this version could carry a free-text theme label (dark, corporate, …). It never changed a deck's colours — only the palettes do — and is no longer part of the design. Where one is still set, Configuration shows it as Search label (legacy) with a Clear action; older agent instructions that looked templates up by that word keep working until it is cleared.

Templates are shared like every other resource: private to you, shared with groups, or company-managed for everyone. The Export action downloads the whole template as a package (metadata plus assets) that Import on the Templates page recreates on another platform.

docs.title: Generate a template with AI
docs.text:
Rather than typing color values by hand, let the assistant draft the template. Generate with AI is available on the Templates page, on the creation form, and on the Configuration tab of an existing template.

  1. Write a design brief in plain language: the audience, the mood, two or three colors — "a light corporate deck for quarterly reviews, navy and gold, understated".
  2. Add palette hints if you have them: a hex value or a color word, one chip each.
  3. If the template already holds an image asset, pick it under Sample colours from a logo: the dominant colors of the image are handed to the assistant so the palette sits naturally around your logo.
  4. Click Generate. A live preview of a sample deck in the proposed palette appears next to the result, together with the name, labels, layout catalog and agent guidance the assistant drafted, and the colors it read from the logo.
  5. Refine in follow-up rounds — Refine this result with "warmer accent" or "swap the heading font for a geometric sans" — or Regenerate from the brief to start over.
  6. Apply to form fills the fields. Nothing is saved until you save the template, and every field stays editable.

When you generate from the Configuration tab, Start from the current configuration keeps whatever the brief does not mention; turn it off for a fresh design. The proposal is checked against what the renderer supports: a value it would ignore is listed as an adjustment rather than silently dropped.

A logo first

To build a template around a logo, create the template, upload the logo on the Assets tab with the role logo (and the dark-on-light variant as logo_light), then run Generate with AI from Configuration with the logo selected. The logo is then drawn on every slide of the decks made from the template, and the palette is sampled from it.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
The Assets tab holds the files a template brings to a deck. Each asset has a role that tells the renderer and the agents what it is: logo, logo_light, logo_mark, product_logo, partner_logo, integration_logo, customer_logo, people_photo, background, illustration, diagram, screenshot, badge, icon, image, font, or other — and a free-text description that says what the file shows. A template holds up to 400 assets; the tab filters them by role (each role with its count) and by a keyword in the name or the description — the same two handles an assistant uses.

  • The logo asset (and logo_light on the light theme) is drawn by the deck chrome on every slide.
  • Other images are placed by the assistant when you ask for them — a product logo on the title slide, a background on a section divider, a diagram in an image block, several logos at once in a logo grid.
  • The description is what an assistant picks an asset by ("the architecture diagram", "the dark-surface variant"), so write it for a reader who cannot see the file: what it shows, and whether it is drawn for a dark or a light surface.

You can add, relabel, replace and remove assets independently of the rest of the template. Replacing a file keeps its identity, so decks that already reference it pick up the new version. SVG files are cleaned on upload: scripts and remote references are removed before the file is stored.

docs.title: Ask an agent to author a template
docs.text: The built-in Template Designer agent creates and refines templates from a conversation: describe the brand, answer its questions, and it creates the template, attaches the logos you uploaded to the chat, writes the deck defaults and the guidance, and generates a preview deck for you to judge. It cannot read colors out of an image — for that, use Generate with AI in the UI and bring the result back to the agent to refine.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Generate a deck in your new brand: see Presentations.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tools are the actions agents can take directly. This page gives you a quick tour of the Tools screens.

Custom tools are off by default

In XTM One, custom tools are switched off by default, and the Tools page shows the built-in tools only. An administrator turns them on by switching off Disable custom tools in Settings > Security, or with its environment variable (see Settings > Security options).

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, open Tools & Integrations > Tools. The page opens on the Built-in Tools tab: platform-provided capabilities such as Files, Web, Design, Threat Intelligence, Coordination, and Platform. A capability this deployment has switched off, such as the code interpreter, is not listed. So this page is often less about configuration and more about understanding what the platform already makes available to agents. Each card tells you whether the tool is a standard platform capability, whether it is active, and what category of action it adds.

The Browser tool browses without a sign-in by default. Give an agent browser profiles and it opens those applications signed in, without seeing the credentials. To review a page as a person sees it, the agent can set the window size (from 320 x 240 to 3840 x 2160; each session opens at 1280 x 720), hover an element to see its tooltip or hover state (the pointer goes to a point of the element itself, so a thin curved line such as a graph edge is reached even when the middle of its box is covered by a layer beneath), drag an element by a given distance with real pointer input (a resize handle or a slider follows it as it would a person's mouse), capture one element instead of the whole window, and read the messages and errors the page logged to its console since it was opened. A script the agent runs on a page stops after 30 seconds (the agent may give it up to 2 minutes), so a page busy with a long task never holds the conversation. When the agent's browser session is closed for being idle or its browser stops, the next session gets back the cookies and site storage the last one had - a site it signed in to stays signed in - and the agent is told the session was re-created. Closing the session on purpose signs it out.

Each card is one capability. Several former cards now share one: Files covers file generation, reading and editing, HTML rendering and image generation; Web covers reading web pages and the browser; Design covers template search, template authoring and reading the design of a source document; Threat Intelligence covers the STIX bundle validator, the grounded STIX extraction (extract_stix_from_document, which turns a report into a STIX 2.1 bundle on the agent's own model) and the FIMI analytics; Coordination covers work items, shared state and worksets; Platform covers managing the platform from chat (agents, assignments, knowledge bases and the other resources) and fleets. An agent configured before the change keeps exactly the functions it had: its former tools are shown under the new card, and an agent can still be configured through the API with a former tool name, listed as deprecated.

When an administrator has turned custom tools on, a second tab, Custom Tools, lists them. It behaves like the other resource libraries, with search, visibility and tag filters, and an Add Tool action. A third tab, Repositories, syncs custom tools from a GitHub or GitLab repository (see Sync custom tools from a repository).

The Platform tool acts as the person the agent works for, and offers only what that person may do: a function only an administrator may run (cancelling runs, reading and starting evaluations) is not offered to anyone else, and every other change stays limited to the resources the person may manage.

The General Assistant and the CTEM Assistant start with the same tools: Platform, Files, Presentations, Reports, Design, Web, Threat Intelligence and, for administrators, Platform Insights. Video Studio and the code interpreter are part of that set too, but both are off by default: Video Studio is an off-by-default feature (see Feature flags), and the code interpreter is off in XTM One until an administrator turns it on (see Settings > Security options). An administrator can remove any of these tools in Settings > General Assistant.

The Computer Use (Runners) tool reads, writes and lists files on an enrolled machine with runner_read_file, runner_write_file and runner_list_dir. Their former names read_file, write_file and list_dir are still accepted, so an agent or an allow list that names them keeps working.

docs.title: Built-in tool detail pages
docs.text:
Opening a built-in tool leads to a detail page with Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

  • Overview shows what the tool does and whether it is used in real workflows — how many agents use it, how many runs it has, and (for Files, which includes image generation) the current image model.
  • Configuration is usually informational. For Files it exposes the platform-wide image model: admins can change it, non-admins can only see it — so the experience differs by role even though the page is visible to everyone.
  • Activity shows runs linked to agents using the tool.

docs.title: Custom tool detail pages
docs.text:
When an administrator has turned custom tools on, each custom tool has a detail page with Overview, Configuration, Tests and Activity tabs, with Test Tool, Run tests and delete actions in the header.

  • Overview summarizes the tool: what it does, its language and timeout, its input parameters, and which agents use it.
  • Configuration is where you define and edit the tool. The parts that matter are durable:
    • parameters define what the tool expects
    • code (JavaScript or Python) defines what the tool does
    • a timeout defines how long the platform will wait
    • visibility and sharing settings define who can discover and reuse it

Next to the code field, Generate with AI writes the code from a short description of what it should do. It reads the form as it stands: the language, the tool's name and description, and the parameters you declared. When the field already holds code, the button reads Improve with AI and reworks that code instead of starting over. The result lands in the editor for you to review; nothing is saved until you save the tool. The same button is offered in a flow, when you choose Write a new script on a script node.

Test Tool opens a dedicated test dialog — the fastest way to validate a custom tool before binding it to an agent. Its Dry run switch runs the tool with dry_run set to true (see Dry run).

docs.title: Tests and dry run
docs.text:
A custom tool can declare its own tests, in its Tests tab, in two forms you can combine:

  • Data cases: a name, the inputs, whether the case is a dry run, and what the output must look like (equals, contains, not_contains, regex, json_subset), or that the tool must fail (expect_error, error_contains). Each case is one run of the tool, exactly as an agent runs it.
  • Test code, in the tool's language. In Python, test_* functions or unittest classes call run_tool(inputs, dry_run=True); in JavaScript, test(name, fn) with assert (Node's assert) calls await runTool(inputs, { dryRun: true }). Both return what the tool printed and raise ToolError when the tool fails. Only the language's standard library is available.

Run tests in the header, or Run all tests in the tab, runs everything and shows each result with its output; the badge in the header keeps the outcome of the last full run. Dry run only skips the cases that are not dry runs and runs the test code with dry_run forced to true. Each data case also has its own button. Tests run in the same sandbox as the tool, with your variables.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: Every run of a custom tool receives a dry_run variable ($dry_run in JavaScript): false when an agent calls the tool, true for a dry-run case or the Dry run switch of Test Tool. A tool that changes something (creates a ticket, blocks an address, sends a message) should check it and only describe what it would do. The platform cannot do it for the tool: the sandbox lets the tool reach the network, because a tool needs it to read too.

docs.title: Sync custom tools from a repository
docs.text:
The Repositories tab of the Tools page syncs custom tools from a GitHub or GitLab repository. Add a repository asks for the repository (owner/repository, group/project, or its address), a branch, tag or commit (the default branch when empty), a sub-directory, a credential and how often to sync. A public repository on github.com or gitlab.com needs no credential; a private one, or a self-managed GitLab, is read with a connected GitHub or GitLab integration you can use.

Each directory holding a tool.yaml becomes one custom tool:

tools/whois-lookup/
  tool.yaml        # name, description, input_schema, timeout, tags, tests
  main.py          # the code (main.py, main.js or index.js, or the file named by "entry")
  test_main.py     # optional test code (test_main.py or main.test.js, or "test_file")

name: Whois lookup
description: Looks a domain up in WHOIS
timeout: 60
tags: [osint]
input_schema:
  type: object
  properties:
    domain: { type: string, description: The domain }
  required: [domain]
tests:
  - name: dry run
    inputs: { domain: example.com }
    dry_run: true
    expect: { contains: [example.com] }

Each sync reads the commit the branch points at, then:

  • a tool whose files did not change is left as it is;
  • a new or changed tool runs its tests, and the new version is activated only when they pass. A tool that declares no tests is activated too, and the report says it is untested. When the tests fail, the active version stays and the report shows the failures; a new tool is not created;
  • a tool removed from the repository is disabled, not deleted, because agents may use it. When its directory comes back, the sync enables it again (once its tests pass, if it changed); a tool you disabled yourself stays disabled;
  • a tool that cannot be read (an invalid tool.yaml, a missing file) is reported and left as it is.

Sync now syncs at once, unless a sync of the same repository is already running, and Last sync report shows what the last sync did, tool by tool. Every sync that changes a tool is recorded in the audit log.

A synced tool is read-only on its page: its name, code, parameters and tests change in the repository. You can still share it, enable or disable it, and hide it from chat. Detach turns it into an ordinary tool you can edit; the repository no longer updates it (Sync it again in the report undoes that for the next sync). Deleting a repository keeps its tools, detached, unless you choose to delete them too. A repository you add is yours; an administrator can add a company-managed one, whose tools are company-managed.

docs.title: Waiting is a tool too
docs.text:
Some capabilities are not on the Tools page because every agent has them. wait is one: it lets an agent pause on purpose — typically after handing a long task to another agent — and re-check when the work is likely done, instead of asking for a status update over and over.

You will see it in the chat as a countdown with the agent's own explanation of what it is waiting for, next to a Continue now link. Under it, each task or run the agent is waiting for is listed with its state (Pending, Running with how long it has been running, Completed, Failed...), updated as it changes:

  • Continue now ends the pause and lets the agent carry on with whatever it has.
  • The usual stop button cancels the whole response, pause included.

The agent also wakes up on its own as soon as the work it named has finished, so a five-minute wait often costs far less. That work can be a task it handed to another agent, or an assignment or flow run it started, for example a test run of an assignment. Admins set the ceilings in Settings > General Assistant.

An assignment run the agent starts from the chat (trigger_assignment) reports back to that conversation when it ends: if the agent was not waiting for it, the run's outcome - its status, how long it took and its result - resumes the conversation, and the agent tells you what came out. A run you cancel is not reported. When the agent asks to start an assignment that is already running, it is told which run is in progress, so it can wait for that one instead.

docs.title: Read-only expectations
docs.text: Built-in tools are part of the platform: visible and understandable, but not treated like personal resources. The main experience is usually inspection and understanding rather than ownership and creation.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use the tool description to understand capability before attaching it to an agent.
  • Check Agents Using before changing shared tool settings.
  • Treat the image model of the Files tool as platform-wide, not per-agent.
  • Expect built-in tools to be the main visible part of this page, unless custom tools are turned on.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables store reusable values that resolve at runtime in personas, prompts, skills, and tools, so you do not repeat key values by hand. This page explains what the Variables page shows and how it works.

Variables are off by default

In XTM One, custom variables are switched off by default, and Variables does not appear in the left navigation. An administrator turns them on by switching off Disable custom variables in Settings > Security, or with its environment variable (see Settings > Security options).

Unlike most other resources, variables do not use a list page plus detail page pattern. They use one management page with create and edit dialogs.

docs.title: The management page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, open Tools & Integrations > Variables. The page is a board of reusable values that resolve at runtime in personas, prompts, skills, and tools. You can search by name, description, or value pattern and filter by tags, then create, edit, copy, or delete a variable. If you have permission, New Variable adds one.

Each variable is a card, not a table row. The card shows enough to decide quickly whether it is the right variable, whether it is sensitive, and whether it still looks current. Non-secret variables show their value preview directly; secret variables mask it behind a lock icon and a Secret badge, with a reveal toggle on the card itself. Each card also has a copy action for the variable reference.

docs.title: Editing behavior
docs.text:
Clicking a card opens an edit dialog — there is no separate detail page or tabs. The create and edit dialogs share the same fields; the key decision is whether to mark the variable Secret, which changes how it is displayed and handled later.

For a secret variable, the value field does not reveal the stored value on edit. The placeholder tells you to enter a new value only when you want to update it, which reinforces that secret handling differs from plain text.

A secret variable can also read its value from a vault an administrator granted you: From a vault opens the secret picker, and the field then shows the vault, the path and the key instead of a value. The value is read from the vault each time a run needs it. See Secret vaults.

docs.title: Inserting a variable
docs.text: The Variable button next to a persona, an agent's instructions, an assignment prompt, a prompt of the library, a skill, a flow node's text or a custom tool lists the variables you may use, secret ones badged Secret, and inserts the reference at the cursor. Create a secret variable from a vault secret, at the bottom of that list, picks a secret from a vault, creates a secret variable holding its reference (only you see it until you share it) and inserts it: a prompt never holds a vault reference itself.

docs.title: Copying a reference
docs.text: The UI lets you copy the reference format directly instead of typing it. The copied format uses the variable ID (for example {{var_id.<id>}}) and can be reused in personas, prompts, skills, and tools.

docs.title: A secret variable in an integration credential
docs.text:
An integration's API key or client secret may hold a reference to a secret variable, alone or inside a longer value: users API-Key {{var_id.<id>}}. The reference is stored as written and replaced by the variable's value each time the integration calls its service, so the key itself never has to be pasted into the integration.

  • Only a secret variable can be referenced there. Saving the integration is refused when the variable does not exist, is not secret, or is not visible to you and to the integration's owner.
  • The reference resolves for the integration's owner, with the same visibility rules as below (company-managed variables only for an integration with no owner).
  • If the variable is later deleted, made non-secret, emptied or no longer shared with the owner, the integration's calls fail with "secret unavailable" until the reference is fixed. The value stays out of traces and logs, as for any secret variable.
  • A key without a reference behaves exactly as before.

docs.title: Who a reference resolves for
docs.text:
A reference is replaced by its value only for the person the work runs as, and only if that person can see the variable: their own variables, the ones shared with them or one of their groups, and company-managed ones (unless restricted to an audience they are not in). In a chat that is the person chatting. An assignment runs as the person who triggered it, else its run-as user, else its owner. A flow runs as its owner, or as the person who ran it. Administrators get no exception.

When an agent's automations run as someone else, share the variable with that person or their group, or make it company-managed. Otherwise the reference is sent to the model as written. The agent's page lists the variables it references that have no value yet, and the references to variables that no longer exist.

docs.title: Where a secret value goes
docs.text:
The value of a secret variable, stored in XTM One or read from a vault, reaches the model and the tools it calls. It is never kept anywhere else in clear:

  • What a run or a chat stores (its messages, the tool calls and their results, an approval waiting for a reviewer) holds a marker instead of the value. When the work resumes (an approved tool call, an answered question, the next message of a conversation, the next step of a flow), the model and the tools get the value back.
  • Traces and server logs hold the same marker, error messages included (a failing tool's output, for instance).
  • What an agent remembers of a run or a chat, and what it remembers about you, holds the marker too. A later run or conversation reads that memory with the marker, never the value.
  • A command an agent runs on XTM One Desktop gets the value on your machine. The command history and the approval card show [secret], and so does what the command prints back, wherever the value appears in it: the agent reads [secret] there too. If the variable is no longer shared with you by the time the machine picks the command up, the command gets the marker instead of the value. If the value changes, or stops being readable, while the command runs, what it prints back is not kept: the command is recorded as failed, since that output could hold the old value. A command that uses a secret variable is never added to the machine's allowed or blocked commands.
  • When the model repeats the value in its answer, you see [secret]: in the chat while it streams, in the conversation afterwards (its reasoning and tool calls included), in its title, in a channel, in a notification, and in the answers of the OpenAI-compatible API, the MCP agent tools and the browser extension. A reviewer approving a tool call sees [secret] in its arguments too.
  • An error recorded for a failed flow or background task shows [secret] in place of the value.

A value shorter than 8 characters is not replaced: it would turn unrelated words and numbers into markers. Keep credentials longer than that, which they are in practice. The marker belongs to the run or the conversation that wrote it: copied into another one, it is never turned back into the value. What you type in a message is never turned back into a value either: the model reads [secret] there. Each message of a conversation resolves the variables you may read at that moment, so once a variable is no longer shared with you, the next message no longer gets its value.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use Secret for credentials or sensitive values.
  • Copy the reference instead of typing it from memory.
  • Add clear descriptions so other users know where the variable should be used.
  • Use tags when the same workspace contains many operational variables.

docs.title: XTM One in the XTM Suite
docs.text:
This section explains how XTM One appears inside the other products of the XTM Platform: OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ.

XTM One is the core platform of the XTM Platform. It holds what the products share: the context of your organization, central authentication, shared integrations, and agents that work across products. OpenCTI (threat intelligence), OpenAEV (adversarial exposure validation) and OpenCRQ (governance, risk and compliance) are its modules, and each one keeps ownership of its own use case.

You do not always have to open the XTM One application directly to use XTM One capabilities. In some deployments, those capabilities are surfaced inside the product where you are already working.

docs.title: What this section is for
docs.text:
Use these pages when you want to understand:

  • where XTM One features can appear outside the main XTM One application
  • what the user experience usually looks like in another product
  • why some AI actions are available, hidden, or disabled
  • how OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ expose XTM One to end users
  • which access point to use for a given task

docs.title: What stays the same across products
docs.text:
Even when you use XTM One from another XTM Suite product, a few principles stay the same:

  • the product you are in remains the main working context
  • XTM One provides the shared context and the agents behind the feature
  • your current user permissions still matter
  • feature availability depends on how your administrators configured the platform

docs.title: How a product knows which agent to use
docs.text:
Each connected product declares the AI capabilities it needs — summarize this container, generate this message, process this bundle. In XTM One, those capabilities are called intents, and an administrator binds an agent to each one. That binding decides which of your agents answers when a user clicks an AI action in OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ, and whether the action appears at all.

You do not need to configure anything to use the features: XTM One ships with bindings for its built-in agents. If your organization wants its own agent behind one of these actions, see Intents.

docs.title: What can vary by deployment
docs.text:
Not every organization exposes the same XTM One features in the same way.

What can vary includes:

  • which actions are available
  • which objects can trigger those actions
  • which assistant or agent is used behind the scenes
  • whether the result is immediate, streamed, or handled in the background

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Common experience across the XTM Suite
  • XTM One in OpenCTI
  • Indicator decay re-check
  • XTM One in OpenAEV
  • XTM One in OpenCRQ

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Start with Common experience across the XTM Suite, then move to the product-specific pages that match your environment.

docs.title: Common experience across the XTM Suite
docs.text: When XTM One is exposed inside another XTM Suite product, the experience is usually contextual rather than standalone.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
You usually start from the product you are already using, not from the XTM One home page.

That means:

  • you stay inside the current product
  • the current object or workflow provides the context
  • XTM One is used to interpret, summarize, plan, or automate based on that context

docs.title: How a request usually works
docs.text:
The common pattern looks like this:

  1. You open an object or workflow in the current product.
  2. You trigger an XTM One action from that context.
  3. The product sends the relevant context to XTM One.
  4. XTM One routes the request to the right assistant or agent.
  5. The result comes back into the product, or continues as a longer-running task.

From an end-user perspective, the important point is simple: you do not need to re-explain everything manually. The current product context is part of the request.

docs.title: How permissions work
docs.text:
XTM One is not meant to silently bypass the permissions of the product you are in.

In practice, this means:

  • what you can trigger still depends on your current account
  • what XTM One can read or do is scoped by the connected product and your access
  • an AI action should not grant you broader rights than you already have

docs.title: Why an action may be hidden or disabled
docs.text:
An XTM One action can be unavailable for several reasons:

  • the product is not connected to XTM One
  • the feature is not enabled in your deployment
  • no agent is bound to that use case — see Intents
  • the relevant capability is not available for your business context
  • your permissions do not allow the underlying operation

If a button or menu entry is missing, that does not automatically mean something is broken.

docs.title: What results can look like
docs.text:
Depending on the feature, the result may appear as:

  • a summary
  • extracted information
  • a proposed action or draft
  • a streamed answer
  • a background task that finishes later

Some workflows can also include a human review step before anything sensitive is applied.

docs.title: The in-product assistant panel
docs.text:
When the product's version supports it, the assistant panel of OpenCTI and OpenAEV also carries what the XTM One chat offers around a conversation:

  • Your usage quota: the same count and limit as the indicator of the XTM One chat, for the same period. It is not shown on Community Edition, where AI is off.
  • Your prompts: the prompts you can use in the XTM One chat - your own, the ones shared with you or your groups, and the company-managed ones - newest first. A prompt set to Hide from chat is not offered.
  • Rating an answer: a thumbs up or down, with an optional comment of up to 2,000 characters. It is the same rating as in the XTM One chat: rating again replaces it, removing it takes it back, the agent's managers see it in its Feedback tab, and it is still there when you reopen the conversation.
  • Reports, presentations and videos: the assistant of each product writes reports, builds presentations and makes videos from your data. Each one is a card in the answer, with its title, its size (slides, sections, scenes and length) and Open in XTM One; where the product supports it, the card also downloads it (PDF or PowerPoint for a presentation, PDF for a report, MP4 for a finished video) and follows a video while it renders. A product on an older version shows a link to the same XTM One page.

docs.title: How to use the feature well
docs.text:
• Start the action from the most relevant object, not from a generic page.
  • Expect the answer to be tailored to the current context.
  • Review the result before using it in an operational decision.
  • If the action is unavailable, check with your administrator whether the integration or routing is configured.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with XTM One in OpenCTI, then read XTM One in OpenAEV if your organization uses it.

docs.title: Indicator decay re-check
docs.text:
OpenCTI's indicator decay lowers an indicator's score over time and revokes the indicator when the score reaches the decay rule's revoke score. Some indicators are revoked while their observable is still malicious. XTM One ships two built-in agents that re-check every indicator about to be revoked:

  • Indicator Decay Guardian finds the indicators that decay revokes in the next 48 hours, enriches their observables with the threat-intelligence integrations it is given, and applies the verdicts. It never decides on its own.
  • Indicator Decay Judge decides, from the enrichment evidence alone, whether each indicator is still malicious. It runs on the platform routing model, the lightweight model an administrator sets in Settings > AI Models, and has no tools.

When the judge finds an indicator still malicious with a confidence of at least 70, the Guardian raises its score. OpenCTI then restarts the decay from the new score, so the indicator is not revoked; the Guardian also adds a note with the evidence and the verdict, and the label decay-reenriched. Otherwise nothing changes in OpenCTI and the decay continues. An indicator whose enrichment failed, or whose evidence is not enough to decide, is left alone and reported as degraded, never as kept.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Configure a routing model in Settings > AI Models. Without one, the judge runs on the platform default model, and its configuration page says so.
  2. Give the Guardian its enrichment sources: as an administrator, open the Guardian's Configuration tab and bind the threat-intelligence integrations it should query (VirusTotal, GreyNoise, AbuseIPDB, Shodan, urlscan.io, ...). It uses the OpenCTI integration of whoever it runs as.
  3. Try it: an administrator runs Re-check indicators about to decay from the Guardian's assignments. It runs as that administrator, with their OpenCTI access.
  4. Automate it: open Hourly indicator decay re-check, choose the account it runs as under Run As, then turn it on. It is off on a new install and stays as you leave it across restarts.

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text: Each run reports how many indicators it examined, kept (with their new score), left to decay, and degraded, with the reason. The Guardian keeps one record per indicator in its workset (Work > Operations > Worksets), with the evidence and the verdict, and does not judge an indicator again within 24 hours. A degraded indicator is the exception: its first attempt decided nothing, so the Guardian tries it again about 2 hours later instead of 24, if decay has not revoked it by then.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One run examines at most 20 indicators, the ones closest to revocation; the report says when more are waiting. The hourly run picks them up next.
  • Enrichment uses the integrations bound to the Guardian, not the enrichment connectors of OpenCTI.

docs.title: XTM One in OpenAEV
docs.text: In OpenAEV, XTM One supports adversarial exposure validation work without requiring you to leave the OpenAEV experience. As in OpenCTI, the capabilities appear inside the product, attached to the scenario, inject, or exercise you are working on.

docs.title: Access points inside OpenAEV
docs.text:
Each access point is powered by a named capability — an intent — answered by an agent your administrators chose. These are the agents that handle them out of the box.

Where it applies What you can do Capability Default agent The in-product AI assistant Hold a conversation about the current OpenAEV context — scenarios, simulations, results global.assistant CTEM Assistant, which hands the conversation over to the OpenAEV Assistant Text and description fields Summarize, explain, shorten, expand, fix spelling and grammar, change the tone of the content you are writing global.summarize, global.explain, global.make_it_shorter, global.make_it_longer, global.fix_spelling, global.change_tone OpenAEV Assistant Exercise content Generate the messages used in an adversary emulation exercise aev.message_generator OpenAEV Assistant Exercise content Generate a media article for an adversary emulation exercise aev.media_article_generator OpenAEV Assistant Phishing content Generate a phishing lure email (subject, HTML body, and plain-text fallback) for an authorized phishing simulation aev.phishing_email_html_generator AEV Phishing Email Generator Phishing content Generate a phishing landing page (HTML and CSS) for an authorized credential-capture simulation aev.phishing_landing_page_html_generator AEV Phishing Landing Page Generator Detection and remediation Turn a malware behavior description into detection rules, with the processes, commands, files, and ATT&CK techniques it relies on aev.detection_rules_generator AEV Detection Rules Generator Document analysis Extract tactics, techniques, and procedures from a document cti.ttp_harvester CTI TTP Harvester (Filigran AI)

The exact wording of buttons and menu entries depends on your OpenAEV version, and an administrator can bind a different agent to any of these capabilities.

Beyond these contextual actions, the OpenAEV Assistant and the scenario and payload agents can also be used from XTM One itself — to design a scenario, propose injects, or review the outcome of an exercise, with the results written back into OpenAEV.

The OpenAEV Assistant also turns your results into a deliverable: a validation readout as a report or a presentation for a review meeting, in your report and deck templates. See Presentations.

docs.title: Autonomous attack path
docs.text:
On OpenAEV Enterprise Edition, a chained scenario can be launched as an autonomous attack path: you give OpenAEV an objective and a scope, and XTM One drives the run. The OpenAEV Attack Path Orchestrator (capability aev.attack_path_orchestrator) plans the attack path, launches techniques in OpenAEV, reads the findings as they arrive, records each step on the run's timeline, and adapts the next step to what it found.

  • You stay in control from OpenAEV. The orchestrator follows the directions you send during the run, asks you a question when it needs a decision, and stops when you cancel the run.
  • Slow results cost nothing while they wait. A step whose result takes hours, such as a phishing email waiting for a click, parks the run until the finding arrives or a deadline passes: no model call runs in between.
  • Plan without running. A run can design the attack path only, never executing a technique, so you can review it before a live run follows it.
  • Specialists. The orchestrator consults the OpenAEV Payload Creator (capability aev.attack_path_additional_agent) for payloads, code and exploitation support, plus any other agent selected for the run in OpenAEV.

XTM One accepts an autonomous run only with Enterprise features: a connected Enterprise Edition platform or a Filigran license (see Editions and licensing). An administrator's emergency stop on the whole platform also cancels autonomous runs.

docs.title: React to OpenAEV events
docs.text:
An assignment can run its agent when something happens in OpenAEV. Give the assignment an Integration event trigger on the OpenAEV integration and pick one or more events:

Event When it fires Simulation finished A simulation reaches the finished status Inject or atomic test finished An inject or atomic test ends executed, partial or in error Finding created A new finding is created

XTM One sets up OpenAEV to call it: under the integration's own OpenAEV account, it creates a webhook notifier and one notification trigger per event, named XTM One - <fleet> - <purpose>. It checks them every 15 minutes, recreates one that was deleted in OpenAEV, restores one that was edited, and removes them when the assignment stops asking, is disabled, or is deleted.

  • An administrator first sets the webhook_secret field on the OpenAEV integration in XTM One. OpenAEV sends it with every event; without it, nothing is set up and the assignment never receives an event.
  • The assignment's trigger must ask for this setup in its configuration. The assignment page does not offer it yet: an assignment created through the API or by an agent can.

docs.title: What to expect when you use it
docs.text:
When you trigger an XTM One action from OpenAEV:

  • the current OpenAEV context is reused, so you do not have to restate it
  • XTM One routes the request to the agent bound to that capability for the aev business context
  • the result comes back as part of the OpenAEV experience

Longer-running work can continue in the background; those runs appear in Operations in XTM One.

docs.title: Why a feature may be unavailable
docs.text:
An action can be hidden or disabled if:

  • the OpenAEV instance is not registered with XTM One
  • no agent is bound to that capability, or the bound agent is disabled
  • the bound agent is private rather than company-managed or shared with a group
  • the binding targets another business context than aev
  • your OpenAEV permissions do not allow the related operation

Administrators can review and fix the routing on the Intents page.

docs.title: Permissions and review
docs.text:
As with other suite products, you should expect:

  • the action to respect your current OpenAEV permissions
  • results to be treated as operational assistance, not final truth by default
  • some sensitive workflows to include a review or validation step

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Start the action from the scenario or exercise that already contains the relevant context.
  • Review generated proposals before applying them to an operational workflow.
  • Ask your administrator if the expected action is missing or unavailable.

docs.title: OpenAEV MCP server
docs.text:
Connecting OpenAEV to XTM One also activates a native MCP server for the platform.

Any MCP-compatible client (Cursor, Claude Desktop, custom agents) can connect to https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev with a personal XTM One API key and search, read, and manage scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, atomic tests, and findings — with your own OpenAEV permissions.

Find your endpoint and a ready-to-copy client configuration in My Profile > MCP Endpoint, and see Platform MCP servers for the full guide.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Return to the main XTM One guide for the broader platform chapters, starting with Home Dashboard when needed. Administrators who need to change which agent answers a capability should read Intents.

docs.title: XTM One in OpenCRQ
docs.text: OpenCRQ is the governance, risk and compliance module of the XTM Platform. It owns frameworks, controls, assessments, risk scenarios and the financial quantification of cyber risk. XTM One brings its agents into OpenCRQ, gives your own agents OpenCRQ tools, and keeps the primary assets of your organization profile in line with OpenCRQ's assets.

docs.title: The embedded assistant
docs.text:
Once OpenCRQ is registered with XTM One, the OpenCRQ header shows an Ask Ariane button. It opens the XTM One chat in a side panel, without leaving OpenCRQ. The button appears only when the OpenCRQ deployment is connected to XTM One and runs Enterprise Edition; a Community Edition deployment does not show it.

Each request goes through the OpenCRQ backend to XTM One, under your own identity, so the answer stays within what your OpenCRQ account can see.

Capability What it does Default agent global.assistant The conversation behind Ask Ariane CTEM Assistant, which hands the conversation over to the OpenCRQ Assistant

OpenCRQ declares this capability when it registers, and an administrator can bind a different agent to it on the Intents page.

docs.title: OpenCRQ tools for your agents
docs.text:
